What is an ontology?

An ontology is a shared list of the kinds of things in one area. It also says how these things relate. We start in a bike shop. Then we look at philosophy and at computer science.

  • Say in one sentence what an ontology is.
  • Tell the philosophy meaning from the computer meaning.
  • Explain Gruber's 1993 definition in simple words.
  • Give five reasons why software needs an ontology.
  • Put six tools in order, from a word list to a knowledge graph.

Start in a bike shop

Mia opens a small bike shop. On the first day she writes one page for her team. The page has two lists.

List 1: the kinds of things

  • Bike
  • City bike
  • Mountain bike
  • Wheel
  • Customer
  • Order

List 2: how they relate

  • A city bike is a kind of bike.
  • A mountain bike is a kind of bike.
  • A wheel is part of a bike.
  • A customer places an order.
  • An order contains bikes.

Now everyone in the shop uses the same words. A new worker reads the page and understands the shop. You can draw the same page as a picture.

This page is a small ontology. It has three parts.

  • Kinds of things. We call each kind a class.
  • Links between the kinds. We call each link a relation.
  • Agreement. The whole team uses the same page.

An ontology answers two questions. What kinds of things do we talk about? How do they relate to each other?

The page does not say "bike number 7 is red". That is a fact about one single bike. An ontology talks about kinds first. Facts about single things are data. You will see the difference in The building blocks.

One word, two meanings

Read these two sentences. Look at the small word "an".

  • Ontology is an old part of philosophy.
  • Our team wrote an ontology for the bike shop.

The first sentence talks about a field of study. You cannot count it. The second sentence talks about a thing. You can make it, count it and save it in a file.

The philosophy meaning

Philosophy asks very general questions. Ontology is the part that asks one of them. What is there? Do numbers exist? What is a thing, and what is a feature of a thing?

The word has Greek roots. "On" means being. The ending "-logy" means study. The Latin word ontologia is quite young. The oldest known book with this word is from 1606. Jacob Lorhard wrote it.

The questions are much older than the word. Aristotle sorted all things into ten kinds more than 2,300 years ago. You can read this story in Ancient and medieval roots.

The computer meaning

In computer science an ontology is a made thing. It is a file that a program can read. It names the kinds of things in one area and their relations. People call such an area a domain.

In 1998 the researcher Nicola Guarino wrote about this difference. With a big O, Ontology is the field of study. With a small o, an ontology is one thing among many.

The two meanings side by side
PhilosophyComputer science
Grammar"Ontology", no article"an ontology", "two ontologies"
Main questionWhat is there in the world?What does this system talk about?
SizeEverythingOne domain
ResultA theory in a bookA file for people and programs
TestGood argumentsReal questions and real data
ExampleAristotle's ten kinds of thingsSchema.org, the Gene Ontology

The two meanings are linked. Both sort things into kinds. Both name the relations between the kinds. This is why computer people borrowed the word.

A software ontology does not tell you what "really" exists. It tells you what one system needs to talk about. For a program, a thing exists only when the program can name it.

Gruber's definition, word by word

In 1993 Tom Gruber worked at Stanford University. He wanted AI programs to share their knowledge. His paper in the journal Knowledge Acquisition has one famous sentence.

An ontology is an explicit specification of a conceptualization.

Tom Gruber, 1993

The sentence has three hard words. Read it from the end to the start.

  1. Conceptualization. This is a simple view of one part of the world. You choose the things and relations that matter for your goal. Mia's view has bikes, wheels, customers and orders. It does not have the weather.
  2. Specification. This is an exact description in writing. The view is not only in Mia's head. It is on the page.
  3. Explicit. This means said openly and clearly. In much software the meaning hides in a short name like cust_tp. An explicit page says "customer type" and tells you what it means.
  4. All together. An ontology is a clear, written description of your simple view of one area.

Other researchers soon made the sentence stronger. In 1997 a thesis by W. N. Borst asked for two more things. The description must be formal. The view must be shared by a group. In 1998 Rudi Studer and two colleagues put all these words into one definition. Here it is in simple words.

An ontology is a formal and clear description of the kinds of things in one domain and of their relations. A group of people agrees on it.

Use the definition as a test with four questions.

Is Mia's page an ontology?
QuestionMia's page
Is it about one domain?Yes. A bike shop.
Is it written down clearly?Yes. Two lists on one page.
Does a group agree on it?Yes. The team uses it.
Can a machine read it?Not yet. It is plain English.

The last answer is "not yet". To fix it, we write the page in a formal language. Here is one line of Mia's page in a language called Turtle.

@prefix shop: <http://example.org/shop#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

shop:CityBike rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike .   # a city bike is a kind of bike

You will write a full file like this in Your first ontology.

Gruber wrote about the idea again in 2009. He named the usual parts of an ontology: classes, attributes and relationships. He also said where an ontology sits. A database schema says how data is stored. An ontology says what the data means.

Why software needs an ontology

Mia's shop grows. Now it has two programs. The sales program has a table named client. The repair program has a table named customer. A new report needs both tables.

Somebody must know that a client and a customer are the same kind of thing. Today this knowledge is in one person's head. When this person leaves, the knowledge leaves too. An ontology writes it down for people and for programs.

Software gets five things from an ontology.

Five needs and what an ontology gives
NeedWithout an ontologyWith an ontology
Shared meaningEach team means something different by "customer".One written meaning. People and programs use it.
Joining dataYou guess which tables match.Both tables point to the same class, Customer.
CheckingWrong data comes in and nobody sees it.A checker reports an order with no customer.
ReasoningThe program knows only what you typed.The program finds new facts from rules.
Context for AIAn AI model guesses what a name means.The model looks up the type and the links.

A closer look at reasoning

Reasoning is the need that surprises most people. Here is the smallest example.

  1. The ontology says that every city bike is a bike.
  2. The data says that B7 is a city bike.
  3. The program adds a new fact. B7 is a bike. Nobody typed this fact.

Context for AI

A language model is good with words. But it can mix up two things with the same name. Is "Jaguar" an animal or a car maker? An ontology gives each thing a type and clear links. The model can look them up before it answers.

Many teams build such systems now. In 2024 researchers at Microsoft described a method called GraphRAG. A model first builds a graph of things from your documents. Then it uses the graph to answer broad questions. Read more in Ontologies and AI and in Context graphs and agent memory.

Here is one more reason for engineers. An ontology keeps knowledge out of the code. The rule "a city bike is a bike" lives in one file. It does not hide in ten if lines. Natalya Noy and Deborah McGuinness gave this reason in their 2001 guide.

An ontology is not magic. People must agree on the words, and this takes time. Start with a small domain and one real question.

From a word list to a knowledge graph

Not every list of words is an ontology. There is a line of tools, from very simple to very rich. Each step adds one thing. Walk through the six steps with Mia's shop.

Word list

The team agrees on its words: bike, wheel, order. Each thing has one name. Nobody writes "cycle" in one place and "bike" in another.

A fixed list like this is a controlled vocabulary. With a short meaning for each word, it is a glossary.

Taxonomy

Now the words form a tree. Bike is on top. City bike and mountain bike are below it.

A taxonomy has one kind of link. The link means "is a kind of".

Thesaurus

A thesaurus adds two more links. The first link joins words with the same meaning. For "bicycle", use "bike". The second link means "related". A bike is related to a helmet.

Libraries use a thesaurus to make search better.

Schema

A schema describes data for one system. An order has a number, a date and a customer. The number is a whole number.

Now a program can store and check data. But the meaning of each name is still in people's heads.

Ontology

An ontology adds meaning that a machine can use. It has many kinds of relations, and it has rules. Every order has one customer. Nothing is both a bike and a customer.

Now a program can find mistakes and new facts.

Knowledge graph

Fill the ontology with facts about single things. B7 is a city bike. Lea placed order 12. Order 12 contains B7.

This is a knowledge graph. Things are nodes. Relations are arrows.

Look at step 2 again. A taxonomy is a tree, and every line has the same meaning.

Compare this tree with the graph in the first section. The tree cannot say that a wheel is part of a bike. It cannot say that a customer places an order. The graph can, because it has many kinds of links.

This line of steps has a name. It is the ontology spectrum. Deborah McGuinness drew a well-known version with about ten points. It appeared in a book in 2003. She uses the name "ontology" only for the richer points. For her, an ontology needs a fixed word list, clear meanings and strict "is a kind of" links.

The last step is different from the others. Steps 1 to 5 add meaning. Step 6 adds data. A knowledge graph is not a stronger ontology. It is an ontology with many facts inside.

Use this quick test. One kind of link makes a taxonomy. Many kinds of links and some rules make an ontology. Add facts about single things, and you have a knowledge graph.

Many people call every tree of categories an ontology. A folder tree of products is a taxonomy. It is useful, but a program cannot reason much with it.

Three one-minute examples

Here are three real projects. Each one takes a minute to understand. Each one sits at a different place on the line.

Schema.org: words for web pages

You search for a book on the web. The result shows the author and the year. How does the search engine know them? The web page has a small block of data for machines. The block uses words from Schema.org.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Book",
  "name": "The Left Hand of Darkness",
  "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "Ursula K. Le Guin" },
  "datePublished": "1969"
}

Here Book and Person are classes. The words name and author are relations. Google, Microsoft and Yahoo started Schema.org in June 2011. Version 30.1 from September 2026 has 826 types and 1,540 properties.

The Gene Ontology: one name for each job in a cell

Two labs study the same gene. One lab works with mice. The other lab works with yeast. Each lab has its own words for the job of the gene. So no program can join their results. The Gene Ontology gives every job one name and one number.

Look at "Hexose biosynthesis". It has two parents. So this ontology is a graph and not a simple tree. The project started in 1998 with three databases, for the fly, yeast and the mouse.

The release of August 2026 has 38,092 terms. Scientists have used them in more than 15 million annotations.

Wikidata: a graph of general knowledge

Wikidata is a free knowledge graph. Anyone can edit it. Every thing has a number that starts with Q. Every relation has a number that starts with P. Numbers work in every language.

@prefix wd:  <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> .
@prefix wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/> .

wd:Q42 wdt:P31 wd:Q5 .        # Douglas Adams - instance of - human
wd:Q42 wdt:P69 wd:Q691283 .   # Douglas Adams - educated at - St John's College

Wikidata opened in October 2012. In November 2026 it has about 124 million items. Most of it is facts about single things. So it sits on the last step of the line.

The three examples on the line
ProjectDomainPlace on the lineSize in 2026
Schema.orgWeb pagesA light ontology826 types, 1,540 properties
Gene OntologyBiologyAn ontology with strict links38,092 terms
WikidataGeneral knowledgeA knowledge graphAbout 124 million items

These numbers change with every release. Check the linked pages for the numbers of today.

Patterns to remember

An ontology is made of a few sentence shapes. Learn these shapes. You will use them in every chapter of this book.

Sentence shapes for talking about an ontology
PatternPurposeModelNote
A is a kind of BPut one class under a wider classA city bike is a kind of bike.Use it for kinds, not for single things.
X is a BSay what one single thing isB7 is a city bike.B7 is one thing. It is not a kind.
A is part of BLink a part to its wholeA wheel is part of a bike.A part is not a kind. A wheel is not a bike.
A + verb + BName a relation between two classesA customer places an order.Name the relation with a verb.
Every A has a BState a ruleEvery order has a customer.A rule is about all members of the class.
"Word" means ...Fix one meaning for a word"Order" means one purchase by one customer.One word, one meaning.
For X, use YJoin words with the same meaningFor "bicycle", use "bike".This is a thesaurus link. It is about words.
A here is the same as B thereJoin data from two systems"Client" in sales is the same as "customer" in repair.Check the meaning first. Similar names can lie.
If ..., then ...Find a new factIf B7 is a city bike, then B7 is a bike.The new fact comes from a rule, not from typing.
Thing, relation, thingWrite one fact of a knowledge graphLea, placed, order 12.One fact has exactly three parts.

Practice

Which sentence uses the computer meaning of the word?

  • Ontology is a part of philosophy.
  • Our team published an ontology for bike parts.
  • Aristotle was interested in ontology.

"An ontology" is a made thing that you can count. The other two sentences talk about the field of study.

In Gruber's sentence, what is a "conceptualization"?

  • A database with many tables
  • A programming language for AI
  • A simple view of one area, made for a goal

You choose the things and relations that matter. The ontology writes this view down.

A shop has a tree of product kinds. It has only "is a kind of" links. What is it?

  • A knowledge graph
  • A taxonomy
  • A thesaurus

One kind of link in a tree makes a taxonomy. A thesaurus also has same-meaning and related links.

Nobody typed "B7 is a bike". The program knows it anyway. Which need is this?

  • Joining data
  • Shared meaning
  • Reasoning

The program used a rule and a fact to find a new fact.

What does a knowledge graph add to an ontology?

  • Stronger rules
  • Many facts about single things
  • A list of synonyms

The ontology gives the kinds and the relations. The knowledge graph fills them with data.

Fill in the missing words.

Gruber published his famous definition in the year ?.

"A wheel is ? a bike" links a part to its whole.

A word list with a short meaning for each word is a ?.

  1. Write a small ontology page for a coffee shop. Give five kinds of things and four relations.
    Answer

    One possible page. Kinds: Drink, Coffee, Tea, Customer, Order. Relations: Coffee is a kind of drink. Tea is a kind of drink. A customer places an order. An order contains drinks. Your page can be different. There is no single correct model.

  2. Your team has a JSON schema for orders. Is it an ontology? Answer in three sentences.
    Answer

    Not yet. It describes the fields and types of data for one system. It does not say what the things mean or how the classes relate, so a program cannot reason with it.

  3. Put these four on the line: a list of country codes, Wikidata, a folder tree of products, the Gene Ontology.
    Answer

    The list of country codes is a word list. The folder tree is a taxonomy. The Gene Ontology is an ontology. Wikidata is a knowledge graph.

  4. Explain this sentence with an example. "For a program, a thing exists only when the program can name it."
    Answer

    Mia's ontology has no class for a helmet. So her programs cannot store a helmet or ask about one. For these programs, helmets do not exist. When Mia adds the class Helmet, helmets start to exist for the system.

Key takeaways

  • An ontology is a shared, written list of kinds of things and their relations.
  • In philosophy, Ontology is the study of what there is. In computing, an ontology is a file.
  • Gruber's 1993 definition means a clear, written description of a simple view of one domain.
  • Software uses an ontology for shared meaning, joining data, checking, reasoning and AI context.
  • The line goes from word list to taxonomy, thesaurus, schema, ontology and knowledge graph.
  • A taxonomy has one kind of link. An ontology has many kinds of links and rules.

Sources

  • A Translation Approach to Portable Ontology Specifications. Tom Gruber's 1993 paper with the famous definition.
  • Ontology (definition). Gruber's later entry for the Encyclopedia of Database Systems.
  • Logic and Ontology. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on the philosophy meaning.
  • Formal Ontology and Information Systems. Nicola Guarino's 1998 paper on the two meanings.
  • Ontologies Come of Age. Deborah McGuinness on the ontology spectrum.
  • Ontology Development 101. The guide by Noy and McGuinness, with reasons to build an ontology.

The building blocks

Every ontology is made from the same few blocks. You need classes, individuals, properties and rules. This chapter takes one sentence apart and names each block. At the end you can read a small university ontology.

  • Name the five building blocks of an ontology and find them in a sentence.
  • Tell "is a kind of", "is an instance of" and "is part of" apart.
  • Predict what a domain and a range let a program conclude.
  • Split an ontology into schema (TBox) and data (ABox).
  • Explain the open world, closed world and unique names with one example.

One sentence, five blocks

Read this short story from a university.

Ada is a professor. She teaches Logic 101. Logic 101 has 5 credits. Every course has at most one teacher.

The story looks simple. But it already holds all five blocks of an ontology. Go through them one by one.

Class

"Professor" and "course" are kinds of things. A kind of thing is a class.

Many single things belong to one class.

Individual

"Ada" and "Logic 101" are single things. A single thing is an individual.

You can point at an individual. You cannot point at a class.

Object property

"Teaches" links Ada to Logic 101. It joins two individuals.

This link is an object property.

Data property

"Has 5 credits" links Logic 101 to the number 5. A number is a plain value, not a thing.

This link is a data property.

Axiom

"Every course has at most one teacher" is a rule about all courses.

A rule like this is an axiom.

The five blocks and the words in the story
BlockWords in the storySimple test
Classprofessor, courseCan you say "a ..." and "many ..."?
IndividualAda, Logic 101Is there exactly one of it?
Object propertyteachesIs there a thing at both ends?
Data propertyhas 5 creditsIs a number, text or date at the end?
Axiomevery course has at most one teacherDoes it talk about all members?

Classes are the nouns for kinds. Individuals are the names. Properties are the verbs. Axioms are the rules with "every" or "no".

Beginners often make "Logic 101" a class. Ask the test question. Is there exactly one Logic 101? Yes. So it is an individual. The class is Course.

Classes and individuals

Look at two sentences. Both use the words "is a".

  • Ada is a professor.
  • A professor is a person.

The two sentences are very different. The first one puts one individual into a class. The second one puts a whole class inside a wider class. English uses the same words for both. An ontology language does not.

  • Ada is an instance of the class Professor.
  • Professor is a subclass of the class Person.
@prefix uni:  <http://example.org/uni#> .
@prefix rdf:  <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

uni:ada rdf:type uni:Professor .              # an individual in a class
uni:Professor rdfs:subClassOf uni:Person .    # a class inside a class

The first link is called instance of. In Turtle it is rdf:type. You can also write the short word a. The second link is called subclass of. In Turtle it is rdfs:subClassOf.

A class is a set

Think of a class as a set of individuals. The class Professor is the set of all professors. Ada is one member of that set. A subclass is a smaller set inside a bigger set. So every member of Professor is also a member of Person.

Programs use this. When Ada is a professor, a program concludes that Ada is a person. Nobody needs to type that fact.

Class A is a subclass of class B when every individual in A is also in B.

Most ontologies have one top class. In OWL it is owl:Thing. Every individual is a member of it. There is also an empty class, owl:Nothing. No individual can be a member of it.

Do not write uni:ada rdfs:subClassOf uni:Professor. That sentence says Ada is a set of things. Use rdf:type for individuals. Use rdfs:subClassOf only between two classes.

Properties and attributes

Now look at the links. Some links point to another thing. Other links point to a plain value.

uni:ada      uni:teaches uni:logic101 .   # thing to thing
uni:logic101 uni:credits 5 .              # thing to a number
uni:logic101 rdfs:label  "Logic 101" .    # a name for people to read

A property is a named link. The first line uses an object property. Both ends are things. You can follow the link and learn more about Logic 101.

The second line uses a data property. The end is a value with a datatype. Here the datatype is integer. A value has no links of its own. The number 5 does not teach anything.

The third line is an annotation. It gives a name or a comment for people. Reasoning programs do not use it.

Attributes

Many people say attribute for a data property. Credits, a birth date and an email address are attributes. The word comes from databases and older guides. OWL 2 says data property. In Turtle you write owl:DatatypeProperty.

Three kinds of properties in OWL
KindTurtle classEnd of the linkExample
Object propertyowl:ObjectPropertyAnother individualteaches, takes, offeredBy
Data propertyowl:DatatypePropertyA literal valuecredits, birthDate, email
Annotation propertyowl:AnnotationPropertyAny value, only for peoplerdfs:label, rdfs:comment

Ask one question. Will I ever want to say something about the value? A department has a name, a head and a budget. So "department" is a thing, and you need an object property. A credit number has nothing more to say. So you use a data property.

Do not store a thing as text. uni:ada uni:worksIn "Computer Science" is weak. Another file may write "CS" or "Comp. Sci.". A program cannot join these strings. Make the department an individual and link to it.

Is a kind of, instance of, part of

Three links cause most modelling mistakes. They look alike in English. But they follow different rules. Read the three small chains below.

A link is transitive when you can follow it through a chain. "Is a kind of" is transitive. "Part of" is usually transitive too. "Instance of" is not.

How the three links behave
Questionis a kind ofinstance ofpart of
Between what?Class and classIndividual and classUsually individual and individual
Transitive?YesNoYes, for one kind of part
Do features pass down?Yes. A professor has everything a person has.Yes, from the class to the member.No. A wheel is not a bike.
Turtlerdfs:subClassOfrdf:typeYour own property, like uni:partOf

Part of is not kind of

An engine is part of a car. But an engine is not a kind of car. So never put Engine under Car in a class tree. Use a part-of property for it.

A W3C note on part-whole links gives a second warning. Some links look like "part of", but they are not. Ben is a member of the chess club. The club is a member of the student union. Is Ben a member of the union? Not always. So membership is not transitive.

  • Member of: a person in a club. Not transitive.
  • Contained in: a student in a room. The student is not part of the room.
  • Made of: a statue made of clay. Clay is not a part like an arm.

"Engine is a subclass of CarPart" looks fine. But it says that every engine is a car part. Boats and planes have engines too. Say that a car engine is part of a car instead.

Domain and range

A property can say what is at each end. The domain is the class at the start. The range is the class at the end.

uni:teaches a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain uni:Professor ;    # whoever teaches is a professor
    rdfs:range  uni:Course .       # whatever is taught is a course

uni:chen uni:teaches uni:ai201 .   # no type is written for chen or ai201

Now look at Chen. Nobody wrote "Chen is a professor". We ran the RDFS rules over the file with Python. We used the rdflib and owlrl packages. Here is what came out.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF
import owlrl

UNI = Namespace("http://example.org/uni#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("uni.ttl")
before = len(g)

# add every fact that the RDFS rules allow
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.RDFS_Semantics).expand(g)
print("triples before:", before, "after:", len(g))

for who in ("ada", "chen", "ai201", "logic101", "cs"):
    types = sorted(t.split("#")[1] for t in g.objects(UNI[who], RDF.type)
                   if str(t).startswith(str(UNI)))
    print(who, "is a", ", ".join(types))
triples before: 30 after: 82
ada is a Person, Professor
chen is a Person, Professor
ai201 is a Course
logic101 is a Course
cs is a Department

The program found that Chen is a professor and a person. It found that AI 201 is a course. The domain and the range gave these new facts.

If property P has domain C, and x P y is a fact, then x is a C. If P has range D, and x P y is a fact, then y is a D.

The big surprise: domain is not a check

Many engineers expect a domain to work like a type check in code. They think it rejects bad data. It does not. Watch what happens with a typo.

g.add((UNI.ben, UNI.teaches, UNI.ai201))   # Ben is a student. A typo?
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.RDFS_Semantics).expand(g)
ben is a ['Person', 'Professor', 'Student']

There is no error. The program simply concludes that Ben is also a professor. The OWL 2 Primer warns about this exact mistake. A domain makes new facts. It does not block facts.

Do not give a property two domains to mean "this or that". Two domains mean "this and that". With domains Professor and Student, every teacher becomes both. Use one wider class, or no domain at all.

Do you want real checks? Use a validation language called SHACL. You meet it in SHACL and validation. For now, remember this. A domain describes. It does not guard.

Axioms: the rules

An axiom is any statement that the ontology says is true. "Professor is a subclass of Person" is already an axiom. Richer axioms use the words "every", "no", "at most" and "the same as".

  • Nobody is both a professor and a student.
  • Every course has at most one teacher.
  • "Taught by" is the reverse of "teaches".
  • A full-time student is a student who takes at least one course.
uni:Professor owl:disjointWith uni:Student .

uni:Course rdfs:subClassOf [ a owl:Restriction ;
    owl:onProperty uni:taughtBy ;
    owl:maxCardinality "1"^^xsd:nonNegativeInteger ] .

uni:taughtBy owl:inverseOf uni:teaches .

uni:FullTimeStudent owl:equivalentClass [ owl:intersectionOf ( uni:Student
    [ a owl:Restriction ; owl:onProperty uni:takes ;
      owl:someValuesFrom uni:Course ] ) ] .
DisjointClasses: Professor, Student

Class: Course
    SubClassOf: taughtBy max 1

ObjectProperty: taughtBy
    InverseOf: teaches

Class: FullTimeStudent
    EquivalentTo: Student and (takes some Course)

The second tab is Turtle. The third tab is Manchester syntax. It says the same thing in shorter words. The Protégé editor shows axioms in this form.

Common kinds of axioms
AxiomEnglish shapeWhat a program can do with it
SubclassEvery A is a B.Add the type B to every A.
Disjoint classesNothing is both A and B.Report Ben if he is both.
Equivalent classAn A is exactly a B with ...Sort individuals into A by their links.
CardinalityEvery A has at most n ...Find that two names mean one thing.
Inverse property"Taught by" reverses "teaches".Add the reverse link.
Transitive propertyPart of a part is a part.Follow chains.

The disjoint axiom gives the check we missed above. We added it and ran the stronger OWL RL rules. Now owlrl wrote an error into the graph.

Disjoint classes http://example.org/uni#Professor and http://example.org/uni#Student have a common individual http://example.org/uni#ben

Two words for one idea: a rule that a program can use is an axiom. A whole set of axioms is a theory. You meet the logic behind it in Description logics.

The "only" restriction does not mean "has some". "Every course is taught only by professors" is also true for a course with no teacher. Add "taught by some professor" when the link must exist.

Schema and data: TBox and ABox

Look at the university file again. It has two parts. The top part talks about classes and properties. The bottom part talks about Ada, Ben and Logic 101.

The TBox is the schema part. It holds the axioms about classes and properties. The ABox is the data part. It holds facts about individuals.

The names come from description logic. "T" stands for terminology, the words. "A" stands for assertions, the facts. Some books add an RBox for rules about properties. "Teaches is the reverse of taught by" would go there.

Which box?
StatementBox
Professor is a subclass of Person.TBox
Every course has at most one teacher.TBox
Ada is a professor.ABox
Ada teaches Logic 101.ABox
Logic 101 has 5 credits.ABox

The split matters in practice. The TBox is small and changes slowly. The ABox can hold millions of facts and changes every day. Many teams keep them in different files. Some tools also reason over them in different ways.

In a database, the TBox is like the table definitions. The ABox is like the rows. But the TBox also holds rules that make new rows.

Some people call only the TBox "the ontology". Others call both boxes together "the ontology". Noy and McGuinness call the classes plus the individuals a knowledge base. Say which one you mean.

Open world, closed world, unique names

Ask the university file one question. Does Ada teach AI 201?

from rdflib import Graph

g = Graph()
g.parse("uni.ttl")
print(g.query("""
  PREFIX uni: <http://example.org/uni#>
  ASK { uni:ada uni:teaches uni:ai201 }
""").askAnswer)
False

The query says False. But what does that mean? There are two ways to read it.

Closed world

The data is complete. A fact that is missing is false. So Ada does not teach AI 201.

A train timetable works like this. No train at 9:15 means there is no train.

Open world

The data may be incomplete. A fact that is missing is unknown. Maybe Ada teaches it. The file just does not say.

The web works like this. Another page may add the fact tomorrow.

A database uses the closed world assumption. OWL reasoning uses the open world assumption. The SPARQL engine above only looked at stored triples. Its False means "not found". An OWL reasoner never concludes "false" from a missing fact alone.

Unique names

In a database, two different keys mean two different rows. This is the unique name assumption. OWL does not make it. Two names can point to one thing.

uni:Course rdfs:subClassOf [ a owl:Restriction ;
    owl:onProperty uni:taughtBy ;
    owl:maxCardinality "1"^^xsd:nonNegativeInteger ] .

uni:logic101 a uni:Course ;
    uni:taughtBy uni:ada , uni:lovelace .   # two names

A database would reject this. Two teachers break the rule. But an OWL reasoner thinks differently. One teacher is allowed and two names appear. So the two names must mean the same person. We ran the OWL RL rules and then added one more fact.

owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)
print("same person?", (UNI.ada, OWL.sameAs, UNI.lovelace) in g)

# now say that the two names are two different people
g.add((UNI.ada, OWL.differentFrom, UNI.lovelace))
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)
same person? True
error: 'sameAs' and 'differentFrom' cannot be used on the same subject-object pair

Only the explicit "different" fact makes a real clash. Without it, the reasoner merges the names.

Identity

Each individual needs one stable name. In RDF and OWL that name is an IRI, such as http://example.org/uni#ada. Two files that use the same IRI talk about the same thing. When two IRIs mean one thing, you link them with owl:sameAs.

A harder question is about identity itself. Is Logic 101 in 2025 the same thing as Logic 101 in 2026? The title is the same. The teacher and the students changed. Schema.org splits this into two types. A Course is the subject in the catalogue. A CourseInstance is one run of it, at one time or place. The property hasCourseInstance links them.

Write down the identity rule for each important class. "Two students are the same when they have the same student number." This helps later when you join data from two systems.

Do not use owl:sameAs for "similar". It copies every fact from one name to the other. Linking a city to its football club with it mixes their facts. Use a weaker link, like skos:closeMatch, when you are not sure.

A tiny university ontology

Now put all the blocks together. The graph shows the TBox and the ABox in one picture. Drag the nodes to see them better.

Here is the full file that we tested above. Read the comments. Each one names a block from this chapter.

@prefix uni:  <http://example.org/uni#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# ---- schema (TBox): classes
uni:Person     a owl:Class .
uni:Professor  a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf uni:Person .
uni:Student    a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf uni:Person .
uni:Course     a owl:Class .
uni:Department a owl:Class .

# ---- schema (TBox): properties with domain and range
uni:teaches   a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain uni:Professor ; rdfs:range uni:Course .
uni:takes     a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain uni:Student ;   rdfs:range uni:Course .
uni:offeredBy a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain uni:Course ;    rdfs:range uni:Department .
uni:credits   a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain uni:Course ;    rdfs:range xsd:integer .

# ---- data (ABox): individuals and facts
uni:ada  a uni:Professor ; rdfs:label "Ada" ; uni:teaches uni:logic101 .
uni:ben  a uni:Student ;   rdfs:label "Ben" ; uni:takes uni:logic101 .
uni:logic101 rdfs:label "Logic 101" ; uni:credits 5 ; uni:offeredBy uni:cs .
uni:cs   rdfs:label "Computer Science" .
uni:chen uni:teaches uni:ai201 .   # no type written for chen or ai201

The file has 30 triples. After the RDFS rules it has 82. Most new triples are types, like "Ada is a person". Some are small facts about the vocabulary itself.

The Department to Faculty link is only in the picture. It shows where a part-of property would go. Try to add it to the file in the practice section.

You build a full ontology like this, step by step, in Your first ontology.

Patterns to remember

Building block patterns in Turtle
PatternPurposeModelNote
C a owl:ClassDeclare a classuni:Course a owl:Class .Class names start with a capital letter.
x a CPut an individual in a classuni:ada a uni:Professor .Never use subClassOf for an individual.
A rdfs:subClassOf BPut a class inside a wider classuni:Professor rdfs:subClassOf uni:Person .Only for real kinds, not for parts.
x P y (object)Link two individualsuni:ada uni:teaches uni:logic101 .Use it when the end has its own facts.
x P value (data)Give an individual an attributeuni:logic101 uni:credits 5 .Do not store a thing as a string.
P rdfs:domain CSay what starts the linkuni:teaches rdfs:domain uni:Professor .It makes new types. It does not check.
P rdfs:range DSay what ends the linkuni:credits rdfs:range xsd:integer .Two ranges mean both, not either.
A owl:disjointWith BSay nothing is bothuni:Professor owl:disjointWith uni:Student .This is how OWL finds wrong data.
x partOf yLink a part to its wholeuni:cs uni:partOf uni:science .Membership and containment are not parts.
x owl:sameAs yJoin two names for one thinguni:ada owl:sameAs uni:lovelace .It copies all facts. Never use it for "similar".
x owl:differentFrom ySay two names are two thingsuni:ada owl:differentFrom uni:ben .OWL has no unique names. Say it when it matters.
x rdfs:label "text"Give a name for peopleuni:cs rdfs:label "Computer Science" .Labels are for people. Reasoners ignore them.

Practice

Which one is an individual?

  • Course
  • Logic 101
  • Department

There is exactly one Logic 101. Course and Department are kinds with many members.

"Logic 101 has 5 credits." What kind of property is "credits"?

  • Object property
  • Data property
  • Annotation property

The end of the link is a plain number, not a thing.

Ada is a professor. Professor is an academic rank. What follows?

  • Ada is an academic rank.
  • Nothing new about Ada.
  • Academic rank is a subclass of Professor.

"Instance of" is not transitive. You cannot follow it through a chain.

"Teaches" has domain Professor. The data says "Rex teaches Logic 101". Rex is a dog. What does an RDFS reasoner do?

  • It reports an error.
  • It deletes the fact.
  • It concludes that Rex is a professor.

A domain makes new facts. It never rejects data. Only a disjoint axiom, like "no dog is a person", can show a clash.

The data has no fact "Ben takes AI 201". What does an OWL reasoner conclude?

  • Ben does not take AI 201.
  • It is unknown.
  • The data has an error.

OWL uses the open world assumption. A missing fact is unknown, not false.

Fill in the missing words.

The class at the start of a property is its ?.

The part of an ontology with facts about individuals is the ?.

In Turtle, the short word for rdf:type is ?.

What is the difference between a class and an individual?

A class is a kind with many members. An individual is one single thing.

Is "part of" a kind of "is a"?

No. A wheel is part of a bike, but a wheel is not a bike.

What does the unique name assumption say?

Different names mean different things. Databases use it. OWL does not.

What is in the TBox?

Classes, properties and rules about them. The schema part.

  1. Sort these into TBox and ABox. "Ben takes Logic 101." "Every student is a person." "CS is a department." "Takes has range Course."
    Answer

    TBox: "Every student is a person" and "Takes has range Course". ABox: "Ben takes Logic 101" and "CS is a department".

  2. Add a part-of link for the CS department to uni.ttl. Write two Turtle lines.
    Answer

    One possible answer: uni:partOf a owl:ObjectProperty, owl:TransitiveProperty . and uni:cs uni:partOf uni:scienceFaculty . The first line makes the property transitive. So chains of parts work.

  3. A teammate writes uni:worksIn rdfs:domain uni:Professor, uni:Admin. They want "a professor or an admin works in a department". What goes wrong? How do you fix it?
    Answer

    Two domains mean "and". Every person who works somewhere becomes a professor and an admin. Fix it with one wider class, like Staff, as the domain. Or use a union class: rdfs:domain [ owl:unionOf ( uni:Professor uni:Admin ) ].

  4. Your database says each course has one teacher. The data has "Logic 101 taught by A. Lovelace" and "Logic 101 taught by Ada L.". What does a database do? What does an OWL reasoner do? Why?
    Answer

    The database rejects the second row, because it breaks the rule. The OWL reasoner concludes that the two names are one person. OWL has no unique name assumption, so two names may mean one thing. Only a differentFrom fact makes a clash.

  5. Design question: should "Logic 101 in 2026" be an individual of Course? Give one problem and one better model.
    Answer

    Problem: the teacher and students change each term. One individual would collect facts from many terms and mix them. Better: keep Course for the subject in the catalogue. Add a class CourseInstance, as schema.org does, with a term, a teacher and students. Link each course to its instances.

Key takeaways

  • The five blocks are classes, individuals, object properties, data properties and axioms.
  • Use rdf:type for an individual in a class. Use rdfs:subClassOf between classes.
  • "Is a kind of" is transitive. "Instance of" is not. "Part of" is not "kind of".
  • Domain and range make new facts. They do not reject wrong data.
  • The TBox is the schema with rules. The ABox is the data about individuals.
  • OWL uses the open world and no unique names. Databases use the closed world and unique names.
  • Give each thing one stable IRI. Use owl:sameAs only for "exactly the same".

Sources

  • OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Primer (Second Edition). The W3C introduction to classes, properties, the open world and unique names.
  • RDF Schema 1.1. The W3C rules for type, subclass, domain and range.
  • Simple part-whole relations in OWL ontologies. A W3C draft note on part-of and its common mistakes.
  • Ontology Development 101. Noy and McGuinness on classes, slots, instances and knowledge bases.
  • owlrl on PyPI. The Python package we used for the RDFS and OWL RL rules (version 7.6.2 with rdflib 7.6.0).

Your first ontology, step by step

In this chapter you build a real ontology for a bug tracker. You start with questions and a list of words. You end with a Turtle file, three answers from SPARQL and one new fact from a rule. Every program here was run, and the output is real.

  • Write three competency questions for a small domain.
  • Sort a list of terms into classes, properties, individuals and values.
  • Write the ontology in plain sentences and then in Turtle.
  • Load the file with Python rdflib and ask questions in SPARQL.
  • Add a rule, see a new fact appear, and compare with a property graph.

Choose a domain and three questions

Your team uses a bug tracker. People report bugs. Developers fix them. Some issues block other issues. The team lead asks three questions every Monday.

  1. Which open issues does Mia have?
  2. How many issues does each component have?
  3. Which open bugs have nobody assigned?

These are competency questions. They set the size of the ontology. A term that helps to answer them goes in. A term that does not help stays out for now.

Here is the whole plan. You will follow it in this chapter.

Ask

Write three questions that the ontology must answer.

List

Write down every word that people use in the domain. Do not sort yet.

Sort

Mark each word. Is it a class, a property, a single thing or a value?

Link

Add properties with a domain and a range.

Say

Write the model in plain sentences. Show them to a teammate.

Write

Write the model and some data in Turtle.

Query

Load the file with Python. Answer the three questions with SPARQL.

Reason

Add one rule. Watch a new fact appear.

Compare

Store the same data as a property graph. See what changes.

This plan follows the classic guide Ontology Development 101 by Natalya Noy and Deborah McGuinness. Their first step is also to fix the domain and the questions.

Do not start with "all of software development". That domain has no end. Start with three questions from real people. You can grow the ontology later.

List the terms and sort them

Talk to the team for ten minutes. Write down every word they use. Here is the list from our team.

issue, bug, feature, task, title, status, open, in progress, closed, assignee, reporter, developer, person, Mia, Sam, Lea, project, web shop, component, checkout, search, release, 2.0, blocks, created date

Now sort the words. Use the tests from The building blocks.

The terms, sorted
KindTermsTest
ClassIssue, Bug, Feature, Task, Person, Project, Component, Release, StatusMany members
IndividualMia, Sam, Lea, web shop, checkout, search, release 2.0Exactly one
Value of a value setopen, in progress, closedA short fixed list
Object propertyassigned to, reported by, in component, part of, targets, blocksA thing at both ends
Data propertytitle, created dateText or a date at the end

Two words are missing from the table: "assignee" and "reporter". They are not new classes. They are roles that a person plays for one issue. So we turn them into properties: assigned to and reported by. The word "developer" is out for now. No question needs it.

Next, arrange the classes in a tree. Bug, Feature and Task are kinds of Issue.

Why is "open" not a class?

You could make a class OpenBug under Bug. But a bug is open today and closed next week. Its class would change. A class should hold things for their whole life. A bug is always a bug. It is not always open.

Philosophers call a class like Bug rigid. A class like OpenBug is not rigid. A changing state is better as a value. So Status is a small class with three individuals. This is a value set.

Do not turn every word into a class. "Assignee" sounds like a class. But Mia is an assignee for BUG-1 and not for BUG-5. A role that depends on another thing is usually a property.

Add properties

Each property gets a domain and a range. Remember: they describe the ends of a link. They do not check data.

The properties of the bug tracker
PropertyKindDomainRange
assignedToobjectIssuePerson
reportedByobjectIssuePerson
inComponentobjectIssueComponent
partOfobjectComponentProject
hasStatusobjectIssueStatus
targetsobjectIssueRelease
blocksobjectIssueIssue
titledataIssuestring
createddataIssuedate

Look at the names. Classes start with a capital letter: Issue. Properties start with a small letter and a verb: assignedTo. Noy and McGuinness give the same advice. Pick one style and keep it.

Read each property as a sentence. "An issue is assigned to a person." If the sentence sounds wrong, the domain or the range is wrong.

Do not use a property name in both directions. assignedTo goes from the issue to the person. If you also need the other way, make a second property, like assignedIssue. Then say they are inverses.

Say it in plain sentences

Before you write any code, write the model in English. A product owner can check English. Most product owners cannot check Turtle.

  • A bug, a feature and a task are kinds of issue.
  • An issue is assigned to a person and reported by a person.
  • An issue is in a component. A component is part of a project.
  • An issue has a status. A status is open, in progress or closed.
  • An issue targets a release. An issue can block another issue.
  • An issue has a title and a created date.
  • BUG-1 is a bug. Its title is "Payment page crashes".
  • BUG-1 is in Checkout. It is open. It is assigned to Mia.
  • FEAT-2 is a feature. It is in progress and assigned to Sam.
  • BUG-1 blocks FEAT-2. FEAT-2 blocks TASK-3.
  • BUG-5 is an open bug in Checkout. Nobody is assigned.

Show the sentences to the team. In our team, Sam asked one question. "Can a bug be in two components?" The answer was no. Write this down. Later you can add it as a rule.

If you cannot say it in a short sentence, you cannot model it yet. Talk more with the team first.

Write it in Turtle

Turtle writes each fact as subject, property and object. A full stop ends a group. A semicolon means "same subject, next property". A comma means "same subject and property, next object".

We use two files. The first one holds the schema, the TBox.

@prefix bt:   <http://example.org/bugs#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# ---------- TBox: classes
bt:Issue     a owl:Class .
bt:Bug       a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bt:Issue .
bt:Feature   a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bt:Issue .
bt:Task      a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf bt:Issue .
bt:Person    a owl:Class .
bt:Component a owl:Class .
bt:Project   a owl:Class .
bt:Release   a owl:Class .
bt:Status    a owl:Class .
bt:open       a bt:Status .   # the three allowed values
bt:inProgress a bt:Status .
bt:closed     a bt:Status .

# ---------- TBox: properties
bt:assignedTo  a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range bt:Person .
bt:reportedBy  a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range bt:Person .
bt:inComponent a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range bt:Component .
bt:partOf      a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Component ; rdfs:range bt:Project .
bt:hasStatus   a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range bt:Status .
bt:targets     a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range bt:Release .
bt:blocks      a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range bt:Issue .
bt:title       a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range xsd:string .
bt:created     a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:domain bt:Issue ; rdfs:range xsd:date .

The second file holds the data, the ABox.

@prefix bt:   <http://example.org/bugs#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# ---------- ABox: people, places, releases
bt:mia a bt:Person ; rdfs:label "Mia" .
bt:sam a bt:Person ; rdfs:label "Sam" .
bt:lea a bt:Person ; rdfs:label "Lea" .
bt:shop     a bt:Project ;   rdfs:label "Web shop" .
bt:checkout a bt:Component ; rdfs:label "Checkout" ; bt:partOf bt:shop .
bt:search   a bt:Component ; rdfs:label "Search" ;   bt:partOf bt:shop .
bt:v2       a bt:Release ;   rdfs:label "2.0" .

# ---------- ABox: issues
bt:BUG-1  a bt:Bug ; bt:title "Payment page crashes" ;
    bt:inComponent bt:checkout ; bt:hasStatus bt:open ;
    bt:assignedTo bt:mia ; bt:reportedBy bt:lea ;
    bt:targets bt:v2 ; bt:blocks bt:FEAT-2 ; bt:created "2026-11-02"^^xsd:date .
bt:FEAT-2 a bt:Feature ; bt:title "Pay with a gift card" ;
    bt:inComponent bt:checkout ; bt:hasStatus bt:inProgress ;
    bt:assignedTo bt:sam ; bt:targets bt:v2 ; bt:blocks bt:TASK-3 .
bt:TASK-3 a bt:Task ; bt:title "Write release notes" ;
    bt:hasStatus bt:open ; bt:assignedTo bt:mia ; bt:targets bt:v2 .
bt:BUG-4  a bt:Bug ; bt:title "Search ignores accents" ;
    bt:inComponent bt:search ; bt:hasStatus bt:closed ; bt:assignedTo bt:sam .
bt:BUG-5  a bt:Bug ; bt:title "Wrong total with two coupons" ;
    bt:inComponent bt:checkout ; bt:hasStatus bt:open ; bt:reportedBy bt:lea .

Each name like bt:BUG-1 is short for a full IRI: http://example.org/bugs#BUG-1. The @prefix line sets up the short form.

Keep the schema and the data in separate files. The schema changes rarely, and people review it with care. The data changes every hour. A tool often writes it.

Do not build IRIs from titles, like bt:PaymentPageCrashes. Titles change. Use a stable key, like the issue number. Put the title in a data property.

Load it and ask three questions

Now load both files with Python. We use rdflib 7.6.0 on Python 3.14. Run it with uv run --with rdflib python3.14 load.py.

from rdflib import Graph, RDF, OWL

g = Graph()
g.parse("tracker.ttl")      # the schema (TBox)
g.parse("data.ttl")         # the data (ABox)
print("triples:", len(g))

g.bind("bt", "http://example.org/bugs#")
classes = sorted(g.qname(c) for c in g.subjects(RDF.type, OWL.Class))
print("classes:", ", ".join(classes))
triples: 89
classes: bt:Bug, bt:Component, bt:Feature, bt:Issue, bt:Person, bt:Project, bt:Release, bt:Status, bt:Task

The graph has 89 triples. Now ask the three Monday questions. SPARQL looks for patterns in the graph. A word with ? is a variable. SPARQL fills it with every value that fits.

from rdflib import Graph

g = Graph()
g.parse("tracker.ttl")
g.parse("data.ttl")
PRE = """PREFIX bt:   <http://example.org/bugs#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
"""

# Q1: Which open issues does Mia have?
q1 = PRE + """
SELECT ?issue ?title WHERE {
  ?issue bt:assignedTo bt:mia ;
         bt:hasStatus  bt:open ;
         bt:title      ?title .
} ORDER BY ?issue"""

# Q2: How many issues does each component have?
q2 = PRE + """
SELECT ?name (COUNT(?issue) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?issue bt:inComponent ?c .
  ?c rdfs:label ?name .
} GROUP BY ?name ORDER BY DESC(?n)"""

# Q3: Which open bugs have nobody assigned?
q3 = PRE + """
SELECT ?bug ?title WHERE {
  ?bug a bt:Bug ; bt:hasStatus bt:open ; bt:title ?title .
  FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?bug bt:assignedTo ?someone }
}"""

for name, q in (("Q1", q1), ("Q2", q2), ("Q3", q3)):
    print(name)
    for row in g.query(q):
        print("  ", " | ".join(str(x).split("#")[-1] for x in row))
Q1
   BUG-1 | Payment page crashes
   TASK-3 | Write release notes
Q2
   Checkout | 3
   Search | 1
Q3
   BUG-5 | Wrong total with two coupons

All three questions have answers. So the ontology passes its first test.

  1. SPARQL looks for any ?issue with the link bt:assignedTo bt:mia. It finds BUG-1 and TASK-3.
  2. It keeps only the ones with bt:hasStatus bt:open. Both stay.
  3. It reads the title of each one into ?title.
  4. It sorts the rows by ?issue and prints them.

Q3 and the closed world

Q3 uses FILTER NOT EXISTS. It asks for bugs with no assignedTo link in the data. This is a closed-world question. The query treats a missing fact as "no". That is fine for a report. But it is not what an OWL reasoner does. A reasoner says "unknown".

Do not write ?issue a bt:Issue in a query and expect bugs. Our data says "BUG-1 is a bug". It never says "BUG-1 is an issue". Plain SPARQL does not use rdfs:subClassOf. You need a reasoner first, or the path a/rdfs:subClassOf*.

Add one rule and watch a new fact appear

BUG-1 blocks FEAT-2. FEAT-2 blocks TASK-3. So, in real life, BUG-1 also blocks TASK-3. You cannot write the release notes while the payment page crashes. But the data does not say so yet.

We add one rule. "If A blocks B and B blocks C, then A blocks C." In OWL this is one line. The property becomes transitive. You can also write the rule as a SPARQL update. Both tabs give the same new fact.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF, OWL
import owlrl

BT = Namespace("http://example.org/bugs#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("tracker.ttl")
g.parse("data.ttl")

def blockers_of(issue):
    return sorted(s.split("#")[1] for s in g.subjects(BT.blocks, issue))

print("before:", blockers_of(BT["TASK-3"]))

# the rule: if A blocks B and B blocks C, then A blocks C
g.add((BT.blocks, RDF.type, OWL.TransitiveProperty))
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)

print("after: ", blockers_of(BT["TASK-3"]))
from rdflib import Graph

g = Graph()
g.parse("tracker.ttl")
g.parse("data.ttl")

rule = """
PREFIX bt: <http://example.org/bugs#>
INSERT { ?a bt:blocks ?c }
WHERE  { ?a bt:blocks ?b . ?b bt:blocks ?c }"""

# run the rule again and again until no new triple appears
while True:
    size = len(g)
    g.update(rule)
    print("triples:", len(g))
    if len(g) == size:
        break

Here is the output of the OWL version. It uses the owlrl package 7.6.2.

before: ['FEAT-2']
after:  ['BUG-1', 'FEAT-2']

And here is the output of the SPARQL version.

triples: 90
triples: 90

The first run added one triple: BUG-1 blocks TASK-3. The second run added nothing. So the loop stopped. A state where the rules add nothing new is a fixed point. Every forward-chaining reasoner runs until it reaches one.

The OWL version also added many other facts. For example, it found that BUG-1 is an Issue, from the subclass axiom. The SPARQL version adds only what your one rule says. You learn more about rule engines in Rules and Datalog.

Do not store the new facts in the same file as the typed facts without a mark. Later you cannot tell them apart. When BUG-1 is fixed, the old "blocks TASK-3" fact must go too. Keep inferred facts in a separate graph, or compute them again.

The same data as a property graph

Many teams store graphs in a property graph database instead. Neo4j is the best-known one. Its query language is Cypher. Here is the same data in Cypher (shortened).

CREATE (:Person {name: 'Mia'}), (:Person {name: 'Sam'}), (:Person {name: 'Lea'});
CREATE (:Component {name: 'Checkout'}), (:Component {name: 'Search'});
CREATE (:Issue {key: 'BUG-1', kind: 'Bug', title: 'Payment page crashes', status: 'open'});
CREATE (:Issue {key: 'FEAT-2', kind: 'Feature', title: 'Pay with a gift card', status: 'inProgress'});
CREATE (:Issue {key: 'TASK-3', kind: 'Task', title: 'Write release notes', status: 'open'});
CREATE (:Issue {key: 'BUG-5', kind: 'Bug', title: 'Wrong total with two coupons', status: 'open'});

// an edge can carry its own fields, like the date of the assignment
MATCH (i:Issue {key: 'BUG-1'}), (p:Person {name: 'Mia'})
CREATE (i)-[:ASSIGNED_TO {since: date('2026-11-03')}]->(p);

MATCH (a:Issue {key: 'BUG-1'}), (b:Issue {key: 'FEAT-2'})
CREATE (a)-[:BLOCKS]->(b);

Now compare two questions side by side. Pick a tab.

SELECT ?issue ?title WHERE {
  ?issue bt:assignedTo bt:mia ;
         bt:hasStatus  bt:open ;
         bt:title      ?title .
} ORDER BY ?issue
MATCH (i:Issue {status: 'open'})-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(:Person {name: 'Mia'})
RETURN i.key, i.title ORDER BY i.key;

The Cypher query draws the pattern with arrows. The answer is the same: BUG-1 and TASK-3. Now look at the chain of blockers. Cypher has no rule for it. Instead, the query follows the chain.

MATCH (a:Issue)-[:BLOCKS*1..5]->(t:Issue {key: 'TASK-3'})
RETURN a.key ORDER BY a.key;
['BUG-1']
['FEAT-2']

The part *1..5 means "follow one to five BLOCKS edges". The Neo4j manual says this older form still works. Its newer form is -[:BLOCKS]->{1,5}, which follows the ISO GQL standard.

RDF graph and property graph, on the same data
QuestionRDF graph (Turtle)Property graph (Cypher)
Names of thingsGlobal IRIs that any file can reuseInternal ids plus your own key field
Fields on an edgeNot direct. You need an extra pattern.Yes. since sits on ASSIGNED_TO.
Kinds of issueClasses with subClassOfA label or a kind field. No subclass.
StatusIndividuals in a value setA plain string
New factsRules and reasonersPath queries at question time
StandardsW3C: RDF, OWL, SPARQLISO GQL (2024). Cypher came first.
How we tested the Cypher

We did not run a Neo4j server. We ran the same statements in Kuzu 0.11.3, a small graph database inside Python. Kuzu needs table definitions first, so we added six CREATE NODE TABLE and CREATE REL TABLE lines. The outputs above come from that run. The Kuzu project was archived in October 2025. A community fork called LadybugDB continues it.

RDF puts the meaning in the data and rules. A property graph puts the data in nodes and edges with fields, and leaves the meaning to your queries and code.

Do not choose a model because one query looks shorter. Choose by your needs. Do you join data from many sources and need shared meaning? RDF helps. Do you need fast path queries inside one app? A property graph helps. Data models compared goes deeper.

Make it ready for real use

The tracker works. But a real team needs a few more things. Here is a short list, from easy to hard.

  1. Labels. Give every class and property an rdfs:label and an rdfs:comment. People read these, not the IRIs.
  2. A real namespace. Replace example.org with a domain that your team owns. IRIs should never change.
  3. A version. Add owl:versionInfo "0.1" to the ontology. Change it when the schema changes.
  4. Checks. "Every issue has exactly one title." OWL does not check this. Use SHACL shapes. See SHACL and validation.
  5. Reuse. Do not invent bt:title if a common one fits. Many teams use dcterms:title from Dublin Core.
  6. Tests. Keep the three competency questions as tests. Run them after every change.

A typical exam task gives you a short story. You must find classes, individuals and properties, then write Turtle. Check two things first. Did you use a for individuals? Did you keep roles as properties?

Patterns to remember

Patterns for building a first ontology
PatternPurposeModelNote
Which ... does ... have?Write a competency questionWhich open issues does Mia have?Write questions before classes.
A is a kind of BBuild the class treebt:Bug rdfs:subClassOf bt:Issue .Only for things that stay that kind for life.
Role as propertyModel a role for one thingbt:BUG-1 bt:assignedTo bt:mia .Do not make a class Assignee.
State as value setModel a changing statebt:open a bt:Status .Do not make a class OpenBug.
Schema file, data fileKeep TBox and ABox aparttracker.ttl, data.ttlThe data changes often. The schema does not.
g.parse(file)Load Turtle in Pythong.parse("data.ttl")rdflib guesses the format from the file ending.
SELECT ... WHERE { pattern }Ask a question?i bt:hasStatus bt:openPlain SPARQL ignores subClassOf.
FILTER NOT EXISTS { ... }Find missing linksOpen bugs with no assigneeThis is a closed-world check in the query.
P a owl:TransitivePropertyFollow chains with a rulebt:blocks a owl:TransitiveProperty .Keep inferred facts apart from typed facts.
INSERT { } WHERE { }Write a rule in SPARQLAdd ?a bt:blocks ?cRepeat until no new triple appears.
(a)-[:REL*1..n]->(b)Follow chains in Cypher-[:BLOCKS*1..5]->The path is computed at query time, not stored.

Practice

What is a competency question?

  • A test for the people who build the ontology
  • A question the finished ontology must answer
  • A question in a job interview

Competency questions set the scope. They also become tests later.

The team says "reviewer". How do you model it?

  • A class Reviewer under Person
  • A property reviewedBy from Issue to Person
  • An individual bt:reviewer

A reviewer is a role a person plays for one issue. Roles are usually properties.

Why is "closed" a member of Status and not a class ClosedBug?

  • Classes cannot have long names.
  • A bug changes its status, but it stays a bug.
  • SPARQL cannot query classes.

A class should hold a thing for its whole life. A state that changes is a value.

The query SELECT ?i WHERE { ?i a bt:Issue } returns no rows on our data. Why?

  • The file has a syntax error.
  • rdflib cannot read classes.
  • The data only says "a bt:Bug". Plain SPARQL does not follow subClassOf.

Run a reasoner first, or write ?i a/rdfs:subClassOf* bt:Issue.

Fill in the missing words.

In Turtle, a ? means "same subject, next property".

The state where rules add nothing new is a ?.

  1. Write the plain sentence for this Turtle line: bt:BUG-4 bt:hasStatus bt:closed .
    Answer

    BUG-4 has the status closed. Or: BUG-4 is closed.

  2. Write a SPARQL query for "Which issues target release 2.0?".
    Answer

    SELECT ?i WHERE { ?i bt:targets bt:v2 } With our data it returns BUG-1, FEAT-2 and TASK-3.

  3. Add a new issue in Turtle. TASK-6 "Update the help page" is open, in Search, and nobody is assigned. Which of the three questions changes its answer?
    Answer

    bt:TASK-6 a bt:Task ; bt:title "Update the help page" ; bt:inComponent bt:search ; bt:hasStatus bt:open . Q2 changes: Search now has 2 issues. Q3 does not change, because TASK-6 is a task, not a bug.

  4. Write a SPARQL rule that adds "the person is a developer" for everyone who has an assigned issue.
    Answer

    INSERT { ?p a bt:Developer } WHERE { ?i bt:assignedTo ?p } One run is enough. The rule does not use its own output, so no loop is needed.

  5. The team wants to record when each issue was assigned. Show how you store it in the property graph. Why is it harder in plain RDF?
    Answer

    In Cypher the date goes on the edge: [:ASSIGNED_TO {since: date('2026-11-03')}]. In plain RDF a triple cannot hold extra fields. You need an extra node for the assignment, with its issue, person and date. The 15 modelling patterns shows this n-ary pattern.

Key takeaways

  • Start with three competency questions. They decide what goes in.
  • List the words, then sort them into classes, individuals, values and properties.
  • Roles become properties. Changing states become values in a value set.
  • Write the model in plain sentences before you write Turtle.
  • rdflib loads Turtle in two lines. SPARQL answers questions with patterns.
  • One rule, like a transitive property, adds facts that nobody typed.
  • A property graph stores fields on edges and follows chains at query time.

Sources

  • Ontology Development 101. The seven-step guide by Noy and McGuinness, with naming advice.
  • Querying with SPARQL (rdflib docs). How rdflib runs queries and updates.
  • SPARQL 1.1 Query Language. The W3C standard for SELECT, FILTER NOT EXISTS and GROUP BY.
  • Cypher manual: variable-length patterns. The Neo4j page on path quantifiers and the older star form.
  • KuzuDB graph database abandoned. News on the end of the Kuzu project in October 2025.

The 15 modelling patterns

Most ontologies are built from the same small moves. This chapter gives you 15 of them as patterns. Each pattern has a purpose, a small model in Turtle and one warning. Learn them once and use them in every domain.

  • Name the 15 patterns and put them into five groups.
  • Pick the right pattern for a modelling problem.
  • Write each pattern in Turtle and test it with Python.
  • Avoid the classic mistake that comes with each pattern.

What a modelling pattern is

Look at two sentences from Mia's bike shop.

  • Lea bought bike B7.
  • Lea gave bike B7 four stars on 12 November.

The first sentence fits into one triple: Lea, bought, B7. The second sentence has four parts: Lea, B7, four stars and a date. One triple cannot hold it. Every ontology builder meets this problem. And there is a known answer. You make a new node for the rating. You link the four parts to that node.

A known answer to a problem that comes back again and again is a pattern. In ontology work people say ontology design pattern. W3C working groups wrote notes about some of them in 2005 and 2006. Research groups keep libraries of them today.

Every pattern in this chapter has four parts. They are the same four columns as the pattern tables in this book.

The four parts of a pattern
PartQuestion it answers
PatternWhat is the name of the move?
PurposeWhen do I use it?
ModelWhat does it look like in Turtle?
NoteWhat is the one mistake to avoid?

The 15 patterns fall into five groups. Open the tree to see them.

All models below use the same short prefixes. Here they are once, so the models can stay short.

@prefix shop: <http://example.org/shop#> .
@prefix crm:  <http://example.org/crm#> .
@prefix wd:   <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .
@prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> .
@prefix qudt: <http://qudt.org/schema/qudt/> .
@prefix unit: <http://qudt.org/vocab/unit/> .
@prefix dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .

A pattern is a recipe. You do not invent a new way to model time or units. You use the recipe that others already tested.

Do not use a pattern because it looks clever. Every pattern adds nodes and work. Use it only when your competency questions need it.

Things and kinds: patterns 1 to 4

These four patterns are the base of every model. You met them in The building blocks. Here each one gets its pattern card.

Pattern 1: Class and instance

shop:CityBike a owl:Class .   # a kind of thing
shop:b7 a shop:CityBike .     # one single bike of that kind

Purpose: say that one thing belongs to a kind. Note: ask "is there exactly one?". If yes, it is an instance. Use a, never rdfs:subClassOf, for an instance.

Pattern 2: Subclass

shop:CityBike rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike .
shop:EBike    rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike .

Purpose: put a narrow kind under a wider kind. Every city bike is a bike. Note: the narrow kind must hold for the whole life of the thing. A "bike for sale" is not a good subclass. It stops being for sale when somebody buys it.

Pattern 3: Object property

shop:placedBy a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:domain shop:Order ; rdfs:range shop:Person .
shop:o12 shop:placedBy shop:lea .

Purpose: link one thing to another thing. Note: name it with a verb and read it as a sentence. "Order 12 is placed by Lea." Remember that the domain and the range add types. They do not check data.

Pattern 4: Data property

shop:orderDate a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain shop:Order ; rdfs:range xsd:date .
shop:o12 shop:orderDate "2026-11-03"^^xsd:date .

Purpose: give a thing a plain value, like a date or a number. Note: always write the datatype. Without ^^xsd:date, the value is only text. Then a query cannot sort the orders by date.

Pattern 4 is wrong for things with their own facts. A colour name like "red" looks like a value. But if you need a list of allowed colours, use pattern 10.

Links between things: patterns 5, 6 and 13

These patterns say more about the links themselves. Look at an example first.

  1. The data says: order 12 is placed by Lea.
  2. Pattern 5 says places is the reverse of placed by. So the reasoner adds: Lea places order 12.
  3. The data says: spoke 12 is part of the front wheel. The front wheel is part of B7.
  4. Pattern 6 says part of is transitive. So the reasoner adds: spoke 12 is part of B7.

Pattern 5: Inverse

shop:places owl:inverseOf shop:placedBy .
# from "o12 placedBy lea" a reasoner adds "lea places o12"

Purpose: read one link in both directions. Note: store only one direction in the data. Let the reasoner or the query make the other one. If people type both, sooner or later one side is missing.

Pattern 6: Part-whole

shop:partOf  a owl:ObjectProperty , owl:TransitiveProperty .
shop:hasPart owl:inverseOf shop:partOf .
shop:spoke12     shop:partOf shop:frontWheel7 .
shop:frontWheel7 shop:partOf shop:b7 .

Purpose: link a part to its whole, so chains of parts work. Note: a part is not a kind. A wheel is not a bike, so never write shop:Wheel rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike.

The W3C note on part-whole links adds one more idea. Sometimes you want only the next level, like the parts of a wheel but not the parts of those parts. Then make a second property, directPartOf. Make it a subproperty of partOf, but not transitive.

Pattern 13: Identity link

shop:lea owl:sameAs crm:customer-881 .   # one person, two systems
shop:Bike skos:exactMatch wd:Q11442 .    # Wikidata item "bicycle"

Purpose: say that two names point to the same thing. The shop system calls her shop:lea. The customer system calls her crm:customer-881. Note: owl:sameAs copies every fact from one name to the other. Use it only for "exactly the same individual". For mapping concepts between vocabularies, use the SKOS links skos:exactMatch or skos:closeMatch.

A team links its node for the city of Paris to a node for a Paris football club with owl:sameAs. Now the club has a population, and the city has a stadium. Identity links must be checked by a person.

Context: patterns 7, 8 and 9

A plain triple has no room for "when", "in which role" or "how much". These three patterns make that room. They all use the same trick. You turn a link into a node.

Pattern 7: Role

shop:lea-customer a shop:CustomerRole ;
    shop:playedBy shop:lea ;
    shop:customerNumber "C-0881" ;
    shop:since "2025-04-01"^^xsd:date .
shop:lea-staff a shop:EmployeeRole ;
    shop:playedBy shop:lea ;
    shop:since "2026-09-01"^^xsd:date .

Purpose: let a person play roles that start, end and have their own data. Lea is a customer and, since September, also a worker. Note: Customer is not a kind of person for life. So the simple model shop:Customer rdfs:subClassOf shop:Person breaks when roles change or need data. Pattern libraries call this the agent role pattern.

Pattern 8: Event with time

shop:Repair rdfs:subClassOf prov:Activity .
shop:repair31 a shop:Repair ;
    shop:onBike shop:b7 ;
    shop:doneBy shop:mia ;
    prov:startedAtTime "2026-11-10T09:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime ;
    prov:endedAtTime   "2026-11-10T10:30:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .

Purpose: record something that happens, with who, what and when. Note: always write a time zone. The Z at the end means UTC. Without it, 09:00 in Tokyo and 09:00 in Berlin look the same.

The model reuses two properties from PROV-O, a W3C standard from 2013. For harder time questions, use OWL-Time. It has instants, intervals and words like "before" and "during". Its property time:inXSDDateTimeStamp requires a time zone.

Pattern 9: N-ary relation

shop:rating5 a shop:Rating ;
    shop:ratedBy   shop:lea ;
    shop:ratedItem shop:b7 ;
    shop:stars     4 ;
    shop:ratedOn   "2026-11-12"^^xsd:date .

Purpose: hold a relation with three or more parts. An n-ary relation is the general case. Roles and events are two common kinds of it. Note: give the node a class, like shop:Rating, and a name. The W3C note on n-ary relations calls this pattern 1: a new class for the relation.

Named node or blank node? The W3C note gives a simple test. Can two different ratings have exactly the same parts? Then each needs its own name. Lea can rate B7 with four stars twice, on two days.

Do not use old RDF reification (rdf:Statement, rdf:subject) for an n-ary relation. It talks about a statement, not about a rating in the world. The W3C note says the same.

Values: patterns 10, 11 and 14

Values look easy. But three kinds of values cause trouble again and again: fixed lists, numbers with units and ordered lists.

Pattern 10: Value set

shop:Colour a owl:Class ;
    owl:equivalentClass [ owl:oneOf ( shop:red shop:blue shop:black ) ] .
[] a owl:AllDifferent ;
    owl:distinctMembers ( shop:red shop:blue shop:black ) .
shop:b7 shop:colour shop:red .

Purpose: allow only a short, fixed list of values. Note: owl:oneOf closes the list. But OWL has no unique names. So also say that the values are all different. Otherwise red and blue could be one colour.

A W3C note from 2005 shows a second way. Each value is a subclass, like RedThing. Both ways work. The note gives one firm rule: pick one way and do not mix them in one ontology. For lists that people edit often, like product categories, many teams use a SKOS concept scheme instead.

Pattern 11: Quantity with unit

shop:b7 shop:weight [
    a qudt:QuantityValue ;
    qudt:value   14.2 ;
    qudt:hasUnit unit:KiloGM ] .

Purpose: store a number together with its unit. Note: a bare number is a trap. Is 14.2 in kilograms or pounds? Put the unit in the data. Here we use QUDT, a big open set of units. unit:KiloGM is its IRI for the kilogram.

We checked these names in the QUDT schema, version 3.5.3, in November 2026. Older QUDT examples on the web use qudt:numericValue and qudt:unit. Web pages often use schema.org instead: a schema:QuantitativeValue with schema:value and schema:unitCode.

A cheap version also works: shop:weightKg 14.2. The unit sits in the property name. It is fine for one app. It is weak for joining data, because a machine cannot read units from names.

Pattern 14: List and order

shop:assembly shop:hasStep shop:s1 , shop:s2 , shop:s3 .
shop:s1 shop:position 1 ; rdfs:label "Fit the wheels" .
shop:s2 shop:position 2 ; rdfs:label "Adjust the brakes" .
shop:s3 shop:position 3 ; rdfs:label "Test ride" .
shop:assembly shop:steps ( shop:s1 shop:s2 shop:s3 ) .

Purpose: keep things in a fixed order. Note: the triples of a graph have no order. You must write the order into the data.

The second tab is short. Turtle turns ( ... ) into a chain of rdf:first and rdf:rest links. But such lists are hard to query. They also take an OWL ontology outside OWL 2 DL. That is the part of OWL that reasoners can fully handle. The n-ary note uses its own ordering property for this reason. The first tab is longer, but ORDER BY ?pos just works.

Trust and change: patterns 12 and 15

Data comes from somewhere, and ontologies change. These two patterns record both facts.

Pattern 12: Provenance

The supplier says that B7 weighs 14.2 kg. Mia weighed it and wrote 14.6 kg. Both facts are useful, but you must know who said what. Provenance is that record. The common way puts facts into a named graph. Then you describe the graph.

shop:supplierData {
    shop:b7 shop:weightKg 14.2 .
}
shop:mia-scale {
    shop:b7 shop:weightKg 14.6 .
}
shop:supplierData prov:wasAttributedTo shop:velocorp ;
    prov:generatedAtTime "2026-10-01T08:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .
shop:mia-scale prov:wasAttributedTo shop:mia .

Purpose: say who said a fact and when. Note: one named graph holds many facts from one source. That is cheap and fast. Do not make one named graph for every single triple.

What if you really need a note on one triple? RDF 1.2 adds that. A triple can be the object of another triple, called a triple term. Turtle 1.2 has a short form for it.

PREFIX shop: <http://example.org/shop#>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>

shop:b7 shop:weightKg 14.2 ~ shop:claim1 {| prov:wasAttributedTo shop:velocorp |} .

The part after ~ names the claim. The part in {| |} describes it. We loaded this file with pyoxigraph 0.5.13. It gave three triples, one of them with rdf:reifies and a triple term.

RDF 1.2 is not a final standard yet. On 15 November 2026 the W3C page for RDF 1.2 Concepts is a Candidate Recommendation Draft. The Turtle 1.2 page is a Working Draft. Many tools cannot read the new syntax. Check the W3C pages: this can change.

Pattern 15: Versioning

<http://example.org/shop> a owl:Ontology ;
    owl:versionIRI  <http://example.org/shop/1.2.0> ;
    owl:versionInfo "1.2.0" ;
    owl:priorVersion <http://example.org/shop/1.1.0> .

shop:Cycle a owl:Class ;
    owl:deprecated true ;              # do not use any more
    dcterms:isReplacedBy shop:Bike .   # use this instead

Purpose: say which version this is and what changed. Note: never delete a term that others use. Old data still points to it. Mark it as deprecated and point to the new term.

The ontology IRI stays the same in every version. The version IRI changes with each release. Tools can load "the latest" or "exactly 1.1.0".

Use version numbers with three parts, like 1.2.0. Change the first number when old data breaks. Change the second for new terms. Change the third for fixes in labels and comments.

All 15 cards

Here are the 15 patterns as cards. Each card is one move. Swipe through them to review.

Class and instance

Put one thing into a kind.

shop:b7 a shop:CityBike .

Use a, not subClassOf.

Subclass

Put a kind under a wider kind.

shop:CityBike rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike .

Only for kinds that last for life.

Object property

Link two things.

shop:o12 shop:placedBy shop:lea .

Domain and range add types. They do not check.

Data property

Give a thing a plain value.

shop:o12 shop:orderDate "2026-11-03"^^xsd:date .

Always write the datatype.

Inverse

Read a link both ways.

shop:places owl:inverseOf shop:placedBy .

Store one direction only.

Part-whole

Link a part to its whole.

shop:partOf a owl:TransitiveProperty .

A part is not a kind.

Role

A person plays a role with its own data.

shop:lea-customer shop:playedBy shop:lea .

A role is not a subclass for life.

Event with time

Record what happened and when.
