shop:repair31 prov:startedAtTime "2026-11-10T09:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .

Always add a time zone.

N-ary relation

A relation with three or more parts.

shop:rating5 shop:ratedBy shop:lea ; shop:stars 4 .

Give the node a class and a name.

Value set

Allow only a fixed list.

shop:Colour owl:equivalentClass [ owl:oneOf ( shop:red shop:blue ) ] .

Also say the values are all different.

Quantity with unit

A number and its unit together.

[] qudt:value 14.2 ; qudt:hasUnit unit:KiloGM .

A bare number is a trap.

Provenance

Who said it, and when.

shop:supplierData prov:wasAttributedTo shop:velocorp .

One named graph per source, not per triple.

Identity link

Two names, one thing.

shop:lea owl:sameAs crm:customer-881 .

Never use sameAs for "similar".

List and order

Keep a fixed order.

shop:s2 shop:position 2 .

Triples have no order. Write it into the data.

Versioning

Name the version, deprecate old terms.

shop:Cycle owl:deprecated true .

Never delete a used term.

Test the patterns with Python

Patterns are only useful if they work. We put all the Turtle models from this chapter into one file, patterns.ttl. The provenance model went into provenance.trig. Then we ran the RDFS and OWL RL rules and asked four questions.

from rdflib import Graph, Dataset, Namespace
import owlrl

SHOP = Namespace("http://example.org/shop#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("patterns.ttl")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)

# patterns 5 and 6: facts that nobody typed
print("lea places o12:", (SHOP.lea, SHOP.places, SHOP.o12) in g)
print("spoke12 part of b7:", (SHOP.spoke12, SHOP.partOf, SHOP.b7) in g)

# pattern 14: steps in order
q = """PREFIX shop: <http://example.org/shop#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?label WHERE { shop:assembly shop:hasStep ?s .
  ?s shop:position ?pos ; rdfs:label ?label } ORDER BY ?pos"""
print("steps:", [str(r.label) for r in g.query(q)])

# pattern 12: who said what?
ds = Dataset()
ds.parse("provenance.trig", format="trig")
q = """PREFIX shop: <http://example.org/shop#>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
SELECT ?kg ?who WHERE { GRAPH ?g { shop:b7 shop:weightKg ?kg }
  ?g prov:wasAttributedTo ?who } ORDER BY ?kg"""
for r in ds.query(q):
    print("b7 weighs", r.kg, "kg according to", r.who.split("#")[1])
lea places o12: True
spoke12 part of b7: True
steps: ['Fit the wheels', 'Adjust the brakes', 'Test ride']
b7 weighs 14.2 kg according to velocorp
b7 weighs 14.6 kg according to mia

We used Python 3.14 with rdflib 7.6.0 and owlrl 7.6.2. All four answers match what the patterns promise. Two facts came from rules. The order came from the position values. The sources came from the named graphs.

In the TriG file, the triples about the graphs sit outside any named graph. They are in the default graph. So the query finds them outside the GRAPH block.

Choose the right pattern

When you meet a modelling problem, ask the questions in this table. The first "yes" points to a pattern.

From a question to a pattern
Your questionPattern
Does the link need a date, a score or a third thing?9 N-ary relation
Is it something that happened at a time?8 Event with time
Does a person get this label only for a while?7 Role
Is the value from a short, fixed list?10 Value set
Is it a measured number?11 Quantity with unit
Does the order matter?14 List and order
Do two sources disagree?12 Provenance
Do two systems name the same thing?13 Identity link
Is it a piece of a bigger thing?6 Part-whole
Will other teams use your terms?15 Versioning

Patterns also combine. A repair (pattern 8) can have a mechanic in a role (pattern 7). It can have a cost with a unit (pattern 11). It can come from a source system (pattern 12). Real models are made from many small patterns.

Exam tasks often hide an n-ary relation in a sentence. Look for a link with extra words like "on", "for", "since" or "with". "Ada taught Logic in 2025 to 40 students" needs a node for the teaching.

Do not turn every link into a node "just in case". The graph gets three times bigger, and queries get longer. Start with a plain link. Turn it into a node when a real question needs the extra parts.

Patterns to remember

The 15 modelling patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
1 Class and instancePut one thing into a kindshop:b7 a shop:CityBike .Use a for instances, never subClassOf.
2 SubclassPut a kind under a wider kindshop:CityBike rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike .Only for kinds that last for the whole life.
3 Object propertyLink two thingsshop:o12 shop:placedBy shop:lea .Domain and range add types. They do not check.
4 Data propertyGive a thing a plain valueshop:o12 shop:orderDate "2026-11-03"^^xsd:date .Always write the datatype.
5 InverseRead one link both waysshop:places owl:inverseOf shop:placedBy .Store one direction. Let rules add the other.
6 Part-wholeLink parts to wholes in chainsshop:partOf a owl:TransitiveProperty .A part is not a kind. Members are not parts.
7 RoleA role with its own data and timeshop:lea-customer shop:playedBy shop:lea .Roles change. Do not make them subclasses for life.
8 Event with timeRecord what happened and whenprov:startedAtTime "2026-11-10T09:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTimeAlways write a time zone.
9 N-ary relationA relation with three or more partsshop:rating5 shop:ratedBy shop:lea ; shop:stars 4 .Give the node a class. Do not use old reification.
10 Value setAllow only a fixed listowl:oneOf ( shop:red shop:blue shop:black )Add AllDifferent. Do not mix with value classes.
11 Quantity with unitKeep a number with its unit[] qudt:value 14.2 ; qudt:hasUnit unit:KiloGM .A bare number is a trap.
12 ProvenanceSay who said it and whenshop:supplierData prov:wasAttributedTo shop:velocorp .One named graph per source. RDF 1.2 is still a draft.
13 Identity linkJoin two names for one thingshop:lea owl:sameAs crm:customer-881 .sameAs copies all facts. Use SKOS for "close".
14 List and orderKeep a fixed ordershop:s2 shop:position 2 .Triples have no order. RDF lists are hard to query.
15 VersioningName versions and retire termsshop:Cycle owl:deprecated true .Never delete a term that others use.

Practice

"Sam worked at the shop as a mechanic from 2024 to 2026." Which pattern fits best?

  • Subclass: Mechanic under Person
  • Role, with a start and an end date
  • Value set

The role has its own time. A subclass would make Sam a mechanic for life.

A file says shop:b9 shop:length 180 . What is the main problem?

  • The number is too big.
  • Nobody knows the unit.
  • A length must be text.

180 centimetres and 180 millimetres are very different. Use pattern 11.

Which pattern keeps the steps of a repair in order and stays easy to query?

  • An RDF list with ( ... )
  • A position number on each step
  • The order of the lines in the file

Triples have no order. A position number works with ORDER BY.

Two systems call one customer by two IRIs. Which link joins them?

  • rdfs:subClassOf
  • skos:closeMatch
  • owl:sameAs

It is exactly the same individual. closeMatch is for similar concepts.

Fill in the missing words.

A relation between three or more things is an ?.

To retire a term, set owl:<span class="blank" data-answer="deprecated">?</span> true.

A set of triples with its own name is a ?.

  1. Name the pattern for each sentence. (a) A wheel belongs to B7. (b) B7 is red. (c) The price list comes from the supplier.
    Answer

    (a) Part-whole, pattern 6. (b) Value set, pattern 10. (c) Provenance, pattern 12.

  2. Write Turtle for "Lea rented B7 from 1 to 3 December 2026 for 45 euros." Use patterns 8, 9 and 11.
    Answer

    One possible model: shop:rental7 a shop:Rental ; shop:renter shop:lea ; shop:rentedItem shop:b7 ; prov:startedAtTime "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime ; prov:endedAtTime "2026-12-03T23:59:59Z"^^xsd:dateTime ; shop:price [ a qudt:QuantityValue ; qudt:value 45 ; qudt:hasUnit unit:CCY_EUR ] . QUDT names the euro unit:CCY_EUR. Some teams store money with schema.org instead.

  3. A teammate writes shop:Customer rdfs:subClassOf shop:Person . and shop:lea a shop:Customer . Lea starts to work at the shop. What problems can follow, and how does pattern 7 help?
    Answer

    Lea must now be a customer and a worker at once. If someone adds "Customer and Employee are disjoint", the data clashes. There is also no place for "customer since" or a customer number per role. With pattern 7, Lea plays two role nodes. Each role has its own dates and data.

  4. Your ontology renames shop:Cycle to shop:Bike in version 2.0.0. Write the Turtle that keeps old data working.
    Answer

    shop:Cycle owl:deprecated true ; dcterms:isReplacedBy shop:Bike ; owl:equivalentClass shop:Bike . The equivalent class axiom lets a reasoner treat old data as bikes. Also change owl:versionIRI and add owl:priorVersion.

  5. Explain why owl:oneOf alone does not stop "red" and "blue" from being one colour.
    Answer

    OWL has no unique name assumption. Two names can point to one thing. oneOf says the class has at most these members. It does not say they are different. Add owl:AllDifferent to make three distinct colours.

Key takeaways

  • A pattern is a tested answer to a modelling problem that comes back.
  • The 15 patterns fall into five groups: things and kinds, links, context, values, trust and change.
  • Roles, events and n-ary relations use one trick: turn the link into a node.
  • Values need care: close value sets, keep units with numbers, write order into the data.
  • Named graphs record who said what. RDF 1.2 triple terms are still a draft in 2026.
  • Never delete a used term. Deprecate it and point to its replacement.

Sources

  • Defining N-ary Relations on the Semantic Web. W3C note (2006) with the new-class pattern and the ordered list pattern.
  • Representing Specified Values in OWL. W3C note (2005) on value sets and value partitions.
  • Simple part-whole relations in OWL ontologies. W3C draft note on part-of and direct parts.
  • PROV-O: The PROV Ontology. W3C Recommendation (2013) for provenance and activities.
  • RDF 1.2 Turtle. The W3C draft with triple terms and the annotation syntax.
  • GeoLink Agent Role pattern. A published role pattern with start and end times.

Ancient and medieval roots

People asked "what kinds of things are there?" long before computers. Greek, Indian and Islamic thinkers made the first lists of kinds. Medieval teachers drew the first class trees. Many ideas in OWL and knowledge graphs start here.

  • Name Aristotle's ten categories and give an example of each.
  • Tell a substance from an accident, and a genus from a species.
  • Draw Porphyry's tree and read a definition from it.
  • Explain the medieval fight about universals in three positions.
  • Connect Llull, the Vaisheshika school and Avicenna to modern tools.

The first question: what is there?

Look at a river. Today the water is high. Tomorrow it is low. Is it the same river? Or a new one each day?

Questions like this started Greek philosophy. One of the first thinkers to answer them with pure argument was Parmenides. He lived in Elea, a Greek town in southern Italy. He wrote one poem. Only parts of it survive.

His main idea is simple and strange. "What is, is. What is not, is not." Nothing can come from nothing. So, for Parmenides, real being cannot start, end or change. Change is only how things look to us.

We do not know when Parmenides was born. An old Greek source counts back from his "best years" and gives about 540 BC. Plato's dialogue Parmenides suggests about 515 BC. Scholars still argue about which source is better. Both put his work in the early 400s BC.

Why does a computer scientist care? Parmenides asked the first ontology question. What exists? Every data model must answer it too. Your database has a table for customers. So, for the database, customers exist.

Do not read old texts as early software manuals. Parmenides did not plan a database. We only borrow his question. The answers belong to his time.

Plato: the forms and their copies

Think of all the round things you know. A coin, a wheel, a plate. None of them is perfectly round. But you still know what "round" means. Where does this idea come from?

Plato lived in Athens, from about 428 to about 348 BC. His answer was the Forms. A Form is a perfect pattern. It does not change and you cannot touch it. Real things are imperfect copies of the Forms.

  • Many beautiful things share one Form: Beauty.
  • Many round things share one Form: Roundness.
  • The things change and break. The Forms stay the same.

In the dialogue Phaedrus, Plato gives advice for good thinking. Divide things into kinds at their natural joints. Do not break the parts like a bad butcher. Ontology engineers still like this picture. A good class tree cuts the world where it really divides.

For Plato there are two worlds. One world has the many changing things. The other world has the one perfect pattern for each kind.

Plato's birth year is not certain. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives 429 BC with a question mark. Other books give 428 or 427 BC. He died in 348 or 347 BC.

A Form is not a thought in someone's head. For Plato, Forms are more real than the things we see. This is the opposite of what many people expect.

Aristotle's ten categories

Here is a short story. Read it and count the kinds of information.

Lea is a human. She is 170 cm tall and clever. She is taller than Ben. She is in the office on Monday morning. She is sitting and wears boots. She writes code, and she is being watched by her cat.

One sentence about one person holds ten kinds of information. Aristotle (384 to 322 BC) noticed this. He studied with Plato for about twenty years. Then he made his own system. His short book Categories sorts everything we can say into ten top kinds. We call them categories.

The ten categories with the story about Lea
CategoryQuestion it answersIn the story
SubstanceWhat is it?a human
QuantityHow much? How big?170 cm tall
QualityWhat is it like?clever
RelationCompared with what?taller than Ben
PlaceWhere?in the office
TimeWhen?on Monday morning
PositionIn what posture?sitting
HavingWhat does it have on?wears boots
ActingWhat does it do?writes code
Being affectedWhat is done to it?is being watched

Aristotle gave his own classic examples, like "in the market place" and "yesterday". The list sits in chapter 4 of the Categories. He says the list covers everything, but he does not prove it. Much later, Immanuel Kant criticised it for this reason. You meet Kant in From Leibniz to modern logic.

Substance and accident

Look at the table again. One row is special. Lea is a human all her life. But she is not always sitting or in the office.

A substance exists on its own. An accident exists only in a substance. "Clever" cannot float around alone. It is always the cleverness of someone. The other nine categories are kinds of accidents.

Aristotle also split substance in two. A primary substance is one single thing, like this horse. A secondary substance is a kind, like "horse" or "human". You can say the kind of many things. You cannot say Lea of anything else.

This is the same split as individual and class. Lea is an individual. Human is a class. "Lea is a human" is the instance-of link of The building blocks.

Did Aristotle write the Categories? Most scholars say yes, and they think it is an early work. But some doubt it, and the title probably comes from later editors. The Stanford Encyclopedia lists both points as open questions.

Do not model an accident as a class of things. "Sitting" is not a kind of person. Lea sits now and stands later. In a data model, this is a changing property or an event with a time.

Genus, species and the syllogism

How do you define "human"? Aristotle's method has two parts. First, name the wider kind. Then name what makes this kind special.

  • The wider kind is the genus. For a human, it is "animal".
  • The special feature is the difference. For a human, it is "rational", or able to think.
  • Together they give the species. A human is a rational animal.

This old recipe is still alive in OWL. The class Human equals the class of things that are both an Animal and a RationalThing.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

ex:Animal        a owl:Class .                 # the genus (the wider kind)
ex:RationalThing a owl:Class .                 # the difference

ex:Human a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "human" ;
    owl:equivalentClass [                      # human = animal AND rational
        a owl:Class ;
        owl:intersectionOf ( ex:Animal ex:RationalThing )
    ] .

ex:socrates a ex:Human .                       # one individual

Nobody typed "Socrates is an animal". A reasoner finds it. Here we run the OWL RL rules from the Python package owlrl.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF
from owlrl import DeductiveClosure, OWLRL_Semantics

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/")
g = Graph()
g.parse("genus.ttl", format="turtle")

print("before:", (EX.socrates, RDF.type, EX.Animal) in g)
DeductiveClosure(OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)   # run the OWL RL rules
print("after: ", (EX.socrates, RDF.type, EX.Animal) in g)
before: False
after:  True

The syllogism: the first reasoning rule

Aristotle also made the first system of logic. Its unit is the syllogism. Here is the most famous form.

  1. Every animal is a living body.
  2. Every human is an animal.
  3. So every human is a living body. This line must be true when the first two are true.

Medieval teachers gave each valid form a name to help memory. This form is called Barbara. The three letters "a" stand for three "every" sentences. Today we call this rule transitivity. A reasoner uses it on every rdfs:subClassOf chain.

Here is Barbara as a tiny program. It repeats the rule until no new fact appears.

# Each pair means: every A is a B.
every = {
    ("human", "animal"),
    ("animal", "living body"),
    ("living body", "body"),
}

def barbara(pairs):
    """Every A is B. Every B is C. So every A is C."""
    facts = set(pairs)
    while True:
        new = {(a, c) for (a, b) in facts for (b2, c) in facts if b == b2}
        if new <= facts:          # nothing new: stop
            return facts
        facts |= new

for a, c in sorted(barbara(every) - every):
    print(f"every {a} is a {c}")
use std::collections::BTreeSet;

type Pair = (&'static str, &'static str); // (A, B): every A is a B

// Every A is B. Every B is C. So every A is C.
fn barbara(start: &BTreeSet<Pair>) -> BTreeSet<Pair> {
    let mut facts = start.clone();
    loop {
        let mut new: BTreeSet<Pair> = BTreeSet::new();
        for &(a, b) in &facts {
            for &(b2, c) in &facts {
                if b == b2 && !facts.contains(&(a, c)) {
                    new.insert((a, c));
                }
            }
        }
        if new.is_empty() {
            return facts; // nothing new: stop
        }
        facts.extend(new);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let every: BTreeSet<Pair> = BTreeSet::from([
        ("human", "animal"),
        ("animal", "living body"),
        ("living body", "body"),
    ]);
    for (a, c) in barbara(&every).difference(&every) {
        println!("every {a} is a {c}");
    }
}
every animal is a body
every human is a body
every human is a living body

This loop is a small forward-chaining reasoner. You build a full one in Build a reasoner.

"Every A is B" does not mean "every B is A". Every human is an animal. But not every animal is a human. Many students flip the arrow of rdfs:subClassOf in the same way.

Porphyry's tree

Porphyry was a Greek philosopher. He lived from about 234 to about 305 AD. He wrote a short book called the Isagoge, which means "Introduction". For more than a thousand years, students read it before Aristotle's logic.

The book explains five ways to say something about a thing. Later writers called them the five predicables.

The five predicables with a human as the example
PredicableMeaningExample
Genusthe wider kindanimal
Speciesthe kind itselfhuman
Differencewhat separates it in its genusrational
Propertya feature that only this kind has, alwaysable to laugh
Accidenta feature that can come and gositting

Porphyry also walked down from the top kind, step by step. At each step one difference splits a genus in two. Follow the steps.

Substance

Start at the top. Split substance by one difference: with a body or without a body.

Body

Take the bodies. Split them: living or not living. A stone is a body that does not live.

Living body

Split living bodies: they can sense, or they cannot. A tree lives but does not sense.

Animal

An animal is a living body that senses. Split animals: rational or not rational.

Human

A human is a rational animal. Below the human there are no more kinds. There are only single people, like Socrates and Plato.

Read a definition straight from the tree. Go up from "Human" and collect the differences. A human is a substance with a body, alive, able to sense and rational.

This tree is one of the oldest pictures of a taxonomy. It has the same shape as a class tree in Protégé.

Porphyry did not draw a tree. He wrote the steps in words. The name "Porphyry's tree" and the picture came from later teachers. The Latin translation by Boethius made the book standard in medieval Europe.

Socrates is not a subclass of Human. He is an instance. The last line of the tree changes the link from "is a kind of" to "is a member of". Mixing these two links is a classic modelling error.

The medieval fight about universals

At the start of the Isagoge, Porphyry asks three questions. Then he refuses to answer them. They are too deep for beginners, he says.

  1. Do genera and species really exist, or are they only in our thoughts?
  2. If they exist, do they have a body or not?
  3. Do they exist apart from things, or only in things?

"Human" and "animal" are universals. Many single things share them. For about a thousand years, teachers in Europe argued about Porphyry's questions. This is the problem of universals.

Boethius translated the Isagoge into Latin. He wrote two commentaries on it. He was born around 475 to 480 and died in 524 or 526. Sources differ. His answer was careful. Universals exist in the mind, and the mind takes them from real things.

Three answers to Porphyry's first question
PositionMain claimWhoA modern echo
RealismUniversals are real things. "Humanity" is in every human.William of Champeaux, Abelard's teacherA class names a real kind in the world.
Moderate realismA common nature is in the things. The mind makes it universal.Thomas Aquinas (about 1225 to 1274)Classes come from real features of things.
NominalismOnly single things exist. Universals are words or concepts.William of Ockham (about 1287 to 1347)A class is just a set of instances we chose.

Peter Abelard (1079 to 1142) sits between the camps. He attacked his teacher's realism. For Abelard only words are universal. But words still have a real basis. Two humans share the "state" of being human, even if this state is not a thing.

Ockham and his razor

Ockham was an English friar. He said there is no thing called "felinity". There are only single cats, and they are alike. The word "cat" is a concept in the mind. It is universal only because it applies to many cats.

His name is on a famous rule, Ockham's razor. Do not add more things to a theory than you need. Ockham used this idea often. But the short form "entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity" is not in his books. Later writers made that sentence.

The razor is good advice for modellers. Do not add a class like RedCar when a property color does the job. Every class costs time to define, test and explain.

Modern ontologists still disagree. The team behind BFO, an upper ontology, says classes should stand for real kinds in the world. Others say an ontology describes the concepts of a community. See Formal ontology and upper ontologies.

Nominalism is not "nothing is real". Nominalists believe in real single things. They doubt only that kinds are extra things.

Ramon Llull's turning wheels

Imagine three paper rings on one pin. Each ring has nine letters. You turn the inner rings and read one column. Now you have a new combination of three ideas. Turn again, and you have the next one.

Ramon Llull lived on Majorca, from 1232 (perhaps 1233) to 1316. He was a writer and a missionary. He wanted a method to prove his beliefs to anyone, step by step. He called it his Art and rewrote it many times. A short version, the Ars brevis, is from 1308.

Llull used nine letters: B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K. Latin at that time had no separate J. In the first meaning, each letter stands for one divine quality.

The nine letters in their first meaning
BCDEFGHIK
goodnessgreatnessdurationpowerwisdomwillvirtuetruthglory

How many different groups of three letters are there? A computer counts them in a moment.

from itertools import combinations

letters = "BCDEFGHIK"            # Llull's nine letters (no J)

pairs = list(combinations(letters, 2))
triples = list(combinations(letters, 3))

print(len(pairs), "pairs, first:", "".join(pairs[0]))
print(len(triples), "triples, first:", "".join(triples[0]))
print(len(triples) * 20, "cells in the big table")
fn main() {
    let letters: Vec<char> = "BCDEFGHIK".chars().collect(); // nine letters, no J
    let n = letters.len();

    let mut pairs: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    let mut triples: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..n {
        for j in (i + 1)..n {
            pairs.push(format!("{}{}", letters[i], letters[j]));
            for k in (j + 1)..n {
                triples.push(format!("{}{}{}", letters[i], letters[j], letters[k]));
            }
        }
    }

    println!("{} pairs, first: {}", pairs.len(), pairs[0]);
    println!("{} triples, first: {}", triples.len(), triples[0]);
    println!("{} cells in the big table", triples.len() * 20);
}
36 pairs, first: BC
84 triples, first: BCD
1680 cells in the big table

The numbers match Llull's own work. His Third Figure has 36 boxes, one for each pair. The large table in his Ars generalis ultima has 84 columns with 20 cells each. That makes 1,680 cells. The short Ars brevis prints only seven columns and leaves the rest to the reader.

Llull's idea was new. Thinking can be a mechanical process: combine a fixed set of basic ideas by rules. About 350 years later, Leibniz took this idea further. His plan for a calculus of thought is in the next chapter.

Sources differ on the details of the Fourth Figure. One translation of the Ars brevis says the outer ring is fixed and the two inner rings turn. Some later descriptions say all three rings move. Llull's death date is also unclear. We only know he died in 1316, after March.

Llull's wheels did not compute answers like a computer. They produced combinations. A person still had to read each one and build an argument from it.

Beyond Greece and Europe

Greece was not the only place with category lists. Two other traditions matter for our story.

India: the Vaisheshika categories

The Vaisheshika school is one of the classic schools of Indian philosophy. Its founding text is the Vaisheshika Sutra. Tradition names its author Kanada. The school sorts all that exists into six categories.

The six Vaisheshika categories (padartha)
SanskritEnglishExample
dravyasubstancea pot of clay
gunaqualitythe red colour of the pot
karmamotion, actionthe pot falls
samanyauniversalpot-ness, shared by all pots
visheshaparticularitywhat makes one atom differ from another
samavayainherencethe tie between the red and the pot

The school counts nine substances: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self and mind. The first four are made of atoms. Later writers added a seventh category: absence. "There is no pot on the table" names a real absence.

Two ideas look very modern. Inherence is a named relation. It ties a quality to its substance and a universal to its members. That is close to the instance-of link. Absence is a first step toward thinking about negative facts.

Kanada's dates are very uncertain. The Stanford Encyclopedia puts him in the 2nd century BC. Other scholars give dates centuries earlier. The great commentator Prashastapada is put in the 5th or the 6th century AD. Sources also differ on who first added "absence".

The Islamic world: Avicenna

Avicenna, in Arabic Ibn Sina, was a Persian doctor and philosopher. He was born near Bukhara and died in 1037. His huge book The Cure (Kitab al-Shifa) has a part on metaphysics. For him metaphysics studies being as being.

His most famous idea is a split. A thing's essence is what it is. Its existence is the fact that it is there. You can know what a unicorn is. That does not tell you that unicorns exist. He also said that horseness, taken in itself, is just horseness. It is neither one nor many.

His metaphysics reached Europe in Latin. Scholars in Toledo translated it in the second half of the 1100s. Thomas Aquinas and many others built on it.

Avicenna's split works like a good ontology file. A class definition says what a thing is. It does not say that any instances exist. In OWL you can define Unicorn and leave it empty. Schema and data are separate, just like essence and existence.

Avicenna's birth year is uncertain. Many books say 980. The Stanford Encyclopedia says about 970, perhaps as early as 964. His death in 1037 is not in doubt.

Do not tell this history as "Greece, then Europe" only. Ideas travelled from Greek into Arabic and then into Latin. Indian thinkers built their own system with no Greek help.

The long story on one line

Here are the main dates of this chapter. Dates with "about" are not certain.

  1. c. 500 BC Parmenides. Asks what being is. He is active in the early 400s BC.
  2. c. 428-348 BC Plato. Forms as perfect patterns. Cut nature at its joints.
  3. 384-322 BC Aristotle. Ten categories, substance and accident, genus and species, the syllogism.
  4. c. 2nd c. BC? Kanada. The Vaisheshika categories. The date is much debated.
  5. c. 234-305 Porphyry. The Isagoge, five predicables and three questions about universals.
  6. c. 480-525 Boethius. Latin translation of the Isagoge, with two commentaries. Exact years differ by source.
  7. c. 970-1037 Avicenna. Essence and existence in The Cure.
  8. 1079-1142 Peter Abelard. Attacks realism. Universals are words with a real basis.
  9. c. 1225-1274 Thomas Aquinas. A common nature in things, made universal by the mind.
  10. 1308 Ramon Llull, Ars brevis. Turning wheels combine nine basic ideas.
  11. c. 1287-1347 William of Ockham. Only single things exist. The razor.
What did each thinker give to modern tools?

Aristotle gave classes, individuals and properties. Porphyry gave the class tree. The syllogism gave the first reasoning rule. Llull gave the idea of mechanical combination. Avicenna gave the split between schema and data.

Why are so many dates uncertain?

Most old books survive only as later copies. Birth records did not exist. Historians count back from known events, and different sources give different events.

Where does the word "ontology" come from?

Not from this period. The Latin word ontologia first appears in 1606. You read that story in the next chapter.

Patterns to remember

These old ideas became reusable modelling moves. Each row joins an old idea to a modern model.

Old ideas as modelling patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
X is a C (substance)Say what a single thing isex:lea a ex:Human .The type stays while the thing exists.
X has feature F (accident)Record a feature that can changeLea is sitting now.Use a property or an event, not a class.
Species = genus + differenceDefine a class exactlyHuman = Animal and RationalIn OWL, use owl:intersectionOf.
Every A is B, every B is CFind new class linksHuman, animal, living bodyThe arrow goes one way only.
Split a genus by one differenceBuild a clean class treeBody: living or not livingUse one difference per split.
Kinds above, members belowKeep class and instance apartSocrates is a member of Human.An instance is never a subclass.
Ask for each categoryCheck that a model is completeWhere? When? How much?Missing place or time is a common gap.
Do not add what you do not needKeep the model smallProperty color, no class RedCarOckham's razor. Add a class only for a real need.
Combine a few basic termsGenerate all options to check36 pairs from 9 lettersCombinations grow very fast.
Name the tie itselfMake a relation explicitInherence ties red to the pot.A link is information too.
What it is, not that it isSplit schema from dataDefine Unicorn, add no instance.A class can be empty.

Practice

"Lea is in the office." Which category is "in the office"?

  • Substance
  • Place
  • Position

Place answers "where?". Position answers "in what posture?", like sitting.

Which one is a primary substance?

  • Horse
  • White
  • This horse in the field

A primary substance is one single thing. "Horse" is a kind, so it is a secondary substance. "White" is an accident.

In "a human is a rational animal", what is "animal"?

  • The genus
  • The difference
  • An accident

The genus is the wider kind. "Rational" is the difference.

Who drew the first picture of Porphyry's tree?

  • Porphyry himself
  • Aristotle
  • Later teachers, after Porphyry

Porphyry wrote the steps in words. The picture and the name came later.

"Only single things exist. 'Cat' is a concept that applies to many cats." Which position is this?

  • Realism
  • Nominalism
  • Platonism

This is Ockham's view. Realists say the kind itself is real.

Fill in the missing words.

Aristotle sorted everything we can say into ? categories.

The Barbara syllogism is the rule we now call ?.

Nine letters give ? groups of three letters.

Avicenna split what a thing is (essence) from the fact that it is (?).

  1. Write one sentence about your laptop that uses at least five of the ten categories. Label each part.
    Answer

    One possible answer. "My laptop (substance) is 1.4 kg (quantity) and silver (quality). It is on my desk (place) this evening (time). It is running a build (acting)." Your sentence can be different.

  2. Continue Porphyry's tree for vehicles. Start with "Vehicle" and use one difference per split. Make three levels.
    Answer

    Vehicle splits into "with an engine" and "without an engine". Engine vehicles split into "on land" and "not on land". Land vehicles with engines split into "two wheels" (motorbike) and "four wheels" (car). Each split uses only one difference.

  3. A teammate makes a class SittingPerson under Person. What would Aristotle say? What do you suggest?
    Answer

    Sitting is an accident, in the category of position. It can change in a minute. So it should not be a class of people. Use a property like posture or an event with a start and end time.

  4. The Python Barbara program loops until nothing new appears. Why must it stop on a finite list of pairs?
    Answer

    It only makes pairs of names that are already in the list. With n names there are at most n × n pairs. Each loop adds at least one new pair or stops. So after at most n × n loops it must stop. This is the fixed-point idea of Rules and Datalog.

  5. Explain the problem of universals with a database example. Use the words "class" and "instance".
    Answer

    A table customer has rows for single customers. The rows are instances. The class "Customer" is the universal. A realist says the class names a real kind of thing. A nominalist says the class is only our name for a chosen set of rows. For the software both work the same, but the debate changes how you choose classes.

Key takeaways

  • Parmenides asked the first ontology question: what is there?
  • Plato's Forms are perfect patterns. Real things copy them.
  • Aristotle gave ten categories, substance and accident, genus and species, and the syllogism.
  • Porphyry's steps became the tree picture: the ancestor of every class tree.
  • The fight about universals asks if kinds are real. It is still alive in upper ontologies.
  • Llull combined basic ideas by turning wheels: an early dream of mechanical thought.
  • Vaisheshika named inherence and absence. Avicenna split essence from existence.
  • Many dates here are uncertain. Good history says so.

Sources

  • Aristotle's Categories. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the ten categories, substance and open questions.
  • Porphyry. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the Isagoge, the predicables and the later tree.
  • The Medieval Problem of Universals. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius, Abelard, Aquinas, Ockham.
  • Ramon Llull. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the Art, the nine letters and the figures.
  • Parmenides of Elea. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the poem and the two birth dates.
  • Ibn Sina's Metaphysics. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: essence, existence and the Shifa.

From Leibniz to modern logic

Between 1600 and 1950, ontology got its name and logic got its symbols. Thinkers turned "is a kind of" into numbers, algebra and formulas. Every tool in this book, from OWL to SPARQL, stands on their work.

  • Tell the story of the word "ontology" with the right names and years.
  • Explain Leibniz's dream and test his number code for concepts.
  • Read a Boolean class formula and a predicate logic formula.
  • Explain Russell's paradox and why OWL keeps classes and individuals apart.
  • Say what Husserl, Lesniewski, Carnap, Quine and Tarski gave to modern tools.

A new word: ontologia

Look at an old school book from 1606. Its first pages show a big diagram of all subjects. One box has a new Latin word: ontologia. The book is the Ogdoas scholastica, printed in St. Gallen in Switzerland.

The author was Jacob Lorhard (1561 to 1609). He was a teacher and the head of a school in St. Gallen. For him, ontologia was another name for metaphysics. It studies everything that we can think about.

The word grew slowly after that.

  • 1613. Rudolph Goclenius uses the word in his Lexicon philosophicum. It is only a short note in the margin. He calls it the philosophy of being.
  • 1613. Lorhard's book comes out again in Basel with a new title, Theatrum philosophicum. The word moves from the cover to the inside.
  • 1730. Christian Wolff publishes Philosophia prima, sive Ontologia. This means "First philosophy, or Ontology". Wolff's books were read in many universities. After him, "ontology" was a normal word.

For a long time, many writers said Goclenius made the word in 1613. Later research found Lorhard's book from 1606. Most experts now call Lorhard's book the first known use. An older book could still turn up. So say "the first known use", not "the first use".

The word is new, but the questions are old. Aristotle never used the word "ontology". When we call his work ontology, we use a later name. See Ancient and medieval roots.

Leibniz: a language for thought

Two people argue about a hard question. Imagine they could stop talking and start calculating. The answer would come out like the sum of a bill. Nobody could argue with it.

This was the dream of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716). He was a German philosopher and mathematician. He wanted two things.

  • A universal characteristic: a symbol language for all basic concepts.
  • A calculus ratiocinator: rules to calculate with these symbols.

In several texts he wrote one Latin word for this moment: Calculemus. It means "let us calculate".

The idea started early. In 1666, when he was about 20, he published Dissertatio de arte combinatoria, a study of combinations. He knew Ramon Llull's wheels well. He liked the idea but criticised the details. Llull's basic ideas were too few, and he did not use all combinations.

Concepts as numbers

In papers from 1679, Leibniz tried a clever trick. Give each basic concept a prime number. A complex concept is the product of its parts. He used animal = 2 and rational = 3, so human = 6.

Now "every human is an animal" becomes a small calculation. Does 2 divide 6? Yes. So the sentence is true. Here is the same idea with a few more concepts.

from math import gcd

# Basic concepts get prime numbers (Leibniz's idea, 1679).
living, sensing, rational, green = 2, 3, 5, 7

animal = living * sensing        # 6
human = animal * rational        # 30
plant = living * green           # 14

def every(a, b):
    """Every a is a b, if b's number divides a's number."""
    return a % b == 0

print("every human is an animal:", every(human, animal))
print("every animal is a human: ", every(animal, human))
print("every plant is an animal:", every(plant, animal))
print("shared part of human and plant:", gcd(human, plant))
// Basic concepts get prime numbers (Leibniz's idea, 1679).
const LIVING: u32 = 2;
const SENSING: u32 = 3;
const RATIONAL: u32 = 5;
const GREEN: u32 = 7;

// Every a is a b, if b's number divides a's number.
fn every(a: u32, b: u32) -> bool {
    a % b == 0
}

fn gcd(a: u32, b: u32) -> u32 {
    if b == 0 { a } else { gcd(b, a % b) }
}

fn main() {
    let animal = LIVING * SENSING; // 6
    let human = animal * RATIONAL; // 30
    let plant = LIVING * GREEN; // 14

    println!("every human is an animal: {}", every(human, animal));
    println!("every animal is a human:  {}", every(animal, human));
    println!("every plant is an animal: {}", every(plant, animal));
    println!("shared part of human and plant: {}", gcd(human, plant));
}
every human is an animal: True
every animal is a human:  False
every plant is an animal: False
shared part of human and plant: 2

The Rust program prints the same lines with true and false in small letters. Look at the last line. The greatest common divisor is 2, which means "living". It finds the most specific concept that human and plant share. Modern reasoners compute the same thing. They call it the least common subsumer.

Leibniz also wrote about binary numbers, using only 0 and 1. His paper appeared in the volume of the Paris Academy for 1703. Some catalogues say 1705, because that volume was printed later. He also gave a famous rule. Two things that share every property are one thing. In OWL, owl:sameAs says that two names point to one thing.

The number trick has limits. Leibniz needed negative numbers for "not", and the system grew complex. It only works if you can list all basic concepts. Nobody can do that for the whole world.

Linnaeus: names and ranks for all life

Before 1750, a plant often had a long Latin name of many words. Each book used a different long name. Scientists could not be sure that they meant the same plant.

Carl Linnaeus (1707 to 1778) was a Swedish doctor and botanist. He gave every species a short name of two words. The first word is the genus. The second word picks out the species. Humans are Homo sapiens. The dog rose is Rosa canina. This is binomial naming.

He also put the kinds into fixed levels, called ranks.

Three books matter most.

  • 1735. The first Systema Naturae. It had only a few very large pages.
  • 1753. Species Plantarum names all plants known to him. Plant names officially start here.
  • 1758. The 10th edition of Systema Naturae uses two-word names for animals. Animal names officially start here.

Linnaeus gave ontology two lasting tools. The first is a fixed set of levels. The second is one stable name for each kind. Today the Gene Ontology and other biology ontologies do the same with number codes.

A binomial name works like a unique ID. Two labs use different common names, but Homo sapiens means one thing. In RDF the same job is done by an IRI.

Ranks are not classes. "Genus" is not a kind of animal. Homo is a genus. Its rank is a label on the class, not a parent class. Mixing these levels is a common error in biology data.

Kant: the categories in the mind

Aristotle listed ten categories of being. Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804) asked a different question. Which basic concepts does our mind need to think about anything at all?

His answer is in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781, second edition 1787). He found twelve categories in four groups. He took them from the forms of logical judgment. He also criticised Aristotle's list, because it had no clear principle behind it.

Kant's twelve categories
GroupCategoriesA question it lets you ask
Quantityunity, plurality, totalityOne, some or all?
Qualityreality, negation, limitationIs it so, not so, or so only in part?
Relationsubstance and accident, cause and effect, communityWhat carries what? What causes what? Which things act on each other?
Modalitypossibility, existence, necessityCan it be? Is it? Must it be?

The big change is where the categories live. For Aristotle, they are kinds of things in the world. For Kant, they are concepts that the mind brings to experience.

Aristotle sorted the world. Kant sorted the tools we use to think about the world.

Kant's groups make a good checklist. Does your model say how many (quantity)? What is not true (negation)? What causes what (relation)? What must be true and what only might be (modality)?

Logic becomes algebra and then formulas

Boole: classes as algebra

Write x for "animals" and y for "living things". Then xy means things that are both. George Boole (1815 to 1864) built a whole algebra from this idea. His books are The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847) and The Laws of Thought (1854).

  • The symbol 1 means the whole universe. The symbol 0 means nothing.
  • The product xy means the members of both classes.
  • The class 1 − x means everything that is not in x.

One law looks strange in normal algebra: x^2 = x. But it is true for classes. "Animals that are animals" are just animals. From it, Boole got x(1 - x) = 0. Nothing is both an animal and not an animal.

A computer stores a class as bits. Each bit is one thing in the universe. Here is Boole's algebra on four things.

# A tiny universe of four things. One bit for each thing.
names = ["Lea", "Rex", "Oak", "Rock"]
ONE, ZERO = 0b1111, 0b0000      # Boole's 1 (everything) and 0 (nothing)

living = 0b0111                  # Lea, Rex, Oak
animal = 0b0011                  # Lea, Rex

def show(x):
    return [n for i, n in enumerate(names) if x >> i & 1]

print("x * x = x:        ", animal & animal == animal)
print("x * (1 - x) = 0:  ", animal & (ONE ^ animal) == ZERO)
print("living * animal = ", show(living & animal))
print("1 - living =      ", show(ONE ^ living))
// A tiny universe of four things. One bit for each thing.
const NAMES: [&str; 4] = ["Lea", "Rex", "Oak", "Rock"];
const ONE: u8 = 0b1111; // Boole's 1 (everything)
const ZERO: u8 = 0b0000; // Boole's 0 (nothing)

fn show(x: u8) -> Vec<&'static str> {
    (0..4).filter(|i| x >> i & 1 == 1).map(|i| NAMES[i]).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let living: u8 = 0b0111; // Lea, Rex, Oak
    let animal: u8 = 0b0011; // Lea, Rex

    println!("x * x = x:         {}", animal & animal == animal);
    println!("x * (1 - x) = 0:   {}", animal & (ONE ^ animal) == ZERO);
    println!("living * animal =  {:?}", show(living & animal));
    println!("1 - living =       {:?}", show(ONE ^ living));
}
x * x = x:         True
x * (1 - x) = 0:   True
living * animal =  ['Lea', 'Rex']
1 - living =       ['Rock']

Boole's product is owl:intersectionOf in OWL. Later logicians made his sum into a normal "or", which is owl:unionOf. His 1 − x is owl:complementOf. Every SQL WHERE a AND b also uses his algebra.

Frege: predicate logic

Boole's algebra cannot say "every parent has some child". You need to talk about two things and a relation between them. Gottlob Frege (1848 to 1925) solved this in a small book in 1879, the Begriffsschrift ("concept writing").

Frege made the first full system of predicate logic. Two ideas were new.

  • A sentence is not split into subject and predicate. It is a function applied to arguments, like hasChild(anna, ben).
  • A quantifier binds a variable: "for all x" or "there is an x".

For Frege, a concept is a function. It takes an object and gives back true or false. The concept "is a planet" gives true for Mars.

Here is one OWL class and its meaning in predicate logic. A parent is someone who has some child who is a person.

@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/> .
@prefix owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .

ex:hasChild a owl:ObjectProperty .
ex:Person   a owl:Class .

ex:Parent a owl:Class ;
    owl:equivalentClass [
        a owl:Restriction ;
        owl:onProperty     ex:hasChild ;   # the relation
        owl:someValuesFrom ex:Person       # "there is some" child who is a Person
    ] .
\forall p \, \big( \text{Parent}(p) \leftrightarrow \exists x \, ( \text{hasChild}(p, x) \land \text{Person}(x) ) \big)

The word someValuesFrom is Frege's "there is". The word allValuesFrom is his "for all". The description logics behind OWL are careful pieces of his logic. See Description logics.

Charles Sanders Peirce in the United States found quantifiers on his own, a few years after Frege. His papers of 1883 and 1885 used Σ for "some" and Π for "all". Frege's two-dimensional notation was hard to print. Our modern symbols come from later writers.

"Every parent has a child" and "there is a child of every parent" are different. The order of the quantifiers matters. The first says each parent has some child. The second says one child belongs to all parents.

Peirce: logic you can draw

Look at the picture below. It is a sentence. It is drawn, not written.

Peirce (1839 to 1914) called these drawings existential graphs. He started them around 1896. They first appear in print in 1897. By 1903 he had a full system with rules for proofs. The parts are simple.

  • The sheet of assertion is the page. Everything drawn on it is claimed as true.
  • A cut is an oval. It means "not".
  • A line of identity is a thick line. It means "something", the same thing in each place it touches.

He had three levels. Alpha graphs match propositional logic. Beta graphs match predicate logic. Gamma graphs go further, into modal logic.

Why does this matter today? John Sowa based his conceptual graphs on Peirce's ideas. His first paper on them came in 1976, and his book in 1984. More broadly, Peirce showed that a graph can carry exact logic. Every knowledge graph tries to do the same. You meet Sowa in AI and knowledge representation.

An oval in a Peirce graph is not a set or a class. It means "not". Two ovals, one inside the other, cancel out, like "not not".

Russell's paradox and the theory of types

A librarian makes a catalogue of all catalogues that do not list themselves. Should this new catalogue list itself? If it does, it should not. If it does not, it should. There is no good answer.

This is the shape of a paradox found by Bertrand Russell (1872 to 1970) in 1901. Take the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Is it a member of itself? Both answers lead to a contradiction.

On 16 June 1902 Russell wrote to Frege. Frege's second volume of the Grundgesetze was already being printed. One of Frege's basic laws allowed exactly this kind of set. Frege added an appendix, but his project never recovered.

Russell gave different months for his discovery: May, June or "spring" 1901. The German mathematician Ernst Zermelo found a similar problem around the same time, perhaps earlier. The exact date is not known.

A program can ask the same question. In Python, a function that asks "do you NOT hold of yourself?" runs forever.

# R(f) is True when f does NOT hold of itself.
def R(f):
    return not f(f)

try:
    print(R(R))          # Does R hold of itself?
except RecursionError:
    print("RecursionError: the question never ends")
// R(f) is true when f does NOT hold of itself.
fn r<F: Fn(&F) -> bool>(f: &F) -> bool {
    !f(f)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", r(&r)); // Does R hold of itself?
}
Python:  RecursionError: the question never ends

Rust:    error[E0308]: mismatched types
           println!("{}", r(&r)); // Does R hold of itself?
                            ^^ recursive type with infinite-size name

Look at the difference. Python starts the question and never finishes. Rust refuses to compile, because no type can fit. The Rust compiler does what Russell proposed.

Russell's fix was the theory of types. Things live on levels. Individuals are on level 0. Classes of individuals are on level 1. Classes of classes are on level 2. A class may only contain things from the level below. So "a set that contains itself" cannot even be written.

  • 1903. A first, simple version, in an appendix to The Principles of Mathematics.
  • 1908. A fuller version in the paper "Mathematical Logic as Based on the Theory of Types".
  • 1910 to 1913. Principia Mathematica, three volumes with Alfred North Whitehead.

OWL 2 DL keeps the same discipline. A name can be used as a class and as an individual. This trick is called punning. But the reasoner treats the two uses as separate things. Freer OWL Full allows classes inside classes, and then reasoning is no longer guaranteed to finish.

Do not make ex:Eagle both a subclass of ex:Bird and an instance of ex:Bird. One eagle is a bird. The species Eagle is not a bird. It is a species. Put it in a separate class, like ex:Species.

Parts, frameworks and commitment

Four thinkers of the early 1900s gave ontology its modern questions. Each slide shows one thinker, in order of their main work.

Edmund Husserl: formal ontology

Husserl (1859 to 1938) wrote the Logical Investigations in 1900 and 1901. One part sketches a theory of parts and wholes. Some parts are dependent. The red of an apple cannot exist without the apple.

Later, in Ideas I (1913), he split formal ontology from regional ontologies. Formal ontology studies forms like object, part, unity and number. A regional ontology studies one area, like nature.

Stanislaw Lesniewski: mereology

Lesniewski (1886 to 1939) was a Polish logician. In 1916 he published the first strict theory of parts and wholes. It is called mereology.

For him a "class" is a whole made of parts, not an abstract set. He also built a logic of the word "is" and named it Ontology. In 1940 Henry Leonard and Nelson Goodman published a similar "calculus of individuals".

Rudolf Carnap: frameworks

Carnap (1891 to 1970) tried to build all science from experience in Der logische Aufbau der Welt (1928). In 1950 he wrote "Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology".

His point: a question like "is there a prime above 100?" makes sense inside a framework of numbers. "Do numbers really exist?" is different. For Carnap it is really a practical choice of which framework to use.

W. V. O. Quine: commitment

Quine (1908 to 2000) gave a test for what a theory says exists. Write the theory in predicate logic. Its ontological commitment is everything its variables must range over.

The short slogan is "to be is to be the value of a variable". He also said "no entity without identity". If you cannot say when two things are the same, do not add them.

These four ideas have direct uses in engineering.

From philosophy to modelling practice
ThinkerIdeaIn a modern ontology
Husserldependent partsA quality, like a colour, depends on its bearer. BFO and DOLCE model this.
LesniewskimereologyPart-of is transitive. A wheel's spoke is part of the bike.
CarnapframeworksEach ontology is a framework. "Does a Customer exist?" depends on the model.
QuinecommitmentA schema commits you to every type its queries range over.
QuineidentityEvery class needs an identity rule: a key or a clear sameAs policy.

Most books link the slogan "to be is to be the value of a variable" to Quine's paper "On What There Is" (1948). That paper states the idea in longer words. One commentary says the short form already ends his 1939 paper "Designation and Existence". This book could not check the 1939 text directly. Quote the 1948 paper for the idea.

"Ontology" in Lesniewski's work is not the same as an OWL ontology. It is his name for a logical system about the word "is". The name is a coincidence of history.

Tarski: truth and models

When is the sentence "snow is white" true? When snow is white. This sounds silly. But Alfred Tarski (1901 to 1983) turned it into exact mathematics.

His paper on truth appeared in Polish in 1933, and soon after in German. It gives a test for any theory of truth, called Convention T. The sentence "S" is true if and only if S. Then he defined truth for formal languages, step by step from the parts of a formula.

From this grew model theory. Tarski proposed the name "theory of models" in 1954. Three words are key.

  • An interpretation gives every name and predicate a meaning in some domain.
  • A model of some sentences is an interpretation where all of them are true.
  • Sentences A entail a sentence B when B is true in every model of A.

Here is a tiny model checker. It tests "every human is mortal" in two structures.

# A structure: a domain plus a meaning (a set) for each predicate.
domain = {"socrates", "plato", "rex"}
m1 = {"Human": {"socrates", "plato"}, "Mortal": {"socrates", "plato", "rex"}}
m2 = {"Human": {"socrates", "plato"}, "Mortal": {"socrates", "rex"}}

def every_is(m, p, q):
    """True in m: for all x, if p(x) then q(x)."""
    return all(x in m[q] for x in domain if x in m[p])

def counterexamples(m, p, q):
    return sorted(x for x in domain if x in m[p] and x not in m[q])

for name, m in [("m1", m1), ("m2", m2)]:
    print(name, every_is(m, "Human", "Mortal"), counterexamples(m, "Human", "Mortal"))
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet};

type Structure = BTreeMap<&'static str, BTreeSet<&'static str>>;

// True in m: for all x, if p(x) then q(x).
// We return the x that break the rule. An empty list means "true".
fn counterexamples(m: &Structure, domain: &[&'static str], p: &str, q: &str) -> Vec<&'static str> {
    domain.iter().copied().filter(|x| m[p].contains(x) && !m[q].contains(x)).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let domain = ["plato", "rex", "socrates"];
    let m1: Structure = BTreeMap::from([
        ("Human", BTreeSet::from(["socrates", "plato"])),
        ("Mortal", BTreeSet::from(["socrates", "plato", "rex"])),
    ]);
    let m2: Structure = BTreeMap::from([
        ("Human", BTreeSet::from(["socrates", "plato"])),
        ("Mortal", BTreeSet::from(["socrates", "rex"])),
    ]);
    for (name, m) in [("m1", &m1), ("m2", &m2)] {
        let bad = counterexamples(m, &domain, "Human", "Mortal");
        println!("{name} {} {:?}", bad.is_empty(), bad);
    }
}
m1 True []
m2 False ['plato']

The sentence is true in m1 and false in m2. Plato is the counterexample in m2. So m1 is a model of the sentence, and m2 is not.

This is exactly how the W3C defines meaning for RDF. The RDF 1.1 Semantics document defines a model-theoretic semantics. One graph entails another when every interpretation that makes the first true also makes the second true. OWL 2 has a model-theoretic semantics too. See Logic for ontology.

"True in one model" is not "entailed". Our checker found one model where the sentence holds. Entailment needs truth in every model of the premises. A reasoner proves this without listing all models.

What each thinker gave to today's tools

The story is a chain of ideas. Each arrow shows one idea passing from one person to the next, or into a modern tool.

  1. 1606 Lorhard. First known printed use of ontologia, in Ogdoas scholastica.
  2. 1613 Goclenius. The word in a margin note of the Lexicon philosophicum.
  3. 1666 Leibniz. De arte combinatoria. Later, in 1679, concepts as prime numbers.
  4. 1730 Wolff. Philosophia prima, sive Ontologia makes the word standard.
  5. 1735-1758 Linnaeus. Systema Naturae, ranks and two-word names.
  6. 1781 Kant. Critique of Pure Reason, twelve categories.
  7. 1847-1854 Boole. Logic as an algebra of classes.
  8. 1879 Frege. Begriffsschrift, the first predicate logic.
  9. 1896-1903 Peirce. Existential graphs.
  10. 1900-1901 Husserl. Logical Investigations, parts and wholes.
  11. 1901-1902 Russell. The paradox and the letter to Frege. Types follow in 1903 and 1908.
  12. 1916 Lesniewski. The first strict mereology.
  13. 1933 Tarski. The definition of truth for formal languages.
  14. 1948 Quine. "On What There Is". Carnap answers in 1950.
  15. 1954 Tarski. Proposes the name "theory of models".
Why did computer science need all this logic?

A computer cannot guess meaning. It needs exact rules for what follows from what. Frege gave the language, Tarski gave the meaning, and Russell showed the dangers. Description logics later chose a safe part that a computer can always finish.

Which of these ideas is most used every day?

Boole's algebra. Every search filter, SQL query and OWL class expression with "and", "or" and "not" uses it.

Did any of these thinkers build a computer ontology?

No. Leibniz came closest in spirit. The first computer ontologies came with AI research after 1956. That is the next chapter.

Patterns to remember

Logical patterns from 1600 to 1950
PatternPurposeModelNote
Concept = product of partsTest "every A is B" by calculationhuman = 2 × 3 × 5, animal = 2 × 3Works only with a closed list of basic concepts.
Most specific shared parentFind what two classes sharegcd(30, 14) = 2: livingReasoners call it the least common subsumer.
Genus + species nameGive each kind one stable nameHomo sapiensIn RDF, use one IRI per thing.
Rank as a labelRecord the level of a classHomo has rank genus.A rank is not a parent class.
xy, x + y, 1 − xBuild classes from classesowl:intersectionOf, owl:unionOf, owl:complementOf"Not" is wide: 1 − animal includes rocks.
There is some x with RRequire at least one linkowl:someValuesFromFrege's "there is".
For all x with RLimit what links can point toowl:allValuesFromTrue even when there are no links at all.
Levels of typesAvoid self-membershipEagle (species) vs. an eagle (bird)Keep classes and individuals apart.
A depends on BModel qualities and partsThe red depends on the apple.No bearer, no quality.
No entity without identityDecide when two records are oneSame tax number, same companyWrite the rule before you merge data.
True in every modelDefine entailmentm1 is a model, m2 is not.One model is not enough for entailment.

Practice

Which book has the first known printed use of the word ontologia?

  • Goclenius, Lexicon philosophicum, 1613
  • Lorhard, Ogdoas scholastica, 1606
  • Wolff, Philosophia prima, sive Ontologia, 1730

Lorhard's 1606 book is the first known use. Goclenius came in 1613. Wolff made the word standard in 1730.

In Leibniz's code, human = 30 and animal = 6. What does 30 % 6 == 0 tell you?

  • Every human is an animal.
  • Every animal is a human.
  • Humans and animals share nothing.

The smaller concept's number divides the larger one. So all parts of "animal" are inside "human".

Which of Kant's groups holds cause and effect?

  • Quantity
  • Modality
  • Relation

Relation has substance and accident, cause and effect, and community.

In Boole's algebra, what does x(1 - x) = 0 say?

  • Every x is a 1.
  • Nothing is both x and not x.
  • x is empty.

1 − x is everything outside x. The product with x is empty.

Why does Rust refuse to compile r(&r)?

  • Rust has no functions as arguments.
  • No type can contain itself, so the type would be infinite.
  • The function has a spelling mistake.

This is the idea of Russell's theory of types. Levels stop self-application.

Fill in the missing words.

Frege published the Begriffsschrift in ?.

Russell wrote to Frege about the paradox in the year ?.

The logic of parts and wholes is called ?.

B is true in every model of A. Then A ? B.

  1. Give "bird" a Leibniz number. Use living = 2, sensing = 3 and a new prime for "flying". Is every bird an animal? Is every bird a plant (plant = 2 × 7)?
    Answer

    Choose flying = 11. Then bird = 2 × 3 × 11 = 66. Animal is 6, and 66 % 6 == 0, so every bird is an animal. Plant is 14, and 66 % 14 is 10, so a bird is not a plant. But gcd(66, 14) = 2, so both are living.

  2. Write "no animal is a rock" in Boole's algebra, with a for animals and r for rocks.
    Answer

    ar = 0. The class of things that are both animals and rocks is empty. In OWL you would write owl:disjointWith.

  3. Write "every person has some parent who is a person" in predicate logic.
    Answer

    \forall x \, ( \text{Person}(x) \to \exists y \, ( \text{hasParent}(x, y) \land \text{Person}(y) ) ). In OWL: Person is a subclass of "hasParent some Person".

  4. A data model has ex:Lion a ex:Species and ex:Lion rdfs:subClassOf ex:Animal. Is this a problem? Use Russell's idea.
    Answer

    The name Lion is used on two levels: as an individual (a species) and as a class (of animals). In OWL 2 DL this is punning, and the reasoner treats them as two separate things. It is allowed, but you must not expect facts about the species to flow to single lions.

  5. Your company merges two customer tables. Use Quine's "no entity without identity" to say what you must decide first.
    Answer

    You must decide when two rows are the same customer. For example: same tax number, or same email and same name. Without this rule you cannot count customers. You also cannot link their orders.

Key takeaways

  • The first known use of ontologia is Lorhard's book of 1606. Wolff made it standard in 1730.
  • Leibniz dreamed of reasoning by calculation. His prime-number code is an early subsumption test.
  • Linnaeus gave fixed ranks and one stable two-word name per species.
  • Kant moved the categories from the world into the mind.
  • Boole made logic an algebra of classes. OWL's and, or, not come from him.
  • Frege's predicate logic, with quantifiers, is the root of description logics.
  • Russell's paradox led to types. OWL keeps classes and individuals apart for the same reason.
  • Husserl, Lesniewski, Carnap and Quine gave dependence, parts, frameworks and identity.
  • Tarski's models give RDF and OWL their exact meaning.

Sources

  • Gottlob Frege. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the Begriffsschrift and Russell's letter.
  • Russell's Paradox. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the dates and the theory of types.
  • George Boole. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: his two books and the law x² = x.
  • Peirce's Deductive Logic. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: existential graphs and quantifiers.
  • Stanislaw Lesniewski. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: mereology and his Ontology.
  • RDF 1.1 Semantics. The W3C document with the model theory for RDF.

AI and knowledge representation (1956-1990)

The first AI programs needed to know things about the world. How do you put knowledge inside a computer? Between 1956 and 1990, researchers tried networks, frames, rules and logic. Their answers became today's ontologies, rule engines and knowledge graphs.

  • Explain semantic networks, frames and scripts with a small example.
  • Describe the "what's in a link" problem and how KL-ONE answered it.
  • Run a tiny inheritance network, a MYCIN-style rule combiner and a Prolog program.
  • Explain the frame problem and the knowledge acquisition bottleneck.
  • Say what survived the AI winter and where it lives today.

The Dartmouth start

In August 1955, four researchers wrote a short funding request. They wanted ten people to work together for two months, in the summer of 1956. The place was Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, USA.

The four authors were John McCarthy (Dartmouth), Marvin Minsky (Harvard), Nathaniel Rochester (IBM) and Claude Shannon (Bell Labs). Their request is dated 31 August 1955. It used a new name for the field: artificial intelligence.

The request had a bold idea. Every part of learning and intelligence can, in principle, be described so exactly that a machine can copy it. One topic on their list was how machines could use language.

Three years later, McCarthy wrote "Programs with Common Sense". He presented it in 1958, and it was printed in 1959. He described the Advice Taker, a program that would keep its knowledge as sentences in logic. The program would find new facts from old ones. This is the start of knowledge representation, or KR.

Early AI asked two questions. How do we write knowledge down for a machine? How does the machine use it to find answers?

Sources differ on the exact dates of the 1956 meeting. The request asked for two months. Not all invited people came for the whole time. The date of the written request, 31 August 1955, is certain.

Dartmouth did not produce a working AI system. It produced a name, a community and a research plan. The real programs came in the years after.

Semantic networks: knowledge as a graph

Answer these three questions fast. Can a canary sing? Can a canary fly? Does a canary have skin?

Most people answer the first question fastest and the last one slowest. Why? In 1969 Allan Collins and Ross Quillian tested this in a lab. They measured how long people took to say "true". Their idea was that memory is a network.

"Can sing" is stored on the canary node. "Can fly" is one link up, on bird. "Has skin" is two links up, on animal. More links take more time, and the lab results agreed.

A semantic network stores knowledge as nodes and labelled arrows. A node gets the properties of the nodes above it. This is inheritance.

Who was first?

  • 1956. Richard Richens in Cambridge, England, used the term "semantic net". He wanted a shared language of meaning for machine translation.
  • 1966. Ross Quillian finished his PhD on "semantic memory" at the Carnegie Institute of Technology. A version appeared in a 1968 book edited by Minsky.
  • 1969. Collins and Quillian published the canary experiment.

Inheritance with an exception

Look at the penguin. It is a bird, and birds fly. But the penguin node says "cannot fly". The nearest fact wins. This is a default: true unless a closer node says otherwise.

# Each node: its parent ("is a") and its own properties.
net = {
    "animal":  (None,     {"has skin": True, "can breathe": True}),
    "bird":    ("animal", {"can fly": True, "has wings": True}),
    "canary":  ("bird",   {"can sing": True, "is yellow": True}),
    "penguin": ("bird",   {"can fly": False}),        # an exception
}

def ask(node, prop):
    """Walk up the is-a links. Return the answer and the links used."""
    steps = 0
    while node is not None:
        parent, props = net[node]
        if prop in props:
            return ("yes" if props[prop] else "no"), steps
        node, steps = parent, steps + 1
    return "unknown", steps                 # nobody knows

questions = [("canary", "can sing"), ("canary", "can fly"), ("canary", "has skin"),
             ("penguin", "can fly"), ("canary", "can swim")]
for node, prop in questions:
    answer, steps = ask(node, prop)
    print(f"{node} {prop}? {answer} (links: {steps})")
use std::collections::HashMap;

// Each node: its parent ("is a") and its own properties.
type Net = HashMap<&'static str, (Option<&'static str>, Vec<(&'static str, bool)>)>;

// Walk up the is-a links. Return the answer and the links used.
fn ask(net: &Net, start: &str, prop: &str) -> (&'static str, u32) {
    let mut node = Some(start);
    let mut steps = 0;
    while let Some(n) = node {
        let (parent, props) = &net[n];
        if let Some((_, v)) = props.iter().find(|(p, _)| *p == prop) {
            return (if *v { "yes" } else { "no" }, steps);
        }
        node = *parent;
        steps += 1;
    }
    ("unknown", steps) // nobody knows
}

fn main() {
    let net: Net = HashMap::from([
        ("animal", (None, vec![("has skin", true), ("can breathe", true)])),
        ("bird", (Some("animal"), vec![("can fly", true), ("has wings", true)])),
        ("canary", (Some("bird"), vec![("can sing", true), ("is yellow", true)])),
        ("penguin", (Some("bird"), vec![("can fly", false)])), // an exception
    ]);
    let questions = [("canary", "can sing"), ("canary", "can fly"), ("canary", "has skin"),
                     ("penguin", "can fly"), ("canary", "can swim")];
    for (node, prop) in questions {
        let (answer, steps) = ask(&net, node, prop);
        println!("{node} {prop}? {answer} (links: {steps})");
    }
}
canary can sing? yes (links: 0)
canary can fly? yes (links: 1)
canary has skin? yes (links: 2)
penguin can fly? no (links: 0)
canary can swim? unknown (links: 3)

The last answer is "unknown", not "no". The network does not say that canaries cannot swim. It just does not know.

Defaults and exceptions do not exist in OWL. In OWL, if every bird flies and a penguin is a bird, then a penguin flies. A "cannot fly" fact then makes the ontology inconsistent. Model exceptions with a narrower class, like FlyingBird, or with rules.

Frames and scripts

You open the door of a hotel room. Before you look, you already expect a bed, a bathroom and a window. You do not check for each one. Your mind fills in the usual things.

Marvin Minsky built on this idea. His paper "A Framework for Representing Knowledge" came out as an MIT memo in June 1974. A version was printed in a book in 1975. A frame is a structure for a usual situation. It has named parts called slots. Each slot can have a default value.

frame HotelRoom
  is-a:      Room
  beds:      default 1          # used unless we learn more
  bathroom:  default yes
  window:    default yes
  price:     must be a number   # a rule for the slot
  guest:     must be a Person

frame Room_412
  is-a:      HotelRoom
  beds:      2                  # overrides the default
  guest:     Lea

Room 412 inherits "bathroom: yes" and "window: yes". It overrides the number of beds. Frames look a lot like classes in object-oriented programming. Both ideas grew in the 1970s.

Scripts: frames for events

Roger Schank and Robert Abelson took the idea to events. Their 1977 book Scripts, Plans, Goals and Understanding describes a script. A script is the usual order of steps in a common event. Their best-known example is a visit to a restaurant.

Enter

The customer comes in, looks for a table and sits down.

Order

The customer reads the menu. The waiter comes. The customer orders food.

Eat

The cook makes the food. The waiter brings it. The customer eats.

Leave

The customer gets the bill, pays and leaves.

Now read this story. "Lea went to a restaurant. She ordered fish. She left a big tip." The story never says that Lea ate or paid. A program with the script can still answer "Did Lea eat?". Their program SAM used scripts to read short stories.

A script is an early event model. Today you model events with a start time, an end time, participants and steps. See the event pattern in The 15 modelling patterns.

Scripts break when life is unusual. If the restaurant is closed, the script gives wrong guesses. Schank and Abelson knew this. For unusual cases, they added plans and goals.

What's in a link?

Look at this one arrow: Car --color--> Red. What does it mean?

  • Every car is red?
  • Cars are usually red?
  • Some car is red?
  • Cars have a colour, and red is one possible value?

The arrow does not say. In 1975 William Woods asked exactly this in a paper called "What's in a Link: Foundations for Semantic Networks". He worked at the company BBN. His point was hard but simple. Networks had pictures but no clear meaning. Two programs could read the same arrow in two different ways.

Woods said a network needs clear semantics. One important split is between a definition and a fact. "A bachelor is an unmarried man" defines a concept. "Ben is a bachelor" states a fact about one person.

The many meanings of IS-A

In 1983 Ronald Brachman wrote "What IS-A Is and Isn't". He listed the different meanings of the IS-A link in systems of his time. Here are three that you meet every day.

One arrow, three meanings
NetworkReal meaningIn RDF or OWL
Canary IS-A BirdEvery canary is a bird.rdfs:subClassOf
Tweety IS-A CanaryThis one thing is a canary.rdf:type
Canary IS-A Yellow thingCanaries have a colour, yellow.a property, like ex:color

This confusion is still common in 2026. Teams draw one "is a" arrow for both subclass and instance. Then a query for "all birds" misses Tweety, or counts "Canary" as a bird. Always ask: is this a kind or one thing?

KL-ONE and the birth of description logics

Brachman did not only criticise. In the late 1970s he and his colleagues built KL-ONE. It was a network language with exact meaning. Brachman and James Schmolze described it in a 1985 paper.

KL-ONE had three big ideas.

  • Concepts and roles. A concept is a class, like Parent. A role is a relation, like hasChild.
  • Defined and primitive concepts. A defined concept has a full definition: a parent is a person with at least one child. A primitive concept has only necessary conditions.
  • Classification. The system can place a new defined concept in the right spot of the tree by itself.

The key reasoning task is subsumption. Does concept A always contain concept B? Is every mother a parent? The system answers from the definitions alone.

  1. Definitions: a Parent is a Person with at least one child. A Mother is a Woman with at least one child. Every Woman is a Person.
  2. Question: where does Mother go in the tree?
  3. The system checks subsumption. Every Mother is a Woman, so a Person. She has a child. So Mother goes under Parent and under Woman. Nobody wrote "Mother is a Parent".

Power costs speed

In 1984 Brachman and Hector Levesque published a short paper with a big message. They studied subsumption in a very small frame language. Add one more small feature, and the problem became intractable.

The lesson: the more a language can say, the slower its reasoning can become. This trade-off shaped all later work. Designers now pick a language that is strong enough, but not stronger.

The family grew under many names: terminological systems, concept languages and others. Later it was called description logics. In 1991 Manfred Schmidt-Schauss and Gert Smolka described the logic ALC. It is still the standard first description logic. OWL, from 2004, is built on this family. See Description logics.

Nobody agrees on one birth date for the name "description logics". Overviews say the name came during the 1980s or around 1990. The earlier names were used for years at the same time.

Conceptual graphs

John Sowa at IBM took another path. His first paper on conceptual graphs came in 1976, and his book Conceptual Structures in 1984. He joined AI networks with Peirce's existential graphs, which you met in From Leibniz to modern logic. Conceptual graphs later became one of the formats of ISO Common Logic.

Ask "what's in a link?" in every review. For each arrow, write one sentence that says what it means for all things, for some things, or for one thing.

Expert systems and MYCIN

A doctor thinks: "If the test shows X and the patient has Y, then Z is likely." Can a program hold hundreds of such rules?

An expert system does exactly this. It has two parts. The knowledge base holds the rules. The inference engine applies them. The two parts are separate, so you can change the rules without changing the engine.

DENDRAL, started at Stanford in 1965, is often called the first expert system. It helped chemists identify molecules. The most famous one came next.

MYCIN

MYCIN was built at Stanford in the 1970s. Edward Shortliffe wrote it for his PhD, with Bruce Buchanan and others. It advised doctors on blood infections and meningitis, and on which drugs to use. It was written in Lisp and grew from about 200 rules to several hundred.

A rule in MYCIN's style looks like this, simplified.

IF   the organism stains gram-negative
AND  the organism is rod-shaped
AND  the organism grows without air
THEN there is suggestive evidence (0.6) that the organism is Bacteroides
