The number 0.6 is a certainty factor. It goes from −1 (surely false) to +1 (surely true). When two rules support the same conclusion, MYCIN combines them. For two positive factors x and y, the result is x + y(1 - x).

def combine(x, y):
    """MYCIN's formula when two rules both support a conclusion."""
    return x + y * (1 - x)

cf = 0.0                                   # no evidence yet
for rule, strength in [("rule 1", 0.6), ("rule 2", 0.4), ("rule 3", 0.3)]:
    cf = combine(cf, strength)
    print(f"after {rule}: {cf:.2f}")
// MYCIN's formula when two rules both support a conclusion.
fn combine(x: f64, y: f64) -> f64 {
    x + y * (1.0 - x)
}

fn main() {
    let mut cf = 0.0; // no evidence yet
    for (rule, strength) in [("rule 1", 0.6), ("rule 2", 0.4), ("rule 3", 0.3)] {
        cf = combine(cf, strength);
        println!("after {rule}: {cf:.2}");
    }
}
after rule 1: 0.60
after rule 2: 0.76
after rule 3: 0.83

Each new rule adds belief, but the value never passes 1. The order of the rules does not change the result.

How good was it?

A blind test was published in 1979. Eight experts judged drug choices for ten cases of meningitis. They did not know which choices came from the program. MYCIN's choices were rated acceptable 65% of the time. Five Stanford specialists scored between 42.5% and 62.5%.

Still, MYCIN was never used in daily hospital work. Doctors had to type answers to many questions. It did not connect to hospital systems. There were also questions about who is responsible for a wrong answer. The team later made EMYCIN: the engine without the medical rules, so others could add their own.

Certainty factors are not probabilities. Later studies showed that they only behave like probabilities under strong assumptions. Do not mix them with real probability numbers.

Prolog and logic programming

Write two facts and one rule. Then ask a question. The computer finds the answer by itself. This is the idea of logic programming.

Prolog was born in Marseille, France, in 1972. Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel built it. The name comes from French: programmation en logique. Robert Kowalski in Edinburgh gave the theory. A Prolog rule is a Horn clause: one conclusion, any number of conditions.

% Facts: parent(Parent, Child).
parent(ana, ben).
parent(ben, cara).
parent(cara, dan).

% Rules: an ancestor is a parent, or a parent of an ancestor.
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y).

We ran three questions with Tau Prolog 0.3.4, a Prolog system in JavaScript.

?- ancestor(ana, Who).
Who = ben
Who = cara
Who = dan
false.

?- ancestor(Who, dan).
Who = cara
Who = ana
Who = ben
false.

?- ancestor(ana, eve).
false.

The final "false" after each list means "no more answers". Look at the last question. Prolog says "false" because it cannot prove it. Eve is not in the data at all. This is negation as failure. It assumes a closed world.

OWL and RDF work the other way. They assume an open world. "Not in the data" means "unknown", not "false". Many bugs come from mixing the two. See The building blocks.

In 1982 Japan started its Fifth Generation Computer project. Logic programming was at its centre. The project ended in 1992 without the hoped-for breakthrough. A small part of Prolog for databases became Datalog. It lives on in modern rule engines. See Rules and Datalog.

Cyc: all of common sense

Ask a program: "If you put a cup of water upside down, what happens?" A medical expert system has no idea. It knows meningitis, but not water. This is brittleness.

Douglas Lenat had a plan against brittleness. In 1984 he started Cyc at MCC in Austin, Texas. MCC was a research group paid for by many US companies. The name comes from "encyclopedia". The goal was to write down the common sense that every adult knows. Water flows down. People are born and die. A thing cannot be in two places at once.

His 1985 paper in AI Magazine named two problems in its title: brittleness and knowledge acquisition bottlenecks. Cyc would solve both with a huge base of everyday facts and rules, written by hand in a logic language called CycL.

  • At the end of 1994, the project moved out of MCC into a company, Cycorp. Some sources say January 1995.
  • Lenat led Cycorp until his death on 31 August 2023.
  • Cyc never reached the general intelligence it aimed for. But it showed how large and how hard a common-sense ontology is.

Cyc is the biggest test of the hand-written approach. It worked well inside companies for some tasks. It also proved the bottleneck: writing all of common sense by hand takes decades. Today, language models learn much common sense from text. But they cannot show their reasons the way Cyc could.

Two hard problems

The frame problem

A robot paints a box red. What changed? The box's colour. What did not change? Its place, its size, the colour of the walls, the time of day, and millions of other facts.

In 1969 John McCarthy and Patrick Hayes wrote "Some Philosophical Problems from the Standpoint of Artificial Intelligence". They described what is now called the frame problem. In pure logic, you must write a rule for every fact that an action does not change. With many actions and facts, the number of these rules explodes.

The fix is a default: things stay the same unless something changes them. Pure logic cannot say "unless" easily. So researchers built non-monotonic reasoning, in which a new fact can remove an old conclusion. The Stanford Encyclopedia says the technical problem is now more or less solved. The wider philosophical version is still debated.

The knowledge acquisition bottleneck

Building MYCIN took years of talks between doctors and programmers. The experts often could not say how they knew things. Every rule had to be found, written, tested and fixed by hand.

Edward Feigenbaum named this in 1977. Getting knowledge out of experts is the slow part, the bottleneck, of building expert systems. Most later books on the subject cite him or a 1983 book by Frederick Hayes-Roth and colleagues.

The bottleneck is still with us. Ontology engineering methods answer it with reuse, shared upper ontologies and competency questions. Language models now help to draft terms and extract facts. People must still check them. See The ontology engineering method and Ontologies and AI.

The frame problem is not about Minsky's frames. The two names are only similar. The frame problem is about what does not change after an action.

The AI winter and what survived

Hype came first, then disappointment, then cuts in money. People call such a period an AI winter.

  • 1973. In the UK, the Lighthill report judged that AI had failed its big goals. Funding fell in the UK, and also in the USA in the following years.
  • 1984. At the yearly AAAI meeting, Roger Schank and Marvin Minsky warned that a new winter was coming. The phrase "AI winter" comes from about this time.
  • 1987. The market for special Lisp machines collapsed. Cheaper desktop computers could run Lisp too. Many expert-system companies failed in the following years.

But good ideas did not die. They changed their names and moved into normal software.

  1. 1955-56 Dartmouth. The funding request (31 August 1955) and the summer meeting name the field.
  2. 1956 Richens. The term "semantic net", for machine translation.
  3. 1958 McCarthy. The Advice Taker: knowledge as logic sentences.
  4. 1965 DENDRAL. An early expert system for chemistry, at Stanford.
  5. 1966-69 Quillian. Semantic memory. The canary test with Collins in 1969.
  6. 1969 McCarthy and Hayes. The frame problem.
  7. 1972 Prolog. Colmerauer and Roussel in Marseille.
  8. 1974-75 Minsky. Frames. Woods. "What's in a Link" (1975).
  9. 1976 MYCIN book by Shortliffe. Sowa's first paper on conceptual graphs.
  10. 1977 Schank and Abelson. Scripts. Feigenbaum names the bottleneck.
  11. late 1970s KL-ONE. Exact network language with classification.
  12. 1983-85 Brachman. IS-A paper (1983), the trade-off with Levesque (1984), KL-ONE overview (1985).
  13. 1984 Cyc starts. The phrase "AI winter" appears.
  14. 1987 Lisp machine market collapses. The second winter begins.
  15. 1991 ALC. A clean description logic, the start of the road to OWL.
Why do ontologists study this period?

Most mistakes in modern models were made here first. Unclear links, mixed "is a" arrows, defaults in a logic without defaults, and hand-written knowledge that never ends. Knowing the history helps you avoid them.

Did neural networks exist in this period?

Yes. Simple neural networks existed from the 1950s, and they had their own ups and downs. This chapter follows the symbolic line, because ontologies come from it.

What came right after 1990?

Researchers wanted to share and reuse knowledge instead of writing it again. This led to Gruber's definition and the ontology engineering era. See The ontology engineering era.

Patterns to remember

Knowledge representation patterns from early AI
PatternPurposeModelNote
Store a fact as high as possibleAvoid repeating facts"can fly" on Bird, not on each birdChildren inherit it.
Nearest fact winsAllow exceptionsPenguin: cannot flyOWL has no defaults. Use rules or narrower classes.
Frame with slotsDescribe a usual kind of thingHotelRoom: beds, bathroom, windowA slot type is a constraint. A default is a guess.
Script of scenesDescribe a usual evententer, order, eat, leaveAdd time and participants for a real event model.
One meaning per arrowMake links exactsubClassOf vs. type vs. propertyAsk: all, some, typical or one?
Defined conceptLet the system classifyParent = Person with at least one childOnly defined concepts get placed by the reasoner.
Strong enough, not strongerKeep reasoning fastChoose a light logic if it is enough.Each extra feature can cost a lot of speed.
IF conditions THEN conclusionWrite expert knowledge as rulesIF rod-shaped AND ... THEN ...Keep rules apart from the engine.
x + y(1 − x)Combine two positive certainty factors0.6 and 0.4 give 0.76Not a probability.
head :- bodyWrite a logic ruleancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).Prolog assumes a closed world.
Things stay the same unless changedHandle the frame problemThe box moves, the walls keep their colour.Needs default reasoning.
Reuse before you writeFight the bottleneckImport a shared ontology for time.Writing all knowledge by hand never ends.

Practice

Which year is on the Dartmouth funding request?

  • 1955
  • 1956
  • 1958

The request is dated 31 August 1955. The meeting itself was in the summer of 1956.

In the Collins and Quillian network, which answer takes the longest?

  • A canary can sing.
  • A canary can fly.
  • A canary has skin.

"Has skin" is stored two links up, on Animal. More links take more time.

"Tweety IS-A Canary." What does this link mean in RDF?

  • rdfs:subClassOf
  • rdf:type
  • owl:sameAs

Tweety is one thing, an instance. The instance link is rdf:type.

What was the main message of Brachman and Levesque in 1984?

  • Frames are better than logic.
  • More expressive power can make reasoning much slower.
  • Subsumption is always easy.

One small extra feature made subsumption intractable. Power costs speed.

Prolog answers "false" to ancestor(ana, eve). What would an OWL reasoner say about the same open-world question?

  • False
  • True
  • Unknown

Prolog uses a closed world: not provable means false. OWL uses an open world: not provable means unknown.

Fill in the missing words.

Minsky's paper on frames first came out as an MIT memo in ?.

The famous example script of Schank and Abelson is a visit to a ?.

Two positive certainty factors 0.5 and 0.5 combine to ?.

Lenat started the Cyc project in ?.

  1. Add an ostrich to the semantic network. Ostriches are birds, cannot fly and can run fast. What are the answers for "ostrich can fly" and "ostrich has skin"?
    Answer

    Add "ostrich": ("bird", {"can fly": False, "can run fast": True}). "Ostrich can fly" gives no after 0 links, because the ostrich's own fact wins. "Ostrich has skin" gives yes after 2 links, inherited from Animal.

  2. Write a frame for a "Meeting" with four slots. Give two slots a default value.
    Answer

    One possible frame. Meeting: is-a Event. Room: default "main room". Length: default 30 minutes. Organizer: must be a Person. Participants: must be one or more Persons. Your slots can be different.

  3. The arrow Employee --manager--> Person is in a diagram. Write two different meanings it could have.
    Answer

    Meaning 1: every employee has some manager who is a person. Meaning 2: if an employee has a manager, the manager must be a person, but some employees have none. In OWL the first is someValuesFrom, the second is allValuesFrom or a range.

  4. Add a rule sibling(X, Y) to the Prolog program: two different people with the same parent. Which built-in do you need?
    Answer

    sibling(X, Y) :- parent(P, X), parent(P, Y), X \= Y. The built-in \= means "cannot be unified", so a person is not their own sibling. In our data nobody has a sibling, so every query fails.

  5. A robot moves a cup from the table to the shelf. List three facts that change and three that do not. Which problem does the second list show?
    Answer

    Change: the cup's place, what is on the table, what is on the shelf. No change: the cup's colour, the room's size, the robot's name. The second list shows the frame problem. It could go on forever, so we need a default that unchanged things stay the same.

  6. Explain in four sentences why MYCIN scored well in tests but was never used in hospitals.
    Answer

    In a blind test, experts rated its drug choices acceptable 65% of the time, better than five specialists. But doctors had to type answers to many questions. It did not connect to hospital systems. There were also open questions about responsibility for mistakes.

Key takeaways

  • The 1955 Dartmouth request named AI. McCarthy's Advice Taker started knowledge representation in logic.
  • Semantic networks store knowledge as a graph with inheritance. Collins and Quillian tested this with the canary.
  • Frames add slots and defaults. Scripts add the usual order of events.
  • Woods and Brachman showed that links need exact meaning. KL-ONE gave it, with subsumption and classification.
  • Brachman and Levesque showed that power costs speed. This led to description logics and later OWL.
  • MYCIN showed that rules can match experts, but tests are not the same as real use.
  • Prolog brought logic programming and a closed world. Datalog came from it.
  • Cyc tried to write all common sense by hand and proved the bottleneck.
  • The frame problem led to default reasoning. The AI winter killed the hype, not the ideas.

Sources

  • A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence. The 1955 request, reprinted in AI Magazine.
  • Semantic Networks. John Sowa's history: Richens, Quillian, Woods, KL-ONE and conceptual graphs.
  • A Framework for Representing Knowledge. Minsky's 1974 MIT memo on frames.
  • The Certainty-Factor Model. David Heckerman's review of MYCIN's certainty factors and their limits.
  • The Frame Problem. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: McCarthy and Hayes, and later solutions.
  • CYC: Using Common Sense Knowledge to Overcome Brittleness and Knowledge Acquisition Bottlenecks. Lenat and colleagues in AI Magazine, 1985.

The ontology engineering era (1990-2000)

Around 1990, AI teams built every knowledge base from zero. In the next ten years they learned to share and reuse them. Ontology became an engineering job, with languages, methods, tools and the first big success.

  • Explain why the DARPA Knowledge Sharing Effort wanted shared ontologies.
  • Read small examples in KIF, Ontolingua, SHOE and DAML+OIL, and write them in Turtle.
  • Check a model with Gruber's five design rules and with OntoClean.
  • Name the first methods, tools and upper ontologies of the decade.
  • Explain why the Gene Ontology became the first big success.

The problem: every team started from zero

Picture two hospitals in 1990. Each one builds an expert system for heart problems. The first system says "heart attack". The second says "myocardial infarction". Both mean the same thing.

Each knowledge base took years to build. But the second hospital cannot reuse the first one. The words are different, and the file formats are different too.

A 1992 progress report starts with exactly this problem. Teams in the same field, like medicine, each built their own knowledge base from scratch. The authors said this cost too much. It would cost even more as systems grew.

The Knowledge Sharing Effort

The US research agency DARPA paid for a joint answer. It was called the Knowledge Sharing Effort. A 1991 article in AI Magazine described it. Robert Neches coordinated it from November 1989. Other sponsors were the Air Force research office, the NSF and a research organisation called CNRI.

The work was split into four working groups. Each group attacked one wall between systems.

The four working groups and what they made
GroupGoalMain result
InterlinguaOne shared language for knowledgeKIF
Knowledge Representation System Specification (KRSS)Remove small, random differences between languages of the KL-ONE familyA common specification
External InterfacesLet programs ask each other questionsKQML, a message language for agents
Shared, Reusable Knowledge Bases (SRKB)Agree on common words and modulesShared ontologies

Why one shared language saves work

The Interlingua group had a simple counting argument. An interlingua cuts the number of translators.

  1. Without a middle language, each system needs a translator to every other system. For n systems that is n(n-1) one-way translators.
  2. With five systems: 5 \times 4 = 20 translators.
  3. With a middle language, each system needs one translator in and one out. That is 2n translators.
  4. With five systems: 2 \times 5 = 10 translators. With ten systems: 20 instead of 90.

The 1991 article also gave a working meaning of the word ontology. An ontology names the basic terms and relations of a topic. It also gives the rules for combining them. So two systems that share an ontology share their words and the rules for using them.

Knowledge sharing is not file sharing. You can copy a file in a second. But the other system must also understand every word in it. That shared understanding is the ontology.

KIF and Ontolingua: one language, many systems

The Interlingua group wrote the KIF manual. Version 3.0 is dated June 1992. Michael Genesereth and Richard Fikes edited it at Stanford. KIF can say anything that first-order logic can say.

KIF looks like the programming language Lisp. Every sentence is a list in round brackets. Variables start with a question mark. The arrow => means "if ... then".

Tom Gruber at Stanford built Ontolingua on top of KIF. His idea was the translation approach. You write an ontology once, in Ontolingua. Then a program translates it into the languages of several other systems. Gruber described it in a 1992 Stanford report, KSL-92-71. The journal Knowledge Acquisition printed it in 1993.

Here is one rule of Mia's bike shop in three languages. The first two are historical. The third is how you write it today.

;; Every city bike is a bike.
(forall ?x
  (=> (city-bike ?x)
      (bike ?x)))
;; :def gives a necessary condition for the class.
(define-class city-bike (?x)
  "A bike made for streets in a town."
  :def (bike ?x))
@prefix shop: <http://example.org/shop#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

shop:CityBike rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike .

I wrote the KIF and Ontolingua lines with the forms shown in the 1992 progress report and in the Ontolingua reference manual. No tool today runs them, so I could not test them. The Turtle line parses with Python's rdflib.

By 1996 the Stanford team had put Ontolingua on the web. Adam Farquhar, Richard Fikes and James Rice built the Ontolingua Server. People in different places could open, edit and reuse ontologies in a web browser. It kept a library of shared ontologies.

KIF never became a formal standard. But its ideas live on in Common Logic, the ISO/IEC 24707 standard from 2007, revised in 2018. One dialect of Common Logic, CLIF, looks very much like KIF.

KIF is not a programming language. Nothing "runs" a KIF file like a script. KIF is a format for passing knowledge from one program to another.

Gruber's paper and five design rules

You met Gruber's famous 1993 sentence in What is an ontology?. An ontology is an explicit specification of a conceptualization. Here we look at his second paper. It tells you how to design a good ontology.

Gruber first gave this talk at a workshop in Padova, Italy, in March 1993. He revised it in August 1993. The International Journal of Human-Computer Studies printed it in 1995. It proposes five design rules. Each row below uses Mia's bike shop.

Gruber's five design criteria (1995)
RuleMeaningGood exampleBad example
ClarityDefinitions are exact and objective. Give full definitions when you can."A city bike is a bike with mudguards and a bell.""A city bike is a nice bike for town."
CoherenceWhat follows from the rules must agree with the meaning. The rules must not contradict each other.Every bike has at least two wheels. A tricycle is a bike.Every bike has exactly two wheels. A tricycle is a bike.
ExtendibilityYou can add new terms without changing old ones.Add E-bike under Bike later.Rewrite Bike each time a new kind arrives.
Minimal encoding biasChoose terms for their meaning, not for one tool or file format.Price is a decimal number with a currency.Price is text, because the old database stored text.
Minimal ontological commitmentSay only what the shared task needs. Users can add more detail.A customer has a name.Every customer must have a birth date and a shoe size.

The rules can pull against each other. Clarity wants full definitions. Minimal commitment wants you to say as little as possible. A good designer finds a balance for the task.

Say exactly what you mean. Do not contradict yourself. Leave room to grow. Do not let one tool shape the words. Do not force more on users than they need.

Students often think "minimal commitment" means "make it small". It means "do not force extra claims on the people who share it". A big ontology can still make few forced claims.

WordNet: a network of English words

Here is how WordNet sees the word "bicycle". Click a node to open or close it.

WordNet started in 1985 at Princeton University. The psychologist George A. Miller led it. He wanted to model how people store word meanings in the mind. Later Christiane Fellbaum led the project.

WordNet groups words with the same meaning into a synset. The bicycle synset holds four words: bicycle, bike, wheel and cycle. Synsets are linked by a few relations.

  • A hypernym is more general. "Vehicle" is a hypernym of "bicycle".
  • A hyponym is more special. "Tandem" is a hyponym of "bicycle".
  • A meronym names a part. "Pedal" is a meronym of "bicycle".

Princeton's last full release was WordNet 3.0 in 2006. A database for version 3.1 followed in 2011. Today the community project Open English WordNet keeps it alive. Its site lists about 120,000 synsets. In the 1990s WordNet was the biggest free network of meanings. Many AI projects used it as a light ontology. SUMO, which you meet below, was later mapped to it.

WordNet is about word senses, not about things in the world. Look at the synset again. It contains "wheel", because some people say "wheel" for a bike. A real ontology of bikes would never mix the bike and its wheel like this.

Guarino and formal ontology

Nicola Guarino worked at a research institute of the Italian CNR in Padova. With Roberto Poli he organised a workshop on formal ontology there in March 1993. Gruber's design paper was first presented at that workshop.

In June 1998 the first conference called Formal Ontology in Information Systems, or FOIS, met in Trento, Italy. It ran from 6 to 8 June. Guarino edited the proceedings. His paper opens the book and makes three points.

  • Building an ontology needs philosophy and linguistics, not only computer science.
  • An ontology can be the centre of an information system. He called this an ontology-driven information system.
  • Ontologies come in four kinds, from very general to very special.

A top-level ontology describes very general ideas. Guarino said that, at least in theory, many users could agree on one such ontology. A domain ontology and a task ontology make the top-level terms more special. An application ontology uses both for one program.

The first upper ontologies

Guarino's top-level ontology is also called an upper ontology. The first famous ones grew out of the 1990s work. Their first versions appeared just after 2000.

Three upper ontologies that began around 2000
NameStartPeopleToday
SUMO (Suggested Upper Merged Ontology)IEEE project approved in December 2000. Paper at FOIS 2001.Ian Niles and Adam Pease, TeknowledgeWritten in SUO-KIF, a version of KIF. Mapped to WordNet.
DOLCEWonderWeb project reports in 2002 and 2003Masolo, Borgo, Gangemi, Guarino, Oltramari and othersISO/IEC 21838-3 (2023)
BFO (Basic Formal Ontology)2002Barry Smith and Pierre GrenonISO/IEC 21838-2 (2021). Its site says it is used by more than 550 projects.

You study these three in depth in Formal ontology and upper ontologies.

"Formal" here does not mean "polite". It means two things. The theory is written in logic. And it is about form: parts, wholes, identity and time, in any domain.

Methods: from art to engineering

In the early 1990s, each team built ontologies in its own way. It was a craft. Three groups wrote down a method, so that others could repeat it.

TOVE and competency questions

The TOVE project (Toronto Virtual Enterprise) began in the early 1990s. Mark Fox led it at the University of Toronto. In 1995 Michael Grüninger and Fox published its method. Its key idea is the competency question.

Motivating scenarios

Describe the real situation. Mia's shop loses track of bikes in repair.

Informal competency questions

Write the questions in English. "Which bikes are in repair now?" "Who owns bike B7?"

Terminology

Name the terms in logic: Bike, Customer, Repair, owns, inRepairSince.

Formal competency questions

Write each question again with these terms. Later you can write it as a query.

Axioms

Add rules and limits for the terms. The ontology is good when the axioms can answer every question.

The Enterprise Ontology

At the same time, a team in Edinburgh built the Enterprise Ontology. The lead was AIAI at the University of Edinburgh. The partners were IBM, Lloyd's Register, Logica and Unilever. The UK government paid for the project. The full paper appeared in The Knowledge Engineering Review in 1998. Mike Uschold was the first author.

The team first wrote every definition in plain English. They started with basic terms like entity, relationship and actor. Then they defined terms in four areas: activities, organisation, strategy and marketing. Finally they wrote the definitions again in Ontolingua. The paper reports which uses worked and which did not.

METHONTOLOGY

In 1997 Mariano Fernández, Asunción Gómez-Pérez and Natalia Juristo in Madrid published METHONTOLOGY. The paper's title says it all: from ontological art towards ontological engineering. They borrowed ideas from software engineering. Later papers say the process follows the software standard IEEE 1074.

METHONTOLOGY activities
KindActivities
ManagementPlanning, control, quality checks
DevelopmentSpecification, conceptualization, formalization, implementation, maintenance
Support (all the time)Knowledge acquisition, integration, evaluation, documentation

The ontology grows as a series of better and better prototypes. You do not finish one step for ever before the next.

OntoClean: checking the class tree

Many class trees have a hidden error. Look at this one.

Person is a subclass of Customer.

It looks fine in a shop system. Every person in the database bought something. But a person can stop being a customer and still be a person. So the tree says something false.

Nicola Guarino and Christopher Welty built a method for finding such errors. They first published the ideas in 2000. The name OntoClean first appeared in 2002, in Communications of the ACM. The method tags each class with four meta-properties.

The four OntoClean meta-properties
Meta-propertyQuestionExample
Rigidity (+R, -R, ~R)Must every member stay a member while it exists?Person is rigid (+R). Customer is anti-rigid (~R).
Identity (+I, -I)Does the class tell us how to tell two members apart?Person carries identity (+I). An amount of water does not (-I).
Unity (+U, -U, ~U)Is each member one whole thing?An ocean is a whole (+U). Water as stuff has anti-unity (~U).
Dependence (+D, -D)Does each member need something else to exist?A customer needs a shop (+D). A person does not (-D).

Some tags pass down the tree. If the parent has the tag ~R, +I, +U, ~U or +D, then the child must have it too. This short program checks that rule.

# Meta-properties for each class (Guarino and Welty's OntoClean).
# R: "+R" rigid, "-R" non-rigid, "~R" anti-rigid
# I: identity, U: unity ("~U" means anti-unity), D: dependence
meta = {
    "Person":   {"R": "+R", "I": "+I", "U": "+U", "D": "-D"},
    "Student":  {"R": "~R", "I": "+I", "U": "+U", "D": "+D"},
    "Customer": {"R": "~R", "I": "+I", "U": "+U", "D": "+D"},
    "Water":    {"R": "+R", "I": "-I", "U": "~U", "D": "-D"},
    "Ocean":    {"R": "+R", "I": "+I", "U": "+U", "D": "-D"},
}
# Each pair means: the first class is a subclass of the second.
subclass_of = [
    ("Student", "Person"),
    ("Person", "Customer"),   # a modelling mistake
    ("Ocean", "Water"),       # another mistake
]
# If the parent has this tag, the child must have it too.
inherited = ["~R", "+I", "+U", "~U", "+D"]

for child, parent in subclass_of:
    for tag in inherited:
        kind = tag[1]                      # "R", "I", "U" or "D"
        if meta[parent][kind] == tag and meta[child][kind] != tag:
            print(f"{child} under {parent}: parent is {tag}, "
                  f"child is {meta[child][kind]}")
use std::collections::HashMap;

// Tags in the order R, I, U, D. "~R" = anti-rigid, "~U" = anti-unity.
fn main() {
    let meta: HashMap<&str, [&str; 4]> = HashMap::from([
        ("Person",   ["+R", "+I", "+U", "-D"]),
        ("Student",  ["~R", "+I", "+U", "+D"]),
        ("Customer", ["~R", "+I", "+U", "+D"]),
        ("Water",    ["+R", "-I", "~U", "-D"]),
        ("Ocean",    ["+R", "+I", "+U", "-D"]),
    ]);
    // (child, parent): the child is a subclass of the parent.
    let subclass_of = [
        ("Student", "Person"),
        ("Person", "Customer"), // a modelling mistake
        ("Ocean", "Water"),     // another mistake
    ];
    // If the parent has this tag, the child must have it too.
    // The number is the position of the tag in the array.
    let inherited = [("~R", 0), ("+I", 1), ("+U", 2), ("~U", 2), ("+D", 3)];

    for (child, parent) in subclass_of {
        for (tag, i) in inherited {
            let (c, p) = (meta[child][i], meta[parent][i]);
            if p == tag && c != tag {
                println!("{child} under {parent}: parent is {tag}, child is {c}");
            }
        }
    }
}
Person under Customer: parent is ~R, child is +R
Person under Customer: parent is +D, child is -D
Ocean under Water: parent is ~U, child is +U

Both programs print the same three problems. Student under Person passes. The fix for the first mistake is to turn the link around. Customer is a subclass of Person.

Customer is a subclass of Person.

The tags are not facts of nature. They record what you mean in your model. In a game where people turn into ghosts, Person may be anti-rigid. OntoClean shows the logical result of your choices.

Tools and the first web languages

Protégé

Protégé began at Stanford in the 1980s. It started as Mark Musen's doctoral work. Musen dates the first version to 1987. It ran on Xerox Lisp machines. The Java version Protégé-2000 added plug-ins. Support for the web language OWL came in about 2004.

Protégé is still a widely used free editor. The latest stable desktop release is 5.6.9, from March 2026. A first alpha of version 6.0.0 came out in September 2026. There is also WebProtégé, which runs in the browser. The World Health Organization built its disease list ICD-11 with a WebProtégé-based tool.

SHOE: ontologies inside web pages

In 1996 a team at the University of Maryland asked a new question. Can web pages carry ontology data? Their answer was SHOE. Sean Luke, Lee Spector, David Rager, Jeff Heflin and James Hendler worked on it. SHOE added new tags to HTML. One tag declared an ontology. Other tags declared classes, relations and facts.

The SHOE 1.01 specification is dated 28 April 2000 on its own page. Another well-known index gives 3 February 2000. The sources disagree, so I give both.

OIL and DAML+OIL

Around 2000, Europe and the USA both paid for web ontology languages.

  • OIL (Ontology Inference Layer) came from a European project in 2000. Dieter Fensel, Frank van Harmelen, Ian Horrocks, Deborah McGuinness and Peter Patel-Schneider described it in 2001. It joined three ideas: frames for an easy look, description logics for exact meaning, and web standards like RDF. It came in layers: Core, Standard, Instance and Heavy OIL.
  • DAML (DARPA Agent Markup Language) was a US program led by James Hendler. Hendler's own slides say it started in 1999. Some other sources say 2000. Its first language, DAML-ONT, appeared in October 2000.
  • DAML+OIL joined the two in December 2000. A March 2001 version added data types from XML Schema. On 18 December 2001 it was published as a W3C Note.
<ONTOLOGY ID="bike-shop-ontology" VERSION="1.0">
  <DEF-CATEGORY NAME="Bike">
  <DEF-CATEGORY NAME="CityBike" ISA="Bike">
  <DEF-RELATION NAME="soldBy">
    <DEF-ARG POS="1" TYPE="Bike">
    <DEF-ARG POS="2" TYPE="Shop">
  </DEF-RELATION>
</ONTOLOGY>
<daml:Class rdf:ID="CityBike">
  <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="#Bike"/>
  <rdfs:subClassOf>
    <daml:Restriction>
      <daml:onProperty rdf:resource="#hasPart"/>
      <daml:hasClass rdf:resource="#Bell"/>
    </daml:Restriction>
  </rdfs:subClassOf>
</daml:Class>
@prefix shop: <http://example.org/shop#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .

shop:CityBike a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike ,
        [ a owl:Restriction ;              # every city bike ...
          owl:onProperty shop:hasPart ;    # ... has a part ...
          owl:someValuesFrom shop:Bell ] . # ... that is a bell

In DAML+OIL, daml:hasClass means "at least one value is in this class". OWL later renamed it owl:someValuesFrom. The partner daml:toClass means "all values are in this class". OWL calls it owl:allValuesFrom. I checked the SHOE and DAML+OIL lines against their specifications but could not run them. The Turtle version parses with rdflib and gives 6 triples.

The W3C started its Web Ontology Working Group to turn DAML+OIL into a standard. The group's charter gives November 2001 as its start. A 2003 slide by Hendler says November 2002, so the sources disagree here too. The result, OWL, is the story of the next chapter.

Do not mix up hasClass and toClass. "Some part is a bell" and "all parts are bells" are very different claims. The same trap exists in OWL with someValuesFrom and allValuesFrom.

The Gene Ontology: the first big success

Here is one real entry from the Gene Ontology. It is written in the OBO format that biologists use.

[Term]
id: GO:0019319
name: hexose biosynthetic process
namespace: biological_process
def: "The chemical reactions and pathways resulting in the formation of hexose, any monosaccharide with a chain of six carbon atoms in the molecule."
synonym: "hexose biosynthesis" EXACT
is_a: GO:0019318 ! hexose metabolic process
is_a: GO:0046364 ! monosaccharide biosynthetic process

The term has a stable number, a name, a definition, a synonym and two parents. All values come from the QuickGO service. I put them into the OBO layout myself. The real term has three more exact synonyms.

The Gene Ontology, or GO, started in 1998. Three databases of model animals agreed to use the same words: FlyBase for the fruit fly, SGD for yeast and MGD for the mouse. In 2000 the founders published a paper in Nature Genetics. Its title called GO a tool for the unification of biology.

GO has three parts. Each part answers one question about a gene product.

  • Molecular function. What does it do? For example, it binds sugar.
  • Biological process. In which bigger job does it take part? For example, making hexose.
  • Cellular component. Where in the cell does it work? For example, in the cell membrane.

Why did GO succeed when many other ontologies stayed in papers? Here is my reading of the history.

  • A real, painful problem. By 1998 genome data grew very fast. Labs could not compare results without shared words.
  • A simple structure. Terms, definitions, "is a" and "part of" links. No heavy logic at the start.
  • Stable numbers. A GO number never changes its meaning. Old terms become obsolete but are not deleted.
  • People who curate. Experts read papers and link genes to terms every day.
  • Open and free. Anyone can download and use it.

A GO term is not a gene. It describes what a gene product does, where, and in which process. The link between a gene and a term is called an annotation.

The decade on one line

Here are the main dates of this chapter. Where sources disagree, the entry says so.

  1. 1985 WordNet starts. George A. Miller at Princeton.
  2. 1987 First Protégé. Mark Musen at Stanford, on Lisp machines.
  3. Nov 1989 Knowledge Sharing Effort. Robert Neches coordinates the DARPA project.
  4. 1991 AI Magazine article. The four working groups and the plan.
  5. Jun 1992 KIF 3.0 manual. Genesereth and Fikes, Stanford.
  6. 1992-93 Gruber's Ontolingua paper. Report KSL-92-71, then the 1993 journal paper.
  7. Mar 1993 Padova workshop. Formal ontology meets knowledge engineering.
  8. 1995 Design rules and competency questions. Gruber's five criteria. Grüninger and Fox's TOVE method.
  9. 1996 SHOE and the Ontolingua Server. Ontologies meet the web.
  10. 1997 METHONTOLOGY. Ontology building as engineering.
  11. 1998 Gene Ontology, FOIS and the Enterprise Ontology paper. A busy year.
  12. 1999 or 2000 DAML program starts. Sources disagree on the year.
  13. 2000 OIL, DAML-ONT, DAML+OIL, OntoClean ideas. SUMO's IEEE project is approved in December.
  14. Dec 2001 DAML+OIL becomes a W3C Note. The road to OWL begins.
  15. 2002 BFO and DOLCE begin. The name OntoClean appears in print.
What survived from this decade?

Many things. Competency questions are still the first step of most methods. Protégé is still the main free editor. The Gene Ontology is bigger than ever. DAML+OIL became OWL. KIF lives on in Common Logic and in SUMO.

What did not survive?

KIF as a daily language, Ontolingua as a system, and SHOE. Their ideas moved into RDF and OWL, which the web community adopted.

Why does the word "engineering" matter?

Engineering means a repeatable way to build things, with steps, tests and tools. Before 1990 each ontology was a one-time work of art. After 2000, teams could plan, test and maintain ontologies like software.

Patterns to remember

These moves from the 1990s are still used every day. Each row joins an old idea to a model you can write today.

Lessons of the ontology engineering era as reusable patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
Shared middle languageConnect many systems with few translatorsFive systems need 10 translators, not 20.The middle language must be as expressive as the richest system.
Write once, translate many timesKeep one source of truthOntolingua to several target systemsA weak target language loses some meaning.
Competency question firstSet the scope before modelling"Which bikes are in repair now?"No question, no reason for the term.
Plain English, then logicAgree on meaning before syntaxEnterprise Ontology: English text, then OntolinguaKeep the English definition next to the formal one.
Clarity testMake a definition exact"A city bike has mudguards and a bell."Words like "nice" or "usual" fail the test.
Minimal commitmentForce only what the task needsA customer has a name.Optional details stay optional.
Anti-rigid under rigidPlace role classes correctly:Customer rdfs:subClassOf :Person .Never put a rigid class under a role.
Stuff is not a wholeKeep amounts of matter apart from objectsAn ocean is made of water. It is not a kind of water.Use "made of", not "is a".
Some versus allChoose the right restrictionowl:someValuesFrom shop:BellallValuesFrom means every value. It is a much stronger claim.
Stable identifierLet others link to you for yearsGO:0019319Never reuse an old number for a new meaning.
Synset is not a classUse a word network correctlybicycle, bike, wheel, cycleA synset groups words. A class groups things.

Practice

Which working group of the Knowledge Sharing Effort made KIF?

  • External Interfaces
  • Interlingua
  • Shared, Reusable Knowledge Bases

KIF is the shared middle language. External Interfaces made the message language KQML.

An ontology stores prices as text because one old database did. Which of Gruber's rules does it break?

  • Coherence
  • Extendibility
  • Minimal encoding bias

A choice made for one tool or file format is an encoding bias.

Which DAML+OIL word means "at least one value is in this class"?

  • daml:toClass
  • daml:hasClass
  • daml:cardinality

hasClass is the "some" restriction. OWL calls it someValuesFrom.

Which three databases founded the Gene Ontology in 1998?

  • FlyBase, SGD and MGD
  • WordNet, DBpedia and Cyc
  • GenBank, PubMed and UniProt

The fly, yeast and mouse databases agreed to use the same words.

Fill in the missing words.

A set of words with one shared meaning in WordNet is a ?.

A question that the finished ontology must answer is a ?.

With 8 systems and no middle language you need ? one-way translators.

  1. Write this KIF sentence as one Turtle triple: (forall ?x (=> (mountain-bike ?x) (bike ?x))).
    Answer

    shop:MountainBike rdfs:subClassOf shop:Bike . The KIF sentence says every mountain bike is a bike. That is exactly what rdfs:subClassOf says.

  2. A model says "Employee is a subclass of Person" and "Person is a subclass of Employee". Use OntoClean to find the wrong link.
    Answer

    Employee is anti-rigid (~R). A person can stop being an employee. Person is rigid (+R). A rigid class cannot sit under an anti-rigid class, so "Person is a subclass of Employee" is wrong. Keep only "Employee is a subclass of Person".

  3. Write three competency questions for a small library ontology.
    Answer

    One possible set. Which books are on loan now? Which member has borrowed book X? Which books by author Y does the library own? Your questions can be different. Each question should need the ontology to answer it.

  4. Give two reasons why the Gene Ontology succeeded where many 1990s ontologies did not.
    Answer

    It solved a real and urgent problem, because labs could not compare genome data. It also kept a simple structure with stable numbers, so many groups could use it at once. Open access and daily curation also helped.

  5. Hard: Gruber's clarity rule and his minimal commitment rule can pull in opposite directions. Explain with one example.
    Answer

    Clarity asks for a full definition of City bike, for example "a bike with mudguards, a bell and a basket". Minimal commitment asks you not to force extra claims on users. A shop that sells city bikes without baskets cannot use the full definition. A balance is "a bike with mudguards and a bell", which is exact but forces less.

Key takeaways

  • Around 1990 every AI team built its knowledge base from zero. The Knowledge Sharing Effort tried to end this.
  • KIF gave a shared logic language. Ontolingua let you write an ontology once and translate it.
  • Gruber's five rules are clarity, coherence, extendibility, minimal encoding bias and minimal ontological commitment.
  • WordNet is a huge network of word senses. It is useful, but it is about words, not things.
  • Guarino brought formal ontology into information systems. OntoClean checks the class tree with four meta-properties.
  • TOVE, the Enterprise Ontology and METHONTOLOGY turned ontology building into a method.
  • SHOE, OIL and DAML+OIL brought ontologies to the web and led to OWL.
  • The Gene Ontology (1998) succeeded with a real problem, a simple structure, stable numbers and daily curation.

Sources

  • Enabling Technology for Knowledge Sharing. The 1991 AI Magazine article by Neches and others on the Knowledge Sharing Effort.
  • Toward Principles for the Design of Ontologies Used for Knowledge Sharing. Gruber's 1995 paper with the five design criteria.
  • Formal Ontology and Information Systems. Guarino's FOIS 1998 paper with the four kinds of ontology.
  • DAML+OIL (March 2001) Reference Description. The W3C Note of 18 December 2001, with its history.
  • About the Gene Ontology. The GO project's own introduction and history.
  • Protégé releases. The official release list, with 5.6.9 and 6.0.0-alpha-1.

The Semantic Web era (1999-2012)

In the late 1990s Tim Berners-Lee wanted a web that machines could understand. The W3C built standards for it: RDF, RDF Schema, OWL and SPARQL. Some parts changed the world. Other parts never left the lab. This chapter tells both stories.

  • Retell the vision of the 2001 Semantic Web article in your own words.
  • Put RDF, RDF Schema, OWL, OWL 2 and SPARQL on a timeline with correct dates.
  • Write the same data in Turtle, RDF/XML and JSON-LD.
  • Apply the four Linked Data rules and follow links from one dataset to another.
  • Explain what worked in the Semantic Web, what did not, and why.

A dream: a web that machines understand

In May 2001 Scientific American printed a story about two adult children, Pete and Lucy. Their mother needs physical therapy. Lucy asks her software helper to plan it.

  1. Lucy's helper gets the treatment plan from the doctor's helper.
  2. It finds therapists near the mother's home who accept her insurance and have good ratings.
  3. It compares their free times with Pete's and Lucy's calendars.
  4. Pete wants a closer place. His own helper searches again with stricter rules.
  5. The new plan is ready in minutes. The helper can explain how it found the answer.

The helpers in the story are software agents. They do not understand English. They understand data with a clear meaning. The article calls this future the Semantic Web.

The authors were Tim Berners-Lee, James Hendler and Ora Lassila. Berners-Lee invented the web. Hendler ran the DAML program that you met in the last chapter. Lassila co-edited the first RDF standard.

The idea was older than the article. Berners-Lee wrote a "Semantic Web Road map" note in September 1998. His 1999 book Weaving the Web also describes the dream. The article made it famous.

The article names the main parts of the plan.

  • Structured data in web pages, with a meaning that programs can read.
  • URIs as global names for things.
  • RDF to write facts as small three-part statements.
  • Ontologies to define the words, with a taxonomy and rules.
  • Agents that collect data, reason and explain their answers.
  • Proof and trust, with digital signatures, so agents can check who said what.

The Semantic Web was never planned as a second, separate web. The article calls it an extension of the existing web. The same pages and links get extra data that machines can read.

URIs: one global name for each thing

Say the word "Paris". Do you mean the city in France, a town in Texas or a person called Paris? A program cannot guess. A global name solves this.

http://dbpedia.org/resource/Paris           # the city in France
http://dbpedia.org/resource/Paris,_Texas    # the town in Texas

A URI is such a name. A web address (a URL) is one kind of URI. The rules for writing URIs are in the internet standard RFC 3986, from January 2005. It replaced RFC 2396 from August 1998. An IRI is a URI that allows letters from any language. RFC 3987 defines it, also from January 2005.

The Semantic Web uses URIs for things, not only for pages. Mia herself can have a URI. Her shop, her city and the class Bike can have URIs too.

A name for a thing, a page about the thing

Here a problem appears. If you look up Mia's URI, you get a web page. But Mia is not a web page. A W3C note from 3 December 2008, "Cool URIs for the Semantic Web", gives two solutions.

Hash URI

http://example.org/about#mia

The browser drops the part after # before it asks the server. It gets the page about. The page describes Mia, whose name is the full URI.

303 URI

http://example.org/id/mia

The server answers with the code 303, "See Other". It sends you to a page like /doc/mia. The page is about Mia. It is not Mia.

Do not use the address of your home page as your own name in data. If you do, the data says that a web page has a birthday and a phone number. Use a hash URI or a 303 URI for the person.

RDF and RDF Schema

Here is one small fact in four different notations. Each tab shows the same three statements. The tabs were made by Python's rdflib from the Turtle file.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .

ex:mia a foaf:Person ;
    foaf:name "Mia Berg" ;
    foaf:knows ex:leo .
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<rdf:RDF
   xmlns:foaf="http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/"
   xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#"
>
  <rdf:Description rdf:about="http://example.org/mia">
    <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/Person"/>
    <foaf:name>Mia Berg</foaf:name>
    <foaf:knows rdf:resource="http://example.org/leo"/>
  </rdf:Description>
</rdf:RDF>
[
  {
    "@id": "http://example.org/mia",
    "@type": [
      "http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/Person"
    ],
    "http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/knows": [
      {
        "@id": "http://example.org/leo"
      }
    ],
    "http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/name": [
      {
        "@value": "Mia Berg"
      }
    ]
  }
]
<http://example.org/mia> <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/knows> <http://example.org/leo> .
<http://example.org/mia> <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/name> "Mia Berg" .
<http://example.org/mia> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/Person> .

In N-Triples you see the true shape of the data. Every line is one triple: a subject, a predicate and an object. The order of the lines does not matter. It can change from run to run.

RDF became a W3C Recommendation on 22 February 1999. Ora Lassila and Ralph Swick edited it. In 1999 RDF had only one notation, and it was XML. That is the RDF/XML tab.

RDF Schema

RDF gives the shape of facts. RDF Schema (RDFS) gives a small vocabulary for meaning. It has words like rdfs:Class, rdfs:subClassOf, rdfs:domain and rdfs:range.

RDFS took a long road. It was a Proposed Recommendation in March 1999. It became a Candidate Recommendation on 27 March 2000 and stayed there for years. It became a full Recommendation only on 10 February 2004. On that day the W3C published a new set of six RDF documents, with clearer meaning and test cases.

The RDF family, step by step
DateWhat
22 Feb 1999RDF Model and Syntax: Recommendation. Only RDF/XML.
27 Mar 2000RDF Schema 1.0: Candidate Recommendation.
10 Feb 2004RDF Concepts, Semantics, RDF/XML, RDF Schema and more: Recommendations.
16 Jan 2014JSON-LD 1.0: Recommendation.
25 Feb 2014RDF 1.1, with Turtle, N-Triples, TriG and N-Quads as standards.

Turtle feels old, but it became a W3C standard only in 2014. In the Semantic Web years most people saw RDF as XML. Many found it hard to read, and this hurt RDF's image.

RDF is not XML. RDF is a graph of triples. RDF/XML is only one way to write that graph in a file. Turtle and JSON-LD write the same graph.

OWL and OWL 2

RDFS can say "a city bike is a bike". It cannot say "every bike has at least two wheels". For this you need OWL.

@prefix shop: <http://example.org/shop#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# OWL 2: every bike has at least two parts that are wheels.
shop:Bike rdfs:subClassOf [
    a owl:Restriction ;
    owl:onProperty shop:hasPart ;
    owl:minQualifiedCardinality "2"^^xsd:nonNegativeInteger ;
    owl:onClass shop:Wheel
] .

This file parses with rdflib and gives 5 triples. The word owl:onClass counts only parts that are wheels. This "qualified" count is new in OWL 2. The first OWL could only say "at least two parts".

The W3C Web Ontology Working Group started from DAML+OIL. OWL became a Recommendation on 10 February 2004, on the same day as the new RDF documents. It came in three versions, called species.

OWL (2004) and OWL 2 (2009)
VersionDatePartsIdea
OWL10 Feb 2004OWL Lite, OWL DL, OWL FullOWL DL follows a description logic, so a reasoner always finishes. OWL Full allows everything, but no reasoner can always finish.
OWL 227 Oct 2009OWL 2 DL and three profiles: EL, QL, RLMore features, like qualified counts. Each profile is a smaller language that runs fast.
OWL 2, second edition11 Dec 2012SameCorrections and clearer text.

The three OWL 2 profiles each fit one job. EL is for very large class trees, like medical terms. QL is for asking questions over big databases. RL is for rule engines. You learn them in OWL 2.

OWL does not check data like a database. If a bike in your data has only one wheel, OWL does not report an error. It assumes the second wheel exists but is not written down. For checks you need SHACL. See SHACL and validation.

SPARQL: asking the graph

Here is a small dataset for Mia's shop. It uses three shared vocabularies: FOAF for people, Dublin Core for documents and SKOS for topics. You meet them in a later section.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
@prefix dct:  <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .
@prefix skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

foaf:Person rdfs:subClassOf foaf:Agent .        # copied from FOAF

ex:mia a foaf:Person ; foaf:name "Mia Berg" ; foaf:knows ex:leo .
ex:leo a foaf:Person ; foaf:name "Leo Park" .
ex:shop a foaf:Organization ; foaf:name "Mia's Bikes" .

ex:guide1 dct:title "Fixing a flat tyre" ;      # Dublin Core terms
    dct:creator ex:mia ;
    dct:subject ex:tyres .

ex:tyres a skos:Concept ;                        # a SKOS concept scheme
    skos:prefLabel "Tyres"@en ;
    skos:broader ex:bikeParts .
ex:bikeParts a skos:Concept ;
    skos:prefLabel "Bike parts"@en .

Now two questions in SPARQL. The first asks who wrote which guide, about which topic. The second asks for every agent.

from rdflib import Graph
g = Graph().parse("shop.ttl")

q1 = """
PREFIX foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/>
PREFIX dct:  <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?name ?title ?topic ?wider WHERE {
  ?doc dct:creator ?p ; dct:title ?title ; dct:subject ?s .
  ?p foaf:name ?name .
  ?s skos:prefLabel ?topic .
  OPTIONAL { ?s skos:broader/skos:prefLabel ?wider }
}"""
for row in g.query(q1):
    print(row.name, "|", row.title, "|", row.topic, "|", row.wider)

q2 = """
PREFIX foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?name WHERE {
  ?x a/rdfs:subClassOf* foaf:Agent ;   # a type, then zero or more steps up
     foaf:name ?name .
} ORDER BY ?name"""
print([str(r.name) for r in g.query(q2)])
Mia Berg | Fixing a flat tyre | Tyres | Bike parts
['Leo Park', 'Mia Berg']

Look at the second answer. Mia's Bikes is a foaf:Organization. FOAF says that an organization is an agent. But that triple is not in our file. The query knows only what is in the graph. To fix it, add foaf:Organization rdfs:subClassOf foaf:Agent . or load the FOAF vocabulary.

SPARQL became a Recommendation on 15 January 2008. SPARQL 1.1 followed on 21 March 2013. It added updates, counting and grouping, subqueries, property paths like skos:broader/skos:prefLabel, and queries across several endpoints.

SPARQL 1.2 is not finished. The W3C RDF and SPARQL Working Group published a new Working Draft of SPARQL 1.2 Query on 12 November 2026. It is one of twelve SPARQL 1.2 documents. Check the W3C page for the latest status.

An empty answer does not mean "false". It means "not found in this graph". The Semantic Web assumes the world is open. Someone else may know more.

The layer cake

Berners-Lee liked to draw the plan as a stack of layers. People call it the layer cake. Each layer builds on the layers below. The first version is in a talk at the XML 2000 conference, in December 2000. A version on the W3C site from March 2007 looks like this.

December 2000 and March 2007 compared
Level2000 version2007 version
BaseUnicode, URIURI / IRI
SyntaxXML + namespaces + XML SchemaXML (RDF no longer needs it)
DataRDF + RDF SchemaRDF, then RDFS
MeaningOntology vocabularyOWL, plus SPARQL and RIF beside it
TopLogic, Proof, Trust, Digital signatureUnifying logic, Proof, Trust, Crypto, User interface

RIF, the Rule Interchange Format, became a W3C Recommendation on 22 June 2010. The layers above it never became standards. There is still no W3C standard for unifying logic, proof or trust.

The cake is a picture of ideas, not a software design. Real systems often skip layers. Many use RDF and SPARQL with no OWL at all.

Linked Data: the practical turn

By 2006 the full dream looked far away. On 27 July 2006 Berners-Lee wrote a short note called "Linked Data". It asked for something much simpler: publish data on the web and link it. The note gives four rules.

  1. Use URIs as names for things.
  2. Use HTTP URIs, so people can look the names up.
  3. When someone looks up a URI, return useful data in standards like RDF and SPARQL.
  4. Include links to other URIs, so people can find more things.

In 2010 he added a five-star scale for open data. One star means the data is on the web with an open licence. Five stars mean the data uses RDF and links to other people's data.

Rules 3 and 4 make a crawler possible. You start at one URI and follow links from site to site. People call this follow your nose. This program does it on a tiny pretend web.

from collections import deque

# A tiny pretend web. Each URI returns the facts published at it.
web = {
    "http://ex.org/mia": [("name", "Mia Berg"),
                          ("knows", "http://ex.org/leo"),
                          ("worksAt", "http://ex.org/shop")],
    "http://ex.org/leo": [("name", "Leo Park"),
                          ("basedNear", "http://places.example/Berlin")],
    "http://ex.org/shop": [("name", "Mia's Bikes"),
                           ("sameAs", "http://shops.example/42")],
    "http://places.example/Berlin": [("label", "Berlin")],
}   # http://shops.example/42 is missing: a dead link

def follow_your_nose(start, max_depth):
    seen, queue = {start}, deque([(start, 0)])
    while queue:
        uri, depth = queue.popleft()
        facts = web.get(uri)                  # rule 3: look the URI up
        if facts is None:
            print(f"{uri} -> 404, dead link")
            continue
        print(f"{uri} -> {len(facts)} fact(s)")
        if depth == max_depth:
            continue
        for _, obj in facts:                  # rule 4: follow the links
            if obj.startswith("http") and obj not in seen:
                seen.add(obj)
                queue.append((obj, depth + 1))

follow_your_nose("http://ex.org/mia", max_depth=2)
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet, VecDeque};

fn main() {
    // A tiny pretend web. Each URI returns the facts published at it.
    let web: HashMap<&str, Vec<(&str, &str)>> = HashMap::from([
        ("http://ex.org/mia", vec![("name", "Mia Berg"),
            ("knows", "http://ex.org/leo"), ("worksAt", "http://ex.org/shop")]),
        ("http://ex.org/leo", vec![("name", "Leo Park"),
            ("basedNear", "http://places.example/Berlin")]),
        ("http://ex.org/shop", vec![("name", "Mia's Bikes"),
            ("sameAs", "http://shops.example/42")]),
        ("http://places.example/Berlin", vec![("label", "Berlin")]),
    ]); // http://shops.example/42 is missing: a dead link

    let (start, max_depth) = ("http://ex.org/mia", 2);
    let mut seen = HashSet::from([start]);
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([(start, 0)]);
    while let Some((uri, depth)) = queue.pop_front() {
        let Some(facts) = web.get(uri) else {      // rule 3: look it up
            println!("{uri} -> 404, dead link");
            continue;
        };
        println!("{uri} -> {} fact(s)", facts.len());
        if depth == max_depth { continue; }
        for &(_, obj) in facts {                   // rule 4: follow links
            if obj.starts_with("http") && seen.insert(obj) {
                queue.push_back((obj, depth + 1));
            }
        }
    }
}
http://ex.org/mia -> 3 fact(s)
http://ex.org/leo -> 2 fact(s)
http://ex.org/shop -> 2 fact(s)
http://places.example/Berlin -> 1 fact(s)
http://shops.example/42 -> 404, dead link

Both programs print the same lines. The crawler starts at Mia and reaches a second site. It also finds a dead link. Dead links were a real, daily problem of Linked Data.

DBpedia and the Linked Open Data cloud

DBpedia takes the info boxes of Wikipedia and turns them into RDF. Teams at Leipzig University and FU Berlin started it, with help from the company OpenLink. Wikipedia gives the first release as 10 January 2007. An OpenLink blog says February 2007. The main paper, by Sören Auer and colleagues, was presented at the ISWC conference in Busan, Korea, in November 2007.

DBpedia gave everyone URIs for millions of well-known things. So it became the centre of the Linked Open Data cloud. A W3C community project started this cloud in early 2007. Its first diagram, from 1 May 2007, had 12 datasets.

Governments joined too. The UK site data.gov.uk opened on 21 January 2010. Berners-Lee and Nigel Shadbolt helped to build it, and it used Semantic Web technology.

A link is only useful while it works. Many Linked Data sites closed when research money ended. Their URIs then became dead links. Publishing data is a long promise, not a one-time job.

Shared vocabularies

Linked Data works best when many sites use the same words. Five vocabularies from this era are still everywhere. Swipe through them.

Dublin Core

The name comes from a workshop in Dublin, Ohio, in March 1995. OCLC and NCSA organised it. The core set has 15 elements, such as title, creator, date and subject.

It became ISO standard 15836 and IETF RFC 5013. Today people use the larger DCMI Metadata Terms, like dct:creator.

FOAF

FOAF means "Friend of a Friend". Dan Brickley and Libby Miller started it in mid-2000. It describes people, groups and their links: foaf:Person, foaf:name, foaf:knows.

The last specification is version 0.99, dated 14 January 2014.

SKOS

SKOS means Simple Knowledge Organization System. It became a W3C Recommendation on 18 August 2009. It describes thesauri and subject lists: skos:Concept, skos:prefLabel, skos:broader.

SKOS is lighter than OWL. "Broader" does not mean "subclass".

schema.org

Bing, Google and Yahoo started schema.org on 2 June 2011. Yandex joined in November 2011. It gives web pages one shared vocabulary for search engines.

Version 30.1 from 16 September 2026 has 826 types and 1,540 properties.

Why they lasted

All five are small, easy to start with and useful on day one. None of them needs a reasoner. You can use three words from them and ignore the rest.

You can see four of them at work in shop.ttl above. You read schema.org in a web page in What is an ontology?. More detail on each one is in Ontologies in the wild.

Do not read skos:broader as rdfs:subClassOf. In a library list, "Tyres" can sit under "Bike parts". But a tyre is not a kind of bike part list. SKOS links topics, not classes.

What worked, what did not, and why

In 2006 Nigel Shadbolt, Wendy Hall and Berners-Lee looked back in a paper called "The Semantic Web Revisited". They said the main idea was still largely not real. They also saw signs of success in science, where teams used ontologies to share data. Here is my reading of the whole era, up to 2012.

What worked

  • RDF as a simple, shared data model.
  • URIs as global names for things.
  • SPARQL as a standard query language.
  • OWL in life science and medicine, with big class trees.
  • Small vocabularies: Dublin Core, FOAF, SKOS.
  • schema.org markup. Its home page says over 45 million web domains used it in 2024.
  • Open data portals and DBpedia.

What did not

  • Smart agents like Lucy's helper.
  • Reasoning over the whole open web.
  • The proof and trust layers.
  • RDF/XML as a format people liked.
  • Many Linked Data sites, which closed.
  • One shared ontology for everyone.

Why did the big dream fail? Critics gave reasons early. In 2001 the writer Cory Doctorow published an essay called "Metacrap". He said people lie in their data, people are lazy, and people disagree. In November 2003 Clay Shirky wrote that real knowledge rarely fits neat logic rules. Different groups also see the world in different ways.

To these I add four reasons of my own.

  • No reason to publish. Sites did the work, but search engines and agents gave little back. schema.org changed this, because search results got better.
  • Hard tools. RDF/XML and OWL were hard for normal web developers. JSON and simple web APIs were easier.
  • Messy data. Open data has errors and conflicts. Strict logic breaks on one wrong fact.
  • No one pays to keep it. Research projects end. Their servers stop.

The small, practical parts won. The big, clever parts waited. Most ideas came back later in a new form, as you see in the next chapter.

The era on one line

  1. Mar 1995 Dublin Core workshop. Dublin, Ohio.
  2. Sep 1998 Semantic Web Road map. A design note by Berners-Lee.
  3. 22 Feb 1999 RDF Recommendation. RDF/XML only.
  4. 1999 Weaving the Web. Berners-Lee's book describes the dream.
  5. Mar 2000 RDF Schema 1.0. Candidate Recommendation.
  6. mid-2000 FOAF starts. Brickley and Miller.
  7. Dec 2000 First layer cake. XML 2000 conference talk.
  8. May 2001 "The Semantic Web". Scientific American article.
  9. 10 Feb 2004 RDF and OWL Recommendations. RDFS becomes final too.
  10. 27 Jul 2006 Linked Data note. The four rules.
  11. 2007 DBpedia and the LOD cloud. 12 datasets in May.
  12. 15 Jan 2008 SPARQL Recommendation.
  13. Oct 2008 RDFa. RDF inside HTML pages.
  14. Aug 2009 SKOS Recommendation.
  15. 27 Oct 2009 OWL 2 Recommendation. Profiles EL, QL, RL.
  16. 2010 data.gov.uk, RIF and five-star open data.
  17. 2 Jun 2011 schema.org. Bing, Google and Yahoo.
  18. Dec 2012 OWL 2 second edition.
  19. Mar 2013 SPARQL 1.1.

Patterns to remember

These moves come straight from the Semantic Web standards. You will use them in every RDF project.

Semantic Web patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
One thing, one URIName a thing globallyhttp://dbpedia.org/resource/ParisNever reuse a URI for a different thing.
Hash URI for a thingKeep the thing apart from its pagehttp://example.org/about#miaThe page is about. The person is #mia.
Subject, predicate, objectWrite one factex:mia foaf:knows ex:leo .Exactly three parts, then a full stop.
Reuse a known vocabularyLet others understand your datadct:creator instead of ex:authorCheck that the meaning really fits.
Class under classSay every A is a Bfoaf:Person rdfs:subClassOf foaf:Agent .Load the vocabulary, or the query will not know it.
Qualified countCount only parts of one classowl:minQualifiedCardinality 2 ; owl:onClass shop:WheelNew in OWL 2. Not a data check.
Optional data in a queryKeep rows when a value is missingOPTIONAL { ?s skos:broader ?b }Without OPTIONAL the row disappears.
Property pathWalk several links in one stepa/rdfs:subClassOf** means zero or more steps.
Topic under topicBuild a subject listex:tyres skos:broader ex:bikeParts .Broader is not subclass.
Link outConnect your data to the webex:shop owl:sameAs dbr:Some_Shop .sameAs merges all facts. Use it only for true identity.
Follow your noseDiscover more dataLook up a URI, then its linksExpect dead links and handle them.

Practice

Who wrote the 2001 Scientific American article "The Semantic Web"?

  • Gruber, Guarino and Musen
  • Berners-Lee, Hendler and Lassila
  • Brickley, Miller and Guha

Tim Berners-Lee, James Hendler and Ora Lassila wrote it. It appeared in May 2001.

Which date is correct for the first OWL Recommendation?

  • 22 February 1999
  • 10 February 2004
  • 27 October 2009

10 February 2004 is OWL and the new RDF set. 1999 is the first RDF. 2009 is OWL 2.

Which Linked Data rule does a crawler use when it follows a link to another site?

  • Rule 1: use URIs as names
  • Rule 2: use HTTP URIs
  • Rule 4: include links to other URIs

Rule 4 puts the links into the data. Without them, the crawler has nowhere to go.

An OWL ontology says every bike has two wheels. Your data has a bike with one wheel. What does an OWL reasoner do?

  • It reports an error.
  • It assumes the other wheel exists but is not written.
  • It deletes the bike.

OWL uses the open world. Missing data is unknown, not false.

Fill in the missing words.

The four Linked Data rules were written in the year ?.

The three OWL 2 profiles are EL, QL and ?.

In SPARQL, the keyword ? keeps a row when one value is missing.

  1. Write this fact as one Turtle triple: "Leo knows Mia". Use the prefixes from shop.ttl.
    Answer

    ex:leo foaf:knows ex:mia . Note that foaf:knows has a direction. The file says Mia knows Leo. It does not say Leo knows Mia.

  2. Change query 2 so that Mia's Bikes also appears. Give two different ways.
    Answer

    First way: add the triple foaf:Organization rdfs:subClassOf foaf:Agent . to the data. Second way: load the real FOAF vocabulary into the same graph, because it contains that triple.

  3. Why is http://example.org/mia.html a bad name for Mia in RDF data?
    Answer

    It is the address of a web page. Facts like "born in 1990" would then be about the page, not about the person. Use a hash URI like http://example.org/about#mia or a 303 URI.

  4. Name two parts of the layer cake that became W3C standards, and two that did not.
    Answer

    Standards: RDF, RDFS, OWL, SPARQL, RIF. Not standards: unifying logic, proof, trust.

  5. Hard: give three reasons why Lucy's agents never came. Use one critic from the chapter and one reason of your own.
    Answer

    Doctorow said people lie, are lazy and disagree, so web data is not reliable enough. Shirky said real knowledge rarely fits neat logic rules. A reason of your own could be that sites had no reward for publishing rich data until search engines used it. Other good answers mention messy data, hard tools or servers that closed.

Key takeaways

  • The Semantic Web wanted a web of data with a meaning that programs can use. The 2001 article made it famous.
  • URIs name things, not only pages. Hash URIs and 303 redirects keep a thing apart from its page.
  • RDF (1999, 2004) writes facts as triples. RDF Schema adds classes and subclasses. RDF/XML is only one notation.
  • OWL (2004) and OWL 2 (2009) add rich rules. They use the open world and do not check data.
  • SPARQL (2008) and SPARQL 1.1 (2013) query RDF. SPARQL 1.2 is still a Working Draft in November 2026.
  • Linked Data (2006) asked for simple, linked, published data. DBpedia became its centre.
  • Small vocabularies lasted: Dublin Core, FOAF, SKOS and schema.org.
  • The practical parts worked. Agents, web-wide reasoning, proof and trust did not.

Sources

  • The Semantic Web. The May 2001 Scientific American article by Berners-Lee, Hendler and Lassila.
  • Linked Data. Berners-Lee's design note of 27 July 2006, with the five-star scale from 2010.
  • RDF Model and Syntax Specification. The first RDF Recommendation, 22 February 1999.
  • OWL 2 Document Overview. The OWL 2 standard, with links to the 2004 OWL documents.
  • SPARQL 1.2 Query Language. The current Working Draft and its status section.
  • The Linked Open Data Cloud. The diagram and its dataset counts since 2007.

Knowledge graphs and the LLM era (2012-today)

In 2012 Google gave an old idea a new name: the knowledge graph. Since then, graphs of facts have moved into search engines, companies and data platforms. Now they give context to large language models. This chapter tells that story and ends with one timeline from Aristotle to November 2026.

  • Tell the story of Freebase, the Google Knowledge Graph and Wikidata with correct dates.
  • Write the same fact as a property graph in Cypher and GQL, and in RDF 1.2.
  • Check data with SHACL and read a validation report.
  • State the status of RDF 1.2, SPARQL 1.2 and GQL on 15 November 2026.
  • Explain how GraphRAG, agent memory graphs, MCP and the Agentic AI Foundation use or connect graphs.

Things, not strings: 2012

Type "Taj Mahal" into a search box. Do you mean the famous building in India, or the musician with the same name? Old search engines matched letters. They did not know that there are two different things.

On 16 May 2012 Google announced the Knowledge Graph. Amit Singhal, a senior vice president of engineering, wrote the blog post. Its title said "things, not strings". The graph helped search in three ways.

  • Find the right thing. It showed that one name can mean several things.
  • Show a summary. It listed key facts, such as dates of birth and main works.
  • Go deeper. It suggested related things to explore.

At launch the graph had more than 500 million objects and more than 3.5 billion facts. Google built it from public sources such as Freebase, Wikipedia and the CIA World Factbook. In May 2020 Google said the graph had over 500 billion facts about five billion entities.

A knowledge graph is not a new invention. You met the idea as semantic networks in AI and knowledge representation. Google's new name simply stuck.

Freebase: the open graph that Google bought

Much of the early Google graph came from Freebase. The company Metaweb launched it in March 2007. Anyone could add and edit facts, like a Wikipedia for data. Google bought Metaweb in a deal announced on 16 July 2010.

On 16 December 2014 the Freebase team announced the end. Freebase became read-only on 31 March 2015. The plan said the website and API would close by 30 June 2015. Another source says the site went offline only on 2 May 2016. So the final date depends on the source. The data moved to Wikidata, with people checking each imported fact.

A knowledge graph does not need RDF. Google never said which format its graph uses inside. "Knowledge graph" names the idea: things as nodes, facts as links. RDF is one way to store it. A property graph is another.

Wikidata: a knowledge graph anyone can edit

Wikidata knows its own history. This short program asks the public Wikidata query service when five projects started.

import json, urllib.parse, urllib.request

query = """
SELECT ?item ?itemLabel ?inception WHERE {
  VALUES ?item { wd:Q465 wd:Q1453477 wd:Q648625 wd:Q2013 wd:Q1628290 }
  OPTIONAL { ?item wdt:P571 ?inception }
  SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". }
} ORDER BY ?inception"""
url = "https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(
    {"query": query, "format": "json"})
req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "study-book-example/1.0"})
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as r:
    rows = json.load(r)["results"]["bindings"]
for row in rows:
    print(row["item"]["value"].split("/")[-1], row["itemLabel"]["value"],
          row.get("inception", {}).get("value", "-"))
Q465 DBpedia 2007-01-10T00:00:00Z
Q1453477 Freebase 2007-03-01T00:00:00Z
Q1628290 Neo4j 2010-02-01T00:00:00Z
Q648625 Google Knowledge Graph 2012-01-01T00:00:00Z
Q2013 Wikidata 2012-10-29T00:00:00Z

I ran it on 15 November 2026. Your answer can change, because anyone can edit Wikidata. P571 is the property "inception". The Q numbers are the items.

Look closely at two lines. "2012-01-01" for the Google Knowledge Graph does not mean 1 January. Wikidata stores a precision with each date. Here the precision is "year", so it means only "2012". Freebase has month precision: March 2007.

The Neo4j line shows a real disagreement. Wikidata says February 2010. Neo4j's own history page says version 1.0 came out in 2007. Good data keeps both claims with their sources.

The project

Wikidata went online on 29 October 2012. The first edit of item Q42, Douglas Adams, has that date in UTC time. A few reports say 30 October, maybe because of time zones. Wikimedia Deutschland built it. Wikipedias in every language can use its facts. All structured data is free under CC0.

The model is simple. Every thing is an item with a Q number. Every relation is a property with a P number. A statement joins them, and it can carry extra details and references to sources.

Wikidata in numbers
FactValue
Items (content pages)124,059,127 on 15 November 2026
Edits since 2012About 2.57 billion
Query service splitOn 9 May 2025, scholarly articles moved to a second endpoint

The split shows a real limit. The graph grew too big for one query server. Queries that need both parts must now use SPARQL SERVICE to ask both endpoints.

Do not read a Wikidata date without its precision. "2012-01-01" can mean "sometime in 2012". Ask for the precision value too, or check the item page.

Knowledge graphs inside companies

After 2012 many large companies built their own knowledge graphs. In August 2019 people from five of them wrote a joint paper in Communications of the ACM: "Industry-scale Knowledge Graphs: Lessons and Challenges". It grew out of a panel at the ISWC conference in October 2018.

Five company graphs in the 2019 paper
CompanyGraphWhat it holds
MicrosoftBing knowledge graphGeneral knowledge about the world
GoogleKnowledge GraphFacts for search and spoken answers
FacebookIts entity graphThe social graph, plus music, films and places
eBayProduct Knowledge GraphProducts, their parts and their links
IBMWatson Discovery frameworkTools so clients can build their own graph

The graph joins data that used to live in separate systems. The hard part is rarely the graph database. It is deciding which records are the same real thing. You study this in Enterprise and operational ontologies.

Many teams start with a graph database and no ontology. After a year the graph has five kinds of "customer" node. Agree on the classes and their identity rules first.

Property graphs: Neo4j, Cypher and GQL

Mia owns bike B7 since 2021. Where do you put "since 2021"? It belongs to the link between Mia and the bike, not to Mia or the bike. A property graph lets you put it on the link. Here is the same small graph in three notations.

import kuzu, tempfile, os

db = kuzu.Database(os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "shop.kz"))
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Person(name STRING, PRIMARY KEY(name))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Bike(id STRING, model STRING, PRIMARY KEY(id))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE OWNS(FROM Person TO Bike, since INT64)")

conn.execute("""
CREATE (mia:Person {name: 'Mia'}), (leo:Person {name: 'Leo'}),
       (b7:Bike {id: 'B7', model: 'City 3'}), (b9:Bike {id: 'B9', model: 'Trail X'}),
       (mia)-[:OWNS {since: 2021}]->(b7),
       (leo)-[:OWNS {since: 2018}]->(b9)
""")

res = conn.execute("""
