MATCH (p:Person)-[o:OWNS]->(b:Bike)
WHERE o.since >= 2020
RETURN p.name, b.model, o.since
ORDER BY p.name
""")
while res.has_next():
    print(res.get_next())
INSERT (:Person {name: 'Mia'})-[:OWNS {since: 2021}]->(:Bike {id: 'B7', model: 'City 3'})

MATCH (p:Person)-[o:OWNS]->(b:Bike)
WHERE o.since >= 2020
RETURN p.name, b.model, o.since
ORDER BY p.name
import pyoxigraph as ox

data = """
VERSION "1.2"
PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/>
ex:mia ex:owns ex:b7 ~ ex:own1 {| ex:since 2021 |} .  # ~ names the reifier
ex:leo ex:owns ex:b9 ~ ex:own2 {| ex:since 2018 |} .
ex:b7 ex:model "City 3" .
ex:b9 ex:model "Trail X" .
"""
store = ox.Store()
store.load(data.encode(), format=ox.RdfFormat.TURTLE)
for quad in sorted(str(q.triple) for q in store if "own1" in str(q)):
    print(quad)                                      # the triples about own1

query = """
PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/>
SELECT ?p ?model ?since WHERE {
  ?p ex:owns ?b {| ex:since ?since |} .              # SPARQL 1.2 annotation
  ?b ex:model ?model .
  FILTER(?since >= 2020)
}"""
for row in store.query(query):
    print(row["p"].value, row["model"].value, row["since"].value)

The Cypher tab runs with Kuzu 0.11.3 on Python 3.13 and prints one row.

['Mia', 'City 3', 2021]

I tested the Cypher with Kuzu, a small graph database that runs inside Python. Kuzu needs table definitions first, so the script has three CREATE ... TABLE lines. Neo4j does not need them. Note that the Kuzu project was archived in October 2025. Use it for learning, not for new products.

I had no GQL engine, so the GQL tab is not tested. It has two separate statements. The first adds Mia and her bike with INSERT, where Cypher says CREATE. The second is the query, the same as in Cypher. Neo4j's documentation lists INSERT as the GQL statement for adding data. It also says Cypher and GQL differ only a little. The RDF 1.2 tab is explained in the next section.

A short history of property graphs

  • Neo4j. The company says its founders invented the property graph model in 2000, and that Neo4j 1.0 came out in 2007. Wikidata gives February 2010. The sources disagree.
  • Cypher. Neo4j's query language appeared in 2011. Its first public release came with Neo4j 1.4 in July 2011.
  • openCypher. In October 2015 Neo4j opened Cypher so that other databases could use it.
  • SQL/PGQ. In June 2023 ISO added property graph queries to SQL, as ISO/IEC 9075-16:2023.
  • GQL. ISO/IEC 39075:2024 was published in April 2024. The GQL standards site says 17 April. Some standards shops say 11 April.

GQL is a full ISO database language, like SQL. Its pattern part is almost the same as in SQL/PGQ.

The 2024 first edition of GQL is still the current published standard. A Technical Corrigendum, ISO/IEC 39075:2024/Cor 1:2026, was published in July 2026. A second edition is at the Committee Draft stage. Its comment period closed on 30 January 2026. I could not open ISO's own page, so these facts come from national standards catalogues that copy ISO's records. Check the ISO page for the latest.

"Property graph" and "RDF graph" are not enemies. They store the same kind of facts. The big old difference was data on links. RDF 1.2 closes much of that gap.

RDF 1.2: statements about statements

Look at the output of the RDF 1.2 tab above.

<http://example.org/own1> <http://example.org/since> "2021"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer>
<http://example.org/own1> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#reifies> <<( <http://example.org/mia> <http://example.org/owns> <http://example.org/b7> )>>
http://example.org/mia City 3 2021

The part in <<( ... )>> is a triple term. It is a triple used as a value. The node ex:own1 is a reifier. It points to the triple with rdf:reifies. Then you can say things about it, like "since 2021".

The idea is older than the standard. In June 2014 Olaf Hartig and Bryan Thompson published a paper with a new way to do reification in RDF. People called it RDF-star. A W3C working group then turned it into RDF 1.2. The group started as the RDF-star Working Group. Its documents now say RDF and SPARQL Working Group.

RDF 1.2 adds three things to RDF 1.1.

  • Triple terms, in the object position of a triple.
  • Text direction for language-tagged strings, for languages like Arabic.
  • A version label, such as VERSION "1.2", so tools know what to expect.
Status of RDF 1.2, SPARQL 1.2 and SHACL 1.2 at W3C, on 15 November 2026
DocumentLatest versionStage
RDF 1.2 Concepts and Abstract Data Model13 November 2026Candidate Recommendation Draft (first Snapshot: 7 April 2026)
RDF 1.2 Semantics24 September 2026Candidate Recommendation Draft (first Snapshot: 7 April 2026)
RDF 1.2 Turtle11 November 2026Working Draft
RDF 1.2 N-Triples5 November 2026Working Draft
SPARQL 1.2 Query Language12 November 2026Working Draft
SHACL 1.2 Core10 November 2026Working Draft

None of them is a Recommendation yet. A Candidate Recommendation means the group asks for implementations and tests. Oxigraph already supports the new syntax, as the example shows.

A reified triple does not say that the triple is true. The line << ex:mia ex:owns ex:b7 >> ex:claimedBy ex:leo . records a claim by Leo, not a fact. I tested it in Oxigraph: the query ASK { ex:mia ex:owns ex:b7 } answers false. The annotation form {| ... |} is different. It states the triple and describes it.

SHACL: checking data

Mia's shop needs rules for its data. Every bike must have exactly one serial number. The owner must be a person. Here are the rules and the data.

@prefix sh:   <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .

ex:BikeShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass ex:Bike ;               # check every ex:Bike
    sh:property [
        sh:path ex:serial ;
        sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ;    # exactly one serial number
        sh:datatype xsd:string ;
    ] ;
    sh:property [
        sh:path ex:owner ;
        sh:class ex:Person ;               # the owner must be a person
    ] .
@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .

ex:mia a ex:Person .
ex:b7 a ex:Bike ; ex:serial "SN-0007" ; ex:owner ex:mia .
ex:b9 a ex:Bike ; ex:owner ex:shop .       # no serial, and the shop is no person
from pyshacl import validate
from rdflib import Graph, Namespace

SH = Namespace("http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#")
ok, report, _ = validate(Graph().parse("data.ttl"),
                         shacl_graph=Graph().parse("shapes.ttl"))
print("Conforms:", ok)
lines = []
for r in report.subjects(SH.resultSeverity, SH.Violation):
    focus = report.value(r, SH.focusNode).split("/")[-1]
    path = report.value(r, SH.resultPath).split("/")[-1]
    lines.append(f"- {focus} {path}: {report.value(r, SH.resultMessage)}")
print("\n".join(sorted(lines)))
Conforms: False
- b9 owner: Value does not have class ex:Person
- b9 serial: Less than 1 values on ex:b9->ex:serial

This ran with pySHACL 0.40.2. Bike B7 passes. Bike B9 fails twice. The SHACL engine treats missing data as missing. This is the closed-world view that OWL does not take.

SHACL became a W3C Recommendation on 20 July 2017. A Data Shapes Working Group is now writing SHACL 1.2. Its Core document was a Working Draft on 10 November 2026. You learn SHACL fully in SHACL and validation.

SHACL checks, OWL infers. A SHACL check does not add new facts. An OWL reasoner does not report missing data. Most real projects need both kinds of tool.

Catalogs, semantic layers and operational ontologies

In companies, ontology ideas came back under new names. Three of them matter most.

Data catalogs

A data catalog answers the question "what data do we have?". The W3C vocabulary DCAT describes datasets and their files. DCAT became a Recommendation on 16 January 2014. Version 2 followed in February 2020, and version 3 on 22 August 2024. Open-source catalogs include Amundsen, from Lyft, and DataHub, which started at LinkedIn. Databricks opened the code of Unity Catalog in June 2024.

Semantic layers

Two teams calculate "monthly revenue" and get two numbers. A semantic layer defines each metric once, for every tool. On 23 September 2025 Snowflake announced the Open Semantic Interchange (OSI). Salesforce, BlackRock, dbt Labs and RelationalAI were launch partners. The goal is one open, vendor-neutral format, written in YAML, for these definitions.

Operational ontologies

An operational ontology does more than describe data. People and programs act through it. Here is what two vendors document.

Operational ontologies in two data platforms (as documented by the vendors)
PlatformWhat the documentation says
Palantir Foundry OntologyObject types, properties and link types describe the business. Action types and functions describe how things change. Palantir calls it a digital twin of the organization.
Microsoft Fabric IQ OntologyAnnounced at Ignite in November 2025 as a preview. It defines business entities, relationships and rules. Data agents use it for shared business meaning.

My reading: these products bring back the old dream of one shared model. This time it is tied to live data and real actions. The details are in Enterprise and operational ontologies.

A metrics file is not a full ontology. It defines numbers, not the kinds of things and their identity. Use it together with a class model, not instead of one.

LLMs meet graphs

OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Large language models (LLMs) became tools for millions of people. But they have two weak points. They can state wrong facts with confidence. They also do not know your private data. Graphs help with both.

GraphRAG

RAG means that a program first finds useful text, then gives it to the model with the question. Plain RAG finds text that looks similar to the question. It struggles with questions that need several hops.

Microsoft Research described GraphRAG in a blog post on 13 February 2024. The paper by Darren Edge and colleagues followed on 24 April 2024. The code went open source on 2 July 2024. The latest release on GitHub is version 3.3.0, from October 2026.

Extract

An LLM reads all documents. It writes down the entities and the relations between them.

Build the graph

The entities become nodes. The relations become links.

Find communities

The graph is split into groups of closely linked entities, from big groups down to small ones.

Summarise

An LLM writes a short summary of each group before any question arrives.

Answer

For a broad question, each summary gives a partial answer. The partial answers are joined into one final answer.

This toy program shows steps 2 to 4 on hand-written facts. A real system uses an LLM for step 1 and a proper community method for step 3.

from collections import defaultdict

# Step 1 (done by an LLM in real GraphRAG): facts found in the documents.
triples = [
    ("Mia", "owns", "Mia's Bikes"),
    ("Leo", "works at", "Mia's Bikes"),
    ("Mia's Bikes", "sells", "City 3"),
    ("City 3", "is made by", "Velo AG"),
    ("Velo AG", "is based in", "Berlin"),
    ("Ana", "runs", "Cafe Nord"),
    ("Cafe Nord", "serves", "oat latte"),
]
# Step 2: build the graph (links in both directions).
nbrs = defaultdict(set)
for s, _, o in triples:
    nbrs[s].add(o)
    nbrs[o].add(s)

# Step 3: find the group of connected entities (a simple "community").
def community(start):
    seen, stack = {start}, [start]
    while stack:
        for n in nbrs[stack.pop()]:
            if n not in seen:
                seen.add(n)
                stack.append(n)
    return seen

# Step 4: collect the facts of that group as context for the model.
# Question: "Who makes the bikes that Leo sells?"
group = community("Leo")
print(f"{len(group)} entities in Leo's community")
for s, p, o in triples:
    if s in group:
        print(f"{s} {p} {o}.")
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};

fn main() {
    // Step 1 (done by an LLM in real GraphRAG): facts found in the documents.
    let triples = [
        ("Mia", "owns", "Mia's Bikes"),
        ("Leo", "works at", "Mia's Bikes"),
        ("Mia's Bikes", "sells", "City 3"),
        ("City 3", "is made by", "Velo AG"),
        ("Velo AG", "is based in", "Berlin"),
        ("Ana", "runs", "Cafe Nord"),
        ("Cafe Nord", "serves", "oat latte"),
    ];
    // Step 2: build the graph (links in both directions).
    let mut nbrs: HashMap<&str, Vec<&str>> = HashMap::new();
    for (s, _, o) in triples {
        nbrs.entry(s).or_default().push(o);
        nbrs.entry(o).or_default().push(s);
    }
    // Step 3: find the group of connected entities (a simple "community").
    let mut group = HashSet::from(["Leo"]);
    let mut stack = vec!["Leo"];
    while let Some(n) = stack.pop() {
        for &m in &nbrs[n] {
            if group.insert(m) {
                stack.push(m);
            }
        }
    }
    // Step 4: collect the facts of that group as context for the model.
    println!("{} entities in Leo's community", group.len());
    for (s, p, o) in triples {
        if group.contains(s) {
            println!("{s} {p} {o}.");
        }
    }
}
6 entities in Leo's community
Mia owns Mia's Bikes.
Leo works at Mia's Bikes.
Mia's Bikes sells City 3.
City 3 is made by Velo AG.
Velo AG is based in Berlin.

The café facts are left out, because they are in another group. The context links Leo to Velo AG in three hops. A similarity search on the word "Leo" would likely miss the Velo AG sentence.

Agent memory graphs and context graphs

An AI agent works over many sessions. It needs a memory. Some teams store this memory as a graph.

  • Zep and Graphiti. A paper from 20 January 2025 describes a knowledge graph that tracks time. It keeps the history of relationships instead of deleting old ones.
  • Mem0. A paper from 28 April 2025 adds a graph-based memory to its store of facts.
  • Context graphs. On 22 December 2025 the investors Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg published an essay on context graphs. Their idea is a record of decisions, not only of things. It keeps the "why" behind each decision.

The node types and time fields of these systems are a small ontology each. You draw them in Context graphs and agent memory.

MCP and the Agentic AI Foundation

An agent must reach the graph somehow. On 25 November 2024 Anthropic announced the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A data source runs an MCP server. An AI application acts as an MCP client and connects to it. So one graph server can serve many AI apps. The current protocol version is dated 2026-07-28.

On 9 December 2025 the Linux Foundation announced the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). It started with three projects: MCP from Anthropic, goose from Block and AGENTS.md from OpenAI. Its platinum members were Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI.

MCP does not give the model meaning. It only moves requests and data. If the graph behind the server has no clear classes, the model still guesses. The ontology gives the meaning. MCP gives the connection.

From 350 BC to 2026: one timeline

Here is the whole story of this book on one line. Old dates are often uncertain. Where sources disagree, earlier chapters give the details.

  1. c. 350 BC Aristotle's Categories. Ten kinds of being. The exact year is not known.
  2. 3rd century Porphyry's Isagoge. Genus and species, later drawn as a tree.
  3. 1308 Llull's Ars brevis. Turning wheels combine basic ideas.
  4. 1606 Lorhard. First known printed use of the word ontologia.
  5. 1666 Leibniz. A dream of a universal language and calculus of thought.
  6. 1735 Linnaeus. Systema Naturae, a taxonomy of living things.
  7. 1854 Boole. Logic as algebra.
  8. 1879 Frege. Predicate logic.
  9. 1948 Quine. "On What There Is".
  10. 1956 Dartmouth. The field of AI gets its name.
  11. 1966-69 Quillian. Semantic networks.
  12. 1974-75 Minsky. Frames.
  13. 1984 Cyc starts. A huge base of common sense.
  14. 1985 WordNet starts.
  15. 1992 KIF 3.0. The Knowledge Sharing Effort's language.
  16. 1993 Gruber's definition.
  17. 1998 Gene Ontology and FOIS.
  18. 1999 RDF. The first W3C Recommendation for triples.
  19. 2001 "The Semantic Web". The Scientific American article.
  20. 2004 OWL and the new RDF.
  21. 2006 Linked Data rules.
  22. 2007 DBpedia and Freebase.

  27. Oct 2012 Wikidata.

What stayed the same for 2,400 years?

Three questions. What kinds of things are there? How do they relate? How do we know a new fact from old ones? Aristotle asked them. A GraphRAG pipeline still answers them.

What changed most?

Who uses the ontology. First philosophers, then AI researchers, then web developers, then companies. Now language models read ontologies too.

Why do the same ideas keep coming back with new names?

Semantic network, frame, ontology, knowledge graph, context graph. Each new name came with new tools and new money. The core idea, typed things joined by named links, did not change.

Patterns to remember

These patterns come from the knowledge graph years. Use them when you build a graph for search, for a company or for an AI agent.

Knowledge graph patterns since 2012
PatternPurposeModelNote
Things, not stringsTell apart things with the same nameTaj Mahal (building) and Taj Mahal (musician): two nodesGive each thing its own ID, not its name.
Item, property, valueWrite a Wikidata factwd:Q2013 wdt:P571 "2012-10-29"Read the date precision too.
Property on a linkDescribe a relation(mia)-[:OWNS {since: 2021}]->(b7)Put it on the link, not on one end.
Annotated tripleThe same in RDF 1.2ex:mia ex:owns ex:b7 {| ex:since 2021 |} .Annotation states the triple. A bare triple term does not.
MATCH ... RETURNQuery a property graphMATCH (p:Person)-[o:OWNS]->(b) RETURN p.nameSame in Cypher and GQL. Inserts differ.
Shape per classCheck data with closed-world rulessh:targetClass ex:Bike ; sh:minCount 1SHACL checks. It does not infer.
Define a metric onceOne number for all tools"Monthly revenue" in one semantic layer fileA metric is not a class model.
Objects, links, actionsAct on live data through the modelOrder, linked to Customer, with action "Cancel order"Label vendor facts as "documented".
Graph as contextGive an LLM linked factsLeo's community: six entities, five factsSmall, relevant context beats a big dump.
Facts with timeRemember what was true when"Leo works at Mia's Bikes, from 2023 until 2026"Never delete old facts. Close them.
One server, many clientsConnect a graph to AI appsAn MCP server in front of the graphMCP moves data. The ontology gives meaning.
Check the statusCite a standard correctly"RDF 1.2 Concepts: Candidate Recommendation, Nov 2026"Drafts change. Always add the date.

Practice

When did Google announce its Knowledge Graph?

  • March 2007
  • 16 May 2012
  • 29 October 2012

March 2007 is the launch of Freebase. 29 October 2012 is the launch of Wikidata.

What is the status of RDF 1.2 Concepts on 15 November 2026?

  • W3C Recommendation
  • Candidate Recommendation Draft
  • First Public Working Draft

It reached Candidate Recommendation in April 2026. The latest draft is from 13 November 2026. It is not a Recommendation yet.

Which keyword does GQL use to add data, where Cypher uses CREATE?

  • ADD
  • INSERT
  • MERGE

GQL uses INSERT. Neo4j now also accepts INSERT as another word for CREATE.

A SHACL report says "Less than 1 values on ex:b9->ex:serial". What is wrong?

  • Bike B9 has two serial numbers.
  • Bike B9 has no serial number.
  • The serial number has the wrong type.

The shape asks for at least one value. B9 has none.

Which three projects founded the Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025?

  • GraphRAG, Neo4j and Wikidata
  • MCP, goose and AGENTS.md
  • RDF, OWL and SPARQL

Anthropic gave MCP, Block gave goose and OpenAI gave AGENTS.md.

Fill in the missing words.

ISO published the GQL standard, ISO/IEC 39075, in the year ?.

SHACL became a W3C Recommendation in ?.

In RDF 1.2 the node that points to a triple term with rdf:reifies is called a ?.

  1. Write "Leo owns bike B9 since 2018" as one RDF 1.2 line with an annotation.
    Answer

    ex:leo ex:owns ex:b9 {| ex:since 2018 |} . You can also name the reifier: ex:leo ex:owns ex:b9 ~ ex:own2 {| ex:since 2018 |} .

  2. Add a rule to the SHACL shape: every bike has at most one owner.
    Answer

    Add sh:maxCount 1 ; inside the property shape with sh:path ex:owner. The shape then checks the class and the count of the owner.

  3. Wikidata gives "2012-01-01" as the start of the Google Knowledge Graph. Google's blog says 16 May 2012. Do they disagree? Explain.
    Answer

    Not really. The Wikidata value has year precision, so it only says "2012". The blog gives the exact day. A good answer reads the precision before it compares dates.

  4. In the GraphRAG toy, add the fact ("Cafe Nord", "is next to", "Mia's Bikes"). How many entities are in Leo's community now, and why?
    Answer

    Nine. The new link joins the café group to the bike group. So Ana, Cafe Nord and oat latte become part of Leo's community too. This shows why real GraphRAG uses a better community method than simple connection.

  5. Hard: explain why MCP alone does not stop an LLM from giving wrong answers about your company data.
    Answer

    MCP only connects the model to tools and data. If the data has no clear classes, identity rules and checks, the model can still mix up things or read a value wrongly. An ontology gives the meaning, and SHACL can check the data before the model sees it.

Key takeaways

  • Google's Knowledge Graph (16 May 2012) made "knowledge graph" a common word. Freebase was one of its main sources.
  • Wikidata (29 October 2012) is an open knowledge graph with about 124 million items in November 2026.
  • Property graphs put data on links. Cypher came in 2011, SQL/PGQ in 2023 and the ISO GQL standard in April 2024.
  • RDF 1.2 adds triple terms and reifiers. On 15 November 2026 it is a Candidate Recommendation, not yet a Recommendation.
  • SPARQL 1.2 and SHACL 1.2 are still Working Drafts. SHACL 1.0 (2017) checks data with closed-world rules.
  • Data catalogs, semantic layers and operational ontologies bring ontology ideas into company data platforms.
  • GraphRAG (2024) uses an LLM to build a graph and community summaries, then answers from them.
  • MCP (2024) connects AI apps to data. Since December 2025 it belongs to the Agentic AI Foundation.

Logic for ontology

An ontology is a set of statements. Logic gives each statement one exact meaning. Then a program can work out what follows from them. This chapter gives you the logic behind OWL, reasoners and query engines.

  • Write simple English rules in propositional and first-order logic.
  • Check if an interpretation is a model of a set of axioms.
  • Decide if a fact is entailed, with a truth table or a counter-model.
  • Explain sound, complete and decidable, and why OWL gives up power for speed.
  • Predict how the open world and missing unique names change an answer.

Why an ontology needs logic

Read one rule from a university ontology.

Every course has a teacher.

Two engineers read it. Ana thinks each course has its own teacher. Ben thinks one person teaches all courses. Both readings fit the English words. A program cannot guess which one you meant.

Logic fixes this. It gives a statement one meaning only. It has three parts.

  • Syntax: the rules for writing a statement. Which symbols can go where?
  • Semantics: the rules for meaning. When is a statement true?
  • Reasoning: the rules for new facts. What follows from the statements?

OWL, RDFS and SHACL all rest on logic. When you know the logic, you can predict what a reasoner will do. You also understand its error messages.

English lets you be vague. Logic does not. An ontology in logic means the same thing to every person and every program.

Logic does not know the real world. It only knows the statements you wrote. If you forget to say "a professor is a person", logic does not know it.

Propositional logic

Start with three short sentences.

  1. If it rains, the road is wet.
  2. If the road is wet, the road is slippery.
  3. It rains.

You conclude at once: the road is slippery. Propositional logic explains why. Each simple sentence becomes one atom. Here the atoms are rain, wet and slippery. Each atom is true or false.

We join atoms with connectives. The three sentences become rain \to wet, wet \to slippery and rain.

The five connectives
SymbolRead it asTrue when
\neg Anot AA is false
A \land BA and Bboth are true
A \lor BA or Bat least one is true
A \to Bif A then BA is false, or B is true
A \leftrightarrow BA if and only if Bboth have the same value

A truth table

A truth table lists every possible row. Here is the table for "if A then B".

Truth table for A \to B
ABA \to B
truetruetrue
truefalsefalse
falsetruetrue
falsefalsetrue

Only one row is false. The "if" part is true and the "then" part is false. With n atoms the table has 2^n rows. Three atoms give 8 rows.

The arrow is not "because". The sentence "if 2 + 2 = 5, then the moon is green" is true in logic. Its "if" part is false, so the whole sentence is true. Also, "or" is not "one or the other". A \lor B is true when both are true.

Propositional logic is too weak for an ontology. "Ada is a professor" and "Ben is a professor" become two unrelated atoms. It has no way to say "every professor". For that you need the next logic.

First-order logic

Look at the rule "Every professor is a person". In first-order logic you write it like this:

\forall x\, (Professor(x) \to Person(x))

Read it aloud: "for every thing x, if x is a professor, then x is a person". First-order logic can talk about things inside a sentence. It has five new parts.

The parts of first-order logic and their ontology names
PartExampleOntology name
Constant: a name for one thingada, logic101individual
Variable: a placeholderx, y(none)
Predicate with one placeProfessor(x)class
Predicate with two placesteaches(x, y)property
Quantifier\forall every, \exists somerestriction

A predicate is like a function that returns true or false. A quantifier says how many things you mean. First-order logic also has equality: x = y says two names point to one thing.

A fact

"Ada is a professor."

Professor(ada)

Every A is a B

"Every professor is a person."

\forall x\, (Professor(x) \to Person(x))

Some link exists

"Every professor teaches some course."

\forall x\, (Professor(x) \to \exists y\, (teaches(x,y) \land Course(y)))

Nothing is both

"No professor is a student."

\neg \exists x\, (Professor(x) \land Student(x))

At most one

"Every course has at most one teacher."

\forall x \forall y \forall z\, (taughtBy(x,y) \land taughtBy(x,z) \to y = z)

Now the course rule from the start has two clear forms. Ana's reading is \forall x\, (Course(x) \to \exists y\, teaches(y,x)). Ben's reading is \exists y\, \forall x\, (Course(x) \to teaches(y,x)). Only the order of the quantifiers changes. The meaning changes a lot.

The two classic slips

\forall x\, (Professor(x) \land Person(x))

\exists x\, (Professor(x) \to Rich(x))

\forall x\, (Professor(x) \to Person(x))

\exists x\, (Professor(x) \land Rich(x))

The first wrong line says that everything is a professor. The second wrong line is true when one thing is not a professor. A chair makes it true.

Remember the pair. "Every" goes with the arrow. "Some" goes with "and".

Interpretation and model

When is \forall x\, (Professor(x) \to Person(x)) true? It depends on what the words mean. So we pick a small world and test the rule in it. Here are two small worlds, written in Python.

# One interpretation: a domain plus the meaning of each name.
def check(I):
    D = I["domain"]
    prof, person, course, teaches = I["Professor"], I["Person"], I["Course"], I["teaches"]
    axioms = {
        # forall x: Professor(x) -> Person(x)
        "every professor is a person":
            all(x not in prof or x in person for x in D),
        # forall x: Professor(x) -> exists y: teaches(x, y) and Course(y)
        "every professor teaches a course":
            all(x not in prof or any((x, y) in teaches and y in course for y in D)
                for x in D),
        # Professor(ada)
        "Ada is a professor": I["ada"] in prof,
    }
    for text, ok in axioms.items():
        print(f"  {text:34} {ok}")
    print("  model?", all(axioms.values()))

I1 = {"domain": {"d1", "d2", "d3"}, "ada": "d1",
      "Professor": {"d1"}, "Person": {"d1", "d2"}, "Course": {"d3"},
      "teaches": {("d1", "d3")}}
I2 = dict(I1, Person={"d2"})          # same, but d1 is not a person

print("I1"); check(I1)
print("I2"); check(I2)
I1
  every professor is a person        True
  every professor teaches a course   True
  Ada is a professor                 True
  model? True
I2
  every professor is a person        False
  every professor teaches a course   True
  Ada is a professor                 True
  model? False

Each small world is an interpretation. It has two parts.

  • A domain: a set of things that is not empty. Here it is d1, d2 and d3.
  • A meaning for every name. A constant points to one thing. A class becomes a set of things. A property becomes a set of pairs.

An interpretation is a model of a set of axioms when every axiom is true in it.

I1 is a model. I2 is not a model, because d1 is a professor but not a person. This way of giving meaning is called model theory. It goes back to Alfred Tarski. The OWL 2 standard defines its meaning in the same way. The W3C calls it the Direct Semantics.

One ontology usually has many models. Often it has infinitely many. A model may also hold things with no name at all. A professor may teach a course that the data never names.

In logic, "model" does not mean a data model or an AI model. It means one world where all your axioms are true. Keep the two meanings apart when you read reasoner papers.

Entailment

Back to the rainy road. Does the road have to be slippery? A program can check every row of the truth table. It looks for a row where the facts are true but "slippery" is false. Such a row is a counter-model.

from itertools import product

ATOMS = ["rain", "wet", "slippery"]

def implies(a, b):
    return (not a) or b            # "a -> b" is false only when a is true and b is false

def entails(kb, query):
    """KB |= query when every model of the KB makes the query true."""
    for values in product([False, True], repeat=len(ATOMS)):
        v = dict(zip(ATOMS, values))          # one row of the truth table
        if all(f(v) for f in kb) and not query(v):
            return False, v                   # a counter-model
    return True, None

rules = [lambda v: implies(v["rain"], v["wet"]),
         lambda v: implies(v["wet"], v["slippery"])]
fact = [lambda v: v["rain"]]

print(entails(rules + fact, lambda v: v["slippery"]))
print(entails(rules, lambda v: v["slippery"]))
print(entails(rules + fact, lambda v: not v["slippery"]))
(True, None)
(False, {'rain': False, 'wet': False, 'slippery': False})
(False, {'rain': True, 'wet': True, 'slippery': True})
// KB |= query when every model of the KB makes the query true.
fn implies(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool {
    !a || b
}

fn entails(kb: &[fn(&[bool; 3]) -> bool], query: fn(&[bool; 3]) -> bool) -> bool {
    for row in 0..8u8 {
        // one row of the truth table: [rain, wet, slippery]
        let v = [row & 4 != 0, row & 2 != 0, row & 1 != 0];
        if kb.iter().all(|f| f(&v)) && !query(&v) {
            println!("  counter-model: {:?}", v);
            return false;
        }
    }
    true
}

fn main() {
    let rules: [fn(&[bool; 3]) -> bool; 2] = [
        |v| implies(v[0], v[1]), // rain -> wet
        |v| implies(v[1], v[2]), // wet -> slippery
    ];
    let with_fact: [fn(&[bool; 3]) -> bool; 3] = [rules[0], rules[1], |v| v[0]];
    println!("{}", entails(&with_fact, |v| v[2]));
    println!("{}", entails(&rules, |v| v[2]));
}
true
  counter-model: [false, false, false]
false

Read the three Python answers.

  1. Rules plus the fact "rain": "slippery" follows. No counter-model exists.
  2. Rules only: "slippery" does not follow. The dry row is a counter-model.
  3. Rules plus "rain": "not slippery" does not follow either.

A set of axioms K entails a statement \varphi, written K \models \varphi, when \varphi is true in every model of K.

So you prove "it follows" by checking all models. You prove "it does not follow" with one counter-model. The same idea works in first-order logic. But there are too many models to list, so tools use smarter methods.

A set of axioms is consistent when it has at least one model. Otherwise it is inconsistent.

If K has no model, then K \models \varphi for every statement \varphi.

Why? The test is "true in every model". With zero models, nothing can fail the test. So add the facts "rain" and "not rain" to the file, and the program says "yes" to every question. This is why reasoners stop and report an inconsistent ontology first.

"Not entailed" is not "false". Case 3 above shows it. The rules do not entail "slippery", and they do not entail "not slippery". The answer is simply unknown.

Logic books use two turnstile symbols. K \models \varphi is about meaning: true in every model. K \vdash \varphi is about proof: a step-by-step derivation exists. The next section connects them.

Sound and complete

Here is a small ontology. Every employee is a professor or an admin. Both professors and admins are persons. Sam is an employee.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/uni#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .

<http://example.org/uni> a owl:Ontology .
ex:Person a owl:Class .
ex:Professor a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf ex:Person .
ex:Admin a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf ex:Person .
# every employee is a professor or an admin
ex:Employee a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:subClassOf [ a owl:Class ; owl:unionOf ( ex:Professor ex:Admin ) ] .
ex:sam a ex:Employee .

Is Sam a person? Think in cases. If Sam is a professor, Sam is a person. If Sam is an admin, Sam is a person. So yes, in every model. We asked two real tools.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF
import owlrl

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/uni#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("staff.ttl")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)   # rule engine (OWL RL)
print("OWL RL rules: sam is a Person?", (EX.sam, RDF.type, EX.Person) in g)
OWL RL rules: sam is a Person? False
import os
from owlready2 import get_ontology, sync_reasoner

# staff.owl is staff.ttl saved as RDF/XML by rdflib
onto = get_ontology("file://" + os.path.abspath("staff.owl")).load()
with onto:
    sync_reasoner(debug=0)                  # runs the HermiT tableau reasoner (Java)
sam = onto.search_one(iri="*#sam")
print("HermiT: sam is a Person?", onto.Person in sam.INDIRECT_is_a)
HermiT: sam is a Person? True

The rule engine misses the fact. HermiT finds it. We used rdflib 7.6.0, owlrl 7.6.2 and owlready2 0.51, which ships HermiT and needs Java.

A reasoner is sound when every answer it gives is entailed. It is complete when it finds every entailed answer.

Four kinds of reasoner
CompleteNot complete
SoundThe goal. HermiT for OWL 2 DL.Safe but misses answers. OWL RL rules on our file.
Not soundFinds all answers, plus some wrong ones.Wrong answers and missing answers.

Why do the rules miss Sam? OWL RL is a smaller part of OWL. It does not allow "or" on the right side of a subclass axiom. The rules are made for that smaller part. Inside it, and under a few conditions, they find every fact about individuals. Outside it, they stay sound but miss facts.

For first-order logic, Kurt Gödel proved a famous result in his 1929 thesis. It was published in 1930. There are proof systems where \vdash and \models agree. Everything you can prove is entailed. Everything entailed has a proof.

"Incomplete" does not mean "wrong". An incomplete reasoner gives only true answers. It just misses some. An unsound reasoner is the dangerous one. For example, a tool that treats every missing fact as false is unsound for OWL.

Decidable and undecidable

Ask a program one question: "Does K entail \varphi?" For propositional logic, the program can always answer. The truth table is finite. The program checks every row and stops.

A question is decidable when one program always stops with the right answer. Such a program is a decision procedure.

No program can decide entailment for all of first-order logic. Alonzo Church and Alan Turing showed this, each in 1936.

But first-order logic is semi-decidable. Gödel's result gives a method. List all proofs, one by one. If a proof exists, you find it in the end. If no proof exists, the search may never stop. So a "yes" comes in time. A "no" may never come.

Why is first-order logic so hard? A program cannot test every model. There can be infinitely many models, and a model can be infinite. Look at these rules. Every person has a mother who is a person. A mother is an ancestor. An ancestor of an ancestor is an ancestor. Nobody is their own ancestor. Now every model holds an endless chain of mothers. A finite world would need a circle of mothers. But a circle breaks the last rule.

Decidable pieces

Ontology languages use decidable pieces of first-order logic. Description logics are built this way. The basic one, ALC, fits inside the part of first-order logic with only two variables. That part is decidable.

Which questions always get an answer?
LanguageEntailment
Propositional logicDecidable
ALC and other description logicsDecidable
OWL 2 DL (Direct Semantics)Decidable
OWL 2 Full (RDF-Based Semantics)Undecidable
Full first-order logicUndecidable, but semi-decidable

"Undecidable" does not mean "a tool never answers". Provers for first-order logic answer many questions every day. They just cannot promise to stop on every question.

Expressive power and speed

Look at two curves. One grows like n^2. The other grows like 2^n.

A truth table with 30 atoms has more than a billion rows. That is the exponential curve. Most reasoning problems fall into named groups by speed. Such a group is a complexity class. The details come in Description logics.

Speed of reasoning, from the W3C OWL 2 Profiles table, the DL primer and standard results
LanguageHard example it can sayWorst-case time
OWL 2 QLEvery professor teaches something.Queries on data: as easy as SQL
OWL 2 ELA heart disease is a disease of some heart part.Polynomial
OWL 2 RLRules on individuals, like inverse and transitive links.Polynomial for consistency
Propositional logic (SAT)Any mix of and, or, not.NP-complete
ALCAnd, or, not, some, only on classes.Exponential
OWL 2 DL (SROIQ)Counting, inverses, role chains, nominals.Doubly exponential, nondeterministic
First-order logicAnything with every, some and equality.Undecidable

The more a logic can say, the harder its reasoning is in the worst case. Hector Levesque and Ronald Brachman described this trade in 1987.

This is why OWL 2 has three small profiles. You give up some words. You get fast and predictable reasoning. A medical ontology with hundreds of thousands of classes can use EL. A database with a billion rows can use QL, so queries become SQL.

"Worst case" is the slowest possible input. Real ontologies are often much easier. HermiT handles many OWL 2 DL ontologies in seconds. But you get no promise, so test with your own data.

Do not pick the most expressive language "just in case". Every extra feature can slow every user. Pick the smallest language that answers your questions.

Open world, closed world, unique names

The chapter The building blocks met these ideas in plain words. Now we count models. The file says one thing: Ada teaches Logic 101. Does Ada teach AI 201?

from itertools import product

D = [0, 1, 2]                                  # a domain with three things
PAIRS = [(x, y) for x in D for y in D]         # 9 possible links

def relations():
    """Every possible meaning of one binary predicate: 2^9 = 512."""
    for bits in product([False, True], repeat=len(PAIRS)):
        yield {p for p, b in zip(PAIRS, bits) if b}

# Part 1: open world. KB = { teaches(ada, logic101) }. Is teaches(ada, ai201) true?
ada, logic101, ai201 = 0, 1, 2
yes = no = 0
for teaches in relations():
    if (ada, logic101) in teaches:             # this interpretation is a model
        if (ada, ai201) in teaches: yes += 1
        else: no += 1
print("models where the query is true:", yes, " false:", no)

# Part 2: unique names. hasMother is functional (at most one mother).
def functional(r):
    return all(y == z for (x, y) in r for (x2, z) in r if x == x2)

for una in (True, False):
    models, same = 0, 0
    for tom, mary, maria in product(D, repeat=3):      # what each name means
        if una and len({tom, mary, maria}) < 3:
            continue                                     # UNA: names must differ
        for m in relations():
            if (tom, mary) in m and (tom, maria) in m and functional(m):
                models += 1
                same += (mary == maria)
    print(f"UNA={una}: models={models}, mary = maria in {same} of them")
models where the query is true: 128  false: 128
UNA=True: models=0, mary = maria in 0 of them
UNA=False: models=144, mary = maria in 144 of them

Part 1: the open world in logic

The query is true in 128 models and false in 128 models. So the file does not entail it. It does not entail its negation either. The answer is "unknown". This is the open world assumption, said in logic: an answer must hold in every model.

A database thinks differently. It keeps one model only: the smallest one. In it, only stored facts are true. So "Ada teaches AI 201" is false. This is the closed world assumption. SQL, Datalog and SPARQL's FILTER NOT EXISTS all work this way. A missing fact counts as false. This is called negation as failure.

Part 2: unique names in logic

Tom has at most one mother. The data says his mother is Mary. It also says his mother is Maria.

  • With the unique name assumption, Mary and Maria must be two things. Then there are 0 models. The file is inconsistent.
  • Without it, the two names may point to one thing. There are 144 models. In all 144, Mary and Maria are the same. So the file entails mary = maria.

In logic terms, the unique name assumption says one thing. Two different constants never point to the same element. OWL does not make this assumption. The OWL 2 Direct Semantics lets two names point to one thing. You must say owl:differentFrom when it matters.

Four systems, four habits
SystemWorldUnique names?Missing fact means
OWL reasonerOpenNoUnknown
SQL databaseClosedYes (keys)False
Datalog engineClosedYesFalse
SPARQL query, no reasoningClosed for that queryYes, IRIs are comparedNot found

A SPARQL query with FILTER NOT EXISTS is not OWL reasoning. It finds what is missing in the stored data. That is a closed-world check. It is useful, but call it a data check, not an entailment.

Do you need closed-world checks on open-world data? Use shapes. You learn them in SHACL and validation.

Patterns to remember

Logic patterns for ontology work
PatternPurposeModelNote
C(a)Put an individual in a classProfessor(ada)A constant is an individual. A one-place predicate is a class.
∀x (A(x) → B(x))Every A is a B\forall x\, (Professor(x) \to Person(x))Use the arrow under "every", never "and".
∃y (R(x,y) ∧ B(y))Some link to a B exists\exists y\, (teaches(x,y) \land Course(y))Use "and" under "some", never the arrow.
∀y (R(x,y) → B(y))All links go to a B\forall y\, (taughtBy(x,y) \to Professor(y))True when there are no links at all.
¬∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x))Nothing is both\neg \exists x\, (Professor(x) \land Student(x))This is how a reasoner finds bad data.
R(x,y) ∧ R(x,z) → y = zAt most one linkhasMother(x,y) \land hasMother(x,z) \to y = zWithout unique names it merges names.

Find a counter-modelShow that φ does not followthe dry rowOne counter-model is enough.
K has no modelFind an inconsistent ontologyrain and not rainIt entails everything. Fix it first.

Practice

Which sentence is false in propositional logic?

  • false → true
  • false → false
  • true → false

An arrow is false only when the "if" part is true and the "then" part is false.

Which formula says "every student is a person"?

  • \forall x\, (Student(x) \land Person(x))
  • \forall x\, (Student(x) \to Person(x))
  • \exists x\, (Student(x) \to Person(x))

"Every" goes with the arrow. The first formula says that everything is a student.

An interpretation makes two of your three axioms true. Is it a model?

  • Yes, most axioms are true.
  • No. A model makes every axiom true.
  • It depends on the domain size.

One false axiom is enough. Then it is not a model.

A reasoner gives only correct answers, but it misses some. What is it?

  • Sound, not complete
  • Complete, not sound
  • Undecidable

Sound means no wrong answers. Complete means no missing answers.

An ontology has no model at all. What does it entail?

  • Nothing
  • Only its own axioms
  • Every statement

"True in every model" holds for any statement when there are no models.

Fill in the missing words.

A truth table with 4 atoms has ? rows.

A model of the facts where the claim is false is a ?.

Church and Turing showed that first-order logic is ?.

What is an interpretation?

A domain of things plus a meaning for every name: things, sets and sets of pairs.

What does K \models \varphi mean?

φ is true in every model of K.

What is semi-decidable?

A program always finds a "yes". It may run forever on a "no".

Why does OWL have profiles?

Smaller languages reason faster. You trade expressive power for speed.

What does the unique name assumption say in logic?

Two different constants never point to the same element. OWL does not assume it.

  1. Write "No course is a person" in first-order logic.
    Answer

    \neg \exists x\, (Course(x) \land Person(x)). Another correct form is \forall x\, (Course(x) \to \neg Person(x)).

  2. The rules are A \to B and B \to C. Does C follow? Give a counter-model or say why.
    Answer

    No. Make A, B and C all false. Both rules are true, and C is false. That row is a counter-model. You need the fact A to get C.

  3. Write Ben's reading of "every course has a teacher" and explain why it is a stronger claim.
    Answer

    \exists y\, \forall x\, (Course(x) \to teaches(y,x)). It says one single person teaches every course. Ana's reading only needs some teacher for each course, maybe a different one each time.

  4. A teammate says: "Our reasoner is incomplete, so we cannot trust its answers." Is that right?
    Answer

    Not if the reasoner is sound. A sound reasoner gives only entailed answers. Incomplete means it may miss some answers. So you can trust each "yes". You cannot trust a missing answer as a "no".

  5. The data says "Lina's passport number is P1" and "Lina's passport number is P2". The property has at most one value. What does a database do? What does an OWL reasoner do?
    Answer

    A database uses unique names, so P1 and P2 are two values and the rule breaks. It rejects the row. An OWL reasoner has no unique names. If the values are individuals, it concludes P1 = P2. If they are two different literals, like two strings, they cannot be equal, so the ontology becomes inconsistent.

  6. Why can a first-order reasoner never promise to stop, while an ALC reasoner can?
    Answer

    First-order entailment is undecidable (Church and Turing, 1936). A proof search may run forever when no proof exists. ALC is a decidable piece of first-order logic. It fits in the two-variable part, and a decision procedure exists, such as the tableau method.

Key takeaways

  • Logic gives every statement one exact meaning: syntax, semantics and reasoning.
  • A class is a one-place predicate. A property is a two-place predicate. An individual is a constant.
  • "Every" goes with the arrow. "Some" goes with "and". Quantifier order changes the meaning.
  • An interpretation is a domain plus a meaning for each name. A model makes all axioms true.
  • K \models \varphi means φ is true in every model. One counter-model shows it does not follow.
  • Sound means no wrong answers. Complete means no missing answers.
  • First-order logic is undecidable. Description logics and OWL 2 DL are decidable pieces of it.
  • More expressive power means slower reasoning. OWL profiles trade power for speed.
  • OWL uses the open world and no unique names. Databases use the closed world and unique names.

Sources

  • OWL 2 Direct Semantics (Second Edition). The W3C definition of interpretation, model, entailment and consistency for OWL 2.
  • OWL 2 Profiles (Second Edition). Section 5 has the table of reasoning complexity for OWL 2 DL, EL, QL and RL.
  • A Description Logic Primer. Krötzsch, Simančík and Horrocks on models, the open world, unique names and light fragments.
  • Logic, Computability and Incompleteness: computability. A university course page on why first-order logic is undecidable but semi-decidable.
  • forall x: Calgary. A free open textbook on truth tables, first-order logic and interpretations.
  • Levesque and Brachman (1987) in dblp. The record of the paper on expressive power against tractability.

Description logics

Description logics are the logics inside OWL. Each one is a careful piece of first-order logic. It is small enough that a reasoner always finishes. This chapter shows how these logics are built, named and run, from ALC up to SROIQ, EL and DL-Lite.

  • Write concepts with the ALC constructors and read them aloud in English.
  • Sort axioms into TBox, RBox and ABox.
  • Turn subsumption, satisfiability and instance checks into one consistency test.
  • Read a name like SHOIN(D) or SROIQ(D) letter by letter.
  • Run the tableau method by hand and explain why EL and DL-Lite are fast.

Concepts, roles and individuals

Read this description from a university.

A professor who teaches some seminar.

A description logic writes it as one short formula.

Professor \sqcap \exists teaches.Seminar

A description logic (DL) has only three kinds of names.

  • A concept is a class. Professor and Seminar are concepts.
  • A role is a property between two things. teaches is a role.
  • An individual is one named thing, like ada.

From these names you build bigger concepts with constructors. The formula above uses two of them: \sqcap (and) and \exists (some).

One idea in four languages
LanguageThe same idea
Englisha professor who teaches some seminar
Description logicProfessor \sqcap \exists teaches.Seminar
OWL (Manchester syntax)Professor and (teaches some Seminar)
First-order logicProfessor(x) \land \exists y\, (teaches(x,y) \land Seminar(y))

Notice the first-order form. It has one free variable, x. So a concept is a description of one thing. The DL form hides the variables. This keeps the logic small, and it keeps reasoning decidable. You met these ideas in Logic for ontology.

Description logics grew out of semantic networks and frames. The first DL system was KL-ONE, described by Ronald Brachman and James Schmolze in 1985. The story is in AI and knowledge representation.

In DL, "role" means a property, like teaches. It does not mean a job. A job like Teacher is a concept. Do not model "Teacher" as a role.

The ALC constructors

The basic description logic is called ALC. Manfred Schmidt-Schauß and Gert Smolka defined it in 1991. It has eight ways to write a concept. Most DLs in this chapter add to this list. EL and DL-Lite take things away. In the same year, Klaus Schild showed that ALC is a form of modal logic. So older modal logic methods also work for it.

The ALC constructors and their meaning in an interpretation I
DLManchesterEnglishSet of things
\topThinganything\Delta^{\mathcal{I}}, the whole domain
\botNothingnothing\emptyset
ASeminara named conceptA^{\mathcal{I}}
\neg Cnot Cnot a C\Delta^{\mathcal{I}} \setminus C^{\mathcal{I}}
C \sqcap DC and DbothC^{\mathcal{I}} \cap D^{\mathcal{I}}
C \sqcup DC or Dat least oneC^{\mathcal{I}} \cup D^{\mathcal{I}}
\exists r.Cr some Chas an r-link to some Cthings with at least one r-link to a C
\forall r.Cr only Call r-links go to a Cthings whose r-links all end in a C

The last two are the heart of DL. \exists r.C is an existential restriction. \forall r.C is a universal restriction.

Test them on a small world

Here is one fixed interpretation. Three people teach, or do not teach, three courses.

Who belongs to which concept in this world?
Conceptadabenchen
\exists teaches.Seminaryesyesno
\forall teaches.Seminarnoyesyes
\exists teaches.\top \sqcap \forall teaches.Seminarnoyesno
\neg \exists teaches.Coursenonoyes

Look at Chen in the second row. Chen teaches nothing. So "all the things Chen teaches are seminars" is true. Nothing breaks the rule. This is the empty case of "only".

Two rules help you move a "not" inside. \neg \exists r.C is the same as \forall r.\neg C. \neg \forall r.C is the same as \exists r.\neg C. They work like De Morgan's laws for and and or.

"Only" does not mean "some". \forall teaches.Seminar holds for a person who teaches nothing. Write \exists teaches.Seminar \sqcap \forall teaches.Seminar when the link must exist.

TBox, RBox and ABox

A DL knowledge base has three boxes. Read a small one first.

TBox: concepts

Professor \sqsubseteq Person

Lecturer \equiv Person \sqcap \exists teaches.Course

Seminar \sqsubseteq Course

RBox: roles

teaches \sqsubseteq involvedIn

partOf \circ partOf \sqsubseteq partOf

ABox: facts

Professor(ada)

teaches(ada, sem7)

Seminar(sem7)

ada \not\approx ben

The three boxes
BoxAxiom shapesExample in English
TBoxC \sqsubseteq D, C \equiv DEvery professor is a person.
RBoxr \sqsubseteq s, r \circ s \sqsubseteq t, transitive, disjoint rolesTeaching is a kind of involvement.
ABoxC(a), r(a,b), a \approx b, a \not\approx bAda teaches seminar 7.

The axiom C \sqsubseteq D is a concept inclusion. Read it as "every C is a D". The axiom C \equiv D says both directions. The RBox axiom partOf \circ partOf \sqsubseteq partOf is a role chain. Here it says that a part of a part is a part.

Ask the program what it can conclude

From the boxes above a reasoner concludes Lecturer(ada). Ada is a person, because she is a professor. She teaches sem7, which is a course. So she fits the full definition of Lecturer.

A TBox where every axiom is A \sqsubseteq C or A \equiv C, with no cycles, is called acyclic. A TBox with any concept on the left, like \exists teaches.Seminar \sqsubseteq Lecturer, is a general TBox. General TBoxes make reasoning harder. You see the numbers later.

\sqsubseteq and \equiv are very different. With Lecturer \sqsubseteq Person \sqcap \exists teaches.Course, the reasoner never puts Ada into Lecturer. It only knows that lecturers teach. You need \equiv to let the reasoner sort individuals into a class.

Reasoning tasks

Look at one more small TBox.

Student \sqcap Professor \sqsubseteq \bot \qquad TA \sqsubseteq Student \sqcap Professor

No one can be both a student and a professor. But every TA is both. So the class TA can never have a member. A reasoner reports it. In Protégé the class turns red. It is "equivalent to Nothing".

The standard reasoning tasks
TaskQuestionExample
SubsumptionIs every C a D?Is every Professor a Person?
SatisfiabilityCan C have a member?Can TA have a member? No.
ConsistencyDoes the whole knowledge base have a model?Add TA(tim). Now: no.
Instance checkingIs a a member of C?Is Ada a Lecturer? Yes.
ClassificationFind all subsumptions between named concepts.Build the class tree.

A reasoner needs only one engine for all of them. Each task becomes a consistency test.

Let \mathcal{K} be a knowledge base and let a be a new name.

  • C is satisfiable if and only if \mathcal{K} \cup \{ C(a) \} is consistent.
  • C \sqsubseteq D follows if and only if C \sqcap \neg D is not satisfiable.
  • C(b) follows if and only if \mathcal{K} \cup \{ \neg C(b) \} is not consistent.
Why does the second line work?

Suppose some model has a thing in C and not in D. Then that thing is in C \sqcap \neg D, so the concept is satisfiable, and C \sqsubseteq D fails. The other way round is the same idea. No thing in C \sqcap \neg D in any model means every C is a D in every model.

An unsatisfiable class does not make the ontology inconsistent. The TA ontology above is still consistent. It has models, just none with a TA in it. It becomes inconsistent only when an individual is put into TA. Fix red classes early, before data arrives.

The naming scheme

DL names look like codes: ALC, SHIQ, SHOIN(D), SROIQ(D). Each letter adds one feature. Read SHOIN(D) letter by letter.

S: ALC plus transitive roles

S is short for ALC with transitive roles. "Ancestor of" can follow chains.

H: role hierarchy

A role can be a sub-role of another. hasMother \sqsubseteq hasParent.

O: nominals

A concept made from named individuals. \{red, green, blue\} is the class of three colours.

I: inverse roles

You can turn a role around. teaches^{-} means "is taught by".

N: number restrictions

You can count links. \le 1\, hasMother means at most one mother.

(D): datatypes

Values like integers and strings. \exists age.integer is allowed.

The letters in DL names
LetterAddsExample
ALBase: and, atomic not, only, plain somePerson \sqcap \forall hasChild.Doctor
CFull not\neg (A \sqcup B)
UOrCat \sqcup Dog
EFull some\exists teaches.Seminar
SALC with transitive rolespartOf is transitive
HRole hierarchyhasMother \sqsubseteq hasParent
RRole chains, disjoint roles, self and morehasParent \circ hasBrother \sqsubseteq hasUncle
ONominals\{red, green, blue\}
IInverse rolesteaches^{-}
FFunctional roles\le 1\, hasMother
NNumber restrictions\ge 2\, teaches
QQualified number restrictions\ge 2\, teaches.Seminar
(D)Datatypes and values\exists credits.integer

ALC is the same as ALUE. Full "not" already gives you "or" and full "some". So people say ALC. Some letters include others. R includes H. Q includes N, and N includes F.

Remember three pairs. OWL Lite is SHIF(D). OWL DL is SHOIN(D). OWL 2 DL is SROIQ(D). From OWL to OWL 2, two letters changed: H became R (role chains), and N became Q (qualified counts).

Do not read S as "SHIQ". S alone means ALC with transitive roles. Also, ALC has no role axioms at all. A subproperty axiom needs H.

The tableau method

Is every person who teaches a course and teaches only seminars a person who teaches a course that is a seminar? In DL, is C \sqsubseteq D for these two concepts?

C = \exists teaches.Course \sqcap \forall teaches.Seminar \qquad D = \exists teaches.(Course \sqcap Seminar)

The tableau method answers by trying to build a counter-model. It tests C \sqcap \neg D. First, push the "not" inside: \neg D = \forall teaches.(\neg Course \sqcup \neg Seminar). This form, with "not" only on names, is called negation normal form.

  1. Start with one thing x. Its label is \exists teaches.Course, \forall teaches.Seminar, \forall teaches.(\neg Course \sqcup \neg Seminar).
  2. The ∃-rule: x needs a teaches-link to a course. Make a new thing x1 with teaches(x, x1) and Course(x1).
  3. The ∀-rule, twice: every teaches-link of x goes to a seminar, and to a non-course or non-seminar. So x1 also gets Seminar and \neg Course \sqcup \neg Seminar.
  4. The ⊔-rule: try one side at a time. Branch 1 adds \neg Course to x1. But x1 has Course. Clash.
  5. Branch 2 adds \neg Seminar to x1. But x1 has Seminar. Clash.
  6. Every branch has a clash. So C \sqcap \neg D has no model, and C \sqsubseteq D holds.
The four tableau rules for ALC
RuleIf a node hasThen
⊓-ruleC \sqcap Dadd C and D
⊔-ruleC \sqcup D, and neither C nor Dbranch: add C, or else add D
∃-rule\exists r.C, and no r-link to a C yetmake a new node y, an r-link to it, and C at y
∀-rule\forall r.C and an r-link to yadd C at y

A clash is a node with both A and \neg A, or with \bot. Here is the same method as a tiny Python program. It prints every step.

# A tiny ALC tableau. Concepts are tuples in negation normal form:
# ("A",) atom   ("not","A")   ("and",C,D)   ("or",C,D)   ("some",r,C)   ("all",r,C)
def show(c):
    k = c[0]
    if k == "not": return "¬" + c[1]
    if k in ("and", "or"): return "(" + show(c[1]) + (" ⊓ " if k == "and" else " ⊔ ") + show(c[2]) + ")"
    if k in ("some", "all"): return ("∃" if k == "some" else "∀") + c[1] + "." + show(c[2])
    return k

def sat(label, node="x", depth=0):
    pad, todo, label = "  " * depth, list(label), set()
    while todo:                                    # ⊓-rule: split every "and"
        c = todo.pop()
        if c[0] == "and": todo += [c[1], c[2]]
        else: label.add(c)
    print(pad + node + ": " + ", ".join(sorted(show(c) for c in label)))
    if any(("not", c[0]) in label for c in label if len(c) == 1):
        print(pad + "  clash!"); return False       # A and ¬A in one node
    for c in sorted(label, key=show):              # ⊔-rule: try one side, then the other
        if c[0] == "or" and c[1] not in label and c[2] not in label:
            print(pad + "  branch on " + show(c))
            return sat(label | {c[1]}, node, depth + 1) or sat(label | {c[2]}, node, depth + 1)
    for c in sorted(label, key=show):              # ∃-rule, then ∀-rule into the new node
        if c[0] == "some":
            child = {c[2]} | {d[2] for d in label if d[0] == "all" and d[1] == c[1]}
            print(pad + "  new node " + node + "1 via " + c[1])
            if not sat(child, node + "1", depth + 1):
                return False
    return True                                    # no rule applies, no clash: a model exists
from tableau import sat

def neg(c):                                        # push ¬ inward (negation normal form)
    k = c[0]
    if k == "not": return (c[1],)
    if k == "and": return ("or", neg(c[1]), neg(c[2]))
    if k == "or": return ("and", neg(c[1]), neg(c[2]))
    if k == "some": return ("all", c[1], neg(c[2]))
    if k == "all": return ("some", c[1], neg(c[2]))
    return ("not", k)

def subsumed(c, d):                                # C ⊑ D  iff  C ⊓ ¬D has no model
    return not sat({("and", c, neg(d))})

Course, Seminar = ("Course",), ("Seminar",)
C = ("and", ("some", "teaches", Course), ("all", "teaches", Seminar))
D = ("some", "teaches", ("and", Course, Seminar))
print("C ⊑ D ?", subsumed(C, D))
print()
print("∃teaches.Course ⊑ D ?", subsumed(("some", "teaches", Course), D))
x: ∀teaches.(¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), ∀teaches.Seminar, ∃teaches.Course
  new node x1 via teaches
  x1: (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), Course, Seminar
    branch on (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar)
    x1: (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), Course, Seminar, ¬Course
      clash!
    x1: (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), Course, Seminar, ¬Seminar
      clash!
C ⊑ D ? True

x: ∀teaches.(¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), ∃teaches.Course
  new node x1 via teaches
  x1: (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), Course
    branch on (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar)
    x1: (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), Course, ¬Course
      clash!
    x1: (¬Course ⊔ ¬Seminar), Course, ¬Seminar
∃teaches.Course ⊑ D ? False

Look at the second test. The last branch has no clash and no rule left. It is a counter-model: x teaches x1, and x1 is a course but not a seminar. So teaching a course does not mean teaching a seminar.

We checked both answers with HermiT, a real tableau reasoner, through owlready2 0.51. It also says that C is below D, and that "teaches some Course" is not below D.

For ALC concepts, the tableau method always stops. It finds a clash on every branch exactly when the concept is unsatisfiable.

Proof idea

Stops: each new node gets only smaller pieces of the concept, so the tree has a limited depth and width. Sound: a branch with no clash and no rule left reads directly as a model. Complete: if a model exists, it shows which side of every "or" to choose, so some branch never clashes.

Blocking: when the tree could grow forever

Our small program has no TBox. Real ontologies have one. Take one axiom: Person \sqsubseteq \exists hasParent.Person. Every person has a parent who is a person. The ∃-rule makes x1, then x2, then x3, without end.

Real reasoners use blocking. Node x1 has the same label as its parent x. So the reasoner stops at x1 and lets the link point back to x. The model is small: x is their own parent. That is strange, but the axioms allow it. Add more axioms if you want to forbid it.

HermiT, Pellet and FaCT++ are tableau reasoners for OWL 2 DL. They add many tricks: blocking, smart branch order and caching. HermiT uses a "hypertableau" variant. You meet them again in Reasoners and materialisation.

Do not forget negation normal form. The ∀-rule and the clash test only work when "not" stands next to names. Push the "not" inside before you start, or you miss clashes.

Complexity classes in simple words

Each step in the tableau was easy. The cost comes from the branches. Each "or" can double the work. Ten "or" nodes can mean 1024 branches. A complexity class names how fast this cost grows in the worst case.

AC0 and LogSpace: tiny

About as hard as running a fixed SQL query over the data. OWL 2 QL query answering is in AC0 when only the data grows.

P (PTime): polynomial

Time grows like n^2 or n^3. Double the input, and it gets a few times slower. EL reasoning is in P.

NP: guess and check

A good guess is quick to check. But finding it may need many guesses. Propositional SAT is the classic NP problem.

PSPACE: polynomial memory

The memory stays small, but the time can be exponential. ALC without a TBox is here. Our program keeps one path of the tree at a time.

ExpTime: exponential time

Time grows like 2^n. ALC with a general TBox is here.

NExpTime and N2ExpTime: exponential with guessing

OWL DL (SHOIN) is NExpTime. OWL 2 DL (SROIQ) is N2ExpTime: a double exponential, like 2^{2^n}, with guessing.

A problem is complete for a class when it is one of the hardest problems in it. "ALC with a general TBox is ExpTime-complete" means no algorithm can do much better in the worst case.

Worst-case reasoning cost (consistency, subsumption, instance checks)
LogicOWL languageComplexity
DL-LiteOWL 2 QLNLogSpace. In AC0 when only data grows
EL++OWL 2 ELPTime-complete
DLPOWL 2 RLPTime-complete for consistency
ALC, no TBox(none)PSPACE-complete
ALC, general TBox(none)ExpTime-complete
SHOIN(D)OWL DL (2004)NExpTime-complete
SROIQ(D)OWL 2 DL (2009)N2ExpTime-complete

Two kinds of growth matter. Data complexity counts the cost when only the facts grow. Combined complexity lets the schema and the query grow too. For big data, data complexity is the number to watch.

Worst case is not normal case. SROIQ is N2ExpTime-complete, yet HermiT classifies many real OWL 2 DL ontologies in seconds. Complexity tells you what is possible, not what is usual. Measure with your own ontology.

The light families: EL and DL-Lite

Large ontologies need fast reasoning. Two families give it up front. Both drop the features that cause branching.

EL: no "or", no "only", no "not"

EL allows only \sqcap, \exists and \top. Without "or" there is nothing to branch on. A reasoner can just add facts until nothing new appears. This is called saturation. The number of possible facts is polynomial, so the loop ends in polynomial time.

Here is a medical example in EL. A heart disease is a disease located in the heart. An organ disease is a disease located in an organ. The heart is an organ. Carditis is a disease located in the heart. First, a tool rewrites the axioms into four simple shapes. That is the normal form. X1 and X2 are helper names.

# EL classification by saturation. The TBox is already in normal form.
sub  = [("Heart", "Organ"), ("HeartDisease", "Disease"), ("OrganDisease", "Disease"),
        ("Carditis", "Disease")]                                   # A ⊑ B
conj = [("Disease", "X1", "HeartDisease"), ("Disease", "X2", "OrganDisease")]  # A ⊓ B ⊑ C
ex_r = [("HeartDisease", "site", "Heart"), ("OrganDisease", "site", "Organ"),
        ("Carditis", "site", "Heart")]                             # A ⊑ ∃r.B
ex_l = [("site", "Heart", "X1"), ("site", "Organ", "X2")]          # ∃r.A ⊑ B

names = {n for ax in sub + conj + ex_r + ex_l for n in ax if n != "site"}
S = {a: {a} for a in names}          # S[a] = the names we know are above a
R = set()                            # (r, a, b): every a has an r-link to some b
changed, rounds = True, 0
while changed:
    changed, rounds = False, rounds + 1
    new_s = [(a, b) for a in names for (x, b) in sub if x in S[a]]
    new_s += [(a, c) for a in names for (x, y, c) in conj if x in S[a] and y in S[a]]
    new_s += [(a, c) for (r, a, b) in R for (r2, y, c) in ex_l if r == r2 and y in S[b]]
    new_r = [(r, a, b) for a in names for (x, r, b) in ex_r if x in S[a]]
    for a, b in new_s:
        if b not in S[a]: S[a].add(b); changed = True
    for t in new_r:
        if t not in R: R.add(t); changed = True

print("rounds:", rounds)
for a in sorted(n for n in names if not n.startswith("X")):
    print(f"{a:13} ⊑", ", ".join(sorted(b for b in S[a] - {a} if not b.startswith("X"))))
rounds: 5
Carditis      ⊑ Disease, HeartDisease, OrganDisease
Disease       ⊑
Heart         ⊑ Organ
HeartDisease  ⊑ Disease, OrganDisease
Organ         ⊑
OrganDisease  ⊑ Disease
// EL classification by saturation. The TBox is already in normal form.
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet, HashSet};

fn main() {
    let sub = [("Heart", "Organ"), ("HeartDisease", "Disease"), ("OrganDisease", "Disease"),
               ("Carditis", "Disease")];                                  // A ⊑ B
    let conj = [("Disease", "X1", "HeartDisease"), ("Disease", "X2", "OrganDisease")];
    let ex_r = [("HeartDisease", "site", "Heart"), ("OrganDisease", "site", "Organ"),
                ("Carditis", "site", "Heart")];                           // A ⊑ ∃r.B
    let ex_l = [("site", "Heart", "X1"), ("site", "Organ", "X2")];        // ∃r.A ⊑ B
    let mut s: BTreeMap<&str, BTreeSet<&str>> = BTreeMap::new();
    for n in sub.iter().flat_map(|(a, b)| [*a, *b])
        .chain(conj.iter().flat_map(|(a, b, c)| [*a, *b, *c]))
        .chain(ex_r.iter().flat_map(|(a, _, b)| [*a, *b])) {
        s.insert(n, BTreeSet::from([n]));                 // every name is above itself
    }
    let mut r: HashSet<(&str, &str, &str)> = HashSet::new(); // (role, a, b)
    let mut changed = true;
    while changed {
        changed = false;
        let names: Vec<&str> = s.keys().copied().collect();
        let mut new_s = vec![];
        for &a in &names {
            let sa = &s[a];
            for &(x, b) in &sub { if sa.contains(x) { new_s.push((a, b)); } }
            for &(x, y, c) in &conj { if sa.contains(x) && sa.contains(y) { new_s.push((a, c)); } }
            for &(x, role, b) in &ex_r { if sa.contains(x) { changed |= r.insert((role, a, b)); } }
        }
        for &(role, a, b) in &r {
            for &(r2, y, c) in &ex_l { if role == r2 && s[b].contains(y) { new_s.push((a, c)); } }
        }
        for (a, b) in new_s { changed |= s.get_mut(a).unwrap().insert(b); }
    }
    for (a, ups) in s.iter().filter(|(a, _)| !a.starts_with('X')) {
        let list: Vec<&str> = ups.iter().copied().filter(|b| b != a && !b.starts_with('X')).collect();
        println!("{:13} ⊑ {}", a, list.join(", "));
    }
}
Carditis      ⊑ Disease, HeartDisease, OrganDisease
Disease       ⊑
Heart         ⊑ Organ
HeartDisease  ⊑ Disease, OrganDisease
Organ         ⊑
OrganDisease  ⊑ Disease

Nobody wrote "a heart disease is an organ disease". The loop found it. It stopped after five rounds, when nothing new appeared. It never branched and never guessed. This is the idea behind the ELK reasoner. The ELK team says it classifies SNOMED CT, with about 300,000 classes, in a few seconds on a laptop.

DL-Lite: let the database do the work

DL-Lite takes another path. It keeps the data in a normal database. It does not add new facts to the data. Instead it rewrites each query so that it also finds the implied answers. This is called query rewriting.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
  CREATE TABLE teacher(id TEXT);           -- rows typed as Teacher
  CREATE TABLE professor(id TEXT);         -- rows typed as Professor
  CREATE TABLE teaches(who TEXT, course TEXT);
  INSERT INTO teacher   VALUES ('tom');
  INSERT INTO professor VALUES ('ada');
  INSERT INTO teaches   VALUES ('chen', 'ai201');
""")
# TBox:  Professor ⊑ Teacher     ∃teaches ⊑ Teacher
# Query: Teacher(x).  Rewriting adds one SELECT for each axiom that ends in Teacher.
rewritten = """
  SELECT id  FROM teacher
  UNION SELECT id  FROM professor          -- from Professor ⊑ Teacher
  UNION SELECT who FROM teaches            -- from ∃teaches ⊑ Teacher
"""
print("plain query:", [r[0] for r in db.execute("SELECT id FROM teacher")])
print("rewritten:  ", sorted(r[0] for r in db.execute(rewritten)))
plain query: ['tom']
rewritten:   ['ada', 'chen', 'tom']

The axiom \exists teaches \sqsubseteq Teacher means "whoever teaches something is a teacher". DL-Lite keeps every rewriting finite, so the result is plain SQL. This approach is called ontology-based data access. OWL 2 QL is the W3C profile built on DL-Lite.

Why the light families are fast
FamilyWhat it dropsWhat it does insteadTypical use
EL (OWL 2 EL)or, only, notsaturation, no branchesbig medical and life-science ontologies
DL-Lite (OWL 2 QL)or, chains of "some" on the left, transitive rolesquery rewriting into SQLontologies over large databases

One "or" can break a profile. Add Course \sqsubseteq Lecture \sqcup Seminar to an EL ontology, and it is no longer EL. An EL reasoner may skip that axiom or refuse the ontology. Check the reasoner log after every change.

Patterns to remember

Description logic patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
C ⊓ DBoth at onceProfessor \sqcap ResearcherSet intersection.
C ⊔ DAt least oneLecture \sqcup SeminarCauses branching. Not in EL.
∃r.CSome link to a C exists\exists teaches.SeminarThe workhorse of EL.
∀r.CAll links go to a C\forall teaches.SeminarTrue with no links. Add ∃ if needed.
¬∃r.C = ∀r.¬CMove "not" inside\neg \exists teaches.\top = \forall teaches.\botNeeded for negation normal form.
A ⊑ CNecessary conditionProfessor \sqsubseteq PersonNever sorts individuals into A.
A ≡ CFull definitionLecturer \equiv Person \sqcap \exists teaches.CourseLets the reasoner classify.
r ∘ s ⊑ tRole chain (RBox)hasParent \circ hasBrother \sqsubseteq hasUncleNeeds R, so SROIQ.
C ⊑ D testSubsumptionC \sqcap \neg D unsatisfiableOne engine for all tasks.
C(a) testInstance checkingadd \neg C(a), look for a clashOpen world: "no" means "not entailed".
ClashClose a branchCourse and \neg Course at x1All branches closed means unsatisfiable.
BlockingStop an endless treex1 has the same label as xNeeded with a general TBox.
SROIQ(D)Name of OWL 2 DLR, O, I, Q plus datatypesN2ExpTime in the worst case.
EL or DL-LiteFast reasoning on big dataOWL 2 EL, OWL 2 QLStay inside the profile.

Practice

Which concept means "teaches only seminars"?

  • \exists teaches.Seminar
  • \forall teaches.Seminar
  • teaches \sqcap Seminar

∀ is "only". ∃ is "some". A role and a concept cannot be joined with ⊓.

Which axiom belongs in the RBox?

  • Seminar \sqsubseteq Course
  • hasMother \sqsubseteq hasParent
  • teaches(ada, sem7)

The RBox holds axioms about roles. The first one is TBox, the last one is ABox.

What does the letter O add in SHOIN(D)?

  • Object properties
  • Nominals: classes made of named individuals
  • OWL compatibility

O stands for nominals, like the class {red, green, blue}.

The tableau for C \sqcap \neg D finds one open branch with no clash. What follows?

  • C \sqsubseteq D
  • C \sqsubseteq D does not hold
  • The ontology is inconsistent

The open branch is a counter-model: a C that is not a D.

Why is EL reasoning polynomial?

  • EL ontologies are always small.
  • EL has no "or", so the reasoner never branches.
  • EL has no roles.

Without "or", "only" and "not", saturation adds facts in one direction until it stops.

Fill in the missing words.

\neg \exists r.C is the same as ?.

The DL behind OWL 2 DL is ?.

In DL names, the letter for inverse roles is ?.

Concept, role, individual: what are they in OWL?

Class, object property, individual.

How do you test C \sqsubseteq D with a tableau?

Check whether C \sqcap \neg D is satisfiable. If every branch clashes, C \sqsubseteq D holds.

What is blocking?

Stopping a node whose label repeats an ancestor's label, so the tree stays finite.

Data complexity or combined complexity: which matters for a billion facts?

Data complexity. The schema and the query stay small and fixed.

  1. Write "a parent whose children are all doctors" in ALC. Use Person, hasChild and Doctor.
    Answer

    Person \sqcap \exists hasChild.\top \sqcap \forall hasChild.Doctor. The ∃ part makes sure the person really has a child.

  2. Decode the name ALCHIQ.
    Answer

    ALC (and, or, not, some, only) plus H (role hierarchy), I (inverse roles) and Q (qualified number restrictions).

  3. Run the tableau by hand on \exists r.A \sqcap \forall r.\neg A. Is it satisfiable?
    Answer

    Start with x. The ∃-rule makes y with A. The ∀-rule adds ¬A to y. Clash at y. There are no branches, so the concept is unsatisfiable.

  4. How do you check "Is Ada a Lecturer?" with a consistency test only?
    Answer

    Add the fact \neg Lecturer(ada) to the knowledge base. If the result is inconsistent, Ada must be a lecturer. If it is still consistent, the fact is not entailed. Under the open world that means "unknown", not "no".

  5. An EL ontology classifies in two seconds. A teammate adds Course \sqsubseteq Lecture \sqcup Seminar. What can go wrong?
    Answer

    The ontology leaves OWL 2 EL. An EL reasoner like ELK may skip the axiom, so some answers go missing. A full OWL 2 DL reasoner must now branch, and it may be much slower. Model the split another way, or keep it in a separate module.

  6. The TBox is Professor \sqsubseteq Teacher and \exists teaches \sqsubseteq Teacher. Rewrite the query "find all teachers" for tables teacher(id), professor(id) and teaches(who, course).
    Answer

    SELECT id FROM teacher UNION SELECT id FROM professor UNION SELECT who FROM teaches. Each axiom that ends in Teacher adds one SELECT.

Key takeaways

  • A description logic has concepts (classes), roles (properties) and individuals.
  • ALC builds concepts with ⊤, ⊥, ¬, ⊓, ⊔, ∃ and ∀. "Only" is true when there are no links.
  • The TBox is about concepts, the RBox about roles, the ABox about individuals.
  • Subsumption, satisfiability and instance checks all become one consistency test.
  • Each letter in a DL name adds a feature. OWL DL is SHOIN(D). OWL 2 DL is SROIQ(D).
  • The tableau method tries to build a counter-model. A clash on every branch proves the claim.
  • Worst-case cost grows from AC0 and P up to N2ExpTime. Real ontologies are often easier.
  • EL is fast because it never branches. DL-Lite is fast because it rewrites queries into SQL.

Sources

  • A Description Logic Primer. Krötzsch, Simančík and Horrocks on SROIQ, the boxes, the naming scheme, EL, DLP and DL-Lite.
  • An Introduction to Description Logic. The textbook by Baader, Horrocks, Lutz and Sattler (2017), with a chapter on tableau algorithms for ALC.
  • OWL 2 Profiles (Second Edition). The W3C profiles EL, QL and RL and the complexity table in section 5.
  • Tobies: The Complexity of Reasoning with Cardinality Restrictions and Nominals. The JAIR paper (2000) behind the NExpTime results for logics like OWL DL.
  • Description logic (Wikipedia). A summary of the naming letters and of OWL Lite, OWL DL and OWL 2.
  • The ELK Reasoner. The OWL 2 EL reasoner and its SNOMED CT timing.

RDF and RDF Schema

RDF is the data model under OWL, SPARQL and SHACL. It turns all data into small statements with three parts. RDF Schema adds a few words for classes and properties, and some simple rules. This chapter covers both, up to the new triple terms of RDF 1.2.
