  • Break a statement into a triple with IRIs, literals and blank nodes.
  • Read and write one graph in Turtle, N-Triples, JSON-LD and RDF/XML.
  • Use named graphs to record where facts come from.
  • Run the RDFS entailment rules by hand and check them with a program.
  • Write a statement about a statement in RDF 1.1 and in RDF 1.2, and state the RDF 1.2 status today.

The triple

Start with one sentence about a painting.

Blue Harbour was painted by Mira.

RDF cuts it into three parts.

One sentence, one triple
SubjectPredicateObject
Blue Harbourpainted byMira
ex:harbourex:paintedByex:mira

A triple is one statement. The subject is what the statement is about. The predicate is the link. The object is the end of the link. RDF stands for Resource Description Framework.

Here is a small file with more facts about the painting. It is written in Turtle, the most common RDF syntax.

@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/art#> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:harbour a ex:Painting ;
    ex:title "Blue Harbour"@en , "Port bleu"@fr ;
    ex:paintedBy ex:mira ;
    ex:year 1921 ;
    ex:size [ ex:widthCm 60 ; ex:heightCm 45 ] .

ex:mira ex:name "Mira Kovač" .

A set of triples is an RDF graph. Each subject and object is a node. Each triple is one arrow. The file has nine triples. The semicolon in Turtle repeats the subject. The comma repeats the subject and the predicate.

What can stand where (RDF 1.1)
PositionIRIBlank nodeLiteral
Subjectyesyesno
Predicateyesnono
Objectyesyesyes

A literal cannot be a subject. You cannot say anything about the string "Mira Kovač" itself. If you need to, make the thing a node with an IRI, and give it a label.

A graph is a set. If you add the same triple twice, the graph still has it once. Order also does not matter. The file can list triples in any order.

IRIs, literals and language tags

IRIs: global names

The name ex:harbour is short for http://example.org/art#harbour. That long name is an IRI. Two files that use the same IRI talk about the same thing. The prefix ex: only saves typing.

IRIs must match exactly. http://example.org/art#Harbour, https://example.org/art#harbour and http://example.org/art/harbour are three different names. One wrong letter, an "s" or a slash, makes a new thing.

Literals: values with a type

A literal is a value. It has a written form and a datatype. In Turtle, 1921 is short for "1921"^^xsd:integer. Most datatypes come from XML Schema, like xsd:integer, xsd:decimal, xsd:date and xsd:boolean.

A text can carry a language tag, like "Port bleu"@fr. Its datatype is then rdf:langString. Language tags follow BCP 47, so en, fr and pt-BR all work.

Now look at three paintings. Which of them are from the year 1921?

@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/art#> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:harbour ex:year 1921 .                    # xsd:integer
ex:dunes   ex:year "01921"^^xsd:integer .    # same number, other spelling
ex:storm   ex:year "1921" .                  # a plain string, not a number
ex:storm   ex:title "Storm"@en , "Storm"@de , "Storm" .
from rdflib import Graph, Namespace

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/art#")
g = Graph().parse("years.ttl")
q = """PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/art#>
SELECT ?w WHERE { ?w ex:year ?y . FILTER (?y = 1921) } ORDER BY ?w"""
print("year = 1921:", [str(r.w).split("#")[1] for r in g.query(q)])
print("storm titles:", sorted(t.n3() for t in g.objects(EX.storm, EX.title)))
year = 1921: ['dunes', 'harbour']
storm titles: ['"Storm"', '"Storm"@de', '"Storm"@en']

Two results come back. "01921" and "1921" are two spellings of one integer, so both match. The plain string "1921" is text, not a number, so it does not match. The three titles are three different literals, because their language tags differ.

RDF 1.2 adds a text direction for languages written right to left. In Turtle 1.2 you write "يمين"@ar--rtl. The datatype is then rdf:dirLangString.

Do not write numbers and dates in quotes without a datatype. ex:year "1921" is a string. Sorting, filters and sums treat it as text. Write 1921 or "1921"^^xsd:gYear.

Blank nodes

Look at the size in art.ttl: [ ex:widthCm 60 ; ex:heightCm 45 ]. It has no IRI. It is a blank node. In N-Triples it gets a local label like _:b1. The label means something only inside one file.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/art#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("art.ttl")
g.parse("art.ttl")              # load the same file a second time
print("triples:", len(g))       # IRI triples merge, blank node triples do not
print("sizes of harbour:", len(list(g.objects(EX.harbour, EX.size))))
triples: 12
sizes of harbour: 2

The file has 9 triples. Loaded twice, it gives 12, not 9. The six triples with only IRIs and literals merged. The three triples with the blank node did not. Each load made a new blank node. Now the painting has two sizes.

Two graphs that differ only in blank node labels are isomorphic. Tools treat them as the same graph. You see this test in the syntax section below.

Need a stable name later? RDF 1.1 suggests skolemization. You replace each blank node with a fresh IRI. The W3C suggests IRIs under /.well-known/genid/ for this.

Do not use blank nodes for things others must point to. A person, a product or an order needs an IRI. Use blank nodes only for small helper structures, like a size or an address.

Graphs and named graphs

Two sources disagree. The city museum says Blue Harbour is from 1921. An open wiki says 1922. You want to keep both facts, and know who said what.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/art#> .
@prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> .

ex:museumData {                       # a named graph: what the museum says
    ex:harbour ex:year 1921 .
}
ex:wikiData {                         # another named graph: what a wiki says
    ex:harbour ex:year 1922 .
}
# the default graph: facts about the two graphs
ex:museumData prov:wasAttributedTo ex:cityMuseum .
ex:wikiData   prov:wasAttributedTo ex:openWiki .
from rdflib import Dataset

ds = Dataset()
ds.parse("sources.trig", format="trig")
q = """PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/art#>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
SELECT ?year ?who WHERE {
  GRAPH ?g { ex:harbour ex:year ?year }
  ?g prov:wasAttributedTo ?who
} ORDER BY ?year"""
for r in ds.query(q):
    print(r.year, "according to", r.who.split("#")[1])
print(ds.serialize(format="nquads").strip().splitlines()[0])
1921 according to cityMuseum
1922 according to openWiki
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#year> "1922"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> <http://example.org/art#wikiData> .

An RDF dataset has one default graph and any number of named graphs. A named graph is a graph with a name. TriG is Turtle with graph blocks. N-Quads is N-Triples with a fourth part: the graph name. In SPARQL, GRAPH ?g { ... } looks inside named graphs.

RDF does not fix what a graph name means. Is it the source, the file, the time or a version? You decide, and you must write it down. Here the default graph says it: the name stands for a source.

Four syntaxes, one graph

RDF is a model, not a file format. The same graph has many written forms. Here is art.ttl in four of them.

@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/art#> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:harbour a ex:Painting ;
    ex:title "Blue Harbour"@en , "Port bleu"@fr ;
    ex:paintedBy ex:mira ;
    ex:year 1921 ;
    ex:size [ ex:widthCm 60 ; ex:heightCm 45 ] .

ex:mira ex:name "Mira Kovač" .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://example.org/art#Painting> .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#title> "Blue Harbour"@en .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#title> "Port bleu"@fr .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#paintedBy> <http://example.org/art#mira> .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#year> "1921"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#size> _:b1 .
_:b1 <http://example.org/art#widthCm> "60"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> .
_:b1 <http://example.org/art#heightCm> "45"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> .
<http://example.org/art#mira> <http://example.org/art#name> "Mira Kovač" .
{
  "@context": { "ex": "http://example.org/art#" },
  "@id": "ex:harbour",
  "@type": "ex:Painting",
  "ex:title": [ { "@value": "Blue Harbour", "@language": "en" },
                { "@value": "Port bleu", "@language": "fr" } ],
  "ex:paintedBy": { "@id": "ex:mira", "ex:name": "Mira Kovač" },
  "ex:year": 1921,
  "ex:size": { "ex:widthCm": 60, "ex:heightCm": 45 }
}
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<rdf:RDF xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#"
         xmlns:ex="http://example.org/art#">
  <ex:Painting rdf:about="http://example.org/art#harbour">
    <ex:title xml:lang="en">Blue Harbour</ex:title>
    <ex:title xml:lang="fr">Port bleu</ex:title>
    <ex:paintedBy>
      <rdf:Description rdf:about="http://example.org/art#mira">
        <ex:name>Mira Kovač</ex:name>
      </rdf:Description>
    </ex:paintedBy>
    <ex:year rdf:datatype="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer">1921</ex:year>
    <ex:size rdf:parseType="Resource">
      <ex:widthCm rdf:datatype="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer">60</ex:widthCm>
      <ex:heightCm rdf:datatype="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer">45</ex:heightCm>
    </ex:size>
  </ex:Painting>
</rdf:RDF>

Are they really the same? A program can check. It parses all four files and compares the graphs.

from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.compare import isomorphic

files = {"art.ttl": "turtle", "art.nt": "nt", "art.jsonld": "json-ld", "art.rdf": "xml"}
graphs = {f: Graph().parse(f, format=fmt) for f, fmt in files.items()}
base = graphs["art.ttl"]
for f, g in graphs.items():
    # isomorphic: the same graph, even if blank nodes have other labels
    print(f"{f:11} {len(g)} triples, same graph as art.ttl: {isomorphic(g, base)}")
art.ttl     9 triples, same graph as art.ttl: True
art.nt      9 triples, same graph as art.ttl: True
art.jsonld  9 triples, same graph as art.ttl: True
art.rdf     9 triples, same graph as art.ttl: True
Common RDF syntaxes
SyntaxMedia typeGood for
Turtle (.ttl)text/turtleWriting by hand, reading, teaching
N-Triples (.nt)application/n-triplesBig dumps, one triple per line, easy to split
JSON-LD (.jsonld)application/ld+jsonWeb APIs and web pages, like schema.org
RDF/XML (.rdf, .owl)application/rdf+xmlOld tools and many OWL files
TriG and N-Quadsapplication/trig, application/n-quadsDatasets with named graphs

In JSON-LD, the @context maps short keys to IRIs. @id names a node and @type gives its class. A node object without @id, like the size, becomes a blank node.

A JSON key with no meaning in the context is dropped. We tested a file with the keys "title" and "nickname". Only "title" was in the context. The result had one triple, not two. The nickname was silently lost.

The RDFS vocabulary

RDF alone has no idea of classes. RDF Schema (RDFS) adds a small set of words for them. You already used some: rdf:type, rdfs:subClassOf, rdfs:domain. RDF Schema 1.1 is a W3C Recommendation from 25 February 2014.

The RDFS words you use most
TermMeaningExample
rdfs:ResourceThe class of everythingEvery IRI names a resource.
rdfs:ClassThe class of all classesex:Painting a rdfs:Class
rdf:PropertyThe class of all propertiesex:paintedBy a rdf:Property
rdfs:Literal, rdfs:DatatypeValues and their typesxsd:integer a rdfs:Datatype
rdf:typeIs a member ofex:harbour a ex:Painting
rdfs:subClassOfEvery member is also a member ofex:Painting rdfs:subClassOf ex:Artwork
rdfs:subPropertyOfEvery link is also a link ofex:paintedBy rdfs:subPropertyOf ex:creator
rdfs:domain, rdfs:rangeThe class at the start or at the end of a linkex:creator rdfs:range ex:Person
rdfs:label, rdfs:commentA name and a note for peopleex:Painting rdfs:label "painting"@en
rdfs:seeAlso, rdfs:isDefinedByWhere to read moreA link to the vocabulary file

The vocabulary also has rdf:List with rdf:first, rdf:rest and rdf:nil for ordered lists. Turtle writes a list as ( a b c ). Older containers, rdf:Bag, rdf:Seq and rdf:Alt, use rdf:_1, rdf:_2 and so on.

RDF gives you triples. RDFS gives you a handful of words to describe your own words: what is a class, what is a property, and what is inside what.

Do not invent your own label property. Use rdfs:label for display names, with a language tag. Many tools, like Protégé and search indexes, look for it.

RDFS entailment rules, run by hand

Here is a small gallery file. It has five schema triples and three data triples.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/art#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

ex:Painting  rdfs:subClassOf ex:Artwork .           # T1
ex:Artwork   rdfs:subClassOf ex:CreativeWork .      # T2
ex:paintedBy rdfs:subPropertyOf ex:creator .        # T3
ex:creator   rdfs:domain ex:CreativeWork ;          # T4
             rdfs:range  ex:Person .                # T5

ex:harbour a ex:Painting ;                          # T6
           ex:paintedBy ex:mira .                   # T7
ex:sketch9 ex:paintedBy ex:mira .                   # T8: no type given

The W3C RDF Semantics gives a list of entailment rules. Six of them do most of the work.

RuleIf the graph hasThen add
rdfs2P rdfs:domain C, and x P yx rdf:type C
rdfs3P rdfs:range C, and x P yy rdf:type C
rdfs5P subPropertyOf Q, and Q subPropertyOf RP subPropertyOf R
rdfs7P subPropertyOf Q, and x P yx Q y
rdfs9A subClassOf B, and x rdf:type Ax rdf:type B
rdfs11A subClassOf B, and B subClassOf CA subClassOf C

Now apply them by hand. Keep going until no rule adds anything new.

  1. rdfs11 on T1 and T2: ex:Painting rdfs:subClassOf ex:CreativeWork.
  2. rdfs9 on T6 and T1: ex:harbour a ex:Artwork. Then with step 1: ex:harbour a ex:CreativeWork.
  3. rdfs7 on T3 and T7: ex:harbour ex:creator ex:mira. On T3 and T8: ex:sketch9 ex:creator ex:mira.
  4. rdfs2 on T4 and step 3: ex:sketch9 a ex:CreativeWork. For harbour we already have it.
  5. rdfs3 on T5 and step 3: ex:mira a ex:Person.
  6. Try every rule again. Nothing new appears. This is the closure. We found 7 new facts.

Now let a program do the same. We used the owlrl package, version 7.6.2, with rdflib 7.6.0.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF, RDFS
import owlrl

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/art#")
g = Graph().parse("gallery.ttl")
before = set(g)
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.RDFS_Semantics).expand(g)   # apply the RDFS rules
new = set(g) - before
print("triples before:", len(before), " after:", len(g), " new:", len(new))

def short(t):
    return " ".join(x.n3(g.namespace_manager) for x in t)

# keep only new facts about our own names; hide "x a rdfs:Resource" and "p subPropertyOf p"
mine = [t for t in new if str(t[0]).startswith(str(EX)) and str(t[2]).startswith(str(EX))
        and t[0] != t[2]]
for t in sorted(mine, key=short):
    print(" ", short(t))
triples before: 8  after: 38  new: 30
  ex:Painting rdfs:subClassOf ex:CreativeWork
  ex:harbour ex:creator ex:mira
  ex:harbour rdf:type ex:Artwork
  ex:harbour rdf:type ex:CreativeWork
  ex:mira rdf:type ex:Person
  ex:sketch9 ex:creator ex:mira
  ex:sketch9 rdf:type ex:CreativeWork

The program found the same 7 facts. It also added 23 more. They are dull but correct, like "harbour is a resource", "paintedBy is a property" and "creator is a sub-property of itself". The rules rdfs4 and rdfs6, and the RDF rule rdf1, make them.

The full RDFS closure is infinite. The rules know the container properties rdf:_1, rdf:_2, and so on, without end. Real tools add only a finite, useful part. RDF 1.2 Semantics adds rules for triple terms, named rdfs14 and rdfs14a.

Domain and range make new facts. They never reject data. If a dog "paints" something, RDFS concludes that the dog is a person. RDFS has no "not", so a graph almost never becomes inconsistent. The only clashes come from bad literals, like "abc"^^xsd:integer. See The building blocks for this trap, and SHACL and validation for real checks.

Statements about statements

The wiki says the year is 1922. You do not believe it. But you want to record the claim and its source. You need a statement about a statement.

RDF 1.1: reification

@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/art#> .
@prefix rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> .

ex:claim1 a rdf:Statement ;                # RDF 1.1 reification: four triples
    rdf:subject   ex:harbour ;
    rdf:predicate ex:year ;
    rdf:object    1922 ;
    ex:source     ex:openWiki .
from rdflib import Graph
g = Graph().parse("claim11.ttl")
print("triples:", len(g))
print("asserted?", g.query("""PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/art#>
    ASK { ex:harbour ex:year 1922 }""").askAnswer)
triples: 5
asserted? False

This is reification. Four triples describe one triple. The described triple is not asserted. It is only talked about. The method works, but it is long, and RDF 1.1 gives it no special meaning. Many teams used named graphs instead.

RDF 1.2: triple terms and reifiers

RDF 1.2 adds a new kind of term. A triple term is a triple that stands in the object place of another triple. A reifier is a node that points to a triple term with rdf:reifies. Then you describe the reifier.

PREFIX ex:  <http://example.org/art#>
PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#>

# asserted, and annotated through the reifier ex:c1
ex:harbour ex:year 1921 ~ ex:c1 {| ex:source ex:cityMuseum |} .

# only reified: a claim about a triple that is NOT asserted
<< ex:harbour ex:year 1922 ~ ex:c2 >> ex:source ex:openWiki .
import pyoxigraph as ox

store = ox.Store()
store.load(path="claim12.ttl", format=ox.RdfFormat.TURTLE)
nt = store.dump(format=ox.RdfFormat.N_TRIPLES, from_graph=ox.DefaultGraph()).decode()
print("".join(sorted(nt.splitlines(keepends=True))))
ask = "PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/art#> ASK { ex:harbour ex:year 1922 }"
print("1922 asserted?", bool(store.query(ask)))
q = """PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/art#>
SELECT ?year ?src WHERE { << ex:harbour ex:year ?year >> ex:source ?src } ORDER BY ?year"""
for row in store.query(q):
    print(row["year"].value, "according to", row["src"].value.split("#")[1])
<http://example.org/art#c1> <http://example.org/art#source> <http://example.org/art#cityMuseum> .
<http://example.org/art#c1> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#reifies> <<( <http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#year> "1921"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> )>> .
<http://example.org/art#c2> <http://example.org/art#source> <http://example.org/art#openWiki> .
<http://example.org/art#c2> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#reifies> <<( <http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#year> "1922"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> )>> .
<http://example.org/art#harbour> <http://example.org/art#year> "1921"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> .

1922 asserted? False
1921 according to cityMuseum
1922 according to openWiki

Read the N-Triples output. Each Turtle shortcut became plain triples.

  • ~ ex:c1 names the reifier. {| ... |} is the annotation syntax. The 1921 triple is asserted and also described.
  • << ... >> is a reified triple. It makes a reifier and an rdf:reifies link. The 1922 triple is not asserted. The ASK query says False.
  • <<( ... )>> with round brackets is the triple term itself. It appears only as an object.

The query uses the draft SPARQL 1.2 form << ... >> to match a reifier. We ran this with pyoxigraph 0.5.13, which reads Turtle 1.2. rdflib 7.6.0 could not parse the file. It raised a syntax error.

RDF 1.2 is not a W3C Recommendation yet. We checked the W3C pages on 15 November 2026. RDF 1.2 Concepts is a Candidate Recommendation Draft dated 13 November 2026. RDF 1.2 Semantics is a Candidate Recommendation Draft dated 24 September 2026. Both had a Candidate Recommendation Snapshot on 7 April 2026. RDF 1.2 Turtle and N-Triples are still Working Drafts, from 11 and 5 November 2026. The syntax can still change. Check the W3C pages again before you build on it.

  1. 1999 RDF Model and Syntax. The first W3C Recommendation for RDF, with RDF/XML.
  2. 2004 RDF revised. New RDF documents and RDF Schema become Recommendations.
  3. 2014 RDF 1.1. Turtle, N-Triples, TriG and N-Quads become Recommendations. JSON-LD 1.0 too.
  4. 2020 JSON-LD 1.1. A W3C Recommendation on 16 July 2020.
  5. 2026 RDF 1.2 in Candidate Recommendation. Concepts and Semantics reach this stage on 7 April 2026.

A triple term is not a fact. ex:c2 rdf:reifies <<( ... 1922 )>> does not say the painting is from 1922. Write the triple on its own as well if you mean it to be true. The annotation syntax does both in one line.

Common mistakes

These mistakes appear in real RDF data again and again. Each one has a simple fix.

Typing a thing as a string

ex:harbour ex:painter "Mira" cannot be joined with other data. Use an IRI, ex:mira, and give it a label.

Numbers and dates without a datatype

"1921" is text. Write 1921 or "1921"^^xsd:gYear. Otherwise filters and sorting go wrong.

Almost the same IRI

http and https, a slash and a hash, or a capital letter all make new names. Copy prefixes from one shared file.

Blank nodes for real things

Blank nodes cannot be linked from outside, and they do not merge when you load data twice. Give real things IRIs.

subClassOf for an individual

ex:harbour rdfs:subClassOf ex:Painting makes the painting a class. Use rdf:type, written a in Turtle.

Domain and range as checks

They add types. They never reject. Use SHACL for checks.

Missing language tags

"Storm", "Storm"@en and "Storm"@de are three different literals. Pick one rule and keep to it.

A JSON-LD context that misses keys

Keys not in the context vanish when you convert to RDF. Convert once and count the triples.

Reification taken as a fact

Neither rdf:Statement nor a triple term asserts the triple. Assert it separately if it is true.

After every change, convert your file to N-Triples and read it. One triple per line shows every mistake above very clearly.

Patterns to remember

RDF and RDFS patterns in Turtle
PatternPurposeModelNote
s p o .One statementex:harbour ex:paintedBy ex:mira .Subject and predicate are never literals.
s p o1 , o2 .Same subject and predicateex:harbour ex:title "Blue Harbour"@en , "Port bleu"@fr .The comma repeats subject and predicate.
s p1 o1 ; p2 o2 .Same subjectex:harbour a ex:Painting ; ex:year 1921 .The semicolon repeats the subject.
"text"@langText in a language"Port bleu"@frDifferent tags make different literals.
"value"^^typeTyped value"1921"^^xsd:gYearA quoted number with no type is a string.
[ p o ]Small helper nodeex:size [ ex:widthCm 60 ]Blank nodes do not merge across loads.
g { triples }Named graph in TriGex:wikiData { ex:harbour ex:year 1922 . }Write down what the graph name means.
A rdfs:subClassOf BClass inside a classex:Painting rdfs:subClassOf ex:Artwork .Members of A get type B (rdfs9).
P rdfs:subPropertyOf QLink inside a linkex:paintedBy rdfs:subPropertyOf ex:creator .Every P link is also a Q link (rdfs7).
P rdfs:domain CType of the subjectex:creator rdfs:domain ex:CreativeWork .Adds types. Never rejects.
s p o ~ r {| q v |}Assert and describe (RDF 1.2)ex:harbour ex:year 1921 ~ ex:c1 {| ex:source ex:cityMuseum |} .Draft syntax. Check the W3C status.
<< s p o >> q vDescribe without asserting (RDF 1.2)<< ex:harbour ex:year 1922 >> ex:source ex:openWiki .The inner triple is not a fact.

Practice

Which one can be the subject of a triple?

  • The literal "Mira"
  • The blank node _:b1
  • The number 1921

A subject is an IRI or a blank node. Literals can only be objects.

Do 1921 and "01921"^^xsd:integer have the same value?

  • Yes. They are two spellings of one integer.
  • No. The written forms differ.
  • Only in JSON-LD.

The datatype maps both written forms to the number 1921. A SPARQL filter ?y = 1921 matches both.

You load the same Turtle file twice into one graph. It has blank nodes. What happens?

  • Nothing changes.
  • The triples with blank nodes appear twice, with new blank nodes.
  • The tool reports an error.

Blank nodes are local to one load. Each load makes new ones.

Which rule gives ex:mira a ex:Person from ex:creator rdfs:range ex:Person and ex:harbour ex:creator ex:mira?

  • rdfs2
  • rdfs3
  • rdfs9

rdfs3 uses the range and types the object. rdfs2 uses the domain and types the subject.

On 15 November 2026, what is the W3C status of RDF 1.2 Concepts?

  • W3C Recommendation
  • Candidate Recommendation Draft
  • Abandoned

It is a Candidate Recommendation Draft dated 13 November 2026. It is not a Recommendation yet.

Fill in the missing words.

A dataset has one default graph and zero or more ?.

The datatype of "Port bleu"@fr is ?.

In JSON-LD, the key that maps short names to IRIs is ?.

What are the three parts of a triple?

Subject, predicate and object.

What does rdfs9 do?

If A is a subclass of B and x is an A, it adds that x is a B.

What is the difference between <<( s p o )>> and << s p o >>?

The first is a triple term. The second makes a reifier that points to that triple term with rdf:reifies.

When are two graphs isomorphic?

When they are the same except for the labels of blank nodes.

  1. Write this in Turtle with the prefix ex:: "The sketch Dawn was drawn by Ivo in 1930. Its title in German is Morgen."
    Answer

    ex:dawn a ex:Sketch ; ex:drawnBy ex:ivo ; ex:year 1930 ; ex:title "Dawn"@en , "Morgen"@de . The year has no quotes, so it is an integer.

  2. Write the same two triples in N-Triples: ex:dawn ex:drawnBy ex:ivo and ex:dawn ex:year 1930.
    Answer

    <http://example.org/art#dawn> <http://example.org/art#drawnBy> <http://example.org/art#ivo> . and <http://example.org/art#dawn> <http://example.org/art#year> "1930"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> .

  3. Add ex:Sketch rdfs:subClassOf ex:Artwork and ex:drawnBy rdfs:subPropertyOf ex:creator to gallery.ttl, plus exercise 1. Which new facts about dawn and ivo does RDFS add?
    Answer

    rdfs9: dawn is an Artwork, then a CreativeWork (with T2). rdfs7: dawn creator ivo. rdfs2: dawn is a CreativeWork (already found). rdfs3: ivo is a Person.

  4. A JSON-LD file from a partner gives 40 triples. You expected 55. What do you check first?
    Answer

    Check the @context. Keys with no mapping to an IRI are dropped when JSON-LD becomes RDF. Add the missing terms, or use full IRIs as keys.

  5. Two sources give two different birth years for one painter. Show two ways to keep both, with the source of each.
    Answer

    Way 1: put each fact in its own named graph, and describe the graphs in the default graph, as in sources.trig. Way 2 (RDF 1.2, draft): use reifiers, for example << ex:ivo ex:born 1890 ~ ex:r1 >> ex:source ex:archive . and a second reifier for the other year. Named graphs work in every tool today. RDF 1.2 needs a tool that reads it.

  6. Why is the full RDFS closure of any graph infinite? Why does that not hurt real tools?
    Answer

    The RDFS rules and axioms cover the container properties rdf:_1, rdf:_2, and so on, without end. Each of them gets triples such as its type. Real tools add only the triples that matter for the data at hand, so the result stays finite.

Key takeaways

  • A triple is subject, predicate, object. An RDF graph is a set of triples.
  • IRIs are global names. Literals are values with a datatype or a language tag. Blank nodes are local helpers.
  • A dataset holds a default graph and named graphs. Use them to track sources.
  • Turtle, N-Triples, JSON-LD and RDF/XML write the same graphs. Check with an isomorphism test.
  • RDFS adds class, subclass, subproperty, domain, range, label and comment.
  • The RDFS rules add types and links. They never reject data.
  • RDF 1.1 reification and RDF 1.2 triple terms describe a triple without asserting it.
  • On 15 November 2026, RDF 1.2 is a Candidate Recommendation, not yet a Recommendation.

Sources

  • RDF 1.1 Concepts and Abstract Syntax. The W3C definitions of triples, IRIs, literals, blank nodes, skolemization and datasets.
  • RDF Schema 1.1. The W3C list of RDFS classes and properties (Recommendation, 25 February 2014).
  • RDF 1.2 Semantics. The RDFS entailment patterns rdfs1 to rdfs14 and the meaning of triple terms (Candidate Recommendation Draft).
  • RDF 1.2 Concepts and Abstract Data Model. Triple terms, reifiers and base direction. We checked its status line on 15 November 2026.
  • RDF 1.2 Turtle. The draft syntax for triple terms, reified triples and annotations (Working Draft).
  • JSON-LD 1.1. The W3C Recommendation of 16 July 2020 for RDF in JSON.

OWL 2

OWL 2 is the W3C language for rich ontologies. RDF Schema can say "a latte is a coffee". OWL 2 can also say "every latte has some milk" and "nothing is both dairy and plant". A reasoner then finds new facts and hidden errors for you.

  • Write class expressions with and, or, not and the five restrictions.
  • Give each property the right characteristics: transitive, symmetric, functional, inverse.
  • Use equivalence, disjointness, sameAs and datatypes without surprises.
  • Choose the profile EL, QL or RL for a real project.
  • Read and write OWL in Manchester and Turtle syntax, and spot ten classic mistakes.

What OWL 2 adds to RDF Schema

A café owner tells you four things about her menu. Can RDF Schema say them? Look at the table.

Four sentences from a café
SentenceRDF SchemaOWL 2
A latte is a coffee.Yes: rdfs:subClassOfYes
Every latte has some milk.NoYes: a restriction with some
Nothing is both dairy and plant.NoYes: owl:disjointWith
A shop has at most one manager.NoYes: a functional property

RDF Schema gives you classes, subclasses, domain and range. You met them in RDF and RDF Schema. OWL 2 adds the rest of the table. Each new sentence is an axiom.

OWL 2 became a W3C Recommendation on 27 October 2009. A second edition with small fixes followed on 11 December 2012. It replaced OWL 1 from 2004. Old OWL 1 files still work in OWL 2.

One meaning, five syntaxes

OWL 2 has five ways to write the same axiom. RDF/XML is the only one that every tool must read.

In this chapter we use two. Manchester syntax is for people. Turtle is for RDF tools. Pick a tab to see one axiom in four forms.

Class: Latte
    SubClassOf: Coffee, hasIngredient some Milk
:Latte rdfs:subClassOf :Coffee ,
    [ a owl:Restriction ;
      owl:onProperty     :hasIngredient ;
      owl:someValuesFrom :Milk ] .
SubClassOf( :Latte :Coffee )
SubClassOf( :Latte ObjectSomeValuesFrom( :hasIngredient :Milk ) )
Latte ⊑ Coffee
Latte ⊑ ∃hasIngredient.Milk

The Turtle form is longer. The restriction becomes a blank node with three triples. That is why people write Manchester and let tools store Turtle.

Two kinds of meaning

OWL 2 has two official meanings, called semantics. The Direct Semantics reads the ontology as description logic. It is based on the logic SROIQ.

You learn this logic in Description logics. An ontology that follows its rules is OWL 2 DL. Reasoning in OWL 2 DL is decidable. Logic for ontology explains this word.

The RDF-Based Semantics reads any RDF graph as OWL. This is OWL 2 Full. It has no limits, so reasoning is undecidable. In practice, tools work with OWL 2 DL or with one of its profiles.

OWL is not a database schema. An SQL table rejects a bad row. An OWL axiom never rejects data. It describes the world, and the reasoner draws conclusions from it. You see this again and again in this chapter.

Classes and class expressions

Look at these four descriptions of drinks.

  • Coffee: a named class.
  • Coffee or Tea: every drink that is a coffee or a tea.
  • Drink and not Coffee: every drink that is not a coffee.
  • {small, large}: exactly the two sizes small and large.

The last three have no name. Each one is a class expression. You can use it anywhere a class name fits. You can also give it a name with an equivalence axiom. Then it becomes a defined class.

The four basic class constructors
ManchesterTurtleDLMeaning as a set
A and Bowl:intersectionOf ( A B )A \sqcap BIn A and also in B
A or Bowl:unionOf ( A B )A \sqcup BIn A, in B, or in both
not Aowl:complementOf A\neg AEverything outside A
{a, b}owl:oneOf ( a b )\{a, b\}Exactly these individuals

Two classes are always there. owl:Thing holds everything. owl:Nothing holds nothing. A class that must be empty is equal to owl:Nothing.

not Coffee does not mean "not written as a coffee in the data". A reasoner puts a thing in not Coffee only when it can prove it. For example, the thing is a tea, and tea and coffee are disjoint. Missing data is never a proof.

Restrictions: some, only, min, max, value

The café owner describes a latte. "A latte is a coffee. It has some espresso. It has some milk." In Manchester syntax:

Class: Latte
    SubClassOf: Coffee,
        hasIngredient some Espresso,
        hasIngredient some Milk

The part hasIngredient some Milk is a restriction. It is the class of all things with at least one hasIngredient link to a milk. OWL 2 has these restrictions.

Restrictions on a property p
ManchesterDLA thing x is in the class when...Turtle keyword
p some C\exists p.Cx has at least one p link to a Cowl:someValuesFrom
p only C\forall p.Cevery p link of x goes to a Cowl:allValuesFrom
p value a\exists p.\{a\}x has a p link to the individual aowl:hasValue
p min 2 C\geq 2\, p.Cx has 2 or more p links to different Csowl:minQualifiedCardinality
p max 1 C\leq 1\, p.Cx has at most 1 p link to a Cowl:maxQualifiedCardinality
p exactly 2 C= 2\, p.Cboth min 2 and max 2owl:qualifiedCardinality
p Self\exists p.\text{Self}x has a p link to itselfowl:hasSelf true

some is the existential restriction. only is the universal restriction. min, max and exactly are cardinality restrictions. With a class after the number, they are called qualified.

Defined classes and primitive classes

Compare two axioms.

SubClassOf (primitive class)

Class: VeganDrink
    SubClassOf: Drink,
        hasIngredient only Plant

Every vegan drink has only plant ingredients. But a drink with only plant ingredients is not automatically vegan.

EquivalentTo (defined class)

Class: MilkDrink
    EquivalentTo: Drink and
        (hasIngredient some Dairy)

A milk drink has some dairy. And every drink with some dairy is a milk drink. The reasoner finds them.

SubClassOf gives necessary conditions. EquivalentTo gives necessary and sufficient conditions. A class with only necessary conditions is a primitive class.

Run it

Here is a small café ontology and some orders. One order has a mistake. The "vegan" drink contains cow milk.

@prefix : <http://example.org/cafe#> .

:latte1 a :Coffee ; :hasIngredient :shot1 , :milk1 ; :hasSize :large .
:shot1  a :Espresso .
:milk1  a :Milk .
:tea1   a :Tea ; :hasSize :small .
:vegan1 a :VeganDrink ; :hasIngredient :shot2 , :milk2 .   # oops: cow milk
:shot2  a :Espresso .
:milk2  a :Milk .

The full schema cafe.ttl is in the section on Manchester and Turtle below. We run the OWL RL rules of the owlrl package 7.6.2 with rdflib 7.6.0. The command is uv run --with rdflib --with owlrl python3.14 restrictions.py.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF
import owlrl

C = Namespace("http://example.org/cafe#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("cafe.ttl")
g.parse("orders.ttl")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)

def types(x):
    return sorted(t.split("#")[1] for t in g.objects(C[x], RDF.type)
                  if t.startswith(C) and "#" in t)

for x in ("latte1", "tea1", "vegan1", "milk2"):
    print(x.ljust(7), types(x))
latte1  ['Coffee', 'Drink', 'LargeDrink', 'MilkDrink']
tea1    ['Drink', 'Tea']
vegan1  ['Drink', 'MilkDrink', 'VeganDrink']
milk2   ['Dairy', 'Ingredient', 'Milk', 'Plant']

Read the output line by line.

  1. latte1 has some dairy, so it is a MilkDrink. It has the size large, so it is a LargeDrink. Both are defined classes.
  2. tea1 has no ingredients in the data. It gets no extra class.
  3. vegan1 is now a vegan drink and a milk drink. Strange, but not an error yet.
  4. milk2 is now a Plant! The rule "only Plant" did not reject the milk. It concluded that the milk must be a plant.

Now add one axiom: :Dairy owl:disjointWith :Plant. Nothing can be both. Run the rules again.

Disjoint classes :Dairy and :Plant have a common individual :milk2

Now the reasoner finds a real contradiction. The lesson: restrictions infer, disjointness detects. Without disjointness, OWL quietly accepts strange data.

A 2004 paper by Rector and colleagues is about teaching OWL. It lists the same two problems. New users mix up "some" and "only". They also think that classes are disjoint by default. They are not.

Counting needs different names

The class DoubleShot is hasIngredient min 2 Espresso. Cup 1 has the shots shotA and shotB. Is cup 1 a double shot?

We asked the reasoner HermiT. It said no. The two names might mean the same shot.

For cup 2 we added :shotC owl:differentFrom :shotD. Then HermiT said yes. OWL has no unique name assumption.

Do not use only alone and expect a check. "Vegan drinks have only plant ingredients" is true for a drink with no ingredients at all. Add some too, and add disjointness. For full control of the data, use SHACL (see SHACL and validation).

Property characteristics

A café sits in a city. People work there. Here are five facts with five kinds of property.

@prefix :     <http://example.org/cafe#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .

:locatedIn  a owl:ObjectProperty , owl:TransitiveProperty .
:nextTo     a owl:ObjectProperty , owl:SymmetricProperty .
:employs    a owl:ObjectProperty ; owl:inverseOf :worksAt .
:hasManager a owl:ObjectProperty , owl:FunctionalProperty .
:worksIn    a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    owl:propertyChainAxiom ( :worksAt :locatedIn ) .

:beanBar  :locatedIn :kreuzberg ; :nextTo :bookShop ;
          :hasManager :mia , :maria .          # two names
:kreuzberg :locatedIn :berlin .
:sam      :worksAt :beanBar .
from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, OWL
import owlrl

C = Namespace("http://example.org/cafe#")
g = Graph()
g.parse("places.ttl")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)

checks = [
    ("beanBar", C.locatedIn, "berlin"),    # transitive
    ("bookShop", C.nextTo, "beanBar"),     # symmetric
    ("beanBar", C.employs, "sam"),         # inverse
    ("sam", C.worksIn, "berlin"),          # chain
    ("mia", OWL.sameAs, "maria"),          # functional
]
for s, p, o in checks:
    name = p.split("#")[1]
    print(f"{s} {name} {o}?".ljust(28), (C[s], p, C[o]) in g)
beanBar locatedIn berlin?    True
bookShop nextTo beanBar?     True
beanBar employs sam?         True
sam worksIn berlin?          True
mia sameAs maria?            True

Nobody typed these five facts. The reasoner found them. The graph shows the typed links and the new ones.

Property characteristics in OWL 2
CharacteristicRule it addsGood exampleBad example
Transitivex p y, y p z, so x p zlocatedIn, ancestorOfhasParent, knows
Symmetricx p y, so y p xnextTo, marriedToemploys, likes
Asymmetricx p y, so never y p xhasParentnextTo
Reflexiveevery x has x p xsameAgeAshasParent
Irreflexivenever x p xhasParentsameAgeAs
Functionalx p y1, x p y2, so y1 = y2hasBirthDate, hasManagerhasIngredient
Inverse functionalx1 p y, x2 p y, so x1 = x2hasEmailBox (an object)livesIn
Inverse of qx p y, so y q xemploys and worksAtemploys and hires

More property axioms

  • Sub-property. hasManager SubPropertyOf: worksWith. Every manager link is also a "works with" link.
  • Property chain. worksIn SubPropertyChain: worksAt o locatedIn. You saw it work above.
  • Disjoint properties. hasManager and hasCustomer never link the same pair.
  • Keys. HasKey: hasTaxNumber on a class. Two members with the same key value are the same thing. Keys work on named individuals only.

A property that is transitive, or that has a chain, is not simple. In OWL 2 DL, only simple properties may appear in min, max, exactly and Self. Only simple properties may be functional, inverse functional, irreflexive, asymmetric or disjoint. So locatedIn cannot be transitive and asymmetric at the same time. This rule keeps reasoning decidable.

Functional is not a check for "only one value". Our shop has two managers, Mia and Maria. OWL did not report an error. It concluded that Mia and Maria are the same person. You get an error only if you also say :mia owl:differentFrom :maria.

Equivalence, disjointness and individuals

Five axioms connect whole classes.

Axioms between classes
ManchesterTurtleMeaning
Class: A EquivalentTo: Bowl:equivalentClassA and B have the same members
Class: A DisjointWith: Bowl:disjointWithNo member is in both
DisjointClasses: A, B, Cowl:AllDisjointClassesNo two of them share a member
Class: Size DisjointUnionOf: Small, Largeowl:disjointUnionOfSize is exactly Small or Large, never both
EquivalentProperties: p, qowl:equivalentPropertyp and q link the same pairs

Classes overlap by default. Coffee and Tea can share members until you say they cannot. Most real ontologies need many disjointness axioms. The OOPS! pitfall list calls the missing ones "P10 Missing disjointness".

Impossible classes and broken ontologies

Say we add Class: VeganLatte SubClassOf: Latte, VeganDrink. A latte has some milk. Milk is dairy.

A vegan drink has only plant ingredients. Dairy and plant are disjoint. So no vegan latte can exist. The class is unsatisfiable.

An unsatisfiable class is a bug in the schema. If an individual is put into such a class, the whole ontology is inconsistent. An inconsistent ontology entails every statement. So reasoners stop and report it.

Individuals: sameAs and differentFrom

OWL does not assume that two names mean two things. You saw this with Mia and Maria, and with the two shots. Four axioms speak about names.

  • :mia owl:sameAs :maria: one person, two names. All facts of one name hold for the other.
  • :mia owl:differentFrom :sam: two different people.
  • owl:AllDifferent with owl:distinctMembers ( ... ): a whole list of different things.
  • A negative fact. Manchester: Individual: tea1 Facts: not hasSize large. Turtle uses owl:NegativePropertyAssertion.

OWL 2 also allows punning. The IRI :Espresso can name a class and also an individual. The individual can carry facts about the class, like "added to the menu in 2019". The reasoner treats the two uses as separate things.

Do not use owl:sameAs for "very similar". A flat white is like a latte. If you write :flatWhite owl:sameAs :latte, they merge. Every price and recipe of one is now true for the other. For "similar", use your own property or skos:closeMatch.

Datatypes and data ranges

A tea costs 2.50 euros. We want a class of cheap drinks: price below 3.

DataProperty: priceEUR
    Characteristics: Functional
    Range: xsd:decimal

Class: CheapDrink
    EquivalentTo: Drink and (priceEUR some xsd:decimal[< 3.0])

priceEUR is a data property. Its values are literals, not individuals. xsd:decimal[< 3.0] is a data range. The part in square brackets is a facet.

Common datatypes and facets in OWL 2
KindExamples
Numbersxsd:integer, xsd:decimal, xsd:double, owl:real, owl:rational
Textxsd:string, rdf:langString (text with a language tag)
Otherxsd:boolean, xsd:dateTime, xsd:anyURI
Facets< <= > >=, length, minLength, maxLength, pattern, langRange
Your ownDatatype: Euro EquivalentTo: xsd:decimal[>= 0.0]

A data property can be functional. It cannot be transitive, symmetric or inverse. To use a literal value as an identifier, use a key with HasKey.

xsd:date is not in the OWL 2 datatype map. For time, OWL 2 has only xsd:dateTime and xsd:dateTimeStamp. In our test, HermiT stopped with an error on a range of xsd:date. Use xsd:dateTime in axioms, or check dates with SHACL instead.

"2.5" is a string. 2.5 in Turtle is an xsd:decimal. The facet [< 3.0] does not match the string. OWL never converts a value for you. Check the datatype of every literal when you load data.

The three profiles: EL, QL and RL

Full OWL 2 DL can be slow. In the worst case, reasoning time grows extremely fast with size. So the W3C defined three profiles. Each profile removes some features to win speed. Think about three projects.

  1. A medical vocabulary with hundreds of thousands of classes, like SNOMED CT.
  2. Fifty million orders in a PostgreSQL database. Users ask questions in ontology terms.
  3. An RDF knowledge graph that needs rules: transitive, inverse, sameAs.

Project 1 fits OWL 2 EL. Project 2 fits OWL 2 QL. Project 3 fits OWL 2 RL. The table comes from the W3C Profiles document.

The OWL 2 profiles compared
OWL 2 ELOWL 2 QLOWL 2 RL
Built forVery many classesVery much data in databasesRules over RDF data
You can usesome, and, hasValue, chains, transitive, disjoint classes, keys, sameAsinverse, symmetric, disjointness, some (with limits)almost all axioms, with limits on the right side of SubClassOf
You cannot useonly, min, max, or, not, inverse, functional object propertiestransitive, chains, functional, sameAs, hasValue, keyssome on the right side, reflexive, owl:real
Reasoningpolynomial timequery rewriting, very cheap on datapolynomial time with forward rules
Typical toolELKOntopowlrl, RDFox, rule sets in triple stores

Run it: RL rules against a DL reasoner

RL rules are fast, but they miss some things. We tested this. The file dl.ttl holds the latte, a cheap drink class with a facet, and VeganLatte. The script runs owlrl first.

Then it runs HermiT through owlready2 0.51. HermiT needs Java. We used Java 17.

# 1. OWL RL rules (owlrl, pure Python)
g = Graph().parse("dl.ttl")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)
for i, c in QUESTIONS:      # (latte2, MilkDrink), (tea2, CheapDrink)
    print("RL:", i, "is a", c, "?", (C[i], RDF.type, C[c]) in g)
print("RL: problems:", len(list(g.objects(None, ERR))))

# 2. OWL 2 DL reasoner (HermiT inside owlready2)
Graph().parse("dl.ttl").serialize("dl.owl", format="xml")
onto = get_ontology("file://" + os.path.abspath("dl.owl")).load()
with onto:
    sync_reasoner(debug=0)
for i, c in QUESTIONS:
    print("DL:", i, "is a", c, "?", onto[c] in onto[i].INDIRECT_is_a)
bad = [c.name for c in default_world.inconsistent_classes() if c.name != "Nothing"]
print("DL: impossible classes:", bad)
RL: latte2 is a MilkDrink ? True
RL: tea2 is a CheapDrink ? False
RL: problems: 0
DL: latte2 is a MilkDrink ? True
DL: tea2 is a CheapDrink ? True
DL: impossible classes: ['VeganLatte']

Both found the milk drink. Only HermiT used the facet [< 3.0], because RL has no facets. Only HermiT found the impossible class. RL rules work on data. With no vegan latte in the data, no rule fires.

A profile is not a new language. It is a subset of OWL 2.

If your file uses a feature outside RL, an RL engine does not complain. It just misses some answers. Check your ontology against the profile first. Reasoner strategies are in Reasoners and materialisation.

Manchester and Turtle side by side

Here is the whole café schema in both syntaxes. It is the file we tested above. Switch the tabs and compare line by line.

Prefix: : <http://example.org/cafe#>
Ontology: <http://example.org/cafe>

Class: Drink
Class: Coffee     SubClassOf: Drink
Class: Tea        SubClassOf: Drink
Class: Ingredient
Class: Dairy      SubClassOf: Ingredient
Class: Plant      SubClassOf: Ingredient
Class: Milk       SubClassOf: Dairy
Class: OatMilk    SubClassOf: Plant
Class: Espresso   SubClassOf: Plant
Class: Size
Individual: small  Types: Size
Individual: large  Types: Size
ObjectProperty: hasIngredient
ObjectProperty: hasSize

Class: MilkDrink
    EquivalentTo: Drink and (hasIngredient some Dairy)
Class: LargeDrink
    EquivalentTo: Drink and (hasSize value large)
Class: VeganDrink
    SubClassOf: Drink, hasIngredient only Plant
@prefix :     <http://example.org/cafe#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

: a owl:Ontology .
:Drink      a owl:Class .
:Coffee     a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .
:Tea        a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .
:Ingredient a owl:Class .
:Dairy      a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Ingredient .
:Plant      a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Ingredient .
:Milk       a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Dairy .
:OatMilk    a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Plant .
:Espresso   a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf :Plant .
:Size       a owl:Class .
:small a :Size .  :large a :Size .
:hasIngredient a owl:ObjectProperty .
:hasSize       a owl:ObjectProperty .

:MilkDrink owl:equivalentClass [ owl:intersectionOf ( :Drink
    [ a owl:Restriction ; owl:onProperty :hasIngredient ;
      owl:someValuesFrom :Dairy ] ) ] .
:LargeDrink owl:equivalentClass [ owl:intersectionOf ( :Drink
    [ a owl:Restriction ; owl:onProperty :hasSize ;
      owl:hasValue :large ] ) ] .
:VeganDrink rdfs:subClassOf :Drink , [ a owl:Restriction ;
    owl:onProperty :hasIngredient ; owl:allValuesFrom :Plant ] .

Three rules help you read the Turtle form.

  • Square brackets [ ... ] make a blank node. Every restriction is one.
  • Round brackets ( ... ) make an RDF list. and, or and {...} use lists.
  • A restriction always has a owl:Restriction, one owl:onProperty and one keyword like owl:someValuesFrom.

Write in Manchester syntax in Protégé. Save as Turtle for Git and for RDF tools. Turtle diffs are easy to review if you sort the file.

Do not write :Latte owl:someValuesFrom :Milk. A restriction is always a separate node. The class points to it with rdfs:subClassOf or owl:equivalentClass.

Ten classic mistakes

The first mistake is the most common of all. Watch it happen. The schema says "only drinks have a price". Then a muffin gets a price.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF, RDFS
import owlrl

C = Namespace("http://example.org/cafe#")
g = Graph()
g.parse(data="""
@prefix :     <http://example.org/cafe#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
:priceEUR rdfs:domain :Drink .      # "only drinks have a price"
:muffin a :Cake ; :priceEUR 3.5 .   # but the muffin has a price
""", format="turtle")

def run():
    owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)
    return sorted(t.split("#")[1] for t in g.objects(C.muffin, RDF.type)
                  if t.startswith(C))

print("one domain: ", run())
g.add((C.priceEUR, RDFS.domain, C.Food))   # add a second domain
print("two domains:", run())
one domain:  ['Cake', 'Drink']
two domains: ['Cake', 'Drink', 'Food']

No error. The muffin became a drink. With two domains, it became a drink and a food. Now go through all ten.

Domain used as a check

You expect an error. Instead, the subject gets the domain class. The muffin becomes a drink.

Fix: keep domain for meaning. Use SHACL for checks.

Several domains

Two domains mean "both", not "either". The muffin is a drink and a food. OOPS! calls this P19.

Fix: one domain, like Drink or Food, or a common parent class.

"only" without "some"

hasIngredient only Plant is true for a cup of nothing.

Fix: add hasIngredient some Plant when an ingredient must exist.

Missing disjointness

Classes overlap by default. Cow milk became a plant, and nobody noticed.

Fix: make sibling classes disjoint with DisjointClasses.

Functional used as a check

Two values do not give an error. They give sameAs. Mia and Maria merged.

Fix: use SHACL sh:maxCount 1, or state differentFrom.

Unique names assumed

Two IRIs can be one thing. So min 2 did not count two shots.

Fix: add differentFrom or AllDifferent where it matters.

Closed world assumed

A missing fact is unknown, not false. A black coffee is not found as vegan if the data lists only its espresso.

Fix: add a closure axiom, like hasIngredient only Espresso.

"and" inside "some"

hasIngredient some (Milk and OatMilk) means one ingredient that is both. That cannot exist.

Fix: two restrictions: (hasIngredient some Milk) and (hasIngredient some OatMilk).

Wrong transitive or symmetric

hasParent is not transitive. employs is not symmetric. OOPS! calls these P29 and P28.

Fix: test each characteristic with three real individuals.

sameAs for "similar"

sameAs merges every fact. A flat white gets the price of a latte.

Fix: use skos:closeMatch or your own property.

Most OWL mistakes come from one wrong idea. People think OWL checks data. It does not. OWL adds facts. It reports an error only when two facts clash, for example through disjointness.

Patterns to remember

OWL 2 patterns in Manchester syntax
PatternPurposeModelNote
A SubClassOf: p some BEvery A has at least one BLatte SubClassOf: hasIngredient some MilkNecessary only. The reasoner will not find new lattes.
A EquivalentTo: B and (p some C)Define a class so members are foundMilkDrink EquivalentTo: Drink and (hasIngredient some Dairy)Put the parent class inside the definition.
p only BLimit all values of pVeganDrink SubClassOf: hasIngredient only PlantTrue for zero values. It infers, it does not reject.
p some B and p only BClosure: these and nothing elseBlackCoffee SubClassOf: hasIngredient some Espresso, hasIngredient only EspressoNeeded for "only" to classify anything.
p value aLink to one known individualLargeDrink EquivalentTo: Drink and (hasSize value large)Use for value sets like sizes.
p min n B / p max n BCount linksDoubleShot EquivalentTo: hasIngredient min 2 EspressoNeeds differentFrom. No unique names.
DisjointClasses: A, BSay nothing is bothDisjointClasses: Dairy, PlantThe main way to find errors.
Characteristics: TransitiveFollow chainslocatedInNot simple: no cardinality on it.
InverseOf: qRead a link both waysemploys InverseOf: worksAtNot allowed in OWL 2 EL.
SubPropertyChain: p o qJoin two links into oneworksIn SubPropertyChain: worksAt o locatedInThe new property is not simple.
Characteristics: FunctionalAt most one valuehasManagerTwo values give sameAs, not an error.
d some xsd:T[facet v]Classify by a number rangepriceEUR some xsd:decimal[< 3.0]Not in EL or RL. Needs a DL reasoner.

Practice

Which restriction is true for a drink with no ingredients?

  • hasIngredient some Plant
  • hasIngredient only Plant
  • hasIngredient min 1 Plant

"only" checks every link. With zero links, there is nothing to break the rule.

A shop has two values for the functional property hasManager. What does an OWL reasoner do?

  • It rejects the second value.
  • It reports an error at once.
  • It concludes that the two managers are the same individual.

Functional means "at most one". Two names for one value is the only way to make that true.

Your ontology has 400,000 classes and almost no instance data. Which profile fits best?

  • OWL 2 EL
  • OWL 2 QL
  • OWL 2 RL

EL is built for very large class trees, like medical vocabularies.

Which axiom can find a real contradiction in the data?

  • rdfs:domain
  • owl:allValuesFrom
  • owl:disjointWith

Domain and "only" add facts. Disjointness makes two facts clash.

Fill in the missing words.

A class defined with EquivalentTo has necessary and ? conditions.

In Turtle, some becomes owl:?.

OWL does not use the ? assumption, so two IRIs can mean one thing.

  1. Write in Manchester syntax: "A cappuccino is a coffee. It has some espresso and some milk foam."
    Answer

    Class: Cappuccino SubClassOf: Coffee, hasIngredient some Espresso, hasIngredient some MilkFoam

  2. Write Drink and (hasSize value small) in Turtle, as the definition of :SmallDrink.
    Answer

    :SmallDrink owl:equivalentClass [ owl:intersectionOf ( :Drink [ a owl:Restriction ; owl:onProperty :hasSize ; owl:hasValue :small ] ) ] .

  3. Pick a profile for each project. (a) A gene vocabulary with 50,000 classes. (b) Orders in PostgreSQL that users query with ontology words. (c) An RDF graph with transitive and inverse rules.
    Answer

    (a) OWL 2 EL. (b) OWL 2 QL, with a query-rewriting tool like Ontop. (c) OWL 2 RL, with a rule engine.

  4. Our data says :black1 a :Coffee ; :hasIngredient :shot9 . :shot9 a :Espresso . Why is black1 not classified as a VeganDrink (defined with only Plant)? How do you fix it?
    Answer

    Open world: the reasoner cannot know that shot9 is the only ingredient. Fix it in the schema with a closure axiom on a class, like BlackCoffee SubClassOf: hasIngredient only Espresso, and type black1 as BlackCoffee. Our HermiT test then put BlackCoffee under VeganDrink.

  5. The places data says the shop has the managers :mia and :maria. You add :mia owl:differentFrom :maria. What does an RL reasoner say now?
    Answer

    It reports a clash. Functional gives sameAs, and you said differentFrom. owlrl printed: 'sameAs' and 'differentFrom' cannot be used on the same subject-object pair: (:mia, :maria).

  6. Hard. A teammate wants locatedIn to be transitive and asymmetric. Is this allowed in OWL 2 DL? Explain.
    Answer

    No. A transitive property is not simple. The global rules of OWL 2 DL allow only simple properties in asymmetric, irreflexive, functional and disjoint axioms, and in cardinality and Self. The rule keeps reasoning decidable. You can keep it transitive and check for cycles with SHACL or SPARQL instead.

Key takeaways

  • OWL 2 adds restrictions, property characteristics, disjointness and individual axioms to RDF Schema.
  • "some" needs one matching link. "only" limits all links and is true with none.
  • EquivalentTo defines a class, so the reasoner finds its members. SubClassOf only describes.
  • Domain, range, "only" and functional add facts. Only clashes, like disjointness, give errors.
  • OWL has no unique names and no closed world. Use differentFrom, closure axioms or SHACL.
  • EL is for huge class trees, QL for data in databases, RL for rules on RDF.
  • Write Manchester for people. Store Turtle for tools.

Sources

  • OWL 2 Document Overview (Second Edition). Dates, syntaxes, the two semantics and OWL 1 compatibility.
  • OWL 2 Primer (Second Edition). The W3C introduction with examples in all syntaxes.
  • OWL 2 Profiles (Second Edition). What EL, QL and RL allow, their complexity and the RL rules.
  • OWL 2 Structural Specification. Section 11 has the rules on simple properties.
  • OWL 2 Manchester Syntax. The W3C Note with all frame keywords and facets.
  • OOPS! pitfall catalogue. A numbered list of common ontology mistakes, like P10, P19, P28 and P29.

SPARQL

SPARQL is the W3C query language for RDF graphs. You draw a small pattern with variables. The engine finds every place in the graph where the pattern fits. In this chapter every query runs on two engines, rdflib and Oxigraph, and the output is real.

  • Write SELECT queries with triple patterns, FILTER, OPTIONAL, UNION and MINUS.
  • Follow links of any length with property paths.
  • Count and sum with GROUP BY, HAVING and subqueries.
  • Use CONSTRUCT, ASK, DESCRIBE, named graphs, SERVICE and SPARQL Update.
  • Explain entailment regimes and the status of SPARQL 1.2 today.

Your first query

We use a small café graph. It has a menu, three baristas, two shops and eight orders. Here is part of it.

@prefix :     <http://example.org/cafe#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

:Coffee rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .   :Tea rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .
:Latte  rdfs:subClassOf :Coffee .
:latte    a :Latte ;  rdfs:label "Latte"@en , "Milchkaffee"@de ; :priceEUR 3.80 .
:espresso a :Coffee ; rdfs:label "Espresso"@en ; :priceEUR 2.20 .
:greenTea a :Tea ;    rdfs:label "Green tea"@en , "Grüner Tee"@de ; :priceEUR 2.50 .
:muffin   a :Cake ;   rdfs:label "Muffin"@en ; :priceEUR 3.00 .
:mia a :Barista ; :name "Mia" ; :worksAt :beanBar .
:sam a :Barista ; :name "Sam" ; :worksAt :beanBar ; :email "sam@example.org" .
:lea a :Barista ; :name "Lea" ; :worksAt :leafHouse .
:o1 :item :latte ; :servedBy :mia ; :day "2026-11-09"^^xsd:date .
# ... places and the orders o2 to o8 ...

Question: who works at Bean Bar?

PREFIX : <http://example.org/cafe#>

SELECT ?barista ?name
WHERE {
  ?barista :worksAt :beanBar .
  ?barista :name ?name .
}
ORDER BY ?name
barista | name
:mia | Mia
:sam | Sam

The WHERE part holds two triple patterns. A word with ? is a variable. The engine tries every value. A row survives only if both patterns fit with the same ?barista. Each row is a solution.

A group of triple patterns is a basic graph pattern. Joining on a shared variable is the heart of SPARQL. You can shorten the query with Turtle rules: ; repeats the subject, and a means rdf:type.

How to run a query

We run each query file with a small script. Pick the engine you like. We used rdflib 7.6.0 and pyoxigraph 0.5.13 on Python 3.14.

import sys
from rdflib import Graph

g = Graph()
g.parse("cafe.ttl")
for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    res = g.query(open(path).read())
    if res.type == "ASK":
        print(res.askAnswer)
    elif res.type in ("CONSTRUCT", "DESCRIBE"):
        res.graph.bind("", "http://example.org/cafe#")
        print(res.graph.serialize(format="turtle"))
    else:                                   # SELECT
        print(" | ".join(str(v) for v in res.vars))
        for row in res:
            print(" | ".join("-" if v is None else
                  str(v).replace("http://example.org/cafe#", ":")
                  for v in row))
import sys
from pyoxigraph import Store, RdfFormat, QuerySolutions, QueryBoolean

store = Store()                             # in memory
store.load(path="cafe.ttl", format=RdfFormat.TURTLE)

def show(t):
    if t is None:
        return "-"
    return getattr(t, "value", str(t)).replace("http://example.org/cafe#", ":")

for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    res = store.query(open(path).read())
    if isinstance(res, QueryBoolean):
        print(bool(res))
    elif isinstance(res, QuerySolutions):   # SELECT
        names = [v.value for v in res.variables]
        print(" | ".join(names))
        for sol in res:
            print(" | ".join(show(sol[n]) for n in names))
    else:                                   # CONSTRUCT or DESCRIBE
        for t in res:
            print(show(t.subject), show(t.predicate), show(t.object))

Run them with uv run --with rdflib python3.14 run.py q1.rq or uv run --with pyoxigraph python3.14 ox.py q1.rq. From now on we hide the PREFIX lines. The files have them.

Plain SPARQL does not know RDF Schema. ?x a :Drink finds nothing in our graph. No triple says "latte is a Drink" directly. You learn two fixes later: a property path, or a reasoner.

Filters, optional parts, UNION and MINUS

FILTER keeps only some rows

SELECT ?label ?price
WHERE {
  ?item rdfs:label ?label ;
        :priceEUR  ?price .
  FILTER (?price < 3 && lang(?label) = "en")
}
ORDER BY ?price
label | price
Espresso | 2.20
Green tea | 2.50
label | price
Espresso | 2.2
Green tea | 2.5

Both engines give the same values. rdflib keeps the text as typed. Oxigraph writes the shortest form of the decimal. A FILTER uses tests like <, =, &&, ||, ! and functions like lang, regex, contains, bound and isIRI.

OPTIONAL keeps rows with missing data

SELECT ?name ?email
WHERE {
  ?b a :Barista ; :name ?name .
  OPTIONAL { ?b :email ?email }
}
ORDER BY ?name
name | email
Lea | -
Mia | -
Sam | sam@example.org

Without OPTIONAL, only Sam would come back. With it, Lea and Mia stay, and ?email is unbound. This works like a left join in SQL.

UNION gives "this or that"

SELECT ?item ?kind
WHERE {
  { ?item a :Tea  . BIND("tea" AS ?kind) }
  UNION
  { ?item a :Cake . BIND("cake" AS ?kind) }
}
item | kind
:greenTea | tea
:muffin | cake

BIND puts a computed value into a new variable. Here it labels where each row came from.

MINUS and FILTER NOT EXISTS take rows away

SELECT ?name
WHERE {
  ?b a :Barista ; :name ?name .
  MINUS { ?order :servedBy ?b ; :item :latte }
}
name
Lea

The same query with FILTER NOT EXISTS { ... } also returns Lea. So are they the same? Not always. We changed the inner pattern to { ?x :item :latte }. Now it shares no variable with the outer part.

MINUS and NOT EXISTS with no shared variable (tested on both engines)
QueryResultWhy
MINUS { ?x :item :latte }Lea, Mia, SamMINUS removes a row only if they share a variable with equal values. Nothing is shared, so nothing is removed.
FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?x :item :latte }no rowsSome latte order exists, so the test fails for every row.

A FILTER inside a group applies to the whole group, wherever you write it. And a FILTER with an error counts as false. For example, ?price < 3 fails when ?price is unbound. If you want to keep such rows, write !bound(?price) || ?price < 3.

Property paths

A property path follows several links in one pattern. This solves the RDF Schema problem from the first section.

SELECT ?item
WHERE { ?item a/rdfs:subClassOf* :Drink }
ORDER BY ?item
item
:espresso
:greenTea
:latte

Read it as: "item has a type, then zero or more subClassOf steps, then Drink". The latte is a Latte, a Latte is a Coffee, a Coffee is a Drink. The muffin is a Cake, so it is not in the list.

Property path operators
PathMeaningCafé example
p/qp, then q:servedBy/:name
p|qp or q:name|rdfs:label
^pp backwards:beanBar ^:worksAt ?b
p*zero or more prdfs:subClassOf*
p+one or more p:locatedIn+
p?zero or one p:locatedIn?
!(p|q)any property except these!(rdf:type)

Paths can be combined. This query starts at Berlin and walks backwards.

SELECT ?name
WHERE { :berlin ^:locatedIn+/^:worksAt/:name ?name }
ORDER BY ?name
name
Lea
Mia
Sam
  1. ^:locatedIn+: from berlin back to kreuzberg and mitte, then back to beanBar and leafHouse.
  2. ^:worksAt: from each shop back to its baristas: mia, sam, lea.
  3. :name: from each barista forward to the name.

*, + and ? return each node once. Fixed paths keep duplicates.

We tested a small graph where two routes of length two reach node d. :p/:p returned d twice. :p+ returned d once. Both engines agreed.

A path like ?a :knows+ ?b with both ends free can be very slow on a big graph. Fix at least one end to a known IRI. Paths also cannot return the route itself, only the end points.

Aggregates, GROUP BY and subqueries

Which baristas earned more than 5 euros, and how much?

SELECT ?name (COUNT(?o) AS ?orders) (SUM(?price) AS ?revenue)
WHERE {
  ?o :servedBy ?b ; :item ?item .
  ?b :name ?name .
  ?item :priceEUR ?price .
}
GROUP BY ?name
HAVING (SUM(?price) > 5)
ORDER BY DESC(?revenue)
name | orders | revenue
Mia | 4 | 13.60
Sam | 2 | 6.80

Lea earned 4.70, so HAVING removed her. GROUP BY makes one group per name. An aggregate turns each group into one value. SPARQL has COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, SAMPLE and GROUP_CONCAT.

SELECT ?day (COUNT(*) AS ?n)
       (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?who; separator=", ") AS ?baristas)
WHERE { ?o :day ?day ; :servedBy/:name ?who }
GROUP BY ?day
ORDER BY ?day
day | n | baristas
2026-11-09 | 3 | Mia, Sam
2026-11-10 | 4 | Mia, Sam, Lea
2026-11-11 | 1 | Mia
day | n | baristas
2026-11-09 | 3 | Sam, Mia
2026-11-10 | 4 | Lea, Sam, Mia
2026-11-11 | 1 | Mia

Look at the names. The engines put them in a different order. Both are correct. The standard does not fix the order inside GROUP_CONCAT.

Subqueries

Which items cost more than the average? We need the average first. A subquery computes it.

SELECT ?label ?price
WHERE {
  ?item :priceEUR ?price ; rdfs:label ?label .
  FILTER (lang(?label) = "en")
  {
    SELECT (AVG(?p) AS ?avg) WHERE { ?x :priceEUR ?p }
  }
  FILTER (?price > ?avg)
}
ORDER BY DESC(?price)
label | price
Latte | 3.80
Muffin | 3.00

The average is (3.80 + 2.20 + 2.50 + 3.00) / 4 = 2.875. The inner query runs first. Only its selected variable ?avg is visible outside.

Match

Find all matches of each triple pattern and path.

Join

Join the matches on shared variables. Add OPTIONAL, UNION and MINUS parts.

Filter

Apply every FILTER of the group to the joined rows.

Group

Make groups with GROUP BY. Compute the aggregates.

Having

Remove groups that fail HAVING.

Compute

Compute expressions in SELECT, like (SUM(?p) AS ?total).

Order

Sort with ORDER BY. You may sort by a variable you do not select.

Project

Keep only the selected variables. Apply DISTINCT.

Slice

Apply OFFSET and LIMIT last.

Every selected variable must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. SELECT ?name ?price ... GROUP BY ?name is an error. Also, LIMIT without ORDER BY gives random rows. The next run may give other rows.

CONSTRUCT, ASK and DESCRIBE

SELECT returns a table. SPARQL has three more query forms.

CONSTRUCT { ?b :sold ?item }
WHERE     { ?o :servedBy ?b ; :item ?item .
            VALUES ?b { :lea } }
@prefix : <http://example.org/cafe#> .

:lea :sold :espresso,
        :greenTea .
ASK { ?b :worksAt :leafHouse ; :email ?e }
False
DESCRIBE :sam
@prefix : <http://example.org/cafe#> .

:sam a :Barista ;
    :email "sam@example.org" ;
    :name "Sam" ;
    :worksAt :beanBar .
  • CONSTRUCT returns a new graph from a template. Use it to convert data from one vocabulary to another.
  • ASK returns true or false. Use it for tests, for example in a build pipeline.
  • DESCRIBE returns triples about a resource. The standard lets each engine decide which triples. rdflib and Oxigraph both gave Sam's four triples here.

VALUES gives a variable a fixed list of values. It is like a small inline table.

Do not use DESCRIBE in code that must give the same result on every store. Another engine may return more or fewer triples. Write a CONSTRUCT that says exactly what you want.

Named graphs and datasets

A SPARQL engine queries a dataset. It has one default graph and any number of named graphs. Here each shop sends its orders as its own graph. The format is TriG, Turtle with graphs.

PREFIX :  <http://example.org/cafe#>
PREFIX g: <http://example.org/graph/>

# the default graph: the menu
:latte    :priceEUR 3.80 .
:espresso :priceEUR 2.20 .

# one named graph per shop
g:beanBar {
  :o1 :item :latte .
  :o2 :item :espresso .
  :o3 :item :latte .
}
g:leafHouse {
  :o7 :item :espresso .
}
from pyoxigraph import Store, RdfFormat

store = Store()
store.load(path="shops.trig", format=RdfFormat.TRIG)

q = """
PREFIX : <http://example.org/cafe#>
SELECT ?g (COUNT(?o) AS ?orders) (SUM(?price) AS ?revenue)
WHERE {
  GRAPH ?g { ?o :item ?item }      # orders: in a named graph
  ?item :priceEUR ?price .         # prices: in the default graph
}
GROUP BY ?g ORDER BY ?g"""
for row in store.query(q):
    print(row["g"].value, row["orders"].value, row["revenue"].value)

count = "SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o }"
print("default graph:", next(iter(store.query(count)))["n"].value)
print("union of all: ", next(iter(store.query(
    count, use_default_graph_as_union=True)))["n"].value)
http://example.org/graph/beanBar 3 9.8
http://example.org/graph/leafHouse 1 2.2
default graph: 2
union of all:  6

GRAPH ?g { ... } matches inside the named graphs and binds the graph name to ?g. Patterns outside GRAPH match the default graph.

A query can also choose its own dataset. FROM <g:leafHouse> makes that graph the default graph. FROM NAMED picks the named graphs. We tested FROM in Oxigraph. It returned only order o7.

Stores differ here. In Oxigraph the default graph is a separate graph, as the output shows. Some stores make the default graph the union of all graphs. Read your store's manual before you write ?s ?p ?o without GRAPH.

Named graphs are a simple way to record where data came from. One graph per source, per load or per version. You can then drop or replace one source with one command.

SPARQL Update

Coffee prices go up by 10 percent. Here is the change, run in Oxigraph.

store.update(P + """
DELETE { ?item :priceEUR ?old }
INSERT { ?item :priceEUR ?new }
WHERE  {
  ?item a/rdfs:subClassOf* :Coffee ;
        :priceEUR ?old .
  BIND (ROUND(?old * 110) / 100 AS ?new)     # plus 10 percent
}""")
store.update(P + 'INSERT DATA { :o9 :item :greenTea ; :servedBy :sam }')
store.update(P + "DELETE WHERE { :o9 ?p ?x }")
before: espresso=2.2, greenTea=2.5, latte=3.8, muffin=3
after:  espresso=2.42, greenTea=2.5, latte=4.18, muffin=3
orders: 9
orders: 8

Only the two coffees changed. The new order o9 was added and then removed again. SPARQL Update has these operations.

SPARQL 1.1 Update operations
OperationWhat it does
INSERT DATA { ... }Add fixed triples. No variables.
DELETE DATA { ... }Remove fixed triples.
DELETE { } INSERT { } WHERE { }Find rows with WHERE, then delete and add triples for each row.
DELETE WHERE { ... }Short form: delete everything the pattern matches.
WITH <g> ...Run the change inside one named graph.
LOAD <url> INTO GRAPH <g>Read an RDF file from the web into a graph.
CLEAR, DROP, CREATEEmpty, remove or create a graph.
COPY, MOVE, ADDCopy, move or merge whole graphs.

In DELETE/INSERT, the WHERE part runs once, before any change. Do not expect a second round on the new data. Also, an update request with several operations, joined by ;, runs them in order.

Federation and entailment

SERVICE asks another endpoint

Our graph knows the shops. Wikidata knows the names of Berlin in many languages. SERVICE sends part of the query to another SPARQL endpoint. This is federation. We ran this once with rdflib.

PREFIX :     <http://example.org/cafe#>
PREFIX wd:   <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>

SELECT ?shop ?label WHERE {
  ?shop :locatedIn+ :berlin ; :name ?n .        # local data
  SERVICE <https://query.wikidata.org/sparql> {  # remote data
    wd:Q64 rdfs:label ?label .                   # Q64 is Berlin
    FILTER (lang(?label) IN ("de", "ja"))
  }
} ORDER BY ?shop ?label
beanBar Berlin de
beanBar ベルリン ja
leafHouse Berlin de
leafHouse ベルリン ja

The remote part is small and fixed: one item, two labels. That keeps the request cheap. SERVICE SILENT ignores a failing endpoint and keeps the local rows.

Do not send an open pattern like ?x rdfs:label ?l to a public endpoint. It asks for millions of rows and hits a timeout.

Engines also differ in how they send your local values. rdflib sends one request for each local row, with the values of that row in a VALUES clause. We read this in its source code.

So put a fixed IRI or a small VALUES list inside the SERVICE block. Public endpoints also ask for a clear User-Agent and few requests.

Entailment regimes

Remember ?x a :Drink from the first section. It found nothing. We now add the RDF Schema facts with the owlrl package and run the same query.

from rdflib import Graph
import owlrl

q = """PREFIX : <http://example.org/cafe#>
SELECT ?x WHERE { ?x a :Drink } ORDER BY ?x"""

def drinks(g):
    return [str(r.x).split("#")[1] for r in g.query(q)]

g = Graph().parse("cafe.ttl")
print("plain graph:   ", drinks(g))
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.RDFS_Semantics).expand(g)   # add RDFS facts
print("after RDFS:    ", drinks(g))
plain graph:    []
after RDFS:     ['espresso', 'greenTea', 'latte']

The query did not change. The graph changed.

An entailment regime makes this official. It says that a query sees the facts that follow from the data, not only the typed ones.

The SPARQL 1.1 standard defines six: RDF, RDFS, D-entailment (datatypes), OWL 2 RDF-Based, OWL 2 Direct and RIF Core. An endpoint names its regime in its service description with sd:defaultEntailmentRegime.

In practice, most stores do one of three things. They add inferred triples at load time. They rewrite your query with paths. Or they offer a rule set you switch on.

You see these strategies in Reasoners and materialisation. The OWL side is in OWL 2.

SPARQL 1.2: where it stands today

  1. 2008 SPARQL 1.0. W3C Recommendation on 15 January 2008. Queries only.
  2. 2013 SPARQL 1.1. Eleven Recommendations on 21 March 2013: Update, paths, aggregates, federation, entailment, protocols.
  3. 2023 SPARQL 1.2 starts. First Public Working Draft of the query language on 16 May 2023.
  4. 2026 Still a draft. Latest Working Draft of SPARQL 1.2 Query: 12 November 2026.

On 15 November 2026, SPARQL 1.2 is a Working Draft. It is not a Recommendation yet. The W3C history page lists only Working Drafts for SPARQL 1.2 Query.

The other parts are also Working Drafts: Update (25 October 2026), Federated Query (23 April 2026) and Entailment Regimes (9 April 2026). The RDF and SPARQL Working Group writes them. Check the W3C pages: this can change.

SPARQL 1.2 follows RDF 1.2. The main news, from the change list of the draft:

  • Triple terms. A whole triple can be a value: <<( :mia :worksAt :beanBar )>>. New functions: TRIPLE, SUBJECT, PREDICATE, OBJECT, isTRIPLE.
  • Reifiers. << s p o ~ ?r >> matches a statement about a triple and binds its reifier. Annotations {| ... |} add facts about a triple.
  • VERSION. A query can say VERSION "1.2" at the top.
  • Text direction. Literals like "..."@ar--rtl, with LANGDIR, hasLANG, hasLANGDIR and STRLANGDIR.
  • Fixes. A formal meaning for EXISTS, no duplicate variables in VALUES, and other clean-ups.

Oxigraph already reads this draft syntax. We tested it with pyoxigraph 0.5.13. The data says when Mia started at Bean Bar.

from pyoxigraph import Store, RdfFormat

store = Store()
store.load(input="""
PREFIX :    <http://example.org/cafe#>
PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#>
:mia :worksAt :beanBar {| :since "2024-03-01"^^xsd:date |} .
""", format=RdfFormat.TURTLE)
print("triples stored:", len(store))

q = """VERSION "1.2"
PREFIX :   <http://example.org/cafe#>
PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#>
SELECT ?who ?since ?isTriple WHERE {
  << ?who :worksAt :beanBar ~ ?r >> :since ?since .   # reifier ?r
  ?r rdf:reifies ?t .                                  # ?t is a triple term
  BIND (isTRIPLE(?t) AS ?isTriple)
}"""
for row in store.query(q):
    print(row["who"].value, row["since"].value, row["isTriple"].value)
triples stored: 3
http://example.org/cafe#mia 2024-03-01 true

One annotated line became three triples. There is the normal triple, a reifier that rdf:reifies the triple term, and the :since fact on the reifier. The details of triple terms are in RDF and RDF Schema. rdflib 7.6.0 does not parse this syntax yet. We tried, and it gave a parse error.

Do not build production code on draft syntax without a plan. The drafts changed many times since 2023. Pin your engine version, and keep the 1.2 parts small and easy to change.

Patterns to remember

SPARQL patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
SELECT ?v WHERE { s p ?v }Ask for values?b :worksAt :beanBarA shared variable means a join.
FILTER (test)Keep rows that passFILTER (?price < 3)Errors count as false. Unbound values give errors.
OPTIONAL { ... }Keep rows with missing dataOPTIONAL { ?b :email ?e }The variable may be unbound.
{ A } UNION { B }This or that{ ?i a :Tea } UNION { ?i a :Cake }Use BIND to mark which side.
FILTER NOT EXISTS { ... }Rows without a matchbaristas with no latte orderSafer than MINUS when no variable is shared.
?x a/rdfs:subClassOf* CFind instances of subclasses?i a/rdfs:subClassOf* :DrinkWorks without a reasoner.
s p+ ?oFollow a chain:beanBar :locatedIn+ ?placeFix one end on big graphs.
GROUP BY ?k ... HAVINGTotals per groupSUM(?price) ... HAVING (SUM(?price) > 5)Selected variables must be grouped.
{ SELECT (AVG(?p) AS ?avg) ... }Compute a value firstitems above average priceOnly selected variables leave the subquery.
CONSTRUCT { t } WHERE { p }Make a new graph{ ?b :sold ?item }Better than DESCRIBE for exact output.
ASK { ... }Yes or no testASK { ?b :email ?e }Good for data tests in CI.
GRAPH ?g { ... }Match inside named graphsGRAPH ?g { ?o :item ?i }The default graph differs by store.
DELETE { } INSERT { } WHERE { }Change dataraise coffee pricesWHERE runs once, before the change.
SERVICE <url> { ... }Ask a remote endpointWikidata labels for wd:Q64Keep the remote part small and fixed.

Practice

What does OPTIONAL do?

  • It makes the whole query optional.
  • It keeps a row even when the inner pattern has no match.
  • It removes rows with missing values.

OPTIONAL works like a left join. Missing values stay unbound.

Which pattern finds the latte when you ask for drinks, without a reasoner?

  • ?x a :Drink
