  • ?x a/rdfs:subClassOf* :Drink
  • ?x rdfs:subClassOf :Drink

The path follows the type, then any number of subClassOf links.

On 15 November 2026, what is the W3C status of SPARQL 1.2 Query?

  • W3C Recommendation
  • Candidate Recommendation
  • Working Draft

The W3C history page lists only Working Drafts. The latest is from 12 November 2026.

Which query form returns true or false?

  • DESCRIBE
  • ASK
  • CONSTRUCT

ASK only says whether the pattern has at least one match.

Fill in the missing words.

To keep only groups with a total above 5, you write ? after GROUP BY.

The path operator ^ follows a property ?.

  1. Write a query for "Which orders did Lea serve, and on which day?".
    Answer

    SELECT ?o ?day WHERE { ?o :servedBy :lea ; :day ?day } ORDER BY ?day On our data: o4 and o7, both on 2026-11-10.

  2. Count the orders for each item, with the most popular first.
    Answer

    SELECT ?item (COUNT(?o) AS ?n) WHERE { ?o :item ?item } GROUP BY ?item ORDER BY DESC(?n) The latte comes first with 4 orders. Espresso has 2. Green tea and muffin have 1 each.

  3. Write an ASK query that is true if some item has no English label. Is it true on our data?
    Answer

    ASK { ?i :priceEUR ?p . FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?i rdfs:label ?l . FILTER (lang(?l) = "en") } } It is false. All four items have an English label.

  4. A teammate writes MINUS { ?x :item :latte } to remove baristas who sold a latte. Nobody is removed. Why? Fix it.
    Answer

    MINUS only removes a row when both sides share a variable with the same value. ?x is not in the outer part. Fix: MINUS { ?o :servedBy ?b ; :item :latte }, or use FILTER NOT EXISTS with ?b inside.

  5. Write an update that moves Sam from Bean Bar to Leaf House.
    Answer

    DELETE { :sam :worksAt ?old } INSERT { :sam :worksAt :leafHouse } WHERE { :sam :worksAt ?old } The WHERE part finds the old shop. Then the old link goes and the new one comes.

  6. Hard. Your store makes the default graph the union of all named graphs. A colleague's store does not. The same query SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } gives different numbers. How do you write it so both stores agree?
    Answer

    Say which graphs you mean. For all named graphs: SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { GRAPH ?g { ?s ?p ?o } }. For one graph: use FROM <graph-iri> or GRAPH <graph-iri> { ... }. Do not depend on the default graph.

Key takeaways

  • A SPARQL query is a pattern with variables. Shared variables join the patterns.
  • FILTER keeps rows, OPTIONAL keeps rows with gaps, UNION adds rows, MINUS and NOT EXISTS remove rows.
  • Property paths like a/rdfs:subClassOf* follow chains without a reasoner.
  • GROUP BY, aggregates, HAVING and subqueries work like in SQL, with a fixed order of steps.
  • CONSTRUCT makes graphs, ASK tests, DESCRIBE depends on the engine.
  • Named graphs separate sources. The default graph is not the same in every store.
  • SPARQL 1.1 (2013) is the current Recommendation. SPARQL 1.2 is a Working Draft in November 2026.

Sources

  • SPARQL 1.1 Query Language. The W3C Recommendation for patterns, paths, aggregates and the evaluation order.
  • SPARQL 1.1 Update. All update operations and graph management.
  • SPARQL 1.1 Entailment Regimes. The six regimes and how endpoints announce them.
  • SPARQL 1.2 Query Language. The Working Draft of 12 November 2026 and its change list.
  • History of SPARQL 1.2 Query. Every published version and its maturity level.
  • pyoxigraph documentation. The Python API for the Oxigraph store used in this chapter.

SHACL and validation

OWL tells you what follows from your data. It does not tell you what is missing or wrong. SHACL does. You write shapes, like "every drink has exactly one price", and a SHACL engine lists every node that breaks them.

  • Explain why an OWL reasoner does not validate data.
  • Write node shapes, targets and property shapes with the main constraint components.
  • Run pySHACL and read a validation report with severities.
  • Use SHACL-SPARQL for custom checks and SHACL rules for new facts.
  • Describe the status of SHACL 1.2 and compare SHACL with ShEx.

Why OWL does not check your data

Here is some café data with seven problems. Read the comments.

@prefix :     <http://example.org/cafe#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

:Coffee rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .
:Latte  rdfs:subClassOf :Coffee .
:Tea    rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .

:latte    a :Latte ;  rdfs:label "Latte"@en ; :priceEUR 3.80 ; :hasSize :large .
:espresso a :Coffee ; rdfs:label "Espresso"@en ; :priceEUR 2.20 , 2.40 .  # two prices
:greenTea a :Tea ;    rdfs:label "Green tea"@en ; :priceEUR "2.50" .      # text, not a number
:chai     a :Tea ;    rdfs:label "Chai"@en ; :hasSize :huge .              # no price, odd size

:mia a :Barista ; :name "Mia" ; :email "mia@example" .                     # bad email
:o1  a :Order ; :item :latte ; :servedBy :mia ; :day "2026-11-09"^^xsd:date .
:o2  a :Order ; :item :chai ;  :servedBy :sam .                             # no day, unknown sam

We wrote an OWL ontology for it. The price is functional with range xsd:decimal.

Every drink has some price. Every order has some day. The range of servedBy is Barista. Then we ran two reasoners.

What two OWL reasoners found (tested)
ReasonerResult
OWL RL rules (owlrl 7.6.2)0 problems. It also concluded "sam is a Barista" from the range.
OWL 2 DL (HermiT via owlready2)"Inconsistent", with no place named. The cause was the two prices and the text price. After we fixed those two, it said "consistent". Five problems were left.

Why? OWL uses the open world assumption. A missing price is just unknown. OWL has no unique names, so two values can be one thing. And range and domain add facts instead of rejecting data. You saw all of this in OWL 2.

OWL asks: "Can this world exist?" SHACL asks: "Does this data follow our rules?" The first is logic. The second is a data quality check.

For the second question, the W3C made SHACL, the Shapes Constraint Language. It became a W3C Recommendation on 20 July 2017. SHACL uses the closed world assumption inside each check. If a price is missing, the check fails.

Do not add more OWL axioms to "make the reasoner check" your data. Functional and range only add facts. You get strange inferences, like "sam is a Barista", and no useful message. Keep OWL for meaning. Use SHACL for checks.

Shapes, targets and focus nodes

Here is the smallest useful shape.

:DrinkShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Drink ;
    sh:property [
        sh:path :priceEUR ;
        sh:minCount 1 ;
    ] .

Read it as: "Every Drink must have at least one priceEUR." Now the words.

  • A shape is a group of conditions. Shapes live in the shapes graph. The data lives in the data graph.
  • A node shape talks about a node. :DrinkShape is one.
  • A property shape talks about the values at the end of a path. The blank node with sh:path is one.
  • The target picks the nodes to check. Each picked node is a focus node.
  • The values at the end of the path are the value nodes. Conditions like sh:minCount are constraint components.
The five kinds of target in SHACL 1.0
TargetPicksExample
sh:targetClass CEvery instance of C, also through rdfs:subClassOf in the data graphsh:targetClass :Drink
sh:targetNode nOne named nodesh:targetNode :beanBar
sh:targetSubjectsOf pEvery subject of psh:targetSubjectsOf :priceEUR
sh:targetObjectsOf pEvery object of psh:targetObjectsOf :servedBy
implicit class targetA shape that is also an rdfs:Class targets its own instances:Drink a rdfs:Class, sh:NodeShape

A shape without a target checks nothing. It is not an error. The engine just finds no focus nodes. If your report is empty and "conforms" is true, check the targets first.

Property shapes and constraint components

Here is the full shapes file for the café. It has three node shapes.

@prefix :     <http://example.org/cafe#> .
@prefix sh:   <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

:DrinkShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Drink ;                 # every Drink, also via subClassOf
    sh:property [
        sh:path :priceEUR ;
        sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ;     # exactly one price
        sh:datatype xsd:decimal ;
        sh:minExclusive 0 ;
    ] ;
    sh:property [
        sh:path :hasSize ;
        sh:in ( :small :large ) ;           # a fixed list of values
    ] .

:BaristaShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Barista ;
    sh:property [
        sh:path :email ;
        sh:pattern "^[^@ ]+@[^@ ]+\\.[a-z]{2,}$" ;
        sh:severity sh:Warning ;            # not a blocker
        sh:message "The email address looks wrong." ;
    ] .

:OrderShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Order ;
    sh:property [ sh:path :day ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:datatype xsd:date ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path :servedBy ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:class :Barista ] .

SHACL Core has about thirty constraint components. They come in families.

SHACL Core constraint components by family
FamilyComponentsCafé example
Value typesh:class, sh:datatype, sh:nodeKindservedBy points to a Barista
Cardinalitysh:minCount, sh:maxCountexactly one price
Value rangesh:minInclusive, sh:maxInclusive, sh:minExclusive, sh:maxExclusiveprice above 0
Stringsh:minLength, sh:maxLength, sh:pattern, sh:languageIn, sh:uniqueLangemail pattern
Property pairsh:equals, sh:disjoint, sh:lessThan, sh:lessThanOrEqualsstart day before end day
Logicalsh:not, sh:and, sh:or, sh:xonean email or a phone
Shape-basedsh:node, sh:property, sh:qualifiedValueShapethe item must meet DrinkShape
Othersh:closed, sh:ignoredProperties, sh:hasValue, sh:insize is small or large

sh:path takes a SHACL property path. It works like a SPARQL path, written in RDF.

SHACL paths and their SPARQL twins
SHACLSPARQL
sh:path :name:name
sh:path ( :servedBy :name ):servedBy/:name
sh:path [ sh:inversePath :worksAt ]^:worksAt
sh:path [ sh:alternativePath ( :name rdfs:label ) ]:name|rdfs:label
sh:path [ sh:oneOrMorePath :locatedIn ]:locatedIn+

sh:class checks the type in the data. Our order o2 says :servedBy :sam, and nothing says Sam is a Barista. OWL guessed that he is one. SHACL reports him. That is the closed world at work.

Run it with pySHACL

pySHACL is the SHACL engine of the RDFLib project. We used version 0.40.2 on Python 3.14. Run it with uv run --with pyshacl python3.14 validate.py.

from pyshacl import validate

conforms, report, text = validate("data.ttl", shacl_graph="shapes.ttl")
print("conforms:", conforms)

q = """
PREFIX sh: <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#>
SELECT ?focus ?path ?sev ?comp ?value WHERE {
  ?r a sh:ValidationResult ; sh:focusNode ?focus ;
     sh:resultSeverity ?sev ; sh:sourceConstraintComponent ?comp .
  OPTIONAL { ?r sh:resultPath ?path }
  OPTIONAL { ?r sh:value ?value }
} ORDER BY ?focus ?path"""
def short(x):
    return "-" if x is None else str(x).split("#")[-1]
for row in report.query(q):
    print(" | ".join(short(x) for x in row))
conforms: False
chai | hasSize | Violation | InConstraintComponent | huge
chai | priceEUR | Violation | MinCountConstraintComponent | -
espresso | priceEUR | Violation | MaxCountConstraintComponent | -
greenTea | priceEUR | Violation | DatatypeConstraintComponent | 2.50
greenTea | priceEUR | Violation | MinExclusiveConstraintComponent | 2.50
mia | email | Warning | PatternConstraintComponent | mia@example
o2 | day | Violation | MinCountConstraintComponent | -
o2 | servedBy | Violation | ClassConstraintComponent | sam

All seven problems are in the report. The text price "2.50" breaks two rules. It is not a decimal, and it cannot be compared with 0. The report is itself an RDF graph, so we read it with SPARQL. You can also use the command line: pyshacl -s shapes.ttl -f table data.ttl.

Load

Read the shapes graph and the data graph.

Target

For each shape, find the focus nodes from its targets.

Path

For each property shape, follow the path from the focus node. Collect the value nodes.

Check

Test each constraint component on the value nodes. minCount counts them. datatype tests each one.

Report

Write one validation result for each failure, with the focus node, path, value and severity.

Conform

Set sh:conforms. It is true only when there are no results.

Run SHACL in your CI pipeline, like unit tests. A data change that breaks a shape fails the build. The report tells you which node and which rule.

Severity and the validation report

Here is one result from the report, the missing price of chai.

[] a sh:ValidationResult ;
    sh:focusNode :chai ;
    sh:resultMessage "Less than 1 values on :chai->:priceEUR" ;
    sh:resultPath :priceEUR ;
    sh:resultSeverity sh:Violation ;
    sh:sourceConstraintComponent sh:MinCountConstraintComponent .

The engine also adds sh:sourceShape, the shape that failed. A validation report has one sh:conforms value and one sh:result for each problem.

The main parts of a validation result
PropertyWhat it tells you
sh:focusNodeWhich node failed
sh:resultPathWhich path was checked
sh:valueThe bad value, if there is one
sh:sourceShapeWhich shape failed
sh:sourceConstraintComponentWhich kind of rule failed
sh:resultSeverityHow serious it is
sh:resultMessageA text for people, from sh:message or from the engine

Three levels of severity

Every shape has a severity. SHACL 1.0 has three: sh:Violation (the default), sh:Warning and sh:Info. Our email rule is a Warning. Now look at a test with fixed data. Only the bad email is left.

from pyshacl import validate
for allow in (False, True):
    ok, _, _ = validate("fixed.ttl", shacl_graph="shapes.ttl", allow_warnings=allow)
    print("allow_warnings =", allow, "-> conforms:", ok)
allow_warnings = False -> conforms: False
allow_warnings = True -> conforms: True

In the standard, any result makes sh:conforms false, even a Warning. Severity is only a label. pySHACL adds the option allow_warnings to change this. The SHACL 1.2 draft makes this idea official. A report can say which severities break conformance, with sh:conformanceDisallows.

Do not mark a rule as Warning and expect "conforms: true". With default settings, it is still false. Decide in your pipeline what each severity means: stop the build, open a ticket, or just log it.

SHACL-SPARQL: checks that Core cannot write well

Two drinks should never have the same label. SHACL Core has only a trick for this. You follow a path from the label back to every node with that label, and say sh:maxCount 1.

We tested it, and it works. But it is hard to read, and it counts every node with that label, not only drinks. A SPARQL query says it directly. We add a second chai with the label "Chai".

# prefixes that the SPARQL text below may use
: a owl:Ontology ;
  sh:declare [ sh:prefix "" ;     sh:namespace "http://example.org/cafe#"^^xsd:anyURI ] ,
             [ sh:prefix "rdfs" ; sh:namespace "http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#"^^xsd:anyURI ] .

:UniqueLabelShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Drink ;
    sh:sparql [
        a sh:SPARQLConstraint ;
        sh:message "Another drink has the same label: {?other}" ;
        sh:prefixes : ;
        sh:select """
            SELECT $this ?other ?value WHERE {
                $this rdfs:label ?value .
                ?other rdfs:label ?value ;
                       a/rdfs:subClassOf* :Drink .
                FILTER (?other != $this)
            }""" ;
    ] .
conforms: False
chai -> Another drink has the same label: http://example.org/cafe#chai2
chai2 -> Another drink has the same label: http://example.org/cafe#chai

This is SHACL-SPARQL. The rules are simple.

  • $this is the focus node. The engine fills it in for each target.
  • Each row the query returns is one validation result. No rows means no problem.
  • {?other} in the message is replaced by the value of ?other.
  • sh:prefixes points to a node with sh:declare. The query uses those prefixes.

You can also build your own custom constraint component. You declare a parameter, like ex:maxPriceEUR, and a SPARQL validator. Then shape authors use it like sh:minCount, without writing SPARQL.

The SHACL 1.2 Core draft adds sh:uniqueValuesFor for exactly this case: values must be unique across all target nodes. The draft also moves SPARQL-based checks into a separate document, SHACL 1.2 SPARQL-Related Features. pySHACL 0.40.2 follows the 2017 standard, so we used SPARQL here.

A SPARQL constraint runs once for every focus node. A slow query times ten thousand drinks is very slow. Keep the query small, and fix the start node with $this. Test the speed on real data sizes before you go live.

SHACL rules

SHACL can also add facts, like a reasoner. The rules come from SHACL Advanced Features, a W3C Working Group Note of 8 June 2017. It is not a Recommendation. A rule hangs on a shape, and runs for each focus node.

:DrinkRules a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Drink ;
    sh:rule [                                   # a SPARQL rule
        a sh:SPARQLRule ;
        sh:prefixes : ;
        sh:construct """
            CONSTRUCT { $this a :CheapDrink }
            WHERE { $this :priceEUR ?p . FILTER (?p < 3) }""" ;
    ] .

:OrderRules a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Order ;
    sh:rule [                                   # a triple rule
        a sh:TripleRule ;
        sh:subject   sh:this ;
        sh:predicate :servedAt ;
        sh:object    [ sh:path ( :servedBy :worksAt ) ] ;
    ] .
from pyshacl import shacl_rules
from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF

C = Namespace("http://example.org/cafe#")
data = Graph().parse("rule_data.ttl")
before = len(data)
out = shacl_rules(data, shacl_graph="rules.ttl")   # runs the rules
print("triples:", before, "->", len(out))
print("cheap:", sorted(s.split("#")[1] for s in out.subjects(RDF.type, C.CheapDrink)))
print("o1 servedAt:", [o.split("#")[1] for o in out.objects(C.o1, C.servedAt)])
triples: 13 -> 16
cheap: ['espresso', 'greenTea']
o1 servedAt: ['beanBar']

The small data file has three drinks and one order served by Mia at Bean Bar. The SPARQL rule added two types. The triple rule followed the path from o1 to Mia to Bean Bar and added one link. That is three new triples.

Rules in SHACL 1.2

The Data Shapes Working Group is writing new rule documents. Both are Working Drafts in November 2026: SHACL 1.2 Inference Rules and SPARQL 1.2 RL. SPARQL 1.2 RL is a Datalog-style rule language with a SPARQL-like syntax. A rule has the shape RULE { head } WHERE { body }, for example:

RULE { ?o :servedAt ?shop } WHERE { ?o :servedBy ?b . ?b :worksAt ?shop }

The draft also allows negation with NOT { ... }, under stratification. We did not run this syntax. We found no engine for it in our tools. You learn rule engines in Rules and Datalog.

Do not mix rule output and typed data without a mark. Write inferred triples to a separate named graph. Then you can delete and compute them again when the data changes.

Closed-world checks on open-world data

RDF data is open world. SHACL checks are closed world. The two meet at one point: what is in the data graph at check time. This test shows the danger.

# cw_data.ttl
:flatWhite a :Latte .                                        # no price
:lea a :Barista ; :name "Lea" ; :emial "lea@example.org" .   # typo

# cw_onto.ttl (the class tree, in another file)
:Coffee rdfs:subClassOf :Drink .
:Latte  rdfs:subClassOf :Coffee .

The shapes say: every Drink has a price, and a Barista may only have :name and :email. The second shape is closed.

:BaristaShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Barista ;
    sh:closed true ;                        # no other properties allowed
    sh:ignoredProperties ( rdf:type ) ;
    sh:property [ sh:path :name ; sh:minCount 1 ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path :email ] .
run()                                               # data only
run(ont_graph="cw_onto.ttl", inference="rdfs")      # add the class tree first
conforms: False ['lea: ClosedConstraintComponent']
conforms: False ['flatWhite: MinCountConstraintComponent', 'lea: ClosedConstraintComponent']

The closed shape caught the typo :emial both times. But look at the flat white.

In the first run, nobody checked it. The data graph did not say that a Latte is a Drink. So sh:targetClass :Drink did not pick it. The missing price passed in silence.

So the rule is: infer first, then validate. pySHACL does this with ont_graph and inference="rdfs" (or "owlrl", or "both"). Other tools do the same in two steps.

The SHACL 1.2 Core draft has a section on where to look up rdfs:subClassOf triples. It allows the union of the shapes graph and the data graph. Then you can keep the class tree next to your shapes.

A closed shape without sh:ignoredProperties ( rdf:type ) reports every node that has a type, because rdf:type is not in its list. Also, closed shapes check only the properties that leave a node, not the links that point to it.

SHACL 1.2 today, and ShEx in brief

  1. 2017 SHACL 1.0. W3C Recommendation on 20 July 2017. SHACL Advanced Features as a Note on 8 June 2017.
  2. 2025 SHACL 1.2 starts. First Public Working Draft of SHACL 1.2 Core on 18 March 2025.
  3. 2026 Still drafts. Latest Working Draft of SHACL 1.2 Core on 10 November 2026.

On 15 November 2026, SHACL 1.2 is a set of Working Drafts from the W3C Data Shapes Working Group. None is a Recommendation yet. Check the W3C pages: this can change.

SHACL 1.2 documents on 15 November 2026
DocumentStatus and date
SHACL 1.2 CoreWorking Draft, 10 November 2026
SHACL 1.2 SPARQL-Related FeaturesWorking Draft, 22 October 2026
SHACL 1.2 Node ExpressionsWorking Draft, 28 October 2026
SHACL 1.2 Inference RulesWorking Draft, 10 November 2026
SPARQL 1.2 RLWorking Draft, 12 November 2026
SHACL 1.2 User Interfaces, ProfilingWorking Drafts. A compact syntax (SHACL-C) is an Editor's Draft.

The change list in the Core draft is long. These items matter most for daily work.

  • Node expressions: compute nodes, for targets and values.
  • New targets: sh:targetWhere, sh:shape, and the class sh:ShapeClass.
  • New checks: sh:singleLine, sh:someValue, sh:rootClass, sh:subsetOf, sh:uniqueValuesFor, and list checks like sh:memberShape.
  • Unions: sh:class, sh:datatype and sh:nodeKind can take a list of choices.
  • RDF 1.2: sh:reifierShape and the node kind sh:TripleTerm.
  • For AI and tools: sh:intent, sh:agentInstruction, sh:unit, and the severities sh:Trace and sh:Debug.

ShEx in brief

ShEx is a second shape language. It looks like a grammar. Here is our drink rule in ShExC, its compact syntax. We tested it with PyShEx 0.9.0.

PREFIX :    <http://example.org/cafe#>
PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#>

:DrinkShape {
  :priceEUR xsd:decimal ;          # exactly one decimal
  :hasSize  [ :small :large ] ?    # zero or one, from a list
}
:DrinkShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass :Drink ;
    sh:property [ sh:path :priceEUR ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ;
                  sh:datatype xsd:decimal ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path :hasSize ; sh:maxCount 1 ;
                  sh:in ( :small :large ) ] .
latte True
espresso False 2 triples exceeds max {1,1}
chai False No matching triples found for predicate :priceEUR

The ShEx shape has no target. In ShEx you pick the nodes when you call the validator. This is a shape map. We passed each node by hand.

SHACL and ShEx compared
SHACLShEx
StandardW3C Recommendation (2017). 1.2 is in draft.ShEx 2.1, a W3C Community Group report (2019). Not a W3C standard.
Written asRDF (Turtle). Compact syntax in draft.ShExC compact syntax, or JSON (ShExJ)
Which nodesTargets inside the shapesA shape map given at run time
StyleA list of constraintsA grammar for the node's triples
ExtrasSPARQL checks, rules, severitiesClean recursive shapes
Known usersMany data platforms and triple storesWikidata entity schemas

A common question: "SHACL or OWL for data quality?" The answer is SHACL. Give the reasons: open world, no unique names, and domain and range infer instead of check. Then say what OWL is good for: shared meaning and inference.

Patterns to remember

SHACL patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
sh:targetClass CCheck every instance of a classsh:targetClass :DrinkSubclass triples must be in the data graph.
sh:minCount 1A value is requiredsh:path :priceEUR ; sh:minCount 1OWL "some" never does this.
sh:maxCount 1At most one valueone price per drinkOWL functional gives sameAs instead.
sh:datatype TCheck the literal typesh:datatype xsd:decimalThe text "2.50" is not a decimal.
sh:class CCheck the type of a linked nodesh:path :servedBy ; sh:class :BaristaThe type must be in the data.
sh:in ( a b )Allow a fixed listsh:in ( :small :large )Good for value sets.
sh:pattern "regex"Check text formatemail patternEscape the backslash twice in Turtle.
sh:severity sh:WarningMark a soft rulethe email checkStill makes conforms false by default.
sh:closed trueNo unknown propertiescatches :emialAdd sh:ignoredProperties ( rdf:type ).
sh:sparql [ sh:select ... ]A check Core cannot write wellunique labelsReturn $this. One row is one result.
sh:rule [ a sh:SPARQLRule ]Add facts with CONSTRUCT$this a :CheapDrinkSHACL-AF is a Note, not a standard.
validate(..., inference="rdfs")Infer first, then checkfinds the flat whiteWithout it, subclasses can escape.

Practice

The data has a drink with no price. The ontology says "every drink has some price". What does an OWL reasoner do?

  • It reports a missing price.
  • Nothing. It assumes a price exists but is unknown.
  • It deletes the drink.

Open world: a missing fact is unknown, not false.

What is a focus node?

  • The first node in the data file
  • A node that a shape is checking right now
  • The node with the most links

Targets select focus nodes. The engine checks each one against the shape.

The only result in a report has severity sh:Warning. With default settings, what is sh:conforms?

  • true
  • false
  • It depends on the data size.

In SHACL 1.0, any result makes conforms false. Some engines have options to change this.

On 15 November 2026, what is the status of SHACL 1.2 Core?

  • W3C Recommendation
  • W3C Working Draft
  • Community Group report

The latest version is a Working Draft from 10 November 2026. SHACL 1.0 (2017) is the Recommendation.

Fill in the missing words.

In a SPARQL constraint, the variable ? stands for the focus node.

A shape that allows no other properties uses sh:? true.

  1. Write a property shape: every Barista has exactly one name, and it is a string.
    Answer

    :BaristaShape a sh:NodeShape ; sh:targetClass :Barista ; sh:property [ sh:path :name ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ; sh:datatype xsd:string ] .

  2. Write a shape for orders: the item must be a Drink or a Cake. Use sh:or.
    Answer

    :OrderShape sh:property [ sh:path :item ; sh:or ( [ sh:class :Drink ] [ sh:class :Cake ] ) ] . In the SHACL 1.2 draft you could also write sh:class ( :Drink :Cake ).

  3. An order has a start time and an end time. Write a check that the start comes before the end.
    Answer

    sh:property [ sh:path :start ; sh:lessThan :end ] . This is a property pair constraint. It compares the values of two properties of the same focus node.

  4. Your report is empty and conforms is true, but you know the data has errors. Name two possible causes.
    Answer

    The shape has no target, or the target finds no nodes. For example, sh:targetClass :Drink with data that types nodes only as :Latte, and the subclass triples are not in the data graph. Fix: add the class tree, or run inference first.

  5. Write a SHACL-SPARQL constraint: an order must not be served by a barista from another shop than the order's shop (:atShop).
    Answer

    sh:select "SELECT $this ?b WHERE { $this :atShop ?s ; :servedBy ?b . ?b :worksAt ?other . FILTER (?other != ?s) }" on a shape with sh:targetClass :Order. Each returned row is one result.

  6. Hard. A teammate says: "Let us drop SHACL and make every property functional in OWL. The reasoner will find duplicates." What goes wrong? Use the café data.
    Answer

    Functional does not find duplicates of things. It merges them. Two managers become one person through sameAs.

    Two different literal values, like 2.20 and 2.40, do make the ontology inconsistent. But the reasoner only says "inconsistent", not where, and a missing value is never found. SHACL sh:maxCount 1 and sh:minCount 1 name the node and the path.

Key takeaways

  • OWL infers in an open world. It finds clashes, not missing or badly formatted data.
  • SHACL checks data in a closed world: what is not there counts as missing.
  • A node shape has targets. Property shapes check the values at the end of a path.
  • The report is an RDF graph. Each result names the node, path, value, shape and severity.
  • Any result makes conforms false by default, even a Warning.
  • SHACL-SPARQL covers checks that are hard or impossible in Core. SHACL rules add facts.
  • Infer first, then validate, or subclasses can escape the checks.
  • SHACL 1.0 (2017) is the Recommendation. SHACL 1.2 is in Working Draft in November 2026. ShEx is a Community Group report.

Sources

  • Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL). The W3C Recommendation of 20 July 2017.
  • SHACL Advanced Features. The 2017 Working Group Note with rules and custom targets.
  • SHACL 1.2 Core. The Working Draft of 10 November 2026, with its list of changes.
  • History of SHACL 1.2 Core. Every published version and its maturity level.
  • pySHACL on GitHub. The engine used here, with its options for inference and rules.
  • Shape Expressions Language 2.1. The ShEx specification, a final Community Group report.

Rules and Datalog

An ontology says what kinds of things exist. Rules say what follows from the facts you have. Datalog is the small, clean rule language behind many reasoners, program analysers and knowledge graph engines. This chapter shows how it works, by hand and in real engines.

  • Write facts and safe Datalog rules, including recursive rules.
  • Run naive and semi-naive evaluation by hand and in code.
  • Split a program with negation into strata, and spot a program that has none.
  • Compare forward chaining, backward chaining, magic sets and the Rete idea.
  • Place SWRL, RIF, OWL 2 RL and today's engines on one map.

Facts and rules

Start with three small facts about a family.

parent(ana, ben).        % Ana is a parent of Ben
parent(ben, cara).
parent(cara, dan).

grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

The last line is a rule. Read it from right to left. If X is a parent of Y, and Y is a parent of Z, then X is a grandparent of Z. The engine finds two new facts by itself: grandparent(ana, cara) and grandparent(ben, dan).

Now the words. A fact is a plain true statement. A rule has a head and a body. The sign :- means "if". Each piece like parent(X, Y) is an atom. Its name, parent, is the predicate.

  • Constants start with a small letter: ana, ben.
  • Variables start with a capital letter: X, Y. Some engines write ?X.
  • A comma in the body means AND.
  • Two rules with the same head mean OR. Each rule is one way to get the fact.

Database people use two more names. The stored predicates, like parent, form the EDB. The derived predicates, like grandparent, form the IDB.

What makes it Datalog

Datalog is a small part of the logic language Prolog, which you met in AI and knowledge representation. It keeps Prolog's rules but takes away three things.

  1. No function symbols. You cannot write parent(motherOf(X), X). Only constants and variables are allowed.
  2. Every rule must be safe. Each variable in the head must also appear in a positive atom of the body.
  3. No cut and no side effects. The order of rules and facts does not change the answer.

Because of these limits, every Datalog program stops. It always gives the same, finite answer. The name Datalog is usually credited to David Maier.

likes(X, Y) :- person(X).      % Y appears only in the head

Y can be anything at all. The answer has no end.

likes(X, Y) :- person(X), food(Y), eats(X, Y).

Every head variable comes from a body atom. The answer is finite.

Do not read the comma as "then". The body is a set of conditions that must all be true at the same time. Their order does not matter for the result. It can matter for speed in some engines.

Recursion: ancestors and reachability

A grandparent rule looks two steps up. What about all steps up? You cannot write one rule for each length. You write a rule that uses itself.

ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).                  % base case: one step
ancestor(X, Z) :- ancestor(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).  % recursive case: one more step

A rule is recursive when its head predicate also appears in its body. The first rule is the base case. The second rule adds one step to a path that we already know. Together they compute the transitive closure of parent.

The same shape answers a question about graphs. Which nodes can I reach from node a?

reach(a).                               % start here
reach(Y) :- reach(X), edge(X, Y).       % follow one more edge

Look at the cycle a, b, c, a. Does the engine go round forever? No. After reach(a), reach(b) and reach(c), the cycle only gives reach(a) again. That fact is old. Nothing new appears, so the engine stops.

Three shapes of recursion

The same ancestor relation, written three ways
ShapeRecursive ruleNote
Left-linearanc(X,Z) :- anc(X,Y), parent(Y,Z).One recursive atom, first in the body.
Right-linearanc(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), anc(Y,Z).One recursive atom, last in the body.
Non-linearanc(X,Z) :- anc(X,Y), anc(Y,Z).Two recursive atoms. Fewer rounds, more work per round.

All three give the same facts in Datalog. A rule with one recursive atom is called linear. SQL only allows linear recursion, as you will see later.

Prolog runs rules top-down, in the written order. With the left-linear rule, Prolog finds the answers and then calls itself forever, until the stack runs out. Datalog engines work bottom-up from the facts, so the same rule is fine. Prolog systems with tabling, like XSB, also fix this.

Naive evaluation by hand

How does an engine find all ancestor facts? The simplest way is to apply every rule to every fact, again and again. It stops when a round adds nothing new. This is naive evaluation.

Use a chain of five people: ana, ben, cara, dan, eve. There are four parent facts. Each person is the parent of the next.

  1. Round 1. No ancestor facts yet. Rule 1 copies the 4 parent facts: ana-ben, ben-cara, cara-dan, dan-eve. Total: 4.
  2. Round 2. Rule 1 makes the same 4 facts again. Rule 2 joins all 4 ancestor facts with parent. New: ana-cara, ben-dan, cara-eve. Total: 7.
  3. Round 3. Rule 1 repeats its 4. Rule 2 joins all 7 facts. New: ana-dan, ben-eve. Total: 9.
  4. Round 4. Everything again. One new fact: ana-eve. Total: 10.
  5. Round 5. Everything again. Nothing new. Stop. The answer has 10 facts.

The final set has a special property. If you apply the rules to it once more, you get the same set back. A set like this is a fixed point. Naive evaluation finds the smallest one, so it adds no fact that the rules do not force.

But look at the waste. Round 4 makes ana-cara again, for the third time. Every round repeats all the work of the rounds before it.

Naive evaluation is like reading a whole book again each day to find the one new page. It is correct, but slow.

Semi-naive evaluation

A new fact can only come from a join that uses at least one fact that is new since the last round. Old facts joined with old facts give only old facts. So keep a separate set of the newest facts. Call it the delta, written \Delta.

Semi-naive evaluation on the same chain
RoundJoinNew facts (the delta)Total
1rule 1 onlyana-ben, ben-cara, cara-dan, dan-eve4
2delta of round 1 with parentana-cara, ben-dan, cara-eve7
3delta of round 2 with parentana-dan, ben-eve9
4delta of round 3 with parentana-eve10
5delta of round 4 with parentnone: stop10

Same answer, same number of rounds, much less work. This is semi-naive evaluation. It is described in the work of Bancilhon and Ramakrishnan in 1986. Almost every Datalog engine uses it.

The code below runs both methods. It counts every derivation, also the repeated ones. Only one line differs: the join uses all facts, or only the delta.

# ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
# ancestor(X, Z) :- ancestor(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

def run(parent, naive):
    kids = {}                                  # index: Y -> [Z]
    for y, z in parent:
        kids.setdefault(y, []).append(z)
    anc = set(parent)                          # round 1: rule 1
    delta = set(parent)                        # the facts that are new
    rounds, work = 1, len(parent)
    while delta:
        rounds += 1
        base = anc if naive else delta         # THE one difference
        if naive:
            work += len(parent)                # naive also repeats rule 1
        new = set()
        for x, y in base:                      # rule 2
            for z in kids.get(y, []):
                work += 1                      # one derivation
                if (x, z) not in anc:
                    new.add((x, z))
        anc |= new
        delta = new
    return len(anc), rounds, work

for n in (5, 200):
    parent = [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)]   # a chain of n people
    print(f"chain of {n} people")
    for name, naive in (("naive", True), ("semi-naive", False)):
        facts, rounds, work = run(parent, naive)
        print(f"  {name:<10} {facts:>6} facts {rounds:>4} rounds {work:>8} derivations")
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};

// ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
// ancestor(X, Z) :- ancestor(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).
fn run(parent: &[(usize, usize)], naive: bool) -> (usize, u32, u64) {
    let mut kids: HashMap<usize, Vec<usize>> = HashMap::new(); // index: Y -> [Z]
    for &(y, z) in parent { kids.entry(y).or_default().push(z); }
    let mut anc: HashSet<(usize, usize)> = parent.iter().copied().collect(); // round 1
    let mut delta = anc.clone(); // the facts that are new
    let (mut rounds, mut work) = (1, parent.len() as u64);
    while !delta.is_empty() {
        rounds += 1;
        let base = if naive { anc.clone() } else { delta }; // THE one difference
        if naive { work += parent.len() as u64; } // naive also repeats rule 1
        let mut new = HashSet::new();
        for (x, y) in base {
            for &z in kids.get(&y).into_iter().flatten() {
                work += 1; // one derivation
                if !anc.contains(&(x, z)) {
                    new.insert((x, z));
                }
            }
        }
        anc.extend(new.iter().copied());
        delta = new;
    }
    (anc.len(), rounds, work)
}

fn main() {
    for n in [5, 200] {
        let parent: Vec<(usize, usize)> = (0..n - 1).map(|i| (i, i + 1)).collect();
        println!("chain of {n} people");
        for (name, naive) in [("naive", true), ("semi-naive", false)] {
            let (facts, rounds, work) = run(&parent, naive);
            println!("  {name:<10} {facts:>6} facts {rounds:>4} rounds {work:>8} derivations");
        }
    }
}

We ran it with Python 3.14 and Rust 1.99. Both print the same lines.

chain of 5 people
  naive          10 facts    5 rounds       40 derivations
  semi-naive     10 facts    5 rounds       10 derivations
chain of 200 people
  naive       19900 facts  200 rounds  2666600 derivations
  semi-naive  19900 facts  200 rounds    19900 derivations

On a chain, semi-naive makes each fact exactly once. Naive work grows much faster than the answer.

A non-linear rule like anc(X,Z) :- anc(X,Y), anc(Y,Z) needs more care. Using the delta for only one atom misses facts. The engine must use the delta in the first atom, or in the second atom. Engines rewrite each rule into several "delta versions" for this.

Negation and strata

Which nodes can we not reach from a? We need "not".

node(X) :- edge(X, Y).
node(Y) :- edge(X, Y).
reach(a).
reach(Y) :- reach(X), edge(X, Y).
unreached(X) :- node(X), not reach(X).   % negation

Here "not reach(X)" means "reach(X) is not among the facts". This is negation as failure. It is only safe after reach is complete. If we checked too early, d might look unreached, and later become reached. A fact would then have to be taken back.

The fix is to compute in layers. Each layer is a stratum. A predicate used under "not" must sit in a lower stratum. Draw the predicates as a graph. Add an arrow from each body predicate to the head predicate, and mark arrows through "not" as negative.

A program is stratified when its dependency graph has no cycle that contains a negative arrow. Then the predicates can be put into strata 1, 2, 3 and so on. A positive arrow may stay in the same stratum. A negative arrow must go to a strictly higher stratum.

The engine runs stratum 1 to its fixed point, then stratum 2, and so on. This idea comes from Apt, Blair and Walker, and others, in 1988. Every stratified program has one clear answer.

Here is the same program in two real engines. On the left is Nemo, through its Python package. On the right is Ascent, a Datalog library for Rust.

from nmo_python import load_string, NemoEngine

rules = """
edge(a, b). edge(b, c). edge(c, a). edge(c, d). edge(e, f).
node(?X) :- edge(?X, ?Y).
node(?Y) :- edge(?X, ?Y).
reach(a).                                  % start here
reach(?Y) :- reach(?X), edge(?X, ?Y).      % recursion
unreached(?X) :- node(?X), ~reach(?X).     % negation: a higher stratum
"""
engine = NemoEngine(load_string(rules))
engine.reason()
for name in ("reach", "unreached"):
    print(name, sorted(str(row[0]).strip("<>") for row in engine.result(name)))
use ascent::ascent;

ascent! {
    relation edge(char, char);
    relation node(char);
    relation reach(char);
    relation unreached(char);

    node(x) <-- edge(x, _);
    node(y) <-- edge(_, y);
    reach('a');                                  // start here
    reach(y) <-- reach(x), edge(x, y);           // recursion
    unreached(x) <-- node(x), !reach(x);         // negation: a higher stratum
}

fn main() {
    let mut prog = AscentProgram::default();
    prog.edge = vec![('a', 'b'), ('b', 'c'), ('c', 'a'), ('c', 'd'), ('e', 'f')];
    prog.run();
    let mut reach: Vec<char> = prog.reach.iter().map(|r| r.0).collect();
    let mut unreached: Vec<char> = prog.unreached.iter().map(|r| r.0).collect();
    reach.sort();
    unreached.sort();
    println!("reach {reach:?}");
    println!("unreached {unreached:?}");
}
reach ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
unreached ['e', 'f']

Nemo writes negation as ~. Ascent writes it as ! and puts the head on the left of <--. Both found the strata by themselves.

A program with no strata

A game: a position X is winning if you can move to a position Y that is not winning.

win(X) :- move(X, Y), not win(Y).

Here win depends on itself through "not". That is a negative cycle, so there is no stratification. We gave this rule to Nemo 0.10.1. It refused with the message The rules of the program are not stratified.

Programs like this still have meanings, but you need a stronger theory. The well-founded semantics (Van Gelder, Ross and Schlipf, 1991) gives true, false or unknown. The stable model semantics (Gelfond and Lifschitz, 1988) can give several answers. It is the basis of answer set programming.

Negation as failure is closed-world. OWL and RDF are open-world: a missing fact is unknown, not false. When you add "not" rules to an ontology, you change its meaning. Say so in the documentation. See Logic for ontology.

Aggregates like count and sum need the same care. "Ana has 2 children" stops being true when a third child appears. So engines also put aggregates in a higher stratum than the facts they count.

Forward chaining, backward chaining and Rete

There are two directions to use rules. Think about the question: "Is ana an ancestor of eve?"

Forward chaining

Start from the facts. Apply rules until nothing new appears. Store all results. Then look up the answer.

This is materialisation. Queries are fast. Updates cost work.

Backward chaining

Start from the question. Find rules whose head matches it. Turn their bodies into smaller questions. Stop at facts.

Nothing is stored ahead. It only touches what the question needs. Prolog works this way.

Forward chaining is the usual way for Datalog engines and for OWL RL reasoners. Backward chaining is the usual way for Prolog and for query rewriting.

Magic sets: forward chaining with a goal

Can a forward engine focus on one question? Yes. A rewrite called magic sets adds the question as a fact. Bancilhon, Maier, Sagiv and Ullman described it in 1986.

magic(ana).                                       % the question as a fact
ancestor(X, Y) :- magic(X), parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Z) :- magic(X), ancestor(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

We ran the full program and this version in Nemo on the five-person chain. The full program made 10 ancestor facts. The magic version made only 4: the ones that start at ana.

The Rete idea

Business rule engines have a different problem. They have thousands of rules. Facts arrive one at a time, all day. Checking every rule against every fact after each change is too slow.

Charles Forgy at Carnegie Mellon solved this with the Rete algorithm. It first appeared in a 1974 working paper. His thesis followed in 1979, and the best-known paper in 1982. "Rete" is Latin for "net".

Compile the rules

Rule: IF an order is over 100 AND its customer is a VIP, THEN give a discount. The engine turns every condition into a node of a network.

Alpha nodes

An alpha node tests one fact alone. "Is it an order? Is the amount over 100?" Facts that pass wait in an alpha memory.

Beta nodes

A beta node joins two inputs. "Same customer?" It keeps the partial matches it found in a beta memory.

Only the change moves

A new order arrives. It passes only through its own path. Old matches are already stored. The rule fires when a full match reaches the end.

The price

Rete trades memory for speed. It stores many partial matches. OPS5, CLIPS, Jess and Drools used it. Drools later moved to PHREAK, a lazier design that grew from Rete.

Rete and semi-naive evaluation share one idea: do not redo old work. Semi-naive keeps the delta of facts. Rete keeps partial matches. Modern Datalog engines like RDFox also update their stored results when facts are added or deleted.

Production rules are not logic rules. A production rule can delete a fact or call a web service. Then the order of firing changes the result. Datalog rules only add facts, so the order never matters.

Rules for the Semantic Web: SWRL, RIF and OWL RL

OWL is strong, but it cannot say some simple things. "The brother of my parent is my uncle" needs a chain of two properties joined to a third. People wanted rules next to OWL.

SWRL

SWRL, the Semantic Web Rule Language, joins OWL with Horn-like rules. It was published as a W3C Member Submission on 21 May 2004. That is a proposal, not a W3C standard. The uncle example below is close to the one in the submission. It is written in the style that the Protégé editor uses.

hasParent(?x, ?y) ^ hasBrother(?y, ?z) -> hasUncle(?x, ?z)
Person(?p) ^ hasAge(?p, ?a) ^ swrlb:greaterThanOrEqual(?a, 18) -> Adult(?p)

The left side is the body, joined by ^ for AND. The right side is the head. Names starting with swrlb: are built-ins.

There is a catch. The submission itself says that OWL DL plus these rules is undecidable. A popular fix is DL-safe rules (Motik, Sattler and Studer, 2005). A DL-safe rule only matches named individuals, never individuals that OWL only knows must exist.

RIF

The Rule Interchange Format is a W3C Recommendation from 22 June 2010. A second edition followed on 5 February 2013. Its goal is to move rules between different rule engines. It has three dialects.

  • RIF Core. The common part. The spec says it matches Datalog, plus some built-ins.
  • RIF BLD. Basic Logic Dialect: Horn rules with function symbols and equality.
  • RIF PRD. Production Rule Dialect: rules with actions, as in Rete engines.
Forall ?x ?y ?z (
  ex:ancestor(?x ?z) :- And(ex:ancestor(?x ?y) ex:parent(?y ?z))
)

Few products use RIF today. But its documents are still a clear, exact reference for rule meaning.

OWL 2 RL: an ontology language that is a rule set

OWL 2 has a profile called OWL 2 RL. The W3C OWL 2 Profiles document gives it as a list of rules over triples. You can run them with any rule engine. You meet the profile itself in OWL 2. Here are six of its rules.

Six OWL 2 RL rules (names from the W3C Profiles document)
NameIfThen
cax-scoC1 subClassOf C2, and x type C1x type C2
prp-domP domain C, and x P yx type C
prp-rngP range C, and x P yy type C
prp-trpP is transitive, x P y, and y P zx P z
prp-inv1P1 inverseOf P2, and x P1 yy P2 x
cax-dwC1 disjointWith C2, and x type C1 and C2false: an error

Each row is one Datalog rule over a single predicate T(s, p, o) for triples. For example, cax-sco is T(X, type, C2) :- T(C1, subClassOf, C2), T(X, type, C1).

The Python package owlrl runs these rules on an rdflib graph. Here is a bike with parts.

from rdflib import OWL, Graph, Namespace
import owlrl

data = """
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

ex:partOf  a owl:TransitiveProperty ;
           rdfs:domain ex:Part .
ex:hasPart owl:inverseOf ex:partOf .
ex:Wheel   rdfs:subClassOf ex:Part .

ex:spoke1 ex:partOf ex:wheel1 .
ex:wheel1 ex:partOf ex:bike1 ;
          a ex:Wheel .
"""
EX = Namespace("http://example.org/")
g = Graph().parse(data=data, format="turtle")
before = set(g)
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)   # run the OWL 2 RL rules
print(f"{len(before)} triples before, {len(g)} after")
same = 0
for s, p, o in sorted(set(g) - before):
    if p == OWL.sameAs:
        same += 1                                         # rule eq-ref: x sameAs x
    elif all(str(t).startswith(str(EX)) for t in (s, o)): # show only our own names
        print(g.qname(s), g.qname(p), g.qname(o))
print(f"plus {same} triples 'x owl:sameAs x'")

We ran it with owlrl 7.6.2 and rdflib 7.6.0.

7 triples before, 129 after
ex:bike1 ex:hasPart ex:spoke1
ex:bike1 ex:hasPart ex:wheel1
ex:spoke1 ex:partOf ex:bike1
ex:spoke1 rdf:type ex:Part
ex:wheel1 ex:hasPart ex:spoke1
ex:wheel1 rdf:type ex:Part
plus 64 triples 'x owl:sameAs x'

You can name the rule behind each line. The spoke is part of the bike by prp-trp. The bike has its parts by prp-inv1. The spoke is a Part by prp-dom. The wheel is a Part by cax-sco, and also by prp-dom.

Seven triples became 129. Most are dull: the rule eq-ref says every thing is the same as itself, and the engine also adds facts about the OWL words. Do not store a full closure without thinking. Filter it, or let the engine answer queries without saving everything.

The rules are complete only in a limited case. The Profiles document (Theorem PR1) covers OWL 2 RL ontologies and questions about facts on named individuals. Outside that case, the rules may miss consequences of full OWL.

Modern engines in 2026

Datalog was a research topic for years. Now it runs inside code scanners, knowledge graphs and Rust tools. We checked these engines on 15 November 2026.

Datalog engines and their status (checked 2026-11-15)

The same rule in four syntaxes

.decl parent(x: symbol, y: symbol)
.decl ancestor(x: symbol, y: symbol)
.output ancestor
parent("ana", "ben").
ancestor(x, y) :- parent(x, y).
ancestor(x, z) :- ancestor(x, y), parent(y, z).
[?x, :ancestor, ?y] :- [?x, :parent, ?y] .
[?x, :ancestor, ?z] :- [?x, :ancestor, ?y], [?y, :parent, ?z] .
ancestor(?X, ?Y) :- parent(?X, ?Y) .
ancestor(?X, ?Z) :- ancestor(?X, ?Y), parent(?Y, ?Z) .

Datalog inside databases

SQL has had recursive queries since the SQL:1999 standard. WITH RECURSIVE is a linear Datalog rule in SQL clothes.

CREATE TABLE edge(src TEXT, dst TEXT);
INSERT INTO edge VALUES ('a','b'), ('b','c'), ('c','a'), ('c','d'), ('e','f');

WITH RECURSIVE reach(n) AS (
  SELECT 'a'                                    -- start here (rule 1)
  UNION                                         -- UNION drops repeats, so the cycle ends
  SELECT edge.dst FROM reach JOIN edge ON edge.src = reach.n   -- recursion (rule 2)
)
SELECT group_concat(n, ' ') AS reached FROM (SELECT n FROM reach ORDER BY n);
a b c d

We ran it with SQLite 3.51. The PostgreSQL 18 manual describes how it is evaluated. It keeps a "working table" of the rows from the last step, and joins only that table in the next step. That is semi-naive evaluation under another name.

With UNION ALL, the database keeps repeated rows. On a graph with a cycle, the query never stops. Use UNION, or the CYCLE clause in PostgreSQL. The chapter Triple stores and graph databases goes deeper.

The fixed-point idea

You saw it by hand: apply the rules until nothing changes. Now let us say it exactly. Collect all facts in a set I. One round of all rules is a function on sets of facts.

For a program P with facts F, the immediate consequence operator is T_P(I) = F \cup \{\, h\sigma \mid (h \leftarrow b_1, \dots, b_n) \in P \text{ and } b_i\sigma \in I \text{ for all } i \,\} Here \sigma replaces the variables of a rule with constants.

In words: T_P(I) is the facts, plus every rule head whose body is true in I. Naive evaluation computes T_P(\emptyset), then T_P(T_P(\emptyset)), and so on.

Let P be a Datalog program without negation. Then T_P is monotone. The chain \emptyset \subseteq T_P(\emptyset) \subseteq T_P^2(\emptyset) \subseteq \dots reaches a fixed point after finitely many steps. This fixed point is the least fixed point of T_P, and it equals the least model of P.

Proof idea

Monotone: more facts can only make more rule bodies true, never fewer. So each step contains the step before. There are only finitely many possible facts: p predicates, c constants and arity at most k give at most p \cdot c^k. So the chain must stop growing. Every model of P contains F, and is closed under the rules, so by induction it contains every step. So the limit is inside every model: it is the least one. The link between models and fixed points goes back to van Emden and Kowalski (1976) and to Tarski's fixed-point theorem.

Try it with numbers. In our family there are 5 constants and 1 derived binary predicate. So there are at most 5^2 = 25 possible ancestor facts. Each round adds at least one fact, so there are at most 26 rounds. In reality we needed 5.

With fixed rules and growing data, answering a Datalog query takes polynomial time. It is P-complete in data complexity. When the rules are also part of the input, it is EXPTIME-complete.

So Datalog is not a full programming language. It always stops, and on fixed rules it stays polynomial. That is exactly why reasoners like it.

When the guarantee breaks

  • Negation and aggregates are not monotone. With strata, each stratum is still a monotone fixed point.
  • Existential rules invent new values. In Nemo, !v in the head means "some new thing". The process that adds these values is called the chase. It may never stop. Example: every person has a parent, and every parent is a person.
  • Function symbols, as in Prolog, also allow endless new terms.

Before you add an extension, ask: can the set of possible facts still grow forever? If yes, termination is no longer free. Engines like Nemo document which checks they make.

Is Datalog the same as OWL?

No. OWL can say "every person has some parent" without naming the parent. Plain Datalog cannot invent that parent. Datalog can say things OWL cannot, like the uncle chain with a variable shared across atoms. OWL 2 RL is the part of OWL that plain Datalog can run.

When should I use rules instead of more OWL?

Use rules for joins across several properties, for closed-world checks and for computed values. Use OWL for class definitions and classification. For data checks, see SHACL and validation.

Where can I build my own engine?

The chapter Build a reasoner builds a semi-naive OWL RL reasoner step by step. Reasoners and materialisation compares real strategies.

Patterns to remember

Rule and Datalog patterns
PatternPurposeModelNote
p(a, b).State a stored factparent(ana, ben).Constants small, variables capital. End with a full stop.
head :- body.Derive new factsgrandparent(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z).The comma means AND.
Two rules, one headSay ORcontact(X) :- email(X, E). and contact(X) :- phone(X, N).Each rule is one way to get the fact.

Practice

Which rule is unsafe?

  • sibling(X, Y) :- parent(P, X), parent(P, Y).
  • knows(X, Y) :- person(X).
  • adult(X) :- person(X), age(X, A), A >= 18.

Y appears in the head but in no body atom. It could be anything, so the answer has no end.

In semi-naive evaluation, what does rule 2 of the ancestor program join in round 3?

  • All ancestor facts with all parent facts
  • Only the ancestor facts that were new in round 2, with parent
  • Only the parent facts

Old facts joined with old facts give only old facts. The delta of the last round is enough.

Which program cannot be stratified?

  • q(X) :- r(X), not s(X). and s(X) :- t(X).
  • p(X) :- r(X), not q(X). and q(X) :- r(X), not p(X).
  • p(X) :- e(X, Y), p(Y).

p depends on q through "not", and q depends on p through "not". That cycle contains negative arrows.

What is the W3C status of SWRL?

  • W3C Recommendation, 2010
  • W3C Member Submission, 2004
  • Part of OWL 2

SWRL is a 2004 Member Submission. RIF is the W3C Recommendation for rules.

An ontology says ex:Cat rdfs:subClassOf ex:Animal and ex:tom a ex:Cat. Which OWL 2 RL rule gives ex:tom a ex:Animal?

  • prp-trp
  • prp-dom
  • cax-sco

cax-sco moves an instance up the subclass link.

Fill in the missing words.

A chain of 6 people gives ? ancestor facts.

In SQL, recursion starts with the words WITH ?.

A layer of predicates that is computed fully before the next one is a ?.

Soufflé turns Datalog into a program in the language ?.

  1. Write rules for cousin(X, Y): X and Y have parents who are siblings. Use parent and a sibling rule.
    Answer

    sibling(X, Y) :- parent(P, X), parent(P, Y), X != Y. Then cousin(X, Y) :- parent(A, X), parent(B, Y), sibling(A, B). The test X != Y stops a person being their own sibling. Most engines allow it because both variables are already bound.

  2. Run semi-naive evaluation by hand for reach on the graph a to b, b to c, c to a. Start with reach(a). Write the delta of each round.
    Answer

    Round 1: delta {a}. Round 2: from a we get b, delta {b}. Round 3: from b we get c, delta {c}. Round 4: from c we get a, but a is old, so the delta is empty. Stop. Answer: a, b, c.

  3. Put these predicates into strata: big(X) :- size(X, S), S > 10. small(X) :- item(X), not big(X). cheap(X) :- small(X), not rare(X). rare(X) :- found(X, 1).
    Answer

    Stratum 1: size, item, found, big and rare. Stratum 2: small, because it uses "not big". Cheap uses small without "not", so it can share stratum 2. It uses "not rare", and rare is in stratum 1. So cheap also goes in stratum 2. Putting cheap in stratum 3 is also correct.

  4. Write the ancestor relation as a SQL query over a table parent(p, c).
    Answer

    WITH RECURSIVE anc(a, d) AS (SELECT p, c FROM parent UNION SELECT anc.a, parent.c FROM anc JOIN parent ON parent.p = anc.d) SELECT * FROM anc; The first SELECT is rule 1. The second is rule 2.

  5. Explain why hasParent(?x, ?y) ^ hasBrother(?y, ?z) -> hasUncle(?x, ?z) is hard to add to OWL, and what DL-safe rules change.
    Answer

    OWL classes can describe individuals that exist but have no name. A rule that also applies to them can simulate features that make OWL DL undecidable. A DL-safe rule only matches named individuals in the data. Reasoning then stays decidable, but the rule does not fire for unnamed individuals.

  6. A team stores the full OWL RL closure of a 10 million triple graph. Updates are now slow. Give two other designs.
    Answer

    First, use an engine with incremental updates, like RDFox, so a change only touches affected facts. Second, use backward chaining or query rewriting at query time, or a magic-set rewrite for frequent questions. You can also materialise only the rules you need, such as subclass and inverse.

  7. Prove that the rule set "every person has a parent, every parent is a person" makes the chase run forever, starting from person(ana).
    Answer

    Rules: hasParent(?x, !p) :- person(?x). and person(?p) :- hasParent(?x, ?p). From person(ana), we invent n1 with hasParent(ana, n1). Then person(n1). Then we invent n2, and so on. Each round makes a new value, so the set of facts never stops growing. No fixed point is reached.

Key takeaways

  • Datalog is facts plus safe if-then rules, with no function symbols. Every program stops.
  • Recursion uses a base rule and a recursive rule. Cycles in the data are fine.
  • The meaning of a program is its least fixed point: apply the rules until nothing changes.
  • Semi-naive evaluation joins only new facts. It gives the same answer with far less work.
  • Negation needs strata. A cycle through "not" has no stratification, and engines reject it.
  • Forward chaining stores results. Backward chaining starts from the question. Magic sets mix both. Rete keeps partial matches.
  • SWRL is a 2004 submission, RIF a 2010 Recommendation, and OWL 2 RL is OWL written as rules.
  • In 2026, Soufflé, RDFox, Nemo, Ascent, CodeQL and SQL recursive queries all run Datalog ideas.

Sources

  • Datalog lecture, CS294-260, UC Berkeley (2024). Semi-naive evaluation and stratified negation.
  • OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Profiles (Second Edition). W3C, 2012. The OWL 2 RL rule tables and Theorem PR1.
  • SWRL: A Semantic Web Rule Language. W3C Member Submission, 21 May 2004.
  • RIF Overview (Second Edition). W3C, 2013. The RIF dialects and documents.
  • Nemo rule language tour. TU Dresden. Syntax for rules, negation, existential rules and imports.
  • RDFox reasoning documentation. Rule syntax, stratified negation, aggregates and materialisation.

Formal ontology and upper ontologies

Every domain ontology must answer the same big questions. What is a thing? What is a part? What is an event? Upper ontologies answer these questions once, with logic, so that many domain ontologies can share the answers. This chapter shows the main ideas and the main upper ontologies, and helps you choose one, or none.

  • Explain what an upper ontology is for, and what it is not for.
  • Use the axioms of mereology to check a part-whole model.
  • Apply the OntoClean meta-properties to find bad subclass links.
  • Tell continuants from occurrents, and place a term in BFO.
  • Compare BFO, DOLCE, SUMO and UFO, and know their ISO status in 2026.

What an upper ontology is for

Two teams build ontologies. A hospital team writes Patient subClassOf Person. A billing team writes Patient subClassOf Account. Both are "right" for their own work. But you cannot join the two data sets. A patient cannot be a person and a bank account at the same time.

The problem is not about medicine or money. It is about very general ideas. Is a patient a kind of thing, or a role that a thing plays? Is a hospital stay an object or an event? An upper ontology answers these questions for everyone.

An upper ontology is a small set of very general classes and relations. Other names are top-level ontology and foundational ontology. Domain ontologies put their classes under its classes.

The study of these general ideas with logic is called formal ontology. The word "formal" means two things here. The ideas are independent of any one subject. And they are written in exact logic. You met Husserl's use of the term in From Leibniz to modern logic. Nicola Guarino brought it into computer science in the 1990s.

An upper ontology is like the frame of a house. It does not say what is in each room. But every room must fit into it.

An upper ontology is not a big dictionary. BFO has no class for "loan", "invoice" or "patient". It gives you "role", "process" and "object". You still write the domain terms yourself.

Parts and wholes: mereology

A spoke is part of a wheel. The wheel is part of a bike. So the spoke is part of the bike. Every person agrees with this. Logic can make it exact.

The theory of parts and wholes is called mereology, from the Greek word for "part". Stanisław Leśniewski gave the first exact theory in 1916. Leonard and Goodman brought it to a wide audience in 1940. We write P(x, y) for "x is part of y". In mereology, everything counts as a part of itself.

Parthood is a partial order:

  • Reflexive: \forall x\; P(x, x)
  • Antisymmetric: \forall x\, \forall y\; (P(x, y) \land P(y, x) \rightarrow x = y)
  • Transitive: \forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\; (P(x, y) \land P(y, z) \rightarrow P(x, z))

Two more words come from P. A proper part is a part that is not the whole: PP(x, y) \equiv P(x, y) \land x \neq y. Two things overlap when they share a part: O(x, y) \equiv \exists z\, (P(z, x) \land P(z, y)).

The partial order is not enough. Imagine a model where a handlebar has exactly one proper part: its grip. Nothing else. That is strange. If you take the grip away, something must be left. This idea is an extra axiom.

If x is a proper part of y, then y has another part z that does not overlap x:

PP(x, y) \rightarrow \exists z\, (P(z, y) \land \lnot O(z, x))

Ground mereology plus weak supplementation is called minimal mereology. A stronger version, strong supplementation, says: if y is not part of x, then some part of y does not overlap x. It gives a famous result.

With strong supplementation, two things that have proper parts, and have exactly the same proper parts, are the same thing.

Proof idea

Let x and y have the same proper parts, and assume y is not part of x. Strong supplementation gives a part z of y that does not overlap x. If z were a proper part of y, it would also be a proper part of x, so it would overlap x. So z must be y itself. Then y does not overlap x. But y has a proper part w, and w is also part of x, so x and y overlap. This is a contradiction. So y is part of x. In the same way, x is part of y. Antisymmetry gives x = y.

Check this with a bike. Frame A and frame B are made of exactly the same tubes. Extensionality says they are one frame. That sounds right. But a statue and the lump of clay it is made of also have the same parts. Are they one thing? The lump existed before the statue. It survives if you squash the statue. Many philosophers say they are two things. Then extensionality fails. This is why DOLCE uses a separate relation, constitution, for the statue and the clay.

Checking a part-whole model

The code checks three axioms on a bike model. We put two mistakes in it on purpose. In the code, x is a proper part of y when x is part of y but y is not part of x. With antisymmetry, this means the same as x \neq y.

# Direct "proper part of" facts for a bike. Two mistakes are on purpose.
direct = [("spoke1", "wheel1"), ("rim1", "wheel1"), ("wheel1", "bike"),
          ("wheel2", "bike"), ("frame", "bike"), ("handlebar", "bike"),
          ("grip", "handlebar"),                  # the handlebar's ONLY part
          ("seat", "post"), ("post", "seat")]     # a cycle
things = sorted({t for pair in direct for t in pair})

part = {(x, x) for x in things} | set(direct)     # axiom 1: reflexive
delta = set(direct)
while delta:                                      # axiom 3: transitive (semi-naive)
    delta = {(x, z) for (x, y) in delta for (y2, z) in part if y == y2} - part
    part |= delta
print("part-of facts after closure:", len(part))

def overlap(a, b):                                # some z is part of both
    return any((z, a) in part and (z, b) in part for z in things)

for x, y in sorted(part):
    if x < y and (y, x) in part:                  # axiom 2: antisymmetric
        print("antisymmetry broken:", x, "and", y)
for x, y in sorted(part):
    if (y, x) not in part:                        # x is a proper part of y
        if not any((z, y) in part and not overlap(z, x) for z in things):
            print("weak supplementation broken:", x, "in", y)
use std::collections::BTreeSet;

fn main() {
    // Direct "proper part of" facts for a bike. Two mistakes are on purpose.
    let direct = [("spoke1", "wheel1"), ("rim1", "wheel1"), ("wheel1", "bike"),
        ("wheel2", "bike"), ("frame", "bike"), ("handlebar", "bike"),
        ("grip", "handlebar"),                // the handlebar's ONLY part
        ("seat", "post"), ("post", "seat")];  // a cycle
    let things: BTreeSet<&str> = direct.iter().flat_map(|&(a, b)| [a, b]).collect();

    let mut part: BTreeSet<(&str, &str)> = things.iter().map(|&x| (x, x)).collect(); // reflexive
    part.extend(direct);
    let mut delta: BTreeSet<(&str, &str)> = direct.into_iter().collect();
    while !delta.is_empty() { // transitive (semi-naive)
        let new: BTreeSet<_> = delta.iter()
            .flat_map(|&(x, y)| part.iter().filter(move |p| p.0 == y).map(move |p| (x, p.1)))
            .filter(|f| !part.contains(f)).collect();
        part.extend(new.iter().copied());
        delta = new;
    }
    println!("part-of facts after closure: {}", part.len());

    let overlap = |a: &str, b: &str| things.iter().any(|&z| part.contains(&(z, a)) && part.contains(&(z, b)));
    for &(x, y) in &part {
        if x < y && part.contains(&(y, x)) { // antisymmetric
            println!("antisymmetry broken: {x} and {y}");
        }
    }
    for &(x, y) in &part {
        let proper = !part.contains(&(y, x)); // x is a proper part of y
        if proper && !things.iter().any(|&z| part.contains(&(z, y)) && !overlap(z, x)) {
            println!("weak supplementation broken: {x} in {y}");
        }
    }
}

We ran it with Python 3.14 and Rust 1.99. Both print the same lines.

part-of facts after closure: 22
antisymmetry broken: post and seat
weak supplementation broken: grip in handlebar

The closure uses the semi-naive loop from Rules and Datalog. To fix the model, decide which of seat and post is the whole. Then give the handlebar its real second part, the bar itself.

Not every "part of" is the same relation. A spoke is a component of a wheel. Lea is a member of an orchestra. A statue is made of clay. Winston, Chaffin and Herrmann showed in 1987 that chains which mix such relations often sound wrong. Is Lea's arm part of the orchestra? Say which kind of part you mean. BFO has continuant part of, its narrower relation member part of, and occurrent part of.

In BFO 2020, continuant part of means "part at some time". In the OWL file bfo-core.owl, it is not declared transitive. Occurrent part of is declared transitive. Why? "The tyre was part of wheel A at some time" and "wheel A was part of bike B at some time" can be about different times. Then the chain does not hold. BFO's temporal extensions handle time more exactly.

Identity, rigidity and dependence: OntoClean

Look at this small taxonomy. Something is wrong with it, but what?

Apple    subClassOf Food
Student  subClassOf Person
Company  subClassOf Customer

An apple on a tree is not food for anyone yet. A company can stop being a customer and still exist. But a student is always a person. Nicola Guarino and Christopher Welty built a method from questions like these. They published the ideas in 2000. The name OntoClean first appeared in their 2002 paper.

OntoClean gives each class labels called meta-properties.

The four OntoClean meta-properties
Meta-propertyQuestionLabels and examples
RigidityMust every member be in this class for its whole life?+R rigid: Person. ~R anti-rigid: Student. −R: neither.
IdentityDoes the class say how to tell two members apart, and the same member over time?+I: Person, Apple. −I: Red thing.
UnityIs each member one whole, held together in the same way?+U: Person. ~U: Amount of water (any portion is also water). −U: neither.
DependenceDoes each member need some other thing to be in the class?+D: Student needs a school. −D: Person.

The labels matter because some of them pass down the subclass tree.

If class Q is a superclass of class S, then:

  1. If Q is anti-rigid (~R), S must be anti-rigid.
  2. If Q carries an identity criterion (+I), S must carry it too.
  3. If Q carries a unity criterion (+U), S must carry it too.
  4. If Q has anti-unity (~U), S must have anti-unity.
  5. If Q is dependent (+D), S must be dependent.

So "Apple subClassOf Food" breaks rule 1. Food is anti-rigid and Apple is rigid. The code below checks all five rules.

# Meta-properties: rigidity R, identity I, unity U, dependence D.
labels = {
    "PhysicalObject": "+R +I +U -D",
    "AmountOfMatter": "+R +I ~U -D",
    "Person":         "+R +I +U -D",
    "Student":        "~R +I +U +D",
    "Apple":          "+R +I +U -D",
    "Food":           "~R -I -U -D",
    "Company":        "+R +I +U -D",
    "Customer":       "~R +I +U +D",
}
subclass_of = [("Student", "Person"), ("Person", "PhysicalObject"),
               ("PhysicalObject", "AmountOfMatter"),
               ("Apple", "Food"), ("Company", "Customer")]

# If the parent has this label, the child must have it too.
inherited = {"~R": "rigidity", "+I": "identity", "+U": "unity",
             "~U": "anti-unity", "+D": "dependence"}

for child, parent in subclass_of:
    problems = [name for mark, name in inherited.items()
                if mark in labels[parent].split() and mark not in labels[child].split()]
    print(f"{child} -> {parent}:", ", ".join(problems) or "ok")
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    // Meta-properties: rigidity R, identity I, unity U, dependence D.
    let labels: HashMap<&str, &str> = HashMap::from([
        ("PhysicalObject", "+R +I +U -D"),
        ("AmountOfMatter", "+R +I ~U -D"),
        ("Person", "+R +I +U -D"),
        ("Student", "~R +I +U +D"),
        ("Apple", "+R +I +U -D"),
        ("Food", "~R -I -U -D"),
        ("Company", "+R +I +U -D"),
        ("Customer", "~R +I +U +D"),
    ]);
    let subclass_of = [("Student", "Person"), ("Person", "PhysicalObject"),
        ("PhysicalObject", "AmountOfMatter"), ("Apple", "Food"), ("Company", "Customer")];

    // If the parent has this label, the child must have it too.
    let inherited = [("~R", "rigidity"), ("+I", "identity"), ("+U", "unity"),
        ("~U", "anti-unity"), ("+D", "dependence")];

    for (child, parent) in subclass_of {
        let has = |class: &str, mark: &str| labels[class].split(' ').any(|m| m == mark);
        let problems: Vec<&str> = inherited.iter()
            .filter(|(mark, _)| has(parent, mark) && !has(child, mark))
            .map(|(_, name)| *name).collect();
        let text = if problems.is_empty() { "ok".to_string() } else { problems.join(", ") };
        println!("{child} -> {parent}: {text}");
    }
}
Student -> Person: ok
Person -> PhysicalObject: ok
PhysicalObject -> AmountOfMatter: anti-unity
Apple -> Food: rigidity
Company -> Customer: rigidity, dependence

How do you fix each link?

  • Apple and Food. Put Apple under Fruit, a rigid class. Make "food" a role that an apple can play.
  • Company and Customer. Customer is a role. Both companies and people can play it. Do not put Company under it.
  • Physical object and amount of matter. A bike is not a lump of metal. The bike is constituted by the metal. Use constitution, not subclass.

The checker is only as good as the labels. People often disagree about labels, and OntoClean needs careful thinking. The rules find conflicts between labels. They do not tell you which label is wrong.

A quick test for rigidity: "Can a member stop being a member and still exist?" If yes, the class is probably a role or a phase, not a kind. Student, Customer, Child and Employee all fail the test.

Things that last and things that happen

Lea is a person. Lea's morning run is an event. Both are real. But they exist in time in different ways.

At 7:00 and at 7:30, all of Lea is there. She can lose hair or gain weight, but she is the same person. Her run is different. At 7:00 only the first minutes of the run have happened. At 7:30 only the end is happening. The run is never all there at one moment.

A continuant lasts through time and is wholly present whenever it exists. Examples: a person, a bike, the colour of the bike. An occurrent happens. It has parts in time. Examples: a run, a repair, a meeting, the year 2026. DOLCE uses the words endurant and perdurant for the same split.

The two kinds connect through participation. Lea participates in the run. The bike participates in the repair. In BFO, the run has participant Lea.

Dependence

Some continuants cannot exist alone. The red colour of a bike needs that bike. If the bike is destroyed, its red goes with it. BFO calls this a specifically dependent continuant. Qualities, roles, dispositions and functions are all of this kind.

A recipe is different. You can copy it onto a second card, and the same recipe is on both. If one card burns, the recipe still exists. BFO calls this a generically dependent continuant. Information is the main example.

Do not model an event as an object with dates. "Meeting" with fields "start" and "end" is fine in a database. In an upper ontology, a meeting is an occurrent. The people and the room are continuants that participate in it. Mixing the two leads to errors like "the repair is part of the bike".

Some ontologies take a four-dimensional view. In it, a bike is also spread out in time, like a long worm, with a temporal part for each moment. BORO and parts of ISO 15926 work this way. BFO, DOLCE and UFO keep the continuant and occurrent split.

BFO and ISO/IEC 21838

The Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) was developed by Barry Smith and colleagues from the early 2000s. It aims to describe reality as science sees it. Its version BFO 2020 is the content of the international standard ISO/IEC 21838-2:2021.

BFO is small on purpose. We counted the current OWL file, bfo-core.owl, on GitHub: 36 classes and 40 object properties. Here are its main classes.

Three of these classes need care. A realizable entity exists even when it is not active. Its process realizes it.

  • A role comes from a situation. Lea's role as a mechanic exists because of her job, not her body.
  • A disposition comes from the physical make-up of its bearer. Glass is fragile even when nothing breaks it.
  • A function is a disposition that the thing exists for. The heart's function is to pump blood. A brake's function is to stop the wheel.

The ISO/IEC 21838 family

ISO/IEC 21838 is the standard for top-level ontologies. Part 1 says what a top-level ontology must provide. The other parts each hold one ontology. We checked the ISO pages on 15 November 2026.

ISO/IEC 21838 parts (checked 2026-11-15)
PartContentStatus
21838-1:2021RequirementsPublished August 2021. Under systematic review since July 2026, which ISO does every five years.
21838-2:2021BFOPublished November 2021
21838-3:2023DOLCEPublished September 2023
21838-4:2023TUpperPublished September 2023
21838-5UFONot yet published. Final draft ballot started on 13 November 2026. ISO lists the edition for 2027.

Part 1 asks for a lot. A conforming ontology needs a document in plain language, with definitions that are not circular. It needs axioms in OWL 2. Where relevant, it also needs axioms in Common Logic (ISO/IEC 24707). It must cover many areas: space and time, parts, qualities, processes and information.

BFO is the top level for the OBO Foundry ontologies in biology and medicine. It is also the top of the Industrial Ontologies Foundry and the Common Core Ontologies (CCO). CCO released version 2.2 in August 2026. In January 2024, the chief data officers of the US Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community named BFO and CCO as baseline standards for their ontology work.
