The University at Buffalo, where BFO was developed, announced this in February 2024.

Know the two top classes of BFO and their split. Continuant and occurrent are disjoint. Under continuant, know the three branches: independent, specifically dependent and generically dependent. Most placement questions are about these.

DOLCE, SUMO and UFO

BFO is not the only choice. Each upper ontology starts from a different idea of what it should describe.

DOLCE: the world as people talk about it

DOLCE means Descriptive Ontology for Linguistic and Cognitive Engineering. It was built at the Laboratory for Applied Ontology in Italy, in the WonderWeb project. Its first full description is from 2003, by Masolo and colleagues. It is ISO/IEC 21838-3:2023.

The word "descriptive" is the key. DOLCE does not try to describe reality as physics sees it. It describes the categories found in language and common sense. Its four basic categories are endurant, perdurant, quality and abstract.

  • Qualities have positions in a space. The red of a rose and the red of a book cover are two different qualities. If they look the same, they have the same quale in the colour space.
  • Constitution is not identity. A statue and its clay are two things in the same place.
  • Rich logic, light versions. The full theory uses first-order modal logic. For daily use there are OWL versions, such as DOLCE-Lite and DOLCE+DnS UltraLite (DUL).

SUMO: a big upper ontology for reasoning

The Suggested Upper Merged Ontology (SUMO) began at Teknowledge, with a first release in December 2000. Ian Niles and Adam Pease described it in 2001. It was offered to the IEEE Standard Upper Ontology working group as a starting point. It is written in SUO-KIF, a logic language with Lisp-like brackets. SUMO is mapped to the WordNet dictionary. Today Articulate Software maintains it on GitHub, where it was still updated in November 2026.

(partition Entity Physical Abstract)      ; Merge.kif
(subclass Process Physical)               ; Merge.kif
(subclass Cycle LandVehicle)              ; Transportation.kif
(subclass Bicycle Cycle)                  ; Transportation.kif

; our example rule: every bicycle has some wheel as a part
(=> (instance ?B Bicycle)
    (exists (?W) (and (instance ?W Wheel) (part ?W ?B))))

SUMO is much larger than BFO. Beside its upper part, it has many domain files, for example for law, economy and anatomy. It is made to work with automated theorem provers.

UFO and OntoUML: ontology for conceptual models

The Unified Foundational Ontology (UFO) comes from Giancarlo Guizzardi's 2005 PhD thesis. It has three parts. UFO-A covers endurants, UFO-B covers events, and UFO-C covers social things like agents and commitments. UFO puts OntoClean's ideas at the centre.

OntoUML is UML with UFO's categories as stereotypes. A modeller marks each class as a kind, a role, a phase, a relator and so on. Tools then check the model. gUFO is a light OWL 2 DL version of UFO.

@prefix gufo: <http://purl.org/nemo/gufo#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/school#> .

ex:Person a owl:Class, gufo:Kind ;        # rigid: a person is always a person
    rdfs:subClassOf gufo:FunctionalComplex .
ex:Child a owl:Class, gufo:Phase ;        # anti-rigid: changes by itself (age)
    rdfs:subClassOf ex:Person .
ex:Student a owl:Class, gufo:Role ;       # anti-rigid: needs a relation
    rdfs:subClassOf ex:Person .
ex:University a owl:Class, gufo:Kind ;
    rdfs:subClassOf gufo:FunctionalComplex .
ex:Enrollment a owl:Class ;               # the relation as a thing of its own
    rdfs:subClassOf gufo:Relator .
ex:enrolls a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:subPropertyOf gufo:mediates ;
    rdfs:domain ex:Enrollment ; rdfs:range ex:Student .
ex:atUniversity a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:subPropertyOf gufo:mediates ;
    rdfs:domain ex:Enrollment ; rdfs:range ex:University .

We parsed this file with rdflib 7.6.0: 22 triples. The pattern follows gUFO's own examples. A relator, like an enrolment, is a thing in its own right. It has a start date and its own rules. A phase changes because of the thing itself, like age. A role changes because of a relation, like an enrolment.

Other upper ontologies exist too. TUpper (ISO/IEC 21838-4) is built from modules of existing standards. GFO comes from Leipzig. gist is a light upper ontology for business data. In 2022, the journal Applied Ontology compared seven of them on the same modelling cases: BFO, DOLCE, GFO, GUM, TUpper, UFO and YAMATO.

Choosing one, or none

An upper ontology helps most when many teams must share data for a long time. It helps least in a small app with one team. Use this table as a first guide.

A first guide to choosing
Your situationGood fitWhy
Biology, medicine, science dataBFOOBO Foundry ontologies already use it.
Defence, intelligence, industryBFO with CCOBFO and CCO are the baseline in the US DoD and IC. BFO is also the top of the Industrial Ontologies Foundry.
Language, texts, cultural heritageDOLCE or DULBuilt from language and common sense.
UML models, information systemsUFO with OntoUML or gUFOMade for conceptual modelling.
Logic, theorem proving, WordNet linksSUMOLarge, rich axioms in SUO-KIF.
One team, one app, short lifeNone, or a light one like gistThe cost is higher than the gain.

Costs

  • Time to learn the categories.
  • Strict modelling. "Customer" must become a role.
  • Mapping between two upper ontologies is hard.

Gains

  • Joining data with other teams is easier.
  • Clear answers to "kind or role?" and "thing or event?"
  • Reasoners can find category errors, as you will see next.

Even with no upper ontology, use its questions as a checklist. For each class, ask: does it last or happen? Is it a kind, a role or a phase? Does it depend on something? This takes ten minutes and prevents most category errors.

Do not import two upper ontologies "to be safe". Their top classes often conflict. Pick one, and map to others only at the edges, with care.

Mapping a small domain to BFO

Let us map a bike repair shop. First decide, for each term, where it goes. The carousel shows the questions in order.

Does it happen?

Does it unfold in time, with a beginning and an end? Then it is an occurrent, usually a process. Example: a repair.

Can it be copied?

Can the same thing exist on two carriers, like a text on two screens? Then it is a generically dependent continuant. Example: the content of a repair order.

Does it need one bearer?

Does it exist only in one particular thing? Then it is specifically dependent. Example: the red of bike 42.

Quality or realizable?

Is it always fully there, like a colour? Then it is a quality. Does it show itself only in some process? Then it is a role, disposition or function.

Material or not?

Is it made of matter? Then it is a material entity, often an object. Is it a place or a boundary? Then it is an immaterial entity, such as a site.

The bike shop terms in BFO
TermBFO classReason
BicycleobjectMade of matter, one whole thing.
PersonobjectMade of matter, one whole thing.
Mechanicrole (of a person)Lea stays Lea when she changes job.
Frame colourqualityAlways fully present in one bike.
Fragility of a carbon framedispositionShows itself only when the frame breaks.
Brakeobject, with a functionIts function is to stop the wheel.
RepairprocessIt happens and has parts in time.
Repair order contentgenerically dependent continuantThe same content can be on paper and on screen.
Workshop baysiteA space that things are in.
Bikes for saleobject aggregateA group of objects.

Now write it in Turtle with the real BFO IRIs. We copy a small slice of BFO 2020 into the file, with labels as in bfo-core.owl. The last line has a typical mistake.

@prefix obo:  <http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/shop#> .

# A small slice of BFO 2020 (IRIs and labels as in bfo-core.owl)
obo:BFO_0000002 rdfs:label "continuant" .
obo:BFO_0000003 rdfs:label "occurrent" ; owl:disjointWith obo:BFO_0000002 .
obo:BFO_0000004 rdfs:label "independent continuant" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000002 .
obo:BFO_0000040 rdfs:label "material entity" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000004 .
obo:BFO_0000030 rdfs:label "object" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000040 .
obo:BFO_0000020 rdfs:label "specifically dependent continuant" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000002 .
obo:BFO_0000019 rdfs:label "quality" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000020 .
obo:BFO_0000017 rdfs:label "realizable entity" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000020 .
obo:BFO_0000023 rdfs:label "role" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000017 .
obo:BFO_0000015 rdfs:label "process" ; rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000003 .
obo:BFO_0000176 rdfs:label "continuant part of" ; rdfs:domain obo:BFO_0000002 .

# The bike shop, mapped to BFO
ex:Bicycle      rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000030 .  # object
ex:Person       rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000030 .  # object
ex:FrameColour  rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000019 .  # quality
ex:MechanicRole rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000023 .  # role
ex:Repair       rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000015 .  # process

ex:bike42 a ex:Bicycle ; obo:BFO_0000196 ex:red42 .          # bearer of
ex:red42  a ex:FrameColour .
ex:lea    a ex:Person ; obo:BFO_0000196 ex:leaAsMechanic .
ex:leaAsMechanic a ex:MechanicRole .
ex:repair17 a ex:Repair ; obo:BFO_0000057 ex:bike42, ex:lea .  # has participant
ex:repair17 obo:BFO_0000176 ex:bike42 .  # a MISTAKE: "the repair is part of the bike"

The Python script runs the OWL 2 RL rules from Rules and Datalog. Then it prints the BFO classes of each individual, and any error.

import sys
from rdflib import RDF, RDFS, Graph, Namespace, URIRef
import owlrl

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/shop#")
ERROR = URIRef("http://www.daml.org/2002/03/agents/agent-ont#error")  # where owlrl writes errors

g = Graph().parse(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "bike_shop.ttl")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)   # OWL 2 RL rules

for thing in ("bike42", "red42", "lea", "leaAsMechanic", "repair17"):
    labels = sorted(str(g.value(c, RDFS.label))            # BFO labels only
                    for c in g.objects(EX[thing], RDF.type) if (c, RDFS.label, None) in g)
    print(f"{thing:<14}", ", ".join(labels))
for msg in g.objects(None, ERROR):
    print("ERROR:", msg.replace("http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/", "obo:").replace(str(EX), "ex:"))

We ran it with owlrl 7.6.2 on Python 3.14.

bike42         continuant, independent continuant, material entity, object
red42          continuant, quality, specifically dependent continuant
lea            continuant, independent continuant, material entity, object
leaAsMechanic  continuant, realizable entity, role, specifically dependent continuant
repair17       continuant, occurrent, process
ERROR: Disjoint classes obo:BFO_0000003 and obo:BFO_0000002 have a common individual ex:repair17

The domain of continuant part of is continuant. So the mistake made repair17 a continuant. But it is also a process, so an occurrent. The two classes are disjoint, and the reasoner reports it. We deleted the mistake line and ran the script again. The error was gone, and repair17 was only "occurrent, process". The right link is already there: the repair has participant the bike.

Domain and range in OWL are not checks. They add types. Here the domain did not reject the bad triple. It added "continuant", and only the disjointness made the error visible. See OWL 2 for more on this, and SHACL and validation for real data checks.

Patterns to remember

Patterns from formal and upper ontologies
PatternPurposeModelNote
Domain class under an upper classShare top categoriesex:Bicycle rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000030Use the real IRI, not your own copy of the label.
Kind plus roleModel "is a" that can changePerson (kind); Student (role)Anti-rigid classes never go above rigid ones.
Kind plus phaseModel change from withinPerson; Child, Adult (phases)Phases split a kind by its own qualities, like age.
RelatorMake a relation a thingEnrollment mediates Student and UniversityUse it when the relation has its own dates or rules.
Process has participantLink events and thingsrepair17 has participant bike42Never "the repair is part of the bike".
Bearer of a qualityAttach a colour or weightbike42 bearer of red42The quality is a thing that depends on its bearer.
Role realized in a processShow when a role is activerepair17 realizes leaAsMechanicA role exists even when not realized.
Information as GDCModel documents and dataRepair order content: generically dependentThe paper is an object. The content is not.
Part-of with axiomsKeep part trees saneReflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, supplementationCheck for cycles and single-part wholes.
Constitution, not identityStatue and clay, bike and metalThe statue is constituted by the clay.Do not make Statue a subclass of AmountOfMatter.
OntoClean labelsAudit a taxonomyFood ~R above Apple +R: errorThe rules find conflicts. You decide the fix.
Disjoint top classesCatch category errorscontinuant disjointWith occurrentWithout disjointness, the reasoner stays silent.

Practice

Which one is an occurrent?

  • A bridge
  • The building of a bridge
  • The weight of a bridge

Building happens in time and has temporal parts. The bridge and its weight are continuants.

Which subclass link breaks the OntoClean rigidity rule?

  • Student subClassOf Person
  • Person subClassOf Customer
  • Dog subClassOf Animal

Customer is anti-rigid. An anti-rigid class cannot be above a rigid class like Person.

In BFO, what is the content of a PDF report?

  • An object
  • A quality
  • A generically dependent continuant

The same content can be copied to many files and screens. So it is generically dependent.

Which part of ISO/IEC 21838 is not yet published on 15 November 2026?

  • Part 2, BFO
  • Part 3, DOLCE
  • Part 5, UFO

Part 5 is at the final draft ballot stage, which started on 13 November 2026.

A model says a lamp has exactly one proper part, its bulb. Which axiom does it break?

  • Reflexivity
  • Transitivity
  • Weak supplementation

If the bulb is a proper part, the lamp needs another part that does not overlap the bulb.

Fill in the missing words.

DOLCE's words for continuant and occurrent are endurant and ?.

The current OWL file of BFO 2020 has ? classes.

SUMO is written in the logic language ?.

In OntoClean, a class whose members can stop being members is called anti-?.

  1. Place these in BFO: a hammer, the hardness of the hammer, a hammering, a manual for the hammer, the ability of the hammer to drive nails.
    Answer

    Hammer: object. Hardness: quality. Hammering: process. The manual's content: generically dependent continuant (the printed copy is an object). The ability to drive nails: function, because the hammer was made for it.

  2. Give each class OntoClean labels for rigidity and dependence: Employee, Organization, Child.
    Answer

    Employee: ~R (you can stop being an employee) and +D (needs an employer). Organization: +R and −D. Child: ~R, because a child grows up. Child is a phase, so it does not depend on another thing: −D.

  3. A team writes ex:Meeting rdfs:subClassOf obo:BFO_0000030 (object). What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
    Answer

    A meeting happens in time, so it is an occurrent. As an object, it becomes a continuant, and any link that says it has temporal parts or participants will clash. Put Meeting under process (BFO_0000015). The people and the room participate in it.

  4. Show with the axioms that the bike model in the mereology code needs no direct fact "spoke1 part of bike".
    Answer

    We have P(spoke1, wheel1) and P(wheel1, bike). Transitivity gives P(spoke1, bike). The code's closure loop derived it, together with rim1 and grip in bike. That is why 22 facts appear from 9 direct ones and 10 reflexive ones.

  5. Your company builds a small internal app for one team. A colleague wants to import BFO, DOLCE and SUMO. What do you advise?
    Answer

    Import none, or at most one. Three upper ontologies have conflicting top classes and cost much time. For one team and one app, use the upper ontology questions as a checklist: last or happen, kind or role, depends on what. Add BFO or another later if you must share data with other groups.

  6. Why does DOLCE treat a statue and its clay as two things? Use the words constitution and extensionality.
    Answer

    The statue and the clay share all their parts. Extensionality would make them one thing. But they have different histories: the clay existed first and survives if the statue is squashed. So DOLCE keeps them apart. The clay constitutes the statue. Constitution is a relation between two things, not identity.

Key takeaways

  • An upper ontology gives shared, very general categories. Domain ontologies fit under it.
  • Mereology makes part-of exact: a partial order plus supplementation. Strong supplementation gives extensionality.
  • OntoClean labels classes for rigidity, identity, unity and dependence. Five rules find bad subclass links.
  • Continuants last and are wholly present. Occurrents happen and have temporal parts. They meet through participation.
  • BFO 2020 is small, realist and ISO/IEC 21838-2. DOLCE is descriptive and ISO/IEC 21838-3. TUpper is Part 4.
  • UFO is the Part 5 draft, at the final ballot stage in November 2026. SUMO is large and written in SUO-KIF.
  • Choose by community and use. For a small app, choosing none is fine.
  • Map a domain to BFO with real IRIs and disjointness. A reasoner then finds category errors for you.

Sources

  • BFO-2020 repository. The BFO 2020 files for ISO/IEC 21838-2, including bfo-core.owl.
  • ISO/IEC PRF 21838-5 (UFO). ISO page with the life cycle of Part 5. The pages for Parts 1 to 4 have the same form.
  • Mereology. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: axioms, supplementation and extensionality.
  • OntoClean. Overview of the meta-properties and their constraints, with references to Guarino and Welty.
  • DOLCE: A Descriptive Ontology for Linguistic and Cognitive Engineering. Borgo and colleagues, Applied Ontology 2022.
  • gUFO: A Lightweight Implementation of UFO. The OWL version of UFO and its classes.

Data models compared

The same facts can live in tables, in documents, in RDF graphs or in property graphs. Each shape makes some questions easy and others hard. This chapter puts one small story into all four shapes. Then it compares diagrams, schemas, code types and ontologies, so you can choose the right tool.

  • Store one example as tables, documents, RDF triples and a property graph.
  • Read an ER diagram and a UML class diagram, and turn them into an ontology.
  • Explain how a schema and an ontology differ, with one example.
  • Name five key differences between object-oriented classes and ontology classes.
  • Read Rust and Python types as small ontologies, and pick a model for a new project.

One small story, four shapes

Here is the story. We use it in the whole chapter.

  • Ana is an employee. Ben is a contractor.
  • Ana works on project Atlas as the lead, since 2024.
  • Ana also works on project Borealis as a reviewer, since 2025.
  • Ben works on Atlas as a developer, since 2025.

A data model is a set of shapes for data, plus the ways to read and change it. Below is the same story in four data models. Click the tabs.

CREATE TABLE person  (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE project (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE works_on (                       -- the link is a table too
  person  TEXT REFERENCES person(id),
  project TEXT REFERENCES project(id),
  role    TEXT NOT NULL,
  since   INTEGER,
  PRIMARY KEY (person, project));
INSERT INTO person  VALUES ('p1','Ana'), ('p2','Ben');
INSERT INTO project VALUES ('atlas','Atlas'), ('borealis','Borealis');
INSERT INTO works_on VALUES ('p1','atlas','lead',2024),
  ('p1','borealis','reviewer',2025), ('p2','atlas','developer',2025);
[
 {"_id": "atlas", "title": "Atlas",
  "members": [{"name": "Ana", "role": "lead", "since": 2024},
              {"name": "Ben", "role": "developer", "since": 2025}]},
 {"_id": "borealis", "title": "Borealis",
  "members": [{"name": "Ana", "role": "reviewer", "since": 2025}]}
]
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/team#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

ex:Employee rdfs:subClassOf ex:Person .     # schema and data live together
ex:ana  a ex:Employee ; ex:name "Ana" .
ex:ben  a ex:Contractor ; ex:name "Ben" .
ex:atlas    a ex:Project ; ex:title "Atlas" .
ex:borealis a ex:Project ; ex:title "Borealis" .

# a link with extra fields becomes a node of its own
ex:a1 a ex:Assignment ; ex:who ex:ana ; ex:onProject ex:atlas ;
      ex:role "lead" ; ex:since 2024 .
ex:a2 a ex:Assignment ; ex:who ex:ana ; ex:onProject ex:borealis ;
      ex:role "reviewer" ; ex:since 2025 .
ex:a3 a ex:Assignment ; ex:who ex:ben ; ex:onProject ex:atlas ;
      ex:role "developer" ; ex:since 2025 .
CREATE (ana:Person {id:'p1', name:'Ana'}),
       (ben:Person {id:'p2', name:'Ben'}),
       (atlas:Project {id:'atlas', title:'Atlas'}),
       (bor:Project {id:'borealis', title:'Borealis'}),
       (ana)-[:WORKS_ON {role:'lead', since:2024}]->(atlas),
       (ana)-[:WORKS_ON {role:'reviewer', since:2025}]->(bor),
       (ben)-[:WORKS_ON {role:'developer', since:2025}]->(atlas)

Now the words. Each model has its own small vocabulary.

  • Relational. Data lives in tables. A primary key names each row. A foreign key points to a row in another table. Edgar Codd described this model in 1970.
  • Document. Data lives in documents. A document is a tree. It can hold lists and smaller objects inside.
  • RDF. Data is a set of triples. Every thing has a global name, an IRI. You met it in RDF and RDF Schema.
  • Property graph. Data is nodes and relationships. Both can carry key-value properties.
Where does "Ana is the lead on Atlas, since 2024" live?
ModelThe linkThe role and the year
Relationalone row in works_ontwo columns of that row
DocumentAna is copied inside the Atlas documenttwo fields of the copy
RDFa new node ex:a1 with two linkstwo more triples on ex:a1
Property graphone relationship WORKS_ONtwo properties on the relationship

All four models can hold this story. No model is "stronger". They differ in what is short to write and fast to ask.

"A graph database can store things a table cannot." This is false. Every graph fits in a table of edges. The real question is how easy and fast your questions become.

Asking the same two questions

Let us ask each model two questions.

  1. Q1. Who works on Atlas, and in what role?
  2. Q2. Which other projects share a person with Atlas? This is a two-hop question.
q = """SELECT p.name, w.role FROM works_on w
       JOIN person p ON p.id = w.person
       WHERE w.project = 'atlas' ORDER BY p.name"""
print(db.execute(q).fetchall())
# two hops: other projects that share a person with Atlas
q2 = """SELECT DISTINCT w2.project FROM works_on w1
        JOIN works_on w2 ON w2.person = w1.person
        WHERE w1.project = 'atlas' AND w2.project <> 'atlas'"""
print(db.execute(q2).fetchall())
[('Ana', 'lead'), ('Ben', 'developer')]
[('borealis',)]
atlas = next(p for p in projects if p["_id"] == "atlas")
print([(m["name"], m["role"]) for m in atlas["members"]])   # one read

# the reverse question needs a scan of every document
print([p["_id"] for p in projects
       if any(m["name"] == "Ana" for m in p["members"])])
[('Ana', 'lead'), ('Ben', 'developer')]
['atlas', 'borealis']
SELECT ?name ?role WHERE {
  ?a ex:onProject ex:atlas ; ex:who ?p ; ex:role ?role .
  ?p ex:name ?name .
} ORDER BY ?name

SELECT DISTINCT ?other WHERE {      # two hops, through the person
  ?a1 ex:onProject ex:atlas ; ex:who ?p .
  ?a2 ex:who ?p ; ex:onProject ?other .
  FILTER (?other != ex:atlas)
}
Ana lead
Ben developer
['borealis']
MATCH (p:Person)-[w:WORKS_ON]->(:Project {id:'atlas'})
RETURN p.name, w.role ORDER BY p.name;

MATCH (:Project {id:'atlas'})<-[:WORKS_ON]-(:Person)-[:WORKS_ON]->(o:Project)
WHERE o.id <> 'atlas'
RETURN DISTINCT o.id;
['Ana', 'lead']
['Ben', 'developer']
['borealis']

Look at the second question in each tab.

  • SQL uses a join. It matches equal values in two copies of works_on.
  • The document model answers Q1 with one read. But Q2 has no short form. We must scan all documents, or add an index.
  • SPARQL and Cypher draw the path. The query looks like the picture.

So the rule is simple. Tables join by equal values. Documents are fast inside one tree. Graphs follow links, and long paths stay short to write.

In the document model, Ana's name is copied into two documents. If Ana changes her name, you must update both. Copies make reads fast, but every copy must be kept in step. MongoDB's guide says to store together the data you read together. For large or shared data, store a reference instead.

How we tested these queries

The SQL ran in SQLite 3.50 from Python 3.14. The SPARQL ran in rdflib 7.6.0. The Cypher ran in Kuzu 0.11.3 on Python 3.13, because Kuzu has no package for 3.14. Kuzu needs CREATE NODE TABLE and CREATE REL TABLE lines first. Neo4j does not. The Kuzu project was archived in October 2025, as the chapter Your first ontology explains.

The link with extra fields

Our working links carry a role and a year. This small detail separates the models most.

This is the n-ary relation pattern. It costs more triples. But the new node can now take part in any fact. For example, you can say who approved assignment a1.

Four ways to put fields on a link
ModelHowCost
Relationala link table with extra columnsone row per link
Property graphproperties on the relationshipnone extra, but a relationship cannot point to another relationship
RDF 1.1an n-ary node, or old-style reificationabout 4 or 5 triples per link
RDF 1.2a triple term with a reifiersee RDF and RDF Schema

Neo4j's guide says each relationship has a start node, an end node, a direction and exactly one type. A node can have zero or more labels. So a property graph mixes two ideas. Labels work like classes. Relationship types work like properties.

Do not put a list of project ids inside the person node, like projects: ['atlas','borealis']. Then the graph has no edges to follow. Model each link as a relationship.

Diagrams: ER, UML and ontologies

Before code, teams draw. Two diagram styles are common. Here is our story in both.

  • An ER diagram plans a database. Peter Chen published the model in 1976. Entities become tables. M and N say "many on each side".
  • A UML class diagram plans object-oriented code. The OMG standard is at version 2.5.1, from December 2017. The marks 0..* are multiplicities.
  • An ontology is a graph of classes and properties with logical meaning. A program can reason with it.
The same idea in three languages
IdeaERUMLOWL ontology
A kind of thingentityclassowl:Class
A field with a valueattributeattributedata property
A linkrelationshipassociationobject property
How many1, N, M0..1, 1..*cardinality restriction
A link with fieldsrelationship attributeassociation classn-ary class or reifier
Kind ofISA (extended ER)generalization arrowrdfs:subClassOf
Unique keyunderlined attribute{id}owl:hasKey

Each entity table becomes a class

person becomes ex:Person. Each row becomes an individual with an IRI, like ex:p1.

Each plain column becomes a data property

person.name becomes ex:name, with range xsd:string.

Each foreign key becomes an object property

A column that points to another table becomes a link between two individuals.

A link table becomes a property or a class

No extra columns: one object property. Extra columns like role: an n-ary class, like ex:Assignment.

Add what the tables never said

Subclasses, inverse properties, labels in several languages, links to public vocabularies. This step is where the ontology adds meaning.

Steps 1 to 4 can be automatic. W3C made two standards for this in September 2012. The Direct Mapping turns any database into RDF with no setup. R2RML lets you write your own map. Step 5 needs a human who knows the domain.

Diagram marks look alike but mean different things. A UML multiplicity is a rule your code must keep. An OWL cardinality restriction is a statement a reasoner uses to draw conclusions. It does not stop bad data. Read the next section.

Schema and ontology

Try to store a wrong role in both worlds. First, SQL with a check rule.

import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE works_on (person TEXT, project TEXT,
              role TEXT CHECK (role IN ('lead','developer','reviewer')))""")
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO works_on VALUES ('p1', 'atlas', 'boss')")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("SQL said no:", e)
SQL said no: CHECK constraint failed: role IN ('lead','developer','reviewer')

The database refused the row. Now ask the RDF graph a question. The file only says Ana is an ex:Employee. It never says she is a person.

people = P + "SELECT ?p WHERE { ?p a ex:Person }"
print("persons before:", len(g.query(people)))
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.RDFS_Semantics).expand(g)   # add RDFS consequences
print("persons after: ", [str(r.p).split("#")[1] for r in g.query(people)])
persons before: 0
persons after:  ['ana']

The ontology did not refuse anything. It added a fact: Ana is a person. That is the key difference.

  • A schema protects the data you store. It says no to bad rows. It reads data under the closed world.
  • An ontology says what the data means. It lets a reasoner find new facts. It reads data under the open world.
Schema and ontology on the same questions
QuestionSchema (SQL, JSON Schema)Ontology (RDFS, OWL)
Main jobkeep stored data cleanshare meaning, draw conclusions
Missing valueNULL, or an errorunknown
Value of the wrong kindrejecteda new type is inferred, or the ontology becomes inconsistent
Who uses itone application or one databasemany systems, across teams and companies
Nameslocal: works_on.roleglobal IRIs: ex:role

Real systems need both. Use the ontology for meaning. Use a shape language for checks. In RDF that language is SHACL, in SHACL and validation.

Using rdfs:domain as a check. In SQL, a column belongs to one table. In RDF, ex:mentors rdfs:domain ex:Mentor means "whoever mentors is a Mentor". A contractor who mentors becomes a Mentor. Nobody is rejected.

Object-oriented classes and ontology classes

Both worlds say "class". The word means different things. Run this.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF
import owlrl

class Person:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
class Employee(Person): pass
class Mentor(Person): pass

ana = Employee("Ana")
print("Python: Ana is a Mentor?", isinstance(ana, Mentor))   # one class, fixed

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/team#")
g = Graph()
g.add((EX.ana, RDF.type, EX.Employee))
g.add((EX.ana, RDF.type, EX.Mentor))         # just one more triple
print("RDF: types of ana:", sorted(t.split("#")[1] for t in g.objects(EX.ana, RDF.type)))

# a domain is a rule for new facts, not a check
g.parse(data="""@prefix ex: <http://example.org/team#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
ex:mentors rdfs:domain ex:Mentor .
ex:ben a ex:Contractor ; ex:mentors ex:ana .""")
owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.RDFS_Semantics).expand(g)
print("RDF: types of ben:", sorted(t.split("#")[1] for t in g.objects(EX.ben, RDF.type)
                                  if "team#" in t))
Python: Ana is a Mentor? False
RDF: types of ana: ['Employee', 'Mentor']
RDF: types of ben: ['Contractor', 'Mentor']

A Python object is born with one class. To make Ana a mentor too, you need a new class like EmployeeMentor. In RDF, you add one triple. And Ben became a Mentor because of a rule, not because of code.

In 2006 a W3C group wrote a note for software developers about this. Here are its main points, in short.

OO classes and ontology classes (after the W3C note of 2006)
TopicOO class (Java, Python, Rust)Ontology class (RDFS, OWL)
What a class isa template that builds objectsa set of things
Types per thingone classany number of classes
Change of typenot at run timeyes: add a triple, or let a reasoner classify it
Propertiesbelong to a classstand alone, any thing can use them
Domain and rangetype checksrules that add types
Behaviourmethods with codenone: only logical statements
Privacyprivate fieldseverything is public and linkable
Identitya memory address inside one programa global IRI
Missing factsclosed worldopen world

An OO class is a cookie cutter. Every cookie has one shape forever. An ontology class is a label on a box. One thing can sit in many boxes, and a rule can move it into a new box.

Generating one Python class per OWL class and loading individuals into them. This breaks as soon as one individual has two types. Keep a set of types per individual instead, or use a library like Owlready2 that handles this for you.

Types in Rust and Python as small ontologies

Your code already has a small ontology. It is the type system. Look at this Rust file.

#![allow(dead_code)] // keep the demo quiet
// A closed value set: a Role is exactly one of these three.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Role { Lead, Developer, Reviewer }

// A sum type: every worker is an employee OR a contractor, never both.
enum Worker {
    Employee { name: String, mentor: Option<String> }, // 0 or 1 mentor
    Contractor { name: String, day_rate: u32 },
}

struct Assignment { who: String, project: String, role: Role, since: u16 }

// A trait groups types by what they can do.
trait Billable { fn cost_per_day(&self) -> u32; }

impl Billable for Worker {
    fn cost_per_day(&self) -> u32 {
        match self {                       // the compiler checks every case
            Worker::Employee { .. } => 0,  // paid by salary
            Worker::Contractor { day_rate, .. } => *day_rate,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let team = vec![
        Worker::Employee { name: "Ana".into(), mentor: None },
        Worker::Contractor { name: "Ben".into(), day_rate: 600 },
    ];
    for w in &team {
        let name = match w { Worker::Employee { name, .. } | Worker::Contractor { name, .. } => name };
        println!("{name}: {} per day", w.cost_per_day());
    }
    let a = Assignment { who: "Ana".into(), project: "atlas".into(), role: Role::Lead, since: 2024 };
    println!("{} works on {} as {:?} since {}", a.who, a.project, a.role, a.since);
}
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

class Role(Enum):                 # a closed value set
    LEAD = "lead"
    DEVELOPER = "developer"
    REVIEWER = "reviewer"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Assignment:                 # a class with four fields
    who: str
    project: str
    role: Role
    since: int

@runtime_checkable
class Billable(Protocol):         # "anything with cost_per_day()"
    def cost_per_day(self) -> int: ...

@dataclass
class Contractor:
    name: str
    day_rate: int
    def cost_per_day(self) -> int:
        return self.day_rate

a = Assignment("Ana", "atlas", Role.LEAD, 2024)
print(a)
print(isinstance(Contractor("Ben", 600), Billable))   # no inheritance needed
bad = Assignment("Ana", "atlas", "boss", "last year")  # hints are not checked
print(bad.role, bad.since)
print(Role("lead"), [r.value for r in Role])
Ana: 0 per day
Ben: 600 per day
Ana works on atlas as Lead since 2024
Assignment(who='Ana', project='atlas', role=<Role.LEAD: 'lead'>, since=2024)
True
boss last year
Role.LEAD ['lead', 'developer', 'reviewer']

Now add a third kind of worker, Intern, to the Rust enum. Do not touch the match. The compiler stops you.

error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&Worker::Intern { .. }` not covered
  --> types_bad.rs:20:15
   |
20 |         match self {                       // the compiler checks every case
   |               ^^^^ pattern `&Worker::Intern { .. }` not covered

This is a closed world, checked before the program runs. An ontology with the same classes would accept an intern. It would just know nothing about the intern's cost.

Code types read as ontology ideas
RustPythonOntology idea
struct Assignment@dataclassa class with properties that have one value each
enum Role { Lead, ... }class Role(Enum)a value set: owl:oneOf
enum Worker { Employee {..}, Contractor {..} }Employee | Contractora disjoint union: owl:disjointUnionOf
Option<String>str | Noneat most one value: owl:maxCardinality 1
Vec<String>list[str]any number of values (the OWL default)
trait Billable + implan abstract base classa named class you must join on purpose (nominal)
(no direct match)Protocola defined class: anything with the right parts counts (structural)
the compilera type checker like mypya reasoner, but closed world

A sum type like Worker says two things at once. The cases do not overlap. And there are no other cases. In OWL you must say both with axioms. Without them, the open world allows a third kind.

Thinking a dataclass checks types. Look at the output: Assignment("Ana", "atlas", "boss", "last year") ran without an error. The Python docs say @dataclass does not look at the type in the annotation. Use a type checker, a __post_init__ check, or a validation library.

When each model is the right tool

Start from your questions and your users, not from a product.

Strengths and weak points (a first guide)
ModelStrong atWeak atExamples
Relationaltransactions, constraints, reports, mature toolsdeep paths, data with very different shapesPostgreSQL, SQLite
Documentone object per read, flexible fieldsquestions across many documents, shared dataMongoDB, JSON columns
Property graphpaths, neighbours, graph algorithmsglobal meaning, standard exchange across companiesNeo4j, Memgraph
RDF and OWLglobal names, merging sources, reasoning, standardssimple app storage, team skillsJena, GraphDB, Oxigraph

Many teams mix models. A PostgreSQL table can hold a JSON column. An R2RML map can show SQL tables as RDF without copying them. A graph index can sit on top of normal tables. The next chapter, Triple stores and graph databases, opens these systems up.

A classic question: "Why is RDF good for joining data from many sources?" Answer with three points. Names are global IRIs, so the same thing gets the same name. Merging two graphs is just a union of triple sets. The schema travels with the data as more triples.

Choosing a graph database because "our data is connected". All data is connected. Choose it when your main questions follow paths of unknown length, like "who is within four hops of this account?".

Patterns to remember

Patterns for comparing data models
PatternPurposeModelNote
Link table with columnsA many-to-many link with fields, in SQLworks_on(person, project, role, since)Make the pair the primary key, or allow repeats on purpose.
Embed what you read togetherFast reads in a document store{"_id":"atlas","members":[...]}Copies must be updated together. Use references for shared data.
Link as a node (n-ary)A link with fields in RDFex:a1 ex:who ex:ana ; ex:role "lead"Give the node a class, like ex:Assignment.
Properties on a relationshipA link with fields in a property graph-[:WORKS_ON {role:'lead'}]->A relationship cannot point to another relationship.
Entity to class, column to propertyTurn a database design into an ontologyperson.name to ex:nameThen add the meaning tables never had.
Schema for checks, ontology for meaningKeep both jobs clearSQL CHECK plus rdfs:subClassOfOWL does not reject data. Use SHACL for checks on RDF.
Many types per thingModel roles that changeex:ana a ex:Employee, ex:MentorDo not map each OWL class to one code class.
Sum type as disjoint unionSay "exactly one of these"enum Worker { Employee, Contractor }In OWL, say disjointness and covering, or the world stays open.
Option as max 1A field with zero or one valuementor: Option<String>OWL properties allow many values unless you limit them.
Protocol as defined classGroup things by what they haveclass Billable(Protocol)Python checks only method names at run time, not types.
Choose by the main questionPick a data model"follow hops of unknown length" leads to a graphMixing models is normal. Keep one source of truth.

Practice

In which model does a link become a separate node when it needs a role and a year?

  • Property graph
  • Plain RDF (1.1)
  • Relational

RDF 1.1 triples cannot carry fields. You add an n-ary node like ex:a1. Property graphs put properties on the relationship.

The data says ex:ben ex:mentors ex:ana, and the ontology says the domain of ex:mentors is ex:Mentor. Ben is a Contractor. What does an RDFS reasoner do?

  • It reports an error.
  • It deletes the triple.
  • It adds: Ben is a Mentor.

A domain is a rule for new facts. It is not a check.

Which Python construct is closest to an OWL defined class?

  • @dataclass
  • typing.Protocol
  • Enum

A Protocol accepts anything with the right methods. A defined class accepts anything that meets its conditions.

Fill in the missing words.

In a UML class diagram, a link with its own fields is drawn as an ?.

A schema reads data under the ? assumption. An ontology uses the open world.

The W3C language for custom maps from tables to RDF is called ?.

What does a foreign key become in an ontology?

An object property: a link between two individuals.

How many types can one RDF resource have?

Any number. A Python object has one class.

What does a Rust enum with data say in ontology terms?

A disjoint union: the cases do not overlap, and there are no other cases.

Does @dataclass check field types at run time?

No. The annotations are not checked.

  1. Write the table design for "a book has many authors, and each author has a position on the cover (1st, 2nd)".
    Answer

    book(id, title), author(id, name) and wrote(book, author, position). The link table holds the position, like works_on holds the role.

  2. Write the same fact, "Ada is author 1 of book b7", in Cypher and in Turtle.
    Answer

    Cypher: (ada)-[:WROTE {position:1}]->(b7). Turtle with an n-ary node: ex:w1 a ex:Authorship ; ex:author ex:ada ; ex:book ex:b7 ; ex:position 1 .

  3. A team stores each order as a document with the customer's address copied inside. The customer moves. What goes wrong, and what are two fixes?
    Answer

    Old orders keep the old address, and new code may read the wrong one. Fix 1: keep customers in their own collection and store a reference. Fix 2: keep the copy on purpose, as "the address at order time", and name the field that way.

  4. Give two reasons why "one Python class per OWL class" breaks.
    Answer

    An individual can have many types, but an object has one class. A reasoner can add a type later, but an object cannot change its class at run time.

  5. Your Rust enum Worker has two cases. Write the two OWL ideas you need so the ontology says the same.
    Answer

    Disjointness: no thing is both an Employee and a Contractor. Covering: every Worker is an Employee or a Contractor. owl:disjointUnionOf says both in one axiom.

  6. A start-up wants fraud checks like "is this card within three hops of a known bad account?" and also monthly money reports. Which models would you pick?
    Answer

    A relational database for money and reports, because it has transactions and constraints. For the hop question, use recursive SQL first. If the paths get long and the data large, add a graph database or a graph index fed from the same tables. Keep the tables as the source of truth.

Key takeaways

  • Tables, documents, RDF and property graphs can all hold the same facts. They differ in which questions are easy.
  • A link with fields is a link table in SQL, properties on an edge in a property graph, and an n-ary node in RDF 1.1.
  • ER diagrams plan databases. UML plans code. An ontology states meaning that a program can reason with.
  • A schema rejects bad data under the closed world. An ontology adds facts under the open world.
  • An OO class is a template with one type per object. An ontology class is a set, and a thing can be in many.
  • Rust enums and Python Enums are value sets. Sum types are disjoint unions. Option is "at most one".
  • Pick a model by your main questions. Mixing models is normal.

Sources

  • A Semantic Web Primer for Object-Oriented Software Developers. W3C Working Group Note, March 2006, with the table of differences between OO and RDF/OWL classes.
  • R2RML: RDB to RDF Mapping Language. W3C Recommendation of 27 September 2012, with its companion Direct Mapping.
  • Chen: The Entity-Relationship Model, Toward a Unified View of Data. ACM TODS 1(1), March 1976, the paper behind ER diagrams.
  • Neo4j: What is a graph database?. Nodes, labels, relationship types, direction and properties.
  • MongoDB: Data modeling. Embedding, references and schema validation in a document store.
  • Python 3.14: dataclasses. The parameters of @dataclass and the note that annotations are not checked.

Triple stores and graph databases

A triple store keeps RDF data. A graph database keeps property graphs. Inside, both turn names into numbers, sort them in clever orders and join them fast. This chapter opens the box: indexes, query plans, joins and storage. Then it surveys the real systems of November 2026 and shows how far plain PostgreSQL can go.

  • Explain dictionary encoding and the SPO, POS and OSP indexes, and pick the index for any triple pattern.
  • Follow how a query planner orders joins, and show why a bad order costs 100 times more work.
  • Explain index-free adjacency and measure it against a B-tree.
  • Write one path query in Cypher, GQL and SQL/PGQ.
  • Compare today's triple stores, graph databases and graph tools in PostgreSQL, with honest strengths.

From strings to numbers: dictionary encoding

Look at one triple from a real dataset.

<http://example.org/person/42> <http://example.org/worksOn> <http://example.org/project/7>

That is about 80 bytes of text. The same three names appear thousands of times in a big graph. So a triple store does not keep the text in its indexes. It gives each distinct name a small number once. This is dictionary encoding.

We built 30,000 triples about 10,000 people and measured. The code is in the next section.

30000 triples, 10114 distinct terms
as text: 2,435,679 bytes; as 4-byte ids: 360,000 bytes per index

Only 10,114 different names appear in 90,000 positions. With 4-byte numbers, each copy of the data is about 7 times smaller. Comparing two numbers is also much faster than comparing two long strings.

  • The dictionary maps each name to a number, and each number back to the name.
  • The indexes hold only numbers.
  • The engine turns the query's names into numbers first. It turns numbers back into names only for the final answer.

Real systems add tricks. Apache Jena's TDB uses 8-byte ids and finds a name's id through a 128-bit MD5 hash. Small values like integers and dates are stored inside the id itself, so they need no lookup. Oxigraph stores IRIs as 128-bit hashes. Strings shorter than 16 bytes sit inside the key, and longer ones go to a separate id2str table.

Thinking ids sort like values. The id of "Zoe" can be smaller than the id of "Ann". So ORDER BY ?name or FILTER (?age > 30) needs the real values. Inline values help for numbers and dates. For strings, the engine must decode, and that costs time.

Three orders, six orders: SPO, POS, OSP and the hexastore

A query asks for triple patterns, like "who works on project 42?". That is (? worksOn project42): the predicate and the object are known. Which sorted list finds these triples fastest?

Keep the triples sorted in three orders. Each order is a permutation of subject, predicate and object.

import bisect
ORDERS = {"spo": (0, 1, 2), "pos": (1, 2, 0), "osp": (2, 0, 1)}
class Store:
    def __init__(self):
        self.ids, self.terms = {}, []                  # the dictionary
        self.ix = {name: [] for name in ORDERS}        # three sorted indexes
    def enc(self, term):                               # term -> small integer
        if term not in self.ids:
            self.ids[term] = len(self.terms)
            self.terms.append(term)
        return self.ids[term]
    def load(self, triples):
        for t in triples:
            t = tuple(self.enc(x) for x in t)
            for name, order in ORDERS.items():
                self.ix[name].append(tuple(t[i] for i in order))
        for rows in self.ix.values():
            rows.sort()
    @staticmethod
    def choose(bound):                                 # bound = (s?, p?, o?)
        k = sum(bound)
        for name, order in ORDERS.items():             # bound part must be a prefix
            if all(bound[i] for i in order[:k]):
                return name
    def scan(self, s=None, p=None, o=None):
        pat = (s, p, o)
        name = self.choose(tuple(x is not None for x in pat))
        order = ORDERS[name]
        prefix = tuple(pat[i] for i in order if pat[i] is not None)
        rows = self.ix[name]
        i = bisect.bisect_left(rows, prefix)           # binary search to the start
        while i < len(rows) and rows[i][:len(prefix)] == prefix:
            back = [0, 0, 0]
            for pos, i_spo in enumerate(order):        # undo the rotation
                back[i_spo] = rows[i][pos]
            yield tuple(back)
            i += 1
use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashMap};
#[derive(Default)]
struct Store {
    ids: HashMap<String, u32>, terms: Vec<String>,   // the dictionary
    spo: BTreeSet<(u32, u32, u32)>,                    // three sorted indexes
    pos: BTreeSet<(u32, u32, u32)>,
    osp: BTreeSet<(u32, u32, u32)>,
}
impl Store {
    fn enc(&mut self, t: &str) -> u32 {
        if let Some(&id) = self.ids.get(t) { return id; }
        let id = self.terms.len() as u32;
        self.ids.insert(t.to_string(), id);
        self.terms.push(t.to_string());
        id
    }
    fn add(&mut self, s: &str, p: &str, o: &str) {
        let (s, p, o) = (self.enc(s), self.enc(p), self.enc(o));
        self.spo.insert((s, p, o)); self.pos.insert((p, o, s)); self.osp.insert((o, s, p));
    }
    // all subjects with predicate p and object o: a range scan on POS
    fn subjects(&self, p: u32, o: u32) -> Vec<&str> {
        self.pos.range((p, o, 0)..=(p, o, u32::MAX))
            .map(|&(_, _, s)| self.terms[s as usize].as_str()).collect()
    }
}
fn main() {
    let mut st = Store::default();
    st.add("ex:ana", "ex:worksOn", "ex:atlas");
    st.add("ex:ben", "ex:worksOn", "ex:atlas");
    st.add("ex:ana", "ex:worksOn", "ex:borealis");
    st.add("ex:ana", "rdf:type", "ex:Employee");
    let (p, o) = (st.ids["ex:worksOn"], st.ids["ex:atlas"]);
    println!("dictionary: {:?}", st.terms);
    println!("POS keys: {:?}", st.pos);
    println!("on atlas: {:?}", st.subjects(p, o));
}
(1, 1, 0) -> spo
(1, 0, 1) -> osp
(0, 1, 1) -> pos
(1, 0, 0) -> spo
(0, 1, 0) -> pos
(0, 0, 1) -> osp
99 people on project 42
dictionary: ["ex:ana", "ex:worksOn", "ex:atlas", "ex:ben", "ex:borealis", "rdf:type", "ex:Employee"]
POS keys: {(1, 2, 0), (1, 2, 3), (1, 4, 0), (5, 6, 0)}
on atlas: ["ex:ana", "ex:ben"]

Read the Python output. A 1 means "this position is known". For (0, 1, 1) the store uses POS. In POS order, all triples with the same predicate and object sit next to each other. A range scan finds the first one with binary search, then reads forward. The Rust output shows the same idea. In POS, the keys (1, 2, 0) and (1, 2, 3) are neighbours. They are "worksOn atlas" for ana and ben.

A record has n positions. A sorted order can answer a pattern by one range scan when the known positions form a prefix of the order. The smallest number of orders that covers all 2^n patterns is \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}.

In simple words: for triples, n = 3 and \binom{3}{1} = 3. SPO, POS and OSP are enough. For quads with a graph name, n = 4 and \binom{4}{2} = 6. Amazon Neptune's documentation says exactly this: six orders would cover all 16 quad patterns.

Proof idea

The prefixes of one order form a chain of sets: {}, {S}, {S,P}, {S,P,O}. So we must cover all subsets of the positions with chains. Sperner's theorem says the largest family of subsets where no set contains another is the middle layer, with \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} sets. Each chain can hold only one set of that layer, so we need at least that many orders. A known construction, the symmetric chain decomposition, uses exactly that many chains. For n = 3: the chains {S} ⊂ {S,P}, {P} ⊂ {P,O} and {O} ⊂ {O,S} cover every pair.

Three orders are enough to find triples. But some systems keep all six. The hexastore paper by Weiss, Karras and Bernstein (VLDB 2008) did this. With six orders, every pattern's answers can come out sorted by either free position. Sorted inputs allow fast merge joins, as the next section shows. The paper reports a worst-case five-fold growth in index space for this.

Which orders real systems keep (from their documentation)
SystemOrdersNote
Oxigraphspo, pos, osp for the default graph. spog, posg, ospg, gspo, gpos, gosp for named graphs.stored in RocksDB, an LSM-tree key-value store
QLeverall six: PSO, POS, SPO, SOP, OSP, OPScompressed. Each predicate id is stored once per run.
Amazon NeptuneSPOG, POGS, GPSO by defaultoptional OSGP index: up to 20% more storage, inserts up to 23% slower
Apache Jena TDB2three triple indexes and quad indexes, in B+treeseach index holds the whole triple. There is no separate triple table.

Neptune keeps only three of the six quad orders. For a pattern with only the object known, it scans the POGS index once per distinct predicate. Its docs warn that this gets slow when a graph has very many distinct predicates. That is when you turn on OSGP, but only on an empty database.

"More indexes are free." Each index is a full copy of all triples. Every insert and delete must update every copy. Pick the orders your queries need.

How a query is planned and joined

A SPARQL query is a set of triple patterns that share variables. Here is one with three patterns.

SELECT ?p WHERE {
  ?p ex:type    ex:Person .      # pattern A
  ?p ex:livesIn ex:city3 .       # pattern B
  ?p ex:worksOn ex:project42 .   # pattern C
}

The answer is the same in any order. The work is not. Our engine joins pattern by pattern. For each partial answer, it fills in the known variable and scans again. This is an index nested-loop join.

from data import st, EX                  # the 30,000 triples
E = st.enc
Q = [("?p", E(EX + "type"), E(EX + "Person")),        # pattern A
     ("?p", E(EX + "livesIn"), E(EX + "city/3")),     # pattern B
     ("?p", E(EX + "worksOn"), E(EX + "project/42"))] # pattern C

def run(patterns):
    rows, touched = [{}], 0
    for pat in patterns:                    # index nested-loop join
        out = []
        for b in rows:
            s, p, o = (b.get(x, x) if isinstance(x, str) else x for x in pat)
            free = lambda v: None if isinstance(v, str) else v
            for t in st.scan(free(s), free(p), free(o)):
                touched += 1
                nb = dict(b)
                for var, val in zip((s, p, o), t):
                    if isinstance(var, str): nb[var] = val
                out.append(nb)
        rows = out
    return len(rows), touched

def size(pat):                              # statistics: matches with constants only
    return sum(1 for _ in st.scan(*(None if isinstance(x, str) else x for x in pat)))

print("sizes:", {n: size(q) for n, q in zip("ABC", Q)})
print("order A,B,C:", run(Q))
greedy = sorted(Q, key=size)                # smallest first
print("order C,B,A:", run(greedy))
sizes: {'A': 10000, 'B': 1012, 'C': 99}
order A,B,C: (10, 11022)
order C,B,A: (10, 119)

Both orders find the same 10 people. The written order touched 11,022 index rows. The greedy order touched 119, almost 100 times fewer. The rule: start with the most selective pattern, and keep the partial answers small.

Parse

The text becomes a tree of operators: patterns, joins, FILTER, OPTIONAL.

Encode the constants

Each IRI and literal in the query is looked up in the dictionary. An unknown IRI means zero answers, at once.

Estimate sizes

The planner guesses how many rows each pattern and each join gives. It uses statistics, like counts per predicate.

Choose order and join types

It picks the join order and, for each join, nested loop, hash or merge join. Big engines search many plans. Small ones pick greedily.

Scan and join

Range scans read the indexes. Joins combine rows of numbers. Filters run as early as possible.

Decode

Only the final rows go back through the dictionary to become names and values.

Four ways to join two lists of rows
JoinHow it worksGood when
Index nested loopfor each left row, scan an indexthe left side is small
Hash joinput one side in a hash table, look up the otherboth sides are big and unsorted
Merge joinwalk two lists sorted on the join keyboth inputs come sorted, for free, from an index
Worst-case optimal joinjoin all patterns at once, one variable at a timecyclic queries like triangles (next section)

Look at patterns B and C again. A POS scan returns subjects in sorted order, because the subject is the last key part. So both lists come sorted by ?p, and a merge join needs no hash table. This is why the hexastore and RDF-3X keep many orders.

Oxigraph's architecture page says it reorders joins greedily by pattern selectivity and pushes filters down. Its evaluation is single-threaded. Jena's TDB uses a statistics-based optimizer for basic graph patterns.

Trusting the size guesses too much. Most planners assume that patterns are independent. In our data, city and project were random, so the guess "1012 × 99 / 10000 ≈ 10" was right. In real data, "lives in Oslo" and "works for the Oslo office" are strongly linked, and the guess can be 100 times wrong. Research methods like characteristic sets (Neumann and Moerkotte, 2011) count predicates that appear together.

When pairs of joins are not enough

Some queries go round in a circle. A triangle asks for x, y, z with edges x→y, y→z and z→x. Here is a graph made to hurt pairwise joins. A hub has 1,000 edges in and 1,000 edges out. There is also one real triangle.

from collections import defaultdict

m = 1000
E = [(f"in{i}", "hub") for i in range(m)] + [("hub", f"out{j}") for j in range(m)]
E += [("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "a")]              # one real triangle
out, inn = defaultdict(set), defaultdict(set)
for x, y in E:
    out[x].add(y); inn[y].add(x)
print("edges N =", len(E), " AGM bound N^1.5 =", round(len(E) ** 1.5))

# plan 1: binary joins. First E(x,y) JOIN E(y,z), then check E(z,x).
paths = [(x, y, z) for x, y in E for z in out[y]]       # all two-step paths
tri1 = [(x, y, z) for x, y, z in paths if x in out[z]]
print("binary join: middle result", len(paths), "rows, triangles", len(tri1))

# plan 2: generic join, one variable at a time, with set intersection
work, tri2 = 0, []
for x in list(out):
    for y in out[x]:
        a, b = out[y], inn[x]                           # z must be in both sets
        small, big = (a, b) if len(a) <= len(b) else (b, a)
        work += 1 + len(small)                          # one step per edge + intersection
        tri2 += [(x, y, z) for z in small if z in big]
print("generic join: work", work, "steps, triangles", len(tri2))
edges N = 2003  AGM bound N^1.5 = 89644
binary join: middle result 1000003 rows, triangles 3
generic join: work 2006 steps, triangles 3

The pairwise plan built a million two-step paths through the hub. Then it threw almost all of them away. The generic join binds one variable at a time. For each pair x, y it intersects two sets and walks only the smaller one. It did about 2,000 steps. The three answers are the same triangle seen from each corner.

(Atserias, Grohe and Marx, 2008.) If each of the relations R(x,y), S(y,z), T(z,x) has at most N rows, the triangle query has at most N^{3/2} answers, and some inputs reach this. Any plan that joins two relations at a time can need about N^2 steps on some inputs. A worst-case optimal join runs in about N^{3/2} steps on every input.

With numbers: for N = 10^6 edges, N^{3/2} = 10^9 but N^2 = 10^{12}. That is a thousand times more work for the pairwise plan in the worst case. Algorithms like NPRR (2012) and Leapfrog Triejoin (2014) reach the bound. They need sorted indexes in several orders, which triple stores already have.

Proof idea

Split the answers by the number of out-edges of x in R. Call x light if it has at most \sqrt N of them. A triangle with a light x is fixed by one edge T(z,x) and one of at most \sqrt N choices of y. So there are at most N \cdot \sqrt N such triangles. Fewer than \sqrt N values of x are heavy, because R has only N rows. A triangle with a heavy x is fixed by x and one edge S(y,z), so again at most \sqrt N \cdot N. This simple split gives 2N^{3/2}. The exact bound N^{3/2} uses Shearer's lemma. The generic join follows the same idea, because it always walks the smaller of the two sets.

Thinking only "big data" causes slow joins. Skewed data does it too. One hub with a million edges can blow up a small query. Check the plan for huge middle results, not only the table sizes.

Property graph storage and index-free adjacency

A triple store finds neighbours through an index. A native graph database can store, with each node, where its relationships are. We measured both ideas in Rust, in memory. The graph has 200,000 nodes and about 1,000,000 edges. We ran a two-hop walk from 10,000 random start nodes.

// A: each node holds its own neighbour list ("index-free adjacency")
let mut adj: Vec<Vec<u32>> = vec![Vec::new(); n as usize];
for &(a, b) in &edges { adj[a as usize].push(b); }
// B: one global sorted index of (src, dst), like an edge table with a B-tree
let index: BTreeSet<(u32, u32)> = edges.iter().copied().collect();

for &s in &starts {                                   // two hops, list walk
    for &x in &adj[s as usize] { total_a += adj[x as usize].len(); }
}
for &s in &starts {                                   // two hops, index lookups
    for &(_, x) in index.range((s, 0)..=(s, u32::MAX)) {
        total_b += index.range((x, 0)..=(x, u32::MAX)).count();
    }
}
two-hop paths found: 249510 (lists) and 249510 (index)
neighbour lists: 0.5 ms
B-tree index:    12.1 ms

This is index-free adjacency. A hop costs about one step per neighbour. With a B-tree, every hop first searches the tree, about \log_2 E steps. With a million edges, that is about 20 steps per hop, plus jumps through memory.

How Neo4j stores a graph

Neo4j's operations manual lists four store formats. The older aligned and standard formats keep linked-list-like structures on disk. Since version 5.22, new Enterprise databases use the block format by default. Community Edition still uses aligned.

  • In block, each node gets a fixed 128-byte block made of two 64-byte records. One record holds labels and properties. The other holds relationships.
  • Property values under about 31 bytes sit inside the block. Bigger values go to a separate file.
  • The goal is to keep a node's data together, so a query loads fewer pages from disk.

Not every graph database works this way. Amazon Neptune stores property graphs as quads. An edge becomes a statement with the edge id in the G position. Neptune then finds neighbours through its SPOG and POGS indexes. Both designs are fine. They pay in different places.

"Index-free adjacency means no indexes." You still need an index to find the start node, for example a person by email. Index-free adjacency only makes the hops cheap. Also watch for supernodes: a node with millions of relationships makes every walk through it slow.

Query languages: Cypher, GQL and SQL/PGQ

Here is one question in three languages: "who can Ana reach in 1 to 3 KNOWS steps?". The data is a chain Ana → Ben → Chen → Dana → Eli, plus Chen → Ana, which makes a cycle.

import ladybug as lb

db = lb.Database(":memory:")                        # embedded, no server
c = lb.Connection(db)
c.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Person(name STRING PRIMARY KEY)")
c.execute("CREATE REL TABLE KNOWS(FROM Person TO Person)")
for a, b in [("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ben", "Chen"), ("Chen", "Dana"),
             ("Dana", "Eli"), ("Chen", "Ana")]:      # Chen -> Ana makes a cycle
    c.execute(f"MERGE (x:Person {{name:'{a}'}}) MERGE (y:Person {{name:'{b}'}}) "
              f"CREATE (x)-[:KNOWS]->(y)")

r = c.execute("""
    MATCH (a:Person {name:'Ana'})-[e:KNOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
    RETURN b.name AS who, min(length(e)) AS hops
    ORDER BY hops, who""")
while r.has_next():
    print(r.get_next())
['Ben', 1]
['Chen', 2]
['Ana', 3]
['Dana', 3]
MATCH (a:Person WHERE a.name = 'Ana')-[:KNOWS]->{1,3}(b:Person)
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS who
CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH team
  VERTEX TABLES (person)
  EDGE TABLES (knows
    SOURCE KEY (src) REFERENCES person (name)
    DESTINATION KEY (dst) REFERENCES person (name)
    LABEL knows);

SELECT * FROM GRAPH_TABLE (team
  MATCH p = ANY SHORTEST (a:person WHERE a.name = 'Ana')-[k:knows]->{1,3}(b:person)
  COLUMNS (b.name AS who, path_length(p) AS hops));

Look at Ana in the Cypher output. Ana reached herself in 3 steps: Ana → Ben → Chen → Ana. Cypher does not use the same relationship twice in one path, but a node may come back. Add WHERE b <> a if you do not want that.

  • Cypher draws paths with ASCII art: (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b). Many systems speak it, often through the openCypher project.
  • GQL is ISO/IEC 39075:2024, published in April 2024. It took much of its shape from Cypher. Paths repeat with {1,3}.
  • SQL/PGQ is part 16 of the SQL standard, ISO/IEC 9075-16:2023. You declare a graph view over normal tables. Then GRAPH_TABLE runs a pattern and returns rows.

The Neo4j Cypher manual says Cypher supports most mandatory GQL features. For example, it accepts INSERT as another word for CREATE. Support differs a lot between products. LadybugDB 0.22.3 rejected all three GQL forms I tried: the {1,3} quantifier, WHERE inside a node pattern and INSERT.

  1. 1999 SQL:1999. Recursive queries enter the SQL standard.
  2. 2008 Hexastore and RDF-3X. Triple stores with all six index orders.
  3. 2011 Cypher. Neo4j introduces its query language.
  4. 2015 openCypher. Cypher opens up for other vendors.
  5. 2023 SQL/PGQ. Graph queries become part 16 of SQL.
  6. 2024 GQL. ISO publishes ISO/IEC 39075 in April.
  7. 2025 Kuzu archived. The embedded graph database stops in October. Forks such as LadybugDB continue it.
  8. 2026 SQL/PGQ leaves PostgreSQL 19. The feature is removed from the release branch in September.

Expecting *1..3 to be cheap. A variable-length pattern can explode on a dense graph. With 50 neighbours per node, three hops give up to 125,000 paths. Always set an upper bound, and ask for shortest paths when that is what you need.

A survey of systems in November 2026

I checked each system's own website or repository on 15 November 2026. Versions change fast. Check again before you choose.

Here is one small, honest benchmark. We loaded 300,000 generated triples into rdflib and into pyoxigraph 0.5.13. Then we ran one three-pattern query. Each run was a fresh Python 3.14 process.

baseline  load  0.00 s  query    0.0 ms  answer -  peak memory 89 MB
rdflib    load  2.98 s  query  127.9 ms  answer 97  peak memory 560 MB
oxigraph  load  0.35 s  query   46.8 ms  answer 97  peak memory 258 MB

The baseline line is the test data alone, 89 MB. Oxigraph loaded about 8 times faster and used about half the memory. That fits its design: dictionary-encoded keys in Rust, not Python objects. It does not prove Oxigraph is faster for your data. It shows how to measure.

Choosing a database from a vendor's benchmark. Each vendor picks tests it wins. Load your own data, run your own ten most common queries, and measure load time, query time, memory and disk.

Graphs inside PostgreSQL

Many teams already run PostgreSQL. Can it answer graph questions alone? Here is the KNOWS chain again, as a table with columns src and dst. We ran two recursive queries in PostgreSQL 18.3.

CREATE TABLE knows (src text, dst text);
INSERT INTO knows VALUES ('Ana','Ben'), ('Ben','Chen'), ('Chen','Dana'), ('Dana','Eli'), ('Chen','Ana');

-- walks of up to 3 steps that never repeat a person, in breadth-first order
WITH RECURSIVE walk(who, hops, path) AS (
    SELECT 'Ana'::text, 0, ARRAY['Ana']
  UNION ALL
    SELECT k.dst, w.hops + 1, w.path || k.dst
    FROM walk w JOIN knows k ON k.src = w.who
    WHERE k.dst <> ALL (w.path) AND w.hops < 3
) SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY who SET ord
SELECT who, hops, array_to_string(path, ' > ') AS route FROM walk ORDER BY ord;

-- fewest steps to everyone; the CYCLE clause stops at Chen -> Ana
WITH RECURSIVE walk(who, hops) AS (
    SELECT 'Ana'::text, 0
  UNION ALL
    SELECT k.dst, w.hops + 1 FROM walk w JOIN knows k ON k.src = w.who
) CYCLE who SET seen_before USING trail
SELECT who, min(hops) AS fewest_hops FROM walk
WHERE NOT seen_before GROUP BY who ORDER BY 2, 1;
who | hops | route
Ana | 0 | Ana
Ben | 1 | Ana > Ben
Chen | 2 | Ana > Ben > Chen
Dana | 3 | Ana > Ben > Chen > Dana

who | fewest_hops
Ana | 0
Ben | 1
Chen | 2
Dana | 3
Eli | 4
How we ran PostgreSQL without a server

We used PostgreSQL's stand-alone mode, postgres --single, on a scratch data folder. It reads SQL from a file and opens no network port. A short Python script turned its long output into the small tables above.

A recursive CTE has a start part and a step part. PostgreSQL has had WITH RECURSIVE since version 8.4 in 2009. Version 14 added two clauses from the SQL standard.

  • SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY ... SET ord adds a column that sorts rows level by level.
  • CYCLE col SET flag USING path marks a row that returns to a value seen before on its path. Then the walk stops there.

Why does the loop end at all? Each round adds rows, and the set of possible rows is finite. The fixed-point argument is in Rules and Datalog. The Computer Science book proves it with the Knaster-Tarski theorem.

Apache AGE: Cypher inside PostgreSQL

Apache AGE is an extension. You call Cypher through a SQL function and declare the output columns. Version 1.8.0 for PostgreSQL 18 came out in 2026. Release lines follow PostgreSQL versions, so check that yours is supported. This is the shape from the AGE quickstart. I did not run it.

CREATE EXTENSION age;
LOAD 'age';
SET search_path = ag_catalog, "$user", public;
SELECT create_graph('team');
SELECT * FROM cypher('team', $$
    MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Ana'})-[:KNOWS*1..3]->(b:Person)
    RETURN DISTINCT b.name
$$) AS (name agtype);

pgGraph: a graph index over your own tables

The reader's list of open-source projects includes evokoa/pggraph. I read its README and quickstart on 15 November 2026. Here is what it really is.

  • A PostgreSQL extension named graph, written in Rust with pgrx. Version 1.2.1 supports PostgreSQL 14 to 18. The licence is Apache-2.0.
  • Your tables stay the source of truth. graph.build() compiles the links into forward and reverse CSR edge stores. That is index-free adjacency, built as a derived index.
  • The default projection mode is csr_readonly. A mutable_overlay mode also exists.
  • graph.auto_discover('public') registers tables and turns foreign keys into edges. graph.traverse and graph.shortest_path walk the index.
  • The Docker image schedules graph.run_scheduled_maintenance() every five minutes with pg_cron, to keep the index in step with the tables.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS graph;
SELECT * FROM graph.auto_discover('public');      -- tables + foreign keys -> graph
SELECT node_count, edge_count, edge_types FROM graph.status();
SELECT depth, node_table_name, node_id, edge_path
FROM graph.traverse('public.people'::regclass, 'p1', 2, hydrate := false);

I could not run it: the extension is not installed here. The authors publish no benchmark numbers. The chapter Context graphs and agent memory draws its node and edge model.

What happened to SQL/PGQ in PostgreSQL?

A SQL/PGQ implementation was committed for PostgreSQL 19 and then reverted. pgGraph's README says the feature left the 19 release branch on 7 September 2026. On 12 November 2026, PostgreSQL 19 was at release candidate 2. Its draft release notes do not list SQL/PGQ. So for now, graph queries in PostgreSQL mean recursive SQL or an extension. Check the final release notes: this can change.

Three ways to do graphs in PostgreSQL
WayQuery styleHop costExtra cost
Recursive CTEplain SQLan index lookup per hopnothing to install
Apache AGECypher inside cypher()lookups in AGE's own tablesan extension with its own release lines
pgGraphSQL functionsone array step per neighbour (CSR)a derived index to keep in sync

Keeping a path array when you only need "who is reachable". Each row copies its whole path, and the number of walks can grow very fast on a dense graph. For plain reachability, use UNION without a path. It keeps each person once and stops when nothing new appears.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for graph storage and queries
PatternPurposeModelNote
Dictionary encodingStore and compare small numbers, not long strings"ex:ana" -> 0Ids do not sort like values. Decode for ORDER BY and string filters.
Three rotationsCover all 8 triple patterns with range scansSPO, POS, OSPQuads need 6 orders for all 16 patterns.
Six orders (hexastore)Sorted output on any free positionSPO, SOP, PSO, POS, OSP, OPSUp to five times the index space in the worst case.
Most selective firstKeep partial answers small?p worksOn project42 before ?p a PersonSize guesses fail on correlated data.
Merge join on sorted scansJoin without a hash tabletwo POS scans sorted by subjectNeeds an index whose free position comes last.
Worst-case optimal joinCyclic patterns like trianglesbind x, then y, then intersect for zPairwise plans can build huge middle results.
Index-free adjacencyCheap hopsnode → its own relationship listYou still need an index to find the start node.
Bounded path patternWalk a few hops safely-[:KNOWS*1..3]-> or ->{1,3}Paths explode on dense graphs. Always set a maximum.
Graph view over tablesGraph queries on relational dataGRAPH_TABLE (g MATCH ... COLUMNS ...)SQL/PGQ is not in PostgreSQL 19 for now.
Recursive CTE with CYCLEGraph walks in plain PostgreSQLCYCLE who SET seen USING trailPostgreSQL 14 or later.
Derived graph indexFast traversal, tables stay the truthgraph.build() in pgGraphThe index must be kept in sync.
Measure on your dataChoose a system honestlyload time, query time, memoryVendor benchmarks pick their winners.

Practice

A query has the pattern (ex:ana ? ex:atlas): subject and object known. Which of SPO, POS, OSP answers it with one range scan?

  • SPO
  • POS
  • OSP

In OSP order the key starts with object, then subject. Both known parts form the prefix.

Why do triple stores replace IRIs with integers?

  • Integers sort strings in the right order.
  • Integers are smaller and faster to compare, and each name is stored once.
  • SPARQL requires it.

Dictionary encoding saves space and time. It does not keep string order.

What does index-free adjacency make cheap?

  • Finding a node by its email
  • Moving from a node to its neighbours
  • Sorting all nodes by name

Each node points to its relationships. Finding the start node still needs an index.

Fill in the missing words.

For quads with four positions, the smallest number of sort orders that covers every pattern is ?.

The ISO standard number for GQL is ISO/IEC ?.

In PostgreSQL, the clause that stops a recursive walk when it returns to a seen value is ?.

What did the hexastore add over three indexes?

All six orders, so every pattern's answers come sorted by either free position, ready for merge joins.

What is the AGM bound for the triangle query with N edges?

At most N^{3/2} answers. Worst-case optimal joins run in about that time.

Which three indexes does Neptune keep by default?

SPOG, POGS and GPSO. OSGP is optional.

What is pgGraph?

A PostgreSQL extension that builds a derived CSR graph index over normal tables. The tables stay the truth.

  1. List the 8 triple patterns (which positions are known) and name the index from SPO, POS, OSP for each.
    Answer

    None known: any. S: SPO. P: POS. O: OSP. S and P: SPO. P and O: POS. S and O: OSP. All three: any, usually SPO.

  2. A planner sees three patterns with 50,000, 400 and 3 matches. In which order should it join them, and why?
    Answer

    3, then 400, then 50,000, if they share variables. Starting small keeps every partial answer small. Each later pattern becomes a cheap lookup with a known variable.

  3. Your graph has one account with 2 million followers. A "friends of friends" query is slow only for that account's neighbours. What is happening, and what can you do?
    Answer

    It is a supernode. Every walk through it reads millions of relationships. Fixes: filter relationships by type or time before walking, cap the fan-out, precompute results for that node, or model the follow relation as a separate summary.

  4. Rewrite the second PostgreSQL query so it only answers "who is reachable from Ana?", with no path and no CYCLE clause.
    Answer

    WITH RECURSIVE r(who) AS (SELECT 'Ana'::text UNION SELECT k.dst FROM r JOIN knows k ON k.src = r.who) SELECT who FROM r; UNION drops repeats, so the cycle cannot loop forever.

  5. Estimate the space for SPO, POS and OSP over 1 billion triples with 8-byte ids, ignoring compression and tree overhead.
    Answer

    One index row is 3 × 8 = 24 bytes. One index is 24 GB. Three indexes are 72 GB, plus the dictionary. With six orders, 144 GB. That is why QLever and others compress.

  6. A team uses PostgreSQL and wants 2-hop and shortest-path queries on 50 million rows, every few seconds. Compare recursive CTEs, Apache AGE and pgGraph for them.
    Answer

    Recursive CTEs need nothing new, but each hop is an index lookup and shortest paths need care. AGE gives Cypher, but it is another extension to keep in step with PostgreSQL versions. pgGraph gives one array step per neighbour, but its CSR index must stay in sync, and I found no published benchmarks. Test all three on a copy of the real data.

Key takeaways

  • Triple stores turn every name into a number with a dictionary, and keep only numbers in the indexes.
  • SPO, POS and OSP cover all 8 triple patterns. Quads need 6 orders. The hexastore keeps all six for merge joins.
  • The join order decides the work. Most selective first can save 100 times the effort.
  • Cyclic queries can blow up pairwise joins. Worst-case optimal joins stay within the AGM bound.
  • Index-free adjacency makes hops cheap. Neo4j's block format keeps a node's data in one 128-byte block.
  • Cypher, ISO GQL (2024) and SQL/PGQ (2023) all draw path patterns. Support for GQL differs by product.
  • In PostgreSQL 18, use recursive CTEs with SEARCH and CYCLE, Apache AGE, or pgGraph's derived CSR index. SQL/PGQ is not in PostgreSQL 19 for now.

Sources

  • Weiss, Karras and Bernstein: Hexastore (PVLDB 2008). Indexing triples in all six orders.
  • Amazon Neptune: How statements are indexed. The 16 quad patterns, the three default indexes and the optional OSGP index.
  • Oxigraph architecture. Term encoding, the index tables in RocksDB and the greedy join order.
  • Neo4j operations manual: store formats. Block, aligned, standard and high_limit formats and their sizes.
  • Ngo, Ré and Rudra: Skew Strikes Back. A short survey of worst-case optimal joins and the AGM bound.
  • evokoa/pggraph on GitHub. README and quickstart for version 1.2.1, with the note on SQL/PGQ and PostgreSQL 19.

Reasoners and materialisation
