A reasoner is the program that finds what follows from an ontology. There are four big strategies: tableau, consequence-based saturation, rules that store every result, and query rewriting. Each one puts the work in a different place. This chapter runs each strategy, measures its cost with small numbers, and ends with a guide for choosing.

  • Name the reasoning services and run them with HermiT.
  • Explain how tableau, consequence-based, rule-based and rewriting reasoners work, and when each is complete.
  • Measure how materialisation grows, and repair it after a deletion with DRed.
  • Find justifications for an inference, by hand and with Pellet.
  • Choose a reasoning strategy for a real project, with numbers.

What a reasoner does

Here is a small university ontology. It says that professors are persons, that seminars are courses, and that a lecturer is a person who teaches some course. It also has a strange class, RoboProf: a robot that is a professor, while robots are not persons. We ask HermiT, a real reasoner, to look at it.

import os, time
from owlready2 import get_ontology, default_world, sync_reasoner

onto = get_ontology("file://" + os.path.abspath("uni.owl")).load()
t = time.perf_counter()
with onto:
    sync_reasoner(debug=0)                       # HermiT: consistency, classes, individuals
print(f"HermiT: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f} s, including the Java start")
print("unsatisfiable:", [c.name for c in default_world.inconsistent_classes()])
print("TeachingProf is a:", sorted(c.name for c in onto.TeachingProf.is_a if hasattr(c, "name")))
print("ada is a:", sorted(c.name for c in onto.ada.is_a))
HermiT: 0.30 s, including the Java start
unsatisfiable: ['RoboProf', 'Nothing']
TeachingProf is a: ['Lecturer', 'Professor']
ada is a: ['Lecturer', 'Professor']

Nobody wrote "a teaching professor is a lecturer". Nobody wrote "Ada is a lecturer". The reasoner found both. It also found that RoboProf can never have a member. This is what a reasoner does. It computes entailments: things that must be true if the axioms are true.

The standard reasoning services
ServiceQuestionIn the example
ConsistencyCan all axioms be true together?yes
SatisfiabilityCan this class have a member?RoboProf: no
ClassificationWhich class is below which?TeachingProf ⊑ Lecturer
RealisationWhich classes does each individual belong to?ada: Lecturer
Entailment checkDoes this one axiom follow?Professor ⊑ Person: yes
Query answeringWhich things match this query, using the axioms?all lecturers: ada
ExplanationWhy does this follow?a later section

The basic tasks reduce to one: consistency. This was shown in Description logics. A good reasoner is sound and complete for its logic. Four families of reasoners reach this in different ways.

Expecting a reasoner to check data like a database. It works under the open world. A missing value is unknown, not an error. To check that every course has a teacher, use SHACL, from SHACL and validation.

Tableau reasoners: HermiT, Pellet, FaCT++

A tableau reasoner proves "every C is a D" by trying to build a C that is not a D. If every attempt ends in a contradiction, the claim holds. You ran this by hand in Description logics. Here we look at speed. We generated ontologies with a class tree and one defined class per node, D_i \equiv \exists r.C_i, and asked HermiT to classify them.

import sys, time, types
from owlready2 import get_ontology, Thing, ObjectProperty, sync_reasoner

n = int(sys.argv[1])
onto = get_ontology(f"http://example.org/gen{n}#")
with onto:
    class r(ObjectProperty): pass
    C = [types.new_class("C0", (Thing,))]
    for i in range(1, n):                        # a class tree, 3 children each
        C.append(types.new_class(f"C{i}", (C[(i - 1) // 3],)))
    D = []
    for i in range(n):                           # D_i is defined as "r some C_i"
        d = types.new_class(f"D{i}", (Thing,))
        d.equivalent_to = [r.some(C[i])]
        D.append(d)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    sync_reasoner(debug=0)                       # HermiT must find D_i below D_parent
    secs = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"n={n:5}: {2*n} classes, D{n-1} is below D0: {D[0] in D[-1].ancestors()}, {secs:.2f} s")
n=   10: 20 classes, D9 is below D0: True, 0.30 s
n= 1000: 2000 classes, D999 is below D0: True, 0.81 s
n= 4000: 8000 classes, D3999 is below D0: True, 1.50 s
n=16000: 32000 classes, D15999 is below D0: True, 5.33 s

About 0.3 seconds is the cost of starting Java. With 32,000 classes there are about 1 billion pairs of classes. HermiT took 5.3 seconds, so it did not test every pair. Real tableau reasoners use many tricks.

  • Absorption. Turn general axioms into rules that fire only for matching nodes. This removes most branching.
  • Smart classification. Use the subclass links you already know. Test only the pairs that could still be new.
  • Caching. Remember which concept sets were already found satisfiable.
  • Backjumping. After a contradiction, go back straight to the choice that caused it, not just one step.
  • Blocking. Stop building a node whose label repeats an ancestor's label. This keeps the model finite.

HermiT uses a hypertableau method by Motik, Shearer and Horrocks (2009). It turns axioms into rule-like clauses and guesses only when it must.

Tableau reasoners in November 2026
ReasonerOriginState I found
HermiTUniversity of Oxford. Java. LGPL.The Oxford page lists 1.3.8. Owlready2 0.51 bundles 1.3.8.1099. It passes all OWL 2 conformance tests for direct semantics, says its page.
PelletClark & Parsia, the company that later became Stardog. Java. AGPL.Owlready2 0.51 bundles 2.3.1. The community project Openllet builds on Pellet. Its README uses version 2.6.5. Pellet is known for explanations.
FaCT++Tsarkov and Horrocks, Manchester. C++.Hard to trace. Debian packages 1.6.5. I could not confirm a newer upstream release. JFact is a Java port.

Trusting a bundled tool without testing it. In my test, owlready2's Pellet path failed on Java 17. One bundled library is built for a newer Java (class file version 69, which is Java 25). The Pellet command line worked when it used the OWL API loader. Always run one small known case first.

Consequence-based reasoning for EL: ELK

For OWL 2 EL, there is a faster way. Do not build models. Just derive new subclass axioms with a few rules until nothing new appears. Watch it on four axioms from our university.

  1. Told: TeachingProf \sqsubseteq Professor and Professor \sqsubseteq Person. So TeachingProf \sqsubseteq Person.
  2. Told: TeachingProf \sqsubseteq \exists teaches.Seminar.
  3. Told: Seminar \sqsubseteq Course. The existential rule gives TeachingProf \sqsubseteq \exists teaches.Course.
  4. Both parts of Lecturer \equiv Person \sqcap \exists teaches.Course now hold. The conjunction rule gives TeachingProf \sqsubseteq Lecturer.
  5. One more round adds nothing new. Stop.

This is consequence-based reasoning. It is also called saturation. The rules only ever derive two shapes of axiom.

The two shapes and the rules (simplified)
RuleIf you haveThen add
SubclassA \sqsubseteq B and B \sqsubseteq CA \sqsubseteq C
ConjunctionA \sqsubseteq B, A \sqsubseteq C and B \sqcap C is used in the ontologyA \sqsubseteq B \sqcap C
ExistentialA \sqsubseteq \exists r.B and B \sqsubseteq C, and \exists r.C is usedA \sqsubseteq \exists r.C
BottomA \sqsubseteq \exists r.B and B \sqsubseteq \botA \sqsubseteq \bot

Why is this fast? Every derived axiom uses only classes and roles that are already in the ontology. With n concepts and m roles there are at most n^2 + m n^2 possible results. So saturation ends in polynomial time. It never branches, because EL has no "or" and no "not".

ELK is the best-known reasoner of this kind. Its page says it classifies SNOMED CT, with around 300,000 classes, in a few seconds on a modern laptop. It runs rules in parallel on many cores. Version 0.6.0 (May 2024) can trace its inferences. That gives proofs in Protégé, and it improves incremental reasoning after deletions.

Running an EL reasoner on axioms outside EL. It may skip them and give fewer answers, often with only a warning. ELK 0.6.0 tracks the features that make its results incomplete. Read those warnings, or check the profile first.

Rule-based materialisation

The third strategy works on data. Apply rules to the facts and store every new fact. Then every query is a plain lookup. Let us measure the cost on two classic cases. One is a chain of parts with a transitive partOf. The other is one thing with many names linked by owl:sameAs.

import time
from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, OWL, RDF
import owlrl

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/")

def chain(n):                                    # part1 partOf part2 partOf ... part_n
    g = Graph()
    g.add((EX.partOf, RDF.type, OWL.TransitiveProperty))
    for i in range(1, n):
        g.add((EX[f"part{i}"], EX.partOf, EX[f"part{i+1}"]))
    return g

def clique(k):                                   # k names for one thing, one fact each
    g = Graph()
    for i in range(1, k):
        g.add((EX[f"n{i}"], OWL.sameAs, EX[f"n{i+1}"]))
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        g.add((EX[f"n{i}"], EX.label, EX[f"fact{i}"]))
    return g

for name, make, sizes, pred in [("chain", chain, (25, 50, 100), EX.partOf),
                                ("sameAs", clique, (5, 10, 20), EX.label)]:
    for n in sizes:
        g = make(n)
        before = len(list(g.triples((None, pred, None))))
        t = time.perf_counter()
        owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)
        secs = time.perf_counter() - t
        after = len(list(g.triples((None, pred, None))))
        print(f"{name:6} n={n:3}: {pred.split('/')[-1]} triples {before:3} -> {after:5},"
              f" all triples {len(g):6}, {secs:5.2f} s")
chain  n= 25: partOf triples  24 ->   300, all triples    434,  0.07 s
chain  n= 50: partOf triples  49 ->  1225, all triples   1384,  0.27 s
chain  n=100: partOf triples  99 ->  4950, all triples   5159,  1.46 s
sameAs n=  5: label triples   5 ->    25, all triples    162,  0.02 s
sameAs n= 10: label triples  10 ->   100, all triples    317,  0.06 s
sameAs n= 20: label triples  20 ->   400, all triples    927,  0.28 s

A chain of n parts gives n(n-1)/2 triples: 4,950 for 100 parts. With k names for one thing, every fact is copied to every name: k^2 label triples. That is 400 for 20 names. This is materialisation. It is forward chaining run to a fixed point. The semi-naive way to do it is in Rules and Datalog.

Let a set of rules be applied to an RDF graph whose triples use n distinct terms, and let no rule create new terms. Then the materialised graph has at most n^3 triples, and forward chaining stops after at most n^3 rounds.

In simple words: rules like the OWL 2 RL rules only recombine names that already exist. A triple has three places and each place holds one of n terms. So there are at most n^3 possible triples. For the chain with 100 parts, about 102 terms appear, so the bound is about a million triples. The real answer, 4,950, is far below it.

Proof

This follows from the least fixed point theorem for Datalog. Each rule application adds triples built only from the n terms. So every derived triple is one of the n^3 possible ones. Each round adds at least one new triple, or the process stops. So there are at most n^3 rounds, and the result is the least fixed point.

Real engines that materialise:

  • owlrl runs the OWL 2 RL rules on an rdflib graph in Python. It is good for learning and small data.
  • RDFox stores all results in memory and keeps them up to date on change. Its explain shortest command shows a proof with the fewest rule steps.
  • GraphDB materialises with rule sets: rdfs, rdfsplus (the default), owl-horst, owl-max, owl2-ql and owl2-rl.
  • Apache Jena has a rule engine with forward, backward and hybrid modes.

Letting owl:sameAs explode. Entity matching can link thousands of records about one company. Then every fact is copied to every name. GraphDB's documentation describes the fix: keep one representative per group of equal names, instead of the full k^2 copies.

Query rewriting for OWL 2 QL

The fourth strategy stores nothing new. It rewrites the question instead. The data stays in SQL tables. Here the ontology says that professors and lecturers are teachers, that anyone who teaches is a teacher, that anything taught is a course, that seminars are courses, and that giving a seminar is a kind of teaching.

# DL-Lite TBox. ("C", B, A): B ⊑ A.  ("Some", r, A): ∃r ⊑ A.  ("Inv", r, A): ∃r⁻ ⊑ A.  ("R", r, s): r ⊑ s
TBOX = [("C", "professor", "teacher"), ("C", "lecturer", "teacher"),
        ("Some", "teaches", "teacher"), ("Inv", "teaches", "course"),
        ("C", "seminar", "course"), ("R", "gives_seminar", "teaches")]

def step(atom):                                  # all ways to replace one atom
    if len(atom) == 2:                           # concept atom: (A, x)
        a, x = atom
        for kind, b, c in TBOX:
            if c == a and kind == "C":    yield (b, x)
            if c == a and kind == "Some": yield (b, x, "_")
            if c == a and kind == "Inv":  yield (b, "_", x)
    else:                                        # role atom: (s, x, y)
        s, x, y = atom
        for kind, r, t in TBOX:
            if kind == "R" and t == s: yield (r, x, y)

def rewrite(query):                              # query = tuple of atoms
    done, todo = set(), [query]
    while todo:
        q = todo.pop()
        if q in done: continue
        done.add(q)
        for i, atom in enumerate(q):
            for new in step(atom):
                todo.append(q[:i] + (new,) + q[i + 1:])
    return done

A second helper, sql(), turns each rewritten query into one SELECT. The script rewrite_run.py joins them with UNION and runs them in SQLite. The tables hold four people: ada is a professor, ben a lecturer, chen gives seminar 7 and dana teaches logic101.

5 queries: ['gives_seminar', 'lecturer', 'professor', 'teacher', 'teaches']
['ada', 'ben', 'chen', 'dana']
40 queries for: teacher(x), teaches(x,y), course(y)
['chen', 'dana']

"Find all teachers" became 5 SELECTs, and all four people came back. No new row was written. This is query rewriting. The classic algorithm for DL-Lite is PerfectRef, by Calvanese and colleagues (2007). OWL 2 QL is designed so that this always works.

A query with k atoms, where each atom can be replaced in m ways, can need m^k rewritten queries. In our example the three atoms had 5, 2 and 4 options: 5 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 = 40 SELECTs.

So rewriting moves the cost from the data to the query. The data is never copied, and it is always fresh. But each question can grow very large. Real systems prune rewritten queries that add nothing. Ontop also folds the ontology into its mappings, which its papers call T-mappings. Ontop 5.5.0 (14 February 2026) supports RDFS and OWL 2 QL over PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, Snowflake, DuckDB and more. Stardog also reasons at query time: its docs say it does not materialise inferences.

Expecting rewriting to handle a transitive property. "Part of a part of a part..." has no fixed length, so no finite UNION of plain queries can express it. That is why OWL 2 QL has no transitive properties. Use materialisation or recursive SQL for that.

Incremental update when facts change

Materialised results go stale when data changes. Adding facts is easy: run semi-naive evaluation from the new facts only. Deleting is hard. A derived fact may have several reasons. If you delete one reason, the fact may still hold.

We tested this on reachability over a chain of 200 nodes, with a shortcut every 10 nodes. We deleted one edge in two places. We compared DRed with a full recomputation.

def dred(reach, edges, gone):                    # delete one edge, then repair
    old, edges = succ_of(edges), edges - {gone}
    new, (u, v) = succ_of(edges), gone
    over = {(x, v) for x, y in reach if y == u} | {gone}       # 1. over-delete
    work = forward(over, set(over), old)
    reach -= over
    back = {(x, z) for x, z in over                             # 2. re-derive
            if z in new[x] or any(z in new[y] for y in new if (x, y) in reach)}
    reach |= back
    work += len(over) + forward(reach, back, new)              # 3. carry on
    return edges, len(over), len(back), work
delete (190, 191): 20100 -> 19909 facts, over-deleted 1910, put back 1719, DRed work 5157, recompute work 21419, same: True
delete (5, 6): 20100 -> 18930 facts, over-deleted 1170, put back 0, DRed work 2448, recompute work 20517, same: True

Both repairs give the same result as recomputing from zero, with 4 to 8 times less work. Look at the first line. DRed deleted 1,910 facts, then put 1,719 back, because the shortcut from 190 to 192 still reaches them. That wasted work is the weak point of DRed.

Over-delete

Delete the fact, and every stored fact that has at least one derivation through it. Some of these are still true.

Re-derive

For each deleted fact, check if one rule can still derive it from the facts that are left. Put those back.

Carry on

Run forward chaining from the facts you put back, until nothing new appears.

Backward/Forward

Motik, Nenov, Piro and Horrocks (2015) check for another proof before deleting. This avoids most of the wasted over-deletion.

Ways to keep stored results up to date
MethodIdeaCost
Recomputethrow everything away, start againsimple, slow for big data
Countingstore how many derivations each fact hasexact for rules without recursion. Recursion needs more care.
DRed (Gupta, Mumick and Subrahmanian, 1993)over-delete, then re-deriveno extra storage, but wasted work on facts with other proofs
Backward/Forward (2015)look for another proof before deletingless waste, more lookups
GraphDB "smooth delete"forward chain from the deleted facts, then a backward isSupported() checkits docs say tracking every statement would need up to 90% of the storage

Trying to delete a derived fact. If "Ada is a lecturer" was derived, deleting it does nothing useful. The rules derive it again. RDFox, for example, only lets you delete explicit facts. Delete or change the cause instead.

Explanations and justifications

A reasoner says "Ada is a lecturer". A user asks: why? We gave Ada a second course, logic101, so there are two reasons. Pellet and a small Python program both found them.

java -cp "$PELLET_JARS" pellet.Pellet explain --instance ada,Lecturer --max 5 uni2.owl
Axiom: ada type Lecturer

Explanation(s):
1)   Professor subClassOf Person
     Lecturer equivalentTo Person
                           and teaches some Course
     ada type Professor
     sem7 type Seminar
     Seminar subClassOf Course
     ada teaches sem7

2)   Professor subClassOf Person
     Lecturer equivalentTo Person
                           and teaches some Course
     ada type Professor
     ada teaches logic101
     logic101 type Course
from rdflib import Graph, URIRef, RDF
import owlrl

PRE = """@prefix : <http://example.org/uni#> . @prefix owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .\n"""
AXIOMS = {                                       # one Turtle line per axiom
 "A1 Professor ⊑ Person": ":Professor rdfs:subClassOf :Person .",
 "A2 Seminar ⊑ Course":   ":Seminar rdfs:subClassOf :Course .",
 "A3 Lecturer ≡ Person ⊓ ∃teaches.Course": """:Lecturer owl:equivalentClass [ owl:intersectionOf
     ( :Person [ a owl:Restriction ; owl:onProperty :teaches ; owl:someValuesFrom :Course ] ) ] .""",
 "A4 Professor(ada)": ":ada a :Professor .",
 "A5 teaches(ada, sem7)": ":ada :teaches :sem7 .",
 "A6 Seminar(sem7)": ":sem7 a :Seminar .",
 "A7 teaches(ada, logic101)": ":ada :teaches :logic101 .",
 "A8 Course(logic101)": ":logic101 a :Course .",
}
U = "http://example.org/uni#"
GOAL, calls = (URIRef(U + "ada"), RDF.type, URIRef(U + "Lecturer")), 0
def entails(names):                              # the oracle: run the OWL RL rules
    global calls; calls += 1
    g = Graph().parse(data=PRE + "\n".join(AXIOMS[n] for n in names), format="turtle")
    owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)
    return GOAL in g
def shrink(names):                               # black box: drop what is not needed
    keep = list(names)
    for n in list(keep):
        if entails([m for m in keep if m != n]):
            keep.remove(n)
    return keep
found, todo, seen = [], [frozenset(AXIOMS)], set()   # a small hitting-set tree
while todo:
    base = todo.pop()
    if base in seen: continue
    seen.add(base)
    j = next((j for j in found if j <= base), None)      # reuse a known one
    if j is None:
        if not entails(sorted(base)): continue
        j = frozenset(shrink(sorted(base))); found.append(j)
    todo += [base - {n} for n in j]              # remove one axiom of j, look again
for j in found: print(sorted(j))
print("oracle calls:", calls)
['A1 Professor ⊑ Person', 'A3 Lecturer ≡ Person ⊓ ∃teaches.Course', 'A4 Professor(ada)', 'A7 teaches(ada, logic101)', 'A8 Course(logic101)']
['A1 Professor ⊑ Person', 'A2 Seminar ⊑ Course', 'A3 Lecturer ≡ Person ⊓ ∃teaches.Course', 'A4 Professor(ada)', 'A5 teaches(ada, sem7)', 'A6 Seminar(sem7)']
oracle calls: 32

In the Pellet command, PELLET_JARS lists the jar files that owlready2 ships, for example /home/you/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/owlready2/pellet/*. The command line worked on Java 17. The Python script uses owlrl as its yes-or-no oracle, so it finds the same two reasons with RL rules.

A justification for an entailment \alpha of an ontology O is a set J \subseteq O such that J \models \alpha, and no proper subset of J entails \alpha.

Each justification is one complete reason. Remove any axiom from it and that reason breaks. The two reasons share three axioms: A1, A3 and A4.

There are two ways to find justifications.

  • Black box. Use any reasoner as a yes-or-no oracle. Remove axioms one by one while the entailment still holds. To find all justifications, use a hitting-set tree, as in the 2007 work by Kalyanpur, Parsia, Horridge and Sirin. Our 8 axioms needed 32 reasoner calls.
  • Glass box. The reasoner records which axioms each step used. It is faster, but it must be built into the reasoner. Pellet has both methods: --method glass or black.

Justifications can still be hard to read. Matthew Horridge proposed laconic justifications in 2008. They keep only the parts of each axiom that matter. RDFox and ELK give proofs: chains of rule steps, often the shortest one.

Deleting the first axiom you see in an explanation. That axiom may support many good inferences. If there are several justifications, removing one axiom may not even help. You must break every justification. Choose the axiom that is really wrong, not the one that is easy to delete.

Cost in time and memory

Each strategy puts the work in a different place. This picture shows where.

What we measured in this chapter (Apple M2 Pro, Python 3.14, Java 17)
TestSizeResultLesson
HermiT classification32,000 classes5.3 sReal tableau reasoners are far below their worst case on simple trees.
Java start for HermiT20 classes0.3 sFor tiny ontologies, start-up costs more than reasoning.
owlrl, transitive chain100 parts99 → 4,950 triples, 1.5 sTransitive closure grows with the square.
owlrl, sameAs group20 names20 → 400 label triplesEqual names copy every fact.
QL rewriting3 atoms40 SELECTsRewriting grows with the query, not the data.
DRed after one deletion20,100 facts2,448 to 5,157 steps instead of 20,517 to 21,419Incremental repair pays off.

Worst-case theory says the same things in general form. OWL 2 DL is N2ExpTime-complete, EL is polynomial, RL is polynomial in the data, and QL query answering is in AC0 for data complexity. The details are in Description logics and OWL 2.

Memory follows the same pattern. Materialisation stores every inferred triple, so plan disk and RAM for the closure, not for the input. A tableau reasoner keeps the whole ontology and its models in memory, so a schema with millions of axioms needs a big Java heap. Rewriting needs almost no extra memory, but the database must run the big queries.

Choosing a strategy

Start from three questions. What do you reason about: the schema or the data? How often does the data change? Where does the data live?

Strategies side by side
StrategyBest forComplete forMain cost
Tableauschema design, debugging, rich axiomsOWL 2 DLcan be slow on big or tricky schemas
Consequence-basedvery large class hierarchiesOWL 2 ELignores axioms outside EL
Materialisationmany queries over a stable RDF graphOWL 2 RL, RDFS, Datalog rulesload time, storage, repair after changes
Query rewritinglive data in SQL that you cannot copyOWL 2 QL, RDFSbig queries, no transitivity

A common setup uses two of them. Classify the schema with HermiT or ELK when it changes. Store the class tree. Then materialise RL rules over the data, or rewrite queries over SQL, using that tree.

A typical question: "The data changes every second and lives in PostgreSQL. Which strategy?" Answer: query rewriting with OWL 2 QL, because nothing must be recomputed when data changes. Then name the price: no transitive properties, and bigger queries.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for reasoning in practice
PatternPurposeModelNote
Everything is consistencyReduce any check to one testC ⊑ D iff C ⊓ ¬D is unsatisfiableInstance checks work the same way.
Classify once, reuseFast schema answersstore the class tree after each schema changeRe-run when the TBox changes, not for every query.
Saturate ELHuge vocabulariesderive only A ⊑ B and A ⊑ ∃r.BAxioms outside EL may be skipped.
Materialise RLFast queries on RDF dataDeductiveClosure(OWLRL_Semantics)Plan for n(n−1)/2 with transitive chains.
One representative per sameAs groupStop k² copiespick one name, map the others to itShow all names in results if users need them.
Rewrite for QLData stays in SQLteacher(x) becomes 5 SELECTs with UNIONGrows like m^k with query size. No transitivity.
Semi-naive for additionsCheap insertsrun rules from the new facts onlyDeletions need DRed or B/F.
DRed for deletionsRepair stored resultsover-delete, re-derive, carry onWastes work on facts with other proofs.
Delete causes, not conclusionsChange derived factsremove "ada teaches sem7", not "ada is a Lecturer"Derived facts come back after the next run.
Find all justificationsExplain and debugpellet explain --max 5Break every justification, not just one.
Check the profile firstAvoid silent missing answerstest the ontology against EL, QL or RLEngines rarely fail loudly outside their profile.

Practice

Which service finds the most specific classes of each individual?

  • Classification
  • Realisation
  • Satisfiability

Classification is about classes. Realisation is about individuals.

A chain of 200 parts uses a transitive partOf. How many partOf triples does materialisation store?

  • 199
  • 400
  • 19,900

n(n−1)/2 = 200 · 199 / 2 = 19,900.

Why does OWL 2 QL leave out transitive properties?

  • They are rarely used.
  • Queries over them cannot be rewritten into a finite union of plain SQL queries.
  • Tableau reasoners cannot handle them.

A path of any length needs recursion. A finite UNION has a fixed depth.

Fill in the missing words.

The deletion method that over-deletes and then re-derives is called ?.

A smallest set of axioms that still entails a statement is a ?.

The reasoner built for OWL 2 EL that classifies SNOMED CT in seconds is ?.

Where does each strategy put the work?

Materialisation: at load and on change. Rewriting: at each query. Classification: when the schema changes.

Why is EL saturation polynomial?

It only derives A ⊑ B and A ⊑ ∃r.B over existing names, and it never branches.

Black box or glass box: which works with any reasoner?

Black box. It only needs yes-or-no answers.

What does GraphDB do instead of storing k² sameAs copies?

It keeps one representative name per group of equal names.

  1. Use the EL rules to show that TeachingProf \sqsubseteq Person \sqcap \exists teaches.Course. Name the rule at each step.
    Answer

    Subclass rule twice gives TeachingProf ⊑ Person. The told axiom gives TeachingProf ⊑ ∃teaches.Seminar. The existential rule with Seminar ⊑ Course gives TeachingProf ⊑ ∃teaches.Course. The conjunction rule joins the two.

  2. An ontology has 10 people who are all owl:sameAs each other, and each has 5 facts. How many fact triples does full materialisation store, and how many with one representative?
    Answer

    Full: every name gets all 50 facts, so 10 × 50 = 500. With one representative: the 50 facts on one name, plus a map of 10 names.

  3. Rewrite the query "find all courses" with the TBox of this chapter. List the SELECTs.
    Answer

    Four: course(id), seminar(id), the what column of teaches, and the what column of gives_seminar (via gives_seminar ⊑ teaches and ∃teaches⁻ ⊑ Course).

  4. In the DRed test, why were 1,719 facts deleted and then put back when the edge 190→191 was removed?
    Answer

    Every node up to 190 reached 192 to 200 through 191, so DRed deleted those facts first. But the shortcut 190→192 gives another proof. Re-derivation found it and restored them. Only the 191 facts that reach node 191 were really gone.

  5. A class is unsatisfiable with three justifications. They share one axiom, A5. A colleague deletes A2, which is in only one of them. Is the class fixed?
    Answer

    No. Two justifications remain, so the class is still unsatisfiable. Removing A5 breaks all three, but first check that A5 is really wrong, and what else depends on it.

  6. A hospital has 400,000 classes in an EL vocabulary, 50 million patient records in PostgreSQL that change all day, and wants "all patients with any heart disease". Design the reasoning setup.
    Answer

    Classify the vocabulary with ELK when it changes, and store the class tree as a table. Keep patient data in PostgreSQL. Answer the query by rewriting: "heart disease" becomes the list of its subclasses from the stored tree, joined with the records. Nothing is materialised over the changing data. Test with a few known patients first.

Key takeaways

  • A reasoner computes entailments: consistency, satisfiability, classification, realisation and query answers.
  • Tableau reasoners like HermiT and Pellet are complete for OWL 2 DL and use many tricks to stay fast in practice.
  • Consequence-based reasoners like ELK saturate EL axioms in polynomial time, without branching.
  • Materialisation stores every inferred triple. Watch transitive chains (n²/2) and sameAs groups (k²).
  • Query rewriting keeps data in place and grows the query instead. It cannot handle transitivity.
  • Additions are easy to maintain. Deletions need DRed or Backward/Forward.
  • A justification is a minimal set of axioms for an entailment. Break all of them to remove an inference.
  • Choose by what you reason about, how often data changes, and where the data lives.

Sources

  • HermiT OWL Reasoner. The Oxford page: hypertableau, conformance and licence.
  • ELK reasoner releases. What version 0.6.0 adds: tracing, proofs, incompleteness tracking and incremental changes.
  • GraphDB 11.5: Reasoning. Forward chaining, rule sets, smooth delete and the sameAs optimisation.
  • RDFox: Reasoning. Materialisation, incremental updates and explanations with shortest proofs.
  • Ontop guide. A virtual knowledge graph system with RDFS and OWL 2 QL over SQL databases.
  • Stardog: Inference engine. Reasoning at query time by rewriting, without materialisation.

The ontology engineering method

Anyone can write a few classes in Turtle. A team that must keep an ontology alive for years needs a method. This chapter shows that method as everyday work: questions first, reuse, clear names, modules, versions, tests and review.

  • Write competency questions and a scope for a new ontology.
  • Find and reuse terms instead of inventing them.
  • Name, document, split and version an ontology in a way others can follow.
  • Turn competency questions, lint checks and shapes into automatic tests.
  • Plan review, governance and FAIR publication, and pick the right tools.

Start with questions

A security team wants a small ontology about software packages. They want to know which programs are in danger when a library has a flaw. Before they write one class, they write questions.

  1. CQ1. Which releases does the package fastjson have?
  2. CQ2. Which releases need, directly or indirectly, a release with a known flaw?
  3. CQ3. In which release was flaw-42 fixed?
  4. CQ4. Who maintains the packages that a flaw affects?
  5. CQ5. Which releases use a license that our company does not allow?

These are competency questions, or CQs. Michael Grüninger and Mark Fox made them famous in 1995, in the TOVE project. You met that story in The ontology engineering era. Here we use CQs as a working tool.

A CQ does three jobs at once.

  • It sets the scope. No question asks about prices, so prices stay out.
  • It gives you terms. The nouns become candidate classes: package, release, flaw, license, person. The verbs become candidate properties: has, needs, fixed in, maintains.
  • It becomes a test. Later you write each CQ as a SPARQL query with a known answer. If the query fails, the ontology is not finished.

What is a package? Tell me everything about security. Is the data good?

Which releases need a release with a known flaw? The answer is a list of releases.

A good CQ has a clear type of answer: a list of things, a number, yes or no. You can check it with real example data. A weak CQ is a topic, not a question.

Write the scope down

The NeOn method gives a short template for this, the ORSD. Its parts are purpose, scope, implementation language, intended end users, intended uses, requirements and a first glossary of terms. The requirements part holds the CQs. A one-page ORSD is enough for most projects.

Scope of the package ontology
In scopeOut of scope
Packages, releases, dependenciesSource code and files inside a package
Known flaws and the releases that fix themHow to exploit a flaw
Maintainers and licensesPrices, contracts, invoices

Do not start with a long list of classes "just in case". Every class should help answer at least one CQ. A class that answers nothing is cost without value. Remove it, or write the missing question first.

Reuse first

Our team needs a class for a person and a property for a license. Should they write pkg:Person and pkg:license? No. Others solved this years ago.

@prefix foaf:    <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
@prefix dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .

pkg:ana a foaf:Person ; foaf:name "Ana" .            # FOAF already has Person
pkg:fastjson-1.3.0 dcterms:license
    <https://spdx.org/licenses/MIT> .                 # an IRI, not free text

Reuse saves time. It also makes your data join with other data for free. A tool that knows FOAF understands pkg:ana at once. This is the second step of the Ontology 101 guide that you meet below.

Where to look

  • OLS, the Ontology Lookup Service of EMBL-EBI. Its API listed 289 ontologies when we checked on 15 November 2026. Most are from life science.
  • BioPortal and the OBO Foundry list, for biology and medicine.
  • schema.org, for web data about products, people, events and places.
  • LOV, Linked Open Vocabularies, a catalogue of web vocabularies. Its main page gave an error when we checked in November 2026. Check whether it is back.
  • W3C and Dublin Core, for the common core: SKOS, PROV-O, Dublin Core terms, OWL-Time.

The chapter Ontologies in the wild gives a page for many of these.

Three ways to reuse

From light to heavy reuse
WayHowGood for
Use the IRIJust write foaf:Person in your data.Small, common terms. No logic needed.
Extract a moduleCopy only the terms you need, plus what they depend on.A few terms from a huge ontology.
Importowl:imports the whole ontology.You need all its axioms for reasoning.

Before you reuse, check five things. Is there a clear license? Is it still maintained? Do other projects use it? Does its definition mean what you mean? Does every term have a definition?

pkg:fastjson foaf:maintainer pkg:ana .   # FOAF has no such term

You invented a term inside someone else's namespace.

pkg:fastjson pkg:maintainer pkg:ana .    # your own term, your own namespace

New terms live in your namespace. Reused terms keep their real IRIs.

The wrong tab above is called namespace hijacking. The OOPS! scanner calls it pitfall P40 and rates it critical. The opposite mistake is also common: copying foaf:Person to a new IRI pkg:Person. Now two IRIs mean one thing, and your data no longer joins.

The Ontology 101 steps

In 2001 Natalya Noy and Deborah McGuinness at Stanford wrote "Ontology Development 101". It is still the most read first guide. It uses wine and food as its example. It starts with three rules.

  1. There is no one correct model of a domain. The best one depends on the use.
  2. Building an ontology is iterative. You will change your first version.
  3. Classes and properties should be close to the nouns and verbs of the domain.

Then it gives seven steps. Here they are, with our package ontology as the example.

Determine the domain and scope

What does it cover? Who uses it? Which questions must it answer? Our answer: packages and flaws, for a security team, CQ1 to CQ5.

Consider reusing existing ontologies

Search first. We take foaf:Person and dcterms:license.

Enumerate important terms

Write every term you need. Do not sort yet. Package, release, version, flaw, fix, maintainer, license, depends.

Define the classes and the hierarchy

Pick the terms for things that exist on their own: Package, Release, Vulnerability. Build the tree top-down, bottom-up or from the middle.

Define the properties

The guide calls them slots. hasRelease, dependsOn, affects, maintainer, versionString.

Define the facets of the properties

Facets are limits: the value type, how many values, the allowed values. A release has exactly one version string. Today you write many facets as OWL restrictions or SHACL shapes.

Create instances

Add real examples: fastjson, release 1.2.0, flaw-42. Then check them against the CQs.

Steps 4 and 5 go together. The guide itself says it is hard to finish one before the other. In practice you loop through steps 3 to 7 many times.

Top-down, bottom-up or middle-out

For step 4 the guide names three ways. Top-down starts with general classes like Software, then splits them. Bottom-up starts with concrete leaves, like "npm package" and "Rust crate", then groups them. Middle-out starts with the classes people use every day, like Package, then goes up and down. The guide says the middle way is often the easiest.

The guide was written for frame systems like Protégé-2000. Words like "slot" and "facet" come from there. The ideas carry over to OWL. The patterns in The 15 modelling patterns help with steps 4 to 6.

Methods in brief

Ontology 101 is a short guide. Larger projects use a full method. Four are worth knowing by name.

Four ontology engineering methods
MethodFromMain idea
METHONTOLOGYFernández, Gómez-Pérez and Juristo, Madrid, 1997Ideas from software engineering. Management, development and support activities. The ontology grows as a series of prototypes.
NeOnSuárez-Figueroa, Gómez-Pérez and others, 2009 paper, 2012 bookNine scenarios. Each one is a path for a common situation, like reusing a thesaurus or translating an ontology.
eXtreme Design (XD)Presutti, Gangemi and others, 2009Ideas from agile software. Match each small group of CQs to an ontology design pattern. Test each piece.
LOT (Linked Open Terms)Poveda-Villalón and others, 2022A light method for industry. Strong on reuse of terms and on publishing the ontology on the web.

METHONTOLOGY

METHONTOLOGY groups the work into three kinds. Management means planning, control and quality checks. Development means specification, conceptualization, formalization and implementation. Support runs all the time: knowledge acquisition, evaluation, integration, documentation and configuration management. In the conceptualization step you fill tables: a glossary of terms, concept trees, binary relation diagrams and a concept dictionary.

The nine NeOn scenarios

NeOn starts from one fact: you rarely build alone or from zero. So it describes nine paths. Scenario 1 goes from specification to implementation, and every project uses it. The others add work to it.

Ontology design patterns and eXtreme Design

An ontology design pattern is a small model you can copy. The portal ontologydesignpatterns.org collects them. A content pattern solves a domain problem, like "who took part in an event". eXtreme Design uses them like this.

  1. Take one small story from the users and its CQs.
  2. Find a content pattern whose own CQs match yours.
  3. Specialise the pattern for your domain and add it to the ontology.
  4. Write the CQs as tests and run them.
  5. Integrate the piece, run all old tests again, and take the next story.
  1. 1995 Competency questions. Grüninger and Fox publish the TOVE method.
  2. 1997 METHONTOLOGY. Ontology building as engineering, at an AAAI symposium.
  3. 2001 Ontology Development 101. The seven steps, from Stanford.
  4. 2009 NeOn scenarios and eXtreme Design. Networks of ontologies and pattern-based design.
  5. 2014 OOPS! The pitfall scanner is described in a journal paper.
  6. 2016 FAIR principles. Rules for data that people and machines can reuse.
  7. 2022 LOT. A light method for industry, with FAIR in mind.

Do not follow a method like a law. All of them say the same core thing: questions first, reuse, small steps, test, review. Pick the parts your team needs and write them down.

Names, labels and definitions

Look at two real styles. The Gene Ontology names a class GO_0006915. Its label is "apoptotic process". Our package ontology names a class pkg:Release. Its label is "release". Both are fine. They choose a different trade.

Opaque IRIs

An opaque IRI is a number. You can fix a typo in the label and the IRI stays the same. Large ontologies like the OBO ones use this style.

Readable IRIs

A readable IRI is a word, like pkg:dependsOn. Queries are easy to read. But if the name was wrong, the IRI is wrong for ever.

Whatever you pick, follow a written naming convention. This one is common for readable IRIs.

  • Classes: singular nouns in UpperCamelCase: Release, Vulnerability.
  • Properties: verbs or verb phrases in lowerCamelCase: dependsOn, fixedIn.
  • Labels: one rdfs:label per language, in normal words: "depends on"@en.
  • Definitions: one skos:definition per term. Synonyms go in skos:altLabel.

A good definition names the parent class first, then the difference. This shape is called genus and differentia. "A release is a version of a package that the maintainers published."

pkg:Releases a owl:Class .                 # plural
pkg:release_class a owl:Class .            # "class" in the name
pkg:DependsOn a owl:ObjectProperty .       # property with a capital
pkg:Flaw rdfs:label "release"@en .         # two classes, one label
pkg:Release a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "release"@en ;
    skos:definition "A version of a package that the maintainers published."@en .
pkg:dependsOn a owl:ObjectProperty ;
    rdfs:label "depends on"@en .

Persistent IRIs

Your IRIs must work for years. Do not use a server name that may change. The service w3id.org, run by a W3C community group, gives permanent addresses. You add a redirect file to its GitHub repository with a pull request. Then https://w3id.org/yourproject/ sends readers to wherever your files live today.

Do not put a version number inside every term IRI, like pkg/1.0/Release. Then each release makes new terms, and all old data breaks. Version the ontology document. Keep term IRIs stable.

Modules and imports

The package ontology grows. The license part and the security part change at different speeds and have different experts. So the team splits it.

A module is a part of an ontology in its own file, with its own IRI. You join modules with owl:imports.

<http://example.org/pkg-security> a owl:Ontology ;
    owl:imports <http://example.org/pkg-core/1.1.0> .   # pin one version

Imports follow each other. If A imports B and B imports C, then A sees C too. All of this together is the import closure. A reasoner works on the whole import closure.

When you need only a few terms from a big ontology, extract a module instead. ROBOT, a command-line tool from the OBO world, has robot extract. Its methods include:

  • BOT: the seed terms and everything above them. The ROBOT docs call it the most used method.
  • STAR: a small module with the seed terms and the links between them.
  • TOP: the seed terms and everything below them. Often large.
  • MIREOT: copy the terms and their place in the tree, but not all the logic.
robot extract --method BOT --input big.owl \
  --term-file my-terms.txt --output imports/big_import.owl

Do not import a huge ontology for one term. The reasoner then works on all of it. Also watch the closure. OWL 2 says it should not hold two different versions of the same ontology. Pin versions in your imports, and update them on purpose.

Versioning and deprecation

Here is the header of version 1.1.0 of the package ontology. It also retires one old property.

<http://example.org/pkg> a owl:Ontology ;
    owl:versionIRI   <http://example.org/pkg/1.1.0> ;   # this exact version
    owl:versionInfo  "1.1.0" ;
    owl:priorVersion <http://example.org/pkg/1.0.0> ;   # the one before
    dcterms:license  <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/> .

pkg:fixedIn a owl:ObjectProperty ;                     # new in 1.1.0
    rdfs:label "fixed in"@en ;
    skos:definition "Links a flaw to the first release without it."@en .

pkg:licenseName a owl:DatatypeProperty ;               # retired, never deleted
    rdfs:label "license name"@en ;
    owl:deprecated true ;
    dcterms:isReplacedBy dcterms:license .

Each OWL ontology can have two names. The ontology IRI names the series: "the package ontology". The version IRI names one release. Data and imports can point to either one. OWL 2 also has owl:backwardCompatibleWith and owl:incompatibleWith to say how two versions relate.

What kind of change is it?

Many teams borrow semantic versioning from software. It is a team convention, not an ontology standard.

Version numbers for ontology changes
ChangeExampleNew version
Fix text onlyCorrect a typo in a label1.1.0 to 1.1.1
Add or deprecateAdd pkg:fixedIn, retire pkg:licenseName1.0.0 to 1.1.0
Break old dataRemove a term, or change its meaning1.1.0 to 2.0.0

Some groups, like OBO projects, use release dates in the version IRI instead of numbers. That works too. The point is that every release has its own stable IRI.

Deprecate, never delete

Old data and old queries still use the old IRI. If you delete it, they break without a warning. So mark it instead. This is deprecation.

  1. Add owl:deprecated true. OWL 2 defines this annotation for exactly this job.
  2. Point to the replacement. OBO projects use the property "term replaced by" (IAO:0100001). We used dcterms:isReplacedBy.
  3. Remove its logical axioms, so reasoning does not depend on it. Keep its label and definition.
  4. Many OBO projects also start the label with "obsolete". That is a convention. The real signal is owl:deprecated.
  5. Write the change in the release notes. Tell the known users.

The OBO Foundry makes this a rule. Its principle 19, "Term Stability", says the meaning of a term must not change and an obsolete term keeps its identifier.

The worst change is silent. A team keeps the IRI pkg:Release but changes its meaning from "a published version" to "a build". Every old query still runs and now gives wrong answers. If the meaning changes, make a new term and deprecate the old one.

Testing: questions, lints and shapes

Now the CQs from the first section become tests. A test file lists each question, its SPARQL query and the answer we expect from a small set of example data.

# Each competency question: a SPARQL query and the answers we expect.
CQS = [
    ("CQ1 Which releases does fastjson have?",
     "SELECT ?x WHERE { pkg:fastjson pkg:hasRelease ?x }",
     {"fastjson-1.2.0", "fastjson-1.3.0"}),
    ("CQ2 Which releases need a release with a known flaw?",
     "SELECT ?x WHERE { ?v pkg:affects ?bad . ?x pkg:dependsOn+ ?bad }",
     {"tinyhttp-2.0.0", "webapp-0.9.0"}),
    ("CQ3 In which release was flaw-42 fixed?",
     "SELECT ?x WHERE { pkg:flaw-42 pkg:fixedIn ?x }",
     {"fastjson-1.3.0"}),
]

The example data is small. It has three packages, five releases, one flaw and two people. Release webapp 0.9.0 needs tinyhttp 2.0.0, which needs fastjson 1.2.0, which has the flaw.

The checker runs three kinds of test. It runs the CQs. It lints the ontology, like a spell checker for models. It validates the data with a SHACL shape that says "a release has exactly one version string and belongs to exactly one package". You know shapes from SHACL and validation.

import sys
from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, RDF, OWL, Literal
from rdflib.namespace import SKOS, SH
from pyshacl import validate
from cqs import CQS

PKG = Namespace("http://example.org/pkg#")
onto, data = Graph().parse(sys.argv[1]), Graph()
for f in sys.argv[2:]:
    data.parse(f)
fails = 0

for name, query, want in CQS:                       # 1. competency questions
    rows = (onto + data).query(query, initNs={"pkg": PKG})
    got = {str(r[0]).removeprefix(PKG) for r in rows}
    ok = got == want
    fails += not ok
    print("PASS" if ok else "FAIL", name, "" if ok else f"got {sorted(got)}")

kinds = (OWL.Class, OWL.ObjectProperty, OWL.DatatypeProperty)
terms = {t for k in kinds for t in onto.subjects(RDF.type, k)}
used = {p for p in data.predicates() if p.startswith(PKG)}
used |= {c for c in data.objects(None, RDF.type) if c.startswith(PKG)}
problems = [("ERROR no definition:", t) for t in terms if not onto.value(t, SKOS.definition)]
problems += [("ERROR not in ontology:", t) for t in used - terms]
for label, t in sorted(problems):                   # 2. lint the ontology
    fails += 1
    print(label, onto.qname(t))
for t in sorted(used):
    if onto.value(t, OWL.deprecated) == Literal(True):
        print("WARN deprecated term in data:", onto.qname(t))

shapes = Graph().parse("shapes.ttl")                # 3. SHACL on the data
conforms, report, _ = validate(data, shacl_graph=shapes)
for focus in sorted(report.objects(None, SH.focusNode)):
    fails += 1
    print("ERROR shape:", onto.qname(focus))
print(f"{fails} problem(s)")
sys.exit(1 if fails else 0)
use oxigraph::io::RdfFormat;
use oxigraph::model::Term;
use oxigraph::sparql::{QueryResults, SparqlEvaluator};
use oxigraph::store::Store;
use std::collections::BTreeSet;

const PKG: &str = "http://example.org/pkg#";
const CQS: [(&str, &str, &[&str]); 3] = [
    ("CQ1", "SELECT ?x WHERE { pkg:fastjson pkg:hasRelease ?x }",
     &["fastjson-1.2.0", "fastjson-1.3.0"]),
    ("CQ2", "SELECT ?x WHERE { ?v pkg:affects ?bad . ?x pkg:dependsOn+ ?bad }",
     &["tinyhttp-2.0.0", "webapp-0.9.0"]),
    ("CQ3", "SELECT ?x WHERE { pkg:flaw-42 pkg:fixedIn ?x }", &["fastjson-1.3.0"]),
];

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let store = Store::new()?; // in memory
    for f in ["pkg-1.1.0.ttl", "data.ttl", "data-fix.ttl"] {
        store.load_from_reader(RdfFormat::Turtle, std::fs::File::open(f)?)?;
    }
    let mut fails = 0;
    for (name, body, want) in CQS {
        let query = format!("PREFIX pkg: <{PKG}> {body}");
        let mut got = BTreeSet::new();
        let results = SparqlEvaluator::new().parse_query(&query)?.on_store(&store).execute()?;
        if let QueryResults::Solutions(rows) = results {
            for row in rows {
                if let Some(Term::NamedNode(n)) = row?.get("x") {
                    got.insert(n.as_str().trim_start_matches(PKG).to_string());
                }
            }
        }
        let ok = got == want.iter().map(|s| s.to_string()).collect();
        fails += !ok as u32;
        println!("{} {name} {got:?}", if ok { "PASS" } else { "FAIL" });
    }
    println!("{fails} problem(s)");
    std::process::exit(if fails > 0 { 1 } else { 0 });
}

First we run the Python checker on version 1.0.0. That version has no fixedIn yet. We wrote CQ3 before the property, on purpose.

uv run --with rdflib --with pyshacl python3.14 check.py pkg-1.0.0.ttl data.ttl
PASS CQ1 Which releases does fastjson have?
PASS CQ2 Which releases need a release with a known flaw?
FAIL CQ3 In which release was flaw-42 fixed? got []
ERROR no definition: pkg:affects
ERROR shape: pkg:oldlib-0.1.0
3 problem(s)

Three real problems. CQ3 has no answer. A property has no definition. One release in the data belongs to no package. The exit code is 1, so a build server would stop here. Then we fix all three: version 1.1.0 adds fixedIn and the definition, and a small data file adds the fix fact and the missing package.

uv run --with rdflib --with pyshacl python3.14 check.py pkg-1.1.0.ttl data.ttl data-fix.ttl
PASS CQ1 Which releases does fastjson have?
PASS CQ2 Which releases need a release with a known flaw?
PASS CQ3 In which release was flaw-42 fixed?
WARN deprecated term in data: pkg:licenseName
0 problem(s)

Now everything passes. The warning is useful: some data still uses the retired property. A warning does not stop the build. The Rust version runs the same three CQs with Oxigraph and prints PASS three times and 0 problem(s). We ran both with rdflib 7.6.0, pySHACL 0.40.2, Python 3.14, Rust 1.99 and the oxigraph crate 0.5.13.

The same checks with ROBOT

OBO teams run such checks with ROBOT. robot report runs a fixed set of quality queries. It has three levels: ERROR must be fixed before a release, WARN should be fixed soon, INFO should be fixed if possible. By default it fails on any ERROR. robot verify runs your own SELECT queries. Each query finds violations, so an empty result means "pass".

PREFIX owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
# A violation is any class or property with no definition.
SELECT ?term WHERE {
  VALUES ?kind { owl:Class owl:ObjectProperty owl:DatatypeProperty }
  ?term a ?kind .
  FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?term skos:definition ?d }
  FILTER (!isBlank(?term))
}

We ran this query with rdflib. On version 1.0.0 it returns one row, pkg:affects. On version 1.1.0 it returns nothing.

robot report --input pkg.ttl --fail-on ERROR --output report.tsv
robot verify --input pkg.ttl --queries no-definition.rq --output-dir results/

A full test suite has one more layer: a reasoner. It checks that the ontology is consistent and that no class is unsatisfiable. See Reasoners and materialisation, and the tested HermiT run in The Python toolkit.

A CQ test must compare with an expected answer. A test that only checks "the query runs" passes on an empty graph. Also test with data, not only with the ontology. Most CQs ask about instances.

Run the checker on every pull request. The Ontology Development Kit (ODK) from the OBO world packs ROBOT, a reasoner and a standard set of checks into one Docker image with ready workflows.

Review, governance and FAIR

An ontology is shared. Many people depend on it, so changes need rules. This is governance.

How a change moves

  1. A user opens an issue: "We need to know which release fixed a flaw."
  2. An editor writes the CQ and a failing test first.
  3. The editor changes the model in a branch and opens a pull request.
  4. The build server runs the CQ tests, the lint, the shapes and a reasoner.
  5. A domain expert reviews the meaning. A second editor reviews the modelling.
  6. The change is merged. The next release gets a new version IRI and release notes.

The OBO Foundry writes its governance down as principles. The list on its site has 17 of them, numbered with gaps from 1 to 20. Examples: open (1), versioning (4), textual definitions (6), naming conventions (12), notification of changes (13), term stability (19) and responsiveness (20). A small company team can copy this idea: a one-page list of rules that every pull request must follow.

The FAIR principles

In 2016 Mark Wilkinson and many co-authors published the FAIR principles in the journal Scientific Data. FAIR means Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. There are 15 principles, from F1 to R1.3. They were written for data, but an ontology is data too.

What FAIR means for an ontology
LetterPrinciples (short)What you do
F, FindablePersistent identifiers, rich metadata, registered in a searchable placeA w3id IRI, a header with title and creator, a listing in OLS or BioPortal
A, AccessibleGet it by its identifier with an open protocol. Metadata stays even if data goes.The IRI resolves over HTTPS. Old versions stay online.
I, InteroperableA formal shared language, FAIR vocabularies, links to other dataOWL or SKOS in RDF. Reuse terms. Link with sameAs or mappings.
R, ReusableMany attributes, a clear license, provenance, community standardsdcterms:license, version and creator facts, follow OBO or W3C practice

An ontology without a license is not reusable, even if it is online. Many companies may not use it at all. OOPS! lists "no license declared" as pitfall P41. Add dcterms:license to the header on day one.

Tools

We checked these tools on 15 November 2026. Versions change often, so check the project pages.

Common tools for the method
ToolWhat it doesLatest release we found
ProtégéThe best-known desktop ontology editor, from Stanford. Has reasoner plugins.5.6.9, March 2026. A 6.0.0 alpha came out in September 2026.
ROBOTCommand-line tool: report, verify, extract, reason, template, diff.1.9.11, 1 October 2026
ODKOntology Development Kit: ROBOT plus workflows in Docker.1.6.1, March 2026
OOPS!Web scanner from UPM Madrid for 41 known pitfalls.Online service. Its page says the latest revision was April 2023.
WIDOCOMakes HTML documentation pages from an ontology.1.4.26, 23 October 2026

A typical question gives a short story and asks for three CQs, a scope, and two terms to reuse. Then it asks what to do with a wrong term. The expected answer is: deprecate it, point to the replacement, never delete the IRI.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the ontology engineering method
PatternPurposeModelNote
CQ with a typed answerSet scope and requirements"Which releases need a release with a known flaw?"A topic is not a question.
CQ as a testCheck the ontology automaticallySPARQL query + expected set of answersCompare with the answer, not just "it runs".
In scope / out of scopeStop the ontology from growing without endPrices: out. Flaws: in.Every class must serve a CQ.
Reuse by IRIJoin data with others for freepkg:ana a foaf:Person .Never invent terms in another namespace.
Extract a moduleReuse a few terms of a big ontologyrobot extract --method BOTImporting all of it slows the reasoner.
UpperCamelCase className a classpkg:ReleaseSingular. No "Class" in the name.
lowerCamelCase propertyName a propertypkg:dependsOnUse a verb, so the direction is clear.
Label + definitionExplain each term to peopleskos:definition "A version of a package that ..."Parent class first, then the difference.
Ontology headerMake the file findable and reusableowl:versionIRI, owl:versionInfo, dcterms:licenseNo license means no reuse.
Pin the importControl what you depend onowl:imports <.../pkg-core/1.1.0>Two versions in one closure is a conflict.
Deprecate, never deleteRetire a term safelyowl:deprecated true ; dcterms:isReplacedBy ...Never change the meaning of an old IRI.
Violation queryWrite your own lint ruleSELECT terms with no definitionEmpty result means pass.
Shape for dataCheck example and real datash:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1OWL alone does not check data.
Persistent IRIKeep links working for yearshttps://w3id.org/yourproject/No version number inside term IRIs.

Practice

Which one is a good competency question?

  • Everything about software security.
  • Which releases use a license that our company does not allow?
  • Is the ontology good?

It has a clear answer type, a list of releases, and you can check it with data.

You need a class for people. What is the best first move?

  • Create pkg:Person and copy the FOAF definition.
  • Use foaf:Person directly.
  • Create foaf:Maintainer in the FOAF namespace.

Reuse the real IRI. Copying makes two IRIs for one idea. Writing a new FOAF term is namespace hijacking.

A property name was a bad choice. Users already have data with it. What do you do?

  • Delete it in the next release.
  • Keep the IRI and quietly change its meaning.
  • Mark it owl:deprecated true and point to a new property.

Deleting breaks old data. A silent change gives wrong answers. Deprecation keeps old data readable and shows the way forward.

Which change needs a new major version number under semantic versioning?

  • Fixing a typo in a label
  • Adding a new property
  • Removing a class that data already uses

Removing a used term breaks old data. That is a breaking change.

What does robot verify treat as a pass?

  • A query that returns at least one row
  • A query that returns no rows
  • A query that returns true

Each verify query selects violations. No rows means no violations.

Fill in the missing words.

Ontology Development 101 has ? steps.

The NeOn method describes ? scenarios.

The OWL 2 annotation that retires a term is owl:?.

The R in FAIR stands for ?.

  1. Write three competency questions for an ontology of meeting rooms in an office.
    Answer

    One possible set: "Which rooms are free on Monday at 10:00?" "Which rooms have a screen and hold at least 8 people?" "Who booked room B2 today?" Each one has a clear answer type: a list of rooms, a list of rooms, a list of people.

  2. For the meeting room ontology, name one term to reuse and say where it comes from.
    Answer

    For example foaf:Person for the person who books, or schema:Place from schema.org for a room. OWL-Time from the W3C can describe the booking interval.

  3. Find four naming problems: pkg:Packages, pkg:HasMaintainer, pkg:release_class, and two classes with the label "release".
    Answer

    Plural class name. Property with a capital first letter. "class" inside a class name, and an underscore against the camel case rule. Two classes with one label confuse people and tools. OOPS! calls the last one pitfall P32.

  4. Write the Turtle that retires pkg:licenseName and points to dcterms:license. Which version number comes after 1.0.0?
    Answer

    pkg:licenseName owl:deprecated true ; dcterms:isReplacedBy dcterms:license . In OBO style, use IAO:0100001 "term replaced by". Nothing is removed, so it is a minor change: 1.1.0.

  5. Write a CQ test for CQ4: "Who maintains the packages that flaw-42 affects?" Give the query and the expected answer for our data.
    Answer

    SELECT ?m WHERE { pkg:flaw-42 pkg:affects ?r . ?p pkg:hasRelease ?r ; pkg:maintainer ?m }. flaw-42 affects fastjson 1.2.0. fastjson is maintained by Ana. Expected answer: {"ana"}.

  6. Your team imports a medical ontology with 300,000 classes for 12 terms. The reasoner now takes minutes. What do you change, and what do you keep in mind?
    Answer

    Extract a module for the 12 terms, for example with robot extract --method BOT, and import the module instead. Keep a term list file in the repository. Rebuild the module when the source ontology has a new release, and pin that version.

  7. Design a small governance plan for a company ontology used by four teams. Name the roles, the steps of a change and the checks.
    Answer

    Roles: two editors, one domain expert per team, users. Steps: issue, CQ and failing test, branch and pull request, automatic checks, review by an expert and an editor, merge, release with a new version IRI and notes. Checks: CQ tests, a lint for labels and definitions, SHACL on example data, a reasoner for consistency. Rules: deprecate instead of delete, pin imports, license in the header.

Key takeaways

  • Start with competency questions. They set the scope, give you terms and later become tests.
  • Reuse before you invent. Use real IRIs, extract modules from big ontologies, and never write terms into another namespace.
  • Ontology 101 gives seven steps. METHONTOLOGY, NeOn, eXtreme Design and LOT add structure for bigger projects.
  • Follow one written naming convention. Every term gets a label and a definition.
  • Split large ontologies into modules. Pin the versions you import.
  • Every release gets a version IRI. Retire terms with owl:deprecated. Never delete an IRI or change its meaning.
  • Test automatically: CQ queries with expected answers, lint queries, SHACL shapes and a reasoner.
  • Govern changes with issues, reviews and release notes. Publish FAIR: persistent IRI, metadata and a license.

Sources

  • Ontology Development 101. Noy and McGuinness, Stanford, 2001. The three rules, the seven steps and naming advice.
  • OWL 2 Structural Specification (Second Edition). W3C, 2012. Ontology IRI, version IRI, imports and owl:deprecated.
  • ROBOT documentation. The report, verify and extract commands.
  • OOPS! pitfall catalogue. Ontology Engineering Group, UPM. The 41 pitfalls and their importance.
  • FAIR Principles. GO FAIR. The 15 principles from Wilkinson and others, 2016.
  • OBO Foundry principle 19: Term Stability. How to obsolete a term and name its replacement.

Ontologies in the wild

You do not need to invent every class yourself. Thousands of teams already share good vocabularies. In this chapter we visit twelve famous ones. Each gets one short page, one real snippet and one lesson.

  • Read a real snippet from each of the twelve vocabularies.
  • Choose the right vocabulary for web pages, metadata, health, finance, sensors, places and buildings.
  • Query Wikidata's statement model with qualifiers and ranks.
  • Mix several vocabularies in one graph and query them together.
  • Explain what made each vocabulary succeed.

Why look at real ontologies?

Open the source of a recipe page on the web. You will often find a small block of data. It says: this page is a Recipe, it takes 30 minutes, and it has 4.6 stars. A search engine reads this block and shows the stars in its results. The block uses schema.org, the most used vocabulary on the web.

A vocabulary is a set of shared terms. Some are tiny, like Dublin Core with 15 core terms. Some are huge, like SNOMED CT with more than 360,000 concepts. When you reuse a vocabulary, other people and tools understand your data at once.

The twelve at a glance (sizes checked on 15 November 2026)
NameDomainStartedSize todayMain users
schema.orgWeb pages2011826 types, 1,540 properties (V30.1)Websites and search engines
GoodRelationsShops and offers2008 paperMerged into schema.org in 2012Online shops
WikidataGeneral knowledge2012About 124 million itemsWikipedia, researchers, AI
Dublin CoreDocument metadata199515 core elements, more in DCMI TermsLibraries, archives, repositories
SKOSThesauri and code lists2009A small core of classes and propertiesLibraries, governments, catalogues
PROV-OWhere data came from2013A small core of classes and propertiesScience, data pipelines
Gene OntologyGene functions199838,263 terms, 14.7 million annotationsBiologists, databases
SNOMED CTClinical terms2002More than 360,000 conceptsHealth systems in 80+ countries
FIBOFinance2010sTen domains in OWLBanks, regulators
SOSA and SSNSensors and observations2017A small core plus modulesIoT, science data
GeoSPARQLPlaces and shapes2012Classes, properties and functionsMap agencies, geo data
BrickBuildings2016Many equipment and point classes (v1.5.0)Building analytics

The numbers change often. I give the source and the date for each one below. Check them again before you quote them. Each page ends with "Why it worked". That part is my reading, not a fact from the sources.

Making your own ex:Person class when schema:Person exists. Your graph then speaks only to itself. Look for an existing term first. Make a new term only when no good one exists.

Vocabularies of the web

schema.org

Google, Microsoft and Yahoo started schema.org in June 2011. Yandex joined later that year. The goal was simple: one vocabulary for marking up web pages, instead of one per search engine. Release V30.1, dated 16 September 2026, lists 826 types and 1,540 properties. The home page says that in 2024 over 45 million web domains used it.

Websites usually write it in JSON-LD inside the page. Here is a product with an offer, first as a website writes it, then as Turtle.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Product",
  "@id": "https://shop.example/p/kettle-12",
  "name": "Steel kettle 1.2 l",
  "gtin13": "4006381333931",
  "offers": {
    "@type": "Offer",
    "price": "39.90",
    "priceCurrency": "EUR",
    "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock"
  }
}
@prefix schema: <http://schema.org/> .   # the JSON-LD context uses http, not https

<https://shop.example/p/kettle-12> a schema:Product ;
    schema:name "Steel kettle 1.2 l" ;
    schema:gtin13 "4006381333931" ;
    schema:offers [
        a schema:Offer ;
        schema:price "39.90" ;
        schema:priceCurrency "EUR" ;
        schema:availability "https://schema.org/InStock"   # a plain string in JSON-LD
    ] .

Are the two files really the same graph? I tested it with rdflib. The first Turtle file I wrote used https://schema.org/ and wrote the availability as an IRI. The fixed file above uses http and a plain string.

from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.compare import isomorphic

web = Graph().parse("product.jsonld", format="json-ld")   # fetches the schema.org context
for name in ["product.ttl", "product_fixed.ttl"]:
    ttl = Graph().parse(name, format="turtle")
    print(f"{name:18} {len(ttl)} triples, same graph as the JSON-LD: {isomorphic(web, ttl)}")
print("first predicate in the JSON-LD graph:", sorted(web.predicates())[0])
product.ttl        8 triples, same graph as the JSON-LD: False
product_fixed.ttl  8 triples, same graph as the JSON-LD: True
first predicate in the JSON-LD graph: http://schema.org/availability

Two surprises here. First, the official JSON-LD context turns name into http://schema.org/name, with http. If you write https in Turtle, your terms do not match. Second, a string value stays a string. Write {"@id": "..."} if you need a real link. Always test with a parser, not with your eyes.

Why it worked. Search engines gave a clear reward: richer search results. The rules were loose, so a page with a few mistakes still helped. And one small group kept one vocabulary for everybody.

GoodRelations, a short history

Martin Hepp designed GoodRelations, an OWL vocabulary for products, prices and offers. His main paper appeared at the EKAW conference in 2008. Some large online shops used it in RDFa. On 8 November 2012 the schema.org blog announced that GoodRelations would be integrated into schema.org. Terms like priceSpecification and businessFunction come from this work. Their schema.org pages still thank GoodRelations.

Why it matters. It is a success story of a different kind. A research ontology did not win alone. It won by joining the vocabulary that had the users. The product snippet above still carries its ideas.

Wikidata's model

Wikidata started in October 2012 as the shared data store of Wikipedia. Its statistics page said 124,046,273 items when I read it. Anyone can edit it. Its model is richer than a simple triple.

  • An item has an ID starting with Q. Berlin is Q64. Germany is Q183.
  • A property has an ID starting with P. "Capital" is P36.
  • A statement joins an item, a property and a value.
  • A qualifier adds detail to a statement, such as a start time (P580).
  • A reference says where the statement came from.
  • A rank marks the best statement among several.
@prefix wd:  <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> .
@prefix wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/> .
@prefix p:   <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/> .
@prefix ps:  <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/statement/> .
@prefix pq:  <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/qualifier/> .
@prefix wikibase: <http://wikiba.se/ontology#> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/> .

wd:Q183 wdt:P36 wd:Q64 .                 # short form: Germany - capital - Berlin
wd:Q183 p:P36 ex:statement1 .            # long form: a statement node
ex:statement1 ps:P36 wd:Q64 ;            # the value
    pq:P580 "1990-10-03T00:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime ;   # qualifier: start time
    wikibase:rank wikibase:PreferredRank .

Real statement nodes have long generated IDs. I wrote ex:statement1 to keep it short. Now a real query against the public endpoint. It asks for all "capital" statements of Germany with their dates.

import json, urllib.parse, urllib.request

QUERY = """
SELECT ?capitalLabel ?start ?end WHERE {
  wd:Q183 p:P36 ?st .              # Germany -> a statement about "capital"
  ?st ps:P36 ?capital .            # the value of that statement
  OPTIONAL { ?st pq:P580 ?start }  # qualifier: start time
  OPTIONAL { ?st pq:P582 ?end }    # qualifier: end time
  SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". }
} ORDER BY ?start"""
url = "https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({"query": QUERY, "format": "json"})
req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "study-book-example/0.1"})
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
    for row in json.load(r)["results"]["bindings"]:
        start = row.get("start", {}).get("value", "-")[:10]
        end = row.get("end", {}).get("value", "-")[:10]
        print(f'{row["capitalLabel"]["value"]:8} from {start}  until {end}')
Berlin   from 1867-07-01  until -
Bonn     from 1949-01-01  until 1999-01-01
Bonn     from 1973-01-01  until 1990-01-01
Berlin   from 1990-10-03  until -
Berlin   from 1999-01-01  until -

I ran this on 15 November 2026. Real data is messy, and this output shows it well. Bonn appears twice with different dates. The date "1949-01-01" only means "the year 1949". Wikidata stores a precision next to each date, and the simple JSON hides it. When I asked with the short form wdt:P36, I got only one answer: Berlin. The short form returns only the best-ranked statements.

Using wdt: and thinking you see everything. The short form hides old values, qualifiers and references. Use p:, ps: and pq: when time or source matters. And send a clear User-Agent and few queries. The endpoint is shared by everyone.

Why it worked. Wikipedia gave it a reason to exist and many editors. The data is free under CC0. The model allows disagreement: two statements can both stay, with ranks and sources.

Metadata and knowledge organisation

Dublin Core

In March 1995, a workshop met at OCLC in Dublin, Ohio. The name comes from that town, not from Ireland. They chose 15 simple elements to describe any document: title, creator, subject, description, publisher, contributor, date, type, format, identifier, source, language, relation, coverage and rights. ISO 15836-1:2017 now holds these 15. The larger set, DCMI Metadata Terms, lives under http://purl.org/dc/terms/.

@prefix dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .

ex:report7 dcterms:title "Annual water report"@en ;
    dcterms:creator ex:ana ;
    dcterms:issued "2026-03-01"^^xsd:date ;
    dcterms:language "en" ;
    dcterms:license <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/> .

Why it worked. It was small enough to learn in an hour. Every library and archive had the same need. Almost every metadata standard today maps to it.

SKOS

Many groups have word lists, thesauri and code lists. They are not full ontologies. A "broader" topic is not always a superclass. SKOS gives them a simple shared form. It became a W3C Recommendation on 18 August 2009.

@prefix skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .
@prefix ex: <http://example.org/topics/> .

ex:topics a skos:ConceptScheme ; skos:prefLabel "Shop topics"@en .
ex:drinks a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:topics ;
    skos:prefLabel "Drinks"@en ; skos:prefLabel "Bebidas"@es .
ex:tea a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:topics ;
    skos:prefLabel "Tea"@en ; skos:altLabel "Chai"@en ;
    skos:broader ex:drinks .

Each concept has one prefLabel per language and any number of altLabel synonyms. Use broader and narrower for the hierarchy.

Why it worked. It asks for very little logic. A library can publish its subject headings in a week. It is also the right tool for value lists in your own ontology.

Treating skos:broader like rdfs:subClassOf. "Tea" has the broader topic "Drinks". But a tea shop review is not a drink. SKOS links topics, not classes of things.

PROV-O

Where did this chart come from? Who made it, from which table, and when? PROV-O answers this with three classes. An Entity is a thing, such as a file or a chart. An Activity is something that happened, such as a script run. An Agent is someone responsible, a person or a program. It became a W3C Recommendation on 30 April 2013.

@prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .

ex:chart a prov:Entity ;
    prov:wasGeneratedBy ex:run42 ;
    prov:wasDerivedFrom ex:salesTable ;
    prov:wasAttributedTo ex:ana .
ex:run42 a prov:Activity ;
    prov:used ex:salesTable ;
    prov:startedAtTime "2026-11-02T09:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime ;
    prov:wasAssociatedWith ex:ana .
ex:ana a prov:Agent .

Why it worked. Every field needs provenance, and PROV is neutral. Wikidata even uses prov:wasDerivedFrom for its references. The same idea is the heart of agent memory, as in Context graphs and agent memory.

Life science and health

Gene Ontology and the OBO Foundry

In 1998, three databases for the fly, yeast and mouse agreed on shared words for gene functions. That was the start of the Gene Ontology, or GO. It has three parts: molecular function, biological process and cellular component. The release of 19 June 2026 had 38,263 terms and 14,736,040 annotations for 171 species.

An annotation says "this protein takes part in this process", with evidence. The terms form a graph. GO writes it in the OBO format and in OWL.

[Term]
id: GO:0006915
name: apoptotic process
namespace: biological_process
is_a: GO:0012501 ! programmed cell death
@prefix obo:  <http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .

obo:GO_0006915 a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "apoptotic process" ;
    rdfs:subClassOf obo:GO_0012501 .     # programmed cell death

I checked the term and its parent with the QuickGO service of EBI. Note the ID pattern. GO:0006915 in OBO becomes obo:GO_0006915 in OWL. The colon becomes an underscore.

The OBO Foundry grew from GO's success. Its members follow shared principles. The list includes open use, a common format, stable IDs, versioning, clear scope, a text definition for each term, and shared relations. Many members also build on the upper ontology BFO. See Formal and upper ontologies.

Why it worked. Biologists had a real pain: every database used other words. GO gave stable IDs that never get reused. Curators added evidence to every annotation. And the work stayed open and funded for decades.

SNOMED CT and FHIR

SNOMED CT is the clinical terminology of SNOMED International. Its site says the International Edition has more than 360,000 concepts, and that it is used in more than eighty countries. Each concept has a number as its ID and is defined with description logic. Myocardial infarction, a heart attack, is concept 22298006.
