FHIR is the HL7 standard for exchanging health records over web APIs. FHIR gives the structure: a Patient, a Condition, an Observation. SNOMED CT gives the meaning of the codes inside. R4 came out in December 2018 with the first normative parts. R5 came out in March 2023. R6 is being balloted as a fully normative standard. Check hl7.org for its status.

{
  "resourceType": "Condition",
  "clinicalStatus": {
    "coding": [{ "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/condition-clinical",
                 "code": "active" }]
  },
  "code": {
    "coding": [{ "system": "http://snomed.info/sct",
                 "code": "22298006",
                 "display": "Myocardial infarction" }]
  },
  "subject": { "reference": "Patient/example" }
}

The pair system plus code is the real identity. The display text is only for people.

Why it worked. Governments and health systems required it, and they paid for national licences. FHIR made it easy to use with normal web tools. Structure and meaning stayed in two separate standards, so each could change at its own speed.

Matching clinical records by display text. "Heart attack", "MI" and "Myocardial infarction" are one concept. Compare the system and the code. SNOMED CT also needs a licence in most countries, so check before you ship it.

Finance, sensors, places and buildings

FIBO

The Financial Industry Business Ontology, FIBO, is hosted by the EDM Council. Its site says it is also standardised at the Object Management Group. It is written in OWL, released quarterly, and published on GitHub under the MIT licence. It has ten domains, such as Foundations, Business Entities, Securities, Derivatives and Loans.

@prefix fibo-be-le-lei: <https://spec.edmcouncil.org/fibo/ontology/BE/LegalEntities/LEIEntities/> .
@prefix cmns-id: <https://www.omg.org/spec/Commons/Identifiers/> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .

ex:acmeBank a fibo-be-le-lei:LEIRegisteredEntity ;
    cmns-id:isIdentifiedBy ex:acmeLei .
ex:acmeLei a fibo-be-le-lei:LegalEntityIdentifier ;
    cmns-id:identifies ex:acmeBank ;
    rdfs:label "made-up LEI for Acme Bank" .

I took the class and property names from the FIBO source file for LEI entities. FIBO defines a legal entity identifier as the ISO 17442 code that names one legal person. Note that the identifier is its own node, not just a string. This is a common FIBO habit.

Why it worked. After the 2008 crisis, regulators wanted data that banks could compare. Banks needed shared meaning for contracts and parties. FIBO is big and hard, so most teams use a small part of it as a reference, not the whole thing.

SOSA and SSN

A thermometer measures the air in room 101 at 8 o'clock. The reading is 21.5. SOSA models exactly this. SSN adds more detail on top. Both are a joint W3C and OGC standard, a W3C Recommendation since 19 October 2017.

@prefix sosa: <http://www.w3.org/ns/sosa/> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .

ex:obs1 a sosa:Observation ;
    sosa:madeBySensor ex:thermo3 ;
    sosa:observedProperty ex:airTemperature ;
    sosa:hasFeatureOfInterest ex:room101 ;
    sosa:hasSimpleResult 21.5 ;
    sosa:resultTime "2026-11-15T08:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .
ex:thermo3 a sosa:Sensor .

Notice the split. The feature of interest is the room. The observed property is the air temperature. The sensor is a third node. Many home-made models mix these three into one, and then cannot answer simple questions.

Why it worked. The light SOSA core is easy. Heavy users can add SSN. Two standards bodies, W3C and OGC, agreed on one model instead of two.

GeoSPARQL

Which cafes are inside the old town? That needs shapes and spatial functions. GeoSPARQL is the OGC standard for this. Version 1.0 came in 2012. Version 1.1 was published in early 2024. It gives classes (Feature, Geometry), properties such as hasGeometry and asWKT, and functions such as sfWithin.

@prefix geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#> .
@prefix ex:  <http://example.org/> .

ex:plazaDeArmas a geo:Feature ;
    geo:hasGeometry ex:plazaGeom .
ex:plazaGeom a geo:Geometry ;
    geo:asWKT "POINT(-77.0300 -12.0453)"^^geo:wktLiteral .   # longitude, then latitude
PREFIX geo:  <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geof: <http://www.opengis.net/def/function/geosparql/>
SELECT ?place WHERE {
  ?place geo:hasGeometry/geo:asWKT ?wkt .
  FILTER(geof:sfWithin(?wkt,
    "POLYGON((-77.05 -12.06, -77.01 -12.06, -77.01 -12.03, -77.05 -12.03, -77.05 -12.06))"^^geo:wktLiteral))
}

The Turtle and the query parse in rdflib. I did not run the query, because rdflib has no GeoSPARQL functions. You need a store that supports them.

Why it worked. It reused the shape formats that map people already had, such as WKT. It separated the thing (the plaza) from its shape (the point). One thing can then have several shapes.

Swapping latitude and longitude. In WKT with the default system, longitude comes first. Lima is near POINT(-77.03 -12.05), not POINT(-12.05 -77.03). The wrong order puts your cafe near Antarctica.

Brick

A building has air handlers, boxes, rooms and thousands of sensor points. Their names in the control system look like "AHU1.SAT". Brick gives them classes and links. The latest release on GitHub when I checked was v1.5.0, dated 29 October.

@prefix brick: <https://brickschema.org/schema/Brick#> .
@prefix ex:    <http://example.org/building#> .

ex:AHU1 a brick:AHU ;
    brick:feeds ex:VAV1 .
ex:VAV1 a brick:VAV ;
    brick:feeds ex:Room101 ;
    brick:hasPoint ex:SAT1 .
ex:SAT1 a brick:Supply_Air_Temperature_Sensor .
ex:Room101 a brick:Room .

feeds says that air or water flows from one thing into another. hasPoint links equipment to its sensor or setpoint. Each has an inverse: isFedBy and isPointOf.

Why it worked. An analytics app can now ask "every supply air sensor of every box fed by AHU1". It works in every building that uses Brick. Before, each building needed its own scripts. Release 1.5.0 also aligns more closely with RealEstateCore and QUDT.

Mixing vocabularies in one graph

Real graphs use several vocabularies at once. Here is a water report. schema.org says what it is. Dublin Core gives the title. PROV-O says how it was made. SOSA holds the sensor readings. SKOS holds the topics. One SPARQL query walks across all five.

from rdflib import Graph

TTL = """
@prefix schema:  <https://schema.org/> .
@prefix dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .
@prefix skos:    <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .
@prefix prov:    <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> .
@prefix sosa:    <http://www.w3.org/ns/sosa/> .
@prefix xsd:     <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex:      <http://example.org/> .

ex:report1 a schema:Report ;                    # schema.org: the kind of thing
    dcterms:title "Water quality, October" ;    # Dublin Core: catalogue data
    dcterms:subject ex:turbidity ;
    prov:wasGeneratedBy ex:analysis1 .          # PROV-O: where it came from
ex:analysis1 a prov:Activity ;
    prov:used ex:obs1, ex:obs2 ;
    prov:wasAssociatedWith ex:ana .
ex:ana a schema:Person ; schema:name "Ana Torres" .
ex:obs1 a sosa:Observation ; sosa:observedProperty ex:turbidity ;   # SOSA: sensor data
    sosa:madeBySensor ex:sensor7 ; sosa:hasSimpleResult 3.2 .
ex:obs2 a sosa:Observation ; sosa:observedProperty ex:turbidity ;
    sosa:madeBySensor ex:sensor7 ; sosa:hasSimpleResult 4.1 .
ex:turbidity a skos:Concept ; skos:prefLabel "Turbidity"@en ;      # SKOS: topics
    skos:broader ex:waterQuality .
ex:waterQuality a skos:Concept ; skos:prefLabel "Water quality"@en .
"""
g = Graph().parse(data=TTL, format="turtle")
Q = """
SELECT ?title ?who ?topic (AVG(?v) AS ?mean) (COUNT(?o) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?r dcterms:title ?title ; dcterms:subject/skos:broader ?t ;
     prov:wasGeneratedBy ?a .
  ?t skos:prefLabel ?topic .
  ?a prov:wasAssociatedWith/schema:name ?who ; prov:used ?o .
  ?o sosa:hasSimpleResult ?v .
} GROUP BY ?title ?who ?topic"""
for row in g.query(Q):
    print(f"{row.title} | by {row.who} | topic: {row.topic} | mean {float(row.mean):.2f} of {row.n}")
print(len(g), "triples from 5 vocabularies")
Water quality, October | by Ana Torres | topic: Water quality | mean 3.65 of 2
23 triples from 5 vocabularies

I ran it with rdflib 7.6.0 and Python 3.14. The query uses the prefixes from the Turtle text, so it needs no PREFIX lines here. In a real store, write them out.

Here I used https://schema.org/ in Turtle on purpose. Schema.org accepts both http and https. But do not mix them in one graph. Pick one, and convert data from JSON-LD to it.

What made them succeed

Look at the twelve again. They come from different fields, but their stories rhyme. Here are the patterns I see. This part is my reading of the histories above.

  1. 1995 Dublin Core. 15 elements from a workshop in Dublin, Ohio.
  2. 1998 Gene Ontology. Three databases share words for gene functions.
  3. 2002 SNOMED CT. A large clinical terminology appears.
  4. 2008 GoodRelations. The EKAW paper on products and offers.
  5. 2009 SKOS. W3C Recommendation in August.
  6. 2011 schema.org. Search engines agree on one vocabulary.
  7. 2012 Wikidata and GeoSPARQL 1.0. GoodRelations joins schema.org in November.
  8. 2013 PROV-O. W3C Recommendation in April.
  9. 2017 SOSA and SSN. A joint W3C and OGC standard in October.
  10. 2023 FHIR R5. Published in March.
  11. 2024 GeoSPARQL 1.1. A decade later, an update.
  12. 2026 schema.org V30.1 and Brick v1.5.0. Both still grow.
Why each one worked (my reading)
VocabularyMain reasonThe price they paid
schema.orgA clear reward: better search resultsLoose meaning, little logic
GoodRelationsGood design, then joined the winnerLost its own name
WikidataWikipedia's editors and a free licenceMessy, uneven data
Dublin CoreTiny and easyToo simple for detailed work
SKOSFits the lists people already hadNo real class logic
PROV-OEvery field needs provenanceMany ways to say the same thing
Gene OntologyReal pain, stable IDs, evidence, fundingConstant curation work
SNOMED CTRequired by health systemsLicences and great size
FIBORegulators and banks need shared meaningHard to learn
SOSA and SSNA light core with optional detailMany small choices left to users
GeoSPARQLReused the shape formats of map peopleNeeds special engines
BrickOne app runs in many buildingsMust keep up with real equipment

Five lessons follow from the table.

  1. A reward for the user. Stars in search, faster research, reports for the regulator. Without a reward, nobody writes the data.
  2. Stable IDs. GO and SNOMED never reuse an ID. A term can retire, but its ID keeps its old meaning.
  3. Start small, allow growth. Dublin Core, SKOS and SOSA have tiny cores. Extensions come later.
  4. A home and a team. Each one has an owner that answers questions and makes releases.
  5. Easy formats. JSON-LD for web people, JSON for FHIR, WKT for map people. Meet users where they are.

Questions often give a use case and ask for the vocabulary. Sensor reading: SOSA. Where data came from: PROV-O. Topic list: SKOS. Document metadata: Dublin Core. Web page markup: schema.org. Gene function: GO. Know one key class or property of each.

Patterns to remember

Patterns from real vocabularies
PatternPurposeModelNote
Web markup in JSON-LDDescribe a page for search engines"@type": "Product" with offersThe context maps to http://schema.org/.
Statement with qualifiersKeep time and source on a factp:P36, ps:P36, pq:P580wdt: shows only the best rank.
Fifteen-element recordSimple metadata for any documentdcterms:title, dcterms:creatorUse dcterms, not the old elements namespace, for new data.
Concept schemePublish a topic list or code listskos:Concept, skos:broaderbroader is not subClassOf.
Entity, activity, agentRecord where data came fromprov:wasGeneratedBy, prov:usedRecord the activity, not only the source.
Stable term IDNever break old annotationsGO:0006915 becomes obo:GO_0006915Retire terms. Never reuse IDs.
System plus codeExact clinical meaning in a recordhttp://snomed.info/sct + 22298006Never match on display text.
Identifier as a nodeKeep scheme and rules for an IDLEIRegisteredEntity isIdentifiedBy LegalEntityIdentifierA plain string loses its scheme.
Observation nodeStore a sensor readingsosa:Observation with sensor, property, featureDo not merge the room and its temperature.
Feature and geometryPlaces with shapesgeo:hasGeometry, geo:asWKTLongitude first in WKT.
Equipment and pointsPortable building appsbrick:feeds, brick:hasPointfeeds links equipment and spaces along the flow.
Mix, do not copyCombine vocabularies in one graphschema + dcterms + prov + sosa + skosPick one schema.org scheme: http or https.

Practice

A sensor reads 21.5 degrees in room 101.

SOSA: an Observation with a Sensor, an ObservableProperty and a FeatureOfInterest.

A chart was made by a script from a sales table.

PROV-O: Entity, Activity and Agent, with wasGeneratedBy and used.

A list of shop topics in two languages.

SKOS: Concepts with prefLabel per language and broader links.

A recipe page wants stars in search results.

schema.org in JSON-LD inside the page.

A hospital system sends a diagnosis to another system.

FHIR for the structure, SNOMED CT for the code.

An app must find every supply air sensor in a building.

Brick: equipment, feeds and hasPoint.

Which IRI does the official schema.org JSON-LD context produce for name?

  • https://schema.org/name
  • http://schema.org/name
  • http://schema.org/#name

The test in this chapter showed http. Mixing http and https breaks matching.

In Wikidata, which prefix gives only the best-ranked values?

  • wdt:
  • p:
  • pq:

wdt: is the short "truthy" form. p:, ps: and pq: give full statements and qualifiers.

What does skos:broader NOT mean?

  • A wider topic
  • A superclass, so every member of the narrow concept is a member of the broad one
  • A link up a thesaurus hierarchy

SKOS links topics. Use rdfs:subClassOf for class hierarchies.

Dublin Core has ? core elements.

The OWL form of GO:0006915 is obo:?.

  1. Write a SOSA observation: humidity sensor h2 measures 48 in the server room at 10:00 UTC on 15 November 2026.
    Answer

    ex:obs9 a sosa:Observation ; sosa:madeBySensor ex:h2 ; sosa:observedProperty ex:relativeHumidity ; sosa:hasFeatureOfInterest ex:serverRoom ; sosa:hasSimpleResult 48 ; sosa:resultTime "2026-11-15T10:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .

  2. A colleague stores a diagnosis as the text "heart attack". What is wrong, and what should the record hold?
    Answer

    Text cannot be matched reliably. "MI" and "Myocardial infarction" mean the same thing. The record should hold a coding with the system http://snomed.info/sct and the code 22298006. The display text is optional and only for people.

  3. The Wikidata query showed Bonn twice, with different dates. Give two reasons why this can happen.
    Answer

    Different editors added different statements from different sources, and both stay. Also, the dates have different precision and meaning, for example "seat of government" against "official capital". The statements may also have different ranks. Read the qualifiers and references before you trust one.

  4. Your JSON-LD and your Turtle file give different graphs, but they look the same. Name two things to check.
    Answer

    Check the namespace: the context may map to http://schema.org/ while your Turtle uses https. Check value types: a string in JSON-LD stays a literal unless you write {"@id": ...}. Compare with a parser and an isomorphism test.

  5. You build a data catalogue for a city. Which vocabularies would you combine, and for what?
    Answer

    Dublin Core terms for title, creator, date and licence. SKOS for the topic list. PROV-O for how each data set was produced. GeoSPARQL for the area each data set covers. If sensor data is included, SOSA for the readings. Many catalogues also use DCAT, which builds on Dublin Core.

  6. Your company wants its own ontology for buildings. Argue for or against reusing Brick.
    Answer

    For: Brick already has the classes and links for equipment, points and spaces. Apps written for Brick can run on your buildings. It is open and has regular releases. Against: you must follow its releases, and it may lack some local terms. A good middle path is to use Brick and add a small extension namespace for the missing terms.

Key takeaways

  • Reuse first. A shared term makes your data understandable to others at once.
  • schema.org rules the web. Test JSON-LD with a parser, because http and https differ.
  • Wikidata stores statements with qualifiers, references and ranks. The short form hides most of it.
  • Dublin Core, SKOS and PROV-O are small tools you will use in almost every project.
  • GO and SNOMED CT show the power of stable IDs and long-term care.
  • FIBO, SOSA, GeoSPARQL and Brick bring shared meaning to finance, sensors, places and buildings.
  • Vocabularies mix well in one graph. One query can cross all of them.
  • The winners gave users a reward, kept IDs stable, started small and had an owner.

Sources

  • Schema.org: Organization of Schemas. Release V30.1 with counts of types and properties.
  • Wikidata: Statistics. The live item count and edit count.
  • June 2026 GO release. Term, annotation and species counts for the 2026-06-19 release.
  • What is SNOMED CT?. SNOMED International on size and use.
  • Semantic Sensor Network Ontology. The W3C and OGC standard with SOSA, 2017.
  • Brick releases on GitHub. Release notes for Brick v1.5.0.

Enterprise and operational ontologies

A company has many systems, and each one names things in its own way. An enterprise ontology gives them one shared meaning. An operational ontology goes one step further. People and agents can also act through it.

  • Describe what large companies published about their knowledge graphs.
  • Match records with the Fellegi-Sunter model and build a golden record.
  • Explain how a semantic layer keeps one definition for each metric.
  • Separate the documented operational ontology idea from opinions about it.
  • Plan a small first ontology project inside a company.

One customer, five systems

Ana buys from a shop. The sales system calls her "Ana Torres". The billing system calls her "A. Torres". The support system only has her email. The warehouse knows only an address. Marketing has a second record from an old campaign.

Now the boss asks: "How much did Ana spend this year?" Nobody can answer quickly. The data exists, but it is spread over five systems. No system knows that the five records are one person.

An enterprise ontology fixes the meaning. It says: there is one class Customer. A customer has one ID. Orders, invoices and tickets all point to that ID. Every system keeps its own data, but the meaning is shared.

This chapter climbs these layers. First we look at what big companies published. Then we match records, define metrics, model machines, and finally let people act through the ontology.

"We need one big database first." You do not. The ontology can sit on top of the systems you have. Most companies cannot move all data into one place, and they do not need to.

Knowledge graphs at large companies

Large companies built knowledge graphs early. Some of them wrote about it. Here is what they published, in their own public words.

  1. 1969 Fellegi and Sunter. A theory of record linkage. Many matching tools still use it.
  2. May 2012 Google Knowledge Graph. The launch post spoke of more than 500 million objects and 3.5 billion facts. Its slogan was "things, not strings".
  3. 2019 Industry-scale knowledge graphs. Authors from Microsoft, Google, Facebook, eBay and IBM compared their graphs in Communications of the ACM.
  4. 2020 AutoKnow at Amazon. A KDD paper on collecting product knowledge for over 11,000 product types.
  5. Nov 2023 ISO/IEC 30173. An international standard for digital twin terms.
  6. 2025 Semantic layers go open. dbt Labs released MetricFlow under Apache 2.0 in October. Microsoft showed an ontology item in Fabric IQ in November.
  7. 2026 A shared format. The Open Semantic Interchange spec appeared in January. In July it entered the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie.

What the papers teach

  • Things, not strings. Google's post made the main point. A search for "Taj Mahal" should know if you mean the building or the musician. That needs IDs, not words.
  • Different needs, same problems. The 2019 paper came from a panel at the ISWC conference in 2018. The five graphs served search, social links, shopping and enterprise search. Yet the authors found shared problems at scale.
  • The ontology must grow. AutoKnow is about products of thousands of types. Its blog post says the work covers building the ontology, extracting data, cleaning and normalising. A fixed, hand-made type list could not cover that.

I could not open the full text of the 2019 paper. The publisher blocked my reader. So I give only what the abstract and the indexes say. Read the paper yourself for the details of each company.

Copying a big company's design. Their graph serves billions of users and thousands of engineers. Your first graph serves one team. Take their ideas, such as stable IDs and sources for every fact. Do not take their size.

Master data and entity resolution

Back to Ana. We must decide which records are the same person. This job is entity resolution. Its result is one clean record per person, the golden record. Keeping golden records for customers, products and suppliers is called master data management.

The Fellegi-Sunter idea

Compare two records field by field. For each field ask two questions.

  • m: if the two records are the same person, how often does this field agree?
  • u: if they are different people, how often does it agree by chance?

A birth date agrees for the same person almost always, so m is high. It agrees for two strangers rarely, so u is low. A city agrees for strangers quite often, so its u is higher.

For one field, the weight is \log_2 \frac{m}{u} when the values agree and \log_2 \frac{1-m}{1-u} when they differ. A missing value adds 0. The match weight of a pair is the sum over all fields.

In simple words: agreement on a rare thing gives many points. Agreement on a common thing gives few points. Disagreement takes points away. Each point is one bit. Every extra bit doubles the odds that the pair is a match.

  1. Names agree. m = 0.90,\ u = 0.01. Weight \log_2 90 \approx 6.49.
  2. Emails differ. m = 0.95,\ u = 0.001. Weight \log_2 \frac{0.05}{0.999} \approx -4.32.
  3. Birth dates agree. m = 0.97,\ u = 0.003. Weight \log_2 323.3 \approx 8.34.
  4. Cities agree. m = 0.80,\ u = 0.10. Weight \log_2 8 = 3.
  5. Total: 6.49 - 4.32 + 8.34 + 3 = 13.51 bits. Above our limit of 6, so this is a match.

Comparing every pair is too slow. A million records give about 500 billion pairs. So we compare only pairs that share a blocking key, here the family name. The code below does blocking and scoring.

import math
from itertools import combinations

# id, source, name, email, birth date, city
rows = [(1, "crm",     "Ana Torres", "ana.torres@acme.example", "1990-04-02", "Lima"),
        (2, "billing", "Ana Torres", "ana.t@acme.example",      "1990-04-02", "Lima"),
        (3, "support", "A. Torres",  "ana.torres@acme.example", None,         "Lima"),
        (4, "crm",     "Ana Torres", "ana@birch.example",       "1985-11-30", "Quito"),
        (5, "billing", "Bo Chen",    "bo@acme.example",         "1979-01-15", "Lima")]

# m = P(fields agree | same person), u = P(fields agree | different people)
M_U = {2: (0.90, 0.01), 3: (0.95, 0.001), 4: (0.97, 0.003), 5: (0.80, 0.10)}

def weight(a, b):
    """Fellegi-Sunter match weight in bits. Missing values add nothing."""
    total = 0.0
    for f, (m, u) in M_U.items():
        if a[f] is None or b[f] is None:
            continue
        total += math.log2(m / u) if a[f] == b[f] else math.log2((1 - m) / (1 - u))
    return total

block = lambda r: r[2].split()[-1].lower()   # blocking key: the family name
for a, b in combinations(rows, 2):
    if block(a) == block(b):                 # compare only inside one block
        w = weight(a, b)
        print(f"{a[0]}-{b[0]}  weight {w:6.2f}  {'MATCH' if w > 6 else 'no'}")
// A record: id, source, then name, email, birth date, city (None = missing).
type Row = (u32, &'static str, [Option<&'static str>; 4]);

// (m, u) for name, email, birth date, city
const M_U: [(f64, f64); 4] = [(0.90, 0.01), (0.95, 0.001), (0.97, 0.003), (0.80, 0.10)];

/// Fellegi-Sunter match weight in bits. Missing values add nothing.
fn weight(a: &Row, b: &Row) -> f64 {
    let mut total = 0.0;
    for (f, (m, u)) in M_U.iter().enumerate() {
        if let (Some(x), Some(y)) = (a.2[f], b.2[f]) {
            total += if x == y { (m / u).log2() } else { ((1.0 - m) / (1.0 - u)).log2() };
        }
    }
    total
}

// blocking key: the family name
fn block(r: &Row) -> String {
    r.2[0].unwrap().split(' ').last().unwrap().to_lowercase()
}

fn find(parent: &[usize], mut x: usize) -> usize {
    while parent[x] != x { x = parent[x]; }
    x
}

Now we join matched pairs into clusters. Then we build one golden record per cluster. The rule that picks each value is a survivorship rule. Here the most trusted source wins, and a missing value falls back to the next source.

parent = {r[0]: r[0] for r in rows}          # union-find: each row starts alone
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        x = parent[x]
    return x

for a, b in combinations(rows, 2):
    if block(a) == block(b) and weight(a, b) > 6:
        parent[find(b[0])] = find(a[0])      # join the two clusters

TRUST = {"crm": 3, "billing": 2, "support": 1}   # survivorship: best source wins
clusters = {}
for r in rows:
    clusters.setdefault(find(r[0]), []).append(r)
for members in clusters.values():
    best = sorted(members, key=lambda r: -TRUST[r[1]])
    golden = [next((r[f] for r in best if r[f] is not None), None) for f in range(2, 6)]
    print([r[0] for r in members], "->", golden)
fn main() {
    let rows: Vec<Row> = vec![
        (1, "crm", [Some("Ana Torres"), Some("ana.torres@acme.example"), Some("1990-04-02"), Some("Lima")]),
        (2, "billing", [Some("Ana Torres"), Some("ana.t@acme.example"), Some("1990-04-02"), Some("Lima")]),
        (3, "support", [Some("A. Torres"), Some("ana.torres@acme.example"), None, Some("Lima")]),
        (4, "crm", [Some("Ana Torres"), Some("ana@birch.example"), Some("1985-11-30"), Some("Quito")]),
        (5, "billing", [Some("Bo Chen"), Some("bo@acme.example"), Some("1979-01-15"), Some("Lima")]),
    ];
    let mut parent: Vec<usize> = (0..rows.len()).collect(); // union-find: each row alone
    for i in 0..rows.len() {
        for j in i + 1..rows.len() {
            if block(&rows[i]) != block(&rows[j]) { continue; } // compare inside one block
            let w = weight(&rows[i], &rows[j]);
            let verdict = if w > 6.0 { "MATCH" } else { "no" };
            println!("{}-{}  weight {:6.2}  {}", rows[i].0, rows[j].0, w, verdict);
            if w > 6.0 { let (a, b) = (find(&parent, i), find(&parent, j)); parent[b] = a; }
        }
    }
    let trust = |s: &str| match s { "crm" => 3, "billing" => 2, _ => 1 }; // best source wins
    let roots: std::collections::BTreeSet<usize> = (0..rows.len()).map(|i| find(&parent, i)).collect();
    for root in roots {
        let mut members: Vec<&Row> = rows.iter().enumerate()
            .filter(|(i, _)| find(&parent, *i) == root).map(|(_, r)| r).collect();
        members.sort_by_key(|r| -trust(r.1));
        let golden: Vec<&str> = (0..4)
            .map(|f| members.iter().find_map(|r| r.2[f]).unwrap_or("?")).collect();
        let ids: Vec<u32> = members.iter().map(|r| r.0).collect();
        println!("{:?} -> {:?}", ids, golden);
    }
}
1-2  weight  13.51  MATCH
1-3  weight   9.58  MATCH
1-4  weight  -5.05  no
2-3  weight  -4.63  no
2-4  weight  -5.05  no
3-4  weight  -9.80  no
[1, 2, 3] -> ['Ana Torres', 'ana.torres@acme.example', '1990-04-02', 'Lima']
[4] -> ['Ana Torres', 'ana@birch.example', '1985-11-30', 'Quito']
[5] -> ['Bo Chen', 'bo@acme.example', '1979-01-15', 'Lima']

This is the Python output. The Rust program prints the same lines with double quotes. Look closely at records 2 and 3. Their own weight is -4.63, so they do not match. But both match record 1. So the cluster joins all three. This is transitive closure, and it is a risk. One bad link can pull two real people into one cluster.

Splink is an open-source Python library for this work, from the UK Ministry of Justice. It uses the Fellegi-Sunter model and can learn m and u from the data. Version 5.0.0 came out on 28 September 2026. Its page says it links a million records on a laptop in about a minute. In real work you learn m and u. You do not guess them as we did.

Overwriting the source records with the golden record. Keep the sources. Keep a link from each source record to its golden ID. Then you can undo a wrong merge, and you can explain every value.

Where is the ontology here? It says which classes need a golden record. It says which properties identify a thing, such as tax number or email. It also says which properties can only have one value. In OWL that is a functional property, and owl:sameAs records that two IDs name one thing. See OWL 2.

Semantic layers and metrics

Two teams report "revenue" for the same shop. Team A says 520. Team B says 440. Both used the same tables. Team A forgot to remove refunded orders. Now the meeting is about numbers, not about the business.

A semantic layer stops this. Each metric is defined once. Each dimension is defined once. The joins between tables are defined once. Tools ask the layer, and the layer writes the SQL.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customer(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, country TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, day TEXT, amount REAL, status TEXT);
INSERT INTO customer VALUES (1,'PE'),(2,'PE'),(3,'CL');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,'2026-09-03',120,'paid'),(11,2,'2026-09-14',80,'refunded'),
  (12,3,'2026-09-20',200,'paid'),(13,1,'2026-10-02',50,'paid'),(14,3,'2026-10-09',70,'paid');
""")

# The semantic layer: one shared definition per metric and per dimension.
JOIN = "orders o JOIN customer c ON c.id = o.customer_id"
METRICS = {"revenue": "SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN o.amount END)",
           "paid_orders": "COUNT(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 END)"}
DIMS = {"country": "c.country", "month": "substr(o.day, 1, 7)"}

def ask(metrics, by):
    """Compile a metric question to SQL. Nobody writes the joins by hand."""
    cols = [f"{DIMS[d]} AS {d}" for d in by] + [f"{METRICS[m]} AS {m}" for m in metrics]
    sql = f"SELECT {', '.join(cols)} FROM {JOIN} GROUP BY {', '.join(by)} ORDER BY {', '.join(by)}"
    return db.execute(sql).fetchall()

# Two teams wrote "revenue" by hand in two ways:
print("team A:", db.execute("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders").fetchone()[0])
print("team B:", db.execute("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE status='paid'").fetchone()[0])
# With the semantic layer everybody gets the same definition:
print(ask(["revenue", "paid_orders"], by=["month"]))
print(ask(["revenue"], by=["country"]))
team A: 520.0
team B: 440.0
[('2026-09', 320.0, 2), ('2026-10', 120.0, 2)]
[('CL', 270.0), ('PE', 170.0)]

The monthly total is 320 + 120 = 440. The country total is 270 + 170 = 440. Every view gives the same revenue, because every view uses one definition.

A semantic layer and an ontology
QuestionSemantic layerOntology
Main jobCorrect numbers for reportsShared meaning of things and links
Main partsMetrics, dimensions, joinsClasses, properties, links, rules
Typical questionRevenue by month?Which machines feed this tank?
LogicSQL expressionsLogic, shapes and rules
IdentityJoin keysIDs, sameAs, keys

The two are coming together. A semantic layer is a small ontology for numbers. An ontology can carry metrics as properties of its classes.

Putting the metric logic inside each dashboard. Then ten dashboards hold ten copies of "revenue". When the rule changes, you fix nine and forget one.

Digital twins

A water company has 2,000 pumps. Each pump sends its flow rate every minute. Each pump feeds a tank. Engineers want to ask: "Which tanks lose water if pump 17 stops?" They need a model of the real network that stays live.

This model is a digital twin. ISO/IEC 30173, published in November 2023, gives standard terms for it. ISO 23247 (2021) gives a framework for twins in manufacturing. A twin is an ontology plus live data. The ontology says what a pump is. The data says what pump 17 is doing now.

Microsoft's Azure Digital Twins service uses the Digital Twins Definition Language, DTDL. Version 3 is current. A model is an Interface with contents. Here is a small pump model in my own words.

{
  "@context": "dtmi:dtdl:context;3",
  "@id": "dtmi:com:example:Pump;1",
  "@type": "Interface",
  "displayName": "Pump",
  "contents": [
    { "@type": "Telemetry", "name": "flowRate", "schema": "double" },
    { "@type": "Property", "name": "maxPressure", "schema": "double", "writable": true },
    { "@type": "Command", "name": "stop" },
    { "@type": "Relationship", "name": "feeds", "target": "dtmi:com:example:Tank;1" }
  ]
}
DTDL v3 parts and their ontology meaning
DTDL partMeaningOntology word
InterfaceA kind of twin, such as PumpClass
PropertyState, read-only or writableData property
TelemetryA stream of readingsEvent or observation
RelationshipA link to another twinObject property
CommandSomething you can ask the twin to doAction
ComponentAnother Interface inside this onePart-of
extendsInherit from other InterfacesSubclass

The @id is a DTMI. The number after the semicolon is the version. Notice the Command part. A twin model has actions, not only facts. Keep this in mind for the next section.

For buildings, the Brick schema plays a similar role. It is in Ontologies in the wild.

Storing every sensor reading as a graph edge. A pump that reports every minute makes over 500,000 readings a year. Keep readings in a time-series store. Keep the twin graph for the things and their links.

The operational ontology idea

A classic ontology describes the world. People read it, query it and reason with it. But to change something, they leave and open another system. An operational ontology adds the actions to the model. Palantir's Foundry documentation describes this idea in detail. I split this section into two parts. First what the documentation says. Then my own reading.

These points come from Palantir's public Foundry documentation, which I read on 15 November 2026.

  • The Ontology is called an operational layer for the organisation. It sits on top of datasets, virtual tables and models.
  • Semantic elements say what exists: object types, properties and link types.
  • Kinetic elements allow change: action types and functions. Dynamic security is also listed here.
  • An object type is like a dataset. An object is like a row. A property is like a column.
  • An action type is a set of edits that a user applies together, in one transaction. It can have side effects, such as notifications or webhooks.
  • Submission criteria hold validation checks and role-based access.
  • A function is code. It takes inputs, can read objects, and returns outputs.
  • Interfaces describe a shared shape for several object types.
  • The documentation says the Ontology often serves as a digital twin of the organisation.

Here is the same idea as a small program. It is my own teaching model, not Palantir's code or API. Rows back two object types. A function reads. An action checks its rules, then makes one set of edits and writes a log.

# Object types, backed by rows. The key of each row is its identity.
engineers = {"ana": {"team": "db", "on_call": True},
             "bo":  {"team": "db", "on_call": False}}
tickets = {"T-1": {"status": "open", "owner": "bo"},
           "T-2": {"status": "open", "owner": "ana"},
           "T-3": {"status": "closed", "owner": "ana"}}
edit_log = []        # every applied action is written here (the writeback)

def open_load(engineer):
    """Function: read objects, return a value. Changes nothing."""
    return sum(1 for t in tickets.values() if t["owner"] == engineer and t["status"] == "open")

def reassign(ticket, new_owner, user, role):
    """Action type: checks first (submission criteria), then one set of edits."""
    checks = [(role == "lead", "only a lead may reassign"),
              (tickets[ticket]["status"] == "open", "ticket is not open"),
              (engineers[new_owner]["on_call"], f"{new_owner} is not on call"),
              (open_load(new_owner) < 3, f"{new_owner} has too many tickets")]
    failed = [msg for ok, msg in checks if not ok]
    if failed:
        return "REJECTED: " + "; ".join(failed)
    old = tickets[ticket]["owner"]
    tickets[ticket]["owner"] = new_owner                       # the edit
    edit_log.append((user, "reassign", ticket, old, new_owner))
    return f"OK: {ticket} {old} -> {new_owner}"

print(reassign("T-1", "ana", user="cy", role="lead"))
print(reassign("T-2", "bo", user="cy", role="lead"))
print(reassign("T-3", "ana", user="dee", role="member"))
print("load of ana:", open_load("ana"), "| log:", edit_log)
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Ticket { open: bool, owner: &'static str }

struct World {
    on_call: HashMap<&'static str, bool>,      // engineer objects: name -> on call?
    tickets: HashMap<&'static str, Ticket>,    // ticket objects: key -> row
    edit_log: Vec<String>,                     // every applied action (the writeback)
}

impl World {
    /// Function: read objects, return a value. Changes nothing.
    fn open_load(&self, who: &str) -> usize {
        self.tickets.values().filter(|t| t.owner == who && t.open).count()
    }

    /// Action type: checks first (submission criteria), then one set of edits.
    fn reassign(&mut self, ticket: &str, new_owner: &'static str, user: &str, role: &str) -> String {
        let checks = [
            (role == "lead", "only a lead may reassign".to_string()),
            (self.tickets[ticket].open, "ticket is not open".to_string()),
            (self.on_call[new_owner], format!("{new_owner} is not on call")),
            (self.open_load(new_owner) < 3, format!("{new_owner} has too many tickets")),
        ];
        let failed: Vec<String> = checks.into_iter().filter(|c| !c.0).map(|c| c.1).collect();
        if !failed.is_empty() {
            return format!("REJECTED: {}", failed.join("; "));
        }
        let old = std::mem::replace(&mut self.tickets.get_mut(ticket).unwrap().owner, new_owner);
        self.edit_log.push(format!("{user} reassign {ticket} {old} -> {new_owner}"));
        format!("OK: {ticket} {old} -> {new_owner}")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let t = |open, owner| Ticket { open, owner };
    let mut w = World { on_call: HashMap::from([("ana", true), ("bo", false)]),
        tickets: HashMap::from([("T-1", t(true, "bo")), ("T-2", t(true, "ana")), ("T-3", t(false, "ana"))]),
        edit_log: vec![] };
    println!("{}", w.reassign("T-1", "ana", "cy", "lead"));
    println!("{}", w.reassign("T-2", "bo", "cy", "lead"));
    println!("{}", w.reassign("T-3", "ana", "dee", "member"));
    println!("load of ana: {} | log: {:?}", w.open_load("ana"), w.edit_log);
}
OK: T-1 bo -> ana
REJECTED: bo is not on call
REJECTED: only a lead may reassign; ticket is not open
load of ana: 2 | log: [('cy', 'reassign', 'T-1', 'bo', 'ana')]

This is the Python output. The Rust log line prints as one string: "cy reassign T-1 bo -> ana".

Everything in this box is my opinion, not the documentation.

  • The semantic part is a normal ontology with a database flavour. Object types are classes. Link types are object properties. Primary keys give identity.
  • The new part is the kinetic part. Actions turn the ontology into a place where work happens. This looks like the command side of an application, with checks, permissions and a log.
  • There is less formal logic than in OWL. The rules live in code and checks, not in a reasoner. That makes it practical, but you cannot prove much about it.
  • It fits AI agents well. An agent can read objects with functions. It can only change the world through actions. Every action is checked and logged. That is a good safety boundary.

Letting an agent write to tables directly. Give it actions instead. An action has a name, rules, an owner and a log. A raw table update has none of these.

What other data platforms offer now

Many data platforms now ship some kind of ontology or semantic layer. I checked the public pages on 15 November 2026. This changes every few months, so check again before you decide.

Ontology and semantic features in data platforms (checked 15 November 2026)
ProductWhat it offersStatus I found
Microsoft Fabric IQ, ontology itemEntity types, properties, relationships, metrics from Power BI measures, rules in natural language, bindings to data, optional graph. Imports RDF, Turtle and OWL. Exports RDF or Turtle.Preview. The old experience retires on 31 January 2027.
Snowflake semantic viewsLogical tables, facts, dimensions and metrics as a schema object. Cortex Analyst and agents can use them.Definition and querying became generally available in 2025.
Databricks metric viewsMetrics in Unity Catalog with a source, dimensions, measures and joins, written in YAML.The docs I read gave no overall status. Check the release notes.
dbt MetricFlowMetric definitions compiled to SQL for many databases.Apache 2.0 since October 2025.
Apache Ossie (formerly Open Semantic Interchange)A YAML and JSON format to move semantic models between tools: datasets, fields, metrics, relationships.Incubating at Apache since July 2026. Early version.

Azure Digital TwinsTwin graphs with DTDL v3 models and live device data.Available. The docs were updated in August 2026.

Read the Fabric page with the operational idea in mind. Its ontology also binds to data in place. It also carries rules and metrics. It also exists to give AI agents shared context. The words differ, but the direction is the same.

Fabric's documentation says the ontology is not a query engine itself. Agents and dashboards run their queries against the bound sources. A graph is optional. You turn it on when paths matter, for example for shortest-path questions.

Choosing a platform before you have a model. The model is the hard part, and it moves between tools. Write it down first, in plain words and in a portable format such as Turtle or YAML.

How to start small in a company

Big ontology projects often fail. They try to model the whole company before anyone uses anything. Start with one decision that people make every week. Then grow.

Pick one decision

For example: "Which support ticket should we handle next?" One team, one question, one owner.

Write ten questions

Write the questions the model must answer. These are competency questions. "Which open tickets belong to our top customers?"

List five to ten types

Customer, Ticket, Product, Engineer, Contract. Write one sentence of meaning for each.

Choose the keys

Decide the ID of each type. Decide how records from two systems become one. This is where matching starts.

Bind to real tables

Map each type to the tables you already have. Do not copy data if you can read it in place.

Define three metrics

Open tickets, time to first answer, tickets per customer. One definition each.

Add one action

For example "reassign ticket", with checks and a log. Now the model helps people work.

Test and grow

Turn the ten questions into tests. Add shapes for the data. Add a second team only when the first team uses it every week.

We will model the whole company first. Then we will build apps on it next year.

We will model support tickets this month. One team will use it every day. Then we add sales.

Who owns the ontology?

Each type needs a named owner in the business, not only in IT. The owner decides what "customer" means. Without an owner, every team keeps its own meaning.

How do we change it safely?

Give the model versions. Add new properties freely. Mark old ones as deprecated before you remove them. Run the competency question tests on every change.

Do we need an upper ontology?

Not at the start. Reuse small public vocabularies where they fit, such as schema.org or SKOS. An upper ontology like BFO helps later, when many domains must fit together. See Formal and upper ontologies.

How do we show value?

Measure the decision you picked. For example, time to answer a ticket before and after. A number like this keeps the project alive.

Write the first version in a shared document, not a tool. Five types with one-line meanings fit on one page. People can comment on a page. Move it into Turtle or a platform after people agree.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for enterprise and operational ontologies
PatternPurposeModelNote
One ID per real thingJoin data from many systemscustomer:4711 in sales, billing and supportDecide the key before you load data.
Match weightDecide if two records are one thing\sum \log_2 (m/u) over agreeing fieldsLearn m and u from data. Do not guess them.
Blocking keyAvoid comparing every pairSame family name, or same postcodeA bad key hides true matches.
Golden record with linksOne clean view, sources keptsource row -> golden IDNever overwrite the sources.
Survivorship rulePick each value of the golden recordCRM beats billing beats supportWrite the rule per field, not per record.
Metric defined onceSame number in every reportrevenue = SUM(amount) WHERE paidDashboards must not copy the logic.
Twin model with commandsLive model of a real systemDTDL Interface with Telemetry and CommandKeep raw readings in a time-series store.
Object type backed by rowsOntology on top of existing dataTicket objects come from the tickets tableThe key column becomes the identity.
Action with checksSafe changes by people and agentsreassign: role, status, on call, loadLog every applied action.
Read-only functionBusiness logic that agents can callopen_load(engineer)A function must not change data.
Documented versus my readingHonest writing about productsTwo boxes with clear titlesDate every product fact.
One decision firstStart small and show value"Which ticket next?"Add a second team only after real use.

Practice

What is a golden record?

  • The oldest record of a customer
  • The one best record for a real thing, built from all sources
  • A record that is never changed

It joins the matched source records. The survivorship rules choose each value.

Which field should have the highest u value?

  • Tax number
  • Birth date
  • City

u is the chance that two different people agree. Many strangers live in the same city.

In the documented Foundry model, which element is kinetic?

  • Link type
  • Action type
  • Property

Kinetic elements allow change: action types and functions. Link types and properties are semantic.

In DTDL v3, what is a stream of sensor readings?

  • Property
  • Component
  • Telemetry

Telemetry is data the twin sends. A Property is its state.

A field has m = 0.8 and u = 0.1. When it agrees, its weight is ? bits.

Comparing all pairs of 1,000 records needs ? comparisons.

  1. A field has m = 0.95 and u = 0.001. Compute its weight when it agrees and when it differs.
    Answer

    Agree: \log_2 (0.95/0.001) = \log_2 950 \approx 9.89. Differ: \log_2 (0.05/0.999) \approx -4.32.

  2. Records A and B match. Records B and C match. A and C do not. What does union-find do, and why can this be a problem?
    Answer

    It puts A, B and C in one cluster, because matches join clusters. This is transitive closure. If the B and C link is wrong, two real people now share one golden record. Check large clusters by hand, or require a minimum weight inside a cluster.

  3. Team A reports revenue 520. Team B reports 440. The orders table has one refunded order of 80. Explain the gap and how a semantic layer helps.
    Answer

    Team A counted the refunded order and team B did not: 520 - 80 = 440. A semantic layer stores one definition of revenue, with the paid filter. Every report then asks the layer and gets 440.

  4. Write a DTDL v3 Relationship from a Room to at most one Floor.
    Answer

    { "@type": "Relationship", "name": "onFloor", "maxMultiplicity": 1, "target": "dtmi:com:example:Floor;1" }. The maxMultiplicity of 1 says "at most one floor".

  5. An AI agent must be able to close support tickets. Design it in the operational style: what does the agent read, and how does it change data?
    Answer

    The agent reads Ticket and Customer objects through read-only functions, for example open tickets of a customer. It changes data only through an action such as close_ticket. The action checks that the ticket is open, that a resolution note exists, and that the agent has the right role. Each applied action goes into the log with the agent's name.

  6. Your manager wants to "build the company ontology this year". Write a short counter-plan for the first month.
    Answer

    Pick one weekly decision, for example ticket priority, with one owner. Write ten competency questions. Model five to ten types with keys. Bind them to the existing tables. Define three metrics and one action. Turn the questions into tests. Measure one number before and after, then decide on the next team.

Key takeaways

  • An enterprise ontology gives many systems one shared meaning. The data can stay where it is.
  • Big companies taught one lesson again and again: things need IDs, not strings.
  • Entity resolution matches records. Fellegi-Sunter adds evidence in bits. Blocking keeps it fast.
  • Keep source records and link them to the golden record. Then you can undo a wrong merge.
  • A semantic layer defines each metric once. It is a small ontology for numbers.
  • A digital twin is an ontology plus live data. DTDL v3 even has commands.
  • The operational ontology adds actions and functions to objects and links. Actions are a safe door for agents.
  • Platforms change fast. Date every product fact and keep the model portable.
  • Start with one decision, one team and ten questions.

Sources

  • Industry-scale Knowledge Graphs: Lessons and Challenges. Noy and co-authors on the graphs of five companies, 2019.
  • Introducing the Knowledge Graph: things, not strings. Google's launch post, May 2012.
  • Palantir Foundry: Ontology core concepts. Object types, link types, action types, functions and interfaces.
  • What is ontology (preview)? Microsoft Fabric. Entity types, bindings, metrics, rules and the optional graph.
  • Splink on PyPI. Probabilistic record linkage with the Fellegi-Sunter model, version 5.0.0.
  • Digital Twins Definition Language v3. The DTDL specification with Interfaces, Telemetry, Properties, Commands and Relationships.

Ontologies and AI

Language models write fluent text. Ontologies say what is allowed and what is true. In this chapter we join the two. We learn from graphs with vectors, build graphs with language models, and use the ontology to catch wrong answers.

  • Compute a TransE score and a filtered rank by hand.
  • Measure link prediction with MRR and Hits@k.
  • Place a system in one of the six neuro-symbolic types.
  • Check language model output against an ontology before you store it.
  • Choose the right metric for extraction, text to SPARQL and GraphRAG.

Two kinds of AI meet

Ask a language model: "Where was Ana born?" It answers "Lima" in a nice sentence. But it may invent the answer. You cannot see why it said Lima.

Ask a knowledge graph the same question. It answers "Lima" only if the fact ana bornIn lima is stored. It can show the fact and its source. But it cannot read a new email and learn a new fact by itself.

So each side has a strength. Neural AI reads messy text and finds patterns. Symbolic AI keeps clear facts and checks them with rules. An ontology lives on the symbolic side.

The two sides in one table
QuestionNeural (language model, embeddings)Symbolic (ontology, graph, rules)
InputText, images, any messClean facts with known types
StrengthFluent, flexible, fills gapsExact, explainable, checkable
WeaknessCan invent factsNeeds people to model the world
Answer to "why?"Hard to say"Because of these facts and this rule"
Change of knowledgeTrain again or add contextAdd or close a fact

This chapter shows four ways the two sides work together. The tree below is our map.

"The model is big, so it does not need an ontology." A bigger model still invents facts. An ontology does not make the model smarter. It gives you a way to check the model.

Knowledge graph embeddings

Start with a picture in two numbers. Put Peru at the point (0, 0). Put Lima at (1, 0). Now give the relation has_city its own arrow: (1, 0). Peru plus the arrow lands exactly on Lima.

This is the idea of a vector model of a graph. Each entity gets a vector. Each relation gets a vector too. The list of numbers is called an embedding. A good embedding puts true facts close and false facts far.

A score function gives a number to a triple (h, r, t). A higher score means "more likely true". The TransE score is f(h,r,t) = -\lVert \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{t} \rVert, minus the distance between \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{t}.

Check the picture with numbers. Peru plus has_city is (1, 0). The distance to Lima is 0, so the score is 0. The distance to Cusco is \sqrt{0.2^2 + 0.3^2} \approx 0.36, so the score is -0.36. Paris gets -3.61. The best tail is Lima.

TransE came from Bordes and four co-authors at NeurIPS 2013. Many models followed. They differ only in the score function.

Four classic score functions
ModelYearScore ideaGood atWeak at
TransE2013-\lVert \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{t} \rVertChains: r_3 \approx r_1 + r_2One-to-many: all cities of Peru must sit on one point
DistMult2015\sum_i h_i r_i t_iSymmetric relations like "married to"Direction: score of (h,r,t) equals score of (t,r,h)
ComplEx2016\operatorname{Re}\left(\sum_i h_i r_i \overline{t_i}\right) with complex numbersDirection and symmetry bothHarder to explain
RotatE2019\mathbf{t} \approx \mathbf{h} \circ \mathbf{r}, each \lvert r_i \rvert = 1Inverse, symmetric and chain patternsStill weak on many-to-many

Here is the same score in code. The rank function is for the next section.

import math

# Hand-made vectors with 2 numbers, so you can check them on paper.
E = {"Peru": (0.0, 0.0), "Lima": (1.0, 0.0), "Cusco": (1.2, 0.3), "Paris": (3.0, 3.0)}
R = {"has_city": (1.0, 0.0)}

def transe(h, r, t):
    # TransE: h + r should land on t. Score = minus the distance.
    return 0.0 - math.dist([a + b for a, b in zip(E[h], R[r])], E[t])

def rank(h, r, t_true, skip):
    """Place of t_true among all tails. Tails in `skip` are left out."""
    s = transe(h, r, t_true)
    return 1 + sum(1 for t in E
                   if t != t_true and t not in skip and transe(h, r, t) > s)

for t in E:
    print(f"{t:5} score {transe('Peru', 'has_city', t):6.2f}")
train_tails = {"Lima"}   # (Peru, has_city, Lima) is a known training fact
print("raw rank of Cusco:", rank("Peru", "has_city", "Cusco", skip=set()))
print("filtered rank of Cusco:", rank("Peru", "has_city", "Cusco", skip=train_tails))
use std::collections::HashMap;

// TransE: h + r should land on t. Score = minus the distance.
fn transe(e: &HashMap<&str, [f64; 2]>, r: [f64; 2], h: &str, t: &str) -> f64 {
    let (hv, tv) = (e[h], e[t]);
    let dx = hv[0] + r[0] - tv[0];
    let dy = hv[1] + r[1] - tv[1];
    0.0 - (dx * dx + dy * dy).sqrt()
}

/// Place of `t_true` among all tails. Tails in `skip` are left out.
fn rank(e: &HashMap<&str, [f64; 2]>, r: [f64; 2], h: &str, t_true: &str, skip: &[&str]) -> usize {
    let s = transe(e, r, h, t_true);
    1 + e.keys()
        .filter(|t| **t != t_true && !skip.contains(*t) && transe(e, r, h, t) > s)
        .count()
}

fn main() {
    let e: HashMap<&str, [f64; 2]> = HashMap::from([
        ("Peru", [0.0, 0.0]), ("Lima", [1.0, 0.0]),
        ("Cusco", [1.2, 0.3]), ("Paris", [3.0, 3.0]),
    ]);
    let has_city = [1.0, 0.0];
    for t in ["Peru", "Lima", "Cusco", "Paris"] {
        println!("{:5} score {:6.2}", t, transe(&e, has_city, "Peru", t));
    }
    println!("raw rank of Cusco: {}", rank(&e, has_city, "Peru", "Cusco", &[]));
    println!("filtered rank of Cusco: {}", rank(&e, has_city, "Peru", "Cusco", &["Lima"]));
}
Peru  score  -1.00
Lima  score   0.00
Cusco score  -0.36
Paris score  -3.61
raw rank of Cusco: 2
filtered rank of Cusco: 1

People read an embedding as a fact. It is not. A high score says "this looks like the facts I saw". It is a guess. Store it as a guess with a score, never as a checked fact.

Link prediction and how to measure it

The job of an embedding model is link prediction. You give it a question with a hole: (Peru, has_city, ?). It sorts all entities by score. A good model puts the right answer near the top.

Look at the output above. Cusco is a true answer, but Lima scores higher. So the rank of Cusco is 2. But Lima is also true. It was in the training data. Should Cusco lose a place to another right answer? No.

So the standard test uses the filtered setting. You remove every other known true answer before you count. Now Cusco has rank 1.

Take a set Q of test questions. Each question q gives one filtered rank. Then

\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{\lvert Q \rvert} \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{\text{rank}_q} \qquad \text{Hits@}k = \frac{\lvert \{ q : \text{rank}_q \le k \} \rvert}{\lvert Q \rvert}

MRR is between 0 and 1. A perfect model has MRR 1. Hits@k counts how often the right answer is in the top k.

  1. The filtered ranks are 1, 2, 1 and 10.
  2. The reciprocals are 1, 0.5, 1 and 0.1. Their sum is 2.6.
  3. MRR is 2.6 / 4 = 0.65.
  4. Hits@1 is 2/4 = 0.5. Hits@3 is 3/4 = 0.75. Hits@10 is 4/4 = 1.

Training with fake triples

A graph stores only true facts. So where do false examples come from? We make them. We take a true triple and swap the head or the tail for a random entity. This is a negative sample.

The model then learns with a margin \gamma. It wants each true triple closer than its fake triple by at least \gamma:

L = \max\bigl(0,\ \gamma + d(h,r,t) - d(h',r,t')\bigr)

The small program below trains TransE on 28 places. Cities sit in countries. Countries sit in continents. We hide four facts of the form "city in continent". Then we ask the model to guess them.

import random
random.seed(7)

world = {"SouthAmerica": {"Peru": "Lima", "Chile": "Santiago", "Brazil": "Brasilia"},
         "Europe": {"France": "Paris", "Spain": "Madrid", "Italy": "Rome"},
         "Asia": {"Japan": "Tokyo", "India": "Delhi", "China": "Beijing"},
         "Africa": {"Kenya": "Nairobi", "Egypt": "Cairo", "Ghana": "Accra"}}
train, test = [], []
for cont, countries in world.items():
    for i, (country, city) in enumerate(countries.items()):
        train += [(city, "located_in", country), (country, "part_of", cont)]
        # hold out the first city of each continent for the test
        (test if i == 0 else train).append((city, "in_continent", cont))

ents = sorted({x for h, _, t in train + test for x in (h, t)})
rels = ["located_in", "part_of", "in_continent"]
DIM, LR, MARGIN = 16, 0.02, 1.0
vec = {k: [random.gauss(0, 0.3) for _ in range(DIM)] for k in ents + rels}
def dist(h, r, t):   # squared distance between h + r and t
    return sum((a + b - c) ** 2 for a, b, c in zip(vec[h], vec[r], vec[t]))

def mrr(candidates):
    total = 0.0
    for h, r, t in test:
        d = dist(h, r, t)
        total += 1 / (1 + sum(1 for c in candidates if c != t and dist(h, r, c) < d))
    return total / len(test)

continents = list(world)   # the ontology says: the range of in_continent is Continent
print(f"before training: MRR all={mrr(ents):.3f}  typed={mrr(continents):.3f}")
for epoch in range(300):
    random.shuffle(train)
    for h, r, t in train:
        h2, t2 = (random.choice(ents), t) if random.random() < 0.5 else (h, random.choice(ents))
        if MARGIN + dist(h, r, t) - dist(h2, r, t2) <= 0:
            continue                       # the true triple already wins clearly
        for i in range(DIM):
            g = 2 * (vec[h][i] + vec[r][i] - vec[t][i])        # pull the true triple
            g2 = 2 * (vec[h2][i] + vec[r][i] - vec[t2][i])     # push the fake triple
            vec[h][i] -= LR * g; vec[t][i] += LR * g; vec[r][i] -= LR * (g - g2)
            vec[h2][i] += LR * g2; vec[t2][i] -= LR * g2
    for k in ents:                         # keep every entity on the unit sphere
        n = sum(x * x for x in vec[k]) ** 0.5
        vec[k] = [x / n for x in vec[k]]
print(f"after training:  MRR all={mrr(ents):.3f}  typed={mrr(continents):.3f}")
print(len(ents), "entities,", len(train), "train triples,", len(test), "test triples")
before training: MRR all=0.073  typed=0.521
after training:  MRR all=0.875  typed=1.000
28 entities, 32 train triples, 4 test triples

Read the two columns. "All" lets the model choose any entity. "Typed" uses one ontology rule: the answer must be a continent. The rule cuts 28 choices to 4. With the rule, the trained model gets all four right.

TransE learned that in_continent is close to located_in plus part_of. This is the chain pattern from the table. With another seed the numbers change a little. Try it.

Real tests use bigger graphs. FB15k-237 has 14,541 entities, 237 relations and 272,115 training triples. WN18RR has 40,943 entities and 11 relations. Both are cleaned versions of older sets. In the old sets, many test facts had an inverse fact in the training data. A model could copy the inverse and look smart. This is data leakage.

For real work, use a library. PyKEEN is one. Its README lists 40 models and 37 datasets, and version 1.11.1 is from April 2025. Check PyPI for newer versions.

Reporting raw ranks and calling them filtered. Raw ranks punish the model for other right answers. Always say which setting you used. Always say if you used type filters too.

Neuro-symbolic ideas

The type filter was a tiny neuro-symbolic system. A neural part scored the answers. A symbolic part removed the impossible ones.

Henry Kautz named six ways to join the two parts. He gave the talk at AAAI in February 2020. It was printed in AI Magazine in 2022. The names look strange, but each one says who calls whom.

Kautz's six neuro-symbolic types, with his examples
NameWhat happensExample from the article
Symbolic Neuro symbolicWords go in as vectors. Symbols come out.Normal deep learning for language
Symbolic[Neuro]A symbolic solver calls a neural network inside.AlphaGo: tree search with a neural judge
Neuro | SymbolicA network turns pixels into symbols. A reasoner uses them.The Neuro-Symbolic Concept Learner
Neuro: Symbolic → NeuroSymbolic rules make the training data.A transformer that learned symbolic maths
Neuro_{Symbolic}Rules become parts of the network.Logic tensor networks
Neuro[Symbolic]A neural system calls a symbolic engine when it needs one.His favourite. Fast and slow thinking.

This note is my reading, not Kautz's text. A language model agent that calls a SPARQL tool or a reasoner looks like Neuro[Symbolic]. The model decides when to call the tool. The tool gives exact answers. Our type filter is closer to Symbolic[Neuro]. A symbolic rule wraps the neural scores.

Ontologies help neural models in three simple ways.

  • Before training. The ontology adds facts with a reasoner. More true facts make better embeddings.
  • During training. Type rules make better negative samples. A fake "Lima in_continent Peru" is too easy. A fake "Lima in_continent Europe" teaches more.
  • After training. Rules remove answers of the wrong type, as in our program.

"Neuro-symbolic" is not one method. It is a family of designs. When someone uses the word, ask the Kautz question: which part calls which?

Language models build the graph

Here is an email: "Ana joined Acme last May. She grew up in Lima." We want two facts: ana worksFor acme and ana bornIn lima. A language model can read the email and write them. This job is information extraction.

Without help, the model invents its own words. One answer says employedBy. The next says works_at. The graph fills with near copies. The fix is schema-guided extraction. You put the ontology in the prompt. The model may only use those classes and properties.

Send the schema

Give the model the classes, the properties and the allowed patterns. For example: Person worksFor Company.

Ask for structured output

Ask for JSON that follows a JSON Schema. Many model APIs can force this shape.

Link the entities

Turn each name into an ID. "Lima" becomes the city Q2868, not the family name.

Check against the ontology

Check types, domains, ranges and counts. Reject or repair what fails.

Store with the source

Write each fact with the email ID and the model name. Then you can explain it later.

Structured output

Structured output means the model must answer in a fixed shape. OpenAI added this to its API on 6 August 2024. You give a JSON Schema with a strict flag. The answer then matches the schema. Other providers offer similar features. Check each provider's documentation, because the supported parts of JSON Schema differ.

A shape is not a meaning. JSON Schema can say "subject is a string". It cannot say "the subject of worksFor must be a Person". That needs the ontology. We add that check below.

Entity linking

Entity linking turns a name into one ID. It is hard because names are shared. Here is a real search on Wikidata.

import json, urllib.parse, urllib.request

def candidates(name, limit=4):
    """Ask Wikidata for items whose label or alias matches `name`."""
    q = urllib.parse.urlencode({"action": "wbsearchentities", "search": name,
                                "language": "en", "limit": limit, "format": "json"})
    req = urllib.request.Request("https://www.wikidata.org/w/api.php?" + q,
                                 headers={"User-Agent": "study-book-example/0.1"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as r:
        return [(c["id"], c.get("description", "")) for c in json.load(r)["search"]]

for qid, desc in candidates("Lima"):
    print(qid, "-", desc)
Q2868 - capital and largest city of Peru
Q211795 - department of Peru
Q11255517 - family name
Q127940 - genus of molluscs

I ran this on 15 November 2026. The list can change. Which Lima is right? The ontology helps again. The property bornIn has the range City. So a family name and a mollusc are out. The city wins.

  1. Exact ID in the text, for example an email address. Take it.
  2. Exact label or alias match in your own graph. Take it if only one fits.
  3. Search candidates. Remove those of the wrong type.
  4. Still more than one? Compare the context, or ask the model to choose.
  5. Still unsure? Create a "needs review" item. Do not guess.

Libraries now package these steps. The Neo4j GraphRAG Python package has a pipeline that takes node types, relationship types and patterns. Its documentation says the schema guides the model but does not force it. By default it merges nodes with the same label and the same name. The page marks the feature as experimental, so check it before you depend on it.

Merging by name alone. Two people called Ana Torres become one node. Use a key when you have one. Use the type and the context when you do not.

Ontology as a guard against wrong answers

Now the most useful idea of the chapter. Never write model output straight into the graph. Put a guard in front. The guard knows the ontology.

The model below "read" a few emails. Its output has six kinds of problem. The guard finds each one.

import json

# The ontology: domain, range and "at most one value" for each property.
PROPS = {"worksFor": ("Person", "Company", False),
         "bornIn": ("Person", "City", True),          # True = functional
         "headquarteredIn": ("Company", "City", True)}
TYPE = {"ana": "Person", "acme": "Company", "birch": "Company",
        "lima": "City", "arequipa": "City"}           # linked entities

llm_output = """[["ana","worksFor","acme"], ["acme","worksFor","ana"],
 ["ana","bornIn","lima"], ["ana","bornIn","arequipa"], ["ana","bornIn","cusco"],
 ["ana","marriedTo","bob"], ["acme","headquarteredIn","birch"]]"""

def check(triples):
    seen = {}                                   # (subject, property) -> object
    for s, p, o in triples:
        if p not in PROPS:
            yield (s, p, o), "unknown property"; continue
        dom, rng, functional = PROPS[p]
        if s not in TYPE or o not in TYPE:
            yield (s, p, o), "entity not linked"; continue
        if TYPE[s] != dom:
            yield (s, p, o), f"domain: {s} is a {TYPE[s]}, not a {dom}"; continue
        if TYPE[o] != rng:
            yield (s, p, o), f"range: {o} is a {TYPE[o]}, not a {rng}"; continue
        if functional and seen.get((s, p), o) != o:
            yield (s, p, o), f"only one {p} allowed, already {seen[(s, p)]}"; continue
        seen[(s, p)] = o
        yield (s, p, o), "OK"

for triple, verdict in check(json.loads(llm_output)):
    print(" ".join(triple).ljust(32), verdict)
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    // property -> (domain, range, functional)
    let props = HashMap::from([
        ("worksFor", ("Person", "Company", false)),
        ("bornIn", ("Person", "City", true)),
        ("headquarteredIn", ("Company", "City", true)),
    ]);
    let ty = HashMap::from([("ana", "Person"), ("acme", "Company"), ("birch", "Company"),
                            ("lima", "City"), ("arequipa", "City")]);
    // In real code you parse the model's JSON with serde_json.
    let llm = [("ana", "worksFor", "acme"), ("acme", "worksFor", "ana"),
               ("ana", "bornIn", "lima"), ("ana", "bornIn", "arequipa"),
               ("ana", "bornIn", "cusco"), ("ana", "marriedTo", "bob"),
               ("acme", "headquarteredIn", "birch")];
    let mut seen: HashMap<(&str, &str), &str> = HashMap::new();
    for (s, p, o) in llm {
        let verdict = match (props.get(p), ty.get(s), ty.get(o)) {
            (None, _, _) => "unknown property".to_string(),
            (_, None, _) | (_, _, None) => "entity not linked".to_string(),
            (Some((d, _, _)), Some(ts), _) if ts != d => format!("domain: {s} is a {ts}, not a {d}"),
            (Some((_, r, _)), _, Some(to)) if to != r => format!("range: {o} is a {to}, not a {r}"),
            (Some((_, _, true)), _, _) if seen.get(&(s, p)).is_some_and(|x| *x != o) =>
                format!("only one {p} allowed, already {}", seen[&(s, p)]),
            _ => { seen.insert((s, p), o); "OK".to_string() }
        };
        println!("{:32} {}", format!("{s} {p} {o}"), verdict);
    }
}
ana worksFor acme                OK
acme worksFor ana                domain: acme is a Company, not a Person
ana bornIn lima                  OK
ana bornIn arequipa              only one bornIn allowed, already lima
ana bornIn cusco                 entity not linked
ana marriedTo bob                unknown property
acme headquarteredIn birch       range: birch is a Company, not a City

Here domain and range work as checks. That is the closed-world style of SHACL. In OWL, a domain does not reject data. It adds a new type fact instead. See OWL 2 and SHACL and validation. For real graphs, write these checks as SHACL shapes.

What do you do with a rejected fact? You have three choices.

  • Retry. Send the error message back to the model. "acme is a Company, not a Person." Models often fix their answer.
  • Queue. Put it in a review list for a person. This is right for "entity not linked".
  • Drop. Throw it away, but log it. Many drops of one kind show a gap in your ontology.

The JSON was valid, so the facts are correct.

The JSON was valid, so the shape is correct. The ontology checks the meaning. A person or a source checks the truth.

A guard catches impossible facts. It cannot catch possible but false facts. "Ana bornIn Lima" passes every check even if she was born in Quito. Keep the source of each fact, so a person can check it.

Language models ask the graph: text to SPARQL and Cypher

A manager asks: "Who works at Acme?" She does not know SPARQL. A language model can write the query for her. This is text to query. For RDF it is text to SPARQL. For property graphs it is text to Cypher.

The model needs the schema in its prompt. It needs the real names: ex:worksFor, not "employed by". Without the schema it invents names. The query then runs and returns nothing. Nobody sees an error.

So we guard the query too. First, does it parse? Second, does it use only names that exist? Third, does it return the same result as a known good query? The program below does all three with rdflib.

from rdflib import Graph, URIRef
from rdflib.plugins.sparql import prepareQuery

data = """@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .
ex:ana a ex:Person ; ex:worksFor ex:acme ; ex:bornIn ex:lima .
ex:bo  a ex:Person ; ex:worksFor ex:acme ; ex:bornIn ex:cusco .
ex:cy  a ex:Person ; ex:worksFor ex:birch .
ex:acme a ex:Company .  ex:birch a ex:Company ."""
g = Graph().parse(data=data, format="turtle")
# Every IRI the graph uses: classes, properties and entities.
KNOWN = {str(x) for x in set(g.all_nodes()) | set(g.predicates())}

def terms(node, out):            # walk the query tree, collect every IRI
    if isinstance(node, URIRef):
        out.add(node)
    elif isinstance(node, dict):
        for v in node.values(): terms(v, out)
    elif isinstance(node, (list, tuple, set)):
        for v in node: terms(v, out)
    return out

def guard(text):
    try:
        q = prepareQuery(text, initNs={"ex": "http://example.org/"})
    except Exception as e:
        return f"REJECT syntax: {type(e).__name__}"
    used = {str(t) for t in terms(q.algebra, set())}
    unknown = {u for u in used - KNOWN if u.startswith("http://example.org/")}
    if unknown:
        return f"REJECT unknown terms: {sorted(unknown)}"
    return sorted(str(r[0]).split("/")[-1] for r in g.query(q))

gold = "SELECT ?p WHERE { ?p ex:worksFor ex:acme }"
tries = ["SELECT ?p WHERE { ?p ex:employedBy ex:acme }",     # invented property
         "SELECT ?p WHERE { ?p ex:worksFor ex:acme ",        # broken syntax
         "SELECT ?p WHERE { ?p ex:worksFor ex:acme . ?p a ex:Person }"]
print("gold:", guard(gold))
for t in tries:
    r = guard(t)
    print(r if isinstance(r, str) else f"{r}  same result as gold: {r == guard(gold)}")
gold: ['ana', 'bo']
REJECT unknown terms: ['http://example.org/employedBy']
REJECT syntax: ParseException
['ana', 'bo']  same result as gold: True

I ran it with rdflib 7.6.0 and Python 3.14 (uv run --with rdflib). Look at the third query. It is longer than the gold query. But it gives the same people. A text match would call it wrong. A result match calls it right.

PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/>
SELECT ?p WHERE { ?p ex:worksFor ex:acme . }
// The same question on a property graph
MATCH (p:Person)-[:WORKS_FOR]->(c:Company {name: 'Acme'})
RETURN p.name

Public test sets exist. LC-QuAD 2.0 (ISWC 2019) has 30,000 questions with SPARQL for Wikidata and DBpedia. Neo4j published a Text2Cypher set in December 2024 with 44,387 question and query pairs. Use them to compare models. Then build a small test set from your own schema, because your names are not in any public set.

Give the model a few good question and query pairs from your own graph. Show it the real property names and two sample rows. Small, real examples help more than long rules.

Letting the model run any query. A generated query can be slow or can change data. Allow only read queries, set a time limit, and limit the number of rows.

GraphRAG

RAG finds pieces of text and gives them to the model. It works well for "What did the contract say about fees?" It works badly for "What are the main themes in these 5,000 reports?" No single piece of text holds that answer.

GraphRAG builds a graph first. A team at Microsoft described it in April 2024 (Edge and co-authors). Their goal was questions about a whole collection.

Cut the text

Split the documents into chunks. The paper used chunks of 600 tokens with an overlap of 100.

Extract a graph

A language model reads each chunk. It writes entities, relationships and claims.

Find communities

The Leiden method splits the graph into communities. It repeats inside each group, so you get levels.

Summarise each community

The model writes a short report for each community, from the bottom level up.

Answer globally

Each report gives a partial answer and a helpfulness score. The best partial answers are joined into one final answer.

Or answer locally

For a question about one entity, start at that entity and read its neighbours.

The current documentation lists four query modes.

  • Global search. Uses the community reports. For "what are the main themes?"
  • Local search. Starts at an entity and expands to its neighbours.
  • DRIFT search. Local search plus community information.
  • Basic search. Normal vector search over text chunks.

Where is the ontology? In plain GraphRAG the model chooses the entity types. You can give it your own types in the prompt. My view: this is the easiest place to add value. A fixed list of types gives cleaner communities and fewer duplicate nodes.

Indexing everything on day one. The project README warns that indexing can be expensive. The model reads every chunk at least once. Start with a small folder, measure the cost, then grow.

Evaluating all of this

Each task needs its own metric. A single "accuracy" number hides too much. Here is a worked example for extraction first.

  1. A person reads ten emails and writes 20 true facts. This is the gold set.
  2. The model writes 16 facts. 12 of them are in the gold set.
  3. Precision is 12 / 16 = 0.75.
  4. Recall is 12 / 20 = 0.60.
  5. F1 is \frac{2 \cdot 0.75 \cdot 0.60}{0.75 + 0.60} \approx 0.667.
Which metric for which task
TaskMain metricWhat it misses
Link predictionFiltered MRR, Hits@1, Hits@10Whether the top guess is really true in the world
ExtractionPrecision, recall, F1 against a gold setFacts that are true but missing from the gold set
Entity linkingShare of names linked to the right IDNames that should get "no match"
Text to queryExecution accuracySlow queries that still give the right rows
GuardShare of bad facts caught, share of good facts wrongly blockedPossible but false facts
RAG and GraphRAGFaithfulness, context recallA faithful answer to the wrong question

For long answers, people often use another model as the judge. This is LLM-as-a-judge. The GraphRAG paper did this. A judge model compared two answers on comprehensiveness, diversity and empowerment. A fourth criterion, directness, was a control. Tools such as Ragas offer ready metrics like faithfulness and context recall.

Pitfall 1: the test is in the training data

This was the FB15k problem. For language models it is worse. A public benchmark may be inside the model's training text. Keep a private test set from your own data.

Pitfall 2: the judge has favourites

A judge model may prefer longer answers, or the answer it sees first. Swap the order of the two answers and judge again. Check a sample by hand.

Pitfall 3: one run, one number

Models give different answers on different runs. Our TransE run also changes with the seed. Run several times and report the spread.

Pitfall 4: no baseline

Compare with something simple. Plain vector RAG. A query template. A string match for entity linking. A complex system must beat the simple one by enough to pay for itself.

Know the difference between "filtered" and "raw" ranks. Know why FB15k-237 and WN18RR exist. Know that execution accuracy compares results, not query text. These three points come up often.

Patterns to remember
