Patterns for ontologies and AI
PatternPurposeModelNote
Translation scoreScore a triple with vectors-\lVert \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{t} \rVertTransE puts all tails of one-to-many on one point.
Filtered rankFair test of link predictionSkip other known true tails, then countSay "filtered" in every report.
Type-filtered candidatesRemove impossible answersRange of in_continent is ContinentReport results with and without the filter.
Corrupted tripleMake negative examples(Lima, in_continent, Europe)Random fakes are often too easy.
Schema in the promptStop invented property names"Use only: worksFor, bornIn"The model may still break it. Check after.
Structured outputForce the JSON shapeJSON Schema with strict modeShape is not meaning.
Type-checked linkingPick the right ID for a namebornIn needs a City, so Q2868No good candidate means "review", not "guess".
Domain and range guardReject impossible factsacme worksFor ana is rejectedIn OWL these infer types. Use SHACL for checks.
Error back to the modelLet the model fix its output"birch is a Company, not a City"Limit the retries.
Query term checkCatch invented names in SPARQLEvery IRI in the query must existA valid query can still answer the wrong question.
Result matchGrade text to query fairlyCompare result sets, not stringsOrder and duplicates need a rule.
Community summaryAnswer questions about a whole collectionGraphRAG global searchIndexing cost grows with the text.
Fact with sourceLet a person check the truthFact plus email ID plus model nameThe only defence against possible but false facts.

Practice

With TransE, what does a score of 0 mean?

  • The triple is false.
  • \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} lands exactly on \mathbf{t}.
  • The model has not seen the triple.

The score is minus the distance. A distance of 0 gives the best possible score.

Why can DistMult not tell "parent of" from "child of"?

  • It has too few numbers.
  • Its score is the same if you swap head and tail.
  • It uses complex numbers.

\sum_i h_i r_i t_i does not change when h and t swap places. ComplEx fixes this.

A language model agent calls a SPARQL endpoint when it needs an exact fact. Which Kautz type is closest?

  • Symbolic[Neuro]
  • Neuro[Symbolic]
  • Neuro_{Symbolic}

The neural part is in charge and calls a symbolic engine. This is my reading of the taxonomy, not Kautz's own example.

The model's JSON matches your JSON Schema. What do you know?

  • The facts are true.
  • The facts fit the ontology.
  • The facts have the right shape.

JSON Schema checks shape. The ontology guard checks meaning. Sources check truth.

Filtered ranks of five questions are 1, 1, 2, 4 and 5. MRR is ? (two decimals).

In the same set, Hits@3 is ?.

  1. Peru is (0, 0), has_city is (1, 0), Cusco is (1.2, 0.3). Compute the TransE score of (Peru, has_city, Cusco) with Euclidean distance.
    Answer

    \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} = (1, 0). The difference to Cusco is (-0.2, -0.3). The distance is \sqrt{0.04 + 0.09} = \sqrt{0.13} \approx 0.36. The score is about -0.36.

  2. The query is (Peru, has_city, ?). The sorted list is Lima, Arequipa, Cusco, Paris. Lima and Arequipa are in the training data. The test answer is Cusco. Give the raw and the filtered rank.
    Answer

    Raw rank is 3. Filtered rank is 1, because Lima and Arequipa are other known true answers and are skipped.

  3. The model outputs lima headquarteredIn acme. Which check in the guard fails first, and why?
    Answer

    The domain check. headquarteredIn needs a Company as subject, but lima is a City. The guard stops at the first failed check.

  4. The model writes 30 facts. 21 are in the gold set of 28 facts. Compute precision, recall and F1.
    Answer

    Precision is 21/30 = 0.70. Recall is 21/28 = 0.75. F1 is 2 \cdot 0.70 \cdot 0.75 / 1.45 \approx 0.724.

  5. A generated SPARQL query returns the same rows as the gold query, but in another order. Is it right? What rule should your test use?
    Answer

    Usually yes. Compare the results as sets when the question has no order. If the question says "sorted by date", then compare as lists. Write the rule down before you test.

  6. Your team wants GraphRAG over 20,000 support tickets. Give three steps to keep cost and quality under control.
    Answer

    First, index a small sample, for example 500 tickets, and measure tokens and money. Second, give the model a fixed list of entity types from your ontology, such as Customer, Product and Issue. Third, build 30 test questions with known answers and compare GraphRAG with plain vector RAG before you index everything.

  7. Your link prediction model has MRR 0.41 on all entities and 0.62 with a type filter. Your colleague reports only 0.62. What is wrong, and what should the report say?
    Answer

    The filter is part of the system, so 0.62 is fair only if the filter is named. The report should give both numbers, say they are filtered ranks, and say which type rule removed candidates. Then readers can compare with other papers.

Key takeaways

  • Neural AI reads messy text. Symbolic AI keeps clear facts and rules. Ontologies join them.
  • An embedding model scores triples. TransE wants \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} to land on \mathbf{t}.
  • Measure link prediction with filtered MRR and Hits@k. Watch for leakage.
  • A type rule from the ontology removes impossible answers and raises quality.
  • Put the schema in the prompt. Ask for structured output. Then check the meaning with the ontology.
  • Link names to IDs with type checks. When unsure, queue for review.
  • Guard generated queries: parse, check names, compare results.
  • GraphRAG answers questions about a whole collection, but indexing costs money.
  • Choose one metric per task. Keep the source of every fact.

Sources

  • Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data. The TransE paper by Bordes and co-authors, NeurIPS 2013.
  • PyKEEN on PyPI. A Python library for knowledge graph embeddings. Version 1.11.1, list of models and datasets.
  • The Third AI Summer. Henry Kautz's Engelmore lecture in AI Magazine, 2022, with the six neuro-symbolic types.
  • From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization. The GraphRAG paper by Edge and co-authors, 2024.
  • Neo4j GraphRAG Python: knowledge graph builder. Schema-guided extraction and entity resolution.
  • Text2Cypher: Bridging Natural Language and Graph Databases. The Neo4j Text2Cypher dataset and benchmark, 2024.

Context graphs and agent memory

An AI agent forgets everything when its context window ends. A memory system gives it a past. In this chapter we open six real projects and read the ontology inside each one.

  • Explain what a context graph adds to a knowledge graph.
  • Read the node types, edge types and time fields of six real systems.
  • Store a fact with two clocks and ask "as of" questions.
  • Compare identity rules and conflict rules across systems.
  • Design the ontology of your own agent memory with a checklist.

What a context graph is

Start with a small story. A support agent approves a refund of 900 euros. The policy limit is 500 euros. The ticket system stores one line: "refund 900, done".

Now ask four questions. Who allowed the exception? Which rule was used? What did the agent know at that moment? Was there an older case like this one? The ticket system cannot answer.

A context graph can answer. It stores the things, the events and the decisions. Every fact has a time and a source.

A context graph is a graph of entities, events and decisions. Every fact carries a time and a source. A changed fact is closed, not deleted.

You know the knowledge graph from the knowledge graph chapter. A context graph is a knowledge graph with four more things.

  • Events. Every input is stored as it arrived. A message, a file, a tool result.
  • Time. Each fact knows when it became true and when it stopped.
  • Source. Each fact points back to the event that produced it. This is its provenance.
  • Decisions. The graph stores who decided, with which rule and which exception.
Knowledge graph and context graph
QuestionClassic knowledge graphContext graph
What is a fact?A triple: Ana works at AcmeA triple, plus time, plus source
TimeOften noneTrue from, true until, learned on
SourceOften the whole data setThe exact message or document
ChangeOverwrite or deleteClose the old fact and keep it
DecisionsNoWho, which rule, which exception
Typical questionWhat is the capital of Peru?Why did we approve this in June?

The word became popular in December 2025. Two investors, Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg, wrote an essay about it. They call a stored decision a decision trace. Many traces, linked over time, make the graph.

The Graphiti project uses the same word for its graph of facts with time. So vendors use the word in two ways. Always ask what a product really stores.

A context graph is not the private thinking of the model. It stores what was read, which rule was used and who approved. That is enough to explain a decision later.

  1. Jan 2025 Zep paper. It describes the graph inside Graphiti with two clocks.
  2. Apr 2025 Mem0 paper. Memory as short facts taken from chats.
  3. Dec 2025 Hindsight paper. Retain, recall and reflect.
  4. Dec 2025 Context graph essay. Decision traces become a topic.
  5. Apr 2026 Mem0 changes. Its README dates a new add-only method to this month.
  6. Nov 2026 This chapter. I read all six repositories on 15 November 2026.

Time-aware facts: valid time and system time

Here is the example. Ana works at Acme from 10 January 2024. On 1 June 2026 she moves to Birch. The agent hears about it on 20 June. It is 19 days late.

So there are two clocks. Valid time is the clock of the world. System time is the clock of the database. A model with both clocks is bi-temporal.

Four time fields on one fact (the names are from Graphiti)
FieldClockMeaningAcme fact
valid_atWorldThe fact became true2024-01-10
invalid_atWorldThe fact stopped being true2026-06-01
created_atSystemThe system stored the fact2026-03-01
expired_atSystemThe system closed the fact2026-06-20

Take a world day v and a system day k. A fact f answers the question "what did we believe on day k about day v?" when

f.\text{created} \le k \quad\text{and}\quad f.\text{valid} \le v \lt \text{end}_k(f)

Here \text{end}_k(f) is f.\text{invalid} when f.\text{expired} \le k. In all other cases the end is open.

In simple words: the system must already hold the fact on day k. The fact must be true on day v. An end date counts only if the system knew it on day k.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Fact:
    text: str
    valid_at: str              # world time: true from this day
    invalid_at: str | None     # world time: not true from this day
    created_at: str            # system time: the day we stored it
    expired_at: str | None     # system time: the day we closed it

facts: list[Fact] = []

def add(text: str, valid_at: str, today: str, replaces: str | None = None) -> None:
    """Store a new fact. Close the old one. Delete nothing."""
    for old in facts:
        if old.text == replaces and old.invalid_at is None:
            old.invalid_at = valid_at    # the old fact ends in the world
            old.expired_at = today       # we learned that today
    facts.append(Fact(text, valid_at, None, today, None))

def as_of(valid: str, known: str) -> list[str]:
    """What did the system believe on day `known` about day `valid`?"""
    out = []
    for f in facts:
        if f.created_at > known:
            continue                     # not stored yet on that day
        closed = f.expired_at is not None and f.expired_at <= known
        end = f.invalid_at if closed else None
        if f.valid_at <= valid and (end is None or valid < end):
            out.append(f.text)
    return out

add("Ana works at Acme", valid_at="2024-01-10", today="2026-03-01")
add("Ana works at Birch", valid_at="2026-06-01", today="2026-06-20",
    replaces="Ana works at Acme")

print(as_of(valid="2026-05-01", known="2026-07-01"))  # history
print(as_of(valid="2026-06-10", known="2026-07-01"))  # the truth today
print(as_of(valid="2026-06-10", known="2026-06-15"))  # what the agent believed
print(len(facts), "facts stored")
struct Fact {
    text: &'static str,
    valid_at: &'static str,           // world time: true from this day
    invalid_at: Option<&'static str>, // world time: not true from this day
    created_at: &'static str,         // system time: the day we stored it
    expired_at: Option<&'static str>, // system time: the day we closed it
}

/// Store a new fact. Close the old one. Delete nothing.
fn add(facts: &mut Vec<Fact>, text: &'static str, valid_at: &'static str,
       today: &'static str, replaces: Option<&str>) {
    for old in facts.iter_mut() {
        if Some(old.text) == replaces && old.invalid_at.is_none() {
            old.invalid_at = Some(valid_at); // the old fact ends in the world
            old.expired_at = Some(today);    // we learned that today
        }
    }
    facts.push(Fact { text, valid_at, invalid_at: None, created_at: today, expired_at: None });
}

/// What did the system believe on day `known` about day `valid`?
fn as_of(facts: &[Fact], valid: &str, known: &str) -> Vec<&'static str> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for f in facts {
        if f.created_at > known {
            continue; // not stored yet on that day
        }
        let closed = f.expired_at.is_some_and(|d| d <= known);
        let end = if closed { f.invalid_at } else { None };
        if f.valid_at <= valid && end.is_none_or(|e| valid < e) {
            out.push(f.text);
        }
    }
    out
}

fn main() {
    let mut facts: Vec<Fact> = Vec::new();
    add(&mut facts, "Ana works at Acme", "2024-01-10", "2026-03-01", None);
    add(&mut facts, "Ana works at Birch", "2026-06-01", "2026-06-20",
        Some("Ana works at Acme"));

    println!("{:?}", as_of(&facts, "2026-05-01", "2026-07-01")); // history
    println!("{:?}", as_of(&facts, "2026-06-10", "2026-07-01")); // the truth today
    println!("{:?}", as_of(&facts, "2026-06-10", "2026-06-15")); // what the agent believed
    println!("{} facts stored", facts.len());
}
["Ana works at Acme"]
["Ana works at Birch"]
["Ana works at Acme"]
2 facts stored

Both programs print the same lines. Dates are text like 2026-06-01. Text in this form sorts in the right order. Look at the third line. On 15 June the agent still believed "Acme". This explains a decision that the agent made on that day.

Many systems overwrite the old fact. Then the first and the third question have no answer. Other systems keep only one timestamp. Then you cannot separate "true since" from "known since".

Databases know this idea too. The SQL standard of 2011 added tables with both kinds of time. Our small model keeps one row for each fact. A full system-versioned table keeps every old row.

The six projects at a glance

The reader of this book asked for these six projects by name. I opened each repository on 15 November 2026. The table shows what each one really is. Versions change fast, so check the repository again.

Six repositories as I saw them on 15 November 2026
ProjectWhat it isLanguageWhere data livesLicenceVersion seen
GraphitiLibrary that builds a graph of facts with timePythonNeo4j, FalkorDB or Amazon NeptuneApache-2.00.31.2
Mem0Memory layer of short text factsPython, TypeScriptA vector store and an SQLite fileApache-2.0mem0ai 2.2.1
HindsightMemory server: retain, recall, reflectPythonPostgreSQL with pgvectorMIT1.2.1
GraphifyTool that turns a project folder into a graphPythonOne file, graph.jsonApache-2.00.9.108
OmnigraphGraph database with typed schema and branchesRustLance files on disk or object storageMIT0.15.0
pgGraphPostgreSQL extension for graph queries on tablesRustYour tables and a derived indexApache-2.01.2.1

Only the first three call themselves memory systems. The last three are graph engines. All six hold an ontology. Sometimes it is fixed in the code. Sometimes you write it yourself.

An episode arrives

An episode is one message, one document or one tool result. The system stores it first. It is the proof.

Extract

A model or a parser finds the things and the facts. "Ana", "Birch", "works at".

Match

Is this "Ana" already in the graph? The system uses identity rules to decide.

Check conflicts

The new fact may fight with an old fact. The system closes the old one, keeps both, or stops.

Store with time and source

The fact gets its time fields and a link to the episode.

Recall

Later the agent asks a question. The system searches by meaning, by words and by links. It returns a small set that fits the context window.

The ontology inside three memory systems

Each case study has the same five parts. The problem. How it works. A real example. The theory under it. The trade-off.

Graphiti: facts with two clocks

The problem. Chats and business data change every day. A static graph cannot say what was true last month.

How it works. You call add_episode. A language model finds entities and facts. The library matches them to old ones, dates each fact and closes facts that the new fact contradicts.

The ontology in the Graphiti source code
PartWhat the code shows
Node typesEpisodic (raw input), Entity (a thing with name, summary, labels, attributes), Community (a group of entities), Saga (a named series of episodes)
Edge typesMENTIONS, RELATES_TO, HAS_MEMBER, HAS_EPISODE, NEXT_EPISODE
Time fieldsOn a fact: valid_at, invalid_at, created_at, expired_at, reference_time. On an episode: valid_at, created_at
IdentityA uuid on every node and edge. A group_id splits the graph into parts, one for each user or team
SearchVector similarity, BM25 word search and a graph walk. Then a reranker

A real example. I copied the shape of these calls from the Graphiti documentation. I did not run it. It needs a graph database and a model key.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.nodes import EpisodeType

class Person(BaseModel):
    """A human we talk about."""
    occupation: str | None = Field(None, description="Current job")

class Company(BaseModel):
    """A business."""
    industry: str | None = Field(None, description="Main industry")

class Employment(BaseModel):
    """A person works at a company."""
    position: str | None = Field(None, description="Job title")

async def main() -> None:
    graphiti = Graphiti("bolt://localhost:7687", "neo4j", "password")
    await graphiti.add_episode(
        name="chat 41",
        episode_body="user: Ana moved from Acme to Birch on 1 June.",
        source=EpisodeType.message,
        source_description="support chat",
        reference_time=datetime(2026, 6, 20, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
        entity_types={"Person": Person, "Company": Company},
        edge_types={"Employment": Employment},
        edge_type_map={("Person", "Company"): ["Employment"]},
        group_id="team-7",
    )
    for edge in await graphiti.search("Where does Ana work?", group_ids=["team-7"]):
        print(edge.fact, edge.valid_at, edge.invalid_at)   # each hit is a fact edge
    await graphiti.close()

The theory under it. It is the two clocks from the last section, plus one rule for conflicts. I read this rule in the function that closes old edges.

A new fact n contradicts an old fact o. If o.\text{valid} \lt n.\text{valid}, then set o.\text{invalid} = n.\text{valid} and o.\text{expired} = \text{now}. Both facts stay in the graph.

With our numbers: the Acme fact starts in 2024. The Birch fact starts on 1 June 2026. So the Acme fact gets invalid_at 1 June 2026. The graph now has two facts, not one. The code also handles the other order. If the stored fact starts later, the new fact is the one that gets closed.

The trade-off. Each episode needs several model calls. That is slow and it costs money. The README sets a low limit of 10 parallel calls to avoid rate limit errors. You also run a graph database yourself.

The authors publish numbers in their paper of January 2025. With one model, their system answered 71.2% of a long memory test. The full chat history got 60.2%. The answer time was 2.58 seconds against 28.9 seconds. These are the authors' numbers.

Mem0: add only, rank later

The problem. A chat agent must remember what a user likes across many sessions. Sending the full history each time costs too many tokens.

How it works. You call add with messages. One model call extracts short facts. Each fact becomes a text with a vector. The code also finds names in the fact and links them to it.

The ontology in the Mem0 open-source code
PartWhat the code shows
Node typesMemory (one short text fact), Entity (a name found in a fact, kept in a second collection), History row, Message row
Edge typesNo real edges. An entity record holds a list linked_memory_ids. A memory holds user_id, agent_id or run_id
Time fieldscreated_at, updated_at, and an optional expiration_date that hides a memory after that day
IdentityA uuid for each memory. An MD5 hash of the text stops exact copies
SearchVector search finds the candidates. Word search and entity links push good ones up

Older Mem0 versions could write to a graph database. The paper of 2025 describes a graph variant. The open-source code I read has no graph store. The migration guide says graph memory is now a feature of the paid platform only.

A real example. The shape is from the README. I did not run it. It needs a model key.

from mem0 import Memory

memory = Memory()

memory.add(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "I moved to Birch in June. I write Rust now."}],
    user_id="ana",
)

hits = memory.search("Where does Ana work?", filters={"user_id": "ana"}, top_k=3)
for hit in hits["results"]:
    print(hit["memory"], hit["score"], hit["created_at"])

The theory under it. Three searches give three scores. Cosine similarity is between 0 and 1. A raw BM25 score can be 20 or more. You cannot add them raw. Mem0 first presses the BM25 score into the range 0 to 1.

Let s be the similarity, b the raw BM25 score and e the entity boost. With a midpoint m and a steepness a:

\sigma(b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-a(b - m)}} \qquad \text{score} = \frac{s + \sigma(b) + e}{2.5}

Take a short question. The code uses m = 5 and a = 0.7. Memory A has s = 0.62, b = 9 and e = 0.4. Then \sigma(9) = 0.94 and the score is 1.96 / 2.5 = 0.785. Memory B has s = 0.70 and nothing else. Its score is 0.28. The exact name wins over the vague match.

The trade-off. Writes are cheap: one model call. But nothing is closed. The old fact "works at Acme" and the new fact "works at Birch" both stay. The ranking must pick the right one each time. There is no valid time in the open-source code.

The README reports 92.5 on the LoCoMo test with about 7,000 tokens for each query. The README also says these numbers are from the paid platform. So do not expect the same numbers from the open-source code.

Hindsight: what I saw, what I did, what I learned

The problem. An agent should learn and not only remember. It must separate facts about the world from its own actions and from its own conclusions.

How it works. There are three operations. retain stores new content and extracts facts. recall searches. reflect reasons over the memories. Memories live in a bank, one for each user, agent or project.

The ontology in the Hindsight source code
PartWhat the code shows
Node typesBank, Document, Memory unit with fact_type world, experience or observation, Entity. The README adds mental models
Edge typesUnit to entity. Entity to entity with a count of how often they appear together. Unit to unit with link_type temporal, semantic, entity or a causal type, and a weight from 0 to 1
Time fieldsoccurred_start and occurred_end (when it happened), mentioned_at (when it was said), created_at, updated_at. Entities have first_seen and last_seen
IdentityA UUID for each unit. One canonical name for each entity in a bank
SearchFour searches at the same time: meaning, words, graph links and time

The fact type depends on who speaks. "I fixed the login bug" from the agent is an experience. "I bought a car" from a user is a world fact about that user. Later a background job joins many facts into one observation. Each observation keeps links to the facts that support it.

A real example. The shape is from the README. I did not run it. It needs a running server and a model key.

from hindsight_client import Hindsight

client = Hindsight(base_url="http://localhost:8888")

client.retain(
    bank_id="team-7",
    content="Ana moved from Acme to Birch.",
    context="career update",
    timestamp="2026-06-20T10:00:00Z",
)

print(client.recall(bank_id="team-7", query="Where does Ana work?"))
print(client.reflect(bank_id="team-7", query="What changed for Ana this year?"))

The theory under it. Four searches return four lists. Their scores have different scales. Hindsight ignores the scores and uses only the places in each list. The method is reciprocal rank fusion, RRF for short.

An item d has place r_i(d) in list i. Place 1 is the best. With a constant k:

\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{i} \frac{1}{k + r_i(d)}

A list that does not contain d adds nothing.

from collections import defaultdict

def rrf(lists: list[list[str]], k: int) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Reciprocal rank fusion. Rank 1 is the best place in a list."""
    score: dict[str, float] = defaultdict(float)
    for one_list in lists:
        for rank, item in enumerate(one_list, start=1):
            score[item] += 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(score.items(), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])

vector  = ["f7", "f2", "f9", "f4"]   # search by meaning
keyword = ["f2", "f5", "f7"]         # search by words (BM25)
graph   = ["f4", "f2"]               # search by links

for k in (60, 0):
    ranked = rrf([vector, keyword, graph], k)
    print(f"k={k}:", ", ".join(f"{item} {s:.4f}" for item, s in ranked))
k=60: f2 0.0487, f7 0.0323, f4 0.0320, f5 0.0161, f9 0.0159
k=0: f2 2.0000, f7 1.3333, f4 1.2500, f5 0.5000, f9 0.3333

Fact f2 is never first in the vector list. But it is in all three lists, so it wins. Hindsight's code uses k = 60. Graphiti's code uses the form 1/r, which is k = 0 here. A small k gives the top places much more power.

The trade-off. There are many parts: PostgreSQL, a language model, an embedding model and a reranker. Observations are built later, so they can be behind the newest facts. The documentation also says that name matching can join a new short name to the wrong entity.

The paper of December 2025 reports 91.4% on LongMemEval and 89.61% on LoCoMo. The README says two outside groups repeated the test. Still, these are the authors' numbers.

The ontology inside three graph engines

The next three projects do not extract facts from chats for you. They give you a graph to fill or a graph that is built from files and tables.

Graphify: a map of your project

The problem. A coding agent reads the same files again and again. A text search finds words. It does not find structure.

How it works. Graphify reads a folder. It parses code with tree-sitter, without a language model. A model reads documents and images only if you set one up. The result is one file, graph.json, plus a report.

The ontology in the Graphify source code (version 0.9.108)
PartWhat the code shows
Node fieldsid, label, source_file, source_location, and file_type: code, document, paper, image, rationale or concept
Edge fieldssource, target, source_file, a relation such as calls, imports, inherits, references or contains, and a confidence
ConfidenceEXTRACTED (written in the source), INFERRED (worked out), AMBIGUOUS (not sure)
Time fieldsNone. The graph is a picture of the files at one moment
IdentityThe node id comes from the file path under the project root and the name

A real example. These commands are from the README. I could not run the package in my test setup.

uv tool install graphifyy      # the package name has two letters y
graphify install               # register the skill in your coding assistant

# inside the assistant, build the graph for this folder
/graphify .

# then ask the graph, not the files
graphify query "how does a refund reach billing?"
graphify path "refund()" "charge()"
graphify explain "refund()"
{
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "api_refund", "label": "refund()", "file_type": "code",
     "source_file": "api.py", "source_location": "L42"}
  ],
  "edges": [
    {"source": "api_refund", "target": "billing_charge", "relation": "calls",
     "confidence": "INFERRED", "source_file": "api.py"}
  ]
}

The theory under it. Graphify splits the graph into communities with the Leiden method. Leiden looks for a split with high modularity.

A graph has m edges. A community c has e_c edges inside it. The degrees of its nodes sum to d_c. Then

Q = \sum_{c} \left( \frac{e_c}{m} - \left( \frac{d_c}{2m} \right)^2 \right)

Take two triangles joined by one edge. Then m = 7. Each triangle has e_c = 3 and d_c = 7. So Q = 2 \cdot (3/7 - 0.25) = 0.357. Put all six nodes in one community and Q = 0. The split at the bridge is better. Leiden also promises that each community is connected. The older Louvain method could not promise that.

Why does this save tokens? The agent reads one community and its top nodes. It does not read every file.

The trade-off. The graph gets old when files change. You rebuild it, or you use watch mode or a git hook. An INFERRED edge can be wrong. There is no time and no decision history. The README reports recall of 0.497 on a memory test and no model cost to build the graph. These are the authors' numbers.

Omnigraph: your schema, with branches

The problem. Many agents write into one shared model of the world. One bad write can break it for all.

How it works. Omnigraph is a graph database written in Rust. You declare node types and edge types in a .pg file. The engine checks every write against this schema. Changes can go to a branch first, like in Git.

What Omnigraph gives you (documentation for release 0.15.0)
PartWhat the documentation shows
Node and edge typesNone built in. You declare them with node and edge
Constraints@key, @unique, @index, @range, @check, and @card for how many edges a node may have
Time fieldsEvery write is a commit with an id, a parent, an actor and a timestamp. You can read an old commit. That is system time. For valid time you declare your own DateTime property
IdentityThe id of a node comes from its @key values
SearchGraph walk, vector search and text search in one engine, joined with RRF

A real example. The syntax follows the quickstart in the repository. I did not run it. I did not install the binary.

node Decision {
  slug: String @key
  summary: String
  decided_at: DateTime
}

node Policy {
  slug: String @key
  title: String
}

node Person {
  email: String @key
  display_name: String
}

edge Applies: Decision -> Policy
edge ApprovedBy: Decision -> Person {
  reason: String?
}
omnigraph init --schema schema.pg graph.omni
omnigraph branch create agent/refund-42 --target ./graph.omni
omnigraph load --data decisions.jsonl --mode append \
  --branch agent/refund-42 --target ./graph.omni
omnigraph branch merge agent/refund-42 --into main --target ./graph.omni

The theory under it. When both sides changed, Omnigraph does a three-way merge. It compares each side with the merge base. The base is the newest commit that both branches share.

For one entity, let B be its value at the base, S on the source branch and T on the target. If S = B, keep T. If T = B, take S. If S = T, take that value. In all other cases there is a conflict.

Three entities in one merge
EntityBaseSource branchTargetResult
Policy p1, titleRefund ruleRefund rule v2Refund ruleRefund rule v2
Person ana, nameAna S.Ana S.Ana SouzaAna Souza
Decision d7, summaryRefund 500Refund 900Refund 700Conflict

The documentation names seven kinds of conflict. Two examples are divergent_update and orphan_edge. On a conflict the merge publishes nothing. So the main branch never holds a half-merged state.

The trade-off. You must design the schema first. Nothing is extracted from text for you. Some schema changes are refused, for example a new type for an old property. The project is young: the release I saw is 0.15.0.

pgGraph: your tables are the graph

The problem. Your data is already in PostgreSQL tables. A question like "who is two steps from Alice?" needs recursive SQL. That is hard to write and often slow.

How it works. pgGraph is an extension. Your tables stay the truth. You register tables and relationships, or the extension finds them from primary keys and foreign keys. Then graph.build() makes a compact index. SQL functions walk that index.

The ontology in pgGraph (documentation for version 1.2.1)
PartWhat the documentation shows
Node typesThe tables you register
Edge typesForeign keys with a label. A join table with two foreign keys becomes one relationship
Time fieldsNone of its own. Time is whatever columns your tables have
IdentityThe table and its key column
Searchgraph.search, graph.traverse, graph.shortest_path

A real example. These calls are from the quickstart. I did not run them. That needs a PostgreSQL server with the extension.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS graph;

-- register two tables and one relationship by hand
SELECT graph.add_table('public.people'::regclass,
                       id_column := 'id', columns := ARRAY['name']);
SELECT graph.add_table('public.companies'::regclass,
                       id_column := 'id', columns := ARRAY['name']);
SELECT graph.add_edge(
  from_table := 'public.people'::regclass,    from_column := 'company_id',
  to_table   := 'public.companies'::regclass, to_column   := 'id',
  label := 'works_at', bidirectional := true);
SELECT * FROM graph.build();

-- everything within two steps of the person p1
SELECT depth, node_table_name, node_id, edge_path
FROM graph.traverse('public.people'::regclass, 'p1', 2, hydrate := false);

The theory under it. The index is in CSR form. All neighbours of all nodes sit in one long array. A second array says where each node's part starts.

A graph with n nodes and m directed edges needs n + 1 offsets and m targets. The neighbours of node v are the slice from \text{offsets}[v] to \text{offsets}[v+1]. Finding the slice takes two array reads.

use std::collections::VecDeque;

/// Two flat lists. `offsets` has n + 1 numbers. `targets` has one per edge.
fn build_csr(n: usize, edges: &[(usize, usize)]) -> (Vec<usize>, Vec<usize>) {
    let mut offsets = vec![0; n + 1];
    for &(src, _) in edges {
        offsets[src + 1] += 1; // count the edges of each node
    }
    for i in 0..n {
        offsets[i + 1] += offsets[i]; // running total = start position
    }
    let mut targets = vec![0; edges.len()];
    let mut cursor = offsets[..n].to_vec();
    for &(src, dst) in edges {
        targets[cursor[src]] = dst;
        cursor[src] += 1;
    }
    (offsets, targets)
}

/// Breadth-first search with a depth limit.
fn within(offsets: &[usize], targets: &[usize], start: usize, hops: usize) -> Vec<Option<usize>> {
    let mut depth = vec![None; offsets.len() - 1];
    depth[start] = Some(0);
    let mut queue = VecDeque::from([start]);
    while let Some(v) = queue.pop_front() {
        let d = depth[v].unwrap();
        if d == hops {
            continue;
        }
        for &w in &targets[offsets[v]..offsets[v + 1]] { // one slice, no search
            if depth[w].is_none() {
                depth[w] = Some(d + 1);
                queue.push_back(w);
            }
        }
    }
    depth
}

fn main() {
    let names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Acme Bank", "Northwind"];
    let edges = [(0, 3), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 0), (3, 1), (4, 2)]; // (from, to) rows
    let (offsets, targets) = build_csr(names.len(), &edges);
    println!("offsets {:?}", offsets);
    println!("targets {:?}", targets);
    let acme: Vec<&str> = targets[offsets[3]..offsets[4]].iter().map(|&w| names[w]).collect();
    println!("Acme Bank -> {:?}", acme);
    for (v, d) in within(&offsets, &targets, 0, 2).iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(d) = d {
            println!("{} {}", names[v], d);
        }
    }
}
from collections import deque

names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Acme Bank", "Northwind"]
edges = [(0, 3), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 0), (3, 1), (4, 2)]   # (from, to) rows

def build_csr(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]:
    """Two flat lists. offsets has n + 1 numbers. targets has one per edge."""
    offsets = [0] * (n + 1)
    for src, _ in edges:
        offsets[src + 1] += 1            # count the edges of each node
    for i in range(n):
        offsets[i + 1] += offsets[i]     # running total = start position
    targets = [0] * len(edges)
    cursor = offsets[:-1].copy()
    for src, dst in edges:
        targets[cursor[src]] = dst
        cursor[src] += 1
    return offsets, targets

def neighbours(v: int) -> list[int]:
    return targets[offsets[v]:offsets[v + 1]]   # one slice, no search

def within(start: int, hops: int) -> dict[int, int]:
    """Breadth-first search with a depth limit."""
    depth = {start: 0}
    queue = deque([start])
    while queue:
        v = queue.popleft()
        if depth[v] == hops:
            continue
        for w in neighbours(v):
            if w not in depth:
                depth[w] = depth[v] + 1
                queue.append(w)
    return depth

offsets, targets = build_csr(len(names), edges)
print("offsets", offsets)
print("targets", targets)
print("Acme Bank ->", [names[w] for w in neighbours(3)])
print({names[v]: d for v, d in within(0, 2).items()})
offsets [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6]
targets [3, 3, 4, 0, 1, 2]
Acme Bank -> ["Alice", "Bob"]
Alice 0
Bob 2
Acme Bank 1

This is the Rust output. The Python version prints the same numbers in its own style. Five nodes and six edges need 6 + 6 = 12 numbers. One million nodes and five million edges need about 24 MB with 4-byte numbers. The search also has a depth limit. pgGraph has such limits too, so one query cannot walk the whole graph.

The trade-off. The index is derived. After writes you must sync it or build it again. The README also says that each database connection keeps its own copy of the index in memory. And there is no language model here. The graph knows only what your tables say.

Custom types: your own ontology

A memory system starts with general types such as Entity. Real work needs your own types: Person, Company, Decision. Four of the six projects let you declare them. Here is one small ontology in four forms.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Person(BaseModel):
    """A human we talk about."""
    occupation: str | None = Field(None, description="Current job")

class Company(BaseModel):
    """A business."""
    industry: str | None = Field(None, description="Main industry")

class Employment(BaseModel):
    """A person works at a company."""
    position: str | None = Field(None, description="Job title")

entity_types = {"Person": Person, "Company": Company}
edge_types = {"Employment": Employment}
edge_type_map = {("Person", "Company"): ["Employment"]}   # allowed pairs
node Person {
  email: String @key
  display_name: String
  occupation: String?
}

node Company {
  slug: String @key
  name: String
}

edge WorksAt: Person -> Company @card(0..) {
  position: String?
  @unique(@src, @dst)
}
SELECT graph.add_table('public.people'::regclass,
                       id_column := 'id', columns := ARRAY['name']);
SELECT graph.add_table('public.companies'::regclass,
                       id_column := 'id', columns := ARRAY['name']);
SELECT graph.add_edge(
  from_table := 'public.people'::regclass,    from_column := 'company_id',
  to_table   := 'public.companies'::regclass, to_column   := 'id',
  label := 'works_at', bidirectional := true);
@prefix ex:   <https://example.org/memory#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:Person     a owl:Class .
ex:Company    a owl:Class .
ex:Employment a owl:Class ;          # the fact as a node (n-ary pattern)
    rdfs:comment "One job of one person at one company." .

ex:employee   a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Employment ; rdfs:range ex:Person .
ex:employer   a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Employment ; rdfs:range ex:Company .
ex:position   a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Employment ; rdfs:range xsd:string .
ex:validAt    a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:range xsd:dateTime .   # world time
ex:invalidAt  a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:range xsd:dateTime .
ex:createdAt  a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:range xsd:dateTime .   # system time
ex:expiredAt  a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:range xsd:dateTime .

I parsed the Turtle with rdflib 7.6.0. It has 21 triples and 3 classes. The other three tabs follow each project's documentation.

How each system takes your ontology
SystemHow you declare typesWho enforces them
GraphitiPydantic classes for entities and for edges, plus a map of allowed pairsThe model fills them. Pydantic checks the shape
Mem0No types. One text field, custom_instructions, guides the extractionNobody. It is advice to the model
HindsightA mission text for each bank. Optional labels in the form key:value that become entitiesThe model follows the mission. Labels match exactly
GraphifyFixed schema. Your code and files are the inputA validator checks each extraction
OmnigraphA schema file with types, keys and constraintsThe engine, on every write and every merge
pgGraphYour tables, keys and foreign keysPostgreSQL

There are two families. In the first, a model reads text and your types are a strong hint. In the second, your types are a hard rule and wrong data is refused. A hint is flexible. A hard rule is safe.

Do not start with fifty types. The model picks the wrong one more often. Start with three to seven. The Graphiti documentation also forbids some attribute names, such as name and summary. The base node already uses them.

This is the same work as in the ontology engineering method. And the Employment node is the n-ary pattern from the 15 modelling patterns.

Identity, merging and conflict rules

Two messages say "Ana Souza" and "ana souza". Is it one person? This is entity resolution. A wrong "yes" mixes two people. A wrong "no" splits one person in two. Every system needs a rule.

import re
from hashlib import blake2b

def normalize(name: str) -> str:
    """Lower case, and one space between words."""
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", name.lower()).strip()

def shingles(name: str) -> set[str]:
    """All groups of 3 letters, with the spaces removed."""
    s = normalize(name).replace(" ", "")
    return {s[i:i + 3] for i in range(len(s) - 2)}

def jaccard(a: set[str], b: set[str]) -> float:
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b)

def minhash(items: set[str], k: int = 32) -> list[int]:
    """Keep the smallest hash for each of k hash functions."""
    def h(seed: int, item: str) -> int:
        d = blake2b(f"{seed}:{item}".encode(), digest_size=8).digest()
        return int.from_bytes(d, "big")
    return [min(h(seed, x) for x in items) for seed in range(k)]

def estimate(a: set[str], b: set[str], k: int = 32) -> float:
    ma, mb = minhash(a, k), minhash(b, k)
    return sum(x == y for x, y in zip(ma, mb)) / k

print(normalize("  Ana   SOUZA ") == normalize("ana souza"))   # rule 1: same key

pairs = [("Acme Robotics Inc", "Acme Robotics, Inc."),
         ("Acme Robotics Inc", "Acme Robotic Inc"),
         ("Ana Souza", "Ana Sousa")]
for left, right in pairs:
    a = shingles(re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9' ]", " ", left.lower()))
    b = shingles(re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9' ]", " ", right.lower()))
    j = jaccard(a, b)
    verdict = "merge" if j >= 0.9 else "ask the LLM"
    print(f"{left!r} / {right!r}: jaccard {j:.2f}, "
          f"minhash {estimate(a, b):.2f}, {verdict}")
True
'Acme Robotics Inc' / 'Acme Robotics, Inc.': jaccard 1.00, minhash 1.00, merge
'Acme Robotics Inc' / 'Acme Robotic Inc': jaccard 0.67, minhash 0.59, ask the LLM
'Ana Souza' / 'Ana Sousa': jaccard 0.50, minhash 0.53, ask the LLM

This is my own code. It follows the steps I read in Graphiti's helper file. A shingle is a group of three letters. The Jaccard similarity of two sets is the shared part divided by the whole.

Take a random hash function h. For two sets A and B, the smallest hash values are equal with probability

P\big(\min h(A) = \min h(B)\big) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|} = J(A, B)
Proof idea

Look at all items of A \cup B. One of them has the smallest hash. Each item has the same chance to be that one. The two minimum values are equal only when that item is in both sets. There are |A \cap B| such items out of |A \cup B|.

What does it mean? You do not compare full sets. You keep 32 small numbers for each name. The share of equal numbers is close to the true Jaccard value. In the output, 0.59 is close to 0.67. With 32 numbers the error is often near 0.1. So Graphiti uses the numbers only to find candidates fast. Then it computes the exact Jaccard value.

Identity and conflict rules as read in code and documentation
SystemWhen are two things the same?What happens on a conflict?
GraphitiA ladder. Same identity properties. Then one exact match of the cleaned name. Then Jaccard of 0.9 or more on shingles. If still unsure, a model decidesThe old fact is closed with invalid_at and expired_at. It stays
Mem0Memory: same MD5 hash of the text. Entity: same cleaned text, or vector similarity of 0.95 or moreNothing is closed. Both facts stay. The ranking decides
HindsightEntity: similar name by groups of three letters, plus which entities appear with it, plus time. Label entities: exact match onlyRaw facts stay. The observation is rewritten to tell the change. Near-equal observations are merged at similarity 0.97
GraphifySame id from file path and nameEdges carry a confidence tag. You rebuild from the files
OmnigraphSame @key valuesA typed conflict stops the merge. A person or agent resolves it
pgGraphSame table and same keyNo rule of its own. PostgreSQL constraints decide

Short names are dangerous. "Sam" and "Sara" share almost nothing, and "Ann" and "Anne" share almost everything. Graphiti skips the fuzzy step for very short names. It measures how varied the letters are and sends weak names to the model.

A common question: "How do you handle a fact that changes?" A strong answer names three choices. Close the old fact. Keep both and rank. Stop and ask. Then say which one your use case needs.

How the schema choice changes speed and memory

The ontology is not only about meaning. It decides how much work each write costs. It decides how many bytes each fact needs.

Where the work happens
SystemWork at write timeWork at read time
GraphitiSeveral model calls for each episodeThree searches and a rerank. The default search writes no text with a model
Mem0One model call for each addVector search with two boosts
HindsightA model extracts facts. Observations are built laterFour searches, rank fusion, a reranker. Reflect adds model reasoning
GraphifyNo model for code. A model only for documentsA graph query on one file
OmnigraphNo model. The engine checks typesGraph, vector and text search
pgGraphNo model. Build the index from tablesArray scans over the index

Now count bytes. An embedding is a list of numbers. Each number takes 4 bytes. Graphiti's default is 1024 numbers. Hindsight's own embedding model has 384. A common OpenAI model has 1536.

For one million facts the vectors alone need 1.5 GB with 384 numbers. They need 4.1 GB with 1024 numbers. The edges of the same graph need a few megabytes. So this rule helps: edges are cheap, vectors are expensive, and model calls cost the most.

  • Every type with a vector costs memory. Graphiti stores a vector for each entity name and each fact. Ask if both are needed.
  • Keeping episodes costs storage. But without them you have no proof and cannot rebuild.
  • Summaries cost model calls. Communities and observations make reading cheaper and writing more expensive.
  • A partition id is a cheap filter. It makes each search small. Graphiti calls it group_id. Hindsight calls it bank_id.

There is one more cost: errors. A write pipeline is a chain of model steps. If each step is right with probability 0.95, five steps are all right with probability 0.95^5 \approx 0.77. This is why Graphiti asks for models with structured output. A fixed shape removes one kind of error from every step.

Each project reports its own test scores. They use different tests, models and setups. One vendor's 92 and another vendor's 91 do not tell you which is better. Test with your own data.

A design checklist for your own memory ontology

You may build your own memory graph. Maybe on PostgreSQL, as in the build chapter. Use these steps in order.

  1. Write ten questions. The memory must answer them. Add one "why" question and one "as of" question.
  2. Choose the unit. Raw episode, extracted fact, or both. Keep the episode when you need proof.
  3. List the node types. Start with three to seven. Give each one a short description.
  4. List the edge types. Say which pairs of types each edge may join.
  5. Choose identity for each type. Use a key when you have one. If not, write name rules and a threshold.
  6. Choose the clocks. Always keep system time. Add valid time for facts that change.
  7. Choose the conflict rule. Close the old fact, keep both, or stop and ask.
  8. Choose the partition. One id for each user, team or tenant. Filter on it in every query.
  9. Choose what gets a vector. Count the bytes before you say yes.
  10. Plan forgetting. An expiry date, a summary, or delete by source. A user may ask you to delete their data.
  11. Test with a small story. Use twenty episodes with one duplicate name, one changed fact and one late fact.
  1. Questions: "Why did we refund 900 euros?" and "What was the limit on that day?"
  2. Unit: both. Each chat is an episode. Each decision is a node.
  3. Node types: Customer, Policy, Decision, Person, Episode.
  4. Edge types: Decision applies Policy. Decision approved by Person. Decision based on Episode.
  5. Identity: customer number, policy code, staff email. No fuzzy matching is needed.
  6. Clocks: a policy limit has valid time. Every row has system time.
  7. Conflict: a new limit closes the old limit. Old decisions keep their old limit.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for context graphs and agent memory
PatternPurposeModelNote
Episode nodeKeep the raw input as the source of every factEpisode -MENTIONS-> Entity (Graphiti)Never store a fact without its source.
Fact with two clocksAsk what was true and what was knownvalid_at, invalid_at, created_at, expired_atOne timestamp cannot answer "what did we know then?".
Close, do not deleteKeep history when a fact changesold.invalid_at = new.valid_atA delete breaks audits and old decisions.
Add only, rank laterCheap writes with one model callMem0 add() returns only ADD eventsOld and new facts both stay. Ranking must choose.
Fact type by speakerSeparate what was seen, done and learnedfact_type: world, experience, observation (Hindsight)Tell the system who is speaking.
Belief with evidenceFewer and stronger factsObservation -evidence-> FactIt is behind new facts until the job runs.
Confidence tagKnow what was read and what was guessedconfidence: EXTRACTED, INFERRED (Graphify)An INFERRED edge is not proof.
Schema as codeOne enforced model for many agentsnode Decision { slug: String @key }Design the keys first. They are hard to change.
Branch for each agentReview writes before they reach mainbranch create, then branch mergeA conflict stops the merge. Plan who resolves it.
Tables as the ontologyGraph queries on data you already havegraph.add_edge(... label := 'works_at')The index is derived. Sync it after writes.
Identity ladderMerge names safelykey, exact name, Jaccard 0.9, then a modelA low threshold merges two different people.
Fuse by rankJoin results of different searches\sum 1/(k + r)Raw scores of different searches cannot be added.
Partition idKeep each user's memory apartgroup_id, bank_id, user_idA missing filter shows one user's facts to another.

Practice

Which question needs system time, not only valid time?

  • Where did Ana work in May 2026?
  • What did the agent believe on 15 June about Ana's job?
  • Where does Ana work today?

"What did we believe on a day" asks about the database clock. That is system time.

In Graphiti, which edge type holds a fact between two entities?

  • MENTIONS
  • HAS_MEMBER
  • RELATES_TO

MENTIONS links an episode to an entity. HAS_MEMBER links a community to an entity.

What does the open-source Mem0 code store today?

  • Entities and edges in a graph database
  • Text facts with vectors, an entity collection and a history table
  • Only raw chat messages

The graph store was removed from the open-source code. Entities only hold a list of memory ids.

What is the identity of a node in pgGraph?

  • A name that a model extracted
  • The table and the key of the row
  • A hash of the row text

The tables stay the truth. A node is one row of a registered table.

In Graphiti, a closed fact gets a world time in the field ?.

With RRF and k = 60, place 1 in one list adds 1/ ? to the score.

A CSR index for 5 nodes and 6 edges has ? offsets.

  1. The base value of a customer's city is "Lima". Branch A changes it to "Cusco". Branch B changes it to "Quito". What does a three-way merge do?
    Answer

    Both sides differ from the base and from each other. This is a conflict. Omnigraph calls this kind divergent_update. The merge publishes nothing until someone resolves it.

  2. Set A is {ana, nas, aso}. Set B is {ana, nas, asa}. Compute the Jaccard similarity.
    Answer

    Two items are shared: ana and nas. The union has four items. So J = 2/4 = 0.5. This is below 0.9, so there is no automatic merge.

  3. A fact has valid_at 2026-02-01, invalid_at 2026-09-01, created_at 2026-02-03 and expired_at 2026-09-10. Does it answer the question with v = 2026-09-05 and k = 2026-09-07?
    Answer

    Yes. On 7 September the system did not know the end yet, because expired_at is 10 September. So the end is open for this question. The fact was stored before day k and it started before day v.

  4. Why can RRF join a vector list and a BM25 list without changing the scores first?
    Answer

    RRF uses only the place of each item in each list. It never reads the raw scores. So different scales do not matter. An additive method must first press all scores into the same range.

  5. You build a memory for an audit agent in a bank. Each answer must show its source and must be correct for a past date. Which conflict rule do you choose, and which system is the closest fit?
    Answer

    Choose "close, do not delete" with two clocks, and keep every episode. Graphiti is the closest fit, because its facts have valid time, system time and a link to the episode. An add-only store without valid time cannot answer "as of" questions well.

  6. Your memory holds 2 million facts. Each fact has one vector of 1024 numbers. How many bytes do the vectors need? What do you save with 384 numbers?
    Answer

    One vector is 1024 \cdot 4 = 4096 bytes. Two million vectors need about 8.2 GB. With 384 numbers one vector is 1536 bytes, so the total is about 3.1 GB. You save about 5.1 GB. You may lose some search quality, so test it.

Key takeaways

  • A context graph is a knowledge graph plus events, time, source and decisions.
  • Use two clocks. Valid time says when a fact was true. System time says when you knew it.
  • Close old facts. Do not delete them. Then you can explain old decisions.
  • Every memory system has an ontology: node types, edge types, time fields and identity rules.
  • Graphiti closes facts. Mem0 adds and ranks. Hindsight builds observations with evidence.
  • Graphify, Omnigraph and pgGraph give you a graph from files, from a schema or from tables.
  • Edges are cheap, vectors are expensive, and model calls cost the most.
  • Read the code before you trust a product page. Projects change fast.

Sources

  • getzep/graphiti. README and source files for nodes, edges, search and deduplication, version 0.31.2.
  • Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory. The paper behind Graphiti, January 2025.
  • mem0ai/mem0. README, memory source code and the migration guide to the new algorithm.
  • vectorize-io/hindsight. README, database models and the retain, recall and observation documents, version 1.2.1.
  • Graphify-Labs/graphify. README, architecture document and schema validator on the default branch, version 0.9.108.
  • modernrelay/omnigraph. README and the quickstart, schema and merge documents.
  • evokoa/pggraph. README and quickstart document, version 1.2.1.
  • AI's trillion-dollar opportunity: Context graphs. The essay by Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg that made the term popular.

The Python toolkit

Python has a small, mature set of libraries for ontologies and knowledge graphs. This chapter uses each of them end to end: rdflib for graphs and SPARQL, owlready2 for OWL and a real reasoner, pySHACL for checks, and SPARQLWrapper for Wikidata. At the end, one pipeline turns a CSV file into a validated graph.

  • Build, parse, serialise and query RDF graphs with rdflib.
  • Write OWL classes as Python classes and run the HermiT reasoner with owlready2.
  • Validate data with pySHACL and read the validation report in code.
  • Query Wikidata politely with SPARQLWrapper, including rate limits.
  • Build a CSV to RDF to SHACL pipeline, and know when rdflib is too slow.

The toolkit at a glance

Here are the six packages of this chapter. We checked each version on PyPI on 15 November 2026, and we ran every example with these versions and Python 3.14.

The Python ontology toolkit (versions checked 2026-11-15)
PackageVersionJob
rdflib7.6.0 (February 2026)RDF graphs, parsers, serialisers, SPARQL 1.1 query and update
owlready20.51 (June 2026)OWL classes as Python objects, HermiT and Pellet reasoners
pySHACL0.40.2 (October 2026)SHACL validation on rdflib graphs
SPARQLWrapper2.0.0 (March 2022)Send SPARQL to a remote endpoint
owlrl7.6.2 (July 2026)OWL 2 RL and RDFS rules on an rdflib graph
pyoxigraph0.5.13 (October 2026)A fast RDF store and SPARQL engine, written in Rust

SPARQLWrapper has had no release since 2022. It still works, as you will see. The others had releases in 2026.

Install them in a project environment, never into the system Python. With uv you can run a script and name its packages in one line.

uv run --with rdflib --with pyshacl python3.14 check.py
# or, in a virtual environment:
python3.14 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install rdflib pyshacl owlready2 sparqlwrapper owlrl pyoxigraph

Two packages need more than Python. owlready2 starts the reasoners HermiT and Pellet in Java, so you need a Java runtime. We used OpenJDK 17. pyoxigraph ships ready-made binary wheels for common systems.

rdflib: triples, terms and namespaces

Start with a graph about one person. Read the code first. The words come after.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace, Literal, BNode
from rdflib.namespace import RDF, XSD, FOAF

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/")            # your own namespace
g = Graph()
g.bind("ex", EX)                                  # prefix for output

g.add((EX.ana, RDF.type, FOAF.Person))            # one triple = one tuple
g.add((EX.ana, FOAF.name, Literal("Ana")))
g.add((EX.ana, EX.born, Literal("1990-04-02", datatype=XSD.date)))
g.add((EX.ana, FOAF.knows, EX.ben))
addr = BNode()                                    # a node with no IRI
g.add((EX.ana, EX.address, addr))
g.add((addr, EX.city, Literal("Lisbon", lang="en")))

print(len(g), "triples")
print(g.value(EX.ana, FOAF.name))                 # one value
for s, p, o in sorted(g.triples((EX.ana, None, None))):  # None = any
    shown = "a blank node" if isinstance(o, BNode) else o.n3(g.namespace_manager)
    print(g.qname(p), shown)
born = g.value(EX.ana, EX.born)
print(type(born.toPython()).__name__, born.toPython().year)
print((EX.ana, FOAF.knows, EX.ben) in g)
6 triples
Ana
ex:address a blank node
ex:born "1990-04-02"^^xsd:date
rdf:type foaf:Person
foaf:knows ex:ben
foaf:name "Ana"
date 1990
True

A Graph is a set of triples. Each triple is a plain Python tuple of three terms. rdflib has three kinds of term, the same three you know from RDF and RDF Schema.

  • URIRef: an IRI. EX.ana builds one for you.
  • Literal: a value with an optional datatype or language tag.
  • BNode: a blank node, a node with no global name.

A Namespace is a factory for IRIs. EX.ana and EX["ana"] both give http://example.org/ana. rdflib ships namespaces for the common vocabularies: RDF, RDFS, OWL, XSD, FOAF, SKOS, DCTERMS, SH and more. g.bind() only chooses a short prefix for output. It does not change any data.

You read a graph with patterns. g.triples((s, p, o)) treats None as "any". g.value(s, p) returns one object, or None. toPython() turns a typed literal into a Python value. Here the date became a real datetime.date.

g.add((EX.ana, EX.born, Literal("1990-04-02")))   # just a string

This literal is a plain string. SPARQL date functions and SHACL sh:datatype xsd:date will not treat it as a date.

g.add((EX.ana, EX.born, Literal(date(1990, 4, 2))))  # rdflib picks xsd:date

Pass a Python date, or give datatype=XSD.date. Both make a typed literal.

Literal("1") and Literal(1) are different terms. The first is a string. The second is an xsd:integer. A query for one does not find the other. Decide the datatype when you load data, and keep it the same everywhere.

rdflib: parse and serialise

Most data arrives as files. Here a small Turtle file goes in, and three other formats come out.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:ana a foaf:Person ;
    foaf:name "Ana" ;
    foaf:knows ex:ben ;
    ex:joined "2021-03-01"^^xsd:date .
ex:ben a foaf:Person ;
    foaf:name "Ben"@en , "Bem"@pt .
from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.compare import isomorphic

g = Graph().parse("team.ttl")                     # format from the file ending
print("parsed", len(g), "triples")

for fmt in ("nt", "json-ld", "xml"):              # write three other formats
    text = g.serialize(format=fmt)                # returns a str in rdflib 7
    back = Graph().parse(data=text, format=fmt)   # read it back
    print(f"{fmt:8} {len(text):4} chars  same graph: {isomorphic(g, back)}")

print(sorted(g.serialize(format="nt").splitlines())[0])  # one N-Triples line
g.serialize(destination="team.jsonld", format="json-ld", indent=2)
parsed 7 triples
nt        623 chars  same graph: True
json-ld   738 chars  same graph: True
xml       745 chars  same graph: True
<http://example.org/ana> <http://example.org/joined> "2021-03-01"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#date> .

parse() guesses the format from the file ending. For a string, give data= and format=. serialize() returns a string, or writes a file when you give destination=. Since rdflib 6, JSON-LD support is built in.

Format names in rdflib
FormatName in codeNote
Turtleturtle or ttlBest for people. The default for serialize().
N-TriplesntOne triple per line. Good for large files and for grep.
JSON-LDjson-ldFor web developers and APIs.
RDF/XMLxmlOld but still common. Protégé and owlready2 read it.
TriG and N-Quadstrig, nquadsFor several named graphs. Use a Dataset.

Why isomorphic() and not ==? Blank nodes get new random ids each time you parse. Two graphs can have the same shape with different blank node ids. Isomorphic means "the same graph after renaming blank nodes".

Do not compare two graphs with == or by comparing their Turtle text. The order of triples and the blank node ids change from run to run. Use rdflib.compare.isomorphic, or to_isomorphic and graph_diff to see what changed.

rdflib: SPARQL query and update

rdflib has a full SPARQL 1.1 engine for query and update. You met the language in SPARQL. Here is how to call it from Python.

from rdflib import Graph, Namespace
from rdflib.namespace import FOAF

EX = Namespace("http://example.org/")
g = Graph().parse("team.ttl")

q = """
SELECT ?name (LANG(?name) AS ?lang) WHERE {
  ?who foaf:name ?name .
} ORDER BY STR(?name)"""
for row in g.query(q, initNs={"foaf": FOAF}):        # rows act like tuples
    print(row.name, row.lang or "(no language tag)")

ask = "ASK { ?a foaf:knows ?b . ?b foaf:knows ?a }"
print("mutual friends?", g.query(ask, initNs={"foaf": FOAF}).askAnswer)

# initBindings fills a variable before the query runs (no string building)
q2 = "SELECT ?d WHERE { ?p ex:joined ?d }"
print("joined:", [str(r.d) for r in g.query(q2, initNs={"ex": EX}, initBindings={"p": EX.ana})])

g.update("""INSERT { ?b foaf:knows ?a } WHERE { ?a foaf:knows ?b }""",
         initNs={"foaf": FOAF})                       # SPARQL Update
print("mutual friends now?", g.query(ask, initNs={"foaf": FOAF}).askAnswer)

c = g.query("CONSTRUCT { ?p a ex:Member } WHERE { ?p a foaf:Person }",
            initNs={"foaf": FOAF, "ex": EX})
print(len(c.graph), "new triples:", sorted(g.qname(s) for s, _, _ in c.graph))
Ana (no language tag)
Bem pt
Ben en
mutual friends? False
joined: ['2021-03-01']
mutual friends now? True
2 new triples: ['ex:ana', 'ex:ben']
  • SELECT gives rows. You read a column by name, like row.name, or by position.
  • ASK gives askAnswer, a Python bool.
  • CONSTRUCT gives a new graph in .graph. The original graph does not change.
  • update() changes the graph in place. Here it made foaf:knows go both ways.
  • initNs gives prefixes. initBindings fixes a variable to a value before the query runs.

Do not build a query with an f-string from user input, like f"... ex:{name} ...". A strange name can break the query or change its meaning. This is query injection. Pass values with initBindings instead, as in q2.

Did you see ORDER BY STR(?name)? Without STR(), rdflib put "Ben"@en before "Bem"@pt. SPARQL does not fully define the order of literals with different language tags. STR() sorts by the plain text.

owlready2: OWL classes as Python classes

rdflib sees triples. owlready2 sees an ontology. A class in OWL becomes a class in Python, and an individual becomes a Python object. The library comes from Jean-Baptiste Lamy, and it bundles the HermiT and Pellet reasoners.

from owlready2 import (get_ontology, Thing, ObjectProperty, TransitiveProperty,
                       AllDisjoint, sync_reasoner)

onto = get_ontology("http://example.org/pkg.owl")
with onto:                                        # everything below goes into onto
    class Person(Thing): pass
    class Package(Thing): pass
    AllDisjoint([Person, Package])
    class maintains(ObjectProperty):              # a property is a class too
        domain = [Person]
        range = [Package]
    class dependsOn(ObjectProperty, TransitiveProperty):
        domain = [Package]
        range = [Package]
    class Maintainer(Thing):                      # a defined class
        equivalent_to = [Person & maintains.some(Package)]

    webapp, tinyhttp, fastjson = Package("webapp"), Package("tinyhttp"), Package("fastjson")
    webapp.dependsOn = [tinyhttp]
    tinyhttp.dependsOn = [fastjson]
    ana = Person("ana", maintains=[fastjson])

print("before:", ana.is_a, webapp.dependsOn)
with onto:
    sync_reasoner(infer_property_values=True, debug=0)   # HermiT, needs Java
print("after: ", ana.is_a, sorted(p.name for p in webapp.dependsOn))
print(Maintainer.instances())
onto.save(file="pkg.owl", format="rdfxml")
before: [pkg.Person] [pkg.tinyhttp]
after:  [pkg.Maintainer] ['fastjson', 'tinyhttp']
[pkg.ana]

Two things happened. HermiT put ana into Maintainer, because she is a Person who maintains some Package. Python now shows only the most specific class. Second, infer_property_values=True asked for new property values. dependsOn is transitive, so webapp now also depends on fastjson.

  • Person & maintains.some(Package) is the OWL class expression Person and (maintains some Package). See OWL 2.
  • | means "or", Not(...) means "not", and .only(), .min(), .max() and .value() build the other restrictions.
  • sync_reasoner() runs HermiT. sync_reasoner_pellet() runs Pellet, which can also infer data property values.
  • Inside with onto: the inferred facts go into onto. Outside, they go into a separate ontology for inferences.

Domain is a rule, not a check

Now load the saved file. Give bob no class, and let him maintain a package. Then let a package maintain a package.

from owlready2 import (get_ontology, Thing, sync_reasoner,
                       OwlReadyInconsistentOntologyError)

onto = get_ontology("file://pkg.owl").load()      # the file saved before
with onto:
    bob = Thing("bob")                            # no class given
    bob.maintains = [onto.tinyhttp]
    sync_reasoner(debug=0)
print("bob is now:", bob.is_a)                    # domain makes bob a Person

with onto:
    onto.webapp.maintains = [onto.fastjson]       # a Package that maintains?
    try:
        sync_reasoner(debug=0)
    except OwlReadyInconsistentOntologyError:
        print("inconsistent: webapp would be a Person and a Package")
bob is now: [pkg.Maintainer]
inconsistent: webapp would be a Person and a Package

The domain of maintains is Person. HermiT did not reject bob. It concluded that bob is a Person, and then a Maintainer. For webapp the same rule makes it a Person. But Person and Package are disjoint, so the whole ontology became inconsistent. owlready2 raises OwlReadyInconsistentOntologyError.

People add domain to "check" their data. It does not check. It adds facts. Use SHACL, in the next section, when you want "this property is only allowed on persons". The OWL 2 chapter lists this as a classic mistake.

owlready2 keeps its data in its own quadstore, built on SQLite. By default it lives in memory. default_world.set_backend(filename="pkg.sqlite3") keeps it on disk. It also has its own SPARQL engine: default_world.sparql("SELECT ...") returned our three packages as Python objects.

What if Java is missing? Then sync_reasoner() fails. We tried a wrong Java path, and Python raised FileNotFoundError. You can still build, load and save ontologies. You can also set the path by hand, for example owlready2.JAVA_EXE = "/path/to/java". In this book we ran HermiT with OpenJDK 17 on macOS.

pySHACL: validate the data

OWL draws conclusions. SHACL checks rules. You met it in SHACL and validation. pySHACL runs it on rdflib graphs.

@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:Employee rdfs:subClassOf foaf:Person .
ex:joined rdfs:domain foaf:Person .

ex:ana a ex:Employee ; foaf:name "Ana" ;
    ex:joined "2021-03-01"^^xsd:date .
ex:cara a ex:Employee ;          # no name
    ex:joined "March 2021" ;     # not a date
    foaf:knows ex:robot7 .
ex:robot7 a ex:Machine .
ex:dan ex:joined "2020-01-01"^^xsd:date .
@prefix sh:   <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#> .
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/> .
@prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

ex:PersonShape a sh:NodeShape ;
  sh:targetClass foaf:Person ;
  sh:property [ sh:path foaf:name ;
                sh:minCount 1 ] ;
  sh:property [ sh:path ex:joined ;
                sh:datatype xsd:date ;
                sh:maxCount 1 ] ;
  sh:property [ sh:path foaf:knows ;
                sh:class foaf:Person ;
                sh:severity sh:Warning ] .
from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.namespace import SH
from pyshacl import validate

data = Graph().parse("staff.ttl")
shapes = Graph().parse("staff-shapes.ttl")

for inference in ("none", "rdfs"):
    conforms, report, text = validate(data, shacl_graph=shapes, inference=inference)
    print(f"inference={inference}: conforms={conforms}, "
          f"{len(list(report.subjects(SH.focusNode, None)))} result(s)")

rows = []
for r in report.subjects(SH.focusNode, None):     # read the report as a graph
    rows.append((report.value(r, SH.focusNode).n3(data.namespace_manager),
                 report.value(r, SH.resultPath).n3(data.namespace_manager),
                 report.value(r, SH.resultSeverity).fragment))
for row in sorted(rows):
    print(*row)
inference=none: conforms=False, 3 result(s)
inference=rdfs: conforms=False, 4 result(s)
ex:cara ex:joined Violation
ex:cara foaf:knows Warning
ex:cara foaf:name Violation
ex:dan foaf:name Violation

validate() returns three things: a bool, the report as an rdflib graph, and the report as text. Reading the report graph is better for code. Each result has a focus node, a path, a severity and a message.

Look at the two runs. Without inference, there are three results, all about cara. Why is cara checked at all? She is an Employee, not a Person. The answer: SHACL follows rdfs:subClassOf in the data graph when it picks targets. So subclass members are targets even with no inference.

With inference="rdfs", pySHACL first runs the RDFS rules on a copy of the data. The domain of ex:joined makes dan a Person. Now dan is a target, and his missing name is a fourth result.

Useful options of pyshacl.validate
OptionWhat it does
inference"none", "rdfs", "owlrl" or "both". Runs rules on a copy before checking.
ont_graphAn extra ontology graph to mix in, for example your class tree.
allow_warningsWarning results no longer make conforms false. There is also allow_infos.
abort_on_firstStop at the first violation. Fast for a yes or no answer.
advancedTurn on SHACL Advanced Features, like SHACL rules.

Do not decide by the text report or by conforms alone. A single warning makes conforms false unless you pass allow_warnings=True. Read the severity of each result, as the code above does.

SPARQLWrapper: ask Wikidata

Wikidata is a public knowledge graph with a public SPARQL endpoint. SPARQLWrapper sends a query over HTTPS and turns the answer into Python data. Our question: which programming languages were influenced by Python?

import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from SPARQLWrapper import SPARQLWrapper, JSON

endpoint = SPARQLWrapper(
    "https://query.wikidata.org/sparql",
    agent="ontology-book-example/0.1 (learning script) SPARQLWrapper/2.0.0",
)
endpoint.setReturnFormat(JSON)
endpoint.setQuery("""
SELECT ?lang ?langLabel (MIN(YEAR(?start)) AS ?year) WHERE {
  ?lang wdt:P31/wdt:P279* wd:Q9143 ;      # a kind of programming language
        wdt:P737 wd:Q28865 .              # influenced by Python
  OPTIONAL { ?lang wdt:P571 ?start }      # inception
  SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". }
}
GROUP BY ?lang ?langLabel ORDER BY ?year LIMIT 8""")

for attempt in (1, 2):                            # at most two requests
    try:
        data = endpoint.query().convert()
        break
    except HTTPError as err:
        if err.code != 429 or attempt == 2:       # 429 = too many requests
            raise
        wait = min(int(err.headers.get("Retry-After", "60")), 120)
        print(f"HTTP 429, waiting {wait} s as the server asks")
        time.sleep(wait)

for b in data["results"]["bindings"]:
    qid = b["lang"]["value"].rsplit("/", 1)[1]
    print(b.get("year", {}).get("value", "----"), qid, b["langLabel"]["value"])

We ran it on 15 November 2026. Wikidata changes every day, so your answer can differ.

---- Q5166349 Converge
---- Q91440026 Chaos
---- Q115750242 PyScript
1995 Q2005 JavaScript
1995 Q161053 Ruby
2000 Q3503881 Suneido
2001 Q319268 D
2002 Q756175 Io
  • wdt:P31/wdt:P279* is a property path: "instance of", then "subclass of" zero or more times.
  • The label service fills ?langLabel for each ?lang. It is a Wikidata extra, not standard SPARQL.
  • Three languages have no inception date. OPTIONAL kept them. Unbound values sort first.
  • The data says JavaScript was influenced by Python. It is community data. Check surprising claims at their source.

Be polite: the rules of the endpoint

Our first try failed. The server answered HTTP 429 with the note "Aggressively rate-limiting to 1 req / min". That rule was in place during a service problem. We waited and sent one more request. That is why the code above handles 429 and reads the Retry-After header.

The user manual of the Wikidata Query Service, as we read it in November 2026, gives these limits:

  • Each query stops after 60 seconds.
  • Each client (user agent plus IP address) gets 60 seconds of processing time per minute.
  • At most 5 parallel queries per IP address, and 30 failing queries per minute.
  • Clients over the limit get HTTP 429. Clients that ignore 429 can be banned for a while.

Wikimedia also asks for a descriptive User-Agent header. The policy suggests a name, a version and a way to contact you. In your own project, put a project page or a team address there. Generic library names may be blocked.

Wikidata grew too big for its query engine. On 9 May 2025 it split its graph. Scholarly articles moved to a second endpoint, query-scholarly.wikidata.org. The main endpoint keeps everything else. Queries that need both must use federation with SERVICE. The manual also announces a move to a new backend in 2026 and 2027. Check the manual before you build on the endpoint.

Do not loop over thousands of items with one query each. Send one query with VALUES for many items, cache the answers on disk, and download a dump for large jobs. Your script then runs faster, and the service stays up for everyone.

A pipeline: CSV to RDF to a validated graph

Real data often starts as a spreadsheet. Here is a CSV file of software releases. The last row has three problems.

package,version,released,license,maintainer,needs
fastjson,1.2.0,2025-11-02,MIT,Ana,
fastjson,1.3.0,2026-02-10,MIT,Ana,
tinyhttp,2.0.0,2026-01-05,Apache-2.0,Ben,fastjson 1.2.0
webapp,0.9.0,2026-03-01,MIT,,tinyhttp 2.0.0
quick parser,,10/03/2026,MIT,Cara,fastjson 9.9
  1. Map. Turn each row into triples. Make safe IRIs, typed dates and license IRIs.
  2. Validate. Run SHACL shapes on the new graph.
  3. Quarantine. Remove the nodes that failed, and report them.
  4. Publish. Validate again and write Turtle.
import csv
from datetime import date
from urllib.parse import quote
from rdflib import Graph, Literal, Namespace, URIRef
from rdflib.namespace import RDF, XSD, DCTERMS, FOAF

PKG = Namespace("http://example.org/pkg#")
SPDX = "https://spdx.org/licenses/"

def release_iri(package, version):
    return PKG[quote(f"{package}-{version}".replace(" ", "_"))]  # safe IRI

def as_date(text):
    try:
        return Literal(date.fromisoformat(text))  # typed: xsd:date
    except ValueError:
        return Literal(text)                      # keep it, let SHACL complain

def csv_to_graph(path):
    g = Graph()
    g.bind("pkg", PKG); g.bind("dct", DCTERMS)
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            r = release_iri(row["package"], row["version"])
            g.add((r, RDF.type, PKG.Release))
            if row["version"]:                    # empty cell = no triple
                g.add((r, PKG.versionString, Literal(row["version"])))
            g.add((r, DCTERMS.issued, as_date(row["released"])))
            g.add((r, DCTERMS.license, URIRef(SPDX + row["license"])))
            if row["maintainer"]:
                g.add((r, PKG.maintainer, Literal(row["maintainer"])))
            if row["needs"]:
                name, version = row["needs"].rsplit(" ", 1)
                g.add((r, PKG.dependsOn, release_iri(name, version)))
    return g
@prefix sh:  <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#> .
@prefix pkg: <http://example.org/pkg#> .
