@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .

pkg:ReleaseShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:targetClass pkg:Release ;
    sh:property [ sh:path pkg:versionString ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ;
                  sh:pattern "^[0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+$" ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path dct:issued ; sh:datatype xsd:date ; sh:maxCount 1 ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path dct:license ; sh:nodeKind sh:IRI ; sh:minCount 1 ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path pkg:dependsOn ; sh:class pkg:Release ] .
from rdflib import Graph
from rdflib.namespace import SH
from pyshacl import validate
from csv2rdf import csv_to_graph

g = csv_to_graph("releases.csv")                  # step 1: CSV to RDF
print(len(g), "triples from", len(set(g.subjects())), "releases")

shapes = Graph().parse("shapes.ttl")              # step 2: validate
conforms, report, _ = validate(g, shacl_graph=shapes)
bad = {}
for r in report.subjects(SH.focusNode, None):
    node = report.value(r, SH.focusNode)
    bad.setdefault(node, []).append(g.qname(report.value(r, SH.resultPath)))
for node, paths in sorted(bad.items()):
    print("REJECT", g.qname(node), "problems:", ", ".join(sorted(paths)))

for node in bad:                                  # step 3: keep only clean nodes
    g.remove((node, None, None))
g.serialize("releases.ttl", format="turtle")      # step 4: publish
print(len(g), "triples written, conforms now:",
      validate(g, shacl_graph=shapes)[0])
26 triples from 5 releases
REJECT pkg:quick_parser- problems: dct:issued, pkg:dependsOn, pkg:versionString
21 triples written, conforms now: True

The shapes found all three problems in the last row. The version is missing. The date "10/03/2026" is not an ISO date, so it stayed a plain string. And "fastjson 9.9" points to a release that does not exist, so it is not a pkg:Release. Look also at the strange IRI quick_parser-. The empty version made it. That is one more reason to reject the row.

Here is one release from the output file.

pkg:webapp-0.9.0 a pkg:Release ;
    pkg:dependsOn pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 ;
    pkg:versionString "0.9.0" ;
    dct:issued "2026-03-01"^^xsd:date ;
    dct:license <https://spdx.org/licenses/MIT> .

Never paste raw cell text into an IRI. A space or a slash makes a broken IRI. Use urllib.parse.quote, or better, an ID column. Also do not guess dates like "10/03/2026": is it 10 March or 3 October? Let the check reject it and ask the data owner.

Removing a bad node can leave other nodes pointing to it. That is why the pipeline validates a second time before it writes. For bigger mapping jobs, look at RML, a mapping language from a W3C community group. It maps tables, JSON and more to RDF. Morph-KGC is a Python engine for it (version 2.10.0 on PyPI in November 2026). The chapter Build a validator and a service builds the shape checker yourself.

Speed and scale

rdflib keeps every triple as Python objects. That is easy and flexible, but it costs memory and time. pyoxigraph keeps triples in compact Rust structures. We loaded the same generated N-Triples file into both, then ran one two-step join query.

t = time.perf_counter(); g = Graph().parse("big.nt", format="nt")
t_load = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); n = next(iter(g.query(Q)))[0]
print(f"rdflib     load {t_load:5.2f} s  query {time.perf_counter() - t:5.2f} s  n={n}")

t = time.perf_counter(); s = ox.Store()           # pyoxigraph, in memory
s.bulk_load(path="big.nt", format=ox.RdfFormat.N_TRIPLES)
t_load = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); n = next(iter(s.query(Q)))[0]
print(f"pyoxigraph load {t_load:5.2f} s  query {time.perf_counter() - t:5.2f} s  n={n.value}")
N=100000
rdflib     load  3.82 s  query  0.47 s  n=39994
pyoxigraph load  0.40 s  query  0.03 s  n=39994

These are small, rough numbers from one machine. Still, the rule is clear.

  • Up to some hundred thousand triples: rdflib is fine, and its API is the richest.
  • Millions of triples, or a service: use pyoxigraph, or a real triple store. See Triple stores and graph databases.
  • OWL RL rules on rdflib data: use owlrl. The chapter Rules and Datalog runs it, and Build a reasoner writes one yourself.
  • Full OWL classification: use owlready2 with HermiT or Pellet, as above.

A common question: "Which library would you use to validate RDF data against rules?" The answer is pySHACL, not owlready2. A reasoner draws conclusions. A validator reports problems.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for the Python toolkit
PatternPurposeModelNote
Namespace + bindMake IRIs and short prefixesEX = Namespace("http://example.org/")bind changes only the output.
g.add((s, p, o))Add one tripleg.add((EX.ana, FOAF.name, Literal("Ana")))Give a datatype to dates and numbers.
g.value(s, p)Read one valueg.value(EX.ana, FOAF.name)Returns None when missing.
parse / serializeRead and write filesg.serialize("out.ttl", format="turtle")serialize returns a str in rdflib 7.
isomorphic(a, b)Compare two graphsfrom rdflib.compare import isomorphicNever compare with == or text.
g.query(q, initBindings=...)Safe SPARQL with a valueinitBindings={"p": EX.ana}No f-strings with user input.
g.update(...)Change a graph with SPARQLINSERT { ... } WHERE { ... }It changes the graph in place.
Python class = OWL classWrite OWL in Pythonclass Maintainer(Thing): equivalent_to = [...]Work inside with onto:.
sync_reasoner()Classify with HermiTsync_reasoner(infer_property_values=True)Needs Java. Catch the inconsistency error.
validate(data, shacl_graph=...)Check data with shapesconforms, report, text = validate(...)Read the report graph, not the text.
SPARQLWrapper + User-AgentQuery a public endpointSPARQLWrapper(url, agent="name/0.1 (contact)")Handle 429 and wait.
Map, validate, quarantine, publishLoad messy tablesCSV to rdflib to pySHACL to TurtleValidate again after removing nodes.
Switch to pyoxigraphSpeed on big dataStore().bulk_load(path=..., format=...)About 10 times faster loading in our test.

Practice

Which rdflib call reads one value of a property?

g.value(subject, predicate). It returns None when there is no value.

What does serialize() return in rdflib 7?

A string. With destination= it writes a file.

What does owlready2 need to run HermiT?

A Java runtime. We used OpenJDK 17.

What three things does pyshacl.validate return?

A bool conforms, the report as a graph, and the report as text.

What must a script do after HTTP 429 from Wikidata?

Wait as long as Retry-After says. Then retry, or stop.

Which line makes a typed date literal in rdflib?

  • Literal("2026-11-15")
  • Literal("2026-11-15", datatype=XSD.date)
  • URIRef("2026-11-15")

Without a datatype, the literal is a plain string.

Two graphs hold the same data but have different blank node ids. How do you test that they are equal?

  • g1 == g2
  • Compare their Turtle text.
  • isomorphic(g1, g2)

Isomorphism allows blank nodes to be renamed.

owlready2 gives a property a domain of Person. You use it on a thing with no class and run HermiT. What happens?

  • owlready2 raises an error.
  • HermiT concludes the thing is a Person.
  • Nothing changes.

Domain is a rule that adds facts. It only causes an error when the new fact clashes, for example with a disjoint class.

pySHACL returns conforms=False, but all results have severity Warning. Which option makes it true?

  • inference="rdfs"
  • allow_warnings=True
  • abort_on_first=True

allow_warnings stops warnings from making the data fail.

Wikidata answers HTTP 429. What should your script do?

  • Retry at once, ten times.
  • Wait as long as the Retry-After header says, then retry once.
  • Change the User-Agent and retry.

429 means "too many requests". Clients that ignore it can be banned.

Fill in the missing words.

In rdflib, a node with no IRI is a ?.

The owlready2 function that runs HermiT is ?.

owlready2 raises Owlready? when the ontology has no model.

In pySHACL, inference="<span class="blank" data-answer="rdfs">?</span>" runs the RDFS rules before the check.

  1. Write rdflib code that adds "Ben knows Ana" and prints every person Ana knows or who knows Ana.
    Answer

    g.add((EX.ben, FOAF.knows, EX.ana)). Then for o in g.objects(EX.ana, FOAF.knows): print(o) and for s in g.subjects(FOAF.knows, EX.ana): print(s). objects() and subjects() are short forms of triples().

  2. Change q2 in g3_sparql.py so it finds the join date of a person whose IRI comes from user input. Why is initBindings safer than an f-string?
    Answer

    Keep the query text fixed and pass initBindings={"p": URIRef(user_iri)}. The value is bound as one term. It can never add new query text, so it cannot change the meaning of the query.

  3. In owlready2, define CriticalPackage as a Package that some Package depends on. Which packages of our example will HermiT put in it?
    Answer

    class CriticalPackage(Thing): equivalent_to = [Package & Inverse(dependsOn).some(Package)]. tinyhttp and fastjson, because webapp depends on tinyhttp, and tinyhttp depends on fastjson. webapp is not in it.

  4. Add a shape to staff-shapes.ttl so that every person has at most one foaf:name per language. Which SHACL constraint does that?
    Answer

    sh:uniqueLang true on the foaf:name property shape. Ben has "Ben"@en and "Bem"@pt, which is fine. Two English names would be a violation.

  5. The CSV gets a new column homepage. Some cells are empty and some are not URLs. Extend the mapping and the shapes.
    Answer

    In csv_to_graph, add if row["homepage"]: g.add((r, FOAF.homepage, URIRef(row["homepage"]))). In the shape, add sh:property [ sh:path foaf:homepage ; sh:nodeKind sh:IRI ; sh:pattern "^https://" ; sh:maxCount 1 ]. Empty cells make no triple, so they pass. Bad values are rejected.

  6. Your pipeline must load 20 million triples every night and answer SPARQL queries during the day. Which parts of this chapter would you keep, and which would you change?
    Answer

    Keep the mapping idea, the shapes and the quarantine step. Write N-Triples in streams instead of one big rdflib graph. Load into pyoxigraph or a real triple store with a bulk loader. Validate in batches, or with a validator that runs inside the store. Keep rdflib for small tests and tools.

Key takeaways

  • rdflib is the centre of the Python toolkit: terms, graphs, many formats and SPARQL 1.1.
  • Give literals the right datatype. Compare graphs with isomorphic. Pass query values with initBindings.
  • owlready2 makes OWL classes into Python classes and runs HermiT or Pellet through Java.
  • A reasoner adds facts and finds contradictions. Domain and range are rules, not checks.
  • pySHACL checks data and returns a report graph. Read severities, and choose the inference mode on purpose.
  • Public endpoints have limits. Send a descriptive User-Agent, handle 429, batch and cache.
  • A clean pipeline maps, validates, quarantines and publishes, and validates again at the end.
  • For large data, move from rdflib to pyoxigraph or a triple store.

Sources

  • RDFLib documentation. Graphs, namespaces, parsers, serialisers and the SPARQL engine.
  • Owlready2: Reasoning. HermiT and Pellet, Java, inferred facts and the inconsistency error.
  • pySHACL on GitHub. The validate function and its options.
  • SPARQLWrapper documentation. Endpoints, return formats and queries.
  • Wikidata Query Service User Manual. Endpoint, limits, User-Agent and the planned backend move.
  • Wikimedia User-Agent Policy. The format of a good User-Agent header.

The Rust toolkit

Rust has a fast, well kept family of RDF crates around Oxigraph. This chapter first uses them for real work: load Turtle, run SPARQL, stream big files. Then you build a tiny triple store yourself, in plain Rust and in Python, to see what happens inside.

  • Load Turtle and run SPARQL query and update with the oxigraph crate.
  • Stream RDF files with oxttl and keep small graphs in oxrdf.
  • Choose between oxigraph, sophia, horned-owl and older crates like rio.
  • Build a triple store from scratch: string interning, three sorted indexes, patterns and joins.
  • Test the store against a brute-force check and measure the effect of join order.

The crates at a glance

A crate is a Rust package. We checked these on crates.io on 15 November 2026. The first group all live in the Oxigraph repository, and they release together.

Rust crates for RDF and OWL (checked 2026-11-15)
CrateVersionJob
oxigraph0.5.13A full RDF store with SPARQL 1.1 query and update. On disk with RocksDB, or in memory.
oxrdf0.3.5The basic types: NamedNode, Literal, Triple, Quad, plus small in-memory Graph and Dataset.
oxttl0.2.5Streaming parsers and serialisers for Turtle, TriG, N-Triples, N-Quads and N3.
oxrdfio0.2.7One API over all formats, including RDF/XML (oxrdfxml) and JSON-LD (oxjsonld).
spargebra, sparopt, spareval0.4.8, 0.3.9, 0.2.9SPARQL parser, optimiser and evaluator, usable on their own.
sophia0.10.0A generic RDF toolkit built on traits. Partial SPARQL behind a feature.
horned-owl5.0.0OWL 2 as Rust types. Reads and writes several OWL syntaxes.
rio_turtle, rio_xml0.8.6Old parsers. Now marked unmaintained: use oxttl and oxrdfxml.

RocksDB is a C++ database. It is a default feature of oxigraph. It makes the first build slow and large. For tests and small tools, switch it off and use the in-memory store.

[package]
name = "oxi-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
oxigraph = { version = "0.5.13", default-features = false }  # in memory only
oxrdf = "0.3.5"
oxttl = "0.2.5"

Oxigraph is mainly the work of Thomas Pellissier Tanon. The same engine powers the Python package pyoxigraph, which you met in The Python toolkit. There is also a command-line server, the crate oxigraph-cli, version 0.5.13.

Oxigraph: load Turtle and run SPARQL

Here is the package data from The ontology engineering method, in a small store. The program counts releases, marks risky releases with SPARQL Update, and prints them as Turtle. The Python tab does the same with pyoxigraph.

use oxigraph::io::{RdfFormat, RdfSerializer};
use oxigraph::model::{NamedNodeRef, Term};
use oxigraph::sparql::{QueryResults, SparqlEvaluator};
use oxigraph::store::Store;
const PKG: &str = "http://example.org/pkg#";
const DATA: &str = "@prefix pkg: <http://example.org/pkg#> .
pkg:fastjson pkg:hasRelease pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 , pkg:fastjson-1.3.0 .
pkg:tinyhttp pkg:hasRelease pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 .
pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 pkg:dependsOn pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 .
pkg:webapp-0.9.0 pkg:dependsOn pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 .
pkg:flaw-42 pkg:affects pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 .";

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let store = Store::new()?; // in memory (no rocksdb feature)
    store.load_from_slice(RdfFormat::Turtle, DATA)?;
    println!("{} quads loaded", store.len()?);
    let sparql = || SparqlEvaluator::new().with_prefix("pkg", PKG); // shared prefix
    let q = "SELECT ?p (COUNT(?r) AS ?n) WHERE { ?p pkg:hasRelease ?r } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY ?p";
    if let QueryResults::Solutions(rows) = sparql()?.parse_query(q)?.on_store(&store).execute()? {
        for row in rows {
            let row = row?;
            if let (Some(p), Some(Term::Literal(n))) = (row.get("p"), row.get("n")) {
                println!("{p} has {} release(s)", n.value());
            }
        }
    }
    let u = "INSERT { ?r pkg:atRisk true } WHERE { ?v pkg:affects ?bad . ?r pkg:dependsOn* ?bad }";
    sparql()?.parse_update(u)?.on_store(&store).execute()?; // SPARQL Update
    let c = "CONSTRUCT { ?r pkg:atRisk true } WHERE { ?r pkg:atRisk true }";
    if let QueryResults::Graph(triples) = sparql()?.parse_query(c)?.on_store(&store).execute()? {
        let mut out = RdfSerializer::from_format(RdfFormat::Turtle)
            .with_prefix("pkg", PKG)?.for_writer(std::io::stdout());
        for t in triples { out.serialize_triple(&t?)?; }
        out.finish()?;
    }
    let dep = NamedNodeRef::new("http://example.org/pkg#dependsOn")?; // no SPARQL needed
    println!("{} dependsOn triples", store.quads_for_pattern(None, Some(dep), None, None).count());
    Ok(())
}
import pyoxigraph as ox

PKG = "http://example.org/pkg#"
DATA = """@prefix pkg: <http://example.org/pkg#> .
pkg:fastjson pkg:hasRelease pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 , pkg:fastjson-1.3.0 .
pkg:tinyhttp pkg:hasRelease pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 .
pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 pkg:dependsOn pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 .
pkg:webapp-0.9.0 pkg:dependsOn pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 .
pkg:flaw-42 pkg:affects pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 ."""

store = ox.Store()                                  # no path: in memory
store.load(DATA, format=ox.RdfFormat.TURTLE)
print(len(store), "quads loaded")
pre = {"pkg": PKG}                                  # shared prefix

q = "SELECT ?p (COUNT(?r) AS ?n) WHERE { ?p pkg:hasRelease ?r } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY ?p"
for row in store.query(q, prefixes=pre):
    print(row["p"], "has", row["n"].value, "release(s)")

u = "INSERT { ?r pkg:atRisk true } WHERE { ?v pkg:affects ?bad . ?r pkg:dependsOn* ?bad }"
store.update(u, prefixes=pre)                       # SPARQL Update

c = "CONSTRUCT { ?r pkg:atRisk true } WHERE { ?r pkg:atRisk true }"
turtle = ox.serialize(store.query(c, prefixes=pre), format=ox.RdfFormat.TURTLE, prefixes=pre)
print(turtle.decode(), end="")

dep = ox.NamedNode(PKG + "dependsOn")              # no SPARQL needed
print(len(list(store.quads_for_pattern(None, dep, None))), "dependsOn triples")

We ran it with cargo run --bin tour on Rust 1.99, and the Python tab with Python 3.14. Both print the same lines.

6 quads loaded
<http://example.org/pkg#fastjson> has 2 release(s)
<http://example.org/pkg#tinyhttp> has 1 release(s)
@prefix pkg: <http://example.org/pkg#> .
pkg:tinyhttp-2.0.0 pkg:atRisk true .
pkg:webapp-0.9.0 pkg:atRisk true .
pkg:fastjson-1.2.0 pkg:atRisk true .
2 dependsOn triples

Notice pkg:dependsOn*. The star means zero or more steps. So fastjson 1.2.0 itself is at risk: it has the flaw. With + it would not be in the list.

The SPARQL API in version 0.5

  • SparqlEvaluator::new() is the way in. Store::query is deprecated since 0.5.0.
  • with_prefix() adds a prefix to every query you parse with it.
  • parse_query() or parse_update(), then on_store(), then execute().
  • A query returns QueryResults: Solutions for SELECT, Boolean for ASK, Graph for CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE.
  • Each step returns a Result. The ? operator passes errors up to main.
store.load_from_reader(RdfFormat::NTriples, File::open("big.nt")?)?;

One transaction for the whole file. The docs call it slow and memory hungry for big files.

let mut loader = store.bulk_loader();
loader.load_from_reader(RdfFormat::NTriples, File::open("big.nt")?)?;
loader.commit()?; // without this, nothing is saved

The bulk loader is made for large files. Use it for millions of triples.

Do not forget commit() on the bulk loader. We first left it out. The program ran without an error, and the store had 0 quads.

Old blog posts call store.query("..."). It still compiles in 0.5, with a deprecation warning. Move to SparqlEvaluator now, so the next major version does not break your code. Always check the docs for the exact version in your Cargo.toml.

Streaming with oxttl and oxrdf

Sometimes you do not need a store or SPARQL. You want to read a file once, count or filter, and move on. A streaming parser gives you one triple at a time, so memory stays small.

use oxrdf::{Graph, NamedNodeRef, vocab::rdf};
use oxttl::TurtleParser;
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::fs::File;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut graph = Graph::default();                  // oxrdf: a simple in-memory graph
    let mut per_predicate: BTreeMap<String, usize> = BTreeMap::new();
    for triple in TurtleParser::new().for_reader(File::open("data.ttl")?) {
        let triple = triple?;                          // one triple at a time
        *per_predicate.entry(triple.predicate.as_str().to_string()).or_default() += 1;
        graph.insert(&triple);
    }
    for (p, n) in &per_predicate {
        println!("{n:2}  {p}");
    }
    let release = NamedNodeRef::new("http://example.org/pkg#Release")?;
    let releases = graph.subjects_for_predicate_object(rdf::TYPE, release).count();
    println!("{} triples, {releases} releases", graph.len());
    Ok(())
}
from collections import Counter
import pyoxigraph as ox

per_predicate = Counter()
triples = []
for t in ox.parse(path="data.ttl", format=ox.RdfFormat.TURTLE):  # one at a time
    per_predicate[t.predicate.value] += 1
    triples.append(t)
for p, n in sorted(per_predicate.items()):
    print(f"{n:2}  {p}")
rdf_type = ox.NamedNode("http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type")
release = ox.NamedNode("http://example.org/pkg#Release")
releases = sum(1 for t in triples if t.predicate == rdf_type and t.object == release)
print(f"{len(triples)} triples, {releases} releases")
 1  http://example.org/pkg#affects
 2  http://example.org/pkg#dependsOn
 4  http://example.org/pkg#hasRelease
 1  http://example.org/pkg#licenseName
 2  http://example.org/pkg#maintainer
 5  http://example.org/pkg#versionString
11  http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type
 2  http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/name
28 triples, 5 releases

The input is the 28-triple data.ttl of the package ontology. Here the Rust program also keeps all triples in an oxrdf::Graph. That is fine for small files. For a large file, count and drop each triple instead.

Use the parsers from oxttl in Rust code that is not about RDF at all, for example a build tool that reads a small vocabulary file. You get correct Turtle parsing with error positions, and no database.

Other crates in brief

Oxigraph is not the only choice. Here is what else exists, and what we found about its state in November 2026.

sophia: a generic RDF toolkit

Sophia, by Pierre-Antoine Champin, defines RDF as Rust traits: Term, Triple, Graph, Dataset. Any type can implement them. Separate crates give in-memory graphs, Turtle and RDF/XML parsers, JSON-LD 1.1, canonicalisation and partial SPARQL 1.2 query behind a feature flag. Version 0.10.0 came out in May 2026 and aims at RDF 1.2. Choose it when you want to plug your own storage behind a common API.

horned-owl: OWL as Rust types

horned-owl, by Phillip Lord, models OWL 2 axioms as Rust enums and structs. It reads and writes RDF/XML, OWL/XML, Functional Syntax and Manchester Syntax. Its README says it is built for ontologies with very many terms. It is not a reasoner. Its page lists whelk-rs, a Rust version of the Whelk EL reasoner, among its users, and there are Python bindings called py-horned-owl. Version 5.0.0 came out on 13 November 2026.

rio: the old parsers

Rio was the parser family that Oxigraph used before. Its README now says "Rio is unmaintained", and the repository is archived. The crates on crates.io point to oxttl and oxrdfxml. Do not start new code with rio.

Rules and reasoning

For Datalog in Rust, see Ascent (0.8.1) and datafrog (2.0.1) in Rules and Datalog. Nemo is a rule engine written in Rust. The crate reasonable (0.4.4, September 2026) is an OWL 2 RL reasoner. The chapter Build a reasoner writes a small one from scratch.

Which crate for which job
JobFirst choice
SPARQL over a store, in a service or a CLIoxigraph
Read or write one RDF fileoxttl or oxrdfio
Your own storage behind a standard RDF APIsophia
Edit or check OWL axioms in codehorned-owl
Rules over your own Rust dataAscent or datafrog

Do not pick a crate by its download count alone. rio still has many downloads because old projects depend on it, but it gets no fixes. Read the README and the date of the last release.

A triple store from scratch: the plan

Now build your own store. It is about 100 lines of plain Rust, with no crates. The aim is not speed. The aim is to see the three ideas that every real store uses.

  1. Interning. Store each string once and give it a small number, an id. Triples hold only ids.
  2. Sorted indexes. Keep the triples in three sorted orders: SPO, POS and OSP. Any pattern becomes a range in one of them.
  3. Joins. Answer several patterns by filling in variables from one pattern into the next.

Why only three indexes? A triple pattern has three positions. Each is known or unknown, so there are 2^3 = 8 shapes. An index answers a shape when the known positions come first in its order. The table shows that SPO, POS and OSP together cover all eight.

The eight pattern shapes and the index that answers each
Known positionsExampleIndex and prefix
s, p, oIs this exact triple there?SPO with (s, p, o)
s, pWhat does webapp depend on?SPO with (s, p)
sEverything about webappSPO with (s)
p, oWho depends on tinyhttp?POS with (p, o)
pAll dependsOn triplesPOS with (p)
s, oHow is webapp linked to tinyhttp?OSP with (o, s)
oEverything that points to tinyhttpOSP with (o)
noneAll triplesany index, full scan

The idea of keeping triples in several orders is old. The hexastore design of Weiss, Karras and Bernstein (2008) keeps all six orders. Oxigraph's wiki says it keeps SPO, POS and OSP for the default graph, plus six orders for named graphs.

Step 1: interning and the indexes

First the data structure. Interning is also called dictionary encoding. Comparing two u32 numbers is much faster than comparing two long IRIs. A triple of ids takes 12 bytes.

use std::collections::HashMap;

type Id = u32;
type Triple = [Id; 3];

#[derive(Default)]
struct Store {
    ids: HashMap<String, Id>, // string -> id
    names: Vec<String>,       // id -> string
    spo: Vec<Triple>,         // three sorted indexes
    pos: Vec<Triple>,
    osp: Vec<Triple>,
}

impl Store {
    fn intern(&mut self, s: &str) -> Id {
        if let Some(&id) = self.ids.get(s) {
            return id; // seen before: reuse the id
        }
        let id = self.names.len() as Id;
        self.names.push(s.to_string());
        self.ids.insert(s.to_string(), id);
        id
    }

    fn add(&mut self, s: &str, p: &str, o: &str) {
        let t = [self.intern(s), self.intern(p), self.intern(o)];
        self.spo.push(t);
        self.pos.push([t[1], t[2], t[0]]); // the same triple, rotated
        self.osp.push([t[2], t[0], t[1]]);
    }

    fn build(&mut self) {
        for idx in [&mut self.spo, &mut self.pos, &mut self.osp] {
            idx.sort_unstable(); // sort once after loading
            idx.dedup();         // a set: no duplicates
        }
    }
}
from bisect import bisect_left


class Store:
    def __init__(self):
        self.ids = {}                   # string -> id
        self.names = []                 # id -> string
        self.spo, self.pos, self.osp = [], [], []   # three sorted indexes

    def intern(self, s):
        if s not in self.ids:           # new string: give it the next id
            self.ids[s] = len(self.names)
            self.names.append(s)
        return self.ids[s]

    def add(self, s, p, o):
        t = (self.intern(s), self.intern(p), self.intern(o))
        self.spo.append(t)
        self.pos.append((t[1], t[2], t[0]))   # the same triple, rotated
        self.osp.append((t[2], t[0], t[1]))

    def build(self):
        for name in ("spo", "pos", "osp"):    # sort once, drop duplicates
            setattr(self, name, sorted(set(getattr(self, name))))

The dictionary needs two directions. A HashMap goes from string to id when you load. A Vec goes from id back to string when you print. The id is just the position in the Vec.

We load first and sort once at the end. Sorting after each insert would cost far more. dedup() removes repeated triples, because an RDF graph is a set.

This store treats every string the same. A real store must keep the term kind: IRI, blank node or literal, and the datatype and language of literals. "1" as a string and 1 as an integer must get different ids. Oxigraph stores a type byte with every term for this reason.

Step 2: lookups with binary search

A sorted index puts all triples with the same first id next to each other. So "all triples that start with this prefix" is one slice. Two binary searches find its start and its end.

// All rows of a sorted index that start with `prefix`. Two binary searches.
fn range<'a>(idx: &'a [Triple], prefix: &[Id]) -> &'a [Triple] {
    let n = prefix.len();
    let lo = idx.partition_point(|t| t[..n] < *prefix);
    let hi = idx.partition_point(|t| t[..n] <= *prefix);
    &idx[lo..hi]
}

impl Store {
    // Pick the index whose sort order starts with the known positions.
    fn scan(&self, s: Option<Id>, p: Option<Id>, o: Option<Id>) -> Vec<Triple> {
        let from_pos = |r: &[Triple]| r.iter().map(|t| [t[2], t[0], t[1]]).collect();
        let from_osp = |r: &[Triple]| r.iter().map(|t| [t[1], t[2], t[0]]).collect();
        match (s, p, o) {
            (Some(s), Some(p), Some(o)) => range(&self.spo, &[s, p, o]).to_vec(),
            (Some(s), Some(p), None) => range(&self.spo, &[s, p]).to_vec(),
            (Some(s), None, None) => range(&self.spo, &[s]).to_vec(),
            (None, Some(p), Some(o)) => from_pos(range(&self.pos, &[p, o])),
            (None, Some(p), None) => from_pos(range(&self.pos, &[p])),
            (Some(s), None, Some(o)) => from_osp(range(&self.osp, &[o, s])),
            (None, None, Some(o)) => from_osp(range(&self.osp, &[o])),
            (None, None, None) => self.spo.clone(),
        }
    }
}
def prefix_range(idx, prefix):
    """All rows of a sorted index that start with prefix. Two binary searches."""
    if not prefix:
        return idx
    lo = bisect_left(idx, prefix)
    hi = bisect_left(idx, prefix[:-1] + (prefix[-1] + 1,))  # next prefix
    return idx[lo:hi]


def scan(st, s, p, o):
    """Pick the index whose sort order starts with the known positions."""
    from_pos = lambda rows: [(t[2], t[0], t[1]) for t in rows]
    from_osp = lambda rows: [(t[1], t[2], t[0]) for t in rows]
    match (s is not None, p is not None, o is not None):
        case (True, True, True):   return prefix_range(st.spo, (s, p, o))
        case (True, True, False):  return prefix_range(st.spo, (s, p))
        case (True, False, False): return prefix_range(st.spo, (s,))
        case (False, True, True):  return from_pos(prefix_range(st.pos, (p, o)))
        case (False, True, False): return from_pos(prefix_range(st.pos, (p,)))
        case (True, False, True):  return from_osp(prefix_range(st.osp, (o, s)))
        case (False, False, True): return from_osp(prefix_range(st.osp, (o,)))
        case _:                    return st.spo

In Rust, partition_point does the binary search. Slices compare element by element, so t[..n] < *prefix compares only the first n ids. In Python, bisect_left does the same. The end of the range is where the "next prefix" would start: the same prefix with the last id plus one.

The match is the table of the last section, written as code. Rows from POS and OSP are rotated back, so scan always returns triples in s, p, o order. The caller never needs to know which index was used.

Each lookup costs about \log_2 n steps to find the range, plus one step per result. For a million triples, \log_2 10^6 \approx 20.

An off-by-one error at the end of the range is easy to make and hard to see on small data. It only shows up when two prefixes are neighbours. The next step tests scan against a slow but obvious version, on every pattern.

Step 3: patterns, variables and joins

A query is a list of triple patterns. A word that starts with ? is a variable. A binding says which value each variable has in one answer.

type Bindings = HashMap<String, Id>; // variable name -> id

impl Store {
    // Join the patterns one by one. "?x" is a variable, anything else a name.
    fn solve(&self, patterns: &[[&str; 3]]) -> Vec<Bindings> {
        let mut results = vec![Bindings::new()]; // one empty solution
        for pat in patterns {
            let mut next = Vec::new();
            for b in &results {
                let mut key = [None; 3]; // what we know for each position
                for i in 0..3 {
                    key[i] = match pat[i].strip_prefix('?') {
                        Some(var) => b.get(var).copied(), // bound earlier?
                        None => match self.ids.get(pat[i]) {
                            Some(&id) => Some(id),
                            None => return vec![], // unknown name: no answers
                        },
                    };
                }
                for t in self.scan(key[0], key[1], key[2]) {
                    let mut nb = b.clone();
                    let fits = (0..3).all(|i| match pat[i].strip_prefix('?') {
                        Some(var) => *nb.entry(var.to_string()).or_insert(t[i]) == t[i],
                        None => true,
                    });
                    if fits {
                        next.push(nb);
                    }
                }
            }
            results = next;
        }
        results
    }
}
def solve(st, patterns):
    """Join the patterns one by one. '?x' is a variable, anything else a name."""
    results = [{}]                              # one empty solution
    for pat in patterns:
        nxt = []
        for b in results:
            key = []
            for part in pat:                    # what we know for each position
                if part.startswith("?"):
                    key.append(b.get(part[1:]))
                elif part in st.ids:
                    key.append(st.ids[part])
                else:
                    return []                   # unknown name: no answers
            for t in scan(st, *key):
                nb = dict(b)
                if all(nb.setdefault(part[1:], t[i]) == t[i]
                       for i, part in enumerate(pat) if part.startswith("?")):
                    nxt.append(nb)
        results = nxt
    return results

Follow Q2 by hand: ?v affects ?bad . ?r dependsOn ?bad.

  1. Start with one empty binding: {}.
  2. Pattern 1, ?v affects ?bad. Only affects is known, so scan uses POS with prefix (affects). One triple: flaw-42 affects fastjson-1.2.0.
  3. Now one binding: {v: flaw-42, bad: fastjson-1.2.0}.
  4. Pattern 2, ?r dependsOn ?bad. Now ?bad is known. dependsOn and fastjson-1.2.0 are known, so scan uses POS with prefix (dependsOn, fastjson-1.2.0).
  5. One triple: tinyhttp-2.0.0 dependsOn fastjson-1.2.0. The final binding adds r: tinyhttp-2.0.0.

This kind of join is an index nested loop join. For each answer so far, it looks up the next pattern in an index. The check in fits also handles a variable that appears twice in one pattern, like ?x knows ?x.

The last part loads the package data and runs three queries.

fn demo() {
    let mut st = Store::default();
    for (s, p, o) in [
        ("fastjson", "hasRelease", "fastjson-1.2.0"),
        ("fastjson", "hasRelease", "fastjson-1.3.0"),
        ("tinyhttp", "hasRelease", "tinyhttp-2.0.0"),
        ("webapp", "hasRelease", "webapp-0.9.0"),
        ("tinyhttp-2.0.0", "dependsOn", "fastjson-1.2.0"),
        ("webapp-0.9.0", "dependsOn", "tinyhttp-2.0.0"),
        ("webapp-0.9.0", "dependsOn", "fastjson-1.3.0"),
        ("flaw-42", "affects", "fastjson-1.2.0"),
        ("flaw-42", "fixedIn", "fastjson-1.3.0"),
    ] {
        st.add(s, p, o);
    }
    st.build();
    println!("{} terms, {} triples", st.names.len(), st.spo.len());
    println!("first SPO rows as ids: {:?}", &st.spo[..3]);
    println!("Q1 ?r dependsOn ?d");
    show(&st, st.solve(&[["?r", "dependsOn", "?d"]]), &["r", "d"]);
    println!("Q2 ?v affects ?bad . ?r dependsOn ?bad");
    show(&st, st.solve(&[["?v", "affects", "?bad"], ["?r", "dependsOn", "?bad"]]), &["v", "bad", "r"]);
    println!("Q3 ?p hasRelease ?r . ?r dependsOn ?x . ?v fixedIn ?x");
    let q3 = [["?p", "hasRelease", "?r"], ["?r", "dependsOn", "?x"], ["?v", "fixedIn", "?x"]];
    show(&st, st.solve(&q3), &["p", "r", "x"]);
}

// Print each solution as names, one line each, sorted for a stable output.
fn show(st: &Store, rows: Vec<Bindings>, vars: &[&str]) {
    let mut lines = Vec::new();
    for b in rows {
        let names: Vec<&str> = vars.iter().map(|v| st.names[b[*v] as usize].as_str()).collect();
        lines.push(names.join("  "));
    }
    lines.sort();
    for line in lines {
        println!("  {line}");
    }
}
if __name__ == "__main__":
    st = Store()
    for s, p, o in [
        ("fastjson", "hasRelease", "fastjson-1.2.0"),
        ("fastjson", "hasRelease", "fastjson-1.3.0"),
        ("tinyhttp", "hasRelease", "tinyhttp-2.0.0"),
        ("webapp", "hasRelease", "webapp-0.9.0"),
        ("tinyhttp-2.0.0", "dependsOn", "fastjson-1.2.0"),
        ("webapp-0.9.0", "dependsOn", "tinyhttp-2.0.0"),
        ("webapp-0.9.0", "dependsOn", "fastjson-1.3.0"),
        ("flaw-42", "affects", "fastjson-1.2.0"),
        ("flaw-42", "fixedIn", "fastjson-1.3.0"),
    ]:
        st.add(s, p, o)
    st.build()
    print(f"{len(st.names)} terms, {len(st.spo)} triples")
    print("first SPO rows as ids:", st.spo[:3])

    def show(rows, names):
        for line in sorted("  ".join(st.names[b[v]] for v in names) for b in rows):
            print(" ", line)

    print("Q1 ?r dependsOn ?d")
    show(solve(st, [("?r", "dependsOn", "?d")]), ["r", "d"])
    print("Q2 ?v affects ?bad . ?r dependsOn ?bad")
    show(solve(st, [("?v", "affects", "?bad"), ("?r", "dependsOn", "?bad")]), ["v", "bad", "r"])
    print("Q3 ?p hasRelease ?r . ?r dependsOn ?x . ?v fixedIn ?x")
    show(solve(st, [("?p", "hasRelease", "?r"), ("?r", "dependsOn", "?x"),
                    ("?v", "fixedIn", "?x")]), ["p", "r", "x"])

The Python version prints the same lines. The only difference is the id rows: Python shows tuples like (0, 1, 2). The full Rust file has a small main that runs demo(), or the benchmark below when you give it a number.

Q3 is a three-way join. It asks: which package has a release that depends on a release where some flaw was fixed? The answer is webapp, through webapp 0.9.0 and fastjson 1.3.0.

Testing and measuring

Test against brute force

How do you know that scan picks the right index and the right range? Compare it with a version that is too slow for real use but obviously right: look at every triple. Do it for every pattern shape and every id on a random graph.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn scan_matches_brute_force() {
        let mut st = Store::default();
        let mut x: u64 = 7;
        let mut next = || {
            x = x.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(1); // tiny random numbers
            format!("n{}", (x >> 33) % 12)
        };
        for _ in 0..300 {
            let (s, p, o) = (next(), next(), next());
            st.add(&s, &p, &o);
        }
        st.build();
        let n = st.names.len() as Id;
        let choices: Vec<Option<Id>> = std::iter::once(None).chain((0..n).map(Some)).collect();
        let fits = |want: Option<Id>, have: Id| want.is_none_or(|w| w == have);
        for &s in &choices {
            for &p in &choices {
                for &o in &choices {
                    let mut want: Vec<Triple> = st.spo.iter().copied()
                        .filter(|t| fits(s, t[0]) && fits(p, t[1]) && fits(o, t[2]))
                        .collect(); // brute force: look at every triple
                    let mut got = st.scan(s, p, o);
                    want.sort();
                    got.sort();
                    assert_eq!(got, want, "pattern {s:?} {p:?} {o:?}");
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
import random
from itertools import product
from store import Store, scan

random.seed(7)
st = Store()
for _ in range(300):                               # random small graph
    st.add(*(f"n{random.randrange(12)}" for _ in range(3)))
st.build()

ids = range(len(st.names))
checked = 0
for s, p, o in product([None, *ids], repeat=3):    # every pattern shape
    want = sorted(t for t in st.spo
                  if (s is None or t[0] == s) and (p is None or t[1] == p)
                  and (o is None or t[2] == o))    # brute force
    assert sorted(scan(st, s, p, o)) == want, (s, p, o)
    checked += 1
print(f"{len(st.spo)} triples, {checked} patterns checked, all equal")
$ rustc --edition 2024 --test store.rs -o store_test && ./store_test
test tests::scan_matches_brute_force ... ok
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
$ python3.14 check_store.py
277 triples, 2197 patterns checked, all equal

With 12 names there are 13 choices per position, counting "unknown". So the Python test checks 13^3 = 2197 patterns. 300 random triples became 277 after duplicates were removed. This style of test, a fast version checked against a simple one, is called a reference test.

Join order matters

Now a bigger graph: 100,000 releases, each with a type, a version and two dependencies. We ask the same three-pattern query as in the Python chapter, in two orders.

fn bench(n: u32) {
    use std::time::Instant;
    let t = Instant::now();
    let mut st = Store::default();
    for i in 0..n {
        let r = format!("r{i}");
        st.add(&r, "type", "Release");
        st.add(&r, "version", &format!("1.{}.0", i % 10));
        st.add(&r, "dependsOn", &format!("r{}", (i * 7) % n));
        st.add(&r, "dependsOn", &format!("r{}", (i * 13) % n));
    }
    st.build();
    println!("{} triples loaded and indexed in {:.2} s", st.spo.len(), t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
    let as_written = [["?a", "dependsOn", "?b"], ["?b", "dependsOn", "?c"], ["?c", "version", "1.0.0"]];
    let selective_first = [["?c", "version", "1.0.0"], ["?b", "dependsOn", "?c"], ["?a", "dependsOn", "?b"]];
    for (name, q) in [("as written", as_written), ("selective first", selective_first)] {
        let t = Instant::now();
        let rows = st.solve(&q).len();
        println!("{name:16} {rows} rows in {:.3} s", t.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
    }
}
$ ./store_rs 100000
399998 triples loaded and indexed in 0.10 s
as written       39994 rows in 0.247 s
selective first  39994 rows in 0.019 s
$ python3.14 bench_store.py 100000
399998 triples loaded and indexed in 1.04 s
as written       39994 rows in 1.400 s
selective first  39994 rows in 0.120 s

Why 399,998 and not 400,000? For release 0 and release 50,000, both dependency formulas give the same target. The two repeated triples were removed by dedup.

Both orders give 39,994 answers. But "as written" starts with all 200,000 dependsOn triples. "Selective first" starts with the 10,000 releases that have version 1.0.0. Fewer rows at the start means less work at every later step. A pattern that matches few triples has high selectivity.

Our Rust store with a good order is as fast as pyoxigraph here. That is not because it is better. pyoxigraph got the query in the bad order and was still fast. Its optimiser most likely chose a better order by itself. A real engine has a query optimiser that uses counts of the data to do this.

Where real stores go further

  • Term types. IRIs, blank nodes and typed literals get separate ids. Oxigraph inlines strings under 16 bytes and stores longer ones as a 128-bit hash, with the text in a separate table.
  • Updates. Our indexes are sorted vectors, so an insert costs a lot. Real stores use B-trees or LSM trees, which RocksDB uses.
  • Join methods. Sorted indexes allow merge joins, used by RDF-3X (Neumann and Weikum, 2008). Hash joins help when nothing is sorted the right way.
  • Statistics. Counts per predicate and per value let the optimiser pick a good order.
  • Compression and named graphs. Ids are stored compactly, and a fourth position holds the graph name.

The chapter Triple stores and graph databases compares real systems. Build a reasoner uses the same kind of indexes for rules.

A classic question: "Which indexes do you need so that every triple pattern is a prefix lookup?" Answer: three rotations, SPO, POS and OSP, cover all eight patterns. Six orders, as in a hexastore, also give a sorted order for every join.

Patterns to remember

Practice

Which crate holds the RDF types like NamedNode and Triple?

oxrdf.

How do you run SPARQL in oxigraph 0.5?

SparqlEvaluator::new().parse_query(q)?.on_store(&store).execute()?

What replaces the rio parsers?

oxttl for Turtle formats and oxrdfxml for RDF/XML, or oxrdfio for all.

Which three index orders cover every triple pattern?

SPO, POS and OSP.

What is interning?

Storing each string once and using a small number for it everywhere else.

Which index answers the pattern ?x dependsOn tinyhttp-2.0.0 as a prefix lookup?

  • SPO
  • POS
  • OSP

Predicate and object are known. POS starts with p, then o.

Which pattern needs the OSP index with prefix (o, s)?

  • webapp ?p ?o
  • webapp ?p tinyhttp
  • ?s dependsOn ?o

Subject and object are known, the predicate is not. Only OSP has o and s first.

You add oxigraph with default features. The first build takes very long. Why?

  • SPARQL parsing is slow to compile.
  • The default rocksdb feature builds the RocksDB C++ database.
  • oxigraph downloads data at build time.

With default-features = false you get the in-memory store only, and a much faster build.

A query has the patterns ?a dependsOn ?b (200,000 matches) and ?b version "1.0.0" (10,000 matches). Which should a simple engine run first?

  • ?a dependsOn ?b, because it comes first in the text
  • ?b version "1.0.0", because it matches fewer triples
  • It does not matter.

Start with the most selective pattern. Every later step then works on fewer rows.

Fill in the missing words.

In oxigraph 0.5, Store::query is ?.

A triple pattern has 2^3 = ? shapes of known and unknown positions.

Rust's slice method ? does the binary search in our store.

  1. Draw the three index rows for the triple "flaw-42 fixedIn fastjson-1.3.0", using the ids of our demo: flaw-42 is 9, fixedIn is 11, fastjson-1.3.0 is 3.
    Answer

    SPO: [9, 11, 3]. POS: [11, 3, 9]. OSP: [3, 9, 11].

  2. Add a method count(&self, s, p, o) -> usize to the store that counts matches without building a Vec.
    Answer

    Reuse the same match, but return range(...).len() for each case and self.spo.len() for the full scan. No rotation is needed, because only the length matters. This is also the start of statistics for an optimiser.

  3. Change solve so it first sorts the patterns: patterns with more constants come first.
    Answer

    Before the loop, copy the patterns and sort them by the number of parts that do not start with "?", highest first. A better rule uses count from the last exercise to sort by real match counts. Take care: after the first pattern, a pattern that shares a variable with the bound ones is usually cheaper than one with no shared variable.

  4. Our store gives the string "1" and the integer 1 the same id. Change the dictionary key so they differ.
    Answer

    Intern a term, not a string. For example an enum Term { Iri(String), Blank(String), Literal { value: String, datatype: String, lang: Option<String> } } with #[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)], and a HashMap<Term, Id>. Then "1" with xsd:string and "1" with xsd:integer are different keys.

  5. Write the oxigraph code that checks with ASK whether any release depends on a flawed release, and prints true or false.
    Answer

    let a = "ASK { ?v pkg:affects ?bad . ?r pkg:dependsOn+ ?bad }"; then if let QueryResults::Boolean(b) = sparql()?.parse_query(a)?.on_store(&store).execute()? { println!("{b}"); }. On our data it prints true.

  6. Our indexes are sorted vectors. Explain what an insert costs after build(), and propose a structure that makes inserts cheap.
    Answer

    Inserting into a sorted vector moves on average half of the rows, so it costs about n/2 per index. A BTreeSet<[u32; 3]> per index keeps the order and makes insert and range lookup about \log n. Its range() method gives the prefix range directly. Real stores use B-trees or LSM trees on disk.

Key takeaways

  • The Oxigraph family is the main Rust RDF stack in 2026: oxrdf for types, oxttl and oxrdfio for formats, oxigraph for a store with SPARQL.
  • In oxigraph 0.5, run SPARQL through SparqlEvaluator. Turn off the RocksDB feature for an in-memory store.
  • Stream files with oxttl when you do not need a store.
  • sophia gives generic RDF traits, horned-owl gives OWL types, and rio is unmaintained.
  • A triple store is a dictionary plus sorted indexes. SPO, POS and OSP turn every pattern into a prefix range.
  • Joins fill variables from one pattern into the next. Starting with the most selective pattern can save more than ten times the work.
  • Test fast code against a simple brute-force version on every pattern shape.

Build a reasoner

A reasoner turns stated facts into all the facts that follow. In this chapter you build one yourself, in plain Rust and in Python, with no libraries. It runs the RDFS rules and a useful part of OWL 2 RL, first with a naive loop, then with a semi-naive loop. It also remembers why each fact is true, checks itself with tests, and gets measured on a generated graph.

  • Write RDFS and OWL 2 RL rules as data, and match them against indexed facts.
  • Implement the naive and the semi-naive loop and prove on data that they agree.
  • Record a proof for every derived fact and print it as a tree.
  • Detect a contradiction with the disjointness rule cax-dw.
  • Test the reasoner against owlrl, measure it, and explain what real reasoners do better.

What we build

Start with the input. It is a small ontology about software packages, one triple per line. Every word is a prefixed name, and a full stop ends the line. A # starts a comment.

# schema (the TBox)
ex:Maintainer       rdfs:subClassOf     ex:Person .
ex:Person           rdfs:subClassOf     ex:Agent .
ex:maintains        rdfs:domain         ex:Maintainer .
ex:maintains        rdfs:range          ex:Package .
ex:leadMaintainerOf rdfs:subPropertyOf  ex:maintains .
ex:dependsOn        rdf:type            owl:TransitiveProperty .
ex:usedBy           owl:inverseOf       ex:dependsOn .
ex:worksWith        rdf:type            owl:SymmetricProperty .
ex:Person           owl:disjointWith    ex:Package .
# data (the ABox)
ex:ana              ex:leadMaintainerOf ex:fastjson .
ex:ana              ex:worksWith        ex:ben .
ex:webapp           ex:dependsOn        ex:tinyhttp .
ex:tinyhttp         ex:dependsOn        ex:fastjson .
ex:fastjson         owl:sameAs          ex:fast-json .
ex:fast-json        ex:license          ex:MIT .

Nobody wrote "ana is an Agent". But it follows. Ana is lead maintainer of fastjson, so she maintains it. Whoever maintains something is a Maintainer. Every Maintainer is a Person, and every Person is an Agent. Our reasoner must find this, and 21 other facts, by itself.

This is materialisation by forward chaining. You know both words from Rules and Datalog and Reasoners and materialisation. The result, all given facts plus all derived facts, is the closure.

The Rust version uses only the standard library. The Python version uses only the standard library too. Only the tests use rdflib and owlrl, as a reference. Both versions print exactly the same output, so you can read either tab.

We read a toy format, not real Turtle. That keeps the code short and the focus on reasoning. To read real files, plug in the parsers from The Rust toolkit or The Python toolkit.

Rules as data

Here is one rule from the RDF 1.1 Semantics document, called rdfs9. In words: if class A is a subclass of B, and x has type A, then x has type B. The OWL 2 Profiles document has the same rule under the name cax-sco.

T(?x, rdf:type, ?b) :- T(?a, rdfs:subClassOf, ?b), T(?x, rdf:type, ?a).

Every rule in this chapter has this shape. A body of one to three triple patterns, and a head of one triple pattern. Because the shape is always the same, we do not write code for each rule. We write the rules as data, and one function runs them all.

The RDFS rules we use, and their OWL 2 RL names
RDFS nameOWL 2 RL nameIfThen
rdfs2prp-domp domain c, and x p yx type c
rdfs3prp-rngp range c, and x p yy type c
rdfs5scm-spop subPropertyOf q, q subPropertyOf rp subPropertyOf r
rdfs7prp-spo1p subPropertyOf q, and x p yx q y
rdfs9cax-scoa subClassOf b, and x type ax type b
rdfs11scm-scoa subClassOf b, b subClassOf ca subClassOf c

Then the OWL 2 RL part. The scope of this chapter asks for inverse, transitive, symmetric and sameAs.

The OWL 2 RL rules we add (names from the W3C Profiles document)
NameIfThen
prp-inv1, prp-inv2p inverseOf q, and x p y (or x q y)y q x (or y p x)
prp-sympp is symmetric, and x p yy p x
prp-trpp is transitive, x p y, and y p zx p z
eq-sym, eq-transx sameAs y (and y sameAs z)y sameAs x (and x sameAs z)
eq-rep-s, eq-rep-p, eq-rep-ox sameAs y, and x is in a triplethe same triple with y in place of x
cax-dwa disjointWith b, x type a, x type bfalse: a contradiction

In code, a position in a pattern is either a variable or a constant. In Rust it is a small enum. In Python a variable is the tuple ("?", n) and a constant is a plain string.

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum T {
    V(usize), // a variable, by number
    C(Id),    // a constant
}

struct Rule {
    name: &'static str,
    body: Vec<[T; 3]>,
    head: [T; 3],
}

fn owl_rl_rules(d: &mut Dict) -> Vec<Rule> {
    use T::{C, V};
    let mut k = |name: &str| C(d.id(name)); // a constant from the dictionary
    let (ty, sco, spo) = (k("rdf:type"), k("rdfs:subClassOf"), k("rdfs:subPropertyOf"));
    let (dom, rng, inv) = (k("rdfs:domain"), k("rdfs:range"), k("owl:inverseOf"));
    let (trans, sym, same) = (k("owl:TransitiveProperty"), k("owl:SymmetricProperty"), k("owl:sameAs"));
    let (x, y, z, a, b, c) = (V(0), V(1), V(2), V(3), V(4), V(5));
    let r = |name, body: &[[T; 3]], head| Rule { name, body: body.to_vec(), head };
    vec![
        r("cax-sco (rdfs9)", &[[a, sco, b], [x, ty, a]], [x, ty, b]),
        r("scm-sco (rdfs11)", &[[a, sco, b], [b, sco, c]], [a, sco, c]),
        r("prp-spo1 (rdfs7)", &[[a, spo, b], [x, a, y]], [x, b, y]),
        r("scm-spo (rdfs5)", &[[a, spo, b], [b, spo, c]], [a, spo, c]),
        r("prp-dom (rdfs2)", &[[a, dom, c], [x, a, y]], [x, ty, c]),
        r("prp-rng (rdfs3)", &[[a, rng, c], [x, a, y]], [y, ty, c]),
        r("prp-inv1", &[[a, inv, b], [x, a, y]], [y, b, x]),
        r("prp-inv2", &[[a, inv, b], [x, b, y]], [y, a, x]),
        r("prp-symp", &[[a, ty, sym], [x, a, y]], [y, a, x]),
        r("prp-trp", &[[a, ty, trans], [x, a, y], [y, a, z]], [x, a, z]),
        r("eq-sym", &[[x, same, y]], [y, same, x]),
        r("eq-trans", &[[x, same, y], [y, same, z]], [x, same, z]),
        r("eq-rep-s", &[[x, same, y], [x, a, z]], [y, a, z]),
        r("eq-rep-p", &[[a, same, b], [x, a, y]], [x, b, y]),
        r("eq-rep-o", &[[x, same, y], [z, a, x]], [z, a, y]),
    ]
}
def V(n):                    # a variable is ("?", number); a constant is a string
    return ("?", n)

x, y, z, a, b, c = (V(i) for i in range(6))
TY, SCO, SPO = "rdf:type", "rdfs:subClassOf", "rdfs:subPropertyOf"
DOM, RNG, INV, SAME = "rdfs:domain", "rdfs:range", "owl:inverseOf", "owl:sameAs"
RULES = [  # (name, body atoms, head)
    ("cax-sco (rdfs9)",  [(a, SCO, b), (x, TY, a)], (x, TY, b)),
    ("scm-sco (rdfs11)", [(a, SCO, b), (b, SCO, c)], (a, SCO, c)),
    ("prp-spo1 (rdfs7)", [(a, SPO, b), (x, a, y)], (x, b, y)),
    ("scm-spo (rdfs5)",  [(a, SPO, b), (b, SPO, c)], (a, SPO, c)),
    ("prp-dom (rdfs2)",  [(a, DOM, c), (x, a, y)], (x, TY, c)),
    ("prp-rng (rdfs3)",  [(a, RNG, c), (x, a, y)], (y, TY, c)),
    ("prp-inv1", [(a, INV, b), (x, a, y)], (y, b, x)),
    ("prp-inv2", [(a, INV, b), (x, b, y)], (y, a, x)),
    ("prp-symp", [(a, TY, "owl:SymmetricProperty"), (x, a, y)], (y, a, x)),
    ("prp-trp",  [(a, TY, "owl:TransitiveProperty"), (x, a, y), (y, a, z)], (x, a, z)),
    ("eq-sym",   [(x, SAME, y)], (y, SAME, x)),
    ("eq-trans", [(x, SAME, y), (y, SAME, z)], (x, SAME, z)),
    ("eq-rep-s", [(x, SAME, y), (x, a, z)], (y, a, z)),
    ("eq-rep-p", [(a, SAME, b), (x, a, y)], (x, b, y)),
    ("eq-rep-o", [(x, SAME, y), (z, a, x)], (z, a, y)),
]

Look at prp-spo1: [x, a, y] has a variable in the predicate position. That is fine. It is the reason why our facts need an index by predicate and also one by subject and object.

Every rule is safe: each head variable appears in the body. So when the body matches, the head is fully known. The Rust code checks this with expect.

Do not add eq-ref, the rule "every thing is the same as itself". It is correct OWL 2 RL, but it makes three new triples for every term in the graph. The chapter Rules and Datalog showed 64 such triples from 7 input triples with owlrl. Real engines treat equality in a special way instead.

Facts, indexes and matching

The reasoner keeps facts in a set, so a fact is never stored twice. It also keeps three indexes: by subject, by predicate and by object. Each index maps one term to the list of triples that contain it there.

#[derive(Default)]
struct Facts {
    set: HashSet<Triple>,
    by_s: HashMap<Id, Vec<Triple>>,
    by_p: HashMap<Id, Vec<Triple>>,
    by_o: HashMap<Id, Vec<Triple>>,
}

impl Facts {
    fn insert(&mut self, t: Triple) -> bool {
        if !self.set.insert(t) {
            return false; // already known
        }
        self.by_s.entry(t[0]).or_default().push(t);
        self.by_p.entry(t[1]).or_default().push(t);
        self.by_o.entry(t[2]).or_default().push(t);
        true
    }
    // Triples that fit the known positions: take the shortest index list, then filter.
    fn matching(&self, key: [Option<Id>; 3]) -> Vec<Triple> {
        let fits = |t: &&Triple| (0..3).all(|i| key[i].is_none_or(|k| t[i] == k));
        let lists = [(key[0], &self.by_s), (key[1], &self.by_p), (key[2], &self.by_o)];
        let shortest = lists
            .iter()
            .filter_map(|(k, idx)| k.map(|k| idx.get(&k).map_or(&[][..], |v| v.as_slice())))
            .min_by_key(|list| list.len());
        match shortest {
            Some(list) => list.iter().filter(fits).copied().collect(),
            None => self.set.iter().filter(fits).copied().collect(),
        }
    }
}
class Facts:
    def __init__(self):
        self.set = set()
        self.by = [defaultdict(list) for _ in range(3)]   # by subject, predicate, object

    def insert(self, t):
        if t in self.set:
            return False                                   # already known
        self.set.add(t)
        for i in range(3):
            self.by[i][t[i]].append(t)
        return True

    def matching(self, key):
        """Triples that fit the known positions: shortest index list, then filter."""
        lists = [self.by[i].get(k, []) for i, k in enumerate(key) if k is not None]
        candidates = min(lists, key=len) if lists else self.set
        return [t for t in candidates
                if all(k is None or t[i] == k for i, k in enumerate(key))]

Why hash maps here, and not the sorted indexes of The Rust toolkit? A reasoner adds facts all the time. Appending to a list in a hash map is cheap. Inserting into a sorted vector is not.

matching takes a key with known and unknown positions. If several positions are known, it takes the shortest list and filters it. Example: the key (?, rdf:type, ex:Person) uses the object list of ex:Person, which is much shorter than the list of all rdf:type triples.

The dictionary and the loader

As in the last chapter, Rust works with numbers. A dictionary gives each name an id. Python simply keeps the names as strings. Tuples of strings work well as set members.

use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};

type Id = u32;
type Triple = [Id; 3];

#[derive(Default)]
struct Dict {
    ids: HashMap<String, Id>,
    names: Vec<String>,
}

impl Dict {
    fn id(&mut self, s: &str) -> Id {
        if let Some(&id) = self.ids.get(s) {
            return id;
        }
        self.names.push(s.to_string());
        self.ids.insert(s.to_string(), self.names.len() as Id - 1);
        self.names.len() as Id - 1
    }
    fn show(&self, t: Triple) -> String {
        t.map(|id| self.names[id as usize].as_str()).join(" ")
    }
}

fn load(d: &mut Dict, text: &str) -> Vec<Triple> {
    text.lines()
        .map(|line| line.split('#').next().unwrap().trim()) // drop comments
        .filter(|line| !line.is_empty())
        .map(|line| {
            let w: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
            [d.id(w[0]), d.id(w[1]), d.id(w[2])]
        })
        .collect()
}
import sys
from collections import defaultdict


def load(path):
    lines = (line.split("#")[0].split() for line in open(path))
    return [tuple(w[:3]) for w in lines if w]

Matching a rule body

To fire a rule, we must find every way to match its body. The function join takes the atoms from left to right. It keeps a binding for each variable, and the list of triples it used so far. Those triples are the premises of the new fact.

type Found = Vec<(Triple, &'static str, Vec<Triple>)>; // new fact, rule, premises

// Match body atoms from left to right. Atom i reads its facts from src[i].
fn join(rule: &Rule, i: usize, b: [Option<Id>; 6], used: &mut Vec<Triple>, src: &[&Facts], out: &mut Found) {
    let value = |t: T, b: &[Option<Id>; 6]| match t {
        T::C(id) => Some(id),
        T::V(v) => b[v],
    };
    if i == rule.body.len() {
        let head = rule.head.map(|t| value(t, &b).expect("safe rule: head vars are bound"));
        out.push((head, rule.name, used.clone()));
        return;
    }
    let atom = rule.body[i];
    for t in src[i].matching(atom.map(|t| value(t, &b))) {
        let mut nb = b;
        let fits = (0..3).all(|k| match atom[k] {
            T::C(_) => true,
            T::V(v) => *nb[v].get_or_insert(t[k]) == t[k],
        });
        if fits {
            used.push(t);
            join(rule, i + 1, nb, used, src, out);
            used.pop();
        }
    }
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Reasoner {
    all: Facts,
    why: HashMap<Triple, (&'static str, Vec<Triple>)>, // first proof of each derived fact
    rounds: u32,
    firings: u64, // rule matches, also the ones that give old facts
}
def join(body, i, binds, used, src, out):
    """Match body atoms from left to right. Atom i reads its facts from src[i]."""
    if i == len(body):
        out.append((binds, list(used)))
        return
    atom = body[i]
    key = [binds.get(t) if isinstance(t, tuple) else t for t in atom]
    for t in src[i].matching(key):
        nb = dict(binds)
        if all(nb.setdefault(v, t[k]) == t[k]
               for k, v in enumerate(atom) if isinstance(v, tuple)):
            used.append(t)
            join(body, i + 1, nb, used, src, out)
            used.pop()

Note the parameter src. It says, for each atom, which set of facts to read. In the naive loop every atom reads all facts. In the semi-naive loop one atom reads only the new facts. That one parameter is the whole difference, as the next section shows.

  1. Atom 1 is [a, rdfs:domain, c]. The key is (?, rdfs:domain, ?). One match: maintains domain Maintainer. Now a = maintains, c = Maintainer.
  2. Atom 2 is [x, a, y], and a is bound. The key is (?, maintains, ?). One match: ana maintains fastjson. Now x = ana, y = fastjson.
  3. No atoms left. The head [x, rdf:type, c] becomes "ana rdf:type Maintainer". The premises are the two matched triples.

Do not forget the check when a variable is already bound. In [x, a, y] and [y, a, z] of prp-trp, the second atom must use the same y and the same a. The fits test, with get_or_insert in Rust and setdefault in Python, rejects a triple that disagrees with an earlier binding.

The naive loop, then the semi-naive loop

The loop is the heart of the reasoner. Here are both versions in one function, with a flag.

impl Reasoner {
    fn run(&mut self, rules: &[Rule], input: &[Triple], semi_naive: bool) {
        let mut delta = Facts::default();
        for &t in input {
            self.all.insert(t);
            delta.insert(t); // round 1: every input fact is new
        }
        loop {
            self.rounds += 1;
            let mut found = Found::new();
            for rule in rules {
                let n = rule.body.len();
                if semi_naive {
                    for i in 0..n {
                        let mut src = vec![&self.all; n];
                        src[i] = &delta; // atom i must use a new fact
                        join(rule, 0, [None; 6], &mut Vec::new(), &src, &mut found);
                    }
                } else {
                    join(rule, 0, [None; 6], &mut Vec::new(), &vec![&self.all; n], &mut found);
                }
            }
            self.firings += found.len() as u64;
            let mut next = Facts::default();
            for (t, rule, premises) in found {
                if !self.all.set.contains(&t) && next.insert(t) {
                    self.why.insert(t, (rule, premises));
                }
            }
            if next.set.is_empty() {
                return; // fixed point: nothing new
            }
            next.set.iter().for_each(|&t| { self.all.insert(t); });
            delta = next;
        }
    }
}
class Reasoner:
    def __init__(self, rules=RULES):
        self.rules, self.all, self.why = rules, Facts(), {}
        self.rounds = self.firings = 0

    def run(self, triples, semi_naive=True):
        delta = Facts()
        for t in triples:
            if self.all.insert(t):
                delta.insert(t)
        while True:
            self.rounds += 1
            found = []
            for name, body, head in self.rules:
                n = len(body)
                starts = range(n) if semi_naive else [None]
                for i in starts:
                    src = [self.all] * n
                    if i is not None:
                        src[i] = delta                 # atom i must use a new fact
                    matches = []
                    join(body, 0, {}, [], src, matches)
                    for binds, used in matches:
                        fact = tuple(binds[t] if isinstance(t, tuple) else t for t in head)
                        found.append((fact, name, used))
            self.firings += len(found)
            nxt = Facts()
            for fact, name, used in found:
                if fact not in self.all.set and nxt.insert(fact):
                    self.why[fact] = (name, used)      # first proof of the fact
            if not nxt.set:
                return                                 # fixed point: nothing new
            for t in nxt.set:
                self.all.insert(t)
            delta = nxt

Naive: each round, every atom of every rule reads all facts. Old facts joined with old facts give old facts again, so most of the work repeats. The loop stops when a round finds nothing new. That end state is the least fixed point of the rules, as the theorem in Rules and Datalog says.

Semi-naive: keep the facts that are new since the last round, the delta. A rule with n atoms runs n times. In run i, atom i reads only the delta and the others read all facts. So every match uses at least one new fact.

Semi-naive forward chaining. Put all input facts in ALL and in DELTA. Repeat: for every rule and every body position i, match the body with atom i over DELTA and the other atoms over ALL. Let NEW be the matched heads that are not in ALL. If NEW is empty, stop. Otherwise add NEW to ALL and set DELTA to NEW.

Why is the answer the same as naive? Take any match in the naive loop that gives a new fact in round k. If all its premises were known before round k−1, the same match already happened in an earlier round, so its head is not new. So at least one premise is from the last round, the delta. The semi-naive loop tries exactly the matches with at least one delta premise.

On our small ontology, both loops need 4 rounds and reach the same 37 facts. The naive loop makes 216 rule matches. The semi-naive loop makes 112.

For a rule with two atoms over the same kind of facts, like prp-trp, do not use the delta in only one position. Then you miss matches where the new fact is in the other position. Our loop runs every position. It can find the same match twice, when both premises are new. That costs work, not correctness. Exercise 6 removes this double work.

Recording why: proofs

A reasoner that only says "true" is hard to trust. Ours keeps, for every derived fact, the rule and the premises of its first match. That is enough to print a proof tree.

impl Reasoner {
    fn explain(&self, d: &Dict, t: Triple, depth: usize) {
        let pad = "  ".repeat(depth);
        match self.why.get(&t) {
            Some((rule, premises)) => {
                println!("{pad}{}   [{rule}]", d.show(t));
                for &p in premises {
                    self.explain(d, p, depth + 1);
                }
            }
            None => println!("{pad}{}   [given]", d.show(t)),
        }
    }

    // cax-dw: x is in two disjoint classes. That is a contradiction.
    fn clashes(&self, d: &mut Dict) -> Vec<String> {
        let (dw, ty) = (d.id("owl:disjointWith"), d.id("rdf:type"));
        let mut found = Vec::new();
        for [c1, _, c2] in self.all.matching([None, Some(dw), None]) {
            for [x, _, _] in self.all.matching([None, Some(ty), Some(c1)]) {
                if self.all.set.contains(&[x, ty, c2]) {
                    found.push(format!("{} is a {} and a {}", d.names[x as usize], d.names[c1 as usize], d.names[c2 as usize]));
                }
            }
        }
        found.sort();
        found
    }
}
    def explain(self, t, depth=1):
        pad = "  " * depth
        if t in self.why:
            name, used = self.why[t]
            print(f"{pad}{' '.join(t)}   [{name}]")
            for p in used:
                self.explain(p, depth + 1)
        else:
            print(f"{pad}{' '.join(t)}   [given]")

    def clashes(self):
        """cax-dw: x is in two disjoint classes. That is a contradiction."""
        out = []
        for c1, _, c2 in self.all.matching([None, "owl:disjointWith", None]):
            for x_, _, _ in self.all.matching([None, TY, c1]):
                if (x_, TY, c2) in self.all.set:
                    out.append(f"{x_} is a {c1} and a {c2}")
        return sorted(out)

Can a proof tree go round in a circle? No. A fact that is new in round k was matched only from facts known before round k. Its premises are older than the fact itself. So following premises always goes back to earlier rounds, and it ends at given facts. A proof with this property is well-founded. One of the tests checks it.

We keep only the first proof of each fact. A fact can have many proofs. Tools that list all minimal proofs give justifications. See Reasoners and materialisation.

The clashes function runs the rule cax-dw. Its head is "false", so it cannot add a fact. We run it once, after the fixed point, and report every individual that sits in two disjoint classes.

Running the reasoner

The main function loads a file, runs the semi-naive loop, prints all derived facts, explains one, and checks for clashes.

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();
    if args[1] == "--bench" {
        return bench(args[2].parse().expect("a number"));
    }
    let mut d = Dict::default();
    let rules = owl_rl_rules(&mut d);
    let input = load(&mut d, &std::fs::read_to_string(&args[1]).expect("a file"));
    let mut r = Reasoner::default();
    r.run(&rules, &input, true);
    println!("{} given, {} derived, {} rounds", input.len(), r.why.len(), r.rounds);
    let mut derived: Vec<String> = r.why.keys().map(|&t| d.show(t)).collect();
    derived.sort();
    for line in &derived {
        println!("  {line}");
    }
    println!("Why is ana an Agent?");
    let goal = [d.id("ex:ana"), d.id("rdf:type"), d.id("ex:Agent")];
    r.explain(&d, goal, 1);
    println!("Clashes: {:?}", r.clashes(&mut d));
}
if __name__ == "__main__":
    if sys.argv[1] == "--bench":
        bench(int(sys.argv[2]))
        sys.exit()
    given = load(sys.argv[1])
    r = Reasoner()
    r.run(given)
    print(f"{len(given)} given, {len(r.why)} derived, {r.rounds} rounds")
    for t in sorted(" ".join(t) for t in r.why):
        print(" ", t)
    print("Why is ana an Agent?")
    r.explain(("ex:ana", TY, "ex:Agent"))
    print("Clashes:", r.clashes())

We compared the two outputs with diff. They are identical. Read the list with the rules in mind.

  • "ana is an Agent" came through four rules: prp-spo1, prp-dom, scm-sco and cax-sco. The proof used the derived fact "Maintainer subClassOf Agent".
  • usedBy facts come from prp-inv2, and "webapp dependsOn fastjson" from prp-trp.
  • fastjson and fast-json share all facts, through the eq-rep rules. That is how "fastjson license MIT" appeared.
  • "fastjson sameAs fastjson" is real OWL 2 RL. eq-sym gives "fast-json sameAs fastjson", and eq-trans joins the two.
  • The round count includes the last round, which found nothing.

A contradiction

Add one wrong line: ex:fastjson ex:maintains ex:tinyhttp . Now prp-dom makes fastjson a Maintainer, so a Person. prp-rng already made it a Package. Person and Package are disjoint.

$ ./reasoner_rs onto-bad.txt | tail -1
Clashes: ["ex:fastjson is a ex:Person and a ex:Package", "ex:fast-json is a ex:Person and a ex:Package"]

Through sameAs the clash also appears for fast-json. In OWL, an inconsistent ontology entails everything, so a real reasoner stops and reports the problem. Ours reports and lets you decide.

Tests

A reasoner can be wrong in quiet ways: a missed fact, an extra fact, a proof that points to nothing. We test four things.

  1. Naive and semi-naive agree, on the small ontology and on a generated graph.
  2. Expected facts appear, one for each rule family, and the bad file gives a clash.
  3. Every proof is well-founded: each premise is in the closure, there is no circle, and the deepest proof has 3 steps.
  4. A reference engine agrees. owlrl, from the RDFLib project, must derive every fact that we derive.
from rdflib import Graph, URIRef
import owlrl
from reasoner import Reasoner, load, generate, TY
GIVEN = load("onto.txt")
NS = {"ex": "http://example.org/", "rdf": "http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#",
      "rdfs": "http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#", "owl": "http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#"}

def closure(triples, semi_naive=True):
    r = Reasoner()
    r.run(triples, semi_naive)
    return r

def test_naive_and_semi_naive_agree():
    for triples in (GIVEN, generate(300)):
        assert closure(triples, False).all.set == closure(triples, True).all.set

def test_expected_facts_and_clash():
    facts = closure(GIVEN).all.set
    assert ("ex:ana", TY, "ex:Agent") in facts                     # rdfs7, rdfs2, rdfs9
    assert ("ex:fastjson", "ex:usedBy", "ex:webapp") in facts      # prp-trp, prp-inv2
    assert ("ex:fastjson", "ex:license", "ex:MIT") in facts        # eq-sym, eq-rep-s
    bad = GIVEN + [("ex:fastjson", "ex:maintains", "ex:tinyhttp")]
    assert "ex:fastjson is a ex:Person and a ex:Package" in closure(bad).clashes()

def test_every_proof_is_well_founded():
    r, given = closure(GIVEN), set(GIVEN)
    def depth(t, seen=()):                  # fails on a cycle or a missing premise
        assert t not in seen and t in r.all.set
        return 0 if t in given else 1 + max(depth(p, seen + (t,)) for p in r.why[t][1])
    assert max(depth(t) for t in r.why) == 3       # "ana is an Agent" needs 3 steps

def test_owlrl_derives_everything_we_derive():
    iri = lambda name: URIRef(NS[name.split(":")[0]] + name.split(":", 1)[1])
    g = Graph()
    g += [tuple(map(iri, t)) for t in GIVEN]                  # the same input in rdflib
    owlrl.DeductiveClosure(owlrl.OWLRL_Semantics).expand(g)   # the reference engine
    ours = {tuple(map(iri, t)) for t in closure(GIVEN).why}
    assert ours <= set(g), ours - set(g)
    print(f"\nours: {len(ours)} derived, owlrl: {len(g) - len(GIVEN)} derived")
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn closure(d: &mut Dict, input: &[Triple], semi: bool) -> Reasoner {
        let rules = owl_rl_rules(d);
        let mut r = Reasoner::default();
        r.run(&rules, input, semi);
        r
    }

    #[test]
    fn naive_and_semi_naive_agree() {
        let mut d = Dict::default();
        let small = load(&mut d, &std::fs::read_to_string("onto.txt").unwrap());
        let big = generate(&mut d, 300);
        for input in [small, big] {
            let (a, b) = (closure(&mut d, &input, false), closure(&mut d, &input, true));
            assert_eq!(a.all.set, b.all.set);
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn expected_facts_and_proofs() {
        let mut d = Dict::default();
        let input = load(&mut d, &std::fs::read_to_string("onto.txt").unwrap());
        let r = closure(&mut d, &input, true);
        let ana_agent = [d.id("ex:ana"), d.id("rdf:type"), d.id("ex:Agent")];
        assert!(r.all.set.contains(&ana_agent));
        for (fact, (_, premises)) in &r.why {
            assert!(r.all.set.contains(fact));
            assert!(premises.iter().all(|p| r.all.set.contains(p))); // every proof step is real
        }
        let mut bad = input.clone();
        bad.push([d.id("ex:fastjson"), d.id("ex:maintains"), d.id("ex:tinyhttp")]);
        let r = closure(&mut d, &bad, true);
        assert_eq!(r.clashes(&mut d).len(), 2); // fastjson and fast-json
    }
}

We used pytest 9.2.0, rdflib 7.6.0 and owlrl 7.6.2. owlrl derived 156 facts, we derived 22, and all our 22 are among its 156. Where do the other 134 come from? We grouped them with a small script.

The last 6 are interesting. owlrl concluded, for example, "leadMaintainerOf domain Person". That comes from OWL 2 RL schema rules we skipped: scm-dom1, scm-dom2, scm-rng1 and scm-rng2. Exercise 5 adds them.

Testing a new engine against an old one is a reference test. Test in both directions when you can. "Everything we derive, owlrl derives" finds wrong facts. The reverse, on a filtered set, finds missing facts.

Measuring speed

Now a generated graph. A chain of 11 classes, C0 to C10. n instances of C0. A part-of chain of n/10 parts, where part-of is transitive and has an inverse, has-part.

// A generated graph: a chain of 11 classes, n instances, a part-of chain of n/10 parts.
fn generate(d: &mut Dict, n: usize) -> Vec<Triple> {
    let mut text = String::from("ex:partOf rdf:type owl:TransitiveProperty .\nex:hasPart owl:inverseOf ex:partOf .\n");
    for k in 0..10 {
        text += &format!("ex:C{k} rdfs:subClassOf ex:C{} .\n", k + 1);
    }
    for k in 0..n {
        text += &format!("ex:i{k} rdf:type ex:C0 .\n");
    }
    for k in 0..n / 10 {
        text += &format!("ex:p{k} ex:partOf ex:p{} .\n", k + 1);
    }
    load(d, &text)
}

fn bench(n: usize) {
    for semi in [false, true] {
        let mut d = Dict::default();
        let rules = owl_rl_rules(&mut d);
        let input = generate(&mut d, n);
        let start = std::time::Instant::now();
        let mut r = Reasoner::default();
        r.run(&rules, &input, semi);
        let name = if semi { "semi-naive" } else { "naive" };
        println!("{name:10} n={n:5} {:7} facts {:2} rounds {:9} firings {:7.3} s",
                 r.all.set.len(), r.rounds, r.firings, start.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
    }
}
def generate(n):
    """A chain of 11 classes, n instances, a part-of chain of n // 10 parts."""
    g = [("ex:partOf", TY, "owl:TransitiveProperty"), ("ex:hasPart", INV, "ex:partOf")]
    g += [(f"ex:C{k}", SCO, f"ex:C{k + 1}") for k in range(10)]
    g += [(f"ex:i{k}", TY, "ex:C0") for k in range(n)]
    g += [(f"ex:p{k}", "ex:partOf", f"ex:p{k + 1}") for k in range(n // 10)]
    return g


def bench(n):
    import time
    for semi in (False, True):
        r = Reasoner()
        start = time.perf_counter()
        r.run(generate(n), semi_naive=semi)
        name = "semi-naive" if semi else "naive"
        print(f"{name:10} n={n:5} {len(r.all.set):7} facts {r.rounds:2} rounds "
              f"{r.firings:9} firings {time.perf_counter() - start:7.3f} s")
