naive      n=  500    8107 facts  8 rounds    227689 firings   0.016 s
semi-naive n=  500    8107 facts  8 rounds     59183 firings   0.007 s
naive      n= 1000   21157 facts  9 rounds    964802 firings   0.068 s
semi-naive n= 1000   21157 facts  9 rounds    269053 firings   0.026 s
naive      n= 2000   62257 facts 10 rounds   5610115 firings   0.434 s
semi-naive n= 2000   62257 facts 10 rounds   1724977 firings   0.163 s

The Python version found the same facts, rounds and firings. Only the time differs.

Time on our laptop, one run each (Rust 1.99 with -O, Python 3.14)
nRust naiveRust semi-naivePython naivePython semi-naive
5000.016 s0.007 s0.364 s0.103 s
10000.068 s0.026 s1.813 s0.542 s
20000.434 s0.163 s11.319 s4.063 s

What do the numbers say?

  • Rounds grow slowly. prp-trp has two recursive atoms, so the longest known part-of path doubles each round: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. 200 parts need about 8 doubling rounds, plus one for the inverse and one empty round: 10. Compare the linear ancestor rule in Rules and Datalog, which adds one step per round.
  • Semi-naive saves less here than on a chain of parents. The transitive closure itself has many ways to make each fact. A pair (x, z) on a path can be joined through every y between them. Semi-naive removes repeated rounds, not repeated proofs inside one round.
  • Rust is 15 to 26 times faster than Python on the same algorithm. Compact ids and compiled code explain most of it.
  • The closure grows fast. 2,000 instances and 200 parts gave 62,257 facts. The part-of closure alone is about 200^2 / 2 pairs, twice, because of the inverse.

Do not measure a reasoner only on a small hand-made file. Most problems appear with long transitive chains, big sameAs groups and wide class trees. Generate graphs with those shapes, and grow them until the time or memory curve tells you something.

Where real reasoners go further

Our reasoner is correct for its 15 rules, and the tests show it. Real engines go much further.

The full OWL 2 RL rule set

The W3C tables list 78 rules, in six families: equality (eq), properties (prp), classes (cls), class axioms (cax), datatypes (dt) and schema (scm). We have 15 of them, plus the cax-dw check. Missing are, for example, functional properties (prp-fp), property chains (prp-spo2), keys (prp-key), someValuesFrom (cls-svf1) and intersections (cls-int1). Some of them read RDF lists, which need extra code.

Equality without blow-up

The eq-rep rules copy every fact to every alias. A group of k equal names makes k copies of each fact. RDFox instead picks one representative for each group and rewrites all facts to it. Motik, Nenov, Piro and Horrocks describe this rewriting in a 2015 AAAI paper. They report that it can cut reasoning time by orders of magnitude on real data.

Incremental updates

We compute the closure from zero. When one fact is added, semi-naive evaluation can simply continue with that fact as the delta. Deletion is harder, because a fact may have other proofs. Algorithms like DRed first delete too much, then derive back what still holds. See Reasoners and materialisation.

Speed

Real engines plan the join order of each rule, use better indexes, run rules on many cores, and compile rules to native code, as Soufflé does. Specialised code for transitive closure avoids the many repeated proofs we measured.

Beyond rules

OWL 2 RL is a rule-friendly part of OWL. Questions like "every person has some parent" need reasoning about things with no name. Tableau reasoners like HermiT, or consequence-based reasoners like ELK, handle that. See Description logics.

Know the rule names. A common question gives three triples and asks which OWL 2 RL rule derives a fourth. "p inverseOf q, x p y gives y q x" is prp-inv1. "a subClassOf b, x type a gives x type b" is cax-sco, which RDFS calls rdfs9.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for building a reasoner
PatternPurposeModelNote
Rule as dataOne engine for all rules("cax-sco", [(a, SCO, b), (x, TY, a)], (x, TY, b))Every head variable must be in the body.
Index by s, p and oFind matching facts fastby_p[rdf:type], by_o[ex:Person]Take the shortest list, then filter.
Join left to rightMatch a rule bodyBind a, c from atom 1, then look up atom 2Check variables that are already bound.
Naive loopSimplest correct closureAll rules on all facts until nothing is newRepeats old work every round.
Semi-naive loopSame closure, less workAtom i reads the delta, the others read all factsRun every position i of every rule.
First proof per factExplain answerswhy[fact] = (rule, premises)Premises are older, so proofs are well-founded.
Integrity rule after the fixed pointFind contradictionscax-dw: x type a, x type b, a disjointWith bIts head is false: report, do not add.
Skip eq-refAvoid useless factsNo "x sameAs x" for every termReal engines rewrite equality instead.
Naive equals semi-naive testCatch loop bugsassert naive.all.set == semi.all.setAlso run it on generated graphs.
Reference testCatch wrong factsours <= owlrl_closureFilter the reference for the reverse check.
Generated benchmarkFind the real costClass chain, many instances, transitive chainCount firings, not only seconds.

Practice

What is the OWL 2 RL name of rdfs9?

cax-sco: a subClassOf b, x type a, so x type b.

In the semi-naive loop, what does atom i read in run i?

Only the delta, the facts that were new in the last round. The other atoms read all facts.

Why can a proof tree from our reasoner never be circular?

Every premise was known before the derived fact. Following premises always goes back to earlier rounds.

Why do we skip eq-ref?

It adds "x sameAs x" for every term, which is correct but useless and large.

The facts are "ex:knows a owl:SymmetricProperty" and "ex:ana ex:knows ex:ben". Which rule derives "ex:ben ex:knows ex:ana"?

  • prp-trp
  • prp-symp
  • prp-inv1

prp-symp reverses a triple whose property is symmetric.

A naive loop and a semi-naive loop run on the same input. Which statement is true?

  • Semi-naive finds more facts.
  • Both find the same closure. Semi-naive makes fewer rule matches.
  • Semi-naive always needs fewer rounds.

Both reach the least fixed point. In our runs the number of rounds was the same too.

Why does the generated graph need only 10 rounds for a chain of 200 parts?

  • Because Rust is fast.
  • Because prp-trp joins two derived facts, so path lengths double each round.
  • Because the semi-naive loop skips rounds.

A rule with two recursive atoms is non-linear. Paths of length 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on appear in successive rounds.

Fill in the missing words.

The OWL 2 RL rule that reports x in two disjoint classes is cax-?.

The W3C OWL 2 RL tables list ? rules.

Our small ontology has 15 given facts and ? derived facts.

  1. Run the rules by hand: which rules derive "ex:fastjson ex:license ex:MIT"? Write the proof tree.
    Answer

    eq-rep-s, from "fast-json sameAs fastjson" and "fast-json license MIT". The first premise comes from eq-sym on the given "fastjson sameAs fast-json". Our program prints exactly this tree: [eq-rep-s] with the children [eq-sym] and [given].

  2. Why does prp-spo1 need an index by predicate, while cax-sco could live with an index by object?
    Answer

    In prp-spo1, the second atom [x, a, y] has the property a in the predicate position, bound from the first atom. Finding all triples with that predicate needs by_p. In cax-sco, the second atom [x, rdf:type, a] has a known object a, so by_o works, and is shorter than the list of all type triples.

  3. Write the rule cax-eqc1 from the OWL 2 Profiles document in our rule format: if c1 equivalentClass c2, and x type c1, then x type c2.
    Answer

    Python: ("cax-eqc1", [(a, "owl:equivalentClass", b), (x, TY, a)], (x, TY, b)). The partner cax-eqc2 swaps the direction: [(a, "owl:equivalentClass", b), (x, TY, b)] gives (x, TY, a).

  4. Add prp-fp: if p is functional, x p y1 and x p y2, then y1 sameAs y2. What happens with "ex:hasLicense a owl:FunctionalProperty", "ex:lib ex:hasLicense ex:MIT" and "ex:lib ex:hasLicense ex:Expat"?
    Answer

    Rule: ("prp-fp", [(a, TY, "owl:FunctionalProperty"), (x, a, y), (x, a, z)], (y, SAME, z)). It derives MIT sameAs Expat and Expat sameAs MIT, and also MIT sameAs MIT and Expat sameAs Expat. Then the eq-rep rules copy all facts between the two licenses. Under open-world OWL this is not an error. If you want "only one license" as a check, use a SHACL sh:maxCount 1 instead.

  5. Add the four schema rules scm-dom1, scm-dom2, scm-rng1 and scm-rng2. Which new facts appear for onto.txt?
    Answer

    scm-dom1: [(a, DOM, b), (b, SCO, c)] gives (a, DOM, c). scm-dom2: [(b, DOM, c), (a, SPO, b)] gives (a, DOM, c). The range rules are the same with RNG. New facts: maintains domain Person and Agent, leadMaintainerOf domain Maintainer, Person and Agent, and leadMaintainerOf range Package. These are exactly the 6 extra facts about our terms that owlrl found.

  6. Our semi-naive loop can find a match twice when two premises are new. Change it so atoms before i read only the old facts (all facts minus the delta). Is the closure the same? How much work does it save?
    Answer

    Build OLD = ALL minus DELTA at the start of each round. For position i use OLD for atoms before i, DELTA for atom i and ALL for atoms after i. Each match with new premises is then found once, at the first new premise. The closure stays the same. We measured it in Python: 59,183 firings fell to 51,040 for n = 500, about 14 percent less. Most of the remaining work is the many proofs of each transitive pair.

  7. Design a version that handles sameAs with one representative per group, instead of eq-rep-s, eq-rep-p and eq-rep-o. What must change in the facts, the rules and the explanations?
    Answer

    Keep a union-find structure over ids. When x sameAs y is derived, merge their groups and pick a representative, for example the smallest id. Rewrite every stored fact to use representatives, and remove the duplicates that this creates. Before matching, map every constant in a rule to its representative. To answer a query about any alias, map it to the representative first. Explanations must also record the merge steps, so a proof can say "x is the same as y because ...". Motik and others show that getting this right with rules that run in parallel is subtle.

Key takeaways

  • A forward-chaining reasoner is a set of facts, some indexes, rules as data and a loop to a fixed point.
  • RDFS gives six useful rules. OWL 2 RL adds inverse, symmetric, transitive and sameAs rules, with W3C names like prp-inv1 and eq-rep-s.
  • The naive loop is simple and correct. The semi-naive loop gives the same closure and only tries matches with a new premise.
  • Storing the rule and premises of the first match gives a well-founded proof for every derived fact.
  • Contradiction rules like cax-dw run after the fixed point and report problems.
  • Test naive against semi-naive, check every proof, and compare with a reference engine such as owlrl.
  • Measure on generated graphs. Transitive chains and sameAs groups show the real cost.
  • Real reasoners add the full rule set, equality rewriting, incremental updates, join planning and parallel evaluation.

Sources

  • OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Profiles (Second Edition). W3C, 2012. The OWL 2 RL rule tables and their names.
  • RDF 1.1 Semantics. W3C, 2014. The RDFS entailment rules rdfs1 to rdfs13.
  • OWL-RL documentation. The owlrl package that we used as a reference engine.
  • Datalog lecture, CS294-260, UC Berkeley (2024). Naive and semi-naive evaluation.
  • Handling owl:sameAs via Rewriting. Motik, Nenov, Piro and Horrocks, AAAI 2015. Equality by representatives in RDFox.
  • RDFox reasoning documentation. Materialisation and incremental updates in a production engine.

Build a validator and a service

In this chapter you build two real things. First, a small shape checker, in Python and in Rust. Then a small ontology service: PostgreSQL keeps the data, axum and FastAPI serve it, and every write must pass the checker. You will also change the schema without breaking old data.

  • Write a shape checker for required properties, datatypes, classes and counts.
  • Store types, nodes and edges in PostgreSQL with JSONB and pgvector.
  • Serve the graph with axum and FastAPI, and test both without a server.
  • Check every write against the schema and return a clear report.
  • Change the schema safely with numbered migrations and versions.

The plan: one checker, two jobs

Here is the end result first. A client sends a new paper to our service. The paper has four problems. The service does not save it. It answers with this list.

{"error": "invalid", "schema_version": 1, "problems": [
  {"path": "published", "rule": "Datatype", "value": "2026-02-30"},
  {"path": "titel",     "rule": "Closed",   "value": "Oops"},
  {"path": "title",     "rule": "MinCount", "value": "-"},
  {"path": "writtenBy", "rule": "Class",    "value": "node/3"},
  {"path": "year",      "rule": "Datatype", "value": "2026"}]}

The date does not exist. "titel" is a typo. The title is missing. Node 3 is a topic, not a person. The year is text, not a number. The client can fix all five at once.

A service is a program that other programs call. Each address it answers, like POST /nodes, is an endpoint. Our service keeps an ontology: a schema (the TBox) and the data (the ABox). You met these words in The building blocks.

We keep three layers of defence. Each one has a clear job.

Where each check lives, and why
LayerWhat it checksWhy here
JSON parsing (axum, FastAPI)The body is JSON with the right fieldsCheap. Stops garbage before any work.
Shape checker (our code)Counts, datatypes, classes, unknown propertiesGives the client a full list of problems in its own words.
Database constraintsTypes exist, links point to real nodes, props is an objectThe last guard. It also protects against other programs and our own bugs.

Do not trust only the database. A broken write then fails with a 500 error and a message like "violates foreign key constraint". The client cannot act on that. Check early, explain clearly, and keep the database as the last guard.

A shape checker in Python and Rust

We start with a tiny graph of papers. It is a list of triples, like in RDF and RDF Schema. A literal has a text value and a datatype.

S, I, D = "xsd:string", "xsd:integer", "xsd:date"
DATA = [
    ("ex:Student", "rdfs:subClassOf", "ex:Person"),
    ("ex:ann", "rdf:type", "ex:Person"), ("ex:ann", "ex:name", Lit("Ann Lee", S)),
    ("ex:bo", "rdf:type", "ex:Student"), ("ex:bo", "ex:name", Lit("Bo Chen", S)),
    ("ex:kg", "rdf:type", "ex:Topic"), ("ex:kg", "ex:label", Lit("Knowledge graphs", S)),
    # p1 is fine: Bo is a Student, and a Student is a Person
    ("ex:p1", "rdf:type", "ex:Paper"), ("ex:p1", "ex:title", Lit("Shapes in practice", S)),
    ("ex:p1", "ex:year", Lit("2025", I)), ("ex:p1", "ex:writtenBy", "ex:bo"),
    ("ex:p1", "ex:about", "ex:kg"),
    # p2: no title, the year is text, and a topic is not a person
    ("ex:p2", "rdf:type", "ex:Paper"), ("ex:p2", "ex:year", Lit("2026", S)),
    ("ex:p2", "ex:writtenBy", "ex:kg"),
    # p3: two titles, a date that does not exist, and a typo
    ("ex:p3", "rdf:type", "ex:Paper"), ("ex:p3", "ex:title", Lit("A", S)),
    ("ex:p3", "ex:title", Lit("B", S)), ("ex:p3", "ex:published", Lit("2026-02-30", D)),
    ("ex:p3", "ex:writtenBy", "ex:ann"), ("ex:p3", "ex:titel", Lit("C", S)),
]
SHAPES = [
    Shape("ex:Paper", [
        Prop("ex:title", min=1, max=1, datatype=S),
        Prop("ex:year", max=1, datatype=I),
        Prop("ex:published", max=1, datatype=D),
        Prop("ex:writtenBy", min=1, cls="ex:Person"),
        Prop("ex:about", cls="ex:Topic"),
    ], closed=True),
    Shape("ex:Person", [Prop("ex:name", min=1, max=1, datatype=S)]),
]

A Shape is a node shape with a target class. A Prop is a property shape. These are the same ideas as in SHACL and validation, cut down to five rules: min, max, datatype, cls and closed. Now the checker. Pick your language in the tabs.

def validate(g, shapes):
    report = []
    for shape in shapes:
        allowed = {p.path for p in shape.props} | {RDF_TYPE}
        for focus in g.instances(shape.target):
            for p in shape.props:
                values = g.objects(focus, p.path)
                if len(values) < p.min:
                    report.append(Result(focus, p.path, "MinCount"))
                if p.max is not None and len(values) > p.max:
                    report.append(Result(focus, p.path, "MaxCount"))
                for v in values:
                    if p.datatype and not (isinstance(v, Lit) and v.dtype == p.datatype
                                           and well_formed(v)):
                        report.append(Result(focus, p.path, "Datatype", show(v)))
                    if p.cls and (isinstance(v, Lit) or not g.is_a(v, p.cls)):
                        report.append(Result(focus, p.path, "Class", show(v)))
            if shape.closed:                       # no unknown properties
                for pred in sorted(g.preds[focus] - allowed):
                    for v in g.objects(focus, pred):
                        report.append(Result(focus, pred, "Closed", show(v)))
    return sorted(report)
pub fn validate(g: &Graph, shapes: &[Shape]) -> Vec<Problem> {
    let mut report = Vec::new();
    let mut add = |f: &str, p: &str, rule, v: String| report.push(Problem {
        focus: f.to_string(), path: p.to_string(), rule, value: v });
    for shape in shapes {
        for focus in g.instances(&shape.target) {
            for p in &shape.props {
                let values = g.objects(focus, &p.path);
                if values.len() < p.min { add(focus, &p.path, "MinCount", "-".into()); }
                if p.max.is_some_and(|m| values.len() > m) {
                    add(focus, &p.path, "MaxCount", "-".into());
                }
                for v in values {
                    if let Some(dt) = &p.datatype {
                        let ok = matches!(v, Term::Lit { value, dtype }
                            if dtype == dt && well_formed(value, dtype));
                        if !ok { add(focus, &p.path, "Datatype", show(v)); }
                    }
                    if let Some(c) = &p.class {
                        let ok = matches!(v, Term::Iri(n) if g.is_a(n, c));
                        if !ok { add(focus, &p.path, "Class", show(v)); }
                    }
                }
            }
            if shape.closed {                     // no unknown properties
                for pred in &g.preds[focus] {
                    if pred == RDF_TYPE || shape.props.iter().any(|p| &p.path == pred) { continue; }
                    for v in g.objects(focus, pred) { add(focus, pred, "Closed", show(v)); }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    report.sort();
    report
}

Both programs print the same report. We ran python3.14 run_shapes.py and rustc --edition 2024 main.rs with Rust 1.99.

ex:p2  ex:title      MinCount  -
ex:p2  ex:writtenBy  Class     ex:kg
ex:p2  ex:year       Datatype  2026
ex:p3  ex:published  Datatype  2026-02-30
ex:p3  ex:titel      Closed    C
ex:p3  ex:title      MaxCount  -

Is our checker right? We wrote the same data and shapes in Turtle and ran pySHACL 0.40.2 (with rdflib 7.6.0). It found the same six problems, with the same focus nodes, paths and components. So our small checker agrees with a real SHACL engine on this test.

conforms: False
p2 title MinCount
p2 writtenBy Class
p2 year Datatype
p3 published Datatype
p3 titel Closed
p3 title MaxCount

Do not report only the first problem. A client that gets one error at a time needs five round trips for p2 and p3. Collect every problem, sort them, and send the whole list.

Datatypes, classes and the closed world

Three small functions do the hard part. Each one hides a trap.

Is the literal well formed?

The text "2026-02-30" looks like a date. But February 2026 has 28 days. In XML Schema, the text of a literal is its lexical form. A value is well formed when that text is legal for the datatype. SHACL's sh:datatype fails ill-formed literals too, so our checker does the same.

if lit.dtype == "xsd:date":
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}", lit.value):
        return False
    try:
        date.fromisoformat(lit.value)   # rejects 2026-02-30
        return True
    except ValueError:
        return False
"xsd:date" => {
    let p: Vec<&str> = value.split('-').collect();
    if p.len() != 3 || p[0].len() != 4 || p[1].len() != 2 || p[2].len() != 2
        || !p.iter().all(|x| digits(x)) { return false; }
    let (y, m, d): (u32, u32, u32) =
        (p[0].parse().unwrap(), p[1].parse().unwrap(), p[2].parse().unwrap());
    let days = [31, if leap(y) { 29 } else { 28 }, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31];
    (1..=12).contains(&m) && d >= 1 && d <= days[(m - 1) as usize]
}

#[test]
fn dates() {
    assert!(well_formed("2024-02-29", "xsd:date"));   // a leap year
    assert!(!well_formed("2026-02-30", "xsd:date"));  // no such day
    assert!(!well_formed("2026-2-3", "xsd:date"));    // needs two digits
}
running 2 tests
test tests::integers ... ok
test tests::dates ... ok

Why the regular expression in Python? Since Python 3.11, date.fromisoformat also accepts the short form 20260215. That is legal ISO 8601, but it is not a legal xsd:date. The pattern keeps only the long form.

Is the node an instance of the class?

is_a walks up the rdfs:subClassOf links from each type of the node. Bo is a Student. Student is a subclass of Person. So Bo passes cls="ex:Person". A seen set stops the walk if the class tree has a cycle.

def is_a(self, node, cls):
    """True if node has type cls, also through rdfs:subClassOf."""
    todo, seen = list(self.objects(node, RDF_TYPE)), set()
    while todo:
        c = todo.pop()
        if c == cls:
            return True
        if c not in seen:
            seen.add(c)
            todo.extend(self.objects(c, SUBCLASS))
    return False

Are there unknown properties?

A closed shape reports every property it does not list. This catches typos like titel. We always allow rdf:type, like sh:ignoredProperties ( rdf:type ) in SHACL.

Closed shapes and subclasses do not mix well. A Student is checked by the closed Person shape. If Student had its own extra property, like studentId, the Person shape would report it as unknown. Fix: list the subclass properties in the parent shape, or close only the leaf classes.

Our checker is closed world, like SHACL. A missing title is an error. An OWL reasoner would say "the title is unknown". You saw why in Logic for ontology.

The store: an ontology in PostgreSQL

Now the data needs a home. We use PostgreSQL 18.3 with pgvector 0.8.7. Here is the first migration. It creates the schema tables and the data tables.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE schema_version (version int PRIMARY KEY, note text NOT NULL,
                             applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());

-- TBox: the types and one row per property shape
CREATE TABLE node_type (name text PRIMARY KEY, parent text REFERENCES node_type (name));

CREATE TABLE prop_shape (
    type_name  text NOT NULL REFERENCES node_type (name),
    path       text NOT NULL,
    datatype   text CHECK (datatype IN ('string', 'integer', 'date', 'boolean')),
    class_name text REFERENCES node_type (name),
    min_count  int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (min_count >= 0),
    max_count  int  CHECK (max_count >= min_count),
    PRIMARY KEY (type_name, path),
    CHECK ((datatype IS NULL) <> (class_name IS NULL))  -- a literal or a link, never both
);

-- ABox: the instances
CREATE TABLE node (
    id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    type_name  text  NOT NULL REFERENCES node_type (name),
    props      jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}' CHECK (jsonb_typeof(props) = 'object'),
    embedding  vector(3),                                  -- 3 for the demo, 384+ in real life
    schema_ver int   NOT NULL REFERENCES schema_version (version)
);

CREATE TABLE edge (
    src  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES node (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    path text   NOT NULL,
    dst  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES node (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    PRIMARY KEY (src, path, dst)
);

CREATE INDEX edge_by_dst ON edge (dst, path);                     -- walk links backwards
CREATE INDEX node_props ON node USING gin (props jsonb_path_ops); -- fast @> filters
CREATE INDEX node_vec ON node USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

Every line is a decision. Open each one to see the reason.

Why tables for nodes and edges, and not one table per class?

A table per class (a paper table, a person table) is fast and strict. But each new type needs new SQL. An ontology changes often. With node and edge, a new type is one row in node_type. The price: the database cannot check the property rules by itself. Our checker does that.

Why not one triple table (subject, predicate, object)?

A triple table is the most flexible. But every property read becomes a join, and a literal and a link share one column. We keep literals in JSONB and links in edge. Links get real foreign keys. Literals stay together in one row.

Why JSONB for properties?

JSONB stores JSON in a binary form. It is faster to search than json and it can be indexed. It keeps only the last value of a duplicate key and does not keep key order. That is fine for us. The CHECK makes sure props is always an object.

Why a GIN index with jsonb_path_ops?

A GIN index makes props @> '{"year": 2026}' fast. The class jsonb_path_ops is usually much smaller than the default. It supports @> and the jsonpath operators, but not the key test ?.

Why CASCADE on src but RESTRICT on dst?

When you delete a node, its outgoing links mean nothing, so they go too. But links that point to it belong to other nodes. Deleting Ann would leave a paper with no author, and break its min 1 rule. RESTRICT refuses that delete.

Why a vector column and an HNSW index?

An embedding lets you find papers by meaning. pgvector stores it next to the node, so one query can mix graph filters and similarity. HNSW is an approximate index. For the vector type it supports up to 2,000 dimensions. Details are in the Coding book.

Why schema_ver on every node?

It records which version of the rules the node passed. After a schema change you can find the nodes that were never checked against the new rules.

We loaded four types, eight property shapes, six nodes and five edges. No server was allowed here. So we ran the SQL in PostgreSQL's single-user mode, postgres --single -D data -j postgres < file.sql, on a throwaway data folder. Here are four queries and their real output.

-- 1. every Person, also through subClassOf
WITH RECURSIVE sub(name) AS (
    SELECT 'Person'::text
  UNION
    SELECT t.name FROM node_type t JOIN sub ON t.parent = sub.name)
SELECT n.id, n.type_name, n.props->>'name' AS name
FROM node n JOIN sub ON n.type_name = sub.name ORDER BY n.id;

-- 2. JSONB containment: papers from 2026
SELECT id, props->>'title' AS title FROM node WHERE props @> '{"year": 2026}';

-- 3. similar papers, with the author from the graph
SELECT p.id, p.props->>'title' AS title, a.props->>'name' AS author,
       round((p.embedding <=> '[1,0.2,0]')::numeric, 3) AS dist
FROM node p
JOIN edge e ON e.src = p.id AND e.path = 'writtenBy'
JOIN node a ON a.id = e.dst
WHERE p.type_name = 'Paper'
ORDER BY p.embedding <=> '[1,0.2,0]' LIMIT 2;

-- 4. the database refuses junk
INSERT INTO node (type_name, props, schema_ver) VALUES ('Robot', '{}', 1);

INSERT INTO node (type_name, props, schema_ver) VALUES ('Topic', '["not", "an", "object"]', 1);

DELETE FROM node WHERE id = 1;
id = 1  type_name = Person  name = Ann Lee
id = 2  type_name = Student  name = Bo Chen
id = 5  title = Vectors meet graphs
id = 4  title = Shapes in practice  author = Bo Chen  dist = 0.004
id = 5  title = Vectors meet graphs  author = Ann Lee  dist = 0.255
ERROR:  insert or update on table "node" violates foreign key constraint "node_type_name_fkey"
ERROR:  new row for relation "node" violates check constraint "node_props_check"
ERROR:  update or delete on table "node" violates RESTRICT setting of foreign key constraint "edge_dst_fkey" on table "edge"

Query 1 is the SQL twin of is_a: a recursive query. Query 3 mixes three things in one statement: a vector search, a graph join and JSON fields. The operator <=> is cosine distance.

Do not add a WHERE filter to an HNSW search and expect k rows. The filter runs after the index scan. With a rare filter you may get fewer rows. pgvector 0.8 has iterative index scans for this: SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order.

The service in axum

The service turns a JSON write into triples, and calls the same validate from the last section. No second rule engine. This is the most important design choice of the chapter.

Parse

axum's Json extractor turns the body into a NewNode. Bad JSON never reaches our code.

Look up links

One query fetches the stored type of every node the write links to.

Build triples

The node becomes new. Each prop becomes a literal. Each link becomes a triple, plus the type of its target.

Check

Run validate. Keep only problems about new.

Refuse or save

Problems: answer 422 with the list. No problems: insert the node and its edges in one transaction.

Answer

Answer 201 with the new id and the schema version.

Here are steps 3 and 4, in Rust and in Python. The Python version is the FastAPI service from the next section.

/// `link_types` holds the stored type of every node the write links to.
pub fn check(schema: &Schema, n: &NewNode, link_types: &BTreeMap<i64, String>) -> Vec<Problem> {
    let me = "new".to_string();
    if !schema.types.contains(&n.type_name) {
        // No shape targets an unknown type, so the checker would pass it in silence.
        return vec![Problem { focus: me, path: "type".into(), rule: "UnknownType",
                              value: n.type_name.clone() }];
    }
    let mut g = vec![(me.clone(), RDF_TYPE.to_string(), Term::Iri(n.type_name.clone()))];
    for (child, parent) in &schema.parents {
        g.push((child.clone(), SUBCLASS.into(), Term::Iri(parent.clone())));
    }
    for (path, value) in &n.props {
        let values = match value { Value::Array(a) => a.clone(), v => vec![v.clone()] };
        for v in &values { g.push((me.clone(), path.clone(), literal(schema, path, v))); }
    }
    for (path, ids) in &n.links {
        for id in ids {
            let node = format!("node/{id}");
            g.push((me.clone(), path.clone(), Term::Iri(node.clone())));
            if let Some(t) = link_types.get(id) {
                g.push((node, RDF_TYPE.into(), Term::Iri(t.clone())));
            }
        }
    }
    // Linked nodes appear with their type only, so keep problems about `new`.
    let mut problems: Vec<Problem> = shapes::validate(&Graph::new(g), &schema.shapes)
        .into_iter().filter(|p| p.focus == me).collect();
    if let Some(e) = &n.embedding && e.len() != schema.dim {
        problems.push(Problem { focus: me, path: "embedding".into(), rule: "Dimension",
                                value: e.len().to_string() });
    }
    problems
}
def check(schema, node, link_types):
    """Turn one write into triples, then run the same shape checker."""
    if node.type not in schema.types:
        return [Result("new", "type", "UnknownType", node.type)]
    g = [("new", RDF_TYPE, node.type)] + [(c, SUBCLASS, p) for c, p in schema.parents]
    for path, value in node.props.items():
        for v in value if isinstance(value, list) else [value]:
            g.append(("new", path, literal(schema, path, v)))
    for path, ids in node.links.items():
        for i in ids:
            g.append(("new", path, f"node/{i}"))
            if i in link_types:
                g.append((f"node/{i}", RDF_TYPE, link_types[i]))
    problems = [r for r in validate(Graph(g), schema.shapes) if r.focus == "new"]
    if node.embedding is not None and len(node.embedding) != schema.dim:
        problems.append(Result("new", "embedding", "Dimension", str(len(node.embedding))))
    return problems

Three details matter here.

  • Unknown type. No shape targets "Robot". So validate would find no focus node and pass it. We test the type first. The SHACL chapter warned about this: no target, no check.
  • Unknown link. A link to node 99 gets no type triple. The class check then fails. So a missing node is reported as a Class problem, before the database says anything.
  • JSON has no dates. The function literal reads the shape. If the shape wants xsd:date and the JSON value is a string, the literal gets the date datatype. Then well_formed checks it.

Now the web part. We follow the usual axum patterns: shared state in an Arc, typed extractors, and one error type that turns into a response. The store is a trait, so tests can use memory and production can use PostgreSQL.

/// Where nodes live. The tests use memory. Production uses PostgreSQL.
pub trait Store: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn types_of(&self, ids: Vec<i64>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<BTreeMap<i64, String>, AppError>> + Send;
    fn insert(&self, n: NewNode, schema_ver: i32) -> impl Future<Output = Result<i64, AppError>> + Send;
    fn get(&self, id: i64) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Option<Value>, AppError>> + Send;
    fn search(&self, v: Vec<f32>, k: i64) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<Value>, AppError>> + Send;
}

pub fn app<S: Store>(state: Arc<AppState<S>>) -> Router {
    Router::new()
        .route("/health", get(|| async { "ok" }))
        .route("/schema/version", get(version::<S>))
        .route("/nodes", post(create::<S>))
        .route("/nodes/{id}", get(read::<S>))
        .route("/search", post(search::<S>))
        .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(64 * 1024)) // a node is small: refuse big bodies
        .with_state(state)
}

async fn create<S: Store>(
    State(st): State<Arc<AppState<S>>>,
    Json(body): Json<NewNode>,
) -> Result<(StatusCode, Json<Value>), AppError> {
    let ids: Vec<i64> = body.links.values().flatten().copied().collect();
    let link_types = st.store.types_of(ids).await?;     // one query for all links
    let problems = check(&st.schema, &body, &link_types);
    if !problems.is_empty() {
        return Err(AppError::Invalid(st.schema.version, problems));
    }
    let id = st.store.insert(body, st.schema.version).await?;
    Ok((StatusCode::CREATED, Json(json!({ "id": id, "schema_version": st.schema.version }))))
}

Why impl Future + Send in the trait, and not async fn? axum needs handler futures that are Send, so they can move between threads. A plain async fn in a trait does not promise that. The longer form does. The implementations can still use async fn. Note also the path syntax /nodes/{id}. axum 0.8 uses braces. Older versions used /:id.

Test it in memory with oneshot

We test the whole router without a socket. tower::ServiceExt gives the router a oneshot method. It sends one request straight into the service and returns the response. This is an in-process test.

/// Send one request in memory, without a socket. Return status and body.
async fn call(app: &Router, method: &str, uri: &str, body: &str, json_type: bool) -> (StatusCode, Value) {
    let mut req = Request::builder().method(method).uri(uri);
    if json_type {
        req = req.header("content-type", "application/json");
    }
    let res = app.clone().oneshot(req.body(Body::from(body.to_string())).unwrap()).await.unwrap();
    let status = res.status();
    let bytes = to_bytes(res.into_body(), usize::MAX).await.unwrap();
    let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(&bytes).to_string();
    (status, serde_json::from_str(&text).unwrap_or(Value::String(text)))
}

The test seeds Ann, Bo and the topic as nodes 1 to 3. Then it sends twelve requests and checks each status. Here is the real output of cargo test -- --nocapture with axum 0.8.9 (long lines shortened with "...").

POST /nodes -> 422 {"error":"invalid","problems":[{"path":"published","rule":"Datatype",...}
POST /nodes -> 422 {"error":"invalid","problems":[{"path":"type","rule":"UnknownType","value":"Robot"}],...}
GET /nodes/4 -> 200 {"id":4,"links":{"about":[3],"writtenBy":[2]},"props":{"published":"2025-06-01",...}
GET /nodes/99 -> 404 {"error":"not_found"}
GET /nodes/abc -> 400 "Invalid URL: Cannot parse `abc` to a `i64`"
POST /search -> 200 [{"distance":0.004,"id":4},{"distance":0.255,"id":5}]
POST /search -> 400 {"error":"wrong vector size"}

The search distances, 0.004 and 0.255, are the same as in PostgreSQL above. The memory store computes cosine distance itself. That is a good sign that the two stores agree.

The router, the checker and all tests above ran. The PostgreSQL store (src/pg.rs, with sqlx 0.9.0 and the pgvector crate 0.4.2) and main.rs passed cargo check and cargo clippy. They were not run against a live database, because no server was allowed here. Its SQL is the SQL that ran in single-user mode.

async fn insert(&self, n: NewNode, schema_ver: i32) -> Result<i64, AppError> {
    let mut tx = self.pool.begin().await.map_err(internal)?; // node and edges: all or nothing
    let id: i64 = sqlx::query_scalar(
        "INSERT INTO node (type_name, props, embedding, schema_ver) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4) RETURNING id")
        .bind(&n.type_name)
        .bind(json!(n.props))
        .bind(n.embedding.map(Vector::from))
        .bind(schema_ver)
        .fetch_one(&mut *tx).await.map_err(internal)?;
    for (path, dsts) in &n.links {
        for dst in dsts {
            sqlx::query("INSERT INTO edge (src, path, dst) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)")
                .bind(id).bind(path).bind(dst)
                .execute(&mut *tx).await.map_err(internal)?;
        }
    }
    tx.commit().await.map_err(internal)?;
    Ok(id)
}

A transaction keeps the node and its edges together. If one edge fails, the node is not saved either. Every value goes in through $1, $2 and so on. These are bind parameters. They make SQL injection impossible here.

The same service in FastAPI

The Python service has the same endpoints, the same checker and the same answers. FastAPI 0.163.0 with Pydantic 2.14.3 parses the body into a model.

class NewNode(BaseModel):
    type: str
    props: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    links: dict[str, list[int]] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    embedding: list[float] | None = None


def create_app(schema, store):
    app = FastAPI(title="onto-svc")

    @app.get("/health")
    def health():
        return "ok"

    @app.post("/nodes", status_code=201)
    def create(node: NewNode):         # plain def: FastAPI runs it in a thread pool
        ids = [i for group in node.links.values() for i in group]
        problems = check(schema, node, store.types_of(ids))
        if problems:
            body = {"error": "invalid", "schema_version": schema.version,
                    "problems": [{"path": p.path, "rule": p.rule, "value": p.value} for p in problems]}
            return JSONResponse(body, status_code=422)
        return {"id": store.insert(node, schema.version), "schema_version": schema.version}

    @app.get("/nodes/{id}")
    def read(id: int):
        doc = store.get(id)
        return doc if doc else JSONResponse({"error": "not_found"}, status_code=404)

    @app.post("/search")
    def search(q: SearchReq):
        if len(q.vector) != schema.dim:
            return JSONResponse({"error": "wrong vector size"}, status_code=400)
        return store.search(q.vector, q.k)

    return app

Why def and not async def? Our stores are synchronous. A slow synchronous call inside async def blocks the whole event loop. FastAPI runs a plain def endpoint in a thread pool instead. This is the Python twin of the axum rule "never block the runtime".

Test it with TestClient

TestClient calls the app in the same process. No server starts and no port opens. The test sends thirteen requests. Five of the output lines are below.

def client():

                    ("Topic", "label", "Knowledge graphs")]:
        store.insert(NewNode(type=t, props={k: v}), 1)
    return TestClient(create_app(SCHEMA, store))   # no server, no socket

In Python, True is also an int. If literal tests isinstance(v, int) first, "year": true becomes the integer 1 and passes. Test bool before int. The line with "value":"true" above shows the fixed code at work.

With Starlette 1.10.0, the TestClient printed a warning: using httpx is deprecated, install httpx2. With httpx2 2.16.0 the warning went away. The FastAPI testing page still says "install httpx". Check both pages: this can change.
