Changing the schema safely

Schemas change. A rule that is fine today may break old data tomorrow. Here is the plan: make year required on every Paper.

Step 1: a dry run with the checker

Before you change anything, run the old and the new shapes over the stored data. The difference is the list of nodes the change would break. Here we use the triple test data from the start of the chapter. There, p3 has no year.

def dry_run(graph, old, new):
    """Problems that the new shapes add. Run this before you migrate."""
    return sorted(set(validate(graph, new)) - set(validate(graph, old)))


new = copy.deepcopy(SHAPES)
year = next(p for p in new[0].props if p.path == "ex:year")
year.min = 1                                   # the plan: year becomes required
for r in dry_run(Graph(DATA), SHAPES, new):
    print("would break:", r.focus, r.path, r.rule)
would break: ex:p3 ex:year MinCount

Step 2: a migration with a guard

Now the PostgreSQL side. There, node 6, "Cooking with rice", has no year. The migration file checks the data itself. If any Paper has no year, it stops with an error. The whole file runs in one transaction, so nothing changes.

LOCK TABLE node IN SHARE MODE;      -- no writes to node until we commit

DO $$
DECLARE bad int;
BEGIN
  SELECT count(*) INTO bad FROM node WHERE type_name = 'Paper' AND NOT props ? 'year';
  IF bad > 0 THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'stop: % Paper node(s) have no year', bad;
  END IF;
END $$;

UPDATE prop_shape SET min_count = 1 WHERE type_name = 'Paper' AND path = 'year';
INSERT INTO schema_version (version, note) VALUES (3, 'year is required on Paper');
UPDATE node SET schema_ver = 3;     -- the guard proved that all nodes pass version 3

We ran migration 2 (an optional doi), then migration 3. Then a backfill gave node 6 its year: UPDATE node SET props = props || '{"year": 2024}' WHERE id = 6. Then we ran migration 3 again. Our script wraps each file in BEGIN and COMMIT. Steps with no output printed nothing. Here is the real output.

== 0002 optional doi
== 0003 first try
ERROR:  stop: 1 Paper node(s) have no year
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
== versions
version = 1  note = papers, people, topics
version = 2  note = optional doi on Paper
schema_ver = 1  nodes = 6
== backfill node 6
== 0003 again
== versions
version = 1  note = papers, people, topics
version = 2  note = optional doi on Paper
version = 3  note = year is required on Paper
schema_ver = 3  nodes = 6

Each file has a number, and each runs once, in order. A tool records which files already ran. In Rust, sqlx::migrate!("./migrations") embeds the files in the program and records them in a table called _sqlx_migrations. sqlx runs each file in a transaction by default, so our files have no BEGIN. A file that starts with -- no-transaction runs without one. In Python, Alembic is the usual tool.

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?; // never write a password in code
    let pool = PgPoolOptions::new().max_connections(5).connect(&url).await?;
    sqlx::migrate!("./migrations").run(&pool).await?; // apply new files, in order, once
    let schema = load_schema(&pool).await?;
    let state = Arc::new(AppState { schema, store: PgStore { pool } });
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:3000").await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app(state)).await?;
    Ok(())
}

Safe and unsafe changes

Schema changes, from safe to dangerous
ChangeOld dataOld clientsHow
Add a typeSafeSafeOne migration
Add an optional propertySafeSafeOne migration (our 0002)
Raise a min count, lower a max countMay breakMay breakDry run, backfill, guarded migration
Narrow a datatype or a classMay breakMay breakSame as above
Rename a propertyBreaksBreaksExpand and contract
Remove a type or propertyBreaksBreaksContract only after no one uses it

A rename needs expand and contract, also called parallel change. Here is a rename from title to headline.

  1. Expand. Add headline as an optional property (a new schema version). Old clients still send title.
  2. Write both. The service writes both names for every new or changed Paper.
  3. Backfill. UPDATE node SET props = props || jsonb_build_object('headline', props->'title') WHERE type_name = 'Paper' AND NOT props ? 'headline'; We ran this. All three papers then had both names.
  4. Move readers. Clients read headline. Watch the logs until nobody reads title.
  5. Contract. Make headline required, and remove title in a last migration.

Never edit a migration file that already ran somewhere. sqlx stores a checksum of each file. On the next start it stops with "migration 3 was previously applied but has been modified". Tools without checksums are worse: your databases quietly drift apart. Write a new file instead.

Production concerns: the expert part

Races between checking and writing

We check, then we write. Between the two, another request can change the data. This gap is a race condition. Our design closes the gap in three ways.

  • The type of a node never changes. The service has no endpoint that changes type_name. So a class check that passed stays true.
  • Links point only to existing nodes. The foreign key on edge.dst fails if the target vanished in the gap.
  • A target cannot be deleted while it is linked. ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses it.

An update endpoint would need more. Lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, check, and write in the same transaction.

Old rules in a running service

Our service loads the schema once, at start. After migration 3, an old copy of the service still allows papers without a year. One fix is a guarded insert. The service sends the version it checked against. The insert happens only if that version is still the newest one.

INSERT INTO node (type_name, props, schema_ver)
SELECT 'Topic', '{"label": "Vectors"}', 2
WHERE 2 = (SELECT max(version) FROM schema_version) RETURNING id;   -- stale: no row

INSERT INTO node (type_name, props, schema_ver)
SELECT 'Topic', '{"label": "Vectors"}', 3
WHERE 3 = (SELECT max(version) FROM schema_version) RETURNING id;   -- current
id = 9

The first insert returned no row. The service would then answer 409 Conflict and reload the schema. Why is the new id 9, not 7? The two failed inserts in the demo used ids 7 and 8. Identity values are never reused, so gaps are normal. We ran these statements one at a time. We did not test two parallel sessions, because single-user mode has only one.

Speed

Is the checker fast enough to run on every write? We timed both versions on a generated graph of 20,000 papers, about 100,000 triples, on an Apple M2 Pro. Each number is the middle of three runs.

A few microseconds per node is much less than one database round trip. So checking every write costs almost nothing. Our Rust version is not much faster than Python. Both hash string keys for every lookup. The usual fix is to intern strings to integer ids, as in The Rust toolkit.

More things a real service needs

  • Limits. We refuse bodies over 64 KB in axum. Our FastAPI code sets no body limit. Put one in your proxy too, for example nginx client_max_body_size.
  • Timeouts and shutdown. Add a timeout layer and graceful shutdown, so a slow query cannot hold the service forever.
  • Who may write. Add authentication before any public use. Our demo has none.
  • Errors. Log the full database error. Send the client only "internal". Our AppError::Internal does exactly this.

A common design question: "Why not use a triple store and a full SHACL engine?" A good answer: choose them when you need SPARQL, OWL reasoning, or the full SHACL language. Choose this small design when the data already lives in PostgreSQL, the rules are simple, and you need fast writes with clear errors. You can also use both: PostgreSQL for writes, and a nightly export to RDF for SHACL and SPARQL.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for a validator and an ontology service
PatternPurposeModelNote
Collect all problems, then sortOne clear report per writereturn sorted(report)Never stop at the first problem.
datatype = right type + well formedCatch impossible values2026-02-30 fails xsd:dateCheck the text, not only the label.
Walk subClassOf with a seen setClass checks through subclassesBo is a Student, so a PersonThe seen set stops cycles.
Closed shape + allow rdf:typeCatch typos in property namestitel is reportedWatch out for subclass properties.
Test the type firstUnknown types must failUnknownType: RobotNo target means no check.
JSON write to triples, same checkerOne rule engine for batch and APIcheck(schema, node, link_types)Keep only problems about the new node.
node + edge + JSONBA flexible graph in PostgreSQLprops jsonb CHECK (jsonb_typeof(props) = 'object')The database cannot check shapes. Your code must.
RESTRICT on edge.dstDo not break other nodes' rulesDeleting Ann is refusedCASCADE only on the source side.
Store as a trait or classTest without a databaseMemStore and PgStoreBoth must give the same answers.
In-process testsFast, real HTTP testsoneshot, TestClientNo port, no server, no sleep.
Dry run before migrateSee what a change breaksvalidate(new) - validate(old)Run it on a copy of real data.
Guarded migrationStop a change that breaks dataRAISE EXCEPTION in a DO blockOne transaction: all or nothing.
Expand and contractRename without downtimetitle to headlineNever rename in one step.
Version guard on insertOld services cannot use old rulesWHERE 3 = (SELECT max(version) ...)Answer 409 and reload the schema.

Practice

A shape has min=1, max=1 on title. Paper p3 has two titles. Which rule fails?

  • MinCount
  • MaxCount
  • Datatype

Two values are more than the maximum of one.

A client sends {"type": "Robot"}. No shape targets Robot. What does a plain validate call return?

  • A MinCount problem
  • No problems at all
  • A Class problem

No target means no focus node, so nothing is checked. That is why the service tests the type first.

Why is edge.dst declared with ON DELETE RESTRICT?

  • To make deletes faster
  • A delete must not break the rules of nodes that link to it
  • PostgreSQL needs it for indexes

Deleting Ann would leave her paper without a required author.

An axum client sends broken JSON. Which status code did our test get?

  • 400
  • 415
  • 422

axum 0.8.9 answers 400 for a syntax error, 415 for a missing content type, and 422 for JSON with the wrong structure. FastAPI answered 422 in all three cases.

Fill in the blanks.

In axum 0.8, a path parameter is written as /nodes/?.

The GIN operator class that is smaller but has no key test ? is ?.

  1. Add a min_length rule to Prop in the Python checker. Report "MinLength" when a string is too short.
    Answer

    Add min_length: int | None = None to Prop. In the value loop add: if p.min_length and isinstance(v, Lit) and len(v.value) < p.min_length: report.append(Result(focus, p.path, "MinLength", v.value)). Add one test with a too short title.

  2. Why does the service keep only problems whose focus is new?
    Answer

    The mini graph also holds the linked nodes, but only with their type. The Person shape would check Bo and report a missing name, because Bo's name is not in the mini graph. Those reports are false. Bo's own data was checked when Bo was written.

  3. A teammate wants to store every property as a column in a paper table. Give one gain and one cost.
    Answer

    Gain: the database checks types and NOT NULL by itself, and queries are simple and fast. Cost: every new type or property needs a new migration with DDL. For a schema that changes often, the node and edge design is easier.

  4. Write the SQL for a batch check: list every Paper whose year is not a JSON number.
    Answer

    SELECT id FROM node WHERE type_name = 'Paper' AND props ? 'year' AND jsonb_typeof(props->'year') <> 'number'; Note that JSON numbers include 2025.5. A full check also needs (props->>'year') ~ '^-?[0-9]+$'.

  5. You must lower max_count of writtenBy from none to 3. Plan the change.
    Answer

    1. Dry run: list papers with more than 3 authors. 2. Decide with the data owners what to do with them. 3. Fix the data. 4. Run a guarded migration: count papers with more than 3 writtenBy edges and raise an error if any exist, then update prop_shape and add a schema version. 5. Restart or reload all service copies.

  6. Hard. Two requests arrive at the same time. One creates a paper linked to Ann. The other deletes Ann. Walk through what happens in our design.
    Answer

    Case 1: the delete commits first. The paper's check may have seen Ann, but the edge insert then fails on the foreign key, and the whole transaction rolls back. The client gets an error and can retry. Case 2: the paper commits first. The delete then fails because of ON DELETE RESTRICT. In both cases no paper is left without its author. To give the client a 422 instead of a 500, map the foreign key error to a Class problem.

Key takeaways

  • A shape checker needs only a few rules: min, max, datatype, class and closed. Collect every problem.
  • Datatype checks must test the text: 2026-02-30 is not a date.
  • Turn each JSON write into triples and reuse the same checker. One rule engine serves the API and the batch job.
  • Unknown types pass a target-based checker in silence. Test the type first.
  • In PostgreSQL, nodes and edges with JSONB give a flexible graph. Foreign keys and CHECK constraints are the last guard.
  • Test axum with oneshot and FastAPI with TestClient. No server is needed.
  • Change the schema with numbered migrations: dry run, backfill, guarded migration, new version.
  • Rename with expand and contract. Never edit a migration that already ran.

Sources

  • axum documentation. Version 0.8.9: routing with braces, State, Json, and testing.
  • FastAPI: Testing. How TestClient calls the app in the same process.
  • PostgreSQL: JSON types. json and jsonb, containment, and the two GIN operator classes.
  • pgvector on GitHub. Version 0.8.7, HNSW indexes, distance operators and filtering.
  • sqlx: the migrate! macro. Embedded migrations and the _sqlx_migrations table.
  • Parallel Change. The expand, migrate and contract pattern, by Danilo Sato (2014).

Practitioner exam

This chapter is a full practice exam for the whole book. It has 80 questions from easy to hard, five modelling tasks with model answers in Turtle, a reading list, a 30-day study plan and a glossary of 80 terms. Every answer links back to the chapter that teaches it.

  • Name the real certificates in this field and what they cover.
  • Test yourself on every chapter of the book with 80 questions.
  • Solve five modelling tasks and compare your Turtle with tested model answers.
  • Plan 30 days of study and find the right books for the next step.
  • Explain 80 key terms in simple words.

Is there an official certificate?

Many people ask: "Can I get certified in ontology engineering?" We searched in November 2026. We found no official, vendor-neutral certificate for ontology engineering as a whole. No standards body or university group runs one shared exam for the field. Check again before you plan: this can change.

There are vendor certificates. Each one tests one product, plus the ideas around it.

Real certificates near this field (checked on 15 November 2026)
CertificateOwnerFormatWhat it shows
Neo4j Certified ProfessionalNeo4j GraphAcademy80 questions, 60 minutes, pass at 80%, freeProperty graphs and Cypher
Neo4j Graph Data Science CertificationNeo4j GraphAcademy50 questions, 60 minutes, pass at 80%Graph algorithms and graph machine learning
Neo4j & Generative AI CertificationNeo4j GraphAcademy50 questions, 60 minutes, pass at 80%, freeGraphs with LLMs, for example GraphRAG
Foundry Associate exams: Data Engineer, Application Developer, AI EngineerPalantirTimed, open-book, multiple choice, valid for two years. Refreshed on 3 August 2026.Building on Palantir's platform, including its ontology
Learning paths "Knowledge Graph Engineer" and "GraphDB Developer"Graphwise AcademyOnline coursesRDF, SPARQL and GraphDB. We could not confirm a formal certificate at the end.

Palantir also announced hands-on Specialist exams in a live environment. A forum reply dated 22 September 2026 moved their start to 30 September 2026. We did not find an official exam page for them, so treat this as unconfirmed.

No paper says "certified ontology engineer". So show your skill with work: a public ontology, tested queries and shapes, and a small service. This book's last five chapters give you exactly that.

How to use this exam

  • Time. Give yourself 120 minutes for the 80 questions. Then give each modelling task 30 minutes.
  • Rules. Closed book for the questions. Open book and real tools for the modelling tasks.
  • Score. One point per question. For written answers, give the point only if the main idea is in your answer.
  • Pass mark. The pass mark is 64 of 80, which is 80%. The Neo4j exams use the same line.
  • After. For each wrong answer, open the linked chapter. Read the section again, then retry the question in two days.

The questions follow the book. Easy questions come first. Each part ends with written questions, which are harder. Here is how the 80 questions spread over the parts of the book.

Many wrong answers in this field come from one mistake: forgetting which world you are in. Before you answer, ask: "Open world (OWL, RDF) or closed world (SHACL, SQL, Datalog)?"

Practice exam, part 1: basics (questions 1 to 20)

Q1. In computing, what is an ontology?

  • A database of all facts in the world
  • A shared, written list of kinds of things and how they relate
  • A program that answers questions in English

An ontology names the kinds of things in a domain and their relations, so people and programs share one meaning. Chapter: What is an ontology?

Q2. Order by structure: word list, taxonomy, ..., schema, ontology. What comes right after taxonomy?

  • Thesaurus
  • Knowledge graph
  • Ontology

The line goes word list, taxonomy, thesaurus, schema, ontology, knowledge graph. A thesaurus adds "broader", "narrower" and "related" links. Chapter: What is an ontology?

Q3. Gruber (1993) called an ontology an "explicit specification of a conceptualization". What does "explicit" mean here?

  • Secret, for experts only
  • Written down clearly, not only in people's heads
  • Made by a machine

The view of the domain is written down, so others can read and check it. Chapter: What is an ontology?

Q4. The data says :rex rdf:type :Dog and :Dog rdfs:subClassOf :Mammal. What follows?

  • Rex is a subclass of Mammal.
  • Rex is an instance of Mammal.
  • Mammal is an instance of Dog.

Instance-of plus subclass-of gives a new instance-of. "Is a kind of" is transitive. "Instance of" is not. Chapter: The building blocks

Q5. The range of :teaches is :Course. The data says :ann :teaches :bob, and Bob is a Person. What does an RDFS reasoner do?

  • It rejects the triple.
  • It concludes that Bob is also a Course.
  • It deletes Bob.

Domain and range add facts. They never reject data. To catch this error you need a check, like SHACL. Chapter: The building blocks

Q6. Which pair is TBox, then ABox?

  • "Every Student is a Person." and "Ann is a Student."
  • "Ann is a Student." and "Every Student is a Person."
  • "Ann knows Bo." and "Bo knows Cy."

The TBox holds the schema and its rules. The ABox holds facts about individuals. Chapter: The building blocks

Q7. You start a new ontology. What do you write first?

  • The OWL file
  • Competency questions
  • The SHACL shapes

Three to ten questions the ontology must answer set the scope and give you the first terms. Chapter: Your first ontology, step by step

Q8. You must say "Ann worked at Acme as CTO from 2019 to 2023". Which pattern fits?

  • Two data properties on Ann
  • An n-ary relation: a node for the job, with person, company, role, start and end
  • owl:sameAs between Ann and Acme

A link with its own fields becomes a node. Roles, events and n-ary relations all use this trick. Chapter: The 15 modelling patterns

Q9. How should you store "20 kg"?

  • As the string "20 kg"
  • As a quantity node with the number 20 and a unit IRI for kilogram
  • As the number 20 alone

A number without its unit is a bug waiting to happen. A text cannot be compared or converted. Chapter: The 15 modelling patterns

Q10. In Aristotle's terms, which is an accident of Socrates?

  • Being a human
  • Being pale
  • Being a substance

An accident is a property a thing can lose and still be the same thing. Socrates stays Socrates in the sun. Chapter: Ancient and medieval roots

Q11. Porphyry's tree is the ancestor of which modern structure?

  • A hash table
  • A class hierarchy
  • A neural network

It splits a genus into species step by step. Every class tree does the same. Chapter: Ancient and medieval roots

Q12. Where is the first known use of the word "ontologia"?

  • In a book by Jacob Lorhard, 1606
  • In Wolff's book of 1730
  • In Kant's first Critique, 1781

Lorhard used it first. Goclenius used it in 1613. Wolff made it a standard word. Chapter: From Leibniz to modern logic

Q13. Which is true for ontology classes, but not for classes in object-oriented code?

  • A thing has exactly one class.
  • A thing can belong to many classes at the same time.
  • A class cannot have subclasses.

An ontology class is a set. Ann can be a Person, a Student and an Employee at once. Chapter: Data models compared

Q14. Which one is a literal?

  • <http://example.org/ann>
  • "42"^^xsd:integer
  • _:b0

The first is an IRI and the third is a blank node. A literal is a value with a datatype or a language tag. Chapter: RDF and RDF Schema

  1. A query asks "Does Ann have a phone number?" The data has none. What is the answer under the open world, and under the closed world?
    Answer

    Open world (OWL, RDF): "unknown". A phone may exist that we do not know about. Closed world (SQL, SHACL): "no". What is not in the data counts as false. Chapter: The building blocks

  2. A bug tracker has the states Open, In progress and Closed. Should Closed be a class or a value?
    Answer

    A value in a value set, for example an individual of the class Status. A bug changes state over time. Class membership that changes often is a poor fit. Chapter: Your first ontology, step by step

  3. A term in your published ontology turns out to be wrong. Why should you not delete it? What do you do instead?
    Answer

    Other people's data and queries use its IRI. Deleting it breaks them in silence. Mark it owl:deprecated true, explain why in a comment, and point to the new term, for example with dcterms:isReplacedBy. Chapter: The 15 modelling patterns

  4. Name one idea from Frege and one from Tarski that every OWL tool uses today.
    Answer

    Frege: predicate logic with quantifiers. Description logics are pieces of it. Tarski: model theory. RDF and OWL define their meaning with interpretations and models. Chapter: From Leibniz to modern logic

  5. "Ann works at Acme as CTO since 2020." Where do "CTO" and "2020" go in a relational database, a property graph and RDF 1.1?
    Answer

    Relational: columns in a link table employment(person, company, role, since). Property graph: properties on the WORKS_AT edge. RDF 1.1: an n-ary node, like :job1, with links to Ann, Acme, the role and the date. Chapter: Data models compared

  6. Write in Turtle: Ann is a Person, her name is "Ann" in English, and she knows Bo. Use the prefix ex:.
    Answer 
    @prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .
ex:ann a ex:Person ; ex:name "Ann"@en ; ex:knows ex:bo .

    We parsed it with rdflib 7.6.0: three triples about ex:ann. Chapter: RDF and RDF Schema

Practice exam, part 2: intermediate (questions 21 to 40)

Q21. Who proposed frames, with slots and default values?

  • Marvin Minsky
  • Ross Quillian
  • Douglas Lenat

Minsky's frames (1974) grouped facts about a kind of thing. Quillian made semantic networks. Lenat started Cyc. Chapter: AI and knowledge representation

Q22. What did the Cyc project (started 1984) mainly show?

  • Common sense can be learned from text in a week.
  • Writing all common sense by hand is extremely slow and costly.
  • Prolog is always faster than Lisp.

This is the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Getting knowledge from people into machines was the hard part. Chapter: AI and knowledge representation

Q23. Which is NOT one of Gruber's design criteria?

  • Clarity
  • Coherence
  • Maximal ontological commitment

The criterion is minimal ontological commitment: claim as little about the world as you need. The others are extendibility and minimal encoding bias. Chapter: The ontology engineering era

Q24. Which of these came first?

  • SPARQL 1.1
  • OWL 2
  • RDF Model and Syntax

RDF came in 1999, OWL 2 in 2009 and SPARQL 1.1 in 2013. Chapter: The Semantic Web era

Q25. Which is one of the Linked Data principles of 2006?

  • Use HTTP IRIs, so people can look up the names.
  • Always publish in RDF/XML.
  • Never link to other datasets.

The four principles: use IRIs as names, use HTTP IRIs, return useful data with standards, and link to other IRIs. Chapter: The Semantic Web era

Q26. When did ISO publish the GQL standard for property graph queries?

  • 2011
  • 2017
  • 2024

GQL came in April 2024. 2011 is the year Cypher appeared. 2017 is SHACL. Chapter: Knowledge graphs and the LLM era

Q27. On 15 November 2026, what is the status of RDF 1.2 Concepts?

  • W3C Recommendation
  • Candidate Recommendation
  • Abandoned

Its latest version is a Candidate Recommendation Draft of 13 November 2026. RDF 1.1 is still the Recommendation. Chapter: Knowledge graphs and the LLM era

Q28. "Every student reads some book." Let S be Student, B be Book and r be reads. Which formula is right?

  • \forall x\,(S(x) \rightarrow \exists y\,(B(y) \land r(x,y)))
  • \forall x\,(S(x) \land \exists y\,(B(y) \land r(x,y)))
  • \exists y\,\forall x\,(S(x) \rightarrow B(y) \land r(x,y))

"Every" goes with the arrow, "some" goes with "and". The third says one book is read by all students: a different meaning. Chapter: Logic for ontology

Q29. A reasoner is sound but not complete. What does that mean?

  • Every answer it gives is right, but it may miss some answers.
  • It may give wrong answers.
  • It never stops.

Sound means no wrong answers. Complete means no missing answers. Chapter: Logic for ontology

Q30. Which SPARQL keyword keeps a row even when one pattern has no match?

  • FILTER
  • OPTIONAL
  • MINUS

OPTIONAL is like a left join. The variable stays unbound. FILTER and MINUS remove rows. Chapter: SPARQL

Q31. What does ?x a/rdfs:subClassOf* :Animal find?

  • Only direct instances of Animal
  • Instances of Animal or of any of its subclasses
  • All subclasses of Animal

The path follows one type link, then zero or more subclass links. It gives RDFS-style answers without a reasoner. Chapter: SPARQL

Q32. A shape says sh:minCount 1 on :price. A drink has no price. What does a SHACL engine do?

  • It assumes a price exists.
  • It reports a violation.
  • It ignores it unless OWL says so.

SHACL checks in a closed world. A missing value counts as missing. Chapter: SHACL and validation

Q33. A shape has sh:targetClass :Drink. The data has :x a :Latte. The triple :Latte rdfs:subClassOf :Drink is only in a separate ontology file. Is :x checked?

  • Yes, always
  • No, unless you add the class tree or run inference first
  • Only if the shape is closed

targetClass follows subclass triples only in the data graph. Infer first, then validate. Chapter: SHACL and validation

Q34. You need a thesaurus with broader and narrower terms. Which vocabulary do you reuse?

  • SKOS
  • PROV-O
  • GeoSPARQL

SKOS has concepts, labels, broader, narrower and mapping links. PROV-O is for provenance, GeoSPARQL for places. Chapter: Ontologies in the wild

Q35. What makes a Wikidata statement richer than a plain triple?

  • Qualifiers, references and ranks
  • It is written in XML.
  • It has no IRIs.

A statement can say when, according to whom, and how preferred it is. The short "truthy" form hides most of it. Chapter: Ontologies in the wild

Q36. Later in a project, what do competency questions become?

  • Tests: queries with expected answers
  • The name of the ontology
  • The license

Each question becomes a SPARQL query with a known answer. Run them on every change. Chapter: The ontology engineering method

  1. Why did the Gene Ontology (1998) succeed when many earlier ontologies did not? Give three reasons.
    Answer

    It solved a real, shared problem: describing genes the same way across species. Its structure was simple. Its IDs were stable. A community curated it every day. Chapter: The ontology engineering era

  2. Explain with an example why the unique name assumption matters for counting.
    Answer

    Say "a person has at most one mother". The data says Ann's mother is Eva and Ann's mother is Evelyn. A database with unique names reports an error. OWL has no unique names, so the reasoner concludes Eva and Evelyn are the same person. You need owl:differentFrom or a SHACL check. Chapter: Logic for ontology

  3. Write a SPARQL query: count papers per year, newest year first.
    Answer 
    PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/>
SELECT ?year (COUNT(?p) AS ?n)
WHERE { ?p a ex:Paper ; ex:year ?year }
GROUP BY ?year
ORDER BY DESC(?year)

    On three papers from 2025, 2026 and 2026, rdflib printed 2026 2 and 2025 1. Chapter: SPARQL

  4. You must change the meaning of a published class. What is the right way?
    Answer

    Never change the meaning behind an existing IRI. Make a new class with a new IRI. Deprecate the old one and point to the new one. Publish a new version IRI and release notes. Chapter: The ontology engineering method

Practice exam, part 3: hard (questions 41 to 60)

Q41. In one interpretation, Ann has no children. Is Ann in \forall \mathit{hasChild}.\mathit{Doctor} there?

  • No
  • Yes
  • It is undefined.

"All children are doctors" is true when there are no children. Compare Q44: being true in one model is not the same as following from the axioms. Chapter: Description logics

Q42. OWL 2 DL matches which description logic?

  • ALC
  • SHOIN(D)
  • SROIQ(D)

SHOIN(D) is OWL 1 DL. OWL 2 DL added R: complex role inclusions and more. Chapter: Description logics

Q43. Which OWL 2 profile is made for data in relational databases, by query rewriting?

  • EL
  • QL
  • RL

QL rewrites a query into SQL over the tables. EL is for huge class trees. RL is for rules on RDF. Chapter: OWL 2

Q44. Vegan EquivalentTo: Person and (eats only Plant). Ann is a Person. The data has no eats links for Ann. Does a reasoner classify Ann as Vegan?

  • Yes, because "only" is true when there are no links.
  • No. In the open world, Ann may eat things we do not know about.
  • Yes, because every Person is a Vegan.

A reasoner gives only what is true in every model. In some models Ann eats meat. You would need to state a closure, for example eats max 0. Chapter: OWL 2

Q45. Which Datalog program computes ancestors?

  • anc(X,Y) :- parent(X,Y). anc(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), anc(Y,Z).
  • anc(X,Y) :- anc(X,Y).
  • anc(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z).

You need a base rule and a recursive rule. The third finds only grandparents. Chapter: Rules and Datalog

Q46. Why do many engines reject p(X) :- q(X), not p(X).?

  • The program cannot be stratified: it recurses through negation.
  • The variable X is unsafe.
  • Rules cannot have two body atoms.

"not p" must be finished before p is computed. Here p depends on itself through "not". Chapter: Rules and Datalog

Q47. In BFO, which is an occurrent?

  • A heart
  • A surgery
  • The colour of a car

An occurrent happens and has parts in time. A heart and a colour (a quality) are continuants. Chapter: Formal ontology and upper ontologies

Q48. In OntoClean, Person is rigid and Student is anti-rigid. Which subclass link is wrong?

  • Student is a subclass of Person.
  • Person is a subclass of Student.
  • Both are fine.

A rigid class cannot sit under an anti-rigid one. A person who stops studying would stop being a person. Chapter: Formal ontology and upper ontologies

Q49. Which standard holds BFO?

  • ISO/IEC 21838-2
  • ISO 8601
  • ISO/IEC 39075

ISO 8601 is dates and times. ISO/IEC 39075 is GQL. DOLCE is Part 3 of 21838. Chapter: Formal ontology and upper ontologies

Q50. Which three index orders cover all eight triple patterns?

  • SPO, POS, OSP
  • SPO, SOP, PSO
  • SPO alone

Every pattern has its bound parts as a prefix of one of these three. Chapter: Triple stores and graph databases

Q51. What is index-free adjacency?

  • Each node points straight to its neighbours, so a hop needs no index lookup.
  • A database without any index
  • A JSON column with links

It makes long walks cheap. The cost is harder sharding and bulk scans. Chapter: Triple stores and graph databases

Q52. Which reasoner is built for OWL 2 EL with consequence-based reasoning?

  • ELK
  • HermiT
  • Soufflé

HermiT is a (hyper)tableau reasoner for all of OWL 2 DL. Soufflé is a Datalog engine. Chapter: Reasoners and materialisation

Q53. Which sentence about materialisation and query rewriting is true?

  • Materialisation stores inferred facts ahead of time. Rewriting expands each query at run time.
  • Both store every inferred fact.
  • Rewriting needs no ontology.

Materialisation makes queries fast but updates costly. Rewriting keeps data small but makes queries bigger. Chapter: Reasoners and materialisation

Q54. In rdflib, how do you pass a user's value into a SPARQL query safely?

  • Paste it into the query string.
  • Use initBindings.
  • Use eval.

Bindings are values, not query text. A pasted string can change the query, like SQL injection. Chapter: The Python toolkit

  1. How does a tableau reasoner test "Is every Mother a Parent?"
    Answer

    It tests whether \mathit{Mother} \sqcap \lnot \mathit{Parent} is satisfiable. It tries to build a model with one such individual and applies the expansion rules. If every branch ends in a clash, no such individual can exist, so Mother is subsumed by Parent. Chapter: Description logics

  2. Name three classic OWL modelling mistakes and the fix for each.
    Answer

    1. Using domain or range as a check: they add types instead. Use SHACL. 2. Using "only" where you mean "some": "only" is true with no links. 3. Forgetting disjointness: then nothing is ever inconsistent. Other good answers: owl:sameAs for "similar", and expecting unique names. Chapter: OWL 2

  3. Run semi-naive evaluation by hand. Facts: edge(a,b), edge(b,c), edge(c,d). Rules: reach(X,Y) :- edge(X,Y). and reach(X,Z) :- reach(X,Y), edge(Y,Z). What is new in each round?
    Answer

    Round 1: ab, bc, cd (from the base rule). Round 2: join only the new facts with edge: ac, bd. Round 3: ad. Round 4: nothing new, so stop. Six reach facts in total. Chapter: Rules and Datalog

  4. Why does join order matter in a triple store? Give a small example with numbers.
    Answer

    Pattern A matches 10 triples. Pattern B matches 100,000. Start with A and look up B for each of the 10 rows: about 10 index lookups. Start with B: 100,000 rows to check against A. Most selective first. Chapter: Triple stores and graph databases

  5. A fact is deleted from a materialised graph. Why can you not just delete every fact derived from it?
    Answer

    A derived fact may have a second derivation that does not use the deleted fact. Then it must stay. Algorithms like DRed (delete, then rederive) or counting derivations handle this. Chapter: Reasoners and materialisation

  6. You query the public Wikidata endpoint from a script. Give three rules for polite use.
    Answer

    Send a descriptive User-Agent. Handle HTTP 429 and wait as the Retry-After header says. Batch and cache your queries, add LIMIT, and do not send many queries in parallel. Chapter: The Python toolkit

Practice exam, part 4: expert (questions 61 to 80)

Q61. Why does entity resolution use blocking?

  • To compare only records that share a key, so the work is not n squared
  • To block bad users
  • To lock tables during a merge

One million records give about 500 billion pairs. Blocking keeps only pairs with, for example, the same postcode. Chapter: Enterprise and operational ontologies

Q62. TransE gives a triple (h, r, t) a good score when ...

  • \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} is close to \mathbf{t}
  • \mathbf{h} and \mathbf{t} are the same vector
  • \mathbf{r} is zero

A relation is a move in vector space. From the head, the move should land near the tail. Chapter: Ontologies and AI

Q63. In link prediction, what does "filtered" MRR mean?

  • Other true triples are removed from the candidate list before ranking.
  • Rare entities are removed from the test set.
  • Only the top 10 answers are kept.

Without the filter, a correct answer ranked below other correct answers looks like a mistake. Chapter: Ontologies and AI

Q64. "Ann works at Acme" was true from 2020. Your system learned it on 1 March 2024. When does its system time start?

  • 2020
  • 1 March 2024
  • It is unknown.

Valid time says when the fact was true in the world. System time says when you recorded it. Chapter: Context graphs and agent memory

Q65. A new fact contradicts an old one in an agent memory graph. What is good practice?

  • Delete the old fact.
  • Close the old fact's valid time and keep it.
  • Keep both open.

Closed facts keep history. Then you can explain why the agent decided something last week. Chapter: Context graphs and agent memory

Q66. Why does a small triple store intern strings to integer ids?

  • Indexes get smaller and comparisons get fast.
  • To encrypt the data
  • Because Rust has no string type

Each IRI is stored once. The indexes then hold only numbers. Chapter: The Rust toolkit

Q67. Which Rust project is a full SPARQL database on top of RocksDB, with crates like oxrdf and oxttl?

  • Oxigraph
  • Tokio
  • Serde

Oxigraph supports SPARQL 1.1 and has early support for 1.2 drafts. Chapter: The Rust toolkit

Q68. In semi-naive evaluation, what must every rule join in a round use?

  • At least one fact that was new in the last round
  • Only facts from the first round
  • All facts, with no change from naive evaluation

Old-only joins give only old facts again. Skipping them saves most of the work. Chapter: Build a reasoner

Q69. RDFS rule rdfs9: (x rdf:type C) and (C rdfs:subClassOf D) give what?

  • (x rdf:type D)
  • (D rdfs:subClassOf C)
  • (x owl:sameAs D)

Types travel up the class tree. This is the most used rule in any reasoner. Chapter: Build a reasoner

Q70. Why must an ontology service test the type of a new node before it runs a target-based shape checker?

  • No shape targets an unknown type, so the node would pass in silence.
  • It makes the checker faster.
  • JSON needs it.

No target means no focus node, and no focus node means no check. Chapter: Build a validator and a service

Q71. A value is "2026-02-30"^^xsd:date. What does sh:datatype xsd:date say?

  • It passes. The datatype label is right.
  • It fails. The literal is ill-formed.
  • It becomes 2 March 2026.

February 2026 has 28 days. SHACL fails ill-formed literals too. pySHACL and our own checker agreed. Chapter: Build a validator and a service

  1. After entity resolution you have a golden record. Why keep the source records and link them, instead of overwriting them?
    Answer

    Merges can be wrong. With links you can undo a merge. You also keep provenance: which system said what. Auditors and debugging both need it. Chapter: Enterprise and operational ontologies

  2. An LLM writes a SPARQL query from a user's question. Name three guards before you run it.
    Answer

    1. Parse it, and refuse anything that is not a read-only query. 2. Check that every class and property IRI exists in your ontology. 3. Add a LIMIT and a timeout. Also good: compare its results on questions with known answers. Chapter: Ontologies and AI

  3. Design a small memory ontology for a support bot. List four node types, three edge types, and the time fields.
    Answer

    Nodes: User, Product, Ticket, Episode (one conversation). Edges: User REPORTED Ticket, Ticket ABOUT Product, Episode MENTIONS Ticket. Every edge has valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at and a source (the episode it came from). Identity: users by account id, products by SKU. Chapter: Context graphs and agent memory

  4. A store has three sorted indexes: SPO, POS and OSP. Which one answers the pattern (?s, :knows, :bo), and how?
    Answer

    POS. The predicate and the object are fixed. In POS order they form the prefix (knows, bo). One range scan on that prefix gives every subject. Chapter: The Rust toolkit

  5. Your reasoner must explain its results. How do you record why each fact was derived, and why does it help?
    Answer

    When a rule first adds a fact, store the rule name and the premise facts with it. Then you can print a proof tree for any fact. It helps users trust results, helps you find bad axioms, and helps delete facts correctly later. Chapter: Build a reasoner

  6. You must make a property required on one million existing nodes. Give the safe steps.
    Answer

    1. Dry run the new shapes on a copy and list the nodes that would fail. 2. Backfill those nodes. 3. Run a guarded migration in one transaction: it counts failures and stops if any exist. 4. Add a new schema version. 5. Reload every copy of the service, and refuse writes from stale versions. Chapter: Build a validator and a service

  7. OWL or SHACL? Choose for each need. (a) Conclude that every Manager is an Employee. (b) Every order must have exactly one customer. (c) Find class definitions that can have no members.
    Answer

    (a) OWL, with a subclass axiom. (b) SHACL, with sh:minCount 1 and sh:maxCount 1. (c) OWL: a reasoner finds unsatisfiable classes. Chapters: OWL 2 and SHACL and validation

  8. You want to record "The HR system says Ann was born in 1990", and keep the source. Give two ways in RDF.
    Answer

    1. Put the triple in a named graph for the HR system, and describe that graph with PROV-O. 2. Make the claim a node with its own source and time (modelling task 4 below). A third way: an RDF 1.2 triple term with a reifier, but RDF 1.2 is not yet a Recommendation, so check your tools. Chapters: RDF and RDF Schema and The 15 modelling patterns

  9. An agent must answer: "Which suppliers deliver parts for product X, and is any of them blocked?" The data lives in PostgreSQL and in a vendor's API. Sketch a design with an ontology.
    Answer

    1. Write the competency questions. 2. Model Supplier, Part, Product, the links delivers and partOf, and a Status value set with "blocked". 3. Map both sources to these terms, with a source and a time on each fact. 4. Check the result with SHACL. 5. Give the agent a few safe, named queries or actions as tools, for example over MCP, instead of free SQL. 6. Log every answer with the facts it used. Chapters: Enterprise and operational ontologies and Context graphs and agent memory

Five modelling tasks

Each task gives a domain and some competency questions. Write your model in Turtle first. Then open the model answer. Every model answer was parsed with rdflib 7.6.0 and tested with the tool named under it.

Task 1: library loans

A library has books and physical copies. People borrow copies. A loan has a start date, a due date and a status: on loan, returned or lost. Questions: Which books did Ann write? Which loans are overdue on 15 November 2026, and who has them?

Model answer 
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/lib#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# ---- schema (TBox)
ex:Person a owl:Class .
ex:Book   a owl:Class ; rdfs:comment "A work, like a title in the catalogue." .
ex:Copy   a owl:Class ; rdfs:comment "One physical copy of a book." .
ex:Loan   a owl:Class ; rdfs:comment "One borrowing of one copy: an event in time." .
ex:LoanStatus a owl:Class ; owl:oneOf ( ex:onLoan ex:returned ex:lost ) .
ex:onLoan a ex:LoanStatus .  ex:returned a ex:LoanStatus .  ex:lost a ex:LoanStatus .

ex:writtenBy a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Book ; rdfs:range ex:Person .
ex:copyOf    a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Copy ; rdfs:range ex:Book .
ex:item      a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Loan ; rdfs:range ex:Copy .
ex:borrower  a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Loan ; rdfs:range ex:Person .
ex:status    a owl:ObjectProperty , owl:FunctionalProperty ; rdfs:range ex:LoanStatus .
ex:start     a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Loan ; rdfs:range xsd:date .
ex:due       a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Loan ; rdfs:range xsd:date .

# ---- data (ABox)
ex:ann a ex:Person ; rdfs:label "Ann Lee" .
ex:bo  a ex:Person ; rdfs:label "Bo Chen" .
ex:graphs a ex:Book ; rdfs:label "Graphs for Everyone" ; ex:writtenBy ex:ann .
ex:graphs-c1 a ex:Copy ; ex:copyOf ex:graphs .
ex:graphs-c2 a ex:Copy ; ex:copyOf ex:graphs .
ex:loan1 a ex:Loan ; ex:item ex:graphs-c1 ; ex:borrower ex:bo ; ex:status ex:onLoan ;
    ex:start "2026-10-20"^^xsd:date ; ex:due "2026-11-10"^^xsd:date .
ex:loan2 a ex:Loan ; ex:item ex:graphs-c2 ; ex:borrower ex:ann ; ex:status ex:returned ;
    ex:start "2026-10-01"^^xsd:date ; ex:due "2026-10-22"^^xsd:date .
SELECT ?title ?who ?due WHERE {
  ?loan ex:status ex:onLoan ; ex:due ?due ; ex:borrower/rdfs:label ?who ;
        ex:item/ex:copyOf/rdfs:label ?title .
  FILTER (?due < "2026-11-15"^^xsd:date) }
T1 overdue on 2026-11-15: [('Graphs for Everyone', 'Bo Chen', '2026-11-10')]

Key choices: Book and Copy are different classes, because people borrow copies, not works. A Loan is an event node, because it has its own dates. The status is a closed value set. Common mistake: making "OverdueLoan" a stored class. It changes every day, so compute it with a query.

Task 2: hospital staff with OWL

Doctors and nurses are staff, and nobody is both. Doctors treat patients. A ward is part of some hospital, and part-of is transitive. A surgeon is exactly a doctor who performs some surgery. Questions: Who treats Bo? Is Dr Kim a surgeon? Which hospital is ward 3 in?

Model answer 
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/hosp#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .

ex:Staff    a owl:Class .
ex:Doctor   a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf ex:Staff .
ex:Nurse    a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf ex:Staff ; owl:disjointWith ex:Doctor .
ex:Patient  a owl:Class .
ex:Surgery  a owl:Class .
ex:Hospital a owl:Class .
ex:Ward     a owl:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf [ a owl:Restriction ;
                owl:onProperty ex:partOf ; owl:someValuesFrom ex:Hospital ] .
# A surgeon is exactly a doctor who performs some surgery.
ex:Surgeon  a owl:Class ; owl:equivalentClass [ a owl:Class ; owl:intersectionOf ( ex:Doctor
                [ a owl:Restriction ; owl:onProperty ex:performs ; owl:someValuesFrom ex:Surgery ] ) ] .

ex:treats    a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Doctor ; rdfs:range ex:Patient ;
             owl:inverseOf ex:treatedBy .
ex:performs  a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:domain ex:Doctor ; rdfs:range ex:Surgery .
ex:partOf    a owl:ObjectProperty , owl:TransitiveProperty .

ex:drKim a ex:Doctor ; ex:treats ex:bo ; ex:performs ex:op1 .
ex:op1 a ex:Surgery .
ex:ward3 a ex:Ward ; ex:partOf ex:northWing .
ex:northWing ex:partOf ex:cityHospital .
ex:cityHospital a ex:Hospital .

We ran the OWL RL rules of owlrl 7.6.2. Then we added ex:drKim a ex:Nurse and ran them again.

T2 triples: 42 -> 263
T2 bo is a: ['Patient']
T2 drKim is a: ['Doctor', 'Staff', 'Surgeon']
T2 bo treatedBy: ['drKim']
T2 ward3 partOf: ['cityHospital', 'northWing']
Disjoint classes ex:Nurse and ex:Doctor have a common individual ex:drKim

Key choices: EquivalentTo makes Surgeon a definition, so the reasoner finds Dr Kim. The inverse gives treatedBy for free. Disjointness makes the nurse error visible. Common mistake: expecting the range to "check" that Bo is a patient. It made Bo a Patient instead.

Task 3: products with units, checked by SHACL

A shop sells products. Each product has exactly one weight, with a positive number and a unit (kilogram or gram), and an optional colour from a fixed list. Question: Which products break these rules?

Model answer 
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/shop#> .
@prefix owl:  <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix qudt: <http://qudt.org/schema/qudt/> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix unit: <http://qudt.org/vocab/unit/> .

ex:Product a owl:Class .
ex:Color   a owl:Class ; owl:oneOf ( ex:silver ex:black ex:red ) .
ex:silver a ex:Color .  ex:black a ex:Color .  ex:red a ex:Color .
ex:weight  a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:range qudt:QuantityValue .
ex:color   a owl:ObjectProperty ; rdfs:range ex:Color .

ex:kettle a ex:Product ; rdfs:label "Steel kettle" ; ex:color ex:silver ;
    ex:weight [ a qudt:QuantityValue ; qudt:numericValue 1.2 ; qudt:unit unit:KiloGM ] .
ex:mug a ex:Product ; rdfs:label "Big mug" ; ex:color ex:blue ;   # not in the value set
    ex:weight "300 g" .                                           # a string, no unit
ex:ProductShape a sh:NodeShape ; sh:targetClass ex:Product ;
    sh:property [ sh:path ex:weight ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ; sh:node ex:QuantityShape ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path ex:color ; sh:in ( ex:silver ex:black ex:red ) ] .

ex:QuantityShape a sh:NodeShape ;
    sh:property [ sh:path qudt:numericValue ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ;
                  sh:datatype xsd:decimal ; sh:minExclusive 0 ] ;
    sh:property [ sh:path qudt:unit ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:in ( unit:KiloGM unit:GM ) ] .
T3 conforms: False
   mug color In
   mug weight Node

We used pySHACL 0.40.2. The kettle passes. The mug fails twice: blue is not in the list, and "300 g" does not match the quantity shape. Key choices: reuse QUDT for units instead of inventing them. owl:oneOf states the meaning. sh:in enforces it, because OWL alone would not reject ex:blue.

Task 4: conflicting claims with provenance

Two sources give different birth years for Ann. The HR system says 1990. A public web profile says 1991. Each source has a trust score. Questions: Who says what, and when? Which claim comes from the most trusted source?

Model answer 
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/hr#> .
@prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:  <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# Each claim is a node, so it can carry its own source and time.
ex:BirthYearClaim a rdfs:Class ; rdfs:subClassOf prov:Entity .

ex:claim1 a ex:BirthYearClaim ; ex:about ex:ann ; ex:year 1990 ;
    prov:wasAttributedTo ex:hrSystem ;
    prov:generatedAtTime "2024-03-01T09:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .
ex:claim2 a ex:BirthYearClaim ; ex:about ex:ann ; ex:year 1991 ;
    prov:wasAttributedTo ex:webProfile ;
    prov:generatedAtTime "2026-06-10T12:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime .

ex:hrSystem   a prov:Agent ; rdfs:label "HR system" ; ex:trust 0.9 .
ex:webProfile a prov:Agent ; rdfs:label "Public web profile" ; ex:trust 0.4 .
SELECT ?year ?trust WHERE {
  ?c ex:about ex:ann ; ex:year ?year ; prov:wasAttributedTo/ex:trust ?trust .
  FILTER NOT EXISTS {                       # no claim from a more trusted source
    ?c2 ex:about ex:ann ; prov:wasAttributedTo/ex:trust ?t2 . FILTER (?t2 > ?trust) } }
T4 claim: 1990 | HR system | 2024-03-01T09:00:00+00:00
T4 claim: 1991 | Public web profile | 2026-06-10T12:00:00+00:00
T4 most trusted (rdflib): 1990 trust 0.9
T4 most trusted (pyoxigraph): 1990 trust 0.9

Key choices: we keep both claims and never overwrite. The decision rule lives in the query, so you can change it later. Common mistake: storing ex:ann ex:birthYear 1990, 1991. Then nobody knows who said what.

We first wrote this query with a subquery and MAX. pyoxigraph 0.5.13 returned only 1990, which is correct. rdflib 7.6.0 returned both rows. The NOT EXISTS form above gave the right answer in both. Test important queries in two engines.

Task 5: a skills thesaurus with SKOS

Build a small scheme of programming skills. Programming has Systems programming and Scripting below it. Rust is under Systems programming, and Python under Scripting. Give English labels, German labels where you can, and links to Wikidata. Questions: Which skills are anywhere below Programming? Does every concept have at most one preferred label per language?

Model answer 
@prefix ex:   <http://example.org/skills#> .
@prefix skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .
@prefix wd:   <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> .

ex:scheme a skos:ConceptScheme ; skos:prefLabel "Programming skills"@en ;
    skos:hasTopConcept ex:programming .

ex:programming a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:scheme ; skos:topConceptOf ex:scheme ;
    skos:prefLabel "Programming"@en , "Programmierung"@de .
ex:systems a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:scheme ; skos:broader ex:programming ;
    skos:prefLabel "Systems programming"@en , "Systemprogrammierung"@de .
ex:scripting a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:scheme ; skos:broader ex:programming ;
    skos:prefLabel "Scripting"@en .
ex:rust a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:scheme ; skos:broader ex:systems ;
    skos:prefLabel "Rust"@en ; skos:exactMatch wd:Q575650 .
ex:python a skos:Concept ; skos:inScheme ex:scheme ; skos:broader ex:scripting ;
    skos:prefLabel "Python"@en ; skos:altLabel "Python 3"@en ; skos:exactMatch wd:Q28865 .
SELECT ?label ?wd WHERE {
  ?c skos:broader+ ex:programming ; skos:prefLabel ?label .
  FILTER (lang(?label) = "en")
  OPTIONAL { ?c skos:exactMatch ?wd } } ORDER BY ?label
T5 under Programming: Python | http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q28865
T5 under Programming: Rust | http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q575650
T5 under Programming: Scripting | -
T5 under Programming: Systems programming | -
T5 shapes conform: True

Key choices: SKOS, not OWL classes, because a skill tree is a thesaurus, not a set of things. broader+ walks the tree in the query. A SHACL shape with sh:uniqueLang true on skos:prefLabel answers the second question: pySHACL said the data conforms. We checked both Wikidata IDs with the Wikidata API: Q575650 is Rust and Q28865 is Python.

Grade your own model with the same tests. If your Turtle answers every competency question with a query, it is a good answer, even if it looks different from ours.

Reading list and a 30-day plan

These books and specifications are the best next steps after this book. All exist and all details were checked. Free items are marked.

Reading list, from first steps to expert
TitleAuthor or owner, yearWhy read it
Ontology Development 101Natalya Noy and Deborah McGuinness, 2001The classic first guide. Free.
RDF 1.1 PrimerW3C, 2014Short and clear introduction to triples and formats. Free.
OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Primer (Second Edition)W3C, 2012OWL with examples in several syntaxes. Free.
SPARQL 1.1 Query LanguageW3C, 2013The query standard, with many small examples. Free.
Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL)W3C, 2017The validation standard. Free.
Semantic Web for the Working Ontologist, third editionDean Allemang, James Hendler and Fabien Gandon, 2020Practical modelling with RDFS and OWL.
Knowledge GraphsAidan Hogan and others, 2021A wide survey of the whole field. Free to read at kgbook.org.
An Introduction to Ontology EngineeringC. Maria Keet, 2018A full university textbook. The first version is free.

An Introduction to Description LogicFranz Baader, Ian Horrocks, Carsten Lutz and Uli Sattler, 2017The standard book on description logics.
Building Ontologies with Basic Formal OntologyRobert Arp, Barry Smith and Andrew Spear, 2015BFO from its authors, with many examples.

Ideas and history

Days 1 to 7. The idea, the building blocks, your first ontology, the patterns, and the history. Exam part 1 on day 7.

Formal foundations

Days 8 to 14. Logic, description logics, RDF, OWL, SPARQL and SHACL. Exam part 2 on day 14.

Deeper theory and systems

Days 15 to 21. Rules, upper ontologies, data models, stores, reasoners and method. Exam part 3 on day 21.

Practice and building

Days 22 to 29. Real ontologies, companies, AI, agent memory, and the four build chapters.

The full exam

Part 4 and the five modelling tasks. Then mark everything and plan your review.

Glossary: 80 terms in simple words

Each term links to the chapter that explains it best. Cover the middle column and test yourself.

80 key terms
TermSimple meaningChapter
ontologyA shared, written list of kinds of things and their relations.What is an ontology?
taxonomyA tree of kinds, linked only by "is a kind of".What is an ontology?
knowledge graphFacts about real things, stored as a graph.What is an ontology?
classA set of things of one kind.The building blocks
individualOne single thing that belongs to classes.The building blocks
object propertyA link from one thing to another thing.The building blocks
data propertyA link from a thing to a value.The building blocks
axiomA statement that the logic takes as true.The building blocks
TBoxThe schema part: classes and their rules.The building blocks
ABoxThe data part: facts about individuals.The building blocks
domainThe class that every subject of a property gets.The building blocks
rangeThe class or datatype that every value of a property gets.The building blocks
open world assumptionA missing fact is unknown, not false.The building blocks
closed world assumptionA missing fact counts as false.The building blocks
competency questionA question the ontology must be able to answer.Your first ontology
provenanceWhere a fact came from: who, when and how.The 15 modelling patterns
n-ary relationA link between more than two things, made into a node.The 15 modelling patterns
value setA fixed, closed list of allowed values.The 15 modelling patterns
categoryOne of the most general kinds of being.Ancient and medieval roots
syllogismTwo premises that force a conclusion.Ancient and medieval roots
universalA kind or quality that many things share.Ancient and medieval roots
predicate logicLogic with predicates, variables and the quantifiers "all" and "some".From Leibniz to modern logic
mereologyThe logic of parts and wholes.Formal ontology and upper ontologies
semantic networkA graph of concepts with labelled links.AI and knowledge representation
frameA record with slots and default values for one kind of thing.AI and knowledge representation
knowledge acquisition bottleneckGetting expert knowledge into machines is slow and costly.AI and knowledge representation
upper ontologyVery general categories that many domains share.Formal ontology and upper ontologies
OntoCleanA method that checks subclass links with meta-properties.The ontology engineering era
rigidityA rigid class: its members can never stop being in it.Formal ontology and upper ontologies
continuantA thing that lasts and is fully present at each time.Formal ontology and upper ontologies
occurrentA thing that happens and has parts in time.Formal ontology and upper ontologies
IRIA global name for a thing, written like a web address.RDF and RDF Schema
tripleOne fact: subject, predicate, object.RDF and RDF Schema
literalA value like a text, a number or a date.RDF and RDF Schema
blank nodeA node with no global name, local to one graph.RDF and RDF Schema
named graphA set of triples with its own name, for example per source.RDF and RDF Schema
TurtleA short text format for writing RDF.RDF and RDF Schema
JSON-LDRDF written as JSON.RDF and RDF Schema
triple termIn RDF 1.2: a triple used as a value, without stating it.RDF and RDF Schema
Linked DataData published with HTTP IRIs that link to other data.The Semantic Web era
entailmentA statement that is true in every model of the axioms.Logic for ontology
unique name assumptionTwo different names always mean two different things.Logic for ontology
soundA reasoner that never gives a wrong answer.Logic for ontology
completeA reasoner that never misses a right answer.Logic for ontology
decidableA program can always answer yes or no in finite time.Logic for ontology
description logicA decidable logic of concepts, roles and individuals.Description logics
subsumptionOne class is always inside another class.Description logics
tableauA method that tries to build a model and looks for clashes.Description logics
restrictionA class described by the links of its members.OWL 2
OWL profileA smaller part of OWL 2 that reasons faster: EL, QL or RL.OWL 2
disjoint classesClasses that cannot share any member.OWL 2
owl:sameAsSays that two IRIs name exactly the same thing.OWL 2
property pathA query pattern that follows a chain of links.SPARQL
shapeA set of conditions that some nodes must meet.SHACL and validation
focus nodeThe node that a shape is checking right now.SHACL and validation
validation reportThe list of failed checks that a SHACL engine returns.SHACL and validation
DatalogA rule language of facts and if-then rules that always stops.Rules and Datalog
fixed pointThe state where the rules add nothing new.Rules and Datalog
stratified negationUsing "not" only on lower rule layers that are already finished.Rules and Datalog
semi-naive evaluationEach round joins only the facts found in the last round.Rules and Datalog
forward chainingApply rules to known facts until nothing new appears.Build a reasoner
property graphA graph whose nodes and edges carry key-value fields.Data models compared
dictionary encodingStore each name once and use a number for it.Triple stores and graph databases
index-free adjacencyEach node points straight to its neighbours.Triple stores and graph databases
GQLThe ISO query language for property graphs, from 2024.Knowledge graphs and the LLM era
materialisationComputing and storing inferred facts ahead of time.Reasoners and materialisation
query rewritingExpanding a query with the ontology instead of storing inferences.Reasoners and materialisation
justificationA smallest set of axioms that still gives a conclusion.Reasoners and materialisation
FAIRData that is findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.The ontology engineering method
SKOSA W3C vocabulary for thesauri and concept schemes.Ontologies in the wild
entity resolutionFinding records that describe the same real thing.Enterprise and operational ontologies
semantic layerOne shared definition of each business metric and term.Enterprise and operational ontologies
operational ontologyObjects, links and actions on top of live company data.Enterprise and operational ontologies
knowledge graph embeddingVectors for nodes and links that give each fact a score.Ontologies and AI
GraphRAGAn LLM answers from a graph and summaries built from documents.Ontologies and AI
context graphA knowledge graph plus events, time, sources and decisions.Context graphs and agent memory
valid time and system timeWhen a fact was true, and when we recorded it.Context graphs and agent memory
rdflibThe main Python library for RDF graphs and SPARQL.The Python toolkit
interningReplacing each repeated string with one small integer id.The Rust toolkit
migrationA numbered file that changes the database structure once.Build a validator and a service

Patterns to remember

These are patterns for answering exam and interview questions in this field.

Patterns for exam answers
PatternPurposeModelNote
Name the world firstAvoid the most common error"Under OWL's open world, the missing price is unknown."SHACL, SQL and Datalog are closed world.
Infer adds, check rejectsExplain domain, range and shapes"The range made Bob a Course. SHACL would report him."Domain and range never reject data.
Some needs one, only limits allRead restrictions correctly"eats only Plant is true with no eats links."True in one model is not entailed.
Counting needs unique namesExplain max-cardinality surprises"Two mothers become one person."Use differentFrom or SHACL.
Turn the link into a nodeModel time, roles and extra fields:job1 :person :ann ; :role :CTORDF 1.2 triple terms are not yet a Recommendation.
Answer with a counter-modelShow that something does not follow"In this model Ann eats meat, so Vegan is not entailed."One counter-model is enough.
Pick the profile by the jobChoose EL, QL or RL"Huge class tree: EL. Data in SQL: QL. Rules on RDF: RL."Name the reason, not only the letter.
Date every status factAvoid outdated answers"On 15 November 2026, RDF 1.2 is a Candidate Recommendation."Specs and products change fast.
Infer, then validateOrder steps in a data pipeline"Add the class tree, then run SHACL."Otherwise subclasses escape the checks.
Question becomes a testShow method, not only modelling"Each competency question is a SPARQL test in CI."A test needs an expected answer.
Keep claims, decide in the queryHandle conflicting sourcesTwo birth years, each with a sourceNever overwrite a source's claim.
Most selective firstExplain query plans"Start with the 10-row pattern, not the 100,000-row one."Give numbers when you can.

Key takeaways

  • No official, vendor-neutral certificate for ontology engineering exists in November 2026. Vendor certificates from Neo4j and Palantir cover parts of the field.
  • Show skill with work: a published ontology, tests, shapes and a small service.
  • The 80 questions cover every chapter. Each answer links to the chapter to reread.
  • Aim for 64 of 80. Retry wrong questions two days later.
  • A good model answers every competency question with a query. Test it with real tools.
  • Most mistakes come from the world assumption, from domain and range, and from "only".
  • Study 60 to 90 minutes a day for 30 days, and always do the "Do" task.
